title: October 30, 2026
description:
Backup and DR

Feature

You can now edit existing backup plans for Cloud SQL instances to update settings such as backup rules and maximum custom on-demand retention periods. To learn more, see Back up Cloud SQL instances to a backup vault.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use Knowledge Catalog to discover authorized views, logical views, and continuous materialized views. This integration lets you search for these granular data assets alongside your Bigtable instances and tables. This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Manage data assets using Knowledge Catalog.

Datastream

Feature

Datastream integration with Knowledge Catalog is now generally available (GA). For more information, see the documentation.

SAP on Google Cloud

Announcement

Google SecOps for SAP is generally available (GA)

Google SecOps for SAP is generally available (GA). This solution helps you protect your enterprise SAP applications by integrating business-critical telemetry into Google SecOps to provide unified visibility, threat detection, and security response capabilities.

This release includes:

  • Log ingestion from SAP RISE and self-managed SAP environments that run on Google Cloud, on-premises, or other clouds.
  • SAP-specific YARA-L threat detection rules available in the Google SecOps Detection Rules GitHub repository.
  • Automated threat response and containment capabilities by using the SAP RFC Gateway and SOAR playbooks (Preview).

For more information, see Secure SAP applications with Google SecOps.

description:
skills@1.7.0 adds Notion skills databases as an install source for agent skills .

Notion skills are reusable agent skills written as Notion pages. Teams author, review, and update them in the workspace they already use, then install them into any agent the skills CLI supports. No Git repository required.

To browse your Notion workspace's skills, run:

The CLI lists the skill packs shared with you and installs every skill in the packs you select.

To install a single skill, pass its Notion page URL:

Both commands use the Notion CLI (ntn) to authenticate. To set it up:

ntn login requires a Notion personal access token, so your workspace must allow them.

title: Run Terminal-Bench and other Harbor evals on Vercel Sandbox
description:
You can now run Harbor evals on Vercel Sandbox.

Harbor is the open-source harness behind Terminal-Bench, whose registry includes many other benchmarks such as SWE-bench, tau3-bench and OSWorld. Pass --env vercel to harbor run and each trial executes in its own isolated Firecracker microVM, so you can parallelize far beyond what your local machine is capable of.

A task's network policy is enforced at the sandbox firewall, outside the VM. Optional credential injection attaches secrets to matching outbound requests at that firewall, so they never enter the sandbox.

Paired with AI Gateway, one AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY reaches hundreds of models from multiple providers, and benchmarking another model is the same command with a different --model:

Swap --model to vercel_ai_gateway/openai/gpt-5.6-luna to run the same benchmark against an OpenAI model.

Requires Harbor 0.22.0 or later. Follow the step-by-step guide for setup, configuration, and troubleshooting. Learn more in the Sandbox documentation.

Read more

description:
You and your agents can now deploy static artifacts to Vercel in under one second through Vercel CLI.

Run vercel deploy to share a prototype, publish an HTML report, or preview a page created by your coding agent.

Vercel automatically detects eligible deployments, and valid artifacts will skip the build step, immediately returning a live URL.

title: Reproducing, disclosing, and fixing the libheif vulnerability with Hacktron and the maintainers
description:
In August 2026, Hacktron reported what looked like a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Next.js image optimization. Their investigation found that the vulnerable code was not in Next.js itself, but upstream in libheif, an AVIF image decoder used by Next.js, ImageMagick, WordPress, sharp, and much of the web.

Shortly after Hacktron notified us, we worked with them to reproduce the RCE against a current Next.js build and disclose it to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. We then deployed a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and started working with the maintainers on a fix.

The dependency chain

Next.js image optimization lets applications resize and optimize images through the <Image> component (next/image). For AVIF images, the image-processing dependency chain is as follows:

  • <Image> invokes /_next/image,

  • /_next/image calls sharp

  • sharp calls libvips

  • libvips uses libheif to decode the image

That meant the vulnerable code was not in Next.js, but it was still reachable through Next.js image optimization. A malicious AVIF image sent to the image optimization endpoint would invoke libheif through sharp and libvips.

As such, one obvious mitigation was to disable AVIF optimization in Next.js. Malicious AVIF images would then stop at the image optimization endpoint instead of being passed through sharp and libvips to libheif. The exploit would not propagate upstream.

However, only mitigating Next.js, without an upstream fix, posed a disclosure problem.

Disclosing the vulnerability and coordinating the upstream fix

After we worked with Hacktron to successfully reproduce the issue, we rolled out a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and reached out to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif to disclose the vulnerability and begin working on a fix.

Here is the timeline:

  • August 11-12: Hacktron reported the issue to Vercel; Hacktron and Vercel reproduced the RCE with a working proof of concept.

  • August 13: Vercel applied a platform mitigation through its Image Optimization Service.

  • August 19: The Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and began coordination across sharp, libvips, and libheif.

  • August 24: Next.js informed its security partners.

  • August 25: Next.js published a security release that disabled AVIF optimization.

The Vercel security team contacted the maintainers of sharp and libvips by email, and opened coordination with libheif through a GitHub Security Advisory. Hacktron had also submitted vulnerability and exploit details to libheif. On August 19, the Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and aligned on the path forward across sharp, libvips, and libheif. The libheif maintainer continued remediation through Hacktron’s GitHub Security Advisory.

On August 24, Next.js informed its security partners of the libheif vulnerability and its impact on Next.js (partner notifications are a routine part of Next.js’ security release process).

On August 25, six days after the August 19 meeting, the libheif maintainer released v1.23.2, which remediated the RCE.

Vercel and Next.js mitigations

Securing Vercel and its customers was straightforward: all Next.js image optimization requests on Vercel go through a central Image Optimization Service. Therefore, we disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in that central service. Any incoming AVIF images were not passed to libheif for decoding and RCE was not possible on Vercel.

Protecting self-hosted applications required a Next.js release. On August 25, Next.js published a security release that had originally been planned to address a separate issue. After coordinating an upstream fix, we bundled the AVIF mitigation into that release and shipped it a day earlier than planned. The release disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in Next.js; given that the patched libheif release was still propagating downstream, this was the most timely option. We also published a security advisory to communicate the issue’s severity.

Our commitment to making the web more secure

The volume of OSS vulnerabilities discovered continues to increase, and the numbers are overwhelming:

  • In 2026, the CVE program has published more than 35,000 CVEs.

  • Private vulnerability reports on GitHub grew from 500 per week in January to 3,000 per week in May.

  • GitHub also reported 1,560 reviewed advisories in May 2026, the highest monthly volume in the advisory database’s history.

As LLMs accelerate vulnerability research, we expect to see more upstream vulnerabilities like the libheif RCE surface across the OSS ecosystem. There have been a higher number of Next.js security releases in recent months, and we expect that trend to continue as we mitigate new vulnerabilities that both we and the research community uncover.

We are committed to proactively finding vulnerabilities before attackers, responsibly disclosing everything we find, and collaborating with researchers and maintainers on fixes.

Credit

Thanks to Hacktron for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, working with us to reproduce the issue, and coordinating with the upstream maintainers through remediation.

We also want to thank the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. Their work on the upstream fix made coordinated remediation possible across the image processing dependency chain.

We work with a talented set of researchers to secure Next.js and other open source frameworks through Vercel's Open Source Bug Bounty. Anyone interested in contributing to the security of eligible frameworks is encouraged to participate there.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • Vercel security release changelog

  • Just a rumor of a bug is enough to find a security exploit

title: Jev is the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history
description:
Within 24 hours of launching on AI Gateway, Jev from TypeSafe AI reached more than twice as many paid teams as any previous model launch, making it the fastest-adopted model in gateway history.

Jev passed every other comparison model in its first twelve hours and continued to widen its lead for the rest of the day. By hour 24, nearly 13% of paid teams were using it. That's 2x the GPT-5.6 family and more than 6x Fable 5.1's share.

Jev’s launch shows how quickly a specialized model can find a place in production. Its first-day adoption was unmatched among recent launches; the next test is whether that early adoption lasts.

About Jev

Jev was introduced on September 15 as a probabilistic decision model designed to support structured decision-making within software. An application sends it context and a set of questions. Jev evaluates those questions in parallel and returns typed choices, scores, or true-or-false answers, along with probabilities.

Unlike the text produced by a general-purpose language model, Jev’s answers come in a format the code can use directly. Developers can use it to:

  • choose an agent’s next tool or subagent

  • decide whether a workflow should continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • score urgency or risk before taking an action

  • verify model outputs, enforce guardrails, or send uncertain cases for human review

In its own workflow evaluations, TypeSafe AI reports that Jev was up to 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than language models.

See the September AI Gateway Production Index for more model usage data, or try Jev through AI Gateway and build with the AI SDK.

Read more

title: v0 now reads npm credentials from shared environment variables
description:
v0 now installs private packages from npm and custom registries using credentials stored as shared environment variables on Vercel.

This makes it easier for teams to build with their existing design systems, component libraries, and internal packages directly in v0.

To get started, add one of the following as a shared environment variable on Vercel, scoped to Development and/or Preview:

  • Use NPM_TOKEN for private packages hosted on registry.npmjs.org.

  • Use NPM_RC to configure custom or multiple registries.

NPM_RC supports scoped registries and references to other environment variables. For example, configure an organization scope such as @acme for GitHub Packages, or direct package requests through a private JFrog Artifactory registry.

Credentials can be marked sensitive, and v0 never exposes them to the model or writes them to the sandbox filesystem.

You can view the integration status from Settings → Integrations in v0.

Learn more in the private dependencies docs.

Read more

Opt tools in by adding them to the experimental_webMcp object:

Then load the script from your MCP endpoint with the ?webmcp-script parameter:

The script registers those tools with the page and proxies each call back to your MCP server as the signed-in user, so authenticated tools work without a browser-side OAuth flow.

Upgrade to mcp-handler@2.2.0 and read the documentation to get started.

title: Spend Management expands to Enterprise Flexible Commitment plans
description:
Enterprise teams on Flexible Commitment plans can now use Spend Management, already available on Pro, at no additional cost.

You can set a budget at any time in Spend Management settings.

Set a budget per billing cycle, and when your team's metered usage approaches or crosses it, Spend Management can send email notifications, trigger a webhook, or pause the production deployments of all projects. The amount governs the metered usage that draws down from your prepaid balance. Setting an amount does not stop usage on its own; pausing is opt-in, and it does not stop AI Gateway or v0 usage.

Learn more in the Spend Management docs.

title: AI Gateway now supports TypeSafe clients and an HTTP API for Jev
description:
You can now call Jev from TypeSafe AI through AI Gateway using an existing TypeSafe client or the HTTP API, in addition to the AI SDK.

  • TypeSafe client: Point an existing TypeSafe client at AI Gateway without changing its evaluation calls.

  • HTTP API: Call Jev directly from any language or framework.

  • AI SDK: Call Jev from a TypeScript application using AI SDK.

Jev is a probabilistic decision model for software. State goes in, and typed answers come out with probabilities attached, so there's no generated text to parse. Requests are billed through AI Gateway on all three paths, so they appear alongside your other model calls in usage and observability.

Migrate an existing TypeSafe client

Change the base URL and API key. Your systemOne calls, noul questions, and response shapes stay exactly as they are.

Start a new integration

New integrations name the model as typesafe-ai/jev and ask one of three question types: boolean returns a probability from 0 to 1, choice picks one option from a set you name, and score rates against a scale you define. This example asks whether an agent should keep working after fixing a bug and passing its tests.

With the HTTP API, POST to /v1/evaluate:

With the AI SDK, run the same evaluation through evaluate:

You can also use Jev through eve, a framework for building and deploying agents with sandboxed compute, human approvals, and evaluations already built in. eve uses Jev as the default evaluation model for automatic model selection, typed evaluations, and automated tool approvals.

See the TypeSafe-compatible API guide to migrate a client, or the evaluation guide for the HTTP API or AI SDK.

title: Deployments now show billable duration and CPU minutes
description:
Deployments now show their billable duration and CPU minutes in the dashboard, vc inspect, and the REST API. Use it to understand how each build contributes to your usage.

Billable duration is the build and post-build time combined, rounded up to the next whole minute. CPU minutes are that figure multiplied by the machine's vCPUs.

To see the same breakdown from the CLI, update to version 59.23.1 or later with npm i -g vercel@latest, then run vc inspect:

Learn more about build machines and CPU minutes in the docs.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Microsoft Teams
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Microsoft Teams. Creating one gives your organization a Teams bot that your apps and agents run. People can @mention it in channels or message it directly, and your code receives the message and replies as the bot.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel registers the Entra app and Azure Bot resource in your tenant, so there's no client secret to store. A tenant administrator with an Azure subscription completes setup once. Incoming Teams activities are verified and forwarded to your project as Connect trigger.

Create a connector from the dashboard or Vercel CLI:

Once the connector is set up, your code requests a token only when it needs one. Use it with the @vercel/connect SDK, eve channel or Chat SDK adapter:

Each token is scoped to what you request and refreshed automatically, so there's nothing to rotate by hand. Connectors only work in the environments you attach them to, and you can revoke access at any time with vc connect revoke-tokens.

Read the Vercel Connect documentation, view details about the Teams connector in the Vercel Connect catalog, or create a Teams connector to get started.

Read more

title: Claude Opus 5.5 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Opus 5.5 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway as anthropic/claude-opus-5.5.

Opus 5.5 is Anthropic’s strongest Opus model for agentic coding, long-running agent tasks, and professional knowledge work. It communicates progress, findings, and next steps clearly, making extended work easier to supervise.

It has a 1M-token context window and supports up to 128K output tokens. Compared with Opus 5, Anthropic has stated that Opus 5.5 performs at a similar level to Fable 5.1, but is ~30% faster and ~40% cheaper per task than Opus 5.

The new model includes two API changes that can turn previously valid requests into HTTP 400 errors:

  • Thinking is always adaptive. Requests that disable thinking or set a fixed thinking budget are rejected. Use an effort level and prompting to control reasoning depth.

  • Forced tool choice is unsupported. Requests cannot require a tool call or force a specific tool. Use automatic tool selection and prompt the model when it should call a tool. If you previously forced a tool call to return JSON, use structured outputs instead.

To use Claude Opus 5.5:

For lower latency, enable fast mode with speed: 'fast' or use anthropic/claude-opus-5.5-fast. In Claude Code, run /fast to toggle it for the session.

Opus 5.5 also supports regional inference and Zero Data Retention through AI Gateway. Try it in the model playground.

title: Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now in public beta
description:
Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now available in public beta on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. It isn’t tied to a single sandbox, so you can reuse the same Drive across runs and different sandbox instances.

Use Drives to preserve an agent's workspace or on-disk memory, or to reuse datasets, models, and dependency trees.

Create and mount a Drive

Create or retrieve a Drive and mount it at a path when starting a sandbox. Read and write files through the sandbox filesystem at that path.

Anything stored under /data remains on the Drive after the sandbox stops.

Share Drive data across sandboxes

A Drive supports one read-write mount at a time. After the Drive has been written to, multiple sandboxes can read from it concurrently by mounting point-in-time, read-only snapshots.

Each snapshot reflects the Drive at the moment it's mounted. Later writes aren’t included; mount a new snapshot to access them.

Limits and pricing

Each sandbox can mount up to four Drives at separate paths. Drives default to a maximum size of 1 TiB (1 GiB on Hobby) and can be configured up to 16 TiB, with higher limits available by request.

Drives are available in every Sandbox region. Each Drive stays in the region where it was created. Sandboxes that mount it must run in that region and can’t use failover regions.

Drive pricing is based on storage, reads, and writes, with rates varying by region. In iad1, storage costs $0.05 per GB-month, reads $0.0015 per GB, and writes $0.004 per GB. Hobby includes 15 GB of Drive storage and 30 GB each of reads and writes per month. See Sandbox pricing for regional rates and plan details.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: Vercel Connect now supports TanStack AI
description:
Agents built with TanStack AI can now call OAuth-protected MCP servers through Vercel Connect, with no credentials for you to store or rotate.

The new @vercel/connect/tanstack-ai subpath exports connectMCPTransport, which takes a TanStack transport config and attaches a Connect-backed auth provider. The provider is called before every MCP request, so the token is always fresh.

If the user has not granted access, createMCPClient fails with a consent challenge before the model runs. Catch it with getConsentChallenge and redirect to Connect's consent URL. Otherwise, a consent error raised within a tool call would reach the model as an error string rather than the user as a redirect.

Read the TanStack AI integration docs to get started, or see the full list of supported frameworks and adapters for Vercel Connect.

title: How Klaviyo shipped 356 internal apps in two weeks on Vercel
description:
Klaviyo on Vercel

  • Built a platform for shipping internal apps

  • 512 builders and 356 live apps in two weeks

  • Every app ships SSO-gated and private by default

  • Builders go from idea to live app in 3 minutes

Klaviyo is a B2C CRM for more than 200,000 brands. It brings marketing, service, agents, and data together in one platform so brands can deliver customer experiences at scale. Klaviyo built a platform on Vercel for shipping internal apps, then opened it to every employee through a citizen developer program.

In the first two weeks of the program, 512 of Klaviyo’s more than 2,000 employees deployed 356 apps on Vercel. Of those, 196 were full-stack apps with their own databases. The teams that are now shipping software include legal, marketing, and HR. "The next big thing at Klaviyo could be in a marketer's laptop," says Sr. Lead AI Architect Mohamed Ali.

Guardrails instead of walls

Opening deployment to a couple thousand new builders made security the first conversation. The obvious way to keep them safe is to broadly restrict what they can do. Klaviyo went the other way.

Employees aren't just building microsites; they are shipping full-stack apps on top of Klaviyo's own databases, and none of it touches the public network. Every builder is managed through Klaviyo's identity provider, which Vercel made possible through Enterprise Managed Users.

Implementing safeguards across the stack

Secure Compute gives Vercel deployments a private network path into Klaviyo's own infrastructure. Apps built in the program read from and write to Klaviyo's databases without any traffic crossing the public internet. That's what made bring-your-own-database work for Klaviyo.

On top of that connection, Vercel Passport and Klaviyo’s identity provider give every app the same access defaults, with nothing for the builder to configure:

  • Apps are private and SSO-gated through Okta

  • Sensitive environment variables are set at the team level, out of builders' hands

  • Klaviyo's hardened GitHub security is inherited by every project

  • Wiz scans every project, and findings feed Klaviyo's SIEM

  • Public deployment is granted case-by-case, so sales can share microsites with prospects, while internal tools stay private

How Klaviyo's app platform turns an idea into an app

Klaviyo wanted anyone with an idea to be able to describe it in plain language, from Slack, Claude, or Cursor, and get back a working app. They designed K:Forge, an in-house pipeline built on the Vercel SDK, to handle everything in between.

K:Forge creates a GitHub repo, deploys the app on Vercel, connects data through Secure Compute, and applies every security default. The output is a live, SSO-gated app, and the builder never touches infrastructure. Changes work the same way: mid-thread in Slack, someone can tell K:Forge what should be different, then it makes the change and redeploys.

Klaviyo built the pipeline and deliberately didn't build the layer under it. CDN behavior, preview environments, analytics, global scale: all of it is R&D Vercel had already done, so builders and engineers at Klaviyo don't have to think about it.

For bigger builds, citizen developers take an app about 80% of the way, and Klaviyo's platform team steps in for the last 20%, for fine-tuning and safety review. The platform team went from being the bottleneck to being the finishing touch. "We don't worry about scale," Mohamed says. "If 100,000 people hit an app, Vercel already solved that."

What people at Klaviyo are building

Employees build everything from microsites that rework a sales process to full-stack apps for problems too niche for any vendor tool. For K:BOS, Klaviyo's flagship event, the team skipped off-the-shelf registration tooling and built its own. Engineering barely touched it.

Klaviyo was one of the first customers of Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents. The platform gave the company a way to let anyone build full-stack apps, with security handled by default.

What's next

Klaviyo sets a high bar for AI fluency. One in five employees has shipped an app so far, and Mohamed intends to get even more people building. The team is also going deeper into Vercel, with MCP and AI Gateway.

About Klaviyo: Klaviyo is an autonomous B2C CRM that powers more valuable customer experiences. We unify a flexible, scalable data platform, intelligence that gets smarter with every interaction, and action across Marketing and Service to help businesses turn real-time customer data into personalization at scale.

title: The Vercel Bug Bounty Program is now publicly available
description:
In 2022, we launched a private bug bounty program through HackerOne. Over the last several years, we've worked with HackerOne's VIP program to refine our process, targets, and scope, onboarding thousands of their best researchers and hardening security across our platform.

We've translated those learnings into several public bounty programs:

  • The $1 million React2Shell hacker challenge

  • The $1 million Vercel Sandbox hacker challenge

  • Our OSS bug bounty program

Today, we are combining our private and OSS bounty programs into a single, public Vercel bug bounty program.

Why now

AI has fundamentally changed the nature of bug bounty programs, exponentially increasing the number of reports, both valid and invalid. Some companies are responding by moving to private programs.

At Vercel, we’ve found that public reports are still surfacing real, valuable findings. AI enables a much wider range of researchers to discover vulnerabilities, and we believe in evaluating reports on their own merit, so making our entire program public was the logical choice.

In preparation for the public launch, our security engineering team has streamlined our process and built tooling to filter out noise and expedite remediation. We have improved every step, from triaging reports to shipping and verifying fixes.

Our team and processes have been battle tested through our private program and several large public programs in the recent past. We are ready to open a comprehensive program to the public and have the best researchers out there responsibly explore every part of the platform.

What is covered

All products across the Vercel platform and our open-source projects are now part of our unified public program. Read the Scope page on HackerOne for full details on what is covered.

Consolidation makes sense for our processes, but we also received feedback from the research community that having multiple programs made disclosure confusing because there were multiple places to submit reports. A single program simplifies reporting across our platform and open-source projects.

New findings in our open-source projects should be reported to the main Vercel program, but if you already have submissions to the previous OSS program, you don't need to copy them over. We will still review every submission that was made through that program.

How to participate

If you’re a security researcher, visit our HackerOne program page for details, bounties, and guidelines.

To file a report, submit your findings through HackerOne with clear reproduction steps. Our security team reviews every submission and works with researchers via the disclosure process. We're committed to fast response times and transparent communication.

We appreciate the researchers who take the time to dig into our code and report issues responsibly. We would also like to thank all the researchers who have been working in our private program. You have helped build the foundation for this public program, and nothing will change for you. We look forward to your future submissions.

Learn more about security at Vercel.

Join our security team

If this kind of work excites you, we are hiring. Apply to join the Vercel security team.

title: State of agent skills
description:
In seven months, the skills.sh registry grew to one million agent skills and recorded nearly 280 million installs.

A skill gives an AI agent reusable instructions for a particular job. Agents are capable but generic; they can do many jobs, but they don't know how a specific person, team, or company does them. A skill supplies that missing context and can be as simple as a file written in ordinary language.

Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025, and Vercel launched the skills.sh registry three months later.

Using aggregate data from the registry, this report follows a new market through its first million skills: what people teach agents, what gets installed, and where the value is heading.

Skills turn expertise into software

To write a skill, some of the judgment behind a job has to be made explicit, like the steps to follow, what good looks like, and how to evaluate the result. The agent and its tools already supply much of the underlying capability, so the skill only has to provide the judgment and instructions specific to a job.

This makes skills faster and easier to create than conventional software.

skills.sh reached one million skills in seven months. GitHub took 27 months to reach one million repositories. Apple's App Store took just over five years to get to one million apps. npm took more than nine years to reach one million packages.

Far more people can describe how work should be done than program a computer to do it. And once a skill is written, it can be distributed and installed without being rewritten for each agent. Skills pair a much larger pool of creators with software’s capacity for reuse, driving the explosive growth of the ecosystem.

What people are teaching agents

We classified the registry's most-installed skills by the kind of work they help agents do. Together, these skills account for more than four-fifths of all installs. Published listings show supply: what authors have made available to agents; installs show demand: what people want their agents to learn.

Supply leans technical. More than half of listings teach software engineering, agent workflows, data, infrastructure, or security, with software engineering alone accounting for about a quarter.

Demand is more distributed. There's isn't a single category with more than a fifth of installs. Software engineering remains the largest at 18%, followed by agent workflows at 15%, then business operations and writing at nearly 11% each.

To see how each category performs for its size, we also compared its installs per listing with the average.

Business operations, writing and documents, and cloud and infrastructure get the most installs per listing. Demand for that work is split across fewer skills, so each one carries more of it. The average business operations skill draws 74% more installs than the average, writing and documents 50% more, cloud and infrastructure 42% more.

Software engineering, education and productivity, and research are oversupplied. The average software engineering skill draws about 30% fewer installs than average, education and productivity 39% fewer, research 55% fewer.

To write a skill, you need to understand a job. To install one, you need only want the job done. Most skills are technical because they began in developer tools. Installs cover a much broader range of work because agents are useful in every part of a company.

Skills that improve how agents work are among the most installed

Agent workflows and automation account for 14.8% of installs in the classified dataset, second only to software engineering. Among listings with at least 100,000 installs, agent workflows are the largest category.

Agent workflow and automation skills teach agents how to plan, route work, use tools, and automate browsers, abilities that apply across many jobs. A contract-review skill applies to contracts, but a planning skill applies to any job the agent takes on, contracts included.

People are using agents to improve agents. And because agents also help write skills, the catalog grows by improving the very machinery used to build it.

A few skills capture most installs

Install activity is highly concentrated. Nearly half of all skills were installed exactly once. At the other end, 375 skills, or 0.04% of the registry, account for 62% of installs, and the top 1.2% account for 94% of installs.

For all that concentration, there's no single winner. Even the most-installed skill accounts for less than 1% of all installs.

Skills compete within jobs and accumulate across them. Once a team chooses an expense-report skill, it has little reason to install another expense-report skill. But it can use that skill alongside others for spreadsheets, research, and presentations. Each job crowns its own winner, and the winners together carry most of the installs.

Seven in eight installs go to skills any industry can use

We also classified each skill by whether its work was shared across industries or specific to one. Tasks such as cleaning up a spreadsheet or deploying a website recur at banks and hospitals, law firms and restaurants. These cross-industry skills account for 66% of classified skills and 87.5% of installs. On average, they receive 3.6 times as many installs per listing as industry-specific skills.

The advantage is portability, whether a skill reaches across jobs, like agent workflows, or across industries. The skills installed most are the ones the most people can use.

The next generation of skills

The first million skills taught agents what everyone knows. The next million will teach your agents what only you know.

Public skills and better models are making general expertise available to every team, which will turn it into the baseline rather than any kind of advantage. More of the differentiating value will move to company-specific judgment. For example, when a customer gets a refund or what can ship without another review.

The measure of a skill will also shift from popularity to effectiveness. Today, the best signal of a skill's quality is its install count. As models improve, the bar rises, because a skill justifies itself only if the agent does the job better with it than without it. Skills will get tests and benchmarks that measure exactly that.

Skills have already turned expertise into software. The public catalog will continue to grow as supply catches up to demand. And organizations will build on top of it, writing down the knowledge only they have and maintaining it the same way they now maintain code.

Explore the first million, or add to the next, at skills.sh.

About this report

This report uses aggregate skills.sh data. A few notes on measurement:

  • Catalog totals count unique registry listings.

  • Install figures use aggregate registry counters. They do not represent unique people or necessarily independent choices.

  • Function and industry findings describe a classified sample rather than the full catalog.

  • Each analysis uses the latest complete data available. Figures may be revised as the underlying data and methodology improve.

title: Push images to Vercel Container Registry from GitHub Actions
description:
You can now push container images from GitHub Actions to Vercel Container Registry (VCR) without storing long-lived registry credentials.

The new vercel/vcr-action/login action authenticates your workflow using GitHub OIDC. It exchanges the workflow’s OIDC token for a short-lived Vercel access token, then uses that token to log in to vcr.vercel.com. When the job ends, the action logs out and revokes the Vercel token.

To start:

  • Create an OIDC policy on your Vercel team that matches the GitHub repository and workflow, and grants read-write access to VCR.

  • Store your Vercel team ID as a GitHub repo variable, for example VERCEL_TEAM_ID, along with the team slug, project slug, and repo name used in the image tag.

  • Give the workflow or job id-token: write permission.

Then add the login step before you build and push and the image:

The action authenticates Docker by default. Pass engines to use Podman or Buildah instead.

After VCR finishes preparing a linux/amd64 image, you can use it as a custom Vercel Sandbox image. Within the same project, reference it as <repository>:<tag>.

Learn more in the VCR documentation and the GitHub Actions guide.

description:

title: Vercel CDN no longer caches responses with Vary: Cookie
description:
Vercel CDN no longer caches origin responses when Vary includes Cookie.

Vary tells a cache which request headers may change the response. Because cookies often contain visitor-specific values, varying by Cookie can create many cache entries that are rarely reused. The response is still served normally but isn't stored for future requests.

You can identify these responses by checking the x-vercel-cache header and Runtime Logs. The header is set to MISS, and Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie as the cache reason.

If Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie for a route you expect to be cached, check the Vary header returned by your origin:

  • If the response is the same regardless of cookies, remove Cookie from Vary. Vercel CDN can then cache it if it meets the other caching requirements.

  • If the response depends on cookies, keep Cookie in Vary and use Cache-Control: private to prevent personalized responses from being stored in the shared CDN cache.

Caching behavior for other supported Vary headers is unchanged.

Learn more about high-cardinality headers and the vary_key_denied cache reason.

Read more

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
description:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, it caches the data used to produce them. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating catalog records one timestamp, whether the tag covers one entry or a million. The service doesn’t need to find and delete every matching entry.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

When a cache exceeds its storage budget, Runtime Cache evicts its least recently used entries, even if they haven’t reached their expiration time. On Pro and Enterprise, each project and environment has its own budget.

We raised storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day. Projects that rarely reused their cached keys saw no improvement from the additional space.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Descender

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

title: How to Use GPTHuman Origin 5.0 AI Humanizer for Beginners
description:
AI writing tools are brilliant at producing a first draft in seconds, but that draft often sounds stiff, repetitive, and strangely formal. Sentences march in the same rhythm, transitions repeat, and the whole piece feels like it was assembled rather than written. That is exactly the problem GPTHuman Origin 5.0 was built to solve. Launched on 29 October 2026, Origin 5.0 is GPTHuman's newest English-language humanization model, designed to make AI-assisted writing sound more natural while keeping the argument, intent, and central meaning of the original draft intact.

This beginner guide walks you through the whole process step by step: what Origin 5.0 is, how to try it for free, how to prepare a draft that humanizes well, how to check the result for facts and detector scores, and how to use it honestly. By the end, you will have a simple, repeatable workflow you can use for blog posts, emails, product descriptions, and study notes — without losing your own voice in the process.

Step 1: Understand What GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Actually Does

An AI humanizer is not a grammar checker and it is not a paraphraser in the old sense. Grammar tools fix mistakes. Paraphrasers swap words. A humanizer rewrites the flow: it varies sentence length, softens rigid phrasing, replaces predictable transitions, and makes the rhythm sound like a person thinking aloud rather than a machine filling a template.

Origin 5.0 focuses on that flow while trying hard not to change what you meant. According to GPTHuman's launch announcement, the model was tested on 500 AI-written English texts from eight different source models and ten writing categories, including news, blogs, academic writing, SEO content, resumes, and reviews. Each text was processed once, with no retries or hand-picked replacements, and then checked against four external AI detectors: ZeroGPT, Originality.ai, Copyleaks, and QuillBot.

The headline results are worth knowing before you trust any tool blindly. About 92.6 percent of outputs — 463 out of 500 — were classified as human by every one of those four detectors. Almost all outputs, 99.8 percent, passed at least three detectors. Crucially, 100 percent preserved the original meaning, but only 93 percent preserved every single key fact, such as names, numbers, dates, places, and roles. That gap is the whole point of this guide: Origin 5.0 is strong on style, but you are still the fact-checker. A tool that sounds fluent can still quietly drop or soften a detail, and a careful human review catches what a detector never will.

Think of Origin 5.0 as a talented editor, not a replacement author. It improves phrasing, rhythm, transitions, and sentence structure. It does not know whether your price, date, or statistic is correct. Keep that division of labor in mind and the tool becomes genuinely useful instead of quietly risky.

Step 2: Create Your Free GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Account and Open the Tool

Start at the official GPTHuman website and create a free account. You do not need to install anything, and you do not need coding skills. Sign up with your email address, confirm it if asked, and sign in to the dashboard.

Once inside, look for the humanizer workspace and confirm that Origin 5.0 is selected as the model. New models sometimes roll out gradually, so if you see a model picker, choose Origin 5.0 explicitly rather than assuming the default is the newest one. If you cannot find it yet, check for an update notice or a model menu at the top of the editor — and do not pay for a plan until you have tested the free experience on a short piece of your own writing.

Before you paste anything important, spend two minutes learning the layout: where the input box is, where tone or mode controls live, where the output appears, and where the built-in AI detection and similarity tools sit. GPTHuman advertises customizable tone controls, similarity measurement, and built-in AI detection alongside its humanizer, and those three features are the ones you will use in almost every session. Knowing where they are before you start saves you from hunting through menus with a deadline looming.

A practical tip for beginners: use a separate browser profile or a password manager for the account, and never paste passwords, private client data, medical records, or unpublished business information into any online rewriting tool. Humanize public-facing drafts, marketing copy, and study notes — not confidential material.

Step 3: Prepare a Draft That GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Humanizes Well

The quality of the output depends heavily on the quality of the input. A messy, vague draft will humanize into a fluent but still vague piece. A clear draft will humanize into something that actually reads well.

Write or generate your first draft first, then tidy it before humanizing. Break very long paragraphs into shorter ones. Fix obvious errors. Decide what the piece must say in one sentence. If you cannot state that sentence, the draft is not ready, and no humanizer will fix a missing argument.

Keep the draft focused. One idea per paragraph works far better than five ideas crammed into one block, because the model can then vary the rhythm without tangling the logic. Remove filler phrases you already know are weak, such as repeated introductions and empty claims like "in today's fast-paced world". The model can smooth language, but it cannot invent evidence you never gave it.

Finally, save the original draft separately before you humanize anything. Keep a copy in a document or note with the date on it. That original is your safety net: if the humanized version drifts, adds a claim, or drops a fact, you can compare the two side by side and restore what matters. This single habit prevents most humanizer accidents, and it takes less than ten seconds.

Step 4: Paste Your Text Into GPTHuman Origin 5.0 and Choose the Right Tone

Paste your draft into the GPTHuman input box. Start small for your first run: 300 to 600 words is ideal. Short tests let you see how the model handles your style without waiting through a long document or wasting free credits on a draft you have not finished editing.

Next, choose a tone that matches the audience. A blog post usually sounds best in a plain, conversational tone. Business emails need something professional but not stiff, while study notes should stay clear and simple. Avoid the temptation to pick the most dramatic or most casual option on your first try — the goal is natural, not theatrical.

If the tool offers a strength or creativity control, start in the middle. A very light setting may leave the stiff phrasing untouched. A very aggressive setting may rewrite so much that facts and emphasis shift. The middle setting, followed by your own edit, gives you the best balance while you learn how Origin 5.0 behaves with your writing.

Read the input once more before you press the button. Check that names are spelled correctly, numbers are right, and quotes are accurate. Humanizing a draft with a wrong number does not make the number right — it just makes the wrong number sound more convincing.

Step 5: Run GPTHuman Origin 5.0 and Read the Output Like an Editor

Press humanize and wait for the output. Then, instead of copying it straight into your blog or document, read it slowly from start to finish. This is the step beginners skip, and it is the step that matters most.

Ask yourself four questions as you read. Does it still say what I meant? Does each paragraph flow into the next without a jarring jump? Is there any sentence that sounds clever but says nothing? Has any detail changed, softened, or disappeared? Mark anything that feels off, even if you cannot explain why yet — your ear is often right before your analysis catches up.

Pay attention to length changes too. In GPTHuman's benchmark, source samples averaged 318 words while humanized versions averaged 352 words, with shorter words and phrases replacing dense constructions. About 60 percent of outputs became more than 10 percent longer, while only 3 percent became much shorter. So expect the output to breathe a little more. If it suddenly doubles in length, or if a short email becomes a long essay, that is a sign to tighten it yourself rather than accept the expansion.

Read the output aloud if you can. Awkward rhythm, repeated words, and unnatural transitions are much easier to hear than to see on screen. If a sentence makes you stumble when speaking it, rewrite that sentence by hand. The tool did most of the work; your voice finishes it.

Step 6: Fact-Check Every GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Output for Names, Numbers, and Dates

This is the non-negotiable step. Open your original draft beside the humanized version and compare them line by line for facts. Check every name, number, date, place, job title, price, statistic, and quotation. Remember the benchmark: 93 percent of outputs preserved every key fact, which also means 7 percent missed at least one. On a 500-word article with ten facts, that is a real risk, not a theoretical one.

Check meaning as well as facts. A sentence can keep all the same facts and still change the emphasis — turning a suggestion into a promise, a possibility into a certainty, or a criticism into praise. If the tone of a claim has shifted, restore the original wording for that sentence. Your credibility lives in those small shifts.

If you work with sources, keep them open while you check. Do not rely on memory for a statistic you read yesterday. A quick source check takes a minute and prevents an embarrassing correction later. For business and professional writing, this step is even more important: a fluent error in a client email or a product page costs far more than a stiff sentence ever would.

When you find a changed fact, fix it by hand and note the pattern. If the model repeatedly softens numbers, for example, you will learn to watch numbers closely in future runs. That pattern recognition is what turns a beginner into a confident user.

Step 7: Run GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Detection and Similarity Checks

GPTHuman includes built-in AI detection, and Origin 5.0's launch results were measured against four external detectors. Use those checks as a guide, not as a verdict. A "human" score does not prove a piece is good, original, or true — it only suggests the text does not carry the most obvious machine patterns.

Run the detection check on the humanized version, then note the score. If you have access to an external detector, a second check can be useful for important pieces, but do not chase a perfect score by running the text through the humanizer again and again. Repeated humanizing tends to wash out your voice, blur meaning, and produce text that sounds generic rather than human. One careful pass, plus your own edit, beats three automated passes every time.

Also check similarity if the tool offers it. Similarity tells you how close the output stayed to the source — in the benchmark, the average similarity was 92.74 out of 100. Very high similarity may mean the rewrite was too light to help. Very low similarity may mean the meaning drifted. For most purposes, a middle range with a clean fact-check is the sweet spot.

Treat detector scores with humility. Detectors make mistakes in both directions, flagging genuine human writing and missing machine writing. Schools, employers, and publishers increasingly know this, which is why a thoughtful, fact-checked, honestly produced piece matters far more than a score on a screen.

Step 8: Edit Your GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Output by Hand and Put Your Voice Back In

The best humanized writing still needs a human final pass. This is where the piece stops sounding like "good AI writing" and starts sounding like you.

Add one or two details only you would know: a concrete example from your work, a specific place, a real question a customer asked you, or a short personal observation. Replace any generic example with a specific one. Cut any sentence that repeats the previous sentence in different words. Shorten any paragraph that takes four sentences to say what two sentences could say.

Vary the rhythm yourself as well. Mix a short sentence with a longer one. Ask a question where a statement would feel flat. Break a long list into a story or an example. These small moves are what readers actually experience as a human voice — not the absence of detector patterns, but the presence of judgment, selection, and personality.

If a sentence still sounds like the tool wrote it, rewrite that sentence from scratch without looking at the tool's version. Write it the way you would explain it to a friend. Then compare: usually your fresh version is clearer, shorter, and more honest. Keep that version.

Step 9: Use GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Honestly — Know Where the Line Is

Humanizers are powerful, and power needs clear rules. Use Origin 5.0 to improve clarity, fix stiff phrasing, and polish drafts you wrote or genuinely drafted with AI assistance where that assistance is allowed. Do not use it to disguise work you are supposed to produce yourself, to cheat on exams or assignments, to fake authorship, or to mislead readers, teachers, or employers about who wrote something.

Check the rules where you work or study before you use any humanizer on assessed work. Many schools and workplaces have explicit policies on AI assistance and disclosure. When in doubt, disclose: a short note such as "drafted with AI assistance and edited by hand" is honest, professional, and increasingly normal. Hiding assistance creates a bigger problem than the stiff draft ever did.

The same honesty applies to publishing. Readers trust a blog, a newsletter, or a business page because they believe a real person stands behind it. Use the tool to communicate better, not to manufacture a false impression. If a piece required research, say so. If a claim came from a source, cite it. Good writing is not just fluent — it is accountable.

For teams, agree on a shared rule before anyone starts using a humanizer: what kinds of documents may be humanized, who fact-checks them, and how AI assistance is disclosed. A one-paragraph policy prevents awkward conversations later, especially when a client or editor asks how a piece was produced.

Step 10: Build a Repeatable GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Workflow and Save What Works

Once you have a workflow that works, write it down and reuse it. A simple checklist beats a perfect memory, especially when you are producing content regularly.

A practical weekly workflow looks like this. Draft the piece and save the original. Humanize it once with Origin 5.0 at a middle strength and a natural tone. Fact-check names, numbers, and dates against your sources. Run the detection and similarity checks. Edit by hand for voice, examples, and cuts. Read it aloud once. Publish or send it, and keep both the original and final versions filed together.

Save tone settings that worked for each type of writing — blog posts, emails, product descriptions, and social captions often need different settings. Keep a small note of what you changed by hand most often; that note becomes your personal editing checklist and makes each future run faster.

If you run a content team or a small business, this workflow also scales nicely. One person drafts, another humanizes and fact-checks, and a third does the final read-aloud edit. For a digital agency handling client content, that division keeps quality consistent without slowing production down. Similarly, if you publish guides about automation and AI automation services, a documented humanizing workflow shows clients that speed never replaces accuracy.

GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Compared With Other Writing Tools

Beginners often ask how a dedicated humanizer differs from the writing tools they already use. The table below gives a fair, plain-language comparison. Prices and plans change, so check the official site before you buy anything — but the roles of these tools stay fairly stable.

Tool Best for Main limitation Beginner verdict
GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Making AI drafts sound natural while keeping meaning Still needs a full human fact-check; 7 percent of benchmark outputs missed a key fact Best dedicated humanizer to try first for AI drafts
Grammarly Grammar, spelling, clarity, and tone suggestions Not built primarily to rewrite AI rhythm or detector patterns Great everyday editor; pair it with a humanizer, do not replace one with the other
QuillBot Paraphrasing, summarizing, and grammar help Paraphrase can drift in meaning if used aggressively Useful for rewording single sentences; check every paraphrase
Manual editing alone Full control, voice, and accountability Slow on long drafts; easy to miss your own repetitive patterns Always needed as the final pass, even with the best tool

The lesson is simple: no single tool does everything. Grammarly polishes, QuillBot rewords, manual editing adds voice, and Origin 5.0 bridges the gap between a machine-sounding first draft and a natural-sounding final piece. Use them in that order and each tool does the job it is best at.

Common GPTHuman Origin 5.0 Beginner Mistakes to Avoid

First, do not humanize text you have not read. If you do not understand the draft, you cannot judge whether the humanized version kept its meaning. Read first, humanize second.

Second, do not humanize the same text five times chasing a detector score. Each pass moves the text further from your intent and closer to generic filler. One pass plus a real edit is the professional standard.

Third, do not paste confidential or sensitive text into any online tool. Drafts about real clients, private data, or unpublished plans belong in private documents, not in a web editor.

Fourth, do not assume a high human score means the piece is accurate. Detectors measure patterns, not truth. Only your fact-check measures truth.

Fifth, do not publish without reading aloud. The ear catches what the eye forgives, especially repeated transitions, awkward rhythm, and sentences that sound impressive but mean very little.

Finally, do not let the tool erase your voice. If every piece you publish starts to sound the same, the tool is doing too much and you are doing too little. Add examples, opinions, and specifics that only you can add — that is the part readers actually remember.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is GPTHuman Origin 5.0 free to try?

Origin 5.0 is available now in GPTHuman, and the service offers a free way to try it, though exact free limits and paid plans can change. Start with a short test piece, check what the free experience includes, and only consider a paid plan once you know the tool genuinely saves you time on your real writing.

Does Origin 5.0 guarantee that text will pass AI detectors?

No tool can honestly guarantee that. In GPTHuman's own benchmark, 92.6 percent of outputs passed all four external detectors tested, and 99.8 percent passed at least three. Those are strong results, but they are benchmark results on specific texts and detectors, not a promise for every piece you write. Treat scores as a helpful signal and your own edit as the real quality control.

Will humanizing change the meaning of my text?

It should not, but it can soften or shift emphasis, and in the benchmark 7 percent of outputs missed at least one key fact. That is why this guide insists on a side-by-side fact-check. Keep your original saved, compare facts carefully, and restore any detail the rewrite changed.

Can I use GPTHuman for school or work assignments?

Only if the rules where you study or work allow AI assistance, and only with honest disclosure where required. Never use a humanizer to disguise work you were supposed to produce yourself. When in doubt, ask your teacher, manager, or editor before you use it, not after.

Is GPTHuman better than Grammarly or QuillBot?

They do different jobs. Grammarly excels at grammar and clarity, QuillBot excels at paraphrasing, and GPTHuman Origin 5.0 is built specifically to make AI-generated text sound natural while preserving meaning. Many writers use Grammarly for polish, GPTHuman for AI drafts, and manual editing for voice — in that order.

How long should a piece be for a first humanizing test?

Start with 300 to 600 words. That is long enough to see how the model handles your rhythm and tone, and short enough to fact-check carefully. Once you trust the workflow, scale up to full articles, but keep the same checklist no matter how long the piece gets.

Final Thoughts

GPTHuman Origin 5.0, launched on 29 October 2026, is one of the most practical new AI writing tools for beginners because it solves a real, everyday frustration: AI drafts that are correct but sound robotic. Its benchmark results — 92.6 percent passing all four detectors, 100 percent preserving overall meaning — show a model that takes style seriously without casually rewriting substance. But the same benchmark carries a warning every beginner should remember: only 93 percent preserved every key fact. The tool improves how writing sounds; you remain responsible for whether it is true.

Use it the way this guide describes and it becomes a genuine productivity tool. Draft clearly, save the original, humanize once with a natural tone, fact-check every detail, run the detector check, edit by hand for your voice, and read the result aloud before you publish. Follow that workflow and you will produce writing that is both fluent and trustworthy — writing that sounds like you on a good day, not like a machine on autopilot.

Start today with one short draft you already have. Run it through Origin 5.0, fact-check it carefully, and edit it by hand. That single test will teach you more about the tool than any review can, and it will show you exactly where your own editing adds the most value.

For another beginner-friendly AI assistant walkthrough on this site, see our guide to the LegalZoom AI Assistant — it follows the same step-by-step style, with a different tool and use case.

Explore More Free AI Tools

Use them alongside GPTHuman Origin 5.0 to write clearer titles, sharper descriptions, cleaner rewrites, and better-checked pages before you publish.
