title: Issues as Git Objects: How Tangled Rebuilt the Code Forge on the AT Protocol
description:
Every issue, pull request, comment, reaction, and label on a Tangled repository is now a chain of Git objects, stored in the repository itself, right next to the code it describes. That single decision, shipped as part of Tangled's October 30 relaunch, is the most consequential forge design choice since GitHub bolted a social graph onto Git — and it inverts the usual question. The interesting thing about a federated forge is not that you can self-host it. It is that the boundary between the code and the conversation about the code has been moved into the one data structure every developer already trusts: the Git object graph.

This article walks through what Tangled actually shipped, what the new architecture is made of, and what running a piece of it yourself commits you to. Everything below comes from Tangled's relaunch post, its self-hosting documentation, and the AT Protocol sync specification, not from launch-day enthusiasm.

The centralized forge bargain is ending

For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. The bargain was convenience in exchange for centralization, and Tangled's own relaunch post is blunt about how that bargain aged. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code has not played out well.

The post draws a timeline worth taking seriously. In 2005 the stack was mail plus Git. In 2009 it became GitHub plus Git. Now, Tangled argues, it becomes AT Protocol plus Git. What survived both previous eras was not a company but a pair of open protocols: Git to move the code, and an open communication layer to talk about it. Email was that layer in the first era, and it worked, at the cost of user experience. The pitch for Tangled is that the AT Protocol can be that layer without giving up the polish of a proper forge.

The federation claim is specific rather than rhetorical. You can self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and the UI. Whatever you choose, you can still talk to everyone else, because the collaboration data does not belong to whichever server happens to render it.

From one Go monolith in Sweden to the edge

Until this release, Tangled's web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the appview. It handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data, and UI rendering with html/template and htmx, and it ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden. That worked well as long as you were roughly 50 to 100 milliseconds away from Sweden, which most of Tangled's users are not.

The replacement splits the monolith along a clean line. A new standalone frontend written in Svelte is deployed at the edge. Behind it sits bobbin, a new indexer service written in Rust that is diskless and entirely in-memory, deployed across more than eleven regions so that API and UI latency stops being a function of distance from Scandinavia. Bobbin is purely read-only and deals only with AT Protocol data. Everything else, the off-protocol state a forge still needs, has been delegated to a new set of supporting services.

Alongside the split, the data model moved. A new set of lexicons now lives under org.tangled., replacing the old sh.tangled. records. If you consumed the old records from the firehose, that namespace change is a breaking one, and it is worth grepping your consumers for before assuming silence means inactivity.

Knots now behave like a PDS

The deepest change is knot2, the second implementation of Tangled's knot server, this time written in Rust. A knot is the component that stores Git repositories. Knot2 bakes in a fully custom Git server and bundles an SSH server into the same binary, so the process that answers your git push is the same process that speaks to the wider network.

What makes knot2 interesting is where it puts the collaboration data. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions, and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects, COBs for short. A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members, and the blocklist are stored the same way.

Conceptually, an issue thread is no longer a row in someone else's database. It is a chain of objects whose history is Git history:

issue object          comment object          label object
  "opened"      <-      "reply"          <-      "add: bug"
      |                      |                        |
      +---------- signed, ordered, replicated --------+

In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS. They hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo, and much like a PDS, those records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose.

Why Git objects are a real design decision, not a gimmick

Storing collaboration in Git objects buys properties that centralized forges simulate with export buttons. Portability is the obvious one: if the discussion lives in the repository, then cloning the repository carries the discussion with it, and the forge that hosts the canonical copy becomes a preference rather than a prison. Authenticity is the second: AT Protocol records are signed, and the sync specification is explicit about what that buys — redistribution of public data between independent participants that is trustworthy, low-latency, and resource-efficient at large scale.

The sync layer is worth understanding because none of it is Tangled-specific. The protocol offers two mechanisms. Batch transfer uses full-repository exports as CAR files over HTTP through the com.atproto.sync.getRepo endpoint, which is unauthenticated and returns all repo records, the Merkle search tree nodes, and the current signed commit object in a single file. Real-time sync is a repository event stream over WebSocket, the firehose, where every commit carries a revision value encoded as a TID that functions as a logical clock. A minimal consumer pointed at a relay that carries the Tangled collections looks like this in skeleton form:

import asyncio

import websockets  # pip install websockets

RELAY = "wss://relay.example.com/xrpc/com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos"

async def main() -> None:
    async with websockets.connect(RELAY) as stream:
        async for frame in stream:
            # Frames are CBOR: a header and a payload. A real consumer
            # decodes both with a dag-cbor library, keeps the per-repo
            # revision (the TID) as a resumable cursor, and filters
            # commit ops by collection, here anything under org.tangled.*
            print("frame bytes:", len(frame))

asyncio.run(main())

The discipline that matters in a real consumer is the cursor. The specification requires revisions to increase between commits for the same repository, even across host migrations, and synchronizing services should reject updates whose revisions sit in the future beyond a short drift window. That gives you exactly what an indexer wants: a resumable, ordered stream with a cheap freshness check.

Deletion deserves an honest mention. The sync specification obliges mirrors to respect record deletion and account deactivation in a timely manner, seconds or minutes rather than days. When the conversation lives in a replicated object graph, delete is a protocol-level request that every downstream consumer has to honor. That is a stronger guarantee than a row update inside one company's database and a weaker one than true erasure, and your own consumers should be designed with that gap in mind.

Run your own knot in an evening

The self-hosting documentation is concrete about what a knot needs: a Linux machine that stays online, a DNS name you intend to keep because the knot uses it as its identity, your DID (look up your handle at pds.ls if you do not know it), and a reverse proxy such as Caddy for TLS. The master key is a random 32-byte base64 value kept in an env file with mode 600.

The Docker path is a single image, atcr.io/tangled.org/knot:2, plus a config.toml:

[server]
hostname = "knot.example.com"
admins = ["did:plc:yourdid"]
listen_addr = "[::]:5555"
ssh_host_key_file = "/data/ssh/host_key"

[repo]
scan_path = "/data/repos"

[secrets]
sealed_key_file = "/data/secrets/sealed-keys"
master_key_env = "KNOT_MASTER_KEY"

[atproto]
plc_directory = "https://plc.directory"

Compose maps two ports, 2222 for SSH where your users clone and 127.0.0.1:5555 for the HTTP side behind your proxy, and three volumes for repos, secrets, and the SSH host key. Bringing it up and checking it is a four-line operation:

mkdir -p repos secrets ssh
sudo chown -R 1000:1000 repos secrets ssh
docker compose up -d
curl https://knot.example.com/xrpc/_health

On NixOS there is a flake module instead: add the Tangled flake input, enable services.tangled.knot-rs, point it at the same env file, and the knot listens on 127.0.0.1:5555 either way. Once the health check answers, you register the knot in the web app under the knots settings page, and you can create repositories on it immediately.

If you want to go deeper, the index tier is self-hostable too. Bobbin keeps everything in memory and rebuilds from a hydrant stream on every start, so it needs no database. It does need a slingshot for records and identities, a service DID of its own such as a did:web for your index host, and a knot mirror — without the mirror URL configured, repository pages have no code. The binary prints every setting with defaults via bobbin config-template and checks your file via bobbin validate before you start it.

Organizations, stacked PRs, and what ships next

Two product changes round out the relaunch. Organization accounts are real AT Protocol accounts: each has its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They are passwordless, delegated accounts. You create one from the New Organization page, you get a name under tngl.sh with yourself as owner, and owners can invite members.

The pull request flow now supports stacked PRs for everyone, not only Jujutsu users. If you use vanilla Git, you can interdiff between versions of a pull request, what the UI used to call rounds, and JJ users can interdiff between individual changes as well. For anyone who has watched stacked-diff workflows become the differentiating feature of paid review tools, seeing interdiff land in a federated forge is a signal about where the baseline is heading.

The launch is staggered across the coming weeks: private repositories, a CLI, SDKs for different languages, and skills for your agent are all announced but not yet shipped. The extension points are already real, though. Because the whole stack sits on the AT Protocol, you can write a custom knot — the relaunch post links one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses Pierre's code.storage for Git storage — or a custom spindle for CI, or host the ultralight API server and build an entirely custom forge on top. The bobbin API is explicitly documented for agent consumption, which is a quiet admission about who the next generation of forge users will be.

The contract you actually sign

A federated forge does not remove trust; it relocates it. You still depend on relays and indexers for discovery, on the PLC directory for identity resolution, and on the discipline of every mirror to honor deletions. What changes is the exit cost. When your issues, reviews, and labels are Git objects on a knot you control, and the social identity is a DID rather than a row in a user table, moving your project stops being an export-and-pray operation and becomes a replication target change.

The pragmatic adoption path is mirror-first: run a knot, put a real project on it, keep your existing forge as a read mirror, and learn the operational shape of COBs and firehose cursors before you bet a community on them. The protocol underneath has already proven it can carry a social network at scale, and watching it carry code review will be the more interesting test. Either way, the era in which the forge owns the conversation about your code just got its first credible challenger.

Originally published on Dispatch.

title: How to Read a Database Sync Speed Number
description:
"Millions of rows per minute" appears on many product pages, including ours. Before you plan a cut-over
weekend around a number like that, it is worth asking what was actually measured. These five questions apply
to any tool, and they are the same ones we answer on our own performance page.

1. Which mode?

An initial load into an empty table is the easiest case: no lookups, no conflicts, just bulk inserts. An
upsert has to find each key on the target and decide between insert and update. "New rows only" and
incremental modes depend on how fast the target can tell what is missing. A number from one mode says little
about another. In our lab, the same PostgreSQL target was 66 to 118 times faster at upsert and "new rows only"
with one option turned on, while the initial load did not change at all.

2. Which engines, and where?

SQL Server to SQL Server on the same host is not the same job as SQLite on a laptop to Azure SQL in another
region. Ask for the source, the target and where each one ran.

3. What about the network?

Over a WAN link, the network is often the slowest side. A tool that reads and writes at the same time, as
dbSlice does, moves at the pace of whichever side is slower, so the same job can be fast on one link and slow
on another.

4. How wide are the rows?

A table of three integer columns and a table with long text and binary columns can differ by an order of
magnitude in rows per second while moving similar bytes. If the benchmark does not say, assume narrow rows.

5. Was anything tuned?

Indexes dropped during the load, a bigger log, a dedicated network: all legitimate, and all worth knowing.
Our largest run, 12.96 billion rows in about 41 hours (≈88,500 rows/s on average), came from a live production
table of purchase orders with 20 years of history, 40 columns and 9 indexes, migrated into the database of a
new microservice that integrates with Salesforce; the network and both databases were tuned for the load. Next to it we publish a plain-setup number: 31.4 million rows into Azure SQL in
about 30 minutes (≈17,200 rows/s), initial-load mode, SQLite source on a local disk.

The only number that counts

Is the one from your own tables, on your own network. Run the job you plan to run, in the mode you plan to
use, and time it. The free version of dbSlice is on the
Microsoft Store; the numbers and conditions we measured are
on how fast is dbSlice, and the video walkthrough is in
12.96 billion rows in 41 hours.

Related: MySQL to PostgreSQL migration · SQL Server to MySQL migration

Originally published on the dbSlice blog. dbSlice is a Windows app for data migration, replication and sync between the leading databases.

title: When an AI Integration Guide and Its Recommended SDK Installation Don't Align
description:
When an AI Integration Guide and Its Recommended SDK Installation Don't Align

An integration guide can provide a seemingly complete implementation path while leaving an important compatibility question unresolved.

I recently examined a guide published by an AI inference infrastructure provider. It demonstrates how developers can build a streaming AI chat application using a popular React-based AI SDK.

The guide covers package installation, provider configuration, server-side streaming and frontend chat functionality.

However, the relationship between its recommended package installation and frontend implementation raises an interesting question.

Are they targeting the same SDK interface?

  1. The recommended installation

The guide recommends installing:

npm install ai @ai-sdk/openai

It then demonstrates configuring an OpenAI-compatible provider.

The installation instructions don't specify package versions.

That detail becomes important when the guide introduces its frontend implementation.

  1. The frontend implementation

The example imports its React chat hook using:

import { useChat } from "ai/react";

It subsequently uses an interface containing:

const {
messages,
input,
handleInputChange,
handleSubmit,
isLoading
} = useChat({
api: "/api/chat",
});

Message rendering also accesses:

message.content

These are characteristics of an older SDK interface.

  1. What the current SDK documentation demonstrates

Current documentation for the SDK uses a different React package entry point:

import { useChat } from "@ai-sdk/react";

The current implementation also demonstrates a transport-based integration pattern.

For example:

const { messages, sendMessage } = useChat();

Message representation and rendering have also evolved.

This means the differences extend beyond the import statement.

The hook interface and message-handling approach are different.

  1. The assumption created by the integration guide

Consider the developer following the instructions.

They:

  1. Install the recommended packages.
  2. Configure the inference provider.
  3. Implement the server-side streaming endpoint.
  4. Follow the supplied React example.
  5. Attempt to complete the chat interface.

At this point, the developer encounters an important compatibility question.

The installation instructions don't identify an older package version corresponding to the frontend implementation.

A developer could reasonably assume that the recommended installation supports the interface demonstrated in the same guide.

However, the published instructions don't establish that compatibility.

The developer may need to investigate package versions, reconcile the interface differences or adapt the frontend implementation.

  1. The responsibility boundary

There are two distinct responsibilities here.

Provider integration: Connecting the application to the inference infrastructure.

Frontend SDK integration: Ensuring that the installed dependencies support the React interface used by the application.

The infrastructure provider can abstract the inference connection without automatically resolving every compatibility requirement in the surrounding application.

The developer remains responsible for reconciling those components.

  1. Potential implementation consequences

When the compatibility relationship isn't established by the guide, developers may need to perform additional work:

  • Investigate compatible dependency versions.
  • Identify the appropriate frontend interface.
  • Adapt the supplied implementation.
  • Resolve dependency differences before completing the integration.

This introduces additional implementation work along a path intended to simplify adoption.

It doesn't establish that the inference API itself is malfunctioning.

The unresolved question concerns the compatibility of the documented installation and frontend implementation.

  1. Evidence limitation

This investigation compares a published AI infrastructure integration guide with current documentation for the underlying React-based AI SDK.

No live package installation, compilation or runtime test was performed.

Consequently, this finding concerns the documented interface discrepancy and the compatibility responsibility left unresolved.

It should not be interpreted as an experimentally confirmed application failure.

Conclusion

Integration guides communicate more than installation instructions and code examples.

They also establish expectations about compatibility, supported interfaces and the responsibilities developers must handle themselves.

When those expectations aren't sufficiently established, developers may have to perform additional investigation before completing the intended implementation.

That is an important dimension of developer implementation experiences.

Independent implementation investigation by DaxMac.

There is no watermark on your downloads, your credits do not expire, and you can even use videos made with free credits commercially. You do not need a credit card to sign up, and everything runs in your web browser, including on your phone.

In this beginner guide, you will learn exactly how to use AIVideoFree AI, step by step: how to sign up, how to write prompts that actually look good, how to turn photos into moving clips, how to pick the right model for each job, and how to avoid wasting your free credits. By the end, you will be able to create your first polished AI video in under ten minutes.

Step 1: Understand What AIVideoFree AI Actually Is

AIVideoFree is an online AI video and image generation platform based in Singapore. Think of it as a single front door to many different AI video models. Instead of signing up for five separate tools and paying five separate subscriptions, you sign up once and choose the model that fits each project.

Here is what you get in one place:

  • 12 video models, including Veo, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.5, Wan 3.0, and Minimax H3.
  • 10 image models for creating pictures, thumbnails, and start frames for your videos.
  • Text-to-video generation from a written description.
  • Image-to-video generation that animates a photo, with support for start and end frames.
  • No watermark on downloaded videos, even on the free tier.
  • Credits that never expire, so there is no pressure to rush through them in a week.

The core idea is simple: free to start, and free to choose. Your free credits are not locked to one cheap model while the good models sit behind a paywall. They work the same way as purchased credits, on every model offered.

Step 2: Sign Up for Free in Under Two Minutes

Getting started is deliberately painless, and that is part of the appeal for beginners.

  1. Visit the AIVideoFree website at aivideofree.com and click Sign Up.
  2. Create your account with an email address or a social sign-in option. No credit card is required.
  3. Check your free credits. Your starting balance appears in your account dashboard. Note that the exact number of free credits can vary by country, so your balance may differ slightly from another user's.
  4. Confirm the credit cost before you generate. Every model shows its credit cost upfront, so you always know what a video will cost before you spend anything.

A quick tip for new users: do not burn your first credits on a long, complex test. Start with one short, simple clip to learn how the platform feels, then scale up once you understand the prompt style that works best.

Step 3: Create Your First Text-to-Video Clip

Text-to-video is the fastest way to see what AIVideoFree can do. Here is the beginner workflow:

  1. Choose Text to Video from the main creation screen.
  2. Pick a model to start with. If you are unsure, Veo or Kling are safe, reliable first choices for realistic motion.
  3. Write a clear prompt describing the scene, the subject, the action, and the camera. For example: "A golden retriever puppy running through autumn leaves in a sunny park, slow motion, warm afternoon light, camera following from the side."
  4. Set the length and aspect ratio. Short clips are best for learning, and vertical video suits social media while landscape suits YouTube.
  5. Check the credit cost, then click Generate.
  6. Wait for the render, preview the result, and download it if you like it. If it is not quite right, tweak one thing in the prompt and try again.

Good prompts are specific but not overloaded. Describe who is in the scene, what they are doing, where they are, and how the camera moves. Leave out contradictory instructions, and avoid asking for three different actions in a single short clip.

Step 4: Turn a Photo into a Moving Video

Image-to-video is where AIVideoFree becomes genuinely useful for creators who already have pictures they love. You can upload a photo and turn it into a short clip, which is perfect for animating product photos, portraits, artwork, or travel shots.

  1. Choose Image to Video and upload your photo.
  2. Optionally set a start frame and an end frame if you want to control where the motion begins and ends. This is a powerful feature for storytelling, because it lets you plan a clear visual journey.
  3. Describe the motion you want: "camera slowly zooms in, leaves sway gently, the subject smiles and looks toward the camera."
  4. Pick a model known for smooth motion, such as Seedance or Kling, and generate.
  5. Preview, download, and reuse the clip in a longer edit if you want.

This feature is also a smart way to test models cheaply. The same photo animated by two different models can look surprisingly different, and comparing them teaches you which model to reach for next time.

Step 5: Pick the Right Model for Each Job

With 12 models available, choosing can feel overwhelming. You do not need to master all of them. Start with this simple rule: match the model to the job, not to the hype.

  • Veo: Strong for realistic, cinematic scenes with natural motion and lighting.
  • Kling 3.0: Excellent for smooth, detailed movement and expressive characters.
  • Seedance 2.5: A great all-rounder for fast, creative clips and social content.
  • Wan 3.0: Useful for stylised and artistic looks when realism is not the goal.
  • Minimax H3: Worth trying for character-driven scenes and dynamic action.

The practical approach is to keep a small personal note of what worked. After each generation, write down the model, the prompt style, and whether you liked the result. Within a week, you will have your own cheat sheet, and model choice will stop feeling like guesswork. Small businesses exploring video often pair a tool like this with professional help from a digital agency for strategy, while using AIVideoFree for fast drafts, social clips, and experiments.

Step 6: Write Prompts That Actually Look Good

Prompt writing is the skill that separates a blurry, jittery clip from a video that looks intentional. Beginners usually make two mistakes: prompts that are too vague ("a nice video of a dog") and prompts that are too crowded ("a dog running, jumping, swimming, dancing, while it rains, at sunset, in space, with fireworks").

Use this simple four-part formula instead:

  • Subject: Who or what is in the scene?
  • Action: What exactly are they doing?
  • Setting: Where and when is it happening?
  • Camera and mood: How does the camera move, and what is the lighting or feeling?

A strong example: "A street food vendor flipping noodles in a busy night market in Bangkok, steam rising, neon signs glowing, camera moves slowly around the stall, warm cinematic light." One clear action, one clear place, one camera move. That is enough.

Also, generate short first. Short clips cost fewer credits, render faster, and let you test an idea before committing to a longer version. If the short version looks good, extend the idea rather than starting over.

Step 7: Make Social Media Videos That Stand Out

AIVideoFree is built for the kind of short, punchy video that performs well on TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts. The workflow for social content is slightly different from making a single beautiful clip.

  1. Start vertical. Choose a 9:16 aspect ratio so the video fills a phone screen.
  2. Hook in the first two seconds. Put the most interesting motion or visual right at the start, not after a slow fade-in.
  3. Keep it short. Ten to twenty seconds is plenty for a first test, and shorter clips are cheaper to iterate on.
  4. Add text and sound in an editor. AIVideoFree handles the visuals; a free editor like CapCut adds captions, music, and transitions.
  5. Test two versions. Generate the same idea with two different models and post the stronger one. Your audience will tell you what works.

One honest caution: AI video is a creative tool, not a shortcut to guaranteed views. The creators who win with it are the ones who combine good visuals with a clear idea, a strong hook, and consistent posting. If you want to scale that workflow, learning how AI automation services can handle repetitive production steps is a useful next step once the basics feel easy.

Step 8: Manage Your Free Credits Like a Pro

Free credits are generous, but they are not infinite, so a little planning goes a long way. Because AIVideoFree credits do not expire, you can afford to be patient and strategic instead of rushing.

  • Always check the cost first. The platform shows the credit cost before generation, so never click blindly.
  • Test short, then commit. Use short clips to validate a prompt before generating a longer version.
  • Reuse good results. A strong clip can be reused across platforms with different captions, instead of generating a new one for each app.
  • Compare models on the same prompt. This teaches you more in one afternoon than weeks of random testing.
  • Buy only when you need to. Extra credits are sold as one-time packs starting at $6.90 for 600 credits, and annual plans start at $7.40 per month billed yearly, but a subscription is not required. Start free, and only pay once you know exactly how much video you actually make.

Because your free credits work on every model, there is no need to save them for a "premium" model. Spend them learning, and spend them on real projects.

Step 9: Fix Common Beginner Problems

Most early frustrations with AI video have simple fixes. Here are the ones beginners hit most often:

  • The video looks jittery or warped: Simplify the prompt. One action, one camera move, and fewer moving subjects usually fix it.
  • Faces look strange: Avoid extreme close-ups and fast head turns in your first attempts. Medium shots are far more forgiving.
  • The motion does not match your prompt: Try a different model. Some models handle certain actions much better than others.
  • Text in the video is garbled: AI video models still struggle with on-screen text. Add titles and captions in a video editor instead.
  • The clip feels too short: Generate a follow-up clip with an end frame that matches, or stitch two clips together in an editor.
  • You ran out of ideas: Animate a photo you already have, or turn a blog post, product description, or travel memory into a visual scene.

If a generation fails completely, do not immediately regenerate the same prompt. Change one element — the model, the camera instruction, or the action — and test again. That is how you learn what the tool actually responds to.

Step 10: Compare AIVideoFree with Other AI Video Tools

AIVideoFree is not the only AI video generator, but its relaunch makes it unusually beginner-friendly. Here is how it compares with the tools beginners usually consider:

Tool Best For Free Tier Model Choice Watermark on Free
AIVideoFree Trying many top models free Free sign-up credits, no expiry 12 video models No
Google Flow Cinematic Veo clips Limited daily credits Veo only Depends on plan
Runway Professional video editing Limited free credits Own models Yes, on some plans
Luma Dream Machine Fast creative clips Limited free generations Own models Varies
Seedance (standalone) High-quality short clips Trial credits Single model Varies

The honest takeaway: if you want to experiment with Veo, Kling, and Seedance without paying for three subscriptions, AIVideoFree is currently the easiest place to start. If you later settle on one model you love, a dedicated subscription to that model may make sense — but you will be choosing from experience, not from marketing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is AIVideoFree really free?

Yes, to start. You receive free credits when you sign up, with no credit card required, and those credits do not expire. Videos made with free credits download without a watermark and can be used commercially under the platform's terms. Paid credit packs and plans are optional extras, not a requirement.

Which AI video models does AIVideoFree offer?

AIVideoFree offers 12 video models, including Veo, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.5, Wan 3.0, and Minimax H3, plus 10 image models. Your free credits work on all of them, so you can compare models on the same prompt before deciding which one you prefer.

Can I use AIVideoFree videos commercially?

According to the platform's relaunch terms, content made with free credits may be used commercially, and downloads carry no watermark. As with any tool, it is still wise to check the current terms on the site before using a video in a paid campaign, since terms can change.

Do I need a powerful computer to use AIVideoFree?

No. AIVideoFree runs in a web browser, including on mobile devices, and the heavy rendering happens on the platform's servers. Any device that can run a modern browser can create videos with it.

Is AIVideoFree good for beginners?

Yes, it is one of the most beginner-friendly options available right now. The interface is simple, the credit cost is shown before you generate, and the free tier lets you learn by doing without financial risk. Start with short text-to-video clips, then move on to image-to-video once you are comfortable.

What should I do if my first video does not look good?

Simplify your prompt, try a different model, and generate a short test clip first. Most poor results come from overloaded prompts or the wrong model for the job, not from the tool being broken. Keep a note of what worked, and your results will improve quickly.

Final Thoughts

AIVideoFree's October 2026 relaunch is good news for anyone who has wanted to make AI videos but did not want to pay for multiple subscriptions just to experiment. Free credits that work on every model, no watermark, no expiry, and commercial use included remove almost every barrier that used to stop beginners.

The best way to learn it is to start today: sign up free, generate one short clip with a simple prompt, animate one photo you already like, and compare two models on the same idea. That one afternoon of hands-on practice will teach you more about AI video than hours of reading about AI video.

Once you have your first few clips, turn them into real content — a social post, a product teaser, or a short story — and keep iterating. The tools will keep improving, but the creators who benefit most are the ones who start now, while the free tier is this generous.

Explore More Free AI Tools

Want to keep building your AI toolkit? Try these free tools from AIToolSteps: AI Title Generator, Meta Description Generator, AI Rewriter, and Keyword Density Checker. Each one is free, beginner-friendly, and designed to help you create better content faster.

title: I sat through McKinsey's APR framework. Then I ran it on my worst coding habits.
description:
The first time someone said "Awareness, Pause, Reframe" out loud, I almost laughed.

It was in McKinsey's Forward Program, in the Adaptability & Resilience session, and APR was presented as the module's big takeaway: notice your reaction, interrupt it, pick a better story. Three words on a slide. It smelled like the kind of thing that works for people with corner offices and does not work for someone whose production deploy broke at 11pm.

I took the workshop seriously enough to finish it. I did not take APR seriously enough to use it. For a few weeks it lived next to the other good advice I ignore.

Then it got tested three times, by my own work, without me noticing I was running it.

The code review I wanted to answer in four minutes

I had an open-source PR up, tests green, and a maintainer came back with a review that essentially said: your title says you're preferring one option, but your code excludes everything the detector doesn't recognize. When the detector has a gap, users get nothing at all.

My first reaction was instant and physical: a hot, defensive "but it passes, and here's why I did it that way." I had the rebuttal half-written. That was Awareness, except I only recognized it afterward: jaw tight, already composing, treating his comment as an attack on the work rather than information about it.

The Pause was not zen. It was just not hitting reply, because it was late and I was annoyed, and nothing good comes from going through review feedback while angry.

The Reframe happened the next day, when I actually read his argument instead of my defense of it. He wasn't saying my code was bad. He was saying my gate could take away a dev command from a project whose framework we don't recognize yet, and silence is worse than a slightly wrong answer. Correct framing, terrible first reaction. I rewrote the fix as a ranking with a fallback, added the test he asked for, and wrote back agreeing with him.

The uncomfortable part: if APR had been on the slide and nothing else, my four-minute reply would have been public, wrong, and the kind of thing that makes an OSS contributor memorable for the wrong reason.

The 2am version: when the model is confidently, elaborately wrong

The second test is the one that actually changed how I build.

Every agent project I've shipped eventually hits the same wall. The model produces a diff that looks right. The failure message looks right. It explains what it did with total confidence. And it's wrong, not in some exotic way, but in a way a human reviewer would catch in ten seconds.

My old reaction to that was frustration aimed at the model: it's dumb, it hallucinated, prompt harder, add more context. That reaction is Awareness without Reframe. You're just re-describing the trigger with extra vocabulary.

The reframe that mattered: the model isn't the failure here, my harness is. If the only verification is a model saying it worked, then confident and correct are indistinguishable, and no amount of prompting fixes that. So I stopped treating the model's self-assessment as evidence and started gating on things that can't be talked into passing: tests, types, lint, and for code that runs in Docker, the container's exit code. My sandboxing agent terminates its debug loop on an exit code for exactly this reason.

That's Reframe doing real work. The facts didn't change. The reading changed from "the model failed" to "my system has no ground truth," and only one of those is fixable by me that night.

Where APR showed up before I had the words for it

The third one isn't dramatic. My most-downloaded package exists because of a bad reaction I didn't have.

My own agent kept choking on attachments: PDFs, notebooks, DOCX, images, archives. It would guess at content it couldn't read, and guess confidently, which is the worst combination. The reaction I felt was pure irritation at the tool. The reframe I apparently made without labeling it: this isn't an annoying bug, it's an unwritten package. Someone should turn those formats into clean text an agent can actually read. I built it, it shipped, and people download it.

Looking back, that's the same three moves as the PR review. Notice the heat, don't act at the peak of it, then find a reading of the situation that ends in something I control. APR just gave me a name for a sequence I was already running badly and inconsistently.

What I'd change about how they teach it

Since the workshop I went and read around the topic properly, because I've always been suspicious of frameworks that only exist on the slide where they were taught. Two things I'd push on:

They teach it as reflection. Engineers need it as a loop. Reflection is something you do at the end of the day about something that already happened. The failures I care about happen in the next four minutes: the reply, the commit, the rollback decision. APR only pays at the moment of trigger, which means it needs a forcing function, not a reminder. Mine is that any reactive message or commit gets written, then sits for ten minutes. Drafting is free. Sending isn't.

Reframe is the step people quietly skip. Pausing feels productive, so you pause. Reframing feels like work, so you spin instead. The test I use: if my "reframe" doesn't produce a different next action, I didn't reframe anything, I just calmed down. In the PR case the different action was rewriting the fix. In the harness case it was adding a deterministic gate. Calm without a new action is just a nicer version of the original reaction.

What I actually took away

APR is Awareness, Pause, Reframe: catch the reaction while it's still a reaction, insert a gap mechanical enough that you can't skip it, and pick an interpretation that ends in an action you control rather than a story you rehearse.

It's still three words on a slide. The difference is I've now watched it fail in the exact situations it was designed for, which is the only endorsement I trust. My defensiveness on that PR review didn't disappear. It just got a ten-minute delay and a better ending.

If you've done the McKinsey Forward Program, I'd genuinely like to know whether APR landed for you the same way, or whether it took your own version of a code review to make it stick.

Thanks for reading. If this resonated, you can find me on GitHub and on my site. I write about agents, open source, and the parts of engineering that don't show up in a diff.

title: passlib` Ownership Transferred; New Maintainer Seeks Input on Breaking Changes and API Redesigns
description:
Introduction: The Transition of Passlib Maintenance

The passlib Python package, a critical tool for password hashing and verification, has recently undergone a significant shift in stewardship. After the previous maintainer became unreachable, ownership was transferred to a new maintainer who has been actively addressing immediate technical challenges. These include fixing incompatibilities with Python 3.13 and bcrypt 5.0.0, as well as adding type annotations to improve code clarity and maintainability. However, the new maintainer has identified deeper structural issues within the codebase that necessitate a more comprehensive overhaul.

The core problem lies in the original design choices of passlib, which have made the codebase increasingly difficult to maintain and extend. For instance, the PasswordHash class serves a dual purpose, representing both algorithm configuration and the produced hash. This design decision complicates type inference and introduces ambiguity. Similarly, the PasswordHash.using method, which creates subclasses to substitute new parameters, adds unnecessary complexity and makes the API harder to reason about. The overuse of abstraction and multiple inheritance further exacerbates these issues, leading to a codebase that is brittle and resistant to change.

The new maintainer is now faced with a critical decision: how to balance necessary breaking changes with the need to minimize migration difficulties for existing users. Without careful consideration, aggressive API redesigns risk alienating the user base, potentially leading to fragmented adoption of alternative solutions. This fragmentation would not only reduce the long-term viability of passlib but also increase maintenance overhead as users diverge to incompatible forks or replacements.

To mitigate this risk, the maintainer is actively seeking community input on which parts of the API, if altered, would pose the greatest migration challenges. For example, the current CryptContext interface, which relies on string-based scheme names and nested keyword arguments, is cumbersome and lacks type safety. A proposed redesign, such as the one outlined in the libpass-next repository, introduces a more explicit and type-safe interface. However, such changes must be weighed against their impact on existing codebases. If a user’s application heavily relies on the current string-based configuration, migrating to the new interface could require non-trivial refactoring, potentially breaking downstream dependencies.

The stakes are high. Without community collaboration, the redesign process risks becoming a top-down imposition, failing to address the real-world needs of passlib’s users. Conversely, by engaging with the community, the maintainer can ensure that the redesigned API is both future-proof and backward-compatible where it matters most. This approach fosters trust and sustainability, encouraging continued adoption and contribution to the project.

In summary, the transition of passlib maintenance highlights the inherent tension between technical improvement and user continuity. The new maintainer’s call for input is not just a procedural step but a strategic move to align the project’s evolution with the needs of its users. The outcome of this process will determine whether passlib remains a cornerstone of Python password management or becomes a cautionary tale of poorly managed transitions.

Proposed Changes and API Redesigns

The new maintainer of passlib is navigating a delicate balance: modernizing a critical Python package while preserving its usability for existing users. The proposed changes target core structural issues that have made the codebase increasingly difficult to maintain and extend. Below is an analysis of the key redesigns, their rationale, and strategies to mitigate migration challenges.

1. Redesigning PasswordHash to Decouple Roles

The PasswordHash class currently serves a dual purpose: representing both algorithm configuration and the produced hash. This design introduces ambiguity and complicates type inference. For example, when a hash is generated, the object’s role shifts from configuration to output, leading to runtime type confusion. This ambiguity forces type checkers to treat the object as a union type, which propagates uncertainty throughout the codebase.

Proposed Solution: Split PasswordHash into two distinct classes: one for algorithm configuration and another for the hash output. This decoupling aligns with the single responsibility principle, enabling precise type annotations and reducing runtime errors.

Migration Strategy: Provide a deprecation cycle for the unified PasswordHash class, offering a compatibility layer that maps legacy usage to the new classes. This approach minimizes immediate breakage while encouraging adoption of the cleaner API.

2. Replacing PasswordHash.using with Explicit Configuration

The PasswordHash.using method dynamically creates subclasses to inject new parameters, a pattern that obscures the class hierarchy and complicates type checking. For instance, when a new parameter is added, the subclass creation process bypasses static analysis, leading to runtime errors in type-aware code.

Proposed Solution: Replace PasswordHash.using with an explicit configuration mechanism, such as a builder pattern or named arguments. This eliminates the need for dynamic subclassing, making the API more predictable and type-safe.

Migration Strategy: Introduce a wrapper function that mimics the behavior of PasswordHash.using while internally using the new configuration mechanism. This allows existing code to function unchanged while developers transition to the new API.

3. Simplifying CryptContext for Type Safety

The current CryptContext interface relies on string-based configuration, which lacks type safety and forces developers to rely on documentation to avoid errors. For example, misspelling a scheme name or parameter results in runtime exceptions that are difficult to trace.

Proposed Solution: Redesign CryptContext to accept explicit hasher objects, as demonstrated in the libpass-next repository. This approach leverages Python’s type system to catch configuration errors at compile time, reducing the risk of runtime failures.

Migration Strategy: Provide a migration tool that automatically converts string-based configurations to the new object-based format. Additionally, document common pitfalls and provide examples to guide developers through the transition.

4. Addressing Overuse of Abstraction and Multiple Inheritance

The original codebase relies heavily on abstraction and multiple inheritance, leading to a brittle structure where changes in one part of the hierarchy cascade unpredictably. For instance, modifying a base class can inadvertently break derived classes due to the tight coupling of shared state and behavior.

Proposed Solution: Refactor the codebase to favor composition over inheritance, reducing the dependency graph and isolating components. This approach improves modularity and makes the codebase more resilient to changes.

Migration Strategy: Gradually replace inherited functionality with composable utilities, providing backward compatibility layers for deprecated patterns. This phased approach ensures that existing code remains functional while the underlying structure is modernized.

5. Risk Analysis and Decision Dominance

The primary risk of these changes is alienating users by introducing breaking changes without adequate support. However, the current design flaws pose a greater long-term risk: as Python and its ecosystem evolve, passlib’s maintainability will degrade, leading to unfixable bugs and reduced adoption.

Optimal Solution: Prioritize the redesign of CryptContext and PasswordHash, as these changes yield the highest impact on type safety and maintainability. Use compatibility layers and migration tools to minimize immediate disruption, ensuring that users can adopt the new API incrementally.

Rule for Choosing a Solution: If a redesign improves type safety and reduces runtime errors without requiring immediate user action, implement it with a deprecation cycle. If it introduces breaking changes, provide automated migration tools and clear documentation to ease the transition.

By focusing on these targeted improvements and engaging the community, the new maintainer can ensure that passlib remains a reliable and future-proof solution for password management in Python.

Community Feedback and Next Steps

The transition of passlib to a new maintainer marks a critical juncture for the project, balancing the need for technical modernization with the risk of disrupting existing workflows. The new maintainer has already addressed immediate incompatibilities with Python 3.13 and bcrypt 5.0.0, but deeper structural issues remain. These include the dual role of PasswordHash, the complexity introduced by PasswordHash.using, and the overuse of abstraction and multiple inheritance. To navigate this, community input is essential—not as a formality, but as a mechanism to prioritize user pain points and validate proposed redesigns.

How to Provide Feedback

If you rely on passlib in your codebase, your input is critical. The maintainer is specifically seeking answers to:

  • Breaking Changes: Which parts of the API, if altered, would create significant migration challenges for your projects? For example, would a redesign of CryptContext to accept explicit hasher objects (e.g., Argon2Hasher) instead of string-based configurations break your current setup?
  • Refactor Depth: How far should the refactor go? Would a gradual approach (e.g., deprecating PasswordHash.using with a compatibility layer) be more manageable than a complete overhaul?

Share your feedback directly via the GitHub repository or by opening an issue. Specific code examples or migration scenarios are particularly valuable.

Timeline and Implementation Process

The redesign process will follow a phased approach to minimize disruption:

  • Phase 1: Feedback Collection (Immediate - Next 4 Weeks)
    • Gather input on breaking changes and refactor priorities.
    • Identify high-risk areas (e.g., CryptContext and PasswordHash) through user feedback.
  • Phase 2: Proposal Finalization (Weeks 5-8)
    • Synthesize feedback into a concrete redesign plan.
    • Prioritize changes based on impact on type safety and migration difficulty.
  • Phase 3: Implementation with Safeguards (Ongoing)
    • Introduce breaking changes incrementally, with deprecation cycles for legacy APIs.
    • Provide migration tools (e.g., automated conversion scripts for CryptContext configurations) and detailed documentation.
    • Maintain a compatibility layer for critical legacy patterns during transitions.

Why Your Input Matters

Without community involvement, the redesign risks becoming a top-down imposition, leading to fragmented adoption or a fork of the project. For example, if the CryptContext redesign is implemented without understanding downstream dependencies, users may face non-trivial refactoring, causing them to abandon passlib for alternatives. Conversely, a well-informed redesign—one that balances type safety with migration feasibility—can future-proof the package and restore trust in its long-term maintainability.

Join as a Co-Maintainer

The maintainer is actively seeking co-maintainers to share the load. Even short-term contributions—such as reviewing pull requests, testing migration tools, or documenting changes—can significantly accelerate the project’s evolution. Visit the repository to get involved.

Rule of Thumb for Redesign Decisions

If a change improves type safety and maintainability but risks breaking downstream code, use a deprecation cycle and provide migration tools. For example, replacing PasswordHash.using with an explicit configuration pattern should be accompanied by a wrapper function to maintain legacy behavior during the transition.

Conclusion: The Future of Passlib

The proposed changes to passlib are not just cosmetic tweaks but structural overhauls critical for its long-term sustainability. The current codebase, burdened by design choices like the dual role of PasswordHash and the overuse of multiple inheritance, has reached a breaking point. These issues manifest as ambiguous type inference, runtime errors, and a brittle structure that resists extension. For example, the dual role of PasswordHash forces the type system to treat it as both a configuration object and a hash output, leading to type mismatches during compile-time checks. Similarly, the string-based configuration in CryptContext relies on runtime string parsing, which is error-prone and lacks type safety.

The optimal solution lies in redesigning PasswordHash and CryptContext to decouple responsibilities and enforce type safety. Splitting PasswordHash into separate configuration and output classes aligns with the single responsibility principle, eliminating ambiguity. Replacing string-based configurations in CryptContext with explicit hasher objects leverages Python’s type system to catch errors at compile time, not runtime. These changes, while breaking, are mechanistically superior because they address the root causes of maintainability issues, not just symptoms.

However, the risk of alienating users through breaking changes is real. The mechanism of this risk is straightforward: downstream dependencies relying on the current API will fail if not updated, leading to fragmented adoption of alternatives. To mitigate this, a compatibility layer and migration tools are essential. For instance, a wrapper function for PasswordHash.using can maintain legacy behavior while users transition to the new API. Similarly, a migration tool for CryptContext can automatically convert string-based configurations to object-based ones, reducing manual effort.

The community’s role in this process is indispensable. By identifying high-impact migration challenges, users ensure that the redesign prioritizes their needs. For example, feedback on which API changes would be most disruptive allows the maintainer to implement deprecation cycles for critical features, providing a grace period for adoption. Without this collaboration, the redesign risks becoming a top-down imposition, eroding trust and accelerating the project’s decline.

In summary, the future of passlib hinges on balancing technical improvements with user needs. The proposed changes, while disruptive, are mechanistically justified and offer a clear path to sustainability. The community’s input is not just welcomed but essential to ensure that passlib remains a cornerstone of Python password management, avoiding the fate of poorly managed transitions.

Key Takeaways:

  • Structural Overhaul Needed: Current design choices lead to type ambiguity, runtime errors, and brittle code.
  • Optimal Solution: Redesign PasswordHash and CryptContext to enforce type safety and modularity.
  • Risk Mitigation: Compatibility layers and migration tools are critical to avoid alienating users.
  • Community Role: User feedback ensures the redesign aligns with real-world needs, fostering trust and adoption.

Decision Rule:

If a design choice introduces type ambiguity or runtime errors, prioritize refactoring to enforce type safety and modularity. Use compatibility layers and migration tools for breaking changes to minimize user disruption.
