Bun 1.2 vs Node.js 22 vs Deno 2: HTTP Throughput, Native TypeScript & Package Resolution Speed

Executive Summary & Decision Matrix

All benchmarks below were run on identical hardware: AWS c7i.2xlarge (8 vCPU Sapphire Rapids, 16 GiB DDR5-4800), Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, kernel 6.8, ulimit -n 1048576, median of 7 runs with 2 warmup runs discarded. Load generator: wrk -t8 -c512 pinned to a second machine on the same 25 Gbps VPC to eliminate client-side saturation.

Metric Bun 1.2 Node.js 22 (LTS) Deno 2.x
HTTP req/sec (plaintext, Bun.serve / node:http / Deno.serve, 512 conn) 112,400 48,900 71,300
p99 latency @ 20k QPS sustained 2.1 ms 6.8 ms 3.9 ms
p99 latency @ 40k QPS (Bun saturated, Node saturated) 5.5 ms 21.4 ms 9.2 ms
RSS at idle 38 MB 46 MB 62 MB
RAM per 10k keep-alive connections 112 MB 210 MB 168 MB
Cold-start to first request 11 ms 42 ms 27 ms
npm install of express+ws+axios tree (cold cache) 0.9 s 4.1 s 2.3 s (natively), 4.0 s (node-compat)
Native TypeScript execution Yes (strip-types, transpile-on-load) Via --experimental-strip-types (22.6+) Yes (full transpile + TSX transform)
Geekbench 6 (single/multi, JS workload harness) 2,410 / 7,850 2,190 / 6,930 2,320 / 7,410
JSON.parse throughput (64 KB payloads) 1.9 GB/s 1.1 GB/s 1.2 GB/s
Max WebSocket fan-out (per-core, 1M msg/s target) Hits 1.02M msg/s 640k msg/s 780k msg/s
Node-API / npm compatibility ~95% (no node:vm full parity, no N-API threads) 100% ~92% via node: shim layer

Decision matrix in one sentence: Run Bun 1.2 for edge/API-gateway and LLM-proxy workloads that are I/O- and JSON-bound; stay on Node.js 22 when your dependency graph touches native N-API modules (Prisma, sharp, better-sqlite3 with worker threads) or when ecosystem maturity outweighs a 2.3x throughput gap; choose Deno 2 when permission sandboxing, single-binary deploys, or first-party TypeScript matter more than raw req/sec.

Architectural Deep-Dive

Execution pipelines 

flowchart TB
    subgraph Bun["Bun 1.2 — Zig monolith"]
        A1[JS/TS source] --> A2[JavaScriptCore + Bun's Zig transpiler]
        A2 --> A3[Integrated HTTP: SIMD JSON parser,<br/>epoll/kqueue directly in Zig event loop]
        A3 --> A4[Single mmap'd package cache<br/>~/.bun/install/cache]
        A4 --> A5[libuv NOT used —<br/>custom Zig I/O layer]
    end
    subgraph Node["Node.js 22 — V8 + libuv"]
        B1[JS source] --> B2[V8 JIT Ignition/Turbofan/Maglev]
        B2 --> B3[libuv threadpool 4 threads default]
        B3 --> B4[HTTP parser: llhttp]
        B3 --> B5[fs.poll threadpool → SSD]
    end
    subgraph Deno["Deno 2 — V8 + Rust (tokio)"]
        C1[TS/JS source] --> C2[V8 + swc transpile cache]
        C2 --> C3[tokio multi-threaded runtime,<br/>hyper-based HTTP]
        C3 --> C4[Permission sandbox:<br/>--allow-net --allow-read]
        C4 --> C5[Deno cache → node_modules<br/>or global DENO_DIR]
    end

The low-level trade-offs that decide your p99

Bun's event loop is not libuv. Bun replaces libuv with a Zig-native I/O layer that issues epoll_wait batches and avoids the 4-thread UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE bottleneck on filesystem work. This is why fs.readFile on a RAM disk measures 3.1 GB/s on Bun vs 1.4 GB/s on Node with default threadpool sizing — Node caps concurrent file syscalls at 4 threads unless you tune UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16, which most teams never do. The trade-off: Bun's loop has fewer eyes on it. A stalled syscall that libuv would isolate in the threadpool can block Bun's loop directly, which is exactly what happens when Bun.file() hits an NFS mount with 8 ms RTT — we measured head-of-line blocking pushing p99 from 2.1 ms to 240 ms with 50 concurrent readers on network storage.

Node's V8 has the deepest JIT. Turbofan's escape analysis and Maglev tiering mean hot JSON-transform code paths converge 15–20% faster than JavaScriptCore's DFG/FTL over a 10-minute soak. If your workload is CPU-bound transform logic (embedding rerankers, tokenizer glue) rather than proxying, V8's steady-state wins erode Bun's I/O advantage. JSC's trade is the opposite: better memory density and 3.8x faster cold-start because it doesn't run Ignition bytecode warmup first.

Deno pays a sandbox tax on every syscall. Each Deno.serve accept, each op, crosses a Rust-side permission check (~180–400 ns). At 71k req/s that's invisible per-request but it caps the ceiling: the hyper/tokio stack underneath is excellent, yet the op-check boundary and V8 shard-per-permission model keep it from matching Bun's integrated design. What you get in exchange is an OS-grade(ish) sandbox that turns an SSRF into a logged denial instead of a metadata-service credential leak — for inference infrastructure routing requests to internal model endpoints, this is a compliance feature, not a nicety.

Network topology sensitivity. All three runtimes saturate a 25 Gbps NIC differently: Bun's Bun.serve with SO_REUSEPORT across 8 workers hit 24.1 Gbps aggregate; Node's cluster module hit 19.8 Gbps but with 3.1% request reordering at the LB (hash-based upstream mismatch); Deno hit 21.4 Gbps. Behind an NLB with connection-multiplexed gRPC, Bun's per-connection buffer reuse cuts syscalls/sec to the kernel by 40% vs Node — visible in perf stat as lower context-switch counts (18k/s vs 31k/s at equal load).

Package resolution speed: why Bun's installer is structurally faster

Bun's installer does not implement a JS module-graph resolver in JavaScript. It maintains a SQLite-backed lockfile (bun.lockb), performs content-addressed hard-linking from a global cache (no file copies — stat calls drop from ~48k for an express tree to ~1.2k), and parallelizes extraction across all cores with one syscall per package. Cold-cache npm ci on a 1,800-package Next.js tree: 38.4 s (Node/npm 10), 11.2 s (pnpm 9), 4.6 s (Bun). In CI billed at $0.008/min on hosted runners, that's ~$0.0045 saved per pipeline run — trivial per run, ~$1,100/yr at 600 CI runs/day across a 40-repo org.

Deno 2's node_modules compatibility mode writes a real node_modules tree using its own resolver; it's slower than Bun but respects package.json semantics with a lockfile (deno.lock) that hashes integrity per package — catching the npm registry-tarball substitution class of supply-chain issues that npm's --ignore-scripts alone does not.

Real-World Benchmarks & Hard Data

Harness 1: HTTP plaintext + LLM-proxy simulation 

// bench/server.bun.ts — complete, runnable
const UPSTREAM = "http://127.0.0.1:8090";

Bun.serve({
  port: 8080,
  idleTimeout: 30,           // seconds; default 10 kills slow LLM streams
  maxRequestBodySize: 1024 * 1024 * 32,  // 32 MiB for batched prompts
  async fetch(req) {
    try {
      const body = await req.text();
      const upstream = await fetch(UPSTREAM, {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
        body,
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(120_000),  // LLM generation can exceed 60s
      });
      if (!upstream.ok) {
        return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: "upstream", status: upstream.status }), {
          status: 502, headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
        });
      }
      // Stream tokens through without buffering — critical for TTFT
      return new Response(upstream.body, {
        headers: { "content-type": "text/event-stream", "x-runtime": "bun" },
      });
    } catch (err) {
      const timedOut = err instanceof Error && err.name === "TimeoutError";
      return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: timedOut ? "timeout" : "proxy_failure" }), {
        status: timedOut ? 504 : 500,
      });
    }
  },
});

Streaming SSE through this proxy at 8,000 concurrent streams: Bun added 0.9 ms median inter-token latency, Node 1.8 ms, Deno 1.3 ms. Buffering instead of piping upstream.body (the mistake every naive proxy makes) ballooned Bun's RSS from 112 MB to 1.9 GB within 90 seconds at 8k streams — a leak-shaped outcome that's actually buffer amortization, not a leak. Pipe streams; never await upstream.text().

Harness 2: cold-start and TS execution

Scenario Bun 1.2 Node 22 Deno 2
"hello world" HTTP server → first 200 OK 11 ms 42 ms 27 ms
Same, importing a 400-module TS graph 74 ms 310 ms (with tsx) / 190 ms (strip-types) 130 ms
Lambda cold-start (512 MB, measured in AWS us-east-1, p50 of 500 invocations) 68 ms 187 ms 112 ms

Harness 3: CPU-bound JSON transform (tokenizer prep, 1 GB of JSONL)

Runtime wall time notes
Bun + native JSON.parse 6.4 s SIMD-accelerated parser; 1.9 GB/s
Node 11.8 s V8 parser, no SIMD fast path for large bodies
Node + JSON.parse offloaded to worker_pool 7.1 s requires hand-rolled worker pool + backpressure
Deno 10.9 s same V8 parser as Node

Cost-of-Ownership (3 tiers)

Assumptions: inference-proxy fleet, 3 AZs, on-demand pricing, Oct 2026 list prices.

Tier Stack Bun cost/yr Node cost/yr Delta driver
Startup — $100/mo ($1,200/yr) 2× c7i.large + ALB + CloudWatch $1,180 (Bun) $1,520 (Node needs 3 nodes for same p99) Bun's 2.3x throughput → one fewer node; break-even on team-training cost is ~3 engineer-days
Scale-up — $2,500/mo ($30,000/yr) 12× c7i.2xlarge + NLB + APM $30,400 $38,900 Node requires 15 nodes for same 20k QPS p99<8ms SLO; plus ~$900/mo extra APM spans from GC pauses
Enterprise — $25,000/mo ($300,000/yr) 120 nodes, multi-region, 24/7 on-call $301,000 (but risk-adjusted: +$60k/yr regression-testing spend) $312,000 At this size, Node's ecosystem stability offsets compute delta; Bun's edge-case tax (below) dominates TCO

Interpretation: runtime choice moves compute cost ±25% at small scale, but at enterprise scale the deciding variable shifts from req/sec to regression surface and staffing. A 2.3x throughput win is worth $12k/yr; one production incident from an unvetted Bun edge case costs that in on-call time alone.

Failure Modes & Hidden Traps

Trap 1 — Bun's node:vm and worker-thread parity gaps break silently. better-sqlite3, sharp, and anything using worker_threads + N-API raw buffers can pass unit tests and corrupt data under load: Bun's MessagePort transfer of ArrayBuffer historically zero-copied where Node copied, producing use-after-free style crashes (SIGSEGV in release builds, caught only by running with BUN_DEBUG_QUIET_LOGS=0 and core dumps enabled). Debug procedure: ulimit -c unlimited, run bun --smol off, attach lldb to the core; the stack will bottom out in JSC::ArrayBufferContents. Mitigation: pin any native-heavy code path to Node 22, or force --no-worker-threads and validate against your integration suite on every Bun minor bump — Bun's semver discipline on internals is weaker than Node's.

Trap 2 — Node's default idleTimeout and Nagle on SSE kill streaming UX. Node 22's server.keepAliveTimeout default (5 s) plus intermediate ALB idle timeout (60 s) creates the classic "connection reset at exactly 60 s" on LLM streams exceeding the shortest timeout in the chain. The failure shows as ECONNRESET in proxy logs and truncated completions client-side, with zero errors in the runtime itself. Fix requires a four-layer alignment: runtime keep-alive > LB idle timeout > client read timeout, plus socket.setNoDelay(true) — Bun enables TCP_NODELAY by default, Node does not on node:http responses, adding a silent 40 ms per token flush when combined with res.write() of small SSE chunks.

Trap 3 — Deno's permission model inverts under npm: specifiers. deno run --allow-net does not sandbox a pulled npm package that calls process.binding via the compat layer; the shim grants ambient authority to node-compat code to avoid breaking packages that probe the environment. Teams that audited their own code for --allow-read violations routinely miss that a transitive npm dependency (dotenv, for instance) reads .env without any explicit grant warning. Operational consequence: your security review must enumerate npm: imports as trusted-compute, not sandboxed dependencies. The deno audit and lockfile integrity checks help, but the sandbox boundary for node-compat code is advisory, not enforced.

Trap 4 — the unexpected-bill pattern. Bun's low idle RSS (38 MB) tempts teams to overpack containers on small instances. At >8k open WebSockets per 1 GiB of provisioned RAM, Bun.serve per-connection buffer growth (default 64 KB receive buffer, retained) triggers the kernel OOM killer, which AWS charges for via Auto Scaling replacement cycles — a fleet churning 40 replacements/hour at 4-minute minimum billing is a 27% compute bill inflation that looks like a "capacity planning bug" but is a runtime memory-profile mismatch.

Final Buying Decision

There is no license to buy — the real purchase decision is where you host and which managed platform's runtime matrix supports your choice, and that's where the money moves.

  • Prototype-to-Series-A, I/O-bound inference proxy or API gateway: Bun 1.2. On platforms like Railway, Fly.io, or a Koyeb instance, Bun's 2.3x throughput and 4x faster cold-start let you run one tier smaller — real savings of $15–45/mo at the small end, growing linearly. Start with a managed instance that supports custom runtimes and deploy bun.lockb-driven builds for deterministic CI.
  • Series-B-to-enterprise, native-heavy stacks (Prisma, sharp, OpenTelemetry collectors in-process): Node.js 22 LTS. Its --experimental-strip-types covers 80% of the ergonomic win, and V8's maturity under 20k+ QPS sustained load with --max-old-space-size tuned is the lowest-regret choice. Host on platforms with first-class Node LTS images and pay for the compute delta — managed Node 22 on your cloud of choice.
  • Security-sensitive inference routing (multi-tenant, untrusted prompt content, compliance-mandated sandboxing): Deno 2. The permission model on first-party code plus single-binary deno compile deploys shrink your attack surface and image size to ~90 MB vs ~400 MB for a Node Alpine image. Deploy Deno with one-command deploys if you want zero-infra edge placement.

Ratings: Bun 1.2 — 4.8/5 (performance-per-dollar king; cap the blast radius with integration tests on every minor upgrade). Node.js 22 — 4.5/5 (slower and heavier, but zero-surprise semantics and the deepest observability ecosystem: OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation is battle-tested here and merely functional on the other two).

⚡ Snowden SAY | Deep Systems & AI Infrastructure Lab

Production deep-dives on LLM agent memory compaction, Linux kernel eBPF tracing, ultra-low latency C++23 HFT, and 1M+ RPS storage engines:

👉 Join Telegram Channel (@-1004462672501)

Get complete technical monographs and architecture blueprints via Telegram Bot (@Snowden_book_bot).

title: StackSpirit: a local ghost that tells you what to install
description:
I kept watching the same failure. Someone wants to build a Next.js site, or a Python script that clicks through a browser, or an agent with Google's ADK, and they never get to the interesting part. The README says npm install and assumes Node 20. Their machine has Node 16, or Python without venv, or no GOOGLE_API_KEY. The error is real, and it is also useless if you are new.

I wrote StackSpirit for that moment. It is a small open-source CLI. You tell it what you want to build:

stackspirit check "Next.js website"
stackspirit check "AI agent with Google ADK"
stackspirit check "Python automation with Playwright"
stackspirit check "Expo mobile app"

Or you point it at a repo that will not start:

stackspirit scan .

It prints a table. Installed, missing, or wrong version. Then the exact command for the OS it detected — macOS, Linux, or Windows. If you pass --fix, it asks y/N before each command. The default is no. If the command needs sudo, the question says so. It will not invent an API key, and it will not run anything while you are reading.

The ghost bit is light on purpose. A missing dependency is "haunting your build." When the machine is fine, it says the machine is quiet. I did not want a Halloween skin on a tool that people will run when they are already stuck.

What the demo actually shows

On the Linux machine I used while building this, Node 22, Python 3.12, and Go 1.22 were already there. Ollama was not.

stackspirit check "Next.js website" came back quiet and told me to run npx create-next-app@latest. It did not run that for me. create-next-app asks questions, and a tool that starts an interactive installer on its own is not helping.

stackspirit check "AI agent with Google ADK" was the interesting one. Python was new enough (ADK wants 3.11). google-adk was not installed. GOOGLE_API_KEY was not set. The fix was a virtualenv and pip install google-adk, plus a line I have to fill in myself:

export GOOGLE_API_KEY="your-key-here"

stackspirit scan examples/nextjs-site is a folder with a package.json, an .nvmrc of 20, and an empty .env.example. Node 22 was newer than the pin, which the report noted and did not treat as a failure. The real gaps were node_modules and NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL. That is the report I wanted when I clone something and it will not boot.

examples/go-api was quiet. examples/docker-web was not, and the only fix was curl | sudo sh from Docker's own installer, marked as sudo, and not executed.

How the open-source model is actually used

The part I trust is a built-in list: Node and Next.js, React with Vite, Python, Django, FastAPI, Playwright, Docker, Expo, Flutter, Go, Rust, Google ADK, LangChain, the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, and n8n. Versions, packages, env var names, and install commands live in that list. It works with --no-ai, and it works when no model is installed. The samples above were produced that way.

The model has two jobs.

When the sentence is not in the list — "a Hugo site", "a Godot game" — StackSpirit asks a local model to map it. If the model names a stack we already know, we use our commands, not whatever shell line it invented. If it names a new tool, the command has to be boring: one invocation, no pipes, no rm. Anything else is dropped.

When a model is up, it also writes the short "why this matters" paragraph under the table. The table itself stays deterministic. I do not want a model deciding that the install command for Node is something cute.

The default is Ollama and qwen2.5-coder, on 127.0.0.1:11434. You can point the same config at LM Studio, a llama.cpp server, or any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including a free model on OpenRouter if that is what you have. The prompt is the stack name, the OS, and rows like "Playwright: missing". File contents and .env values are not in it. I left a sendCode setting in the config so the policy is visible, and the CLI ignores it. There is no mode that uploads the repository.

Why I don't want a closed model here

A setup tool learns a lot about a computer. Which languages you have. Which versions. Which keys you have not set yet. That is a map of a beginner's machine, and often of a student's laptop. Sending that map to a hosted API so it can return four sentences is a bad trade.

A local open model is free. It works on a train. I can swap qwen2.5-coder for the next open model without rewriting the CLI. And because the knowledge base is there, the tool still works on a machine that is too new to have a model pulled down — which is, awkwardly, the machine this tool is for.

A closed API would also fail in the exact case I care about: the person is offline, or they have not made an account, or the key they were going to use is the thing they are trying to set up. Open and local is not a slogan here. It is the only setup that does not ask them to be finished before they can start.

Repo: https://github.com/AlizayAyesha/StackSpirit

Built by Zar Labs (zarlabs.online).

title: Shopify Adds Promoted Placements to Its AI Shopping Agent Ecosystem
description:
Shopify has introduced a Developer Preview of Promoted Placements for AI shopping experiences built around its Global Catalog. The program gives eligible developers an optional way to earn commission on attributed purchases, adding a paid distribution layer to product discovery through AI agents.

The release is notable because AI-assisted shopping is increasingly becoming a route between a buyer’s question and a merchant’s product. Shopify’s preview does not establish a universal ranking model for AI commerce. It does, however, make the commercial incentives around product routing more explicit, while creating new disclosure and measurement requirements for participating developers.

What Shopify has launched

According to Shopify’s Promoted Placements developer documentation, Promoted Placements extend Global Catalog search with optional paid placements. The program is invite-only during the Developer Preview, and developers must join a waitlist and be onboarded through the Shopify Dev Dashboard.

The current scope is limited. Shopify describes the program as US-only, rather than a general release for every market, merchant, or AI shopping interface.

For an attributed purchase, the base commission is 0.3%. A developer may earn a higher total commission when the merchant is running Shop Campaigns and external platforms are enabled. Shopify describes that total as the base rate plus the merchant-funded commission.

Shopify’s October 2026 changelog also records that the Promoted Placements beta includes Shop Campaigns, corroborating the preview’s connection to that existing merchant campaign mechanism.

How commissions and attribution work

The commercial model has several conditions that matter for developers and merchants assessing the opportunity.

Program element Current documented terms
Program status Invite-only Developer Preview
Base commission 0.3% on attributed purchases
Attribution period 7 days
Higher commission opportunity Base rate plus merchant-funded commission from eligible Shop Campaigns
Shop Campaigns conditions Active US campaign, USD, and purchase completed in Shop or on shop.com
Payout route Shopify Partner payouts

The Shop Campaigns uplift is not a blanket increase on every catalog product or purchase. Shopify says the campaign commission applies only to products in an active campaign in the US, priced in USD, when the buyer completes the purchase in the Shop app or on shop.com. That distinction is important for forecasting: a displayed rate may depend on product, campaign eligibility, checkout destination, and attribution.

Why this matters for AI product visibility

For ecommerce teams, the preview reinforces a distinction that is likely to become more important in AI-assisted commerce: being eligible to appear is not the same as obtaining promoted exposure.

Generative Engine Optimization can still focus on the foundations that help systems understand and retrieve a product, such as accurate product data, clear attributes, consistent availability information, and accessible product pages. Promoted Placements introduce a separate commercial mechanism on top of Global Catalog search. A paid placement should not be treated as evidence that a product has become organically more relevant to an AI system.

For developers of shopping agents, the program offers a defined monetization path tied to purchases rather than an unspecified advertising arrangement. That can influence which integrations, product feeds, and shopping journeys receive engineering attention. Yet the available documentation does not quantify how paid placements are selected, how frequently they appear, or how they affect organic product ordering. Those outcomes remain uncertain in an early preview.

Publishers, affiliates, and comparison services should also pay attention to the broader pattern. As shopping recommendations become more agent-mediated, revenue relationships can affect the presentation of product choices. That does not eliminate the role of editorial selection or product relevance, but it raises the importance of clear separation between sponsored recommendations and other results.

Disclosure is part of the implementation

Shopify requires attribution and earnings disclosures to users to meet FTC and other applicable regional requirements. This is more than a compliance footnote. A user who sees a product suggestion in an agent interface needs sufficient information to understand when a recommendation may result in compensation.

Teams building AI shopping experiences should make disclosure a product and content design requirement from the outset. The exact placement and wording may vary by jurisdiction and implementation, but an obscure disclosure can undermine both regulatory compliance and user trust. Developers should also account for relevant EU and UK rules where they operate, rather than assuming the preview’s US availability removes all wider obligations.

What ecommerce and SEO teams can do now

The preview is too early to justify sweeping claims about AI ranking or traffic shifts. It is still useful as a planning signal.

  • Keep product information complete and consistent across the merchant’s catalog and product pages.
  • Separate organic AI discovery work from campaign and paid-placement decisions in reporting.
  • Ask agent, affiliate, and publisher partners how they label compensated product recommendations.
  • Review Shop Campaign eligibility and checkout conditions before treating a possible commission uplift as expected performance.
  • Track future Shopify documentation for changes to access, markets, selection mechanics, and reporting.

The key practical lesson is that AI commerce visibility may combine retrieval, recommendation, paid placement, and transaction attribution in the same customer journey. Measurement needs to preserve those distinctions instead of grouping every AI-originated product appearance into one visibility metric.

If your product pages need to be evaluated for the information AI systems can retrieve and present, assessing website GEO readiness and identifying optimization opportunities. It provides a practical starting point for assessing website GEO readiness and identifying optimization opportunities, so your team can improve the clarity and accessibility of the product information that supports AI-assisted discovery before deciding where paid distribution fits.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Shopify Promoted Placements?

Promoted Placements are optional paid placements that extend Shopify Global Catalog search for participating AI shopping experiences. They are currently an invite-only Developer Preview.

What commission does Shopify offer for Promoted Placements?

Shopify documents a base commission of 0.3% on attributed purchases. The total can be higher when eligible merchant-funded Shop Campaigns commissions apply.

Are Shopify Promoted Placements available globally?

No. Shopify’s current documentation describes the program as US-only and access is gated through a waitlist and onboarding process.

Do Promoted Placements improve a product’s organic AI ranking?

Shopify’s available documentation describes an optional paid placement program, but it does not establish that participation improves organic product ranking or routing in AI systems.

Conclusion

Shopify’s preview gives AI shopping-agent developers a concrete, commission-based way to monetize product discovery. Its early, US-only status leaves many questions about selection, scale, and performance unanswered, but the model is a clear sign that paid placement and transparent attribution are becoming part of the AI commerce landscape.

title: How to Integrate AI Coding Tools in 2026: Complete Guide
description:
Originally published at nlocoding.com

AI Coding Tool Integration Changes Everything: Microsoft's 24% Productivity Surge

24%More pull requests merged by early adopters of command-line AI coding agents (Microsoft, 2026)

Context: The AI Coding Tool Landscape in 2026 Is Unrecognizable

The way developers work has evolved at breakneck speed—2026 brings over 30 distinct AI coding tools into play, from IDE-integrated agents to cloud orchestration platforms (amux.io). The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is now the backbone for seamless integration, with over 10,000 active MCP servers and 97 million SDK downloads monthly (agenticdevelopercookbook.com).

AI Coding Tools Are Diverse and Purpose-Built

There are now more than 30 AI coding tools, each fitting into categories like IDE-integrated agents, terminal agents, cloud agents, orchestration platforms, and SDKs (amux.io). Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Windsurf lead the pack, but their approaches differ. Cursor is an AI-native IDE at $20/month, GitHub Copilot Pro embeds in editors at $10/month, Claude Code Max runs terminal-native for $100/month, and Windsurf offers a $15/month IDE alternative (sitepoint.com; toolspotter.co).

💡Pro Tip: Choose your tool to match your workflow—don’t assume all AI coding tools are interchangeable.

"AI coding tools have undergone a structural transformation over the past two years. What started as glorified autocomplete has become something different entirely." (sitepoint.com)

The Model Context Protocol Is Now the Integration Standard

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the de facto integration layer for connecting AI coding tools to external services in 2026. Over 10,000 active MCP servers and 97 million monthly SDK downloads show just how deeply MCP is embedded in dev operations (agenticdevelopercookbook.com). MCP has made what used to be a nightmare—getting tools to talk to each other—nearly seamless, regardless of whether your stack is cloud-native or terminal-heavy. If an AI coding tool doesn’t support MCP, you’ll feel the friction immediately.

💡Pro Tip: Prioritize MCP support when shortlisting AI coding tools for integration. You’ll avoid headaches later.

AI Coding Tools Drive Real Productivity Gains

The data shows that integrating AI coding agents isn’t just a nice-to-have—adopters in Microsoft’s 2026 rollout merged 24% more pull requests than they would have otherwise (arxiv.org). The tools automate repetitive tasks, generate boilerplate, and even create tests. But they don’t—and can’t—replace developers. You’ll notice the speed-up, but you’ll also notice that key decisions and code reviews still need a human.

97MMonthly SDK downloads using Model Context Protocol in early 2026

Security Risks Remain: AI Coding Agents Are Vulnerable

Most people get this wrong: AI coding agents are not inherently secure. Claude Code can be manipulated into installing malware from what appear to be clean GitHub repositories (tomshardware.com). Trust, but verify—especially when onboarding new agents or integrating with third-party codebases. This is not a hypothetical concern; it’s the direct result of “helpfulness” gone too far. The lesson is simple: never delegate security reviews or dependency checks entirely to AI.

⚠️Common Mistake: Blindly accepting AI-generated code or installations without manual review exposes your codebase to real-world threats.

Configuration and Integration Mechanisms Define Success

Configuration is not one-size-fits-all. An exploratory study found eight mechanisms for configuring agentic AI coding tools, but Context Files dominate as the preferred approach—often serving as the only mechanism in a repository (arxiv.org). Getting Context Files right is half the battle. Overlooking compatibility with your existing environment, or ignoring the nuances of repository configuration, leads to broken workflows and orphaned agents. Integration is as much about process as it is about technology.

AI-Generated Test Suites Rival Human Output

The data shows that AI-generated tests can achieve code coverage comparable to human-written tests, and frequently deliver positive coverage gains (arxiv.org). The myth that AI test generation is “just for scaffolding” is obsolete. If you’re still writing every test by hand in 2026, you’re probably behind—and probably tired. The caveat: AI is fast, but it still needs a developer’s eye to validate edge cases and business logic.

Comparing Leading AI Coding Tools by Price (2026)

Tool Type Pro/Max Price (USD/mo)
Cursor AI-native IDE $20
GitHub Copilot Pro Editor-integrated $10
Claude Code Max Terminal agent $100
Windsurf AI-native IDE $15

FAQ: How to Integrate AI Coding Tools in 2026

What’s the fastest way to integrate an AI coding tool with my IDE?The fastest integration route is to use tools that support the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which ensures compatibility with most current IDEs and external services.

Are AI coding tools safe to use with sensitive codebases?AI coding tools can be exploited if not properly configured. Manual review of AI-generated code and careful management of third-party dependencies are essential for security.

Do AI coding tools generate tests as well as humans?AI-generated tests offer code coverage similar to human-written suites and often provide positive coverage gains, though human validation remains necessary.

Is it true that AI coding tools can replace developers?AI coding tools automate repetitive and boilerplate tasks but still require developer oversight for complex or context-sensitive code decisions.

What Integration Teaches Us in 2026

This is what actually works. Not the fluffy advice you see everywhere. If you treat AI coding tools as magic wands or as full-time replacements, you’ll get burned—by botched security, broken workflows, or stale skills. But if you’re deliberate, if you make MCP your foundation and Context Files your habit, and if you keep one eye on what the tools automate and the other on what they miss, you get a workflow that’s faster, safer, and more flexible than anything we imagined even two years ago. The boundary between assistant and agent is gone, and so is the excuse for writing code the old way. The future is not about replacing developers; it’s about equipping them to do what only humans can do—faster and better, with an AI copilot that’s finally earned the name.

title: How I connected Apollo's sales data to cognee so an AI agent can answer questions about it
description:
Sales teams keep track of the people and companies they sell to in a CRM, which is a database built for customer records. Apollo.io is one of these tools. It also runs sequences, which are scheduled series of outreach messages sent to a contact.

An AI model can't answer questions about any of that on its own, because every conversation with it starts from zero. cognee is an open source project that gives AI agents a memory. You feed it your data, it builds a knowledge graph (a map of the things in your data and how they connect), and an agent can search that map later.

A connector is the piece of code that moves data from a tool like Apollo into cognee. I built the Apollo connector for Mergetober, a month of open source work on cognee integrations, and it was merged on October 19.

What the connector does

Once your Apollo data is in cognee, you can ask something like "Which contacts at Acme are in an active sequence?" and get an answer based on your own records.

Copying the data once would be simple. The harder part is that a CRM changes every day, so the connector has to handle two things on every later run:

  1. Only process records that changed. Without this, each run would send your whole CRM through the AI processing step again.
  2. Remove records you deleted in Apollo. If you delete a contact, your agent shouldn't keep answering questions about them.

Apollo makes both of these harder than you'd expect, and most of this post is about why.

Trying it

You'll need an Apollo API key, which means a paid plan or a trial, because free plans don't have API access to contact and account search. You'll also need an API key for an AI model provider, since cognee uses one to build the graph.

The connector is in the cognee-community repo, and you run it from there with uv:

git clone https://github.com/topoteretes/cognee-community.git
cd cognee-community/packages/connector/apollo
uv sync
export APOLLO_API_KEY="your-apollo-key"

Put your model key in a .env file as LLM_API_KEY, then run the example:

uv run python examples/example.py

The part of the example that does the work looks like this:

source = apollo_source(api_key=api_key, resource_name="apollo_crm_main")

await cognee.remember(
    source,
    dataset_name="apollo_crm",
    primary_key="id",
    write_disposition="merge",
    max_rows_per_table=0,
)

dataset_name is the place in cognee where this data lives. resource_name is a name you pick for this Apollo account, and it has to stay the same between runs. write_disposition="merge" tells cognee to update existing records. Leave it out and the second sync wipes the first one.

The connector reads your contacts, your company accounts and your sequences. It leaves emails, phone numbers and social profiles out on purpose, and it doesn't use any of the Apollo endpoints that cost credits.

Problem 1: Apollo doesn't tell you what changed

Many services stamp each record with the time it was last updated, so a connector can ask for everything newer than its last run. Apollo has an updated_at field, but it doesn't work for this. I enrolled a contact in a sequence on a live account and the contact's timestamp stayed the same, even though that's the kind of change you'd want your agent to know about. Company records don't come back with the timestamp at all.

So the connector reads every record on each run and turns it into text. It then computes a fingerprint of that text, a short code that changes whenever the text changes. It saves the fingerprints, and on the next run any record with the same fingerprint as before is skipped.

The downside is that reading everything uses up requests, and Apollo limits how many you can make per minute, per hour and per day. The connector stops before it hits a limit, saves its place, and picks up from there on the next run. A large account on a small plan will take several runs to get through.

Problem 2: Apollo doesn't tell you what was deleted

Apollo has no list of deleted records. All the connector can see is that a record it knew about isn't in the list anymore, and that doesn't prove it was deleted. The run might have stopped early, or the list might have been cut off, because Apollo search stops at 50,000 records.

So the connector only acts on a list it read all the way to the end. For each record missing from that list, it asks Apollo about that one record directly. It forgets the record only if Apollo says it's gone, or if the record no longer matches the filters you chose.

What the code review found

Before the connector was merged, goran-radonic, a cognee maintainer, reviewed it over two rounds and left 31 inline comments. Two of the problems they found show how easily the delete logic could go wrong.

The first was about two Apollo accounts sharing one dataset. Both used the same default name, so in the reviewer's test, syncing the second account removed the first account's contacts, and the next sync of the first account removed the second's. The name is now required, and a run refuses to continue from saved progress that belongs to a different Apollo team.

The second was in how I recognized a deleted record. Apollo reports one with an error message, and my check was too loose: a different error, such as "This contact does not exist in the stage you filtered", would also have counted as deleted. The check now accepts only the exact messages Apollo uses for deleted records, plus a plain 404.

Did it work?

I tested it on a real Apollo trial account with records I made for the purpose: two companies, four contacts and one sequence.

What I did What happened
First sync 7 documents stored
Synced again with no changes all 7 skipped
Edited one contact's job title 6 skipped, 1 updated
Deleted a contact and a company in Apollo both removed, nothing else touched

That test covered getting data in and taking it out, and it ran on the version I first submitted. After the review changes I checked the fixes with the automated tests, which run against a fake version of Apollo, and with a few specific calls to the real API. The merged version has 83 tests.

Limits

  • Accounts over 50,000 records need stage or list filters, otherwise deleted records aren't detected.
  • Each contact keeps its latest 50 activity events.
  • Apollo plans to remove the error fields the delete check reads on 16 February 2027, and it hasn't documented a replacement yet, so that check will need updating before then.
  • The dataset contains names, job titles and companies, so share it only with people who are allowed to see your CRM.

The code and setup details are in the Apollo connector folder.

title: Binance hack, Claude Code extension backdoor, Northflank and Mistral Large 4: what each source says
description:
Four developer stories from Friday, October 30, 2026, each read from its own primary source. The biggest is the theft from Binance, where three sources give three different totals. The video has the walkthrough; this article keeps the quotes, numbers and links in one place.

TL;DR

  • Binance wallets on ten blockchains sent funds to one attacker on October 29. TRM Labs counts about $6.36 billion, Elliptic $6.43 billion and Binance estimated around $6.3 billion. Both tracing firms call it the largest crypto theft on record. No government has confirmed who did it.
  • Cursor says a maliciously modified build of Anthropic's Claude Code extension, version 2.1.313, was available in its extension marketplace for about eleven hours on October 29, with at most 5,000 users affected. Cursor's notice does not say how the build got in.
  • Northflank's status page tells all users to assume their environment variables were decrypted and to disable or rotate all keys. It says multiple users confirm their AI keys have been used. No post-mortem yet.
  • Mistral released the weights of Mistral Large 4. Its license is a modified MIT; offering the model to third parties as a hosted service needs a separate commercial license.

Binance: three totals for one theft

TRM Labs published its analysis on October 29. It says an attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes starting at 20:05 UTC, and that the preparation began at least 36 hours earlier. Elliptic's page, updated on October 30, counts $6.43 billion across 11 blockchains and notes that Binance has estimated the impact at around $6.3 billion. Elliptic values each transfer at the time of theft; TRM also gives a figure at current prices, about $6.23 billion. The totals differ because each firm prices and attributes the assets its own way; all of them agree the theft happened. Both call it the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the roughly $1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025.

The mechanism on Ethereum, as Elliptic describes it, uses EIP-7702, a feature of the 2025 Pectra upgrade that lets an ordinary wallet delegate its behavior to a smart contract. The attacker submitted one transaction carrying 50 authorizations, each validly signed with the key of a Binance hot wallet and each covering a different nonce, so that one would match the wallet's transaction count when it landed. That handed control of the wallet to the attacker's sweeper contract, which emptied it about three and a half minutes later. TRM adds that the operator rehearsed the final version of its code on another wallet about four hours before installing it on a Binance hot wallet.

On the other chains, funds left Binance wallets in ordinary signed transfers. TRM reads the pattern as a compromise of Binance's hot wallet signing infrastructure. Elliptic says the attacker appears to have been able to get Binance's own systems to sign transactions, without stealing its private keys.

Binance's account has changed. Its first statement said the incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. A later update says the investigation has uncovered additional points of breach, and Binance has not said what they are. Elliptic compares this with the Bybit theft, where a developer's machine at the wallet provider Safe{Wallet} was the way in.

What Binance and the tracing firms say about the aftermath: Binance says user funds are safe, deposits are unaffected, it will cover all losses, and withdrawals should resume within a day or two. Elliptic has verified $2.84 billion frozen, 44 percent of the theft, almost all of it USDT and USDC; TRM counts about $2.7 billion. The attacker is swapping the rest into assets that cannot be frozen. TRM attributes the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor group with high confidence, Elliptic says North Korea-linked actors are likely responsible, and Elliptic notes that no government has yet confirmed attribution.

For developers the practical lesson is in the machines around the keys. If you run a signing service, list which laptops, containers and services can ask it for a transaction, and what approves them.

Claude Code 2.1.313 in Cursor's marketplace

Cursor's security notice, dated October 29, says that between about 2:27 am and 1:35 pm Pacific a maliciously modified version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension was available in the Cursor extension marketplace. The package is Anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313. Cursor says it was not developed by Anthropic and that at most 5,000 users were affected.

According to Cursor, the extension collects the hostname, username, operating system, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email and public IP address. It then tries to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to authorized_keys, enable the local SSH service and open a reverse SSH tunnel, with persistence through a LaunchAgent on macOS or a scheduled task on Windows, and a retry roughly every 60 seconds. It reports back with an HTTP POST. Cursor says the attacker's server is offline; it worked with the hosting provider to take it down.

Security firm Phorion's write-up adds that the injected code is prepended to the extension's extension.js, so it runs when Node loads the file, before the extension's normal activate function, with no click. Phorion also found a bug on macOS: the script checks whether Remote Login is off with a command that, without admin rights, prints an error and still exits successfully. The script only tries to turn SSH on when the output matches "Off", so it skips that step. Cursor's notice states the consequence: on most macOS and Windows hosts turning on SSH requires admin rights and fails, so the attacker could not have logged in through the tunnel. The extension still adds the key, installs persistence and sends host details. Follow the remediation steps regardless.

Cursor's check for macOS is a one-line grep of ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for the comment svc-telemetry. Cursor also warns that uninstalling the extension may not be sufficient because the payload drops standalone persistence scripts, and it provides removal scripts for macOS and Windows. It recommends rotating credentials reachable from affected hosts, from a trusted system. Cursor removed the version, shut down and rebuilt its marketplace, rotated its keys and found no other tampered extensions. It has no evidence that other versions or the official distribution are affected, and its notice does not say how the modified build reached the marketplace.

Northflank's incident timeline

Northflank's status page for the security incident gives a timeline in UTC on October 30: a Wiz threat alert at 11:43, engineers reviewing it at 11:44, an initial network policy patch at 12:02, more patching at 12:50 and 13:05, and a request for Wiz incident response support at 13:00. At 13:40 the page told customers to rotate environment variables immediately. At 13:58 it said to assume all environment variables have been decrypted and to disable or rotate all keys. It later added that multiple users are confirming their AI keys have been used.

At 15:12 the page said secret rotation on Postgres and MongoDB had been enabled for all users, recommended disabling public expose on add-ons if it was enabled, and again told all users to assume their environment variables are decrypted. It lists secrets on workloads, secret groups and global secrets. The networking, certificates, services, add-ons, jobs, builds and logs components were listed in major outage while the app and API were operational. No post-mortem or cause had been published when this article was prepared, so how the attacker got in is not public.

What to do, following the page: rotate every secret, starting with keys that bill per use such as AI provider keys, then look at each provider's usage page for calls you did not make.

Mistral Large 4: weights and the license clause

On October 6 the Daily Diff covered the preview of Mistral Large 4, with the weights promised for the end of October. Mistral released them on October 29. The model card describes a natively multimodal mixture-of-experts model with about one trillion total parameters and about 49 billion active per token (52 billion including embeddings), 128 routed experts with four active per token, a 1 million token context window, trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own European data centers. A quantized NVFP4 checkpoint targets Blackwell GPUs.

The benchmark numbers come from Mistral's own post. It says Large 4 leads Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 at 19.7 percent, scores 41 percent on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (up 13 points from the preview, with 30 percent fewer output tokens), and is effectively tied with GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index at 48 percent while using 47 percent fewer tokens per task. In Surge Code's blind pairwise preference test, Mistral says only Claude Opus 5.5 ranked ahead among the models evaluated. These are claims from Mistral's own chart; none is an independent result.

The Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License is described in the file as a modified version of the MIT license, with permission granted free of charge for the model, weights and documentation. Clause two says that if the licensee or any of its affiliates operates a Model as a Service business, they must enter into a separate commercial license with Mistral before using the model or derivatives for any commercial purpose. The license defines Model as a Service as giving a third party access to the model or its derivatives for inference or post-training by any means, for instance via API or hosted endpoints, in a way that lets that party exercise meaningful control over inputs, parameters or training data. Clause three exempts internal use that does not make the model available to third parties, and use through Mistral's own products.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

Binance has not named its breach points, Cursor has not said how the build got in, Northflank has no post-mortem yet and the Mistral chart is Mistral's own. Read the primary sources below and act on the concrete checks each one lists.

Sources

  • https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/north-korea-steals-usd-6-36-billion-from-binance-in-the-largest-hack-in-history
  • https://www.elliptic.co/insights/binance-largest-hack-in-history/
  • https://www.wired.com/story/the-dollar63-billion-binance-hack-was-pulled-off-in-just-20-minutes/
  • https://www.npr.org/2026/10/30/g-s1-150902/blockchain-intelligence-firms-link-north-korea-to-6-3b-hack-on-binance
  • https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50305480
  • https://cursor.com/blog/claude-code-extension-security-notice
  • https://phorion.io/blog/offical-claude-code-vsx-compromise/
  • https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50300683
  • https://status.northflank.com/cmvv0rn5a092f14rutwccodpp
  • https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50305025
  • https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/
  • https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B
  • https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50289418

title: From One Chatbot to Five Agents: My AWS Agent Engineer Nanodegree
description:
TL;DR: I finished the Future AWS Agent Engineer nanodegree with three graded projects, each a customer support system for a fictional online store: one chatbot, then one agent, then five agents working together. Each project was harder to build than the one before, and each one gave me fewer problems. Here's how the three compare, what changed between them, and why the last one, which scored 120 out of 120, still got sent back for more proof.

My first project for this nanodegree went in on deadline day in August. It was a chatbot with one system prompt, graded by a rubric written for a product AWS had already stopped offering to new customers. It passed. I spent most of that day worried it didn't count, because I hadn't typed the code.

My second project went in a month later, built in one session. It was one agent that could look up orders, process refunds, and search a product catalog, with an ownership check in code so it wouldn't show you someone else's orders. It also introduced me to a database that bills by the hour just for existing.

My third project went in on a Sunday night in October. It had five agents, two models, three knowledge bases searched at the same time, and a safety filter on every model call. It went from Udacity's untouched starter files to a perfect score on its test suite in under four hours.

Each project was harder than the one before, and each one gave me fewer problems. I didn't expect that, and I wanted to understand why, so this post compares the three side by side.

A junction, a helper, a council

The AWS AI & ML Scholars program runs with Udacity. I was in the Agent Developer track, and its nanodegree, Future AWS Agent Engineer, has three graded projects. All three are customer support systems for a fictional online store. Because the problem stayed the same, I could compare the three builds directly, each one with more tools than the last.

All three ran on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AWS's managed service for the parts of an agent you would otherwise build yourself: calling the model, remembering the conversation, running tools, and hosting the whole thing.

Project one was Nova Trivium, and I wrote about it in Future AWS Agent Engineer? I Didn't Write the Code. Does It Count?. A trivium is where three roads meet. One system prompt sent every message down one of three paths: file a bug report, answer from a pasted FAQ, or redirect to a human.

Project two was Nova Adiutrix, written up in Nova Adiutrix: my second agent built my first project's to-do list. An adiutrix is a helper. One agent tracked orders, processed refunds, searched a product catalog stored in a knowledge base (a managed store the agent can search by meaning instead of exact words), and refused to show you someone else's orders.

Project three is Nova Concilium. A concilium is a council. Five agents, each a specialist, with an orchestrator deciding who speaks.

earlgreyhot1701D / nova-concilium

Nova Concilium: a five-agent customer support system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Strands. A Haiku orchestrator routes to Sonnet specialists for inventory, refunds, policy, and replies, with parallel RAG across three Knowledge Bases, shared DynamoDB state, Bedrock Guardrails, and X-Ray tracing. AWS nanodegree capstone, 120/120.

Nova Concilium — NovaMart Multi-Agent Customer Support

Status: submission README for the nd905 Course 4 final project — complete with the full 120/120 test run and both X-Ray screenshots recorded below. This file is the submission README; the original Udacity starter README is preserved in the git baseline commit 7ea6508 (unmodified starter). Account ID and runtime ARN are intentionally omitted (redacted for public sharing).

Nova Concilium (Latin for "council") is a five-agent customer-support system for the fictional e-commerce company NovaMart, built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Strands Agents SDK. An Orchestrator agent routes each request to specialist worker agents, retrieves grounded policy answers with parallel multi-agent RAG across three Knowledge Bases, enforces a Bedrock Guardrail, keeps shared state in DynamoDB with optimistic locking, and is observable end-to-end through CloudWatch and X-Ray.

What it is

NovaMart's support team handles order status, returns and refunds, and policy questions by…

View on GitHub

Here is how the three compare:

The row I'd read first is "How I knew it worked." The testing got stricter with each project, and the stricter the test, the more I trust everything else in that column.

Each project paid off the last one's list

At the bottom of the Nova Trivium README, I wrote a section called "Not built, and why." It listed three things I left out: retrieval, guardrails, and structured output.

Nova Adiutrix built two of them without my planning it. I noticed halfway through, rereading my old README. That post ended with this: "The third item on that 'Not built, and why' list was guardrails. Still not built. I will let you know how project three goes."

In Nova Concilium, guardrails were a graded requirement. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is a filter that checks what goes into and comes out of the model. Ours blocks competitor talk, price haggling, and legal threats, and it masks personal details. The first sign it worked came from a test that wasn't about it. A customer's email address came back in a test transcript as {EMAIL}.

That finished the list. I didn't pick the order the items got built in. The course did.

The friction moved outward

All three builds had problems. What changed was where the problems came from.

Every lesson showed up again

Here is where each earlier lesson landed:

A knowledge base before a spec

The change I'd credit most happened before any code got written.

On the earlier projects, I handed Kiro a build spec. This time I had Claude, Anthropic's AI model, write a knowledge base first: one markdown file holding every course page, the rubric, the starter repo, and a table of every place those sources disagreed with each other. There were 13. Then, before any spec, Kiro read the starter files and checked all 13. Eleven resolved against a file. The other two had no file to check: a set of names the code hadn't defined yet, and the due date.

Checking the files before writing the spec came straight out of Nova Trivium, where I planned around a starter I had never fully listed. Every value also had to name the file it came from, or get marked UNVERIFIED.

The work split three ways, the same as before. Kiro wrote the code. Claude (Opus 5.5) wrote the knowledge base and reviewed each stage of Kiro's spec against the starter files. I directed, did the Console work, took the screenshots, and made the calls.

Claude's reviews caught four problems in Kiro's requirements. The folder wasn't a git repo yet, so two checkpoints couldn't run. One test was scheduled before the deploy it depends on. The guardrail tests needed example prompts that no file supplied, so Kiro would have had to make them up. And two agents could only be checked after the deploy, so Claude suggested checks that could run earlier.

I over-gated it, then I didn't

The first plan had Kiro stop after every single task and wait for my approval. Early on, I told Claude to stop over-constraining the build. I appreciate thoroughness, but I needed to keep moving.

We cut the stops down to four, the moments that needed me or cost money: before I created the knowledge bases in the Console, before the first deploy, before any git push, and before teardown. Everything else, Kiro ran straight through, pasting output as it went.

The whole run from bare starter files to a perfect score happened after that change, in under four hours. I think the fewer stops are a big part of why it went that fast.

Two agents, one penny

One of the three graded test scenarios asks: how much are 5 items at $29.99 with 10% off?

The exact answer is $134.955, so it has to be rounded. In the latest run, the orchestrator worked it out as $134.96. Then it handed off to the Communication agent, which rounded the discount to $15.00 first and wrote $134.95. The final reply said $134.95. In an earlier run of the same test, the final reply said $134.96.

The rounding rule in the starter code sits in the orchestrator's instructions. The Communication agent, which writes the reply the customer sees, rounded early anyway. As far as I can tell from the logs, the orchestrator's math never made it into the shared record the agents read from, so the Communication agent did the math again its own way.

The test passed anyway. When we wrote the acceptance check, Claude pointed out that the answer depends on rounding mode and suggested accepting either $134.95 or $134.96, since the graded behavior was that the guardrail didn't block a math question. I agreed. Accepting either answer fit the rubric, and it's also why a one-penny disagreement between two of my agents got through every test. Nobody noticed until I read the logs for this post.

This is my second penny this month. In Eight Minutes to Live. Was It Cursor, or Was It the Spec?, a tip calculator I built with Cursor split a 1,437.50 bill three ways into 479.17 each, which adds up to 1,437.51. The extra cent floated because my spec never picked a rule for it.

The comments on that post did more for me than the post did. flatin.pt suggested keeping money in whole cents and handing out the remainder one cent at a time in a fixed order, so the shares always add up. Matt Busel suggested treating the spec as a hypothesis instead of a contract, and updating it every time a check finds a gap. Vlad Zoff suggested keeping the acceptance checks separate from the build, so whoever builds the thing can't redefine what it's judged against.

Vlad's point lands closest to this penny. Loosening the check to accept either answer was a reasonable call for the rubric, but it was still the people building the thing changing the test. Both pennies came from the same gap: in the tip calculator, no rule said who gets the extra cent, and in Nova Concilium, no rule said whose number is the final one. If I follow Matt's advice, the next spec names one agent as the owner of any calculation and has it save the result to the shared record before anyone writes to the customer.

Perfect score, not enough proof

I submitted Nova Concilium that night. The reviewer sent it back less than an hour later.

The feedback was kind. It said the code was a good example of modular, well-documented agent code. Then it asked me to fully deploy my solution, including all the Knowledge Bases and the AgentCore deployment, and to include screenshots of each. Everything it asked for was already deployed and running in my AWS account. The reviewer had no way to see it.

The written deliverables were the code, the knowledge bases, the populated config file, a screenshot of the test score, and a screenshot of the X-Ray service map, which draws every request's path through the agents.

I submitted every one of them. No page asked for Console screenshots or test-run output.

The gap was still mine to catch. The original requirements Kiro wrote said every checkpoint's output gets saved to an evidence folder. When we sped up, the results went into the README as text. Claude didn't flag it in review, and I approved the submission without checking that line. Human approved means the miss is mine.

There's a second lesson in that miss. The rubric says the knowledge bases were "created in the AWS Console" and the system was "deployed to AgentCore Runtime." A reviewer can't log into my account, so for those two lines, a screenshot is the only proof they get. My checklist asked whether each thing was done. It needed to ask whether someone outside my account could see that it was done.

I added the Console screenshots and the test-run output and resubmitted. It passed, and on October 27 the certificate arrived.

Before my course access ended, I had Claude help me turn every lesson into notes: four markdown files, one per course. I wanted to take the knowledge with me, into future builds, instead of losing it when the classroom closes.

What the three projects still can't tell me

  • Whether my process holds up on a project with no starter files to check against.
  • Whether a 120-point suite measures what a customer would care about. It didn't catch the penny.
  • How many of the fights on Nova Concilium were easy only because the first two projects already hurt. ## Does it count?

The first post in this series asked whether directing agents counts as learning, when I never typed the code.

Three projects in, I can name what I learned. I learned where the knowledge lives, where the rules get enforced, and how to write a check that an agent can't talk its way past. On the last project, I learned that a perfect score and a passing submission are different things.

The difficulty went up every time. The building got easier every time. The lessons table is my evidence for why. Seven lessons, each one learned when something broke, and each one built into the next project as a check. That's the skill these three projects gave me: making the next build break in fewer places. I would like to hear from anyone who has built the same thing three times and seen something else.

The certificate says it counts. And..so do I.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect. That is the lens I am writing from.

Built with AI assistance in October 2026. Kiro wrote the code, and Claude (Opus 5.5) wrote the knowledge base, reviewed the spec, and helped draft this post. All three repos are public, so check them before you quote me.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

title: We're NoonLaunch, and here's why we built a launch platform for the AI search era
description:
Hey DEV community 👋

We're NoonLaunch, and this is our first post here. Before we start sharing guides, we want to introduce ourselves properly: who we are, what we're building, and why.

The problem we kept seeing

If you've ever shipped a side project or a SaaS, you probably know this pattern:

  1. You spend weeks (or months) building.
  2. You launch. Traffic spikes for a day or two.
  3. Then it goes quiet, and you're back to wondering how anyone will find your product.

Launch day is a spike, not a strategy. Most launch platforms are built around 24 hours of attention, and once that window closes, your product page gets buried.

At the same time, how people discover software is changing. Buyers still Google things, but more and more of them open ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini or Claude and ask:

"What's the best tool for X?"

If your product isn't mentioned in the places those AI engines learn from, it doesn't make the shortlist. It doesn't matter how good your code is.

What we built

NoonLaunch is a weekly product launch platform that helps AI tools, SaaS and software products get discovered on Google and cited by AI engines like ChatGPT.

A few decisions we made on purpose:

  • Weekly, not daily. A daily leaderboard gives you a few hours of visibility before the next batch pushes you down. A weekly cycle gives every product a real window to be seen.
  • Permanent product pages. Your page doesn't disappear after launch week. It stays live, indexable and findable, long after the launch.
  • Built for search and AI engines. Pages are structured so Google can rank them and AI engines can understand and cite them.
  • A Top 3 weekly badge for the best-performing launches, so there's still a bit of friendly competition.
  • A directory and launch archive, so buyers browsing a category can find you months later.

Free tools, no signup wall

While building NoonLaunch, we kept making small tools for our own launches, so we put them online for free:

  • Startup Name Availability Checker
  • A list of 300+ startup launch directories
  • Product Hunt Launch Planner and Launch Checklist
  • Startup Tagline and Product Description Generators
  • OG Image Generator and Favicon Generator

You can find them all at noonlaunch.com/tools. Use them whether or not you ever launch with us.

What we'll post here

We want this account to be useful, not a stream of ads. Expect posts like:

  • Launch playbooks for indie hackers and small SaaS teams
  • Honest comparisons of Product Hunt and other launch platforms
  • How AI engines pick which products to cite, and what you can do about it
  • SEO basics for new products that developers can actually implement

If you're building something, we'd love to see it.

Over to you 👇

We're curious: how did your last launch go? Did the traffic stick around, or did it fade after a day or two? And have you noticed users finding your product through ChatGPT or Perplexity yet?

Drop your experience in the comments. We read every one, and the best answers will shape what we write next.

Thanks for having us, DEV. 🚀

NoonLaunch team
