title: I built a zero-dependency web compiler in Rust for LLM coding agents: ~34 ms builds
description:
If an LLM builds your frontend, give it a language built for LLMs.

Your agent came to build a button. Your stack handed it a committee: a framework, a bundler, a transpiler, a minifier and a dozen config files. Every one of them is a decision the model has to reconstruct, and context it spends on tooling instead of on your product.

I built BRAINLLM to shorten that path: a compact component language (.brain), one canonical spec and a native compiler written in Rust that tells the agent exactly how to fix its mistakes.

  • 🦀 One native binary: parser, checker, codegen, bundler and minifier. No Vite, webpack, esbuild or Babel in the build pipeline.
  • ⚡ Warm production builds in ~34 ms on our open benchmark.
  • 🤖 Agent-ready diagnostics with exact fix edits, plus CLI and MCP tools.
  • 🍦 Zero runtime dependencies. The output is vanilla JavaScript and CSS. A new app's package.json has no dependencies at all, just the compiler as its only devDependency.

Try it in one command (Node 22+, no Rust install, no npm account):

npm create @christianirack/brainll@latest my-app

The code your agent handles

Components, state and styling live together in .brain files:

<meta props="start:num=0 label:str='Clicks'">

<script>
  let n = sig(start)
  let dbl = drv(() => n * 2)
</script>

<button on:click={n++}>{label}: {n} × 2 = {dbl}</button>

The compiler handles signal reads and writes, derived values update when their inputs change, and styles are scoped to the component. The output is direct-DOM JavaScript: signals update only the affected nodes.

The agent loop

  1. Understand. brain spec serves the implemented language contract. brain map --json maps the project.
  2. Build & correct. The agent writes components with brain add. brain check --json returns diagnostics with the file, location, rule and a proposed fix. Mechanical fixes carry exact replacement edits, and brain fix applies them.
  3. Verify & ship. brain doctor runs checks, tests and diagnostics; brain build compiles production output. Chrome screenshots, accessibility outlines and visual baselines give the agent eyes on the UI it built.

Everything is also exposed over stdio with brain mcp, and brain guide <topic> serves task playbooks (views, data, forms, server, SEO, accessibility, tests, i18n, performance).

Batteries included, zero libraries

A form shouldn't need an ecosystem. Everything below ships in the same toolchain, and the browser runtime has no third-party dependencies:

Built in What you get
Components and reactive state .brain files with markup, BrainScript and scoped styles; sig, drv and fx
Routes and layouts Views, layouts, loaders and guards
Forms and data Form validation, HTTP resources and server contracts
Bundler and minifier Written in Rust, inside the same binary. No Vite, webpack, esbuild or Babel
Diagnostics and repairs JSON diagnostics plus brain fix for mechanical edits
Browser checks Chrome screenshots, accessibility outlines and visual baselines
Size budgets Per-route JS, CSS and HTML budgets that fail oversized builds
Agent tooling Project map, task playbooks (brain guide), CLI and MCP

Show me the numbers

Seven stacks, the same dashboard workflow, 140 measured builds. All seven passed the same nine Chrome interaction checks.

Warm production build Median, 20 runs
BRAINLLM 34.32 ms
React + Vite 155.49 ms
Vue + Vite 211.76 ms
Svelte + Vite 243.53 ms
Astro + React island 504.78 ms
Angular CLI 1,262.50 ms
React + webpack 1,334.54 ms

Apple M5, 24 GiB RAM, two warmups per stack. These are fixture results, not a universal speed claim: output strategies differ. Don't trust the headline, run the benchmark. The method, versions, raw timings and the script to reproduce it are in the repo.

Let your LLM make it better

Every run is a chance to spot a compiler bug, an expensive step or a confusing diagnostic. The agent can turn that finding into a tested proposal and push it to a review branch. Maintainers decide what merges. You stay in control.

Try it

Requires Node 22+. No Rust installation needed.

npm create @christianirack/brainll@latest my-app
cd my-app
npm run dev        # brain run
npx brain spec     # the language contract your agent reads
npm run build      # production build

Or paste the starter brief from the README into your coding agent and describe the app you want.

  • 🌐 Website: https://chrisifm.github.io/BRAINLLM/
  • 💻 GitHub: https://github.com/chrisifm/BRAINLLM
  • 📦 npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@christianirack/brainllm

I'd love feedback on the language design and on the diagnostics format. What would your agent need from a frontend toolchain?

title: We Tested 5 AI Coding Tools on Real Data Science Work. Copilot Won Jupyter, Nobody Expected the Reason.
description:
Most AI coding assistant reviews test the same thing: write a function, fix a bug, build a CRUD app. Data science work looks nothing like that — it's Jupyter cells, half-built DataFrames, and pandas chains nobody wants to retype. So we spent four weeks running Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Tabnine, and Claude Code through exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, model training, and the ETL glue code that nobody writes a blog post about.

The notebook test that separated the field

The clearest gap: Copilot reads the whole notebook's state, not just the current cell. Load a CSV, run df.head(), and its next suggestions — null checks, descriptive stats, distribution plots for the numeric columns it already saw — line up with what you actually loaded. Cursor works fine in .py files but loses cell-to-cell context roughly 20% of the time in our testing: it'll suggest a variable name, or reference a DataFrame, from a different notebook entirely.

For raw pandas/numpy/matplotlib correctness, Copilot was right about 90% of the time; for polars (which has real traction in data science now), that dropped to 80%.

Where the agent-based tools actually win

Ask a notebook tool to "add gradient accumulation and mixed precision to this training loop" and you get a different story. Cursor produced a complete, correct implementation. Copilot's version worked but skipped scaler.update(). Windsurf's had the right shape but wrong accumulation logic. If your data science code has grown past notebooks into a real package — feature store, training script, serving endpoint — Cursor's composer propagates a change (we tested: switching a feature from raw to log-transformed) across all of them. Copilot needed each file updated by hand.

Claude Code is the outlier: no autocomplete, no notebook integration, but it's the only one of the five that can run a pipeline end-to-end, hit a real error (an encoding issue in a CSV, in one of our tests), fix it, and re-run until it's clean. Ask it to reason about an A/B test and it checks normality assumptions before picking a t-test over Mann-Whitney U — that's a different capability than autocomplete, not a better version of it.

The honest tradeoffs

  • Copilot's free tier (2,000 completions/50 chat requests monthly) runs out fast under daily data science use; Pro is $10/month.
  • Cursor at $20/month is twice Copilot's price, which is hard to justify if you live in notebooks rather than production pipelines.
  • Windsurf (now sold as Devin Desktop after Cognition's acquisition) is a reasonable alternative at the same $20/month Cursor charges, but its notebook awareness lags and it sometimes suggests columns that don't exist in your data.
  • Tabnine exists for one real reason: on-prem deployment for teams that legally cannot send data science code — which often contains column names, file paths, and business logic — to an external API.

No tool here wins at everything. The full breakdown, including our methodology and the five datasets we used, is in the complete data science tool comparison.

Disclosure: none of the five tools above are confirmed to run a cash publisher affiliate program with us — most explicitly don't. Nobody paid for placement here.

title: Telling a video stream to a case LCD apart from the commands: JPEG and raw RGB565 in USB captures
description:
Capture the USB traffic of an AIO cooler with a screen on the pump cap, change the brightness four times in the vendor app, and diff the clicks. What you expect is one small command with one byte that follows the slider. What you get is tens of thousands of 1 KB packets, because the app never stops sending the picture to the screen while you click.

This is the fourth post about usb-rea, an open-source tool I built that diffs USB captures per labelled click and writes a pyusb driver. The first one covered commands, the second one naming what the device reports back, the third one handshakes and session tokens. This one is about screens.

The weakness a real capture showed

A user on liquidctl issue 936 shared a public USBPcap capture of an ASUS TUF LC III LCD while changing the brightness. It was the first real capture of that kind I had run usb-rea on, and the old version got it wrong in an instructive way: the video packets landed inside the brightness actions, and the "brightness" usb-rea reported was made of image bytes.

The diff wasn't broken. It did exactly what it was told: find the bytes that change with the label. In a capture full of video, video bytes change with everything.

So since v0.7.4 usb-rea sets image streams aside before anything else runs. On that capture the stream turned out to be a 320x320 JPEG video on its own endpoint, and once it was out of the way the brightness command was easy: byte 4 on EP 0x01 is the percentage.

Encoded images: look for the magic bytes

JPEG, PNG and GIF are the easy case because every image starts with a known marker (FF D8 FF for JPEG). The rule:

  • On one host-to-device channel, at least 3 packets start an image at the same offset. That offset is the per-packet header length.
  • A frame runs from its start packet to the image's end marker (JPEG FF D9, counting embedded thumbnails so an EXIF preview doesn't end the frame early), the next start, or a pause.
  • Each header byte is constant, nn (number of packets in the frame) or ii (index of the packet in the frame).
  • A fixed device-to-host message sent about once per frame is the ack.

Here is the synthetic LCD from the demo, which streams a 240x240 JPEG video next to its brightness command. This is the real output of usb-rea demo --device lcd, with the 64-byte brightness line trimmed:

captured 5 labelled actions, device 1234:abcd

brightness   100%  0x12 | 0x01 | 0x00 | 0x80 | round(value * 1 + 0) | 0x00 | 0x00 | ...

image stream, kept out of the commands: jpeg stream on interrupt EP 0x03: 240x240, 159 frames in 950 packets of 512 bytes, header `08 nn 00 80` then `08 ii 00 00`; ack 08 81 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 on EP 0x84 (driver: send_image())

and the matching part of report.md:

- Frames: 159 (3 to 8 packets each, 950 packets in all, 2 of them from a frame cut off by the capture)
- Image size: 240x240, 1507 to 3985 bytes
- Rate: about 20 frames per second
- Chunk: 512 bytes per packet, the last one padded
- Header (4 bytes): first packet `08 nn 00 80`, then `08 ii 00 00`
- Ack: `08 81 00 00 ...` on EP 0x84, 160x (frames 8, 18, 28, 42, 54)

The image size comes from the JPEG SOF marker, so you also learn the panel resolution for free.

Raw pixels: no magic, so look at the size

Plenty of cheap case screens don't take JPEG at all. They take plain pixels: RGB565 (2 bytes per pixel) or RGB888 (3 bytes), usually behind a short "draw" command. Nothing in those bytes says "image". This is now on main (not released yet), and the trick is arithmetic:

  • Group packets on one channel into runs: large packets with no pause between them, all but the last the same length.
  • A run is a frame when its payload is exactly width x height x bytes per pixel for a common screen size (80x160 up to 1920x480, both orientations).
  • Or, better, when the short packet sent just before the run names a region and the payload is exactly that region. usb-rea tries x, y, width, height and x0, y0, x1, y1 as 16-bit fields in either byte order, plus four 10-bit fields packed into 5 bytes.
  • Three or more frames make a stream. The draw commands go with the pixels; other short commands on the same endpoint stay commands.

The region version matters because these screens rarely redraw everything. A clock or a temperature readout is a small rectangle sent every second, and without the region those frames would look like random large commands.

Output of usb-rea demo --device lcd --raw rgb565, where the synthetic screen is 160x128 and every 4th frame only redraws a 48x16 clock:

image stream, kept out of the commands: raw rgb565 little-endian stream on bulk EP 0x02: 160x128, 79 frames (20 redraw part of the screen) in 4937 packets of 512 bytes, each frame after a command `55 aa 02 00 xx xx yy yy ww ww hh hh`; ack 55 aa 82 00 on EP 0x82 (driver: send_image())

and from the report:

- Screen: 160x128 RGB565, 40960 bytes (2 per pixel) per full frame
- Pixel byte order: little-endian (neighbouring pixels are smooth that way)
- Region: the command gives x, y, width, height as 16-bit little-endian fields from byte 4; 20 of 79 frames redraw only part of the screen

The byte order line is my favourite small heuristic in this release. RGB565 can be sent little or big endian, and the capture doesn't say which. But real pictures are smooth: neighbouring pixels have similar colours. So usb-rea decodes a frame both ways and keeps the order where neighbours differ less. On a flat colour it says it can't tell instead of guessing.

As a ground truth I wrote a test fixture from the public description of the Turing Smart Screen rev A protocol: 6-byte commands with x, y, end x and end y packed as 10-bit fields, DISPLAY_BITMAP = 197, then RGB565 little-endian pixels. usb-rea finds the 320x480 stream, the draw command rr rr rr rr rr c5 (rr = packed region), the partial redraws, and leaves the hello, orientation and brightness commands on the same endpoint alone.

16-bit header fields

Raw frames are big. A 128x160 RGB888 frame in 64-byte packets is 1024 packets, which doesn't fit a one-byte counter, so devices use 16-bit ones. The header description now reads a count or index above 255 as a u16 and shows it doubled, with its byte order: 00 00 nn nn, then ii ii nn nn. The driver fills both bytes in.

The driver side

The generated driver gets send_image(). For a JPEG stream you pass JPEG bytes of the captured size. For a raw stream you pass a Pillow image (converted to RGB565 in the captured byte order) or bytes already in the stream's format, and if the app used region commands you can redraw just part of the screen:

from PIL import Image
from lcd_driver import Device

d = Device()
d.send_image(Image.open("wallpaper.png").resize((160, 128)))
d.send_image(clock_pixels, x=100, y=8, size=(48, 16))   # just the clock

Pillow is optional; the driver doesn't import it.

What it can't do (yet)

  • A screen size that isn't in the list and has no region command is missed.
  • The same byte count can fit several shapes: 320x480 RGB565 is also 480x320, and 320x320 RGB888. The report lists the alternatives so you can check on the device.
  • Region fields are only looked for in the separate draw command, and width is expected before height.
  • RGB888 channel order (RGB or BGR) is not worked out, and streams split over several endpoints are not detected.
  • A frame with a pause longer than 30 ms inside it gets split.

Try it 

pip install -U usb-rea          # 0.7.5
usb-rea demo --device lcd
usb-rea demo --device lcd --raw rgb565

It's also an MCP server (usb-rea mcp), and the streams field in its output carries all of the above. Sending anything to real hardware still needs explicit confirmation from a human.

If you own a case or AIO screen whose app only runs on Windows, a capture while you change one setting would help a lot, especially raw-pixel ones. Issues are open: https://github.com/emirmrkaljevic/usb-rea

I built usb-rea with help from AI coding tools; the inference itself is deterministic and every claim in its reports points at captured frames.

title: What one button becomes in an ApkPy build
description:
When I write a button in ApkPy, I write one line of Python. By the time the app runs on a phone, that line has become a layout entry, a Java listener and a callback method. I want to show the whole path, because it explains why the APK has no Python interpreter inside.

The line:

button(
    "Continue",
    id="continue_button",
    variant="filled",
    command=continue_flow,
    screen=home,
)

home is a Screen. Each screen becomes an Android Activity, and screen= puts the button at the root of that screen. If I pass parent=summary instead, it goes inside a container or card.

The compiler does not run this file and take a screenshot of a desktop window. It parses the Python syntax tree, collects screens, components and callbacks, and resolves the theme and style selectors before writing anything. The style block is a build-time input: the generated project gets colors, drawable shapes and dimensions, not a CSS engine running on the phone.

For the button above, the layout gets this:

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continue_button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:minHeight="48dp"
    android:text="Continue" />

And the Activity gets this:

MaterialButton continue_button = findViewById(R.id.continue_button);
continue_button.setOnClickListener(view -> {
    pythonCallback_continue_flow();
});

The callback is a real Java method generated from my Python function. Conditions, loops, conversions and component calls inside it are translated to their Java equivalents. The snippets are shortened; the real layout also carries margins, colors, accessibility text and drawable references.

One detail worth knowing: helpers are emitted only when the source asks for them. A plain screen does not get a media service. Call audio.play_background and the build adds a foreground service, a MediaSession and the notification. Call https.get and it adds the INTERNET permission and background networking. This is why a simple app stays small.

The generated project is meant to be read. Open the Gradle output from apkpy build in Android Studio and the button is there, with the ID I gave it.

The rule that matters: writehere.py is the source of truth. The generated Android project is an output. Rebuild and the generated files can be replaced, so app behavior stays in Python. apkpy.toml holds the app name, package ID, version and icon.

1.14.1, out on October 25, added classes, dataclasses and custom errors to the translated Python. That reaches the button too: a method can be a command now, command=cart.clear, instead of only a function.

To see the output:

python -m pip install --upgrade apkpy
apkpy start hello
cd hello
python writehere.py

writehere.py opens the Hot Previewer on the desktop. apkpy build writes the Gradle project. apkpy run compiles a debug APK.

title: Beyond Blockchain: Inside the Engineering Vision of Wortex Mainnet
description:
Beyond Blockchain: Inside the Engineering Vision of Wortex Mainnet

A closer look at the technology, architecture, and vision behind an emerging blockchain initiative.

Blockchain technology continues to evolve. Every new generation brings fresh questions about scalability, infrastructure, decentralization, and developer accessibility.

But meaningful innovation is not simply about launching another blockchain. It is about understanding the challenges of existing systems and exploring better ways to build.

This is the vision behind Wortex Mainnet.

A Different Perspective on Blockchain Infrastructure

Wortex Mainnet aims to approach blockchain infrastructure with an engineering-focused mindset.

Rather than relying solely on ambitious promises, the project emphasizes architecture, development, and technical exploration.

Its core vision is to contribute to the ongoing evolution of decentralized technology.

Engineering at the Core

The foundation of any blockchain project is its underlying technology.

Wortex Mainnet's technical direction includes an architecture built around Rust and an emphasis on a lightweight core.

These design choices raise important questions about performance, maintainability, security, and long-term development.

The real measure of success will be how these principles perform under independent technical evaluation and real-world network usage.

Why Decentralization Still Matters

Decentralization is more than a technical concept.

It is about building systems where transparency, participation, and verifiable operations matter.

For blockchain infrastructure to gain meaningful adoption, developers and users need to understand how the network works and what it actually delivers.

Wortex Mainnet seeks to contribute to this broader technological conversation.

title: Lambda Destinations: Catch Failed Async Events
description:
Lambda destinations are one of the most underrated settings in AWS Lambda, in my view. As soon as a service like S3, SNS or EventBridge invokes your function, nobody waits for the response. If something goes wrong, Lambda tries twice more and then quietly throws the event away. No error in the frontend, no ticket, just a line in a log that nobody reads.

That is why I check two things first for every asynchronously invoked function: how often does it retry, and where does an event end up when it fails anyway? In this article you build the answer step by step: a function with limited retries, a failure queue as the on-failure destination, a small script that replays failed events once the fix is in, and tests to go with it.

In short

For asynchronous invocations, Lambda retries failed events twice by default and discards them afterwards. With Lambda destinations, every event that finally fails goes to an SQS queue together with its error message, so you can reprocess it later on purpose. The most common pitfall: destinations do nothing for synchronous invocations or for functions that consume an SQS queue.

What you will learn in this article

  • How Lambda buffers and retries asynchronous invocations internally
  • When Lambda destinations are a better choice than a dead-letter queue
  • How to set up a failure queue with the Serverless Framework and with AWS CDK
  • How to read, analyze and replay failed events
  • Typical mistakes where destinations simply do nothing

What happens during an asynchronous Lambda invocation?

When you invoke a function synchronously, for example through API Gateway, the caller waits for the result and gets an error back directly. An asynchronous invocation works differently: Lambda accepts the event, responds right away with status code 202 and puts it into an internal queue. From there, Lambda invokes your function as soon as there is enough capacity. The caller never hears about the result.

If the function fails, say because your code throws an exception or hits the timeout, Lambda retries the invocation. According to the docs, it makes two more attempts by default: the second after about one minute, the third after another two minutes. Throttling (not enough free concurrency) and system errors are handled differently. In that case the event stays in the queue, and Lambda keeps trying for up to six hours, with intervals growing from one second to five minutes.

After the last attempt, or once the event is too old, Lambda discards it. Without further configuration, all that remains is the AsyncEventsDropped metric. On top of that, the docs point out that the same event can arrive more than once even without an error, because the internal queue is only eventually consistent. So your function needs to be idempotent, as I showed in the article on idempotency in AWS Lambda.

Which services invoke Lambda asynchronously?

Amazon S3 (for example for new objects), Amazon SNS and Amazon EventBridge are among the services that invoke your function asynchronously. You can trigger this yourself with the Event invocation type, for instance via the AWS CLI or the SDK. The pattern “function A kicks off function B and carries on” works exactly like this in many projects.

🎬 How Lambda processes an asynchronous invocation – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Lambda destinations or dead-letter queue?

There are two safety nets for discarded events. The older option is a dead-letter queue (DLQ) on the function: an SQS queue or SNS topic that receives the original event content plus a few attributes. The newer option is Lambda destinations. They send a complete record with request, response and error message to a target of your choice, on success, on failure or both.

Lambda destinations (onFailure) Dead-letter queue
Targets SQS, SNS, Lambda, EventBridge, S3 (failures only) SQS or SNS
Successful invocations yes, with onSuccess no
Content event, error message, number of attempts, function ARN only the event plus attributes (error message cut to 1 KB)
Applies to function, version or alias the function only
Metric for delivery errors DestinationDeliveryFailures DeadLetterErrors

My recommendation is clear: for new functions I use destinations. The record already contains the error message and the number of attempts, which saves you the trip to the logs while debugging. On the other hand, you do not have to rebuild an existing DLQ right away if it works and someone monitors it. Configuring both at the same time is possible, but it makes troubleshooting more confusing.

Which targets make sense?

For failures, an SQS queue is almost always the best choice. Messages stay for up to 14 days, and you can inspect them calmly and replay them on purpose. EventBridge is a good fit for success notifications that other parts of the system should react to. SNS is tricky, because a message there can be at most 256 KB, while asynchronous events can be up to 1 MB. For large events, the docs therefore point to SQS or S3. You can also look up which service fits which purpose in the AWS service finder.

When Lambda destinations do not apply

The most common misconception: destinations are not a general safety net for every Lambda function. They apply to asynchronous invocations and, for failures only, to event source mappings on streams. An event source mapping is the mechanism Lambda uses to poll a source such as SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams itself and feed your function with batches.

Destinations apply to asynchronous invocations and, for failures only, to stream sources.

So if your function consumes an SQS queue, a destination on the function does nothing. There, the dead-letter queue belongs on the source queue, combined with a redrive policy and ideally with partial batch responses. The article on SQS partial batch response shows how. For synchronous invocations through API Gateway or function URLs, the caller gets the error back directly and has to decide what happens next.

Step by step: a failure queue with the Serverless Framework

The example is a fictional bakery that takes preorders online. After each order, a function is invoked asynchronously to email a confirmation to the customer. If the mail service is down or the address is invalid, the order should not get lost but land in a failure queue.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 22 or newer and npm
  • an AWS account with credentials configured for the AWS CLI
  • Serverless Framework v4 (npm i -g serverless, using it requires signing in)
  • basic TypeScript knowledge

Step 1: Create the project

Create a folder and install the dependencies. Serverless Framework v4 builds TypeScript handlers itself with esbuild, so you do not need an extra plugin.

mkdir bakery-preorders && cd bakery-preorders
npm init -y
npm i @aws-sdk/client-lambda @aws-sdk/client-sqs
npm i -D typescript @types/node @types/aws-lambda vitest tsx

The tsconfig.json is deliberately simple. allowImportingTsExtensions allows imports ending in .ts, which tsx and Vitest run directly.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2023",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": ["node"],
    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true
  },
  "include": ["src", "scripts", "test"]
}

Step 2: Write the handler

The handler receives the preorder as its event and sends the email. Sending mail is a placeholder here. Addresses ending in .invalid deliberately trigger an error, so you can see the destination in action right away.

// src/confirm-preorder.ts
export interface Preorder {
  orderId: string;
  customerEmail: string;
  items: string[];
  pickup: string; // ISO date, e.g. "2026-10-31"
}

// Placeholder for a real mail service. Addresses ending in ".invalid"
// simulate a permanent error so you can see the destination at work.
async function sendMail(to: string, subject: string): Promise<void> {
  if (to.endsWith(".invalid")) {
    throw new Error(`Mail service rejected address: ${to}`);
  }
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: "Mail sent", to, subject }));
}

export async function handler(event: Preorder): Promise<{ orderId: string; status: string }> {
  if (!event?.orderId || !event.customerEmail) {
    // An error here ends up in the on-failure destination after all attempts
    throw new Error("Invalid preorder: orderId or customerEmail missing");
  }

  await sendMail(
    event.customerEmail,
    `Your preorder ${event.orderId} is ready for pickup on ${event.pickup}`,
  );

  return { orderId: event.orderId, status: "confirmed" };
}

What matters is that the function really throws an error when something goes wrong. If you catch every exception and return a result anyway, Lambda treats the invocation as successful, and no destination fires.

Step 3: Retries and destination in serverless.yml

Now for the core of it. With maximumRetryAttempts you define how often Lambda retries after a function error (0 to 2). The maximumEventAge value sets, in seconds, how old an event may get (60 seconds to 6 hours). Under destinations.onFailure you attach the failure queue.

# serverless.yml
service: bakery-preorders

provider:
  name: aws
  runtime: nodejs22.x
  region: eu-central-1
  architecture: arm64
  memorySize: 256
  timeout: 10

functions:
  confirmPreorder:
    handler: src/confirm-preorder.handler
    # Asynchronous invocations: at most 1 retry, events at most 1 hour old
    maximumRetryAttempts: 1
    maximumEventAge: 3600
    destinations:
      onFailure:
        type: sqs
        arn:
          Fn::GetAtt: [FailedConfirmations, Arn]

resources:
  Resources:
    FailedConfirmations:
      Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
      Properties:
        QueueName: preorder-confirmation-failed
        MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600 # 14 days, the SQS maximum
        SqsManagedSseEnabled: true

    FailureAlarm:
      Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
      Properties:
        AlarmDescription: Failed confirmations are waiting to be handled
        Namespace: AWS/SQS
        MetricName: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
        Dimensions:
          - Name: QueueName
            Value: !GetAtt FailedConfirmations.QueueName
        Statistic: Maximum
        Period: 300
        EvaluationPeriods: 1
        Threshold: 0
        ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
        TreatMissingData: notBreaching

  Outputs:
    FailureQueueUrl:
      Value: !Ref FailedConfirmations

Because the queue ARN is resolved through Fn::GetAtt, the Serverless Framework needs the type: sqs setting. That is how it can grant the function the matching sqs:SendMessage permission. The alarm fires as soon as a single message sits in the failure queue. Connect it to an SNS topic or your chat channel, otherwise it alarms into the void.

Step 4: Deploy and trigger an error 

serverless deploy

aws lambda invoke \
  --function-name bakery-preorders-dev-confirmPreorder \
  --invocation-type Event \
  --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \
  --payload '{"orderId":"B-1042","customerEmail":"customer@example.invalid","items":["Rye bread"],"pickup":"2026-10-31"}' \
  response.json

The CLI responds right away with "StatusCode": 202. That only means Lambda has accepted the event. After the first failure, Lambda waits about a minute and tries a second time. After that, the record is in the queue. serverless info --verbose shows you the queue URL under outputs.

aws sqs receive-message \
  --queue-url <FailureQueueUrl> \
  --query "Messages[0].Body" --output text

Step 5: Understand the record

The message contains the so-called invocation record. For our example it looks roughly like this:

{
  "version": "1.0",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-27T17:05:12.000Z",
  "requestContext": {
    "requestId": "4f1c2a9e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
    "functionArn": "arn:aws:lambda:eu-central-1:111122223333:function:bakery-preorders-dev-confirmPreorder:$LATEST",
    "condition": "RetriesExhausted",
    "approximateInvokeCount": 2
  },
  "requestPayload": {
    "orderId": "B-1042",
    "customerEmail": "customer@example.invalid",
    "items": ["Rye bread"],
    "pickup": "2026-10-31"
  },
  "responseContext": {
    "statusCode": 200,
    "executedVersion": "$LATEST",
    "functionError": "Unhandled"
  },
  "responsePayload": {
    "errorType": "Error",
    "errorMessage": "Mail service rejected address: customer@example.invalid"
  }
}

You will need three fields almost every time. requestPayload holds the original event you restart with later. condition tells you why the event was given up, here because all attempts were used. And responsePayload contains your function’s error message. So you do not have to pick this structure apart by hand everywhere, here is a small module with types and a validation function:

// src/invocation-record.ts
// Shape of the record Lambda sends to a destination
export interface InvocationRecord<TRequest = unknown> {
  version: string;
  timestamp: string;
  requestContext: {
    requestId: string;
    functionArn: string;
    condition: string; // e.g. "RetriesExhausted" or "Success"
    approximateInvokeCount: number;
  };
  requestPayload: TRequest;
  responseContext?: {
    statusCode: number;
    executedVersion: string;
    functionError?: string;
  };
  responsePayload?: unknown;
}

function isObject(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown> {
  return typeof value === "object" && value !== null;
}

// Validates an SQS message body and returns the typed record
export function parseInvocationRecord(body: string): InvocationRecord {
  let data: unknown;
  try {
    data = JSON.parse(body);
  } catch {
    throw new Error("Message is not valid JSON");
  }
  if (!isObject(data) || !isObject(data.requestContext) || !("requestPayload" in data)) {
    throw new Error("Message is not a Lambda invocation record");
  }
  const ctx = data.requestContext;
  if (typeof ctx.functionArn !== "string" || typeof ctx.condition !== "string") {
    throw new Error("requestContext is incomplete");
  }
  return data as unknown as InvocationRecord;
}

// Short, readable failure description for logs and tickets
export function describeFailure(record: InvocationRecord): string {
  const payload = record.responsePayload;
  const message =
    isObject(payload) && typeof payload.errorMessage === "string"
      ? payload.errorMessage
      : "no error message";
  return `${record.requestContext.condition} after ${record.requestContext.approximateInvokeCount} attempt(s): ${message}`;
}

Step 6: Replay failed events

A failure queue is only as good as the way back. Once the mail service is reachable again or the bug is fixed, you want to reprocess the collected events. The following script reads the queue, prints every error message and invokes the function asynchronously again with the original event. Only then does it delete the message.

// scripts/replay-failures.ts
// Reads failed events from the queue and invokes the function again asynchronously.
// Usage: npx tsx scripts/replay-failures.ts <QueueUrl> [--dry-run]
import { InvokeCommand, LambdaClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-lambda";
import { DeleteMessageCommand, ReceiveMessageCommand, SQSClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";
import { describeFailure, parseInvocationRecord } from "../src/invocation-record.ts";

const [queueUrl, flag] = process.argv.slice(2);
if (!queueUrl) {
  console.error("Please provide the queue URL");
  process.exit(1);
}
const dryRun = flag === "--dry-run";

const sqs = new SQSClient({});
const lambda = new LambdaClient({});
let replayed = 0;

while (true) {
  const { Messages = [] } = await sqs.send(
    new ReceiveMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: queueUrl, MaxNumberOfMessages: 10, WaitTimeSeconds: 2 }),
  );
  if (Messages.length === 0) break;

  for (const message of Messages) {
    const record = parseInvocationRecord(message.Body ?? "");
    console.log(`${record.requestContext.requestId}: ${describeFailure(record)}`);
    if (dryRun) continue;

    await lambda.send(
      new InvokeCommand({
        FunctionName: record.requestContext.functionArn.replace(/:\$LATEST$/, ""),
        InvocationType: "Event",
        Payload: new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(record.requestPayload)),
      }),
    );
    await sqs.send(new DeleteMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: queueUrl, ReceiptHandle: message.ReceiptHandle }));
    replayed++;
  }
  if (dryRun) break;
}

console.log(dryRun ? "Dry run finished, nothing changed" : `${replayed} event(s) sent again`);

# First look at what is in there
npx tsx scripts/replay-failures.ts <FailureQueueUrl> --dry-run

# Then actually send them again
npx tsx scripts/replay-failures.ts <FailureQueueUrl>

During the dry run, messages are read but not deleted. They stay invisible for the queue’s visibility timeout (30 seconds by default) and then show up again. A replayed invocation that fails again simply lands in the queue again. So you lose nothing, but you should not replay blindly in a loop while the cause is still there.

Step 7: Test

The tests check reading the record, the failure description and the handler’s behavior. They run without AWS access.

// test/invocation-record.test.ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { describeFailure, parseInvocationRecord } from "../src/invocation-record.ts";
import { handler } from "../src/confirm-preorder.ts";

const failureBody = JSON.stringify({
  version: "1.0",
  timestamp: "2026-10-27T17:05:12.000Z",
  requestContext: {
    requestId: "4f1c2a9e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
    functionArn: "arn:aws:lambda:eu-central-1:111122223333:function:bakery-preorders-dev-confirmPreorder:$LATEST",
    condition: "RetriesExhausted",
    approximateInvokeCount: 2,
  },
  requestPayload: { orderId: "B-1042", customerEmail: "customer@example.invalid", items: ["Rye bread"], pickup: "2026-10-31" },
  responseContext: { statusCode: 200, executedVersion: "$LATEST", functionError: "Unhandled" },
  responsePayload: { errorType: "Error", errorMessage: "Mail service rejected address: customer@example.invalid" },
});

describe("parseInvocationRecord", () => {
  it("reads a failure record", () => {
    const record = parseInvocationRecord(failureBody);
    expect(record.requestContext.condition).toBe("RetriesExhausted");
    expect(record.requestPayload).toMatchObject({ orderId: "B-1042" });
  });

  it("rejects unrelated messages", () => {
    expect(() => parseInvocationRecord('{"hello":"world"}')).toThrow(/not a Lambda invocation record/);
    expect(() => parseInvocationRecord("not json")).toThrow(/not valid JSON/);
  });

  it("describes the failure in a readable way", () => {
    const text = describeFailure(parseInvocationRecord(failureBody));
    expect(text).toBe("RetriesExhausted after 2 attempt(s): Mail service rejected address: customer@example.invalid");
  });
});

describe("handler", () => {
  it("confirms a valid preorder", async () => {
    const result = await handler({ orderId: "B-1", customerEmail: "customer@example.com", items: ["Pretzel"], pickup: "2026-10-31" });
    expect(result).toEqual({ orderId: "B-1", status: "confirmed" });
  });

  it("throws for a rejected address", async () => {
    await expect(
      handler({ orderId: "B-2", customerEmail: "customer@example.invalid", items: [], pickup: "2026-10-31" }),
    ).rejects.toThrow(/rejected address/);
  });
});

npx tsc --noEmit
npx vitest run

Expected result: the type check finishes without output, and Vitest reports five passing tests.

The same with AWS CDK

If you prefer AWS CDK, three properties on the function are enough. retryAttempts and maxEventAge match the values from serverless.yml, and onFailure takes a destination from the aws-lambda-destinations module. CDK adds the permission to send to the queue automatically.

// lib/preorder-stack.ts
import { Duration, Stack, type StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Runtime, Architecture } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda";
import { SqsDestination } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-destinations";
import { NodejsFunction } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs";
import { Queue } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-sqs";
import type { Construct } from "constructs";

export class PreorderStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    const failed = new Queue(this, "FailedConfirmations", {
      retentionPeriod: Duration.days(14),
    });

    new NodejsFunction(this, "ConfirmPreorder", {
      entry: "src/confirm-preorder.ts",
      runtime: Runtime.NODEJS_22_X,
      architecture: Architecture.ARM_64,
      retryAttempts: 1,
      maxEventAge: Duration.hours(1),
      onFailure: new SqsDestination(failed),
    });
  }
}

Running cdk synth turns this into a resource of type AWS::Lambda::EventInvokeConfig with MaximumRetryAttempts: 1, MaximumEventAgeInSeconds: 3600 and the queue as the OnFailure target. For a success notification to EventBridge, add onSuccess: new EventBridgeDestination().

Tuning retries for asynchronous invocations

The default of two retries is a sensible starting point, but it does not always fit. For errors that will not resolve themselves, such as an invalid address or a validation error, more attempts bring nothing but cost. For short outages of a third-party system, on the other hand, they help. My rule of thumb: one retry for business functions that call third-party systems, zero retries if the function already retries properly with backoff.

Watch out for multiplied retries

If your code retries three times internally and Lambda retries twice more, a single event can hit the partner up to nine times. I described this multiplication in detail in the article on exponential backoff with jitter. So decide deliberately which layer retries, and dial the others back.

How old may an event get?

The maximum age deserves some thought as well. An order confirmation that arrives six hours late confuses more than it helps. With maximumEventAge: 3600 it lands in the failure queue after one hour, and you decide on purpose whether to still send it. There is also a handy emergency brake: if you set a function’s reserved concurrency to 0, Lambda sends new asynchronous events straight to the on-failure destination without any attempt. That helps when a function is currently producing garbage and you still want to keep the events.

Typical mistakes with Lambda destinations

All of the following pitfalls are described in the docs, but they often only show up in production.

  • FIFO as a target: SQS FIFO queues and SNS FIFO topics are not supported. Delivery fails, and only the DestinationDeliveryFailures metric gives it away.
  • SNS with large events: If the record is larger than 256 KB, it does not arrive. Prefer SQS for failures.
  • Destination on an SQS-triggered function: It never fires. Configure the DLQ on the source queue instead.
  • Swallowed errors: A try/catch that only logs turns every failure into a success.
  • Configuration in the wrong place: The settings belong to the function, a version or an alias. If your sources invoke an alias, the configuration has to apply where the invocations arrive.
  • Failure queue without an alarm: A queue nobody looks at is just a slower trash can.

Cost and security

The cost is low. You pay for the extra Lambda attempts, the SQS requests and one CloudWatch alarm, which comes to cents at normal error rates. Data protection matters more: the record contains the complete event, in our example email addresses. Encrypt the queue (in the example with SqsManagedSseEnabled), restrict read access and do not keep messages longer than necessary. If you use an S3 bucket as a destination, remove the destination before deleting the bucket. Otherwise someone else could create a bucket with the same name and receive your failure records.

My take

I consider an on-failure destination mandatory for every asynchronously invoked function, much like a timeout on every HTTP call. The effort is a few lines of YAML, and the benefit shows the first time a third-party system goes down. Without a destination, you have to reconstruct lost events from logs by hand. With one, you replay them with a single command.

Where I disagree is the idea of seeing destinations as a substitute for proper error design. A failure queue collects symptoms. You still have to fix the causes, and that needs someone on the team who feels responsible. Who on your team checks the failure queue in the morning? Once that question is answered, the pattern works really well. If it stays open, after a few months you will find thousands of messages there that nobody can make sense of anymore.

FAQ

What is the difference between Lambda destinations and a DLQ?

A dead-letter queue only receives the original event and a few attributes. Lambda destinations deliver a complete record with the error message and the number of attempts, support more targets and can report successes as well.

Do Lambda destinations work with API Gateway?

No. API Gateway invokes Lambda synchronously, so the error goes straight back to the client. Destinations only apply to asynchronous invocations and, for failures, to stream sources such as Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams.

How often does Lambda retry an asynchronous invocation?

For function errors, twice by default, about one and two minutes apart. With MaximumRetryAttempts you set 0 to 2 retries. When throttled, Lambda keeps trying until the maximum event age, which is six hours by default.

Can I use a FIFO queue as a destination?

No. Lambda only supports standard queues and standard topics. With a FIFO target, delivery fails and the DestinationDeliveryFailures metric goes up.

A failure queue only helps when delivery fails. If your code accepted an event and calculated something wrong, you need something else: I show how to replay events from an archive after a bug fix in the article EventBridge replay: Reprocess events after a bug fix.

Your next step

Pick one function today that is invoked by S3, SNS or EventBridge, and check whether it has an on-failure destination. If not, the few lines from step 3 plus an alarm are all it takes. And then an honest question for you: how many events did your most important asynchronous function silently discard last month? The AsyncEventsDropped metric will tell you. Let me know in the comments what you found.

Sources

  • AWS Lambda: How Lambda handles errors and retries with asynchronous invocation
  • AWS Lambda: Configuring error handling for asynchronous invocation
  • AWS Lambda: Capturing records of asynchronous invocations
  • AWS Lambda: Types of metrics for Lambda functions
  • Serverless Framework: AWS Lambda Functions (destinations, maximumRetryAttempts, maximumEventAge)
  • Tested with Node.js 22.23, TypeScript 7.0.2, Vitest 5.0.5 (5 tests), @aws-sdk/client-lambda and @aws-sdk/client-sqs 3.1157.0, and aws-cdk-lib 2.275.0 (template synthesis with EventInvokeConfig). The serverless.yml was validated as YAML, not deployed.

This post was created with AI assistance.
