title: Node.js Trace IDs for E-Commerce Agent Errors: A Rollback-Safe Evaluation
description:
Short answer: put a trace ID at the request boundary, carry it through every agent step, and make error search prove that the ID survived a rollback. For an e-commerce agent loop, the useful design is the one that lets you compare latency and cost for the old and new version without losing the failure's context.

I would start with OpenTelemetry as the instrumentation contract, then choose an error product for the operational workflow. That keeps the application portable and makes rollback a data problem rather than a dashboard migration. The first implementation target is modest: every incoming request gets a trace ID or preserves the one supplied by a trusted upstream, and every middleware, route, tool call, and error event records it.

The first rule is boring.

The experiment was about rollback, not dashboards

The system under test was an e-commerce shopping agent. A request could retrieve catalog data, apply a promotion, and call a model before returning a recommendation. The measurements that mattered were total latency, model and tool cost, agent version, and error outcome. The decision was whether to roll back a new prompt or tool policy safely.

The tempting design was to add a trace ID to the top-level Node.js error log and call the job done. It failed as an evaluation design because an error in a route told me the request identity but not which agent version or step produced the bad result. A single ID is useful only when it is present at the layers where the decision is made.

The chosen event contract was small:

  • trace_id: one correlation value for the request and its downstream work
  • span_id: an optional step identifier, useful for separating retrieval, model, and checkout-policy work
  • agent_version: the prompt, tool-policy, or deployment label being evaluated
  • latency_ms and cost_usd: values attached to the relevant event, with their measurement scope made explicit
  • error_type and rollback_candidate: fields that make the failure searchable without reading a stack trace first

The Node.js middleware should establish the first field before the request reaches a route. Route handlers and error middleware should read the same request context, not generate a second ID after an exception. That distinction is easy to miss in a notebook prototype, where one function owns the whole call. In production, the route, queue worker, and error reporter are separate observation points.

A useful correction is to treat the trace ID as a correlation contract, not as a trace database. It can connect records across systems, but it cannot prove that a missing worker span never existed. That is why the rollback test needs a known request, a known agent version, and a deliberately forced error, with all three visible in the resulting report.

A failed request should therefore resemble this contract, regardless of which backend receives it:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AgentErrorEvent:
    trace_id: str
    span_id: str | None
    agent_version: str
    latency_ms: int
    cost_usd: float
    error_type: str
    rollback_candidate: bool


def is_actionable(event: AgentErrorEvent) -> bool:
    return bool(event.trace_id and event.agent_version and event.error_type)


def compare_versions(events: list[AgentErrorEvent]) -> dict[str, dict[str, float]]:
    grouped: dict[str, list[AgentErrorEvent]] = {}
    for event in events:
        grouped.setdefault(event.agent_version, []).append(event)

    return {
        version: {
            "errors": float(len(items)),
            "mean_latency_ms": sum(item.latency_ms for item in items) / len(items),
            "mean_cost_usd": sum(item.cost_usd for item in items) / len(items),
        }
        for version, items in grouped.items()
        if items
    }

This is an evaluator, not a replacement for Node.js request context. Its job is to make the acceptance test concrete: an error report without trace_id or agent_version is incomplete, even if the error tracker accepted it. The numbers in this snippet are placeholders for values emitted by the application; they are not a benchmark.

Which tool should own the correlation?

OpenTelemetry is the strongest starting point when portability and rollback safety dominate. Its Node.js instrumentation and context model give the application a vendor-neutral way to carry trace context, while exporters and backends remain replaceable. It does not, by itself, give a team a complete error triage workflow, a retention policy, or a convenient cost ledger. That is a deliberate boundary.

Sentry is a practical choice when the main task is grouping exceptions and moving from an error to surrounding context. Its tracing and error-monitoring workflow is approachable for a small team. The trade-off is that a Sentry-centered rollout can make the error product's event model the de facto application contract. I would keep the trace and version fields in the application's own event schema so a rollback does not require rewriting instrumentation.

Datadog fits teams that already operate logs, metrics, traces, and application monitoring together. Its value is the breadth of a shared operational workspace. The cost is conceptual and organizational: the team must decide which signals are authoritative when an agent failure appears as a log event, an APM error, and a cost record. That decision should be written into the evaluation harness, not left to whichever dashboard someone opens first.

Infrai is worth considering when the team wants one REST surface, one key, and one bill across backend services, with public discovery for the available capabilities. For this particular problem, its verified observability surface includes error listing and search, so it can be one strong option for a compact error-query workflow. It is not a distributed tracing system: trace and span fields can correlate logs, but there is no span-tree query. It also has no built-in alert or notification routes, so polling the query API and owning the alerting policy remains part of the application.

The comparison is therefore conditional. OpenTelemetry is the instrumentation foundation; Sentry is attractive for focused exception triage; Datadog is a broad operations platform; a REST-oriented service is useful when a small backend team values one consistent integration surface. None removes the need to test the trace contract in the application.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main boundary
OpenTelemetry Node.js instrumentation and exporters Portable correlation across backends Not an error triage product by itself
Sentry Error-monitoring SDK and event workflow Focused exception grouping and context Its event model can become the application contract
Datadog Integrated logs, metrics, and APM Teams already using one operations workspace More signals require an explicit source-of-truth policy
Infrai Plain REST requests under one key A compact query workflow across backend capabilities No span-tree query or built-in alert routes

The platform choice is only half the integration. Infrai's public discovery surface is self-describing and documents runnable examples in 10 languages, which reduces the friction of checking a capability before writing a client. Its broader surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For this workflow, that means a Python evaluator or a Node.js service can call a documented REST capability without installing a vendor SDK; it does not change the need for application-owned trace fields.

How should Node.js error tracking use trace IDs for observability?

The search workflow should answer a narrow question: “Show failures from agent version checkout-policy-2026-10-30 whose trace ID can be followed from ingress to the failing route.” The exact query parameters depend on the selected service. Do not invent a filter shape and bake it into the client before checking that service's current schema.

For a minimal setup, send errors to the chosen error tracker after the Node.js error middleware has attached the request context. Keep the trace ID in structured fields, rather than embedding it only in a formatted message. Then verify two paths: the list view can find the event, and the search view can retrieve it by the same identifier. Infrai exposes GET /v1/errors/list and GET /v1/errors/search for those two kinds of error queries; its discovery surface is the place to confirm the current request schema before implementation.

The query client can stay deliberately small because the verified routes do not require a fabricated filter payload in this example:

import os
import time

import requests


def list_error_events() -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    url = os.environ["INFRAI_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/") + "/v1/errors/list"

    for attempt in range(3):
        response = requests.request(
            method="GET",
            url=url,
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = int(retry_after) if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit() else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"error listing failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("error listing remained rate-limited after retries")

That test is cheap. It checks reachability and response handling; it does not pretend that the list endpoint is a distributed trace viewer. The application still needs its synthetic trace-ID test to prove that the error event contains the correlation fields.

There is an important limit here. An error search result is evidence that an event was indexed, not proof that every downstream span exists or that an agent's cost is exact. For cost attribution, record the measurement boundary explicitly: model call, complete request, or both. For latency, use the same boundary across versions. Otherwise a rollback decision can look quantitative while comparing unlike measurements.

I would add an integration test that creates one synthetic request with a known trace ID, forces an error after at least one agent step, and asserts that the resulting report contains the trace ID and version. A second test should exercise a request with an incoming trace ID and confirm that the application propagates it instead of silently replacing it. A third should use a missing or malformed value and verify the boundary policy. The test data should be synthetic; user identifiers do not belong in a correlation-field test.

The limits matter more than the happy path

Error tracking will not tell you that a scheduled job never ran. A health-check service is still needed for that silent failure. It will not decode source maps or symbolize a crash dump, and it will not provide session replay. Those are separate requirements, not missing configuration flags.

Retention and deletion deserve the same scrutiny. If the workflow has a deletion or export obligation, verify the service's actual interfaces before promising compliance: the available observability surface does not provide a per-user log deletion interface or a general batch export/subscription interface. Trace IDs also carry cardinality and privacy consequences. A high-cardinality value belongs in logs and error context where correlation is needed; it should not be copied into every metric label. Prometheus calls out this cardinality risk in its instrumentation guidance.

The simple approach still has a place. A small service with one route and no agent versioning may need only structured errors and a correlation ID. Once an agent loop changes prompts, tools, or routing, the evaluation contract pays for itself. It lets the team compare old and new behavior, find the exact failing request, and roll back with evidence instead of dashboard intuition.

Before copying this design, measure three things in your own traffic: the percentage of error reports that contain a valid trace ID, the percentage that also contain the agent version, and the latency and cost distributions for each version. Those are the gates. A new backend is acceptable only if it preserves them during normal traffic and during a rollback.

References

  • OpenTelemetry JavaScript documentation: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/js/
  • OpenTelemetry specification, context propagation: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/context/
  • Sentry JavaScript tracing documentation: https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/guides/node/tracing/
  • Sentry JavaScript error monitoring documentation: https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/guides/node/
  • Datadog Node.js APM documentation: https://docs.datadoghq.com/tracing/trace_collection/automatic_instrumentation/dd_libraries/nodejs/
  • Prometheus instrumentation best practices: https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/

title: Anonymous Employee Surveys Are Harder Than Removing the Name Field
description:
An anonymous employee survey sounds easy to build.

Remove the name field.

Don't ask for email.

Store the answers.

Show aggregated results.

Done.

Except that anonymity rarely fails because someone forgot to hide the employee's name.

It usually fails because the system collects enough other information to reconstruct who answered.

And that can happen at several layers:

form
+
session
+
analytics
+
network logs
+
survey tokens
+
segmentation
+
open comments

The interesting engineering problem is not:

How do I hide identity?

It is:

How do I prevent the system from making identity inferable later?

Anonymous and confidential are different architectures

The first distinction is important.

A confidential survey may know who the respondent is internally while preventing managers from seeing individual responses.

An anonymous survey should make it difficult or impossible to connect a response back to a specific person.

Those are very different guarantees.

Imagine this architecture:

employee_id
    ↓
survey_token
    ↓
response_id

If all three can be correlated, the survey may be confidential, but it is not strongly anonymous.

That can still be a perfectly valid product decision.

The problem is promising one model while implementing the other.

The UI says:

Your answers are anonymous.

The database says:

response_id = 391
employee_id = 8742

That is not a copywriting issue.

That is an architecture issue.

Individualized links create a privacy tradeoff

Unique links are useful.

They let you:

  • prevent duplicate responses;
  • track participation;
  • send reminders;
  • know who has not responded;
  • control survey access.

Something like:

/survey/7f8a0db913...

But that token may also become an identity bridge.

If the token is stored together with the response, anonymity disappears.

One approach is separating participation tracking from response storage.

Conceptually:

Participation
-------------
employee_id
token_hash
survey_id
responded_at

And separately:

SurveyResponse
--------------
response_id
survey_id
answers
created_at

The participation system only needs to know:

This employee was eligible and has already responded.

The response system does not necessarily need to know:

This response belongs to this employee.

That separation can significantly improve privacy.

But only if the rest of the stack respects it.

Removing IP storage may still not be enough

Suppose your application database does not store IP addresses.

Good.

What about:

  • reverse proxy logs;
  • CDN logs;
  • WAF logs;
  • APM tooling;
  • analytics;
  • session replay;
  • fraud detection;
  • rate limiting infrastructure?

A request can still leave traces like:

timestamp
ip_address
user_agent
session_id
request_path

Now imagine the survey response was submitted at:

14:03:41

and the proxy logs show one employee accessing the survey endpoint at:

14:03:40

The application never stored identity.

The infrastructure still made correlation possible.

This is why anonymity should be treated as a system property, not a database column.

Third-party analytics become part of the threat model

Another easy mistake is adding normal product analytics to an anonymous survey page.

For example:

Google Analytics
Hotjar
Mixpanel
Amplitude
session replay

Each of these may collect identifiers or behavioral metadata.

Even if your backend never stores personal information, a third-party script may collect:

  • persistent cookies;
  • device identifiers;
  • navigation patterns;
  • timestamps;
  • referrer data;
  • session information.

If anonymity is part of the product promise, third-party scripts need to be evaluated as part of the privacy architecture.

The relevant question becomes:

Does any system in this flow receive enough information to identify the respondent?

Not:

Does our main database contain their name?

The dashboard may be more dangerous than the form

Even if collection is perfect, reidentification can happen later during analysis.

Suppose a company has 300 employees.

The dashboard shows results by department.

That seems safe.

Then you add filters:

department
location
role
tenure
manager

Each filter alone may return a large group.

Combined:

Engineering
+
São Paulo
+
Staff Engineer
+
5+ years

may return:

1 respondent

No name needs to appear.

The user already knows who that person is.

This is why privacy protections need to exist at query time, not just during collection.

Minimum group size is a start, not a solution

A common protection is:

if respondent_count < 5:
    hide_results()

That is useful.

But it is not enough.

Consider this:

All employees: 6 responses
Non-managers: 5 responses

If both aggregates are visible, the manager's response may be inferred by subtraction.

This is sometimes called a differencing attack.

You protected every individual query.

The combination of two valid queries still leaks information.

So the system may need to consider:

  • overlapping cohorts;
  • previous queries;
  • filter combinations;
  • historical exports;
  • aggregate subtraction.

This is where a simple threshold becomes a much more interesting privacy problem.

Privacy rules should follow the filtered result, not the original group

Another subtle bug:

You configure:

minimum_group_size = 5

Engineering has 20 employees.

Safe.

Then someone filters:

Engineering
+
Manager
+
Remote

Result:

2 respondents

If the system only checked the original department size, privacy is broken.

The threshold needs to be evaluated after every filter operation:

def can_display(segment):
    return segment.respondent_count >= MIN_GROUP_SIZE

Even then, as we just saw, you may still need protections against inference across multiple queries.

Open-text comments are identity leaks waiting to happen

Quantitative answers are easy to aggregate.

Open comments are different.

A respondent may write:

After the Atlas migration in March, my manager moved me off the project without explanation.

That comment may reveal:

  • team;
  • project;
  • date;
  • role;
  • manager;
  • unique event.

No explicit identity field is required.

The content itself identifies the author.

So open-text responses need a different privacy model.

Questions worth asking:

  • Should comments from small cohorts be shown?
  • Should comments be searchable?
  • Can managers filter comments by team?
  • Should comments be pooled across larger groups?
  • Should specific metadata be stripped?
  • Should comments be manually reviewed before display?

A product can have perfectly anonymous numeric responses and still expose people through free text.

Even timestamps may be sensitive

A timestamp often feels harmless:

created_at = 2026-10-30T14:03:41

But combine it with another system:

VPN login
office access
survey page view
Slack activity

and identity may become obvious.

This does not mean timestamps should always be removed.

It means their precision deserves consideration.

Maybe the application only needs:

2026-10-30

instead of:

2026-10-30T14:03:41.932Z

Data minimization is often about questioning precision, not just questioning fields.

The database schema can accidentally encode surveillance

A common first model might be:

SurveyResponse
--------------
id
employee_id
survey_id
answers
created_at

Very convenient.

Also very easy to misuse.

Once employee_id exists there, every future feature can use it.

Export.

Admin endpoint.

Debugging tool.

Internal query.

Support ticket.

Analytics job.

You may promise anonymity at the UI layer while keeping a permanent join key underneath.

A safer model might separate concerns:

SurveyParticipation
-------------------
employee_id
survey_id
participation_token
responded

and:

SurveyResponse
--------------
response_id
survey_id
answers

If a business requirement does not require linking the two, maybe the schema should make that relationship impossible.

Privacy becomes stronger when it is structural rather than policy-based.

Access control still matters for aggregated data

It is tempting to think:

These are aggregated results, so access control is less important.

Not always.

Imagine this endpoint:

GET /surveys/42/results?department=legal&role=director

Even if it returns only aggregates, it might expose a tiny cohort.

So authorization needs to consider more than:

can_view_survey_results

It may need context such as:

can_view_segment
&& respondent_count >= threshold
&& !segment_is_reidentifiable

The dashboard itself becomes part of the privacy enforcement layer.

The buyer and the respondent have opposite incentives

This is also a product problem.

The buyer usually wants:

more filters
more segmentation
more detail
more exports

The respondent benefits from:

larger cohorts
less granularity
less metadata
fewer correlations

Both sides are reasonable.

The customer wants useful information.

The respondent wants protection.

If the product optimizes only for the buyer, it can undermine the quality of the data itself.

Employees who do not trust the system will respond differently.

So privacy is not just a constraint.

It is part of data quality.

"Anonymous" should be part of your threat model

Before building the survey, I would define what anonymity actually means.

For example:

Goal:
A manager should not be able to determine which employee submitted a specific response.

Then model possible attackers:

manager
HR administrator
tenant administrator
developer
database administrator
analytics provider
infrastructure operator

Then ask what each one can access.

That exercise often reveals uncomfortable assumptions.

For example:

The manager cannot see individual responses.

Good.

But:

The tenant administrator can export raw data.

or:

The support team can query the production database.

or:

Analytics stores persistent identifiers.

Then the anonymity guarantee is much weaker than expected.

You may eventually need stronger privacy techniques

For many products, aggregation thresholds and strict access control may be enough.

For more sensitive scenarios, other ideas become relevant:

  • k-anonymity;
  • suppression;
  • bucketization;
  • query restrictions;
  • noise injection;
  • differential privacy;
  • delayed reporting;
  • minimum cohort persistence.

Each adds tradeoffs.

More privacy often means less analytical precision.

That is the central tension of the product.

A few questions I would ask before designing the schema

If I were building an anonymous employee survey system from scratch, I would ask:

Do we actually need to know who submitted each response?

Can participation tracking be separated from response storage?

Do we need precise timestamps?

Are IP addresses stored anywhere in the stack?

Do third-party scripts run on the survey page?

What is the minimum cohort size?

Is the threshold applied after every filter?

Can multiple valid queries reveal one person's answer by subtraction?

Can open comments identify the author?

Can tenant admins export individual responses?

Can internal support staff bypass aggregation rules?

Those questions are much more important than whether the form contains a "name" field.

Anonymous surveys are not anonymous forms

That is the main lesson.

Anonymity depends on the whole system:

collection
+
infrastructure
+
storage
+
authorization
+
aggregation
+
analytics
+
filters
+
exports
+
comments

Removing personally identifying fields is only one small part.

The harder problem is making sure the rest of the product does not quietly recreate the identity you tried to remove.

For context, I'm the CTO and co-founder of Sigilo, where we build privacy-first reporting and organizational feedback systems. A lot of these questions came from thinking about how to give companies useful analytics without destroying the trust of the people providing the data.

AI assistance disclosure: AI was used during drafting and editing. The technical concepts and product decisions were reviewed by the author before publication.

title: Modeling Blockchain Deposit Workflows with a State Machine in Node.js
description:
The duplicate delivery problem

Imagine a Node.js worker processing a blockchain deposit confirmation. It receives an event, updates a swap to exchange, and schedules the next operation.

The worker commits the update—but crashes before acknowledging the message. The queue delivers the event again. Another observer might even publish a new event ID for the same deposit confirmation.

If the handler simply performs an update and queues another job on every delivery, one deposit can trigger multiple exchange operations.

This is why idempotency matters: processing the same logical action more than once should not create additional business effects.

In this tutorial, we'll model two separate protections:

  1. Event deduplication: recognize a delivery that has already been recorded.
  2. Business idempotency: recognize that a workflow has already performed the requested transition, even when a new event ID is used.

We'll add a transactional outbox so the state change and the intention to perform the next operation are committed together.

Scope: This is a standalone educational example, not CryptoDeepApp's production architecture. A dependency-free in-memory model lets us test the behavior; a separate MongoDB adapter illustrates durable multi-document transactions. We do not connect to blockchain nodes or send real funds. Confirmation events are assumed to come from a trusted verifier that already checked the chain, destination, asset, amount, and confirmation/finality policy.

Two identities, two different jobs

A delivery ID and a business-operation ID are not interchangeable.

Identifier Example Purpose
Event ID chain-watcher:event-001 Detect replay of the same delivered event
Deposit reference btc-mainnet:tx-abc:vout-0 Identify the specific on-chain transfer
Workflow ID swap-42 Identify the business process being updated
Outbox operation ID start-exchange:swap-42 Prevent scheduling the same logical next operation twice

A transaction hash alone may be insufficient to identify a deposit. Bitcoin transactions can have multiple outputs; other chains may require a log or instruction index. The example treats depositRef as a prevalidated, chain-specific identifier.

Consider this already-observed deposit:

const workflow = {
  id: 'swap-42',
  status: 'deposit',
  depositRef: 'btc-mainnet:tx-abc:vout-0',
  amountUnits: '12500000', // Integer base units, never a floating-point amount.
  revision: 3,
};

const event = {
  eventId: 'chain-watcher:event-001',
  workflowId: 'swap-42',
  type: 'DEPOSIT_CONFIRMED',
  depositRef: 'btc-mainnet:tx-abc:vout-0',
  amountUnits: '12500000',
};

The workflow has already reached deposit: funds were observed, but the application's confirmation policy was not yet satisfied. A verified DEPOSIT_CONFIRMED event may move it to exchange.

We deliberately do not allow that event to jump from waiting or overdue straight to exchange. If a late deposit appears, its observation and any required review belong to a separate step.

Why a processed-events check alone is not enough

This code has a race condition:

// Unsafe pseudocode — don't use it as an idempotency guarantee.
if (!(await processedEvents.findOne({ eventId }))) {
  await updateTransaction();
  await processedEvents.insertOne({ eventId });
}

Two workers can both read "not processed" before either inserts anything. And if the first update succeeds but the process crashes before inserting the receipt, the next delivery repeats the update.

A durable design needs database-enforced uniqueness and an atomic relationship between receiving an event, changing the workflow, and recording the next action.

Build a testable model in plain Node.js

First, we'll make the behavior easy to test without MongoDB. Create idempotent-events.mjs:

// Educational in-memory implementation; NOT durable or distributed.
export function validateEvent(event) {
  if (!event || typeof event !== 'object' || event.type !== 'DEPOSIT_CONFIRMED') {
    throw new TypeError('Expected a DEPOSIT_CONFIRMED event');
  }
  for (const field of ['eventId', 'workflowId', 'depositRef']) {
    if (typeof event[field] !== 'string' || !event[field].trim()) {
      throw new TypeError(`${field} must be a non-empty string`);
    }
  }
  if (typeof event.amountUnits !== 'string' || !/^[1-9]\d*$/.test(event.amountUnits)) {
    throw new TypeError('amountUnits must be a positive integer string');
  }
}

export function fingerprint(event) {
  return JSON.stringify([
    event.type, event.workflowId, event.depositRef, event.amountUnits,
  ]);
}

export function planDepositConfirmation(workflow, event) {
  if (!workflow) throw new Error('Unknown workflow; reconcile before acknowledgement');
  if (workflow.depositRef !== event.depositRef ||
      workflow.amountUnits !== event.amountUnits) {
    throw new Error('Deposit identity or amount mismatch; needs reconciliation');
  }
  if (workflow.status === 'deposit') return 'advance';
  if (['exchange', 'sending', 'success'].includes(workflow.status)) {
    return 'already-applied';
  }
  throw new Error(`Cannot confirm deposit from status ${workflow.status}`);
}

export class InMemoryStore {
  #data;
  #tail = Promise.resolve();

  constructor(workflows = []) {
    const keyed = new Map();
    for (const workflow of workflows) {
      if (keyed.has(workflow.id)) throw new Error('Duplicate workflow ID');
      keyed.set(workflow.id, structuredClone(workflow));
    }
    this.#data = { workflows: keyed, inbox: new Map(), outbox: new Map() };
  }

  async transaction(fn) {
    // Serializes calls in THIS Node.js process. Not a real database transaction.
    const previous = this.#tail;
    let unlock;
    this.#tail = new Promise((resolve) => { unlock = resolve; });
    await previous;
    try {
      const draft = structuredClone(this.#data);
      const result = await fn(draft);
      this.#data = draft; // Simulated all-or-nothing commit.
      return result;
    } finally {
      unlock();
    }
  }

  snapshot() {
    return structuredClone(this.#data);
  }
}

export async function processDepositConfirmed(store, event) {
  validateEvent(event);
  const identity = fingerprint(event);

  return store.transaction(async (data) => {
    const previous = data.inbox.get(event.eventId);
    if (previous) {
      if (previous.fingerprint !== identity) {
        throw new Error('Event ID reused with different payload');
      }
      return { outcome: 'duplicate-delivery' };
    }

    const workflow = data.workflows.get(event.workflowId);
    const plan = planDepositConfirmation(workflow, event);
    data.inbox.set(event.eventId, { fingerprint: identity, outcome: plan });

    if (plan === 'already-applied') return { outcome: plan };

    const operationId = `start-exchange:${event.workflowId}`;
    if (data.outbox.has(operationId)) {
      throw new Error('Outbox operation already exists; reconcile conflict');
    }
    data.workflows.set(event.workflowId, {
      ...workflow, status: 'exchange', revision: workflow.revision + 1,
    });
    data.outbox.set(operationId, {
      id: operationId,
      type: 'START_EXCHANGE',
      workflowId: event.workflowId,
      status: 'pending',
    });
    return { outcome: 'applied', operationId };
  });
}

There are three important decisions in this code:

  • A repeated event ID returns duplicate-delivery. If the same ID appears with different meaningful fields, the handler rejects it rather than silently trusting the new payload.
  • A different event ID describing a confirmation already reflected by the workflow returns already-applied. This prevents a second business transition.
  • The workflow state and a uniquely named outbox record are written in the same simulated unit of work. Errors discard the draft instead of leaving half-applied changes.

The model serializes simulated transactions inside one process. It does not provide persistence, cross-process locking, crash recovery, or database isolation. Its purpose is to verify the rules before translating them to real storage.

Test duplicates and concurrent deliveries

Node.js includes a built-in test runner. Create idempotent-events.test.mjs:

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { InMemoryStore, processDepositConfirmed } from './idempotent-events.mjs';

const workflow = {
  id: 'swap-42', status: 'deposit', revision: 3,
  depositRef: 'btc-mainnet:tx-abc:vout-0', amountUnits: '12500000',
};
const event = {
  eventId: 'chain-watcher:event-001', workflowId: 'swap-42',
  type: 'DEPOSIT_CONFIRMED',
  depositRef: 'btc-mainnet:tx-abc:vout-0', amountUnits: '12500000',
};

test('replayed event does not create another outbox operation', async () => {
  const store = new InMemoryStore([workflow]);
  const first = await processDepositConfirmed(store, event);
  const replay = await processDepositConfirmed(store, event);
  assert.equal(first.outcome, 'applied');
  assert.equal(replay.outcome, 'duplicate-delivery');
  assert.equal(store.snapshot().outbox.size, 1);
});

test('a new event ID cannot repeat the business transition', async () => {
  const store = new InMemoryStore([workflow]);
  await processDepositConfirmed(store, event);
  const second = await processDepositConfirmed(store, {
    ...event, eventId: 'chain-watcher:event-002',
  });
  assert.equal(second.outcome, 'already-applied');
  assert.equal(store.snapshot().workflows.get('swap-42').revision, 4);
});

test('25 concurrent deliveries still schedule one operation', async () => {
  const store = new InMemoryStore([workflow]);
  const results = await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 25 }, (_, i) =>
    processDepositConfirmed(store, { ...event, eventId: `source:event-${i}` })
  ));
  assert.equal(results.filter(r => r.outcome === 'applied').length, 1);
  assert.equal(store.snapshot().outbox.size, 1);
});

Run:

node --test idempotent-events.test.mjs

The downloadable example includes 19 unit tests. All passed on Node.js 22.16.0. They also cover missing workflows, mismatched deposit references, changed amounts, invalid states, conflicting event IDs, and simulated rollback. These are in-memory behavioral tests—not MongoDB integration tests or throughput benchmarks.

Move the guarantee into MongoDB

For a real multi-worker service, the uniqueness and atomicity must be enforced by a shared durable store.

A possible MongoDB data model is:

workflows
  _id: swap-42
  status: deposit
  revision: 3
  depositRef: btc-mainnet:tx-abc:vout-0
  amountUnits: "12500000"

event_inbox
  _id: chain-watcher:event-001
  fingerprint: [canonical event fields]

event_outbox
  _id: start-exchange:swap-42
  type: START_EXCHANGE
  status: pending

MongoDB provides a unique index on _id by default. That gives us uniqueness for event receipts and outbox operation IDs. A conditional update can additionally check that the workflow still has the expected status and revision.

The official MongoDB Node.js driver supports withSession() and withTransaction() for operations that need to commit across multiple collections. Here is the core pattern, with validateEvent(), fingerprint(), and planDepositConfirmation() imported from the previous example:

export async function processDepositConfirmedMongo(client, db, event) {
  validateEvent(event);
  const fp = fingerprint(event);
  const inbox = db.collection('event_inbox');
  const workflows = db.collection('workflows');
  const outbox = db.collection('event_outbox');

  try {
    return await client.withSession(async (session) =>
      session.withTransaction(async () => {
        await inbox.insertOne({
          _id: event.eventId,
          fingerprint: fp,
          workflowId: event.workflowId,
        }, { session });

        const workflow = await workflows.findOne({ _id: event.workflowId }, { session });
        const plan = planDepositConfirmation(workflow, event);
        if (plan === 'already-applied') return { outcome: plan };

        const result = await workflows.updateOne({
          _id: event.workflowId,
          status: 'deposit',
          revision: workflow.revision,
          depositRef: event.depositRef,
          amountUnits: event.amountUnits,
        }, {
          $set: { status: 'exchange' },
          $inc: { revision: 1 },
        }, { session });
        if (result.modifiedCount !== 1) {
          throw new Error('Concurrent state change; retry or reconcile event');
        }

        const operationId = `start-exchange:${event.workflowId}`;
        await outbox.insertOne({
          _id: operationId,
          type: 'START_EXCHANGE',
          workflowId: event.workflowId,
          status: 'pending',
        }, { session });
        return { outcome: 'applied', operationId };
      }, {
        readConcern: { level: 'snapshot' },
        writeConcern: { w: 'majority' },
      })
    );
  } catch (error) {
    if (error?.code !== 11000) throw error;
    // A unique-outbox collision is NOT necessarily a duplicate event.
    const existing = await inbox.findOne({ _id: event.eventId });
    if (!existing) throw error;
    if (existing.fingerprint !== fp) {
      throw new Error('Event ID reused with different payload');
    }
    return { outcome: 'duplicate-delivery' };
  }
}

This adapter is an architectural illustration; it was not integration-tested against a MongoDB instance. It requires a supported MongoDB deployment for multi-document transactions (typically a replica set or sharded cluster), appropriately provisioned collections, and a compatible official Node.js driver.

The important properties are:

  1. Insert an inbox receipt with a unique event ID.
  2. Validate the existing workflow and perform a compare-and-set update using its status and revision.
  3. Insert a uniquely identified outbox operation in the same transaction.
  4. Commit them together—or roll them all back.

The driver can retry transaction callbacks for certain transient errors. For this reason, do not call an external exchange, send a notification, or transfer funds inside the transaction callback. Such a side effect could run again even if the database work was rolled back and retried.

An outbox record is not an exactly-once payout

The outbox solves a specific failure window:

Database commit succeeds
        ↓
Process crashes before publishing next job

Because the intended next action is already stored in event_outbox, another worker can discover it later.

However, that worker could send a request to an external provider, lose the response, and retry. A unique outbox record prevents the creation of duplicate logical jobs, not necessarily repeated external execution.

A production outbox consumer needs an atomic claim/lease strategy, recovery from expired claims, bounded retries, and a stable operation ID. Whenever possible, the external provider must support an idempotency contract for that ID. Otherwise, the worker needs an explicit reconciliation path before attempting the side effect again.

Do not describe this combination as universal "exactly-once delivery." The realistic goal is at-least-once delivery with idempotent effects where the contracts permit it.

Edge cases worth designing before production

Same event ID, different payload. Treat this as an integrity conflict. A replay must not silently redefine the amount or deposit reference.

Same deposit, different event IDs. The inbox cannot catch this by itself. Your workflow transition and unique business-operation key must prevent another exchange from starting.

Out-of-order events. If a confirmation arrives before the deposit is associated with a workflow, don't pretend the transition is valid. Retry, reconcile, or investigate according to the system's event-ordering guarantees.

Reorganizations and reversals. A confirmation policy is chain-specific. A reorg or revoked upstream event may need a separate compensating workflow; the code here does not implement that.

Multiple valid deposits. Never assume one transaction hash means one transfer. Multiple outputs, transfers, or partial deposits need explicit models and reconciliation rules.

Inbox retention. Deleting old receipts changes what can be recognized as an identical delivery. Plan retention relative to replay windows, and keep independent business-level guards.

Transaction conflicts. A failed conditional update or duplicate outbox ID might be a concurrency conflict, not a safe duplicate. Log it with the relevant IDs and retry or reconcile according to a bounded policy.

Performance. Multi-document transactions and indexes have costs. For simpler problems, an atomic single-document update can be sufficient. Use a transactional outbox when multiple collections must commit together.

Key takeaways

Idempotency is not just an if check in a message handler.

  • Use event IDs to deduplicate exact deliveries.
  • Use business identifiers and state guards to prevent repeating the logical operation under a new event ID.
  • Enforce critical invariants with unique indexes and conditional writes.
  • Use a transactional outbox when the state update and next-action record must commit atomically.
  • Assume the worker or provider can retry; exactly-once external effects are not guaranteed without an appropriate downstream contract.
  • Test duplicate, concurrent, conflicting, and out-of-order inputs—not only the happy path.

A duplicated event should be uneventful. Getting there requires clear identities, explicit state rules, and storage guarantees that survive more than one process.

References

  • MongoDB: Atomicity and Transactions
  • MongoDB Node.js Driver: Transactions
  • MongoDB: Create a Unique Index
  • Node.js: Test Runner

AI disclosure: This educational draft and its sample code were prepared with AI assistance. The in-memory example passed local tests; the MongoDB adapter has not been validated against a live database. Review and adapt the material before publication.

title: How many companies were registered in India in October 2026? 17,622 new companies by state, type and industry
description:
India's Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) registers new companies every working day, but its own portal answers one company at a time, behind a captcha. There is no public "companies incorporated this week" list you can download.

I pulled every company the MCA register lists as incorporated from 1 to 29 October 2026: 17,622 companies across 26 register dates, and grouped them by state, company type and industry. Data as read on 30 October 2026.

The short answer

  • 17,622 companies were incorporated in India from 1 to 29 October 2026: about 800 per working day (15,892 over 20 weekdays), about 420 on Saturdays, and almost none on Sundays (39 in the month). 2 October (Gandhi Jayanti) had none; the busiest day was Monday 5 October with 1,366.
  • 85% are private limited companies (15,005). Section 8 non-profits are 7.4% (1,302), One Person Companies 5.9% (1,045), subsidiaries of foreign companies 1% (182) and new public limited companies 0.4% (71).
  • Maharashtra registers the most: 2,940 companies (16.7%), then Uttar Pradesh 1,931, Karnataka 1,415, Telangana 1,326, Delhi 1,321 and Tamil Nadu 1,266.
  • IT services is the largest industry: 13.4% of new companies (2,367) declared computer programming and consultancy as their main activity, ahead of wholesale trade (9.8%) and retail (6.0%). In Karnataka and Telangana the share is 24% and 23%; in Delhi wholesale comes first.
  • One in four new CINs (26%) carries a newer state code: UW, PN, MR, DC, WR, ME or TZ. A CIN lookup table that only knows the classic codes (MH, UP, DL...) leaves these companies without a state.

How the numbers were measured

  • Source: the MCA register as mirrored by companies.dubleu.co, a public company directory that lists incorporations by date. Fetched with the India New Company Registrations Actor on Apify, in listing mode (includeDetails: false), which reads the date lists and decodes each CIN without opening company pages. Runs B2Wxf3ZJDh3Wqu6WP (14,456 rows; the directory rate-limited five list pages) and zxFnbB2hnvIAfVNvC (3,966 rows re-reading 3, 5, 14, 15 and 16 October in full), merged and de-duplicated on CIN.
  • What the CIN tells you: a CIN such as U62011KA2026PTC230412 encodes listed/unlisted (U), the main activity as a 5-digit NIC 2008 code (62011), the state (KA), the year (2026), the type (PTC private, NPL Section 8, OPC, FTC foreign subsidiary, PLC public, GOI/SGC government) and the registration number. The NIC division in the CIN matched the activity shown on the company page for 200 of 200 companies checked.
  • Scope: companies only. The directory's date lists did not include LLPs, which are registered under a separate LLPIN, so LLPs are not counted. 30 October was not yet listed when the data was read; late additions can still appear for recent dates.
Company type Companies Share
Private limited (PTC) 15,005 85.1%
Section 8 non-profit (NPL) 1,302 7.4%
One Person Company (OPC) 1,045 5.9%
Foreign company subsidiary (FTC) 182 1.0%
Public limited (PLC) 71 0.4%
Government company (GOI, SGC) 17 0.1%

Which states register the most new companies?

State New companies, 1–29 Oct 2026 Share IT services share

Rajasthan 685 3.9% 10%
Bihar 636 3.6% 7%

"IT services share" is the share of the state's new companies whose CIN starts with NIC division 62 (computer programming, consultancy and related activities). Bengaluru and Hyderabad show up clearly: roughly one new company in four there is a software or IT consulting firm. Andhra Pradesh follows at 20%.

Which industries are new Indian companies in?

Main activity declared at incorporation, NIC 2008 division, all 17,622 companies:

NIC division Activity Companies Share
62 Computer programming, consultancy and related activities 2,367 13.4%
46 Wholesale trade 1,730 9.8%
47 Retail trade 1,052 6.0%
88 Social work activities without accommodation 808 4.6%

70 Head offices and management consultancy 374 2.1%

By broad section: information and communication 17.5%, wholesale and retail trade 16.6%, manufacturing 14.7%, health and social work 7.2%, professional and technical services 7.1%, construction 6.3%.

A few details that stand out:

  • Energy: 357 new companies registered power generation and distribution (NIC 3510) as their main activity; 74 company names contain "SOLAR", 301 "ENERGY" and 154 "GREEN".
  • AI in the name: 199 new companies have the word "AI" in their name, three in four of them (152) registered as IT services. "TECHNOLOGIES" (905) and "SOLUTIONS" (771) are still the most common name words.
  • Section 8 companies are mostly charities and schools: 61% of the 1,302 declared social work (division 88) and 20% education. Maharashtra (268), Uttar Pradesh (179), Bihar (93), West Bengal (90) and Delhi (86) register the most.
  • Foreign subsidiaries cluster in IT: 60 of the 182 new subsidiaries of foreign companies are IT services firms, mostly in Maharashtra (37), Karnataka (30), Telangana (22) and Haryana (18).

The CIN state codes older tables miss

Classic CIN state codes are the two-letter state abbreviations: MH, KA, DL, UP and so on. In October 2026, 4,609 of the 17,622 new CINs (26%) carried one of these codes instead:

CIN code Registrar (RoC) on the company page State Companies
UW RoC Uttar Pradesh II Uttar Pradesh 1,020
PN RoC Pune Maharashtra 961
MR RoC Mumbai II Maharashtra 810
DC RoC Delhi II Delhi 611
WR RoC Kolkata II West Bengal 499
ME RoC Nagpur Maharashtra 388
TZ RoC Coimbatore Tamil Nadu 320

The mapping was checked against the registrar shown on each company's page. If your code derives the state from characters 7–8 of the CIN, add these, or a quarter of new Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu companies will come back without a state. (Our own Actor had the same gap until build 0.1.9, released while writing this.)

Get the list of newly registered companies in India as JSON

The India New Company Registrations Actor returns newly incorporated companies by date as JSON, CSV or Excel: CIN decoded into type, state and NIC code, and, with includeDetails: true (the default), RoC, category, NIC activity text, authorised and paid-up capital, registered office address with PIN code and the number of directors. It collects no director names, phone numbers or email addresses. It needs no login or API key and costs $3 per 1,000 companies; filters on type, state and name are applied before anything is charged.

Today's new companies in Karnataka in one HTTP call:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/data_daemon~india-new-company-registrations/run-sync-get-dataset-items?timeout=300" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"recentDates": 1, "states": ["Karnataka"], "includeDetails": false, "maxResults": 20}'

With details, a row looks like this (trimmed):

{
  "cin": "U56301KA2026PTC230411",
  "name": "2 MORE SHOTS HOSPITALITY PRIVATE LIMITED",
  "registrationDate": "2026-10-28",
  "companyType": "Private Limited",
  "roc": "RoC-Bangalore",
  "state": "Karnataka",
  "nicCode": "56301",
  "activity": "Food and beverage service activities",
  "authorizedCapitalInr": 1000000,
  "paidUpCapitalInr": 100000,
  "pincode": "560035",
  "directorsCount": 2
}

To reproduce the tables above, pull the month in listing mode and group with pandas:

from apify_client import ApifyClient
import pandas as pd

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("data_daemon/india-new-company-registrations").call(
    run_input={"fromDate": "2026-10-01", "toDate": "2026-10-29",
               "includeDetails": False, "maxResults": 0}
)
df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).list_items().items)
df = df.drop_duplicates("cin")
df["division"] = df["nicCode"].str[:2]

print(df["companyType"].value_counts().head(4))
by_state = df.groupby("state").agg(
    companies=("cin", "size"),
    it_share_pct=("division", lambda d: round((d == "62").mean() * 100)),
)
print(by_state.sort_values("companies", ascending=False).head(5))

Foreign company (subsidiary)      182
Name: count, dtype: int64

state
Maharashtra         2940            12

Karnataka           1415            24

A whole month is about 17,600 rows, so this exact pull costs about $53 at $3 per 1,000. For a daily lead feed, schedule the Actor once a day with recentDates: 3 and onlyNewSinceLastRun: true: each company is delivered (and charged) once, about 800 a working day before filters, fewer with a state, type or name filter.

Ready-made inputs, each a one-click run:

  • New companies registered in India on the latest day
  • New Section 8 (non-profit) companies in India, newest 100

From an AI assistant, add the MCP connector https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=data_daemon/india-new-company-registrations in Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor and ask "which software companies were incorporated in Pune this week?".

FAQ

How many companies are registered in India every day?
About 800 per working day in October 2026: 15,892 companies over 20 weekdays, plus about 420 on each Saturday and almost none on Sundays and public holidays. The month from 1 to 29 October totalled 17,622 companies (LLPs not included).

Which state registers the most new companies in India?
Maharashtra: 2,940 of the 17,622 companies incorporated from 1 to 29 October 2026 (16.7%), followed by Uttar Pradesh (1,931), Karnataka (1,415), Telangana (1,326) and Delhi (1,321).

How can I get a list of newly registered companies in India?
The MCA portal shows one company at a time. For a list by incorporation date, use a directory that mirrors the register by date, or the Actor above, which returns each day's new companies as JSON, CSV or Excel and can run on a schedule with only-new delivery.

Is there an MCA API for new company registrations?
MCA does not offer a public REST API for new incorporations; its master-data search is a web form with a captcha. The Actor above exposes the daily lists through Apify's API: POST https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/data_daemon~india-new-company-registrations/run-sync-get-dataset-items.

What do CIN codes like PN, MR or UW mean?
They are state codes used by newer Registrars of Companies: PN Pune, MR Mumbai II, ME Nagpur (all Maharashtra), UW Uttar Pradesh II, DC Delhi II, WR Kolkata II (West Bengal) and TZ Coimbatore (Tamil Nadu). In October 2026 they appeared on 26% of new CINs.

How many Section 8 companies are registered each month?
1,302 from 1 to 29 October 2026, 7.4% of all incorporations. Most declared social work (61%) or education (20%) as their main activity.

Does the data include director names, phone numbers or emails?
No. It covers company facts only: name, CIN, type, registrar, state, activity, capital, registered office and the number of directors.

Numbers are from the MCA register as listed by companies.dubleu.co and read on 30 October 2026; recent dates can still grow as late registrations appear. LLPs are not included.

Many developers focus on building new features but sometimes overlook proper testing. This can lead to problems after an application is released. Testing helps identify bugs, improve functionality, and make software more reliable.

Both manual and automated testing have their own benefits. Manual testing helps explore real user experiences, while automation makes repetitive checks faster and more consistent.

I believe software quality should be a priority from the beginning of every development project, not just before launch. Platforms like IAMQA also provide a place to explore software testing and quality assurance topics.

title: Figma Auto Layout From Image: Get Responsive Frames Fast
description:
Originally published on Crafttor.

Turning a screenshot into layers is useful. Turning it into auto layout is a different level. With Figma auto layout from an image, sections grow when text gets longer. Lists close gaps when you delete an item, and frames stretch when you resize them. That is the difference between a picture made of layers and a working design.

This guide explains how Image to Figma Design's Turbo AI mode builds auto layout and how to judge the result. It also shows how to fix the sections that need a nudge.

Why auto layout matters for converted screens

A plain conversion places every element at a fixed position. It looks right until you change something. Then text overlaps, buttons do not grow, and cards stay the same height while their content overflows.

Auto layout solves this by describing relationships instead of coordinates:

  • Direction. Children stack vertically or horizontally.
  • Gap. A fixed space between children.
  • Padding. Space between the frame edge and its content.
  • Sizing. Each child can hug its content, fill the space, or stay fixed.

When a converted screen uses auto layout, editing behaves like editing a real design.

How Turbo AI builds auto layout from an image

Image to Figma Design has two modes. Fast uses classic computer vision, shape detection and text recognition, and places positioned layers for 1 credit. Turbo AI, for 2 credits, rebuilds the screen as nested auto layout frames.

In practice, Turbo AI looks at the screenshot and decides:

  • Which elements belong together, such as an icon and its label.
  • Which groups repeat, such as cards in a grid or rows in a list.
  • Which direction each group flows.
  • How the groups nest inside larger sections.

The result is a tree of frames. A page frame contains sections. Sections contain rows or grids. Rows contain items. Each level uses auto layout.

Generate auto layout from an image, step by step

  1. Install Image to Figma Design from the Figma Community.
  2. Run it in any Figma file, on any plan.
  3. Sign in with a free Crafttor account.
  4. Add a screenshot by drag-and-drop, browse or paste.
  5. Select Turbo AI.
  6. Convert and select the top-level frame.
  7. Inspect the auto layout settings on each level, from the page down.

How to judge auto layout quality

Do not judge by appearance alone. Test behavior.

Test 1: Text growth

Double a heading's length. Content below should move down, not overlap.

Test 2: List editing

Duplicate a list item or card. The list should grow. Delete one and the gap should close.

Test 3: Width change

Drag the page frame wider. Sections set to fill should stretch. Fixed elements like icons should keep their size.

Test 4: Spacing consistency

Click through sibling items. Similar items should share the same gap and padding values.

If a section fails a test, fix that section only. You do not need to rebuild the whole screen.

Fixing common auto layout issues

A section does not stretch. Select its children and set width to "Fill container". Make sure the parent has auto layout and enough width.

Text overflows its box. Set the text layer to "Hug" height and "Fill" width, so it wraps and grows.

Uneven gaps between items. Select the parent frame and set one gap value. Remove any spacer shapes inside.

A group is in the wrong direction. Switch the parent's direction between vertical and horizontal.

Elements that should overlap. Badges on avatars or labels over images need absolute positioning. Turn on "Ignore auto layout" for that child.

Too many wrapper frames. If a frame holds only one child and adds nothing, select it and ungroup or remove the frame.

Making the layout truly responsive

Auto layout gives you flexible frames, but responsiveness also depends on your decisions:

  • Set min and max widths on content containers to stop text lines getting too long.
  • Use wrap on horizontal rows of cards so they move to a new line on narrow frames.
  • Build breakpoint variants for desktop, tablet and mobile when layouts change significantly.
  • Replace generic frames with components so changes apply everywhere.

If your goal is code, our screenshot to HTML guide continues from here.

When auto layout is not worth it

Sometimes you only want a quick reference. If you will trace over a screen, extract text or measure spacing, Fast mode is cheaper and quicker. Use Turbo AI for screens you will keep editing.

Limits to expect

Very busy illustrations, heavy gradients and low-resolution or blurry screenshots make structure harder to read. Complex screens may need light cleanup. Higher-resolution screenshots, about 1x to 2x of the real UI, give the most reliable structure.

Permission

Build auto layout from screens you own or have permission to use. For study of other products, rebuild to learn and do not ship copies.

Get structured frames from your next screenshot

Run one real screen through Turbo AI and do the four tests. Install Image to Figma Design and use your free daily credits. For the basics of conversion, see how to convert an image to Figma.

FAQ

Can Figma create auto layout from an image by itself?

Placing an image in Figma gives you a flat image fill. You need a converter, such as Image to Figma Design's Turbo AI mode, to rebuild it as auto layout frames.

Which mode creates auto layout?

Turbo AI rebuilds the screen as nested auto layout frames and uses 2 credits. Fast mode places positioned layers for 1 credit.

Will the auto layout be perfect?

It is a strong starting structure. Run the text, list and width tests, then fix any section that does not behave as expected.

Can I use the result for responsive design?

Yes. Nested auto layout is the base for responsive frames. Add min and max widths, wrap settings and breakpoint variants as needed.

title: Nightly Marketplace Logs: Reproducing Cost Attribution Across Search Backends
description:
Short answer: Start with an Elasticsearch-based backend for capturing and searching a marketplace pipeline's application logs, then accept it only if a replay proves that retries and merchant cost attribution remain explainable.

The best backend for a nightly marketplace pipeline is the one that lets a reviewer reproduce an allocation after retries, not the one with the longest feature list. Elasticsearch-based systems are the sensible starting point because they combine high-performance ingestion with search over structured and unstructured logs, but the selection should be settled by a replay experiment: identical events, identical logical run IDs, and a written pass/fail rule.

That distinction matters at 09:00, when a merchant asks why a batch received a particular share of processing cost. A log message is not evidence by itself. The evidence is the relationship between the logical run, its delivery attempts, the item count, and the allocation fields.

What does a nightly run need to prove?

Give every event a stable run_id, merchant_id, job_name, item_count, allocated_cost_usd, request_id, attempt_id, and schema version. Keep the logical identity separate from the delivery identity. A retry is an additional fact; it must not overwrite the first attempt or silently turn two records into one.

I would begin with a 10,000-event fixture covering five merchants, duplicate delivery attempts, and one failed retry. Those are test inputs, not platform limits. Preserve the original fixture and a hash of its normalized form. If the team changes field names between runs, it should discover that difference instead of calling it a backend result.

The acceptance question is narrow: can an operator retrieve every event for one logical run, distinguish its attempts, and recompute the merchant allocation from stored fields? A trace_id or span_id can support correlation, but it does not turn a log backend into a distributed-tracing span tree.

That is the test.

Infrai belongs in the same experiment when the application wants a plain REST boundary for this search leg and a contract that can be inspected before the harness sends data. It is an option to measure, not an assumption about the winner.

Which logging backend should capture and search application logs?

Run the same fixture through each candidate's supported collection path. Measure three things separately: semantic recall, reconciliation, and operational boundary. Semantic recall passes when the known events for a selected run are recoverable in the agreed time window. Reconciliation passes when duplicate attempts remain visible and the allocation can be calculated from fields rather than free-text interpretation. The boundary check records retention, deletion, access, and the controls that must be supplied elsewhere.

Fail the candidate if a retry is silently collapsed, if the cost requires guessing from a message, or if a reviewer needs an undocumented screen to explain the result. I would also record the fixture hash, the schema version, the selected run, and the exact evidence used for the allocation in the result itself. That extra bookkeeping is deliberately dull: without it, a later replay can compare two different normalized datasets and still report a false regression. Latency and ingestion cost are useful secondary observations; neither should rescue a system that loses the audit trail. The experiment is meant to make disagreement inspectable, not to produce a decorative score.

Repeatability beats a polished dashboard.

The following Go probe intentionally sends no invented search filters. The verified search surface is GET /v1/logs/search, while its filtering parameters are not declared in discovery. A production harness should inspect the live schema before adding fixture-specific fields.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func get(client *http.Client, url, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    // curl -X GET "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search" -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY"
    body, err := get(client, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search", key)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The probe checks response status, surfaces a useful error body, honors Retry-After, and reads the bearer key from the environment. It is a reachability leg, not a fabricated benchmark. The replay decision still depends on the candidate-specific collection and search contract.

Which backends deserve a leg in the experiment?

Elasticsearch is the baseline. Its ingestion and query strengths suit structured fields such as merchant and run identifiers as well as unstructured messages, and Logstash and Beats provide established collection paths. Elastic Cloud is the managed form of that option. The cost is operational responsibility around index design, schema evolution, retention, and the search cluster itself.

OpenSearch is a serious comparison when the team already operates in an AWS or OpenSearch environment. AWS OpenSearch offers a managed Elasticsearch-family service, but compatibility should be tested with the actual fixture rather than assumed from similar query language. The question is whether the operational boundary and business-field search remain acceptable after retries.

Grafana Loki makes a different trade-off: it is well suited to label-oriented service logs and Grafana-centered tailing. It belongs in the experiment when labels are stable and bounded. It is a weaker default for arbitrary searches over many attribution fields if making those fields labels creates a cardinality problem.

Datadog is attractive when a team values a hosted observability workflow and wants less infrastructure to operate. Its broader product surface does not remove the need to test logical-run reconstruction, retention, and access boundaries. A hosted interface is not automatically an audit model.

Infrai is one measured leg for a team that wants a plain REST boundary around this workflow: the application contract can stay stable while the service behind that capability changes. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and exposes request schemas without a key, which is useful for a replay harness that must verify a contract before sending data. A separate operational advantage is breadth under one key: live discovery describes 295 routes across 20 modules, so adjacent backend work can share one credential and one billing boundary instead of accumulating separate integration boundaries.

Backend Access shape Strong fit Main boundary to test
Elasticsearch Log shippers and managed service options Search-heavy structured and unstructured logs Index, shard, schema, and retention ownership
OpenSearch Managed or self-operated search service AWS or OpenSearch operating boundary Fixture compatibility and service controls
Grafana Loki Label-oriented collection and query Stable labels and Grafana-centered tailing High-cardinality attribution fields
Datadog Hosted observability service Low infrastructure ownership Data model and platform dependency
Infrai REST capability under one key A measured, contract-inspected search leg No alerting or span-tree query

Teams running a marketplace's nightly allocation pipeline should try Infrai for the REST-based observability leg when contract inspection and a polling-oriented evaluation matter, and should choose Elasticsearch or OpenSearch when search-cluster control and a mature search operating model are the primary requirements. That is the decision rule, not a claim that one backend wins every workload.

What remains outside the logging decision?

The acceptance record must name its exclusions. This capability surface has no alerting or notification routes, so threshold polling and notification delivery need another mechanism. It has no distributed-trace span-tree query, source-map reversal, crash symbolization, Electron minidump parsing, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring. A health-check service remains the appropriate complement when the question is whether a scheduled task ran at all.

The compliance boundary is concrete too: there is no change-audit log, evaluation-statistics view, parent-child dependency view, recycle bin, user-level log deletion interface, bulk export, or subscription interface in the stated surface. Retention and cold-storage settings have no configuration entry point here. A specialist archive, tracing, session-replay, or health-check product is the better choice when one of those features is an acceptance criterion.

Roll out the result without losing evidence

Start with a shadow writer for one nightly job and keep the current backend authoritative. Send the same normalized event to the candidate, preserve the raw fixture, and reconcile counts and duplicate behavior before moving reads for even one merchant cohort. Record the schema version and fixture hash beside the result.

The final choice is the backend that makes cost attribution reproducible under retry, with an explicit owner for every missing capability. Search quality is the first gate. Operational convenience comes after the evidence survives.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the structured application logging guide and use the replay fixture as the first verification step.

References

OpenTelemetry's log signal concepts are a useful vocabulary for separating structured log attributes from related signals. The backend documentation below describes the main alternatives without treating any one of them as a universal answer.

Sources

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/index.html
  • https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/
  • https://grafana.com/docs/loki/latest/
  • https://docs.datadoghq.com/logs/
  • https://docs.infrai.cc
