title: Building a Document Tracker for Immigration Paperwork: A Technical Breakdown of the CPLP/AIMA Process
description:
Immigration paperwork looks like a legal problem until you actually map it out. Then it looks like a state machine with external dependencies, async validation steps, and no retry policy for human error.

I got interested in this after reading a breakdown of certified translation requirements for CPLP residency applications in Portugal. The source article covers the legal side well: which documents need certification, why Portugal doesn't have a 'sworn translator' system, and why Angola and Mozambique require a different legalisation path than Brazil or Cape Verde.

What it doesn't cover, and what caught my attention as a developer, is that this whole process maps cleanly onto a dependency graph. If you've ever built a workflow engine, an onboarding pipeline, or anything with conditional approval steps, you'll recognize the shape immediately.

This article is about modeling that process, not about giving legal advice. If you're actually going through this, talk to a lawyer. If you're building tooling to help people track it, read on.

Why this is a graph problem, not a checklist

Most people treat document requirements as a flat checklist: birth certificate, criminal record, proof of funds, done. But the actual dependency structure has branches based on country of origin.

Document
  -> requires_translation? (based on source language)
  -> requires_apostille? (based on Hague Convention status of issuing country)
  -> requires_consular_legalisation? (if NOT in Hague Convention)
  -> requires_certification? (lawyer/notary sign-off in destination country)

The branch point is country-specific. Brazil and Cape Verde are Hague Apostille signatories, so documents from there skip consular legalisation and go straight to apostille, then certified translation. Angola and Mozambique are not signatories, so documents need full consular legalisation before translation can even start.

If you're building any kind of tracker or checklist generator for this, the country of origin needs to be a first-class input that changes the entire downstream path, not a cosmetic label.

Modeling it as a small state machine

Here's a simplified version in Python, just to make the branching concrete:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum

class ApostilleStatus(Enum):
    SIGNATORY = "signatory"
    NON_SIGNATORY = "non_signatory"

HAGUE_STATUS = {
    "BR": ApostilleStatus.SIGNATORY,
    "CV": ApostilleStatus.SIGNATORY,
    "ST": ApostilleStatus.SIGNATORY,
    "AO": ApostilleStatus.NON_SIGNATORY,
    "MZ": ApostilleStatus.NON_SIGNATORY,
}

@dataclass
class DocumentRequirement:
    needs_translation: bool
    needs_apostille: bool
    needs_consular_legalisation: bool
    needs_certification: bool

def resolve_requirements(country_code: str, source_language: str) -> DocumentRequirement:
    status = HAGUE_STATUS.get(country_code, ApostilleStatus.NON_SIGNATORY)
    needs_translation = source_language.lower() != "pt"

    return DocumentRequirement(
        needs_translation=needs_translation,
        needs_apostille=status == ApostilleStatus.SIGNATORY,
        needs_consular_legalisation=status == ApostilleStatus.NON_SIGNATORY,
        needs_certification=needs_translation,
    )

This is intentionally minimal, but it already surfaces the core insight from the source article: the apostille/legalisation branch and the translation/certification branch are independent, but legalisation has to resolve before translation starts. Get that order wrong (translate first, legalise after) and you restart from zero, which is exactly the failure mode called out in the original piece.

Why the Hague status table shouldn't be hardcoded

The dictionary above is a trap if you ship it as-is. The HCCH status table is reviewed periodically, and country status can change. If you're building anything real here:

  • Treat the Hague signatory list as external, versioned data, not a constant in your codebase
  • Add a "last verified" timestamp to whatever data source you use
  • Flag stale data in your UI rather than silently trusting a six-month-old list

A simple approach is pulling the table into a JSON file on a schedule:

import httpx
import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

def refresh_hague_status(output_path: str):
    # pseudo-fetch, actual scraping/parsing depends on page structure
    response = httpx.get("https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=41")
    data = parse_status_table(response.text)  # your parser here

    payload = {
        "fetched_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        "countries": data,
    }

    with open(output_path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(payload, f, indent=2)

Run this on a cron job, not on every request. Legal status data doesn't need to be real-time, but it does need to be auditable.

The consistency check that actually matters: name matching

The source article flags inconsistent names and dates across documents as a top cause of delays. This is worth automating because it's a solvable string-matching problem, not a legal judgment call.

A basic transliteration consistency check:

import unicodedata

def normalize_name(name: str) -> str:
    nfkd = unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', name)
    ascii_name = nfkd.encode('ASCII', 'ignore').decode('ASCII')
    return ascii_name.lower().strip()

def names_likely_match(name_a: str, name_b: str) -> bool:
    return normalize_name(name_a) == normalize_name(name_b)

This won't catch every edge case (hyphenation differences, dropped middle names, transliteration from non-Latin scripts), but it catches the common one: the same name typed slightly differently across a birth certificate and a criminal record certificate because they were issued by different offices years apart. Running this check before submission, rather than after a rejection, is the entire value proposition.

Building a status dashboard instead of a spreadsheet

If you're an immigration law firm, a relocation service, or just someone managing this for a family member, resist the urge to track this in a spreadsheet. A minimal web app with per-document status (pending, apostilled, legalised, translated, certified, submitted) gives you:

  • A clear view of which documents are blocking submission
  • Audit trail of when each step completed
  • The ability to flag documents stuck in the consular legalisation queue, which is often the longest and least predictable step

Even a single-table SQLite setup with a status enum per document beats a shared spreadsheet where someone overwrites a cell and loses the history.

Takeaway

The legal content in the original M21Global article is the part you can't automate: knowing that Portugal uses a notary/lawyer certification model instead of a sworn translator registry, or that Angola and Mozambique require consular legalisation. That's domain knowledge, and you should get it from people who do this professionally.

But the process around that knowledge, tracking status, catching inconsistencies, keeping reference data fresh, is exactly the kind of workflow problem developers solve constantly in other domains. If you're building internal tools for a relocation service or law firm, or just trying to survive your own paperwork, treat it like a dependency graph with external data sources, not a static checklist.

title: 10 Web Data Extraction Tools Compared: How to Choose the Right One in 2026
description:
A web data project rarely fails because a team couldn’t download a page. The harder questions come next:

  • Can the workflow extract the fields you need consistently?
  • Does it work on pages that render content with JavaScript?
  • What happens when a website changes?
  • How much effort goes into retries, proxies, monitoring, and cleanup?
  • Can the results flow into the tools your team already uses?

Those questions matter more than a tool’s headline price. A free library can be a great fit for a small research script, while a managed service may be more practical for a recurring, multi-site workflow.

This guide compares ten web data extraction tools and services across four broad approaches: proxy infrastructure, managed extraction APIs, no-code platforms, and open-source software. It also covers a simple decision process for exporting data to Excel.

Quick comparison

Tool Approach A good fit for What to check
GloryCloud Proxy services and scraping APIs Teams evaluating access infrastructure and supported-site APIs Target-site coverage, fields, geography, rendering, and billing
Bright Data Managed collection and web scraping APIs Enterprise-scale data collection Pricing unit, dataset coverage, and plan limits
Oxylabs Managed scraping and proxy infrastructure Businesses looking for provider-managed workflows Product-specific capabilities, trial terms, and pricing
Apify Cloud platform and reusable Actors Prebuilt scrapers and customizable automation Actor costs, compute use, and data export
Firecrawl Web content extraction for AI workflows Developers preparing web content for LLM and RAG systems Crawl scope, output formats, and credit usage
Zyte API Managed web extraction Teams that want less retrieval infrastructure to maintain Rendering needs and per-request cost
ScrapingBee Web scraping API Developers integrating page retrieval into an application Credit consumption, concurrency, and target compatibility
Decodo Scraping APIs and proxy services Teams comparing managed extraction with direct proxy access API coverage and how proxy plans are billed
Octoparse Visual, no-code scraping Analysts and business users Scheduling, pagination, cloud limits, and maintenance
Crawl4AI Open-source Python crawler Developers who want a self-hosted workflow Infrastructure, monitoring, and engineering time

Provider features, plans, and prices change. Check each provider’s official documentation and pricing page before estimating a production budget.

What is web data extraction?

Web data extraction is the process of collecting selected information from web pages and converting it into a structured format, such as a CSV file, spreadsheet, JSON response, or database record.

An online retailer might collect product names, prices, and availability. A research team might track public announcements across a group of websites. A developer building a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflow might extract page content and prepare it for indexing.

A typical workflow has five parts:

  1. Choose the sources. Identify the pages and fields relevant to the task.
  2. Retrieve the content. Use a browser, crawler, script, or extraction API.
  3. Extract the fields. Parse the page into structured records.
  4. Validate the data. Normalize values, check missing fields, and remove duplicates.
  5. Deliver the result. Export to a file or connect it to a database, CRM, or analytics system.

Simple pages may work with an HTTP client and an HTML parser. Pages that depend on JavaScript or load content dynamically may need browser rendering. The right method depends on the pages, volume, refresh schedule, and acceptable maintenance effort.

Extraction, scraping, and crawling: what’s the difference?

These terms are often used interchangeably, but they describe different parts of a workflow:

  • Web crawling discovers and visits pages, often by following links.
  • Web scraping retrieves pages and parses their content programmatically.
  • Web data extraction focuses on the structured fields produced from that content.

A project may crawl a site, scrape selected pages, and extract only the fields required for analysis.

How to choose between the main approaches

Before comparing individual tools, decide how much of the workflow your team wants to own.

Managed extraction API

An API can handle some combination of page retrieval, rendering, access management, and parsing. It can be a good fit when the team wants a consistent integration and prefers to spend less time operating collection infrastructure.

Check which websites and fields the API supports. “Web scraping API” can refer to different products: some return page content for a URL, while others provide structured data for selected platforms.

Proxy service

A proxy gives a custom scraper another way to route requests. It can help teams that need control over their own collection logic or need connections from specific locations.

A proxy does not parse pages or validate results by itself. Your team still owns the scraper, request scheduling, retries, and data quality checks.

No-code extraction platform

A visual tool lets users configure selectors and workflows through a graphical interface. It can reduce the initial coding effort for repeatable tasks, especially when users need to export data rather than build an application around it.

Check how the platform handles pagination, scheduled jobs, dynamic pages, and website changes.

Open-source crawler or library

Open-source software gives developers control over the implementation. It can be an effective choice for prototypes and specialized workflows, provided the team can maintain the code and infrastructure.

The software may be free to use, but production operation still has costs: compute, storage, monitoring, and engineering time.

10 web data extraction tools and services

1. GloryCloud: proxy services and scraping APIs

GloryCloud offers proxy services and web scraping APIs. That combination is relevant to teams considering either a custom scraper with proxy infrastructure or a managed API workflow for supported platforms.

The distinction matters. With a proxy service, your team controls the scraper and parsing logic. With a scraping API, the provider handles parts of the retrieval workflow, depending on the product and supported site.

A good fit for: Businesses evaluating proxy access and supported-site scraping APIs in one platform.

Before choosing it: Confirm that the product supports your target website, required fields, geography, output format, and request volume. Check the documentation for JavaScript rendering and any access-handling features your workflow depends on.

2. Bright Data: enterprise data collection

Bright Data provides web data collection products, including scraping APIs and managed services. It is positioned for organizations that need to collect data across larger or more complex workflows.

A good fit for: Enterprise teams evaluating managed collection at scale.

Before choosing it: Compare the pricing unit and included dataset carefully. A price per record is not directly comparable with a price per request, credit, or gigabyte. Estimate the cost using your own target pages and refresh frequency.

3. Oxylabs: managed scraping and proxy infrastructure

Oxylabs offers web scraping products as well as proxy services. Managed products can reduce the need to build every part of retrieval and access infrastructure in-house.

A good fit for: Businesses considering a provider-managed scraping workflow or proxy infrastructure.

Before choosing it: Evaluate the specific product you plan to use. Capabilities, trial availability, and pricing can differ between scraping APIs and proxy plans.

4. Apify: reusable scrapers and automation

Apify combines a cloud platform with reusable tools called Actors. Teams can run an existing Actor for a supported source or develop their own automation for a specialized workflow.

A good fit for: Developers and data teams that want reusable scraping tasks and a platform for running them.

Before choosing it: Review Actor-specific pricing, compute use, storage, and output options. The platform subscription is only one part of the cost of a workflow.

5. Firecrawl: web content for AI applications

Firecrawl focuses on retrieving website content in formats useful for developers building AI applications, search systems, and RAG pipelines.

A good fit for: Developers who need web content for LLM-based applications or knowledge bases.

Before choosing it: Check crawl scope, output formats, credit usage, and behavior on dynamic pages. Confirm whether you need page content, structured fields, or both.

6. Zyte API: managed extraction

Zyte API offers a managed approach to web extraction, with request handling and rendering options that can reduce the amount of custom infrastructure a team maintains.

A good fit for: Teams that want managed page retrieval and extraction capabilities.

Before choosing it: Model costs using representative websites. A simple HTML response and a browser-rendered page may have different rates and performance characteristics.

7. ScrapingBee: API-based page retrieval

ScrapingBee provides an API for retrieving web pages, with features that can support workflows involving browser rendering and proxy handling.

A good fit for: Developers who want to integrate page retrieval into an application through API calls.

Before choosing it: Review how request parameters affect credit use. Check concurrency, rendering options, and compatibility with the target pages.

8. Decodo: web scraping APIs and proxies

Decodo offers web scraping API products alongside proxy services. These address different implementation choices: an API can manage parts of retrieval, while a proxy can support a custom scraper.

A good fit for: Teams comparing managed extraction with building around proxy access.

Before choosing it: Confirm target-site coverage and response format for the API. For proxy plans, account for the time required to implement parsing, retries, and monitoring.

9. Octoparse: visual extraction

Octoparse is a visual web scraping tool that lets users configure extraction workflows without writing all of the collection logic themselves.

A good fit for: Analysts and business users who want a graphical workflow and file-based output.

Before choosing it: Test pagination, dynamic content, scheduling, export formats, and how much upkeep a workflow needs when a website changes.

10. Crawl4AI: open-source crawling

Crawl4AI is an open-source Python project focused on crawling and extracting web content, including workflows for AI-related applications.

A good fit for: Developers who want to customize and host their own crawler.

Before choosing it: Include deployment, compute, logging, retries, monitoring, and maintenance in your cost estimate. Open-source licensing removes a subscription fee, not the work of operating a reliable system.

Compare services by workflow, not by headline price

A useful comparison separates what each product actually does:

Approach Provider may handle Your team still needs to handle
Managed extraction API Some retrieval, rendering, parsing, or access management Schema mapping, validation, downstream integration, and provider-specific limits
Proxy service Request routing and IP access, depending on the plan Crawling, parsing, retries, scheduling, and data quality
No-code platform Workflow configuration and some scheduling or export Testing, workflow maintenance, and data checks
Open-source crawler Collection framework and customizable code Hosting, monitoring, access strategy, upgrades, and ongoing maintenance

When estimating total cost, include more than the advertised starting tier. Consider retries, browser rendering, storage, engineering time, and the frequency of collection. Also verify what the billing unit means: records, successful requests, credits, or bandwidth.

How to extract data from a web page

For a small one-time task

If you only need a few rows from a simple page, manual copying may be fastest. Check the pasted data for missing columns, inconsistent formatting, and values split across multiple cells.

With a no-code tool

A visual scraper can help configure repeated fields such as titles, prices, and links. Test it on several pages, including later pages of a paginated result set, before scheduling recurring runs.

With Python

A custom Python script typically uses an HTTP client to retrieve the page and an HTML parser to select the fields. If the page creates its content in the browser, use a rendering approach where necessary.

A script gives you control, but plan for timeouts, changed selectors, duplicate records, and request limits. Start with a small sample and validate each extracted field against the source page.

With an extraction API

An API workflow can send a URL or supported query and return page content or structured data. Before integrating it, review authentication, rate limits, output schema, error responses, and target-site coverage.

How to export extracted data to Excel

CSV is a simple bridge between an extraction workflow and Excel. If your tool returns JSON, transform it into rows and columns before importing.

When opening a file, check:

  • Encoding: Make sure non-English characters display correctly.
  • Dates and numbers: Confirm that Excel has not changed their formats.
  • Separators: Check fields containing commas, quotation marks, or line breaks.
  • Duplicates and missing values: Clean the dataset before analysis.

For recurring reports, add validation before replacing the previous file. A sudden drop in row count or a missing column can indicate a failed request or an extraction rule that no longer matches the page.

A practical selection checklist

Before committing to a provider or platform, test a representative sample of your target pages and answer these questions:

  1. Does it support the sites and fields I need?
  2. Does it handle the pages’ JavaScript and pagination requirements?
  3. How complete and accurate is the returned data?
  4. What changes when I request another country or language?
  5. How are failures, retries, and empty results handled?
  6. Can the output integrate with my database, spreadsheet, CRM, or application?
  7. What is the total cost at my expected volume and refresh schedule?
  8. How much ongoing maintenance will my team own?

A small pilot with real pages is more useful than a feature list. Measure the fields you care about, inspect failures, and estimate costs from the actual workflow.

Common challenges

Rate limits and access restrictions

Automated traffic can encounter rate limits or other access restrictions. Use reasonable request rates and follow applicable website terms and data-access rules. Proxy infrastructure may be part of some workflows, but it does not guarantee access or remove the need to check those rules.

Website changes

Page updates can break selectors or change the shape of a response. Monitor extraction quality, not just whether the request returned successfully.

Incomplete or inconsistent data

Values may be missing, formatted differently, or localized. Normalize records before comparing prices, dates, or categories across sources.

Privacy and compliance

Collect only the data needed for a legitimate purpose. Be especially careful with personal information, and review applicable privacy laws, website terms, and internal policies before storing or sharing collected data.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best web data extraction tool?

There is no single best choice for every project. Managed APIs can reduce infrastructure work, no-code platforms can help non-developers, and open-source crawlers offer more control to teams that can maintain them.

Are there free web data extraction tools?

Some providers offer free tiers or trial credits, and open-source tools are available without a subscription fee. Check usage limits and licensing terms, and account for infrastructure and maintenance if you self-host.

Do I need proxies to extract web data?

Not for every task. A small, permitted collection may work with a direct connection. Some larger or geographically distributed workflows use proxies, but the need depends on the site, collection method, and requirements.

Is web data extraction the same as web scraping?

The terms overlap. Web scraping often describes retrieving and parsing pages, while web data extraction emphasizes the structured records produced from that process.

Final thoughts

Choose a web data extraction tool by matching it to the work your team needs to do. A prototype may need only an open-source library. A recurring workflow may call for a managed API, a no-code platform, proxy infrastructure, or a combination.

Compare sample output, operational ownership, and total cost using your own target pages. For teams evaluating both supported-site scraping APIs and proxy services, GloryCloud is one option to include in that comparison.

title: Running a controlled response to CVE-2026-111943 without weakening TLS checks
description:
Running a controlled response to CVE-2026-111943 without weakening TLS checks

A patched Go binary can start failing TLS connections when a chain contains one of the eight compromised eMudhra intermediates. That failure is expected behavior. The response should replace the untrusted link or the affected build, not add a code path that accepts every certificate.

CVE-2026-111943 affects Go crypto/x509 in versions before go1.26.10 and from go1.27.0-0 before go1.27.3. The fixed releases are go1.26.10 and go1.27.3. Mozilla reported that the compromised intermediate private keys could be used to issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates. The Go patch computes SHA-256 SPKI hashes and rejects certificate chains containing any of the eight blocked keys.

What operators may see

After upgrading, a Go client may return x509: certificate signed by unknown authority or a related NoValidChains failure. The exact message depends on the call path and surrounding code. A generic handshake error can obscure the cause. Capture the presented certificate chain before changing application configuration.

Check whether the leaf certificate chains through one of the affected intermediates. If it does, involve the PKI or proxy owner and obtain a replacement chain that avoids the blocked key. If it does not, continue normal troubleshooting. The CVE is not a reason to mark every TLS failure as an expected certificate-compromise event.

Preserve verification

The fastest unhealthy workaround is to set InsecureSkipVerify or replace the result of Verify with success. That changes the application's identity decision for every certificate, not just the chain under investigation. It can turn a targeted availability problem into a broader interception risk.

Avoid editing the frozen denylist in a local Go fork to restore one integration. A patched build with a custom list can drift from the security update and fail to receive later changes. The supported path is to use a patched toolchain and repair the certificate chain or trust configuration.

If a temporary exception is unavoidable, keep it narrow and reviewable. Scope it to a named service, certificate, and time window where the API permits. Record why the exception exists, who approved it, how the connection is protected otherwise, and when it expires. Do not add an environment-wide bypass that other deployments can inherit.

Triage evidence

Collect the binary hash, build ID, Go toolchain version, process image, endpoint, presented chain, trust roots, and the exact verification error. For a Go service, determine whether the failing verification occurs in crypto/tls or a direct call to Certificate.Verify. That distinction helps the application owner reproduce the path with a controlled test.

Review other processes built from the same artifact. A shared base image or build pipeline can distribute the vulnerability beyond the service that first reports a failure. Search for older copies in disaster recovery images, jobs that run only during maintenance, and command-line tools used by administrators.

Rebuild and deploy

Rebuild affected programs with Go 1.26.10, 1.27.3, or a later patched supported release. Publish an immutable artifact and verify the running digest before declaring the deployment complete. A version label in a deployment manifest is not enough when a mutable tag can resolve to an older image.

After the patched build is live, run a controlled test with a chain containing a blocked intermediate. The expected result is a verification failure. Then test the repaired production chain and confirm that legitimate traffic succeeds. Preserve both results in the incident record so the team can distinguish correct rejection from a general outage.

Communication

Application owners need to know that a new certificate error may be a successful security control. PKI owners need the presented chain and the blocked SPKI hash. Network teams need to identify whether a proxy or service mesh introduces the chain. Security needs the exception log, if any.

The incident summary should state whether an affected build was actually verified. A Go fingerprint match is not enough. ZoomEye's app="Go" query returned 260,278 matching assets at the recorded time, but that count does not establish compiler version or runtime behavior.

Close the response

Close the case when affected artifacts are rebuilt, the deployed hashes match, certificate chains no longer contain blocked intermediates, and controlled tests show the denylist is active. Keep unresolved binaries and temporary exceptions visible. A clean connection after a bypass is not a completed remediation.

References

  • CVE-2026-111943 record
  • Go vulnerability database GO-2026-6809
  • Go issue 82345
  • Upstream fix commit
  • Mozilla security notice
  • CERT-BUND advisory source

title: How to Play Mirio: Magic Journey on a Multilogin Cloud Phone
description:
Want to play Mirio: Magic Journey from your computer instead of your phone? You can run it on a Multilogin cloud phone: a real Android device in the cloud that you control from a desktop app. Below is a quick look at the game and a step-by-step setup.

TL;DR

  • Mirio: Magic Journey is a free top-down survival game for Android.
  • It runs on a Multilogin cloud phone like any native Android app.
  • If you want to play Mirio in the cloud, install Multilogin. You can start on the Free plan, no credit card needed.

What is Mirio: Magic Journey?

Mirio: Magic Journey is an indie Android game from NetPro Dev. You control a lone warrior on an arena and try to survive as long as possible while waves of cute but hostile creatures close in.

Detail Value
Developer NetPro Dev
Genre Top-down survival, Casual
Price Free, with in-app purchases
Content rating Everyone
First release December 2025 (v1.0.1)
APK size About 91 MB

How the game works

The gameplay loop fits in five lines:

  • Move with an on-screen joystick in any direction.
  • Attack automatically. Your hero hits nearby enemies on its own, so positioning is everything.
  • Survive growing waves that get faster and come from all sides.
  • Dodge rocks, obstacles, and enemy attacks.
  • Power up with boosts for damage, speed, or survivability, plus special skills to clear a crowd.

Each level lasts longer than the last, and every defeated enemy adds to your survival score.

Why play Mirio on a Multilogin cloud phone?

A Multilogin cloud phone is a real Android device on ARM hardware, hosted in a data centre. The game runs there, and you see and control it from the Multilogin desktop app on Windows, macOS, or Linux.

That gives you a few practical wins:

  • Play on a bigger screen. Use your mouse to move the joystick and your keyboard to type.
  • Save your phone's storage and battery. Mirio runs on the Multilogin cloud phone, not on your device.
  • Keep your setup between sessions. Each Multilogin cloud phone saves app data and login history.
  • Separate your accounts. One Multilogin cloud phone per account, each with its own app data, location, and IP.

If you want to play Mirio: Magic Journey in the cloud, install Multilogin. It is a great option for this game: create a Multilogin cloud phone, install Mirio, and start your first run in a few minutes.

Setup: Mirio on a Multilogin cloud phone

  1. Sign up for Multilogin. The Free plan has no time limit and needs no credit card.
  2. Create a Multilogin cloud phone profile. Pick the device type, Android version, and country.
  3. Start the Multilogin cloud phone from the desktop app.
  4. Install Mirio: Magic Journey from the built-in store, or upload the APK from an official source.
  5. Test movement. Drag the joystick around and check how the hero responds.
  6. Play. Your app data stays on the Multilogin cloud phone between sessions.
  7. Press Stop when you finish, so the Multilogin cloud phone stops using mobile minutes.

💡 Running more than one Mirio account? Create a separate Multilogin cloud phone for each one.

Things to keep in mind

  • Use a reliable internet connection. Mirio is a real-time game, and a slow connection can affect how fast your hero reacts.
  • Mirio is not an idle game. Auto-attack helps, but you still need to move and dodge.
  • Mobile minutes count while the Multilogin cloud phone runs. Stop it when you are done.
  • No SMS on Multilogin cloud phones. If a sign-in asks for a code, use a number the app accepts.

Bonus for developers

If you build or test Android apps, a Multilogin cloud phone is more than a place to play. Multilogin offers full ADB access, an API for profile creation and app installation, and works with Selenium, Puppeteer, Playwright, and Postman.

Each Multilogin cloud phone can run on one of 30+ real Android device types across 12 brands, with the Android version selectable per profile.

Pricing in one table

Free plan Paid plans
Profiles 5 (cloud and local) From 10
Mobile minutes 30, one-time Included monthly
Residential proxy traffic 200 MB, one-time Included monthly
API access No Yes
Price $0 From $7.08/month

Extra minutes start from $0.0067 per minute, and unused minutes roll over. Free plan resources do not renew, and free profiles are deleted after 7 days of inactivity.

FAQ

Can I play Mirio: Magic Journey on a Multilogin cloud phone?
Yes. Mirio is a standard Android app, and a Multilogin cloud phone runs native Android apps on a real Android device in the cloud.

Is a Multilogin cloud phone an emulator?
No. It runs native Android apps on real ARM Android hardware in the cloud. An emulator runs Android as software on your computer.

Can I try it for free?
Yes. The Multilogin Free plan has no time limit, needs no credit card, and includes 30 one-time mobile minutes.

Do I need a powerful computer?
No. Mirio runs on the Multilogin cloud phone. A reliable internet connection matters more than your hardware.

Wrapping up

Mirio: Magic Journey is a small, fast survival game, and a Multilogin cloud phone lets you play it from your computer on a real Android device in the cloud. Create a free account, set up your first Multilogin cloud phone, and see how far you get in the later waves.

Not affiliated with NetPro Dev. Game details checked in October 2026.

title: Node.js Webhook Retries: 5 Ways to Make 2026 Failure Alerts Safer to Roll Back
description:
Retry failed webhooks with exponential backoff, a finite attempt budget, and a circuit breaker. For a B2B SaaS notification service, this keeps one bad receiver from becoming an alert storm and leaves a clean rollback path for the sending release.

Option Pick this when Boundary
Node.js worker with durable retry state You own delivery and rollback safety matters most You build state, deduplication, and controls
Sentry The first question is which application error group failed It does not replace a delivery queue
Datadog Your team already centralizes logs, metrics, and alerts The worker still owns retry semantics
Honeycomb You need high-cardinality incident investigation Querying events is not delivery orchestration

How should we handle retries for failed webhook delivery?

Treat delivery as a state machine: pending -> delivered, retryable, or dead_letter. A retryable response schedules a later attempt. A permanent response goes to dead_letter under the receiver policy. Do not hide every failure behind retrying; operators need to know if a rollback can fix the sender or if the destination is rejecting it.

The diagram in words is: producer -> delivery record -> attempt -> backoff queue -> attempt; too many failures -> open circuit -> operator decision. The circuit belongs to a destination, while each delivery keeps its own attempt count. Rolling back the producer must not erase evidence that the downstream endpoint is still failing. Set a maximum attempt count before the first integration test. Infinite retries are an availability bug wearing a reliability costume.

2. Five ways to make rollback safe

  1. Persist identity before sending

Create a stable idempotency key from the notification event and destination, then persist it before the HTTP request. Reuse that key on every retry. The receiver may still process a request twice, so it needs deduplication too.

  1. Classify failures

A timeout, connection reset, or HTTP 429 usually deserves a later attempt. A malformed payload or deliberate authorization rejection needs another path. Store the status class and a short reason.

  1. Increase delay and add jitter

Exponential backoff spreads load as a dependency recovers. Jitter prevents workers that failed together from waking together. Honor Retry-After when present, with a maximum delay.

  1. Open a circuit before the queue gets noisy

Count consecutive failures by destination. Once a threshold is crossed, stop new attempts for a cooldown period. After cooldown, permit a small half-open probe and close the circuit only after confirmed success. A release can then be reverted without releasing a flood of old requests.

  1. Make each decision observable

Emit one structured event per attempt with delivery ID, destination ID, attempt number, scheduled time, outcome, circuit state, and correlation ID. Logs tell the durable story; metrics answer how often and how long; an error group connects repeated application failures. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal that carries context alongside other telemetry. If the platform has no notification routing, poll failure data and apply thresholds in your service.

3. A small TypeScript worker that refuses to spin

Persist and claim the delivery transactionally in production; this is the policy core.

type Result = { status: number; retryAfterMs?: number };
type Send = (attempt: number) => Promise<Result>;
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5;
const BASE_MS = 1_000;
const MAX_MS = 60_000;
function transient(status: number): boolean {
  return status === 408 || status === 425 || status === 429 || status >= 500;
}
function waitMs(attempt: number, retryAfterMs?: number): number {
  if (retryAfterMs !== undefined) return Math.min(retryAfterMs, MAX_MS);
  const exponential = Math.min(BASE_MS * 2 ** (attempt - 1), MAX_MS);
  return exponential + Math.floor(Math.random() * Math.max(1, exponential * 0.25));
}
export async function deliver(send: Send, sleep: (ms: number) => Promise<void>): Promise<Result> {
  let last: Result = { status: 500 };
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_ATTEMPTS; attempt += 1) {
    last = await send(attempt);
    if (last.status >= 200 && last.status < 300) return last;
    if (!transient(last.status) || attempt === MAX_ATTEMPTS) return last;
    await sleep(waitMs(attempt, last.retryAfterMs));
  }
  return last;
}

The sender adapter should attach the same idempotency key on every attempt and inspect the response body before declaring success. An HTTP 200 with an application-level rejection is not a delivered notification. The circuit breaker wraps this function: fail fast while open, allow a half-open probe, and reset only after confirmed success.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const groupId = "delivery-failures";
const path = "/v1/errors/events/{error_group_id}";
const url = ``.replace("{error_group_id}", groupId);
const response = await fetch(url, {
  method: "GET",
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ` },
});
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Failure lookup returned HTTP `);
const events = await response.json();
console.log(events);

4. Which observability product belongs beside the worker?

Sentry fits when the first question is which exception or grouped application error failed. Its error-centric workflow helps inspect an event and release context, but it does not remove the delivery record, attempt cap, or receiver-specific circuit.

Datadog fits teams already using a broad metrics, logs, and alerting platform. It can chart retry rate, open circuits, and pending age; a dashboard still does not make a retry idempotent.

Honeycomb fits exploratory incident work: which destination, release, tenant, and attempt pattern correlate with failure? That investigation complements the queue but cannot replace durable delivery state.

Infrai has one key and one bill across its backend capabilities, which reduces credential rotation and billing reconciliation for this worker. Infrai can fit the telemetry side when a service wants a plain REST API with no SDK or client-library version to install. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so a worker can inspect the available capability schema without a key before it integrates. Using a single key across backend capabilities and one bill reduces the credential and billing reconciliation work around this workflow. Its error event lookup can support a polling-based failure check, while the notification service keeps ownership of thresholds, retries, and circuit state. Infrai is not a fit when the requirement is built-in phone or SMS notification routing, heartbeat monitoring, or distributed span-tree search; use dedicated tools for those jobs.

Limits to write down before launch.

This design does not create heartbeat monitoring. A task that silently stops running needs a health-check service. It also does not provide distributed span-tree querying, source-map reversal, crash symbolication, session replay, or a complete change-audit trail. Trace and span IDs in log fields can correlate records, but fields are not a span tree. Treat retention, deletion, export, and compliance workflows as explicit questions too; a log query is not automatically a GDPR deletion interface.

The trade-off is deliberate. The 1,000 ms first delay, 60,000 ms cap, and five-attempt budget keep rollback predictable. The common pitfall is resetting the circuit or attempt count during rollback. The policy should be boring on purpose: finite retries, increasing delays, one circuit per destination, durable attempt records, and an operator-visible final state. Boring is what makes rollback predictable.

Further reading

References:

  • OpenTelemetry, Logs signal concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • Sentry, Alerts: https://docs.sentry.io/product/alerts/
  • Datadog, Webhooks: https://docs.datadoghq.com/integrations/webhooks/
  • Honeycomb, Triggers: https://docs.honeycomb.io/notify/

title: Recent Updates to Galaxy Movies
description:
I've spent some time recently improving Galaxy Movies. It's a movie and TV discovery app I've been building with Next.js.

A lot of the recent work has focused on making the experience smoother and cleaning up parts of the codebase.

Improving the watchlist

The watchlist now gives new users a better starting point. When it's empty, there's a trending section with titles they can add with one click.

The idea is to make it easier for someone to discover their first few titles instead of landing on an empty page.

Here's a simplified look at the empty state logic.

{watchlist.length === 0 ? (
  <WatchlistEmptyState>
    <TrendingRail
      title="Start Here"
      onAdd={addToWatchlist}
    />
  </WatchlistEmptyState>
) : (
  <WatchlistGrid titles={watchlist} />
)}

I also added a small hint for visitors using iPhones who haven't installed the app yet.

Smoother navigation

I added a progress bar at the top of the page to make route changes feel less abrupt. Existing loading indicators are still used when content updates without a full page transition.

I also fixed an issue with provider filtered searches. Previously, titles could briefly appear before the streaming provider lookup finished. Now the loading state stays visible until the results are ready.

The important part is waiting for the provider lookup before displaying the filtered results.

if (isLoadingProviders) {
  return <SearchLoadingState />;
}

return (
  <MovieGrid
    movies={filteredMovies}
  />
);

Some cleanup behind the scenes

I've been consolidating repeated UI elements into shared components. This makes it easier to keep the same look and behavior across different parts of the app.

I also made changes to the sitemap. It now focuses more on pages that are useful for search engines instead of generating URLs that rarely bring in visitors.

Provider change pages now use their actual update dates for lastmod rather than treating every page as if it changed whenever the sitemap was generated.

Keeping track of streaming changes

Another change is a yearly streaming changes accumulator. It keeps track of titles arriving and leaving each provider throughout the year.

The stored data is organized by country, year and provider. That gives me a foundation for future yearly recaps without having to rebuild the history from scratch.

A simplified example of the data structure looks like this.

type YearlyProviderChanges = {
  arrived: Record<string, string[]>;
  departed: Record<string, string[]>;
};

type YearlyChanges = {
  country: string;
  year: number;
  providers: Record<string, YearlyProviderChanges>;
};

What's next

I'm continuing to work on Galaxy Movies and improve the experience as I go. There's still plenty I'd like to add, but I'm happy with how the project is coming together.

You can check it out at galaxymovies.app.

The source code is available on GitHub.

title: Time-Based One-Time Passwords with HashiCorp Vault and Quarkus
description:
Abstract

This article examines how the Time-Based One-Time Password algorithm (TOTP) can be delegated to the TOTP secrets engine of HashiCorp Vault and consumed by a Quarkus application. It first recalls the theoretical foundations of TOTP and the purpose of Vault. It then describes the use cases of the reference implementation with a UML diagram, analyses the Vault configuration and its bootstrap script, comments on the Java code and its integration tests, and finally presents the deployment topology defined by Docker Compose.

1. What is TOTP and what problem does it solve?

1.1 The weakness of the static password

The static password is the oldest and most widely deployed authentication mechanism in computing. It is also among the most fragile. A password is a shared secret that never changes unless its owner decides otherwise, which in practice means rarely. Once it is captured by phishing, keylogging, database leakage or simple observation over the shoulder, it remains valid for an indefinite period, and the legitimate owner usually has no indication that it has been compromised. The problem is aggravated by the well documented human tendency to reuse the same password across many services, so that the compromise of a modest forum may lead to the
compromise of a bank account. One could say that the static password is a key that its owner copies generously and then leaves under a great number of doormats.

Strictly speaking, the defect does not reside in the password as such but in the fact that it is frequently the only proof of identity required. Whoever holds the password is, from the point of view of the system, the legitimate user, and a single theft is therefore sufficient to usurp an identity.

1.2 Multi-factor authentication

The classical remedy does not consist in abolishing the password, which remains convenient,inexpensive and universally understood, but in depriving it of its exclusive status. The user is required to present several proofs belonging to distinct categories, called authentication factors, which are commonly classified as follows:

  1. something the user knows, such as a password or a PIN;
  2. something the user possesses, such as a smartphone or a hardware token;
  3. something the user is, such as a fingerprint.

The strength of the approach lies in the independence of these categories. The techniques that capture a password, such as phishing or the leakage of a database, do not provide the attacker with a physical device, and the theft of a device does not reveal what its owner knows.

The Time-Based One-Time Password algorithm (TOTP) is a widely adopted means of implementing the second category. At the moment of enrollment, the server generates a random secret, called the
seed, and transmits it once to the user, generally as a QR code scanned with an authenticator application installed on a smartphone. From then on, the application and the server each derive from this seed and from the current time a short numeric code, typically of six digits, which changes every thirty seconds. To authenticate, the user submits the code currently displayed together with the password, and the server accepts it only if it matches the code computed on its side. The possession of the device holding the seed thus becomes a necessary condition for authentication, so that the knowledge of the password alone is no longer sufficient. The mathematical details of this computation are the subject of section 1.3.

When a password is combined with TOTP, an attacker must consequently succeed in two attacks of a different nature against the same person:

  1. obtaining the password, which is usually achieved remotely and on a large scale, by means of a fraudulent login page (phishing), a keylogger installed on the workstation, or the reuse of credentials published after the leakage of another service's database (credential stuffing);
  2. obtaining the seed or the device that holds it, which requires either the physical theft of an unlocked smartphone, the installation of malware on that particular smartphone, or the interception of the QR code during the brief moment of enrollment.

The first attack can be conducted against millions of victims at once from the other side of the world, whereas the second must generally be directed at one specific person and one specific device. Combining them is considerably more difficult than succeeding in either one, and this difference of scale is the essence of the protection. It also explains why TOTP is preferable to codes sent by SMS, whose second factor can be diverted remotely by persuading a mobile operator to transfer the victim's number to a new SIM card (SIM swapping). The password thus ceases to be the weak point of the system and becomes merely one of its two locks. Section 1.3 mentions the notable exception of real-time phishing, in which a single fraudulent page collects both the password and a fresh code and relays them immediately.

It may be observed, not without some irony, that the code produced by the device is itself a kind of password. It differs from the static one, however, in every property that made the latter fragile, since it is generated rather than chosen, changes every thirty seconds, cannot be reused and is never memorized, let alone copied under a doormat.

1.3 The algorithm

TOTP is specified by RFC 6238 and is a direct extension of the HMAC-Based One-Time Password algorithm (HOTP) defined in RFC 4226. HOTP computes a short numeric code from a shared secret K and a counter C according to the following steps:

  1. compute HMAC-SHA1(K, C), which yields a 20 byte value;
  2. apply the so-called dynamic truncation, which uses the four lowest bits of the last byte as an offset in order to extract 31 bits from the HMAC value;
  3. reduce the resulting integer modulo 10^d, where d is the number of digits, usually 6.

The difficulty of HOTP lies in the synchronization of the counter between the client and the server. TOTP removes this difficulty in an elegant manner by replacing the counter with a value that both parties already share without any communication, namely the current time. The counter becomes

T = floor((CurrentUnixTime - T0) / X)

where T0 is the origin of time (usually the Unix epoch) and X is the time step, 30 seconds
by default. The one-time password is then simply HOTP(K, T).

The consequences of this construction are noteworthy:

  1. each code is valid only during a short time window, so that an intercepted code rapidly loses any value for an attacker;
  2. the device that generates the codes needs no network connection, since it only needs the seed and a reasonably accurate clock;
  3. the seed is transmitted only once, at enrolment time, usually through a QR code encoding an otpauth:// URI;
  4. the server must tolerate a small clock drift, which is achieved by also accepting the codes of the adjacent time steps (the so-called skew).

TOTP does not eliminate every threat. A real-time phishing proxy may still relay a fresh code within its validity window, and the seed itself must be protected with the utmost care on the server side. This last point is precisely the reason for introducing Vault into the picture.

2. What is HashiCorp Vault and what is it used for?

HashiCorp Vault is a secrets management system. Its purpose is to store, generate, distribute and revoke sensitive material such as passwords, API keys, certificates and encryption keys, so that this material does not end up scattered across configuration files, environment variables and source code repositories. Every access to Vault is authenticated by a token or by an authentication method, is authorised by policies expressed in the HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL), and may be recorded by an audit device.

Vault organizes its functionalities in pluggable components called secrets engines, each of them mounted at a path of a virtual file system. Among the most frequently used engines are the following:

  1. the key/value engine, which stores arbitrary static secrets;
  2. the database engine, which generates short-lived database credentials on demand;
  3. the PKI engine, which acts as a certification authority;
  4. the transit engine, which offers encryption as a service;
  5. the TOTP engine, which is the subject of this article.

The TOTP engine can play two roles. In the role of a generator, Vault creates the seed, returns a QR code that the user scans with an authenticator application, and later validates the codes submitted by the user. In the role of a provider, Vault receives an existing seed and generates codes on behalf of a client. The present project uses the first role. Its essential benefit is that the seed never leaves Vault after enrollment, and that the application never stores it,
never sees it again and therefore cannot leak it. An application that knows nothing can reveal nothing, which is a principle of security that is far older than computing and has been practised with great success by generations of discreet butlers.

A security-minded reader will notice an apparent paradox. The seed is protected by Vault, but Vault itself requires a secret to be opened. This is solved by the seal mechanism. At startup, the Vault storage is encrypted and Vault is said to be sealed. It must be unsealed by providing a number of key shares produced by Shamir's secret sharing algorithm before it can serve any request. Section 4 shows how this procedure is automated, in a deliberately simplified form,for local development.

3. Use cases

The following diagram presents the actors of the system and the use cases in which they participate, together with their pre-conditions and post-conditions.

The PlantUML source of this diagram is available in diagrams/use-case.puml.

The operator intervenes only once, by starting the stack, after which the bootstrap is fully automated. The end user performs the enrollment and then the authentication, whereas the authenticator application and Vault participate as secondary actors. It is worth noting that the authenticator application and Vault never communicate with each other. They are like two correspondents who agreed on a secret at their only meeting and who, from that day on, prove their acquaintance merely by consulting their watches.

4. Vault configuration

The Vault configuration consists of three files located in the vault/config directory, which is mounted read-only in the containers.

4.1 The server configuration in vault.hcl 

storage "file" {
  path = "/vault/file"
}

listener "tcp" {
  address     = "0.0.0.0:8200"
  tls_disable = 1
}

api_addr      = "http://0.0.0.0:8200"
disable_mlock = true
ui            = true

The storage stanza selects the file storage back-end, which persists the encrypted data of Vault in the /vault/file directory. This directory is backed by the Docker volume vault-file, so that the registered TOTP keys survive the restarts of the container. This
choice is deliberate. Vault also offers a development mode, as does the Quarkus Dev Services mechanism, but both are kept entirely in memory and forget everything when stopped. Such amnesia is acceptable in a test but rather inconvenient for a user who has just scanned a QR code and who would discover at the next restart that the application has no recollection of the enrollment.

The listener stanza opens a TCP listener on all network interfaces on port 8200. The tls_disable directive switches off TLS, which simplifies local development and which would be an unforgivable sin in any other context.

The api_addr parameter defines the address advertised by the server to its clients, in particular for request forwarding in a cluster. With a single node its role is modest.

The disable_mlock parameter prevents Vault from calling the mlock system call, whose purpose is to forbid the operating system to swap memory pages containing secrets to disk. Since containers generally lack the IPC_LOCK capability, this protection is disabled here. In a production deployment it should be kept enabled and the capability should be granted.

Finally, ui = true activates the web interface, available at http://localhost:8200/ui, which is convenient for inspecting the state of the server.

4.2 The access policy in totp-policy.hcl 

path "totp/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

Vault applies a deny by default model. A token can perform only the operations explicitly granted by the policies attached to it. The totp-policy policy grants the application the capabilities create, read, update, delete and list on every path below totp/, and nothing else. The application can therefore create keys (totp/keys/<name>), generate codes and validate them (totp/code/<name>), but it can neither read the key/value secrets of other
teams nor alter the configuration of Vault. This is a direct application of the principle of least privilege. A more restrictive policy is conceivable, for example by removing delete and list if the application never needs them, and the reader is invited to apply such pruning in a real deployment.

4.3 The bootstrap script init.sh

The script is executed by the one-shot container vault-init. Its main property is idempotence, in other words it can be executed any number of times and always leads to the same final state. It proceeds in six stages.

Waiting for the server.

until vault status 2>&1 | grep -qE 'Initialized|Sealed'; do
  sleep 1
done

The depends_on clause of Docker Compose only guarantees that the vault container has been started, not that the Vault process is ready to answer. The script therefore polls the vault status command until its output contains the expected fields. One may observe that the command returns a non-zero exit code when Vault is sealed, which is why the script examines the output rather than the exit code.

Initialisation.

if [ ! -s /init/init.json ]; then
  vault operator init -key-shares=1 -key-threshold=1 -format=json > /init/init.json
fi

The initialization creates the master encryption key, splits it into key shares and produces the initial root token. It is performed only once, when the file /init/init.json does not exist or is empty. In production, the master key is typically divided into five shares with a threshold of three, entrusted to different persons who are expected never to travel on the same aircraft. Here, one share and a threshold of one are sufficient, and the result is stored in clear in the vault-init volume. The script comment explicitly warns that this arrangement is acceptable only for local development.

Unsealing.

UNSEAL_KEY=$(jq -r '.unseal_keys_b64[0]' /init/init.json)
ROOT_TOKEN=$(jq -r '.root_token' /init/init.json)

if vault status -format=json | jq -e '.sealed == true' >/dev/null; then
  vault operator unseal "$UNSEAL_KEY" >/dev/null
fi

With the file storage, Vault is sealed again after each restart. The script extracts the unseal key and the root token with jq, which is installed on the fly by the container entry point, and unseals the server only if it is actually sealed.

Enabling the TOTP engine.

export VAULT_TOKEN="$ROOT_TOKEN"

if ! vault secrets list -format=json | jq -e 'has("totp/")' >/dev/null; then
  vault secrets enable totp
fi

Authenticated with the root token, the script mounts the TOTP secrets engine at its default path totp/, unless it is already mounted.

Writing the policy.

vault policy write totp-policy /vault/config/totp-policy.hcl

This command is naturally idempotent, since writing an identical policy twice leaves it unchanged, and it also guarantees that any modification of the HCL file is taken into account at the next start.

Creating the application token.

if ! vault token lookup dev-app-token >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  vault token create -id="dev-app-token" -policy="totp-policy" \
    -orphan -no-default-policy -period="8760h" -display-name="vault-auth" >/dev/null
fi

This last stage deserves a closer look, since each option carries a precise meaning:

  1. -id="dev-app-token" imposes a known token value, so that the application can be configured statically, which is convenient for development and strongly discouraged elsewhere;
  2. -policy="totp-policy" attaches the least-privilege policy described above;
  3. -no-default-policy removes the default policy, which would otherwise grant a few additional capabilities, such as looking up the token itself;
  4. -orphan detaches the token from its parent, the root token, so that a revocation of the latter does not revoke the application token in cascade;
  5. -period="8760h" makes the token periodic, which means that it has no maximum lifetime and remains valid as long as it is renewed at least once a year;
  6. -display-name="vault-auth" gives the token a readable name in the audit logs.

The application thus receives a token that can do exactly what it needs and nothing more,
which is the ideal relationship between a software component and its privileges, and which
is, regrettably, far less frequent in practice than in textbooks.

5. The application code

The vault-auth module is a Quarkus 3.37 application built with Quarkus REST and the Quarkiverse quarkus-vault extension. Its configuration, in application.properties, is minimal, as shown below.

quarkus.vault.devservices.enabled=false
quarkus.vault.url=http://localhost:8200
quarkus.vault.authentication.client-token=dev-app-token

The Dev Services are disabled for the reason given in section 4.1. The URL and the token designate the Vault server started by Docker Compose and are overridden by the environment variables QUARKUS_VAULT_URL and QUARKUS_VAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLIENT_TOKEN when the application runs in its own container.

5.1 The service TotpService 

@ApplicationScoped
public class TotpService
{
  private VaultTOTPSecretEngine vaultTOTPSecretEngine;

  public TotpService(VaultTOTPSecretEngine vaultTOTPSecretEngine)
  {
    this.vaultTOTPSecretEngine = vaultTOTPSecretEngine;
  }

  public Optional<KeyDefinition> getTotpKeyDefinition(String username)
  {
    CreateKeyParameters params = new CreateKeyParameters("totp-test", username);
    params.setExported(true);
    return vaultTOTPSecretEngine.createKey(username, params);
  }

  public boolean validateCode(String username, String code)
  {
    return vaultTOTPSecretEngine.validateCode(username, code);
  }
}

The class is an application scoped CDI bean, which means that a single instance is shared by all requests. Its only dependency, VaultTOTPSecretEngine, is supplied by the quarkus-vault extension and is injected through the constructor, which makes the dependency explicit and the class easy to instantiate in isolation.

The method getTotpKeyDefinition() creates a TOTP key in Vault. The two-argument constructor of CreateKeyParameters sets the issuer (totp-test), which the authenticator application displays as the name of the service, and the account name, here the user name. This constructor also sets the generate flag to true, which places Vault in its generator role. Vault therefore creates the seed itself instead of expecting one from the caller. The call to setExported(true) asks Vault to return the provisioning material, namely the otpauth:// URL and the QR code as a Base64 encoded PNG image. The key is stored under the path totp/keys/<username>, so that each user owns a distinct key, and a new registration under the same name replaces the previous key.

The period, the algorithm and the number of digits are deliberately left to their default values,namely 30 seconds, SHA1 and 6 digits. This apparent lack of ambition is the result of experience. During the development of the project, the period was initially set to one minute.
The QR code correctly announced a period of 60 seconds, the authenticator application accepted it without any objection, and every single code was then rejected. The explanation is that Google Authenticator ignores the period, algorithm and digits parameters of the URI and always uses the standard values. The application thus faithfully produced codes for a clock that ticked twice as often as the one of Vault. The comment in the source code preserves this lesson for posterity, and the author recommends it to any reader tempted by originality in this domain.

The method validateCode() delegates the verification to Vault, which recomputes the expected code for the current time step and its neighbors and compares it with the submitted one. Vault also records the codes already used and rejects a second submission of the same code within its validity window, which protects the application against replay attacks at no cost. The method returns a simple boolean, and the application never manipulates the seed.

5.2 The resource TotpApi 

@Path("/totp")
public class TotpApi
{
  @Inject
  TotpService totpService;

  @GET
  public Response testTotp(@HeaderParam("X-User") String username,
                           @HeaderParam("X-TOTP-Code") String code)
  {
    return totpService.validateCode(username, code) ? Response.ok("Access granted").build() :
      Response.status(Response.Status.UNAUTHORIZED).entity("Invalid TOTP code").build();
  }

  @GET
  @Path("/register/{username}")
  @Produces(MediaType.TEXT_HTML)
  public String register(@PathParam("username") String username)
  {
    return totpService.getTotpKeyDefinition(username)
      .map(key -> """
        <!DOCTYPE html>
        <html>
            <head><title>Scan QR Code</title></head>
            <body>
                <h2>Scan this QR code with Google Authenticator</h2>
                <img src="data:image/png;base64,%s" alt="TOTP QR Code"/>
            </body>
        </html>
        """.formatted(key.getBarcode()))
      .orElse("Failed to generate TOTP key");
  }
}

The class is a Jakarta REST resource bound to the path /totp and exposes two endpoints.

The endpoint GET /totp/register/{username} performs the enrollment. It obtains the key definition from the service and, if it is present, inserts the Base64 encoded image returned by getBarcode() into a small HTML page by means of a Java text block and the formatted()
method. The image is embedded as a data: URI, so that the browser can display it without any additional request. If the key definition is absent, a short failure message is returned.

The endpoint GET /totp performs the authentication. The user name and the code are read from the custom headers X-User and X-TOTP-Code. A valid code produces the status 200 and the body Access granted, whereas an invalid one produces the status 401 and the body
Invalid TOTP code.

The reader should keep in mind that this resource is a demonstration and not an authentication service ready for production. The registration endpoint is not protected, so that anybody who knows a user name may replace the key of that user, and the absence of a header is not handled specifically. In a real system, enrollment would occur only after a first authentication, for example by password, and the successful validation of the code would lead to the issuance of a session or of a token, typically through the Quarkus OIDC or JWT extensions. These additions are left as an exercise, according to the venerable academic tradition which consists in calling "exercise" what the author did not have the time to write.

5.3 The integration tests

In accordance with the conventions of the project, the tests are integration tests executed against a real Vault server rather than unit tests based on mocks. Two classes are involved.

VaultTestResource implements the QuarkusTestResourceLifecycleManager interface, which allows Quarkus to start an external resource before the application and to stop it afterwards.

@Override
public Map<String, String> start()
{
  vault = new VaultContainer<>(IMAGE)
    .withVaultToken(ROOT_TOKEN)
    .withInitCommand("secrets enable totp");
  vault.start();
  return Map.of(
    "quarkus.vault.devservices.enabled", "false",
    "quarkus.vault.url", vault.getHttpHostAddress(),
    "quarkus.vault.authentication.client-token", ROOT_TOKEN);
}

The method starts a Testcontainers VaultContainer based on the image hashicorp/vault:1.18, which is the same version as in Docker Compose. The method asCompatibleSubstituteFor("vault")informs Testcontainers that the official HashiCorp image may be used in place of the historical vault image it expects. The container runs in Vault development mode with the root token root, and the init command mounts the TOTP engine. The returned map overrides the application configuration, so that the application under test connects to this ephemeral server on its randomly mapped port instead of the persistent one. Here, the ephemeral nature that was a defect
in section 4.1 becomes a virtue, since each test run starts from a perfectly clean state.

TotpApiTest is annotated with @QuarkusTest, which starts the complete application, and with @WithTestResource(VaultTestResource.class), which attaches the resource described above. It contains three test cases written with REST Assured:

  1. registerReturnsQrCode() is a positive test which calls /totp/register/alice and verifies that the response has the status 200 and contains an embedded PNG image;
  2. validCodeGrantsAccess() is a positive test which registers bob, then asks Vault itself to generate the current code by means of generateCode("bob"), and verifies that submitting this code yields the status 200 and the message Access granted;
  3. invalidCodeIsRejected() is a negative test which registers carol, submits the code 000000 and verifies the status 401 and the message Invalid TOTP code.

The second test is particularly instructive. Since no smartphone could reasonably be attached to the build server, the test injects VaultTOTPSecretEngine and lets Vault play the role of the authenticator application. This is possible because the key was created in generator mode, in which Vault is able to compute the current code for its own keys. The third test relies on the fact that 000000 is a valid code with a probability of one in a million for any given time step. Should this test ever fail, the author recommends not correcting it but rather buying a lottery ticket on the same day.

The tests are executed by mvn -pl vault-auth -am test on any workstation with a running Docker daemon, and by the CircleCI pipeline, which uses a machine executor precisely so that
Testcontainers has access to a Docker engine.

6. Deployment

The file docker-compose.yml defines three services, two named volumes and one bind mount. The following diagram represents this topology.

The PlantUML source of this diagram is available in diagrams/deployment.puml.

The service vault runs the Vault server with the configuration of section 4.1. It publishes port 8200 on the host, stores its encrypted data in the volume vault-file and is restarted automatically unless it is explicitly stopped.

The service vault-init uses the same image, runs as root in order to be able to install jq and to write in its volume, executes the script init.sh and then terminates. Its restart policy is no, which is the expected behavior of a one-shot task. Its volume vault-init keeps the file init.json between executions, which is what makes the automatic unsealing possible after a restart.

The service vault-auth runs the Quarkus application, whose image is produced by the Quarkus container image extension during the Maven build. The pull_policy: never clause indicates that the image must exist locally and must not be searched for in a registry. The application starts only once vault-init has completed successfully, which guarantees that Vault is unsealed, that the TOTP engine is mounted and that the token dev-app-token exists at the moment of the first request. Inside the Compose network, the application reaches Vault by its service name, vault, through the environment variable QUARKUS_VAULT_URL.

The whole stack is started by the following commands.

mvn -pl vault-auth -am package -Dquarkus.container-image.build
docker compose up -d

After that, the user opens http://localhost:8080/totp/register/<username>, scans the QR code and checks a code with

curl -H "X-User: <username>" -H "X-TOTP-Code: <code>" http://localhost:8080/totp

The command docker compose down -v removes the volumes and returns the system to its original state of blissful ignorance.

7. Conclusion

This project shows that the implementation of a second authentication factor based on TOTP requires remarkably little application code once the cryptographic responsibilities are delegated to Vault. The Quarkus application contains two short classes and never stores a seed. Vault generates the keys, produces the QR codes, validates the codes and prevents their reuse, while the policy and the periodic orphan token restrict the application to the strict minimum. The integration tests, executed against a real Vault container, give a high degree of confidence in this collaboration without resorting to mocks.

The simplifications adopted for local development, namely the single unseal share stored in clear, the disabled TLS, the fixed token value and the unprotected registration endpoint, must of course be removed before any production use. With this reservation, the approach offers a sound basis on which an authentication service may be built, and the author hopes that the reader, having reached this conclusion without falling asleep, will consider this a valid proof of presence, comparable in rigor to a six digit code.
