title: Discovering API endpoints from source code with zero OpenAPI specs
description:
OpenAPI is great when it exists.

It often doesn't. Or it exists but hasn't been regenerated since the last three sprints. Or it covers the public API but not the internal services. Or it's maintained by hand and is quietly wrong in exactly the places you need it most.

For a testing tool, that's a problem: if you can't enumerate the endpoints, you can't generate tests for them. You're back to hand-authoring requests in Postman, which is where collections go to die.

This is how HTTP Forge discovers endpoints directly from source code — six framework providers, deterministic output, golden fixtures, and drift detection — with no OpenAPI spec required.

Why source code beats a spec

An OpenAPI spec is a derived artifact. Source code is the source of truth.

If discovery reads the source, three useful things follow:

  1. No spec maintenance tax. There's nothing to regenerate before you can test.
  2. Provenance. Every endpoint can point back to file:line — framework, confidence, and the source that produced it.
  3. Drift detection. You can fingerprint the source (git hash + mtime) and know when a stored index is stale.

The tradeoff is parser complexity and the risk of false positives. A wrong endpoint that breaks run_request is worse than a missing endpoint. The design rule I used: incomplete coverage is fine; false positives are not. Unknown patterns get confidence: 'low' rather than a confident guess.

The six providers

One class per framework, all implementing the same ApiDiscoveryProvider contract:

export interface ApiDiscoveryProvider {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly framework: ApiFramework;

  supports(fingerprint: FrameworkFingerprint): ProviderSupport;

  discover(
    context: DiscoveryContext,
    fingerprint: FrameworkFingerprint
  ): Promise<DiscoveryResult>;

  clearCache?(projectRoot?: string): void;
}

Adding a framework means adding a provider and registering it — never editing the orchestrator. That Open/Closed boundary is why the list can grow without destabilizing the existing parsers.

Express — detects the express dependency, scans TS/JS source files, and analyzes route registrations (app.get, router.post, mounts, middleware chains). It emits path params, request body schema hints, and provenance.

NestJS — reads decorators on controllers (@Controller, @Get, @Post, @Body, @Param) and resolves the controller prefix plus method path.

Fastify — follows fastify.get/post/... registrations and inline register() plugins with prefixes. (Known limitation: a variable plugin instance passed to register() isn't traversed.)

AWS Lambda — finds handler exports and serverless-style route definitions, mapping function names to HTTP methods and paths.

Spring — parses Java with java-parser's AST, with a regex fallback for patterns the AST misses. It handles @RestController, @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, path variables, and Pydantic-like model → JSON Schema generation for request bodies.

FastAPI — a pure-JS, balance-aware line walker. No Python runtime, no Python parser dependency. It handles FastAPI()/APIRouter(prefix=...), @app.<method> decorators, {param} paths, Path/Query/Header/Cookie/Body/File/Form parameters, Pydantic BaseModel → JSON Schema, and project-wide include_router prefix resolution (including import ... as aliases and tag merge).

The pipeline

Discovery isn't just "run the parser." The orchestrator does fingerprinting, framework detection, parallel provider execution, seed merging, enrichment, dedupe, and deterministic sorting.

flowchart TD
    start["Project root"] --> fp["Build fingerprint<br/>(package.json / build files / source hints)"]
    fp --> detect["Detect frameworks"]
    detect --> eligible["Select eligible providers"]
    eligible --> parallel["Run providers in parallel"]
    parallel --> seed["Merge explicit seed endpoints"]
    seed --> enrich["Enrich path params, auth, validation"]
    enrich --> dedupe["Dedupe + deterministic sort"]
    dedupe --> index["Build git-native index"]
    index --> persist["Persist discovered index"]

A few details that matter:

  • Language-aware hints. Framework detection scans only relevant extensions — TS/JS for the Node providers, .java for Spring, .py for FastAPI. Without this, app.get( in a Python decorator would falsely trigger the Express hint.
  • Empty source sets fall back. If the TS/JS collector finds nothing, the orchestrator leaves fingerprint.sourceFiles unset so Spring and FastAPI can run their own Java/Python collectors. Otherwise a standalone controller file would never be scanned.
  • Seed merge. If you have an explicit seed (a hand-curated endpoint list), it merges by METHOD + resolvedPath and keeps unmatched seed endpoints with a warning.
  • Deterministic IDs. Endpoint IDs are derived from method, path, and source location — not from timestamps or random values.

Determinism is a feature, not a nicety

Sorted output is what makes discovery diffable:

function compareEndpoints(a: DiscoveredApi, b: DiscoveredApi): number {
  const methodOrder =
    (SORT_METHOD_ORDER[a.method.toUpperCase()] ?? 99) -
    (SORT_METHOD_ORDER[b.method.toUpperCase()] ?? 99);
  if (methodOrder !== 0) return methodOrder;

  const pathA = a.resolvedPath ?? a.pathExpression;
  const pathB = b.resolvedPath ?? b.pathExpression;
  if (pathA !== pathB) return pathA < pathB ? -1 : 1;

  if (a.source.filePath !== b.source.filePath) {
    return a.source.filePath < b.source.filePath ? -1 : 1;
  }
  return a.source.line - b.source.line;
}

Ordering is method ascending (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS), then resolved path, then source file, then line. If two scans of unchanged code produce different output, every downstream diff becomes noise.

There are no timestamps inside endpoint records. The only time-like fields live in the explicit freshness metadata.

Golden fixtures: TDD for parsers

Parser code is easy to write and hard to trust. The anchor is a set of small, real backend projects under test-fixtures/:

  • express-app
  • nestjs-app
  • fastify-app
  • lambda-app
  • spring-app
  • fastapi-app

Each fixture is self-contained and deterministic: 5–8 endpoints, at least one :id path param, one POST-with-body, one DELETE, no dynamic route registration, no generated code. Each ships an expected.endpoints.golden.json.

The convention is deliberately strict:

  1. Sort endpoints identically (method, path, file, line).
  2. Strip volatile fields (id, projectRoot, projectName, timestamps).
  3. Compare relative source paths, never absolute workspace paths.
  4. Deep-equal against the golden file.

Golden files are locked. The test starts red; the provider is written until it's green. Regeneration happens only for a deliberate, reviewed change — and the reason goes in the commit message. You never weaken a golden assertion to make a wrong output pass.

That last rule is the whole game. Without it, "fixing the fixture" becomes the default response to a parser bug, and the suite stops meaning anything.

Drift detection: knowing when the index is stale

A discovered index is a snapshot. The question is: when is it no longer true?

The drift engine computes a freshness fingerprint:

export interface ProjectFreshness {
  gitHash?: string;
  /** Max mtime (ms) of any scanned source file under the project root. */
  maxSourceMtime: number;
}
  • In a git work tree, freshness is keyed on git rev-parse HEAD.
  • In a git-less workspace, it degrades to mtime: a source file newer than the stored scannedAt marks the project stale.
  • No git and no mtime signal means unknown — never a false claim of freshness. 
flowchart LR
    stored["Stored index<br/>(gitHash + scannedAt)"] --> compare{"Current fingerprint"}
    compare -->|"git HEAD matches"| current["current"]
    compare -->|"git HEAD changed"| stale["stale"]
    compare -->|"no stored entry"| unknown["unknown"]
    compare -->|"git-less: source mtime > scannedAt"| stale
    compare -->|"git-less: no newer source"| current

The engine also implements a 3-way diff and a resolver for regenerated artifacts. The rule is regenerate, don't patch: re-derive the artifact from source, then surface which hunks are AI-generated vs user-edited. Only ai_generated regions are regenerable; hand-edited assertions survive regeneration.

That's the part that keeps generated suites from becoming disposable.

What it doesn't do (yet)

Being honest about coverage is part of the trust model:

  • Fastify variable plugin instances passed to register() aren't traversed — routes can be missed or emitted without the mount prefix.
  • FastAPI f-string/expression decorator paths are emitted with confidence: 'low'.
  • No native .NET or Django providers. For those, import an OpenAPI spec (Swashbuckle / drf-spectacular) or let an AI agent infer endpoints from the workspace.
  • Dynamic route registration from config or a database can't be discovered by static analysis. That's a fundamental limit — but it's not a dead end: a custom seed loader module can supply those endpoints at discovery time.

Custom seed loader: the escape hatch for dynamic routes

Set customSeedLoaderModulePath and the orchestrator loads your module and merges its endpoints with the statically discovered ones:

// seed-loader.ts (project-local)
import type { DiscoveredApi } from '@http-forge/core';

export function loadSeedManifestEndpoints(projectRoot: string): DiscoveredApi[] {
  const routes = JSON.parse(readFileSync(`${projectRoot}/routes.json`, 'utf8'));
  return routes.map((route: any) => ({
    id: '', // filled in by the orchestrator
    method: route.method,
    pathExpression: route.path,
    resolvedPath: route.path,
    framework: 'unknown',
    confidence: 0.8,
    source: { filePath: 'routes.json', line: 1 },
    // ...headers, params, body schema as needed
  }));
}

The loader is resolved relative to the project root (or absolute), called with (projectRoot, discoveryContext), and may return either a bare DiscoveredApi[] or { endpoints, warnings }. Matched endpoints merge with the auto-discovered ones; unmatched seed endpoints are kept with a warning rather than silently dropped. Failures surface as seed-loader-failed warnings instead of aborting the scan.

Try it

Discovery runs in the CLI, the VS Code extension, and the MCP server:

http-forge discover --path ./backend --output table
http-forge generate-suite --path ./backend --collection "my-api" --dry-run

Or from an agent, via create_request_from_endpoint and generate_test_suite.

  • Getting started: docs/user-guide/getting-started.md
  • CLI reference: https://github.com/hsl1230/http-forge.cli/blob/main/docs/cli-reference.md
  • HTTP Forge for VS Code: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=henry-huang.http-forge

If you're building your own discovery layer, the two ideas worth stealing are the locked golden fixtures and the deterministic ordering rule. They turn a parser from "seems to work" into something you can refactor without fear.

title: What a ZoomEye match for Go does not say about CVE-2026-111943
description:
What a ZoomEye match for Go does not say about CVE-2026-111943

Asset search can help teams find Go-related services, but CVE-2026-111943 is a toolchain and certificate-verification issue. A ZoomEye result does not reveal which compiler built an application or whether it calls the vulnerable trust path. The measurement needs to be used as a discovery aid, not as a vulnerability verdict.

The affected standard library is Go crypto/x509 before go1.26.10 and from go1.27.0-0 before go1.27.3. Go published fixes in go1.26.10 and go1.27.3. Mozilla reported that eight eMudhra intermediate certificate private keys were compromised. A chain containing one of those intermediates could be accepted by an affected Go verifier, enabling certificate impersonation when an attacker can intercept traffic.

The verified observation

The selected Search query was app="Go". ZoomEye returned 260,278 successful matches at the recorded time and the result passed the Exposure threshold used by this generation task. A second candidate, product="Go", returned the same count. These are query observations, not a census of vulnerable Go binaries.

The Filter query vul.cve="CVE-2026-111943" returned 0 and succeeded. That result does not cancel the Search observation. The selected Exposure rule takes the larger verified count. More importantly, neither count identifies the software version hidden inside an HTTP service.

The canonical search is available through the exact dork in the query record. The public link represents the selected search, not a claim that every result should be treated as compromised.

Why the count is broad

An app fingerprint can represent a server or framework associated with Go. It may reflect a product built with Go even if the exposed component never validates a certificate. It may also miss a Go binary behind a reverse proxy that emits another server fingerprint.

The match count can change as ZoomEye updates its index. It should be saved with the exact dork, timestamp, and scope used for the analysis. Treating a later or differently scoped count as the same observation makes trend comparisons unreliable.

Most importantly, the query cannot tell whether a system contains the patched crypto/x509 denylist. That information comes from build provenance, binary metadata, release packages, and controlled verification tests. A web service can match Go while its TLS is terminated by a non-Go proxy or its certificate validation is implemented outside the standard library.

Turning matches into an investigation

Use the ZoomEye result to find owners and external service boundaries. For each candidate, identify the host, organization, application, deployment path, and responsible team. Then correlate that asset with internal SBOM, image, package, and build records.

An owner can prove a positive build version from signed release metadata. It can also run a controlled test against a certificate chain that includes a blocked intermediate. If neither form of evidence exists, mark the asset as unknown rather than safe. Assign a rebuild task when the binary is reachable or security-critical.

External asset matches require care. A public service may be a front end for a product whose backend has different code. The same hostname may be shared by several applications. Validate the service response and ownership before opening a vulnerability ticket. Do not test certificate interception against third-party systems.

Exposure is not exploitation

The absence of a CVE-indexed filter result is not evidence that no affected system exists. ZoomEye's CVE field depends on its own indexing and banner evidence. The affected condition can sit entirely inside an application and never appear in an exposed banner.

Conversely, a large product-fingerprint count does not mean that an attacker has compromised those assets. The reviewed sources do not report exploitation of CVE-2026-111943 in the wild. The count is an estimate of the population that may deserve a review, while the vulnerability is a defect in a certificate-verification library.

What to record

Save the exact Search and Filter dorks, their successful status, counts, scope, and query times. State which query produced the Exposure value and why it was selected. Keep the asset classification separate from the CVE status.

The useful conclusion is narrow: ZoomEye found 260,278 assets matching app="Go" at the recorded time, and the CVE filter found 0. Those figures support prioritization and further ownership discovery. They do not prove vulnerable builds, active interception, forged certificates, or a compromise.

References

  • CVE-2026-111943 record
  • Go vulnerability database GO-2026-6809
  • Go issue 82345
  • Upstream fix commit
  • Mozilla security notice
  • CERT-BUND advisory source

title: Testing multi-agent crews: forcing split-brain, goal drift, and context drift to happen in CI
description:
Originally published on Loop & Retry — field notes on building LLM agents that survive production.

The multi-agent posts on this blog have covered how a crew breaks (split-brain, goal drift, context drift), how to see it (observability), and how to prevent it at the boundary (tool design). One question is left: how do you know your prevention works before a customer finds out? This post is about writing tests that make each failure happen on purpose, so a regression in your tool boundary fails a build instead of an incident review.

Why your suite is green while your crew is broken

Run a three-agent crew on a happy-path task a hundred times and you will almost never see a coordination failure. That isn't evidence the crew is safe. It's evidence the test schedules agents in a friendly order.

Each failure needs a specific precondition:

  • Split-brain needs two agents to read the same key and then both write. Run them sequentially, or let one finish before the next starts, and the second always reads fresh state.
  • Goal drift needs several lossy handoffs in a row. A two-hop task rarely drifts far enough to matter.
  • Context drift needs a correction to arrive while an agent is mid-task holding the old version. If the objective never changes during a test, nothing can go stale.

So the first rule is that coordination tests cannot be sampled. You don't run the crew and hope the bad interleaving turns up. You construct it. That also means a coordination test almost never needs a real model, and I'd argue it shouldn't use one.

Assert on the state, not on the prose

A model call in the loop makes a test nondeterministic in exactly the place you're trying to pin down. And the output text is the wrong thing to assert on anyway. The question a coordination test asks is not "did the final answer look right?" It's "did the system permit a state it should have refused?" That is a property of the tool layer and the shared store, both of which are ordinary deterministic code.

So replace the model with a scripted agent: a list of tool calls it will make, in order, with no reasoning between them.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable

@dataclass
class ScriptedAgent:
    name: str
    steps: list[Callable[["Harness"], dict]]   # each step makes ONE tool call
    cursor: int = 0
    log: list[dict] = field(default_factory=list)

    def done(self) -> bool:
        return self.cursor >= len(self.steps)

    def advance(self, h: "Harness") -> None:
        result = self.steps[self.cursor](h)
        self.log.append({"agent": self.name, "step": self.cursor, "result": result})
        self.cursor += 1

The harness owns the clock. Instead of letting agents run, it takes an explicit schedule, a list of agent names saying whose step runs next:

class Harness:
    def __init__(self, tools, agents: list[ScriptedAgent]):
        self.tools = tools
        self.agents = {a.name: a for a in agents}
        self.scratch: dict = {}   # values an agent read, for a later step to use

    def run(self, schedule: list[str]) -> None:
        for name in schedule:
            agent = self.agents[name]
            assert not agent.done(), f"schedule over-runs {name}"
            agent.advance(self)
        leftover = [n for n, a in self.agents.items() if not a.done()]
        assert not leftover, f"schedule under-runs {leftover}"

Those two asserts matter more than they look. A schedule that silently skips a step produces a test that passes for the wrong reason, and a green test that never exercised the interleaving is worse than no test.

Test 1: split-brain is an interleaving, so enumerate it

Here is the failure from the split-brain post, written as a test against the versioned read_state / write_state pair from the tool-design post. Two agents each read, then each write.

def agent(name, key, new_value):
    def read(h):
        r = h.tools.read_state(key)
        h.scratch[(name, "read")] = r
        return r
    def write(h):
        r = h.scratch[(name, "read")]
        return h.tools.write_state(key, new_value, expected_version=r["version"])
    return ScriptedAgent(name, [read, write])

def test_concurrent_writers_one_is_rejected(store_tools):
    a, b = agent("A", "plan", "ship friday"), agent("B", "plan", "ship monday")
    h = Harness(store_tools, [a, b])

    h.run(["A", "B", "A", "B"])          # both read, then both write

    results = {x.name: x.log[-1]["result"] for x in (a, b)}
    assert results["A"].get("rejected") is not True
    assert results["B"]["rejected"] is True
    assert store_tools.read_state("plan")["value"] == "ship friday"

The schedule ["A", "B", "A", "B"] is the whole test. It is the interleaving that a sequential run never produces. Two things I'd add before calling this done.

Enumerate, don't pick one. For two agents with two steps each there are only six distinct schedules. Generate all of them and assert the invariant on each:

from itertools import permutations

def all_schedules(agents: dict[str, int]) -> set[tuple[str, ...]]:
    # agents maps name -> number of steps; returns every distinct interleaving
    flat = [n for n, k in agents.items() for _ in range(k)]
    return set(permutations(flat))

def test_no_schedule_leaves_a_lost_update(make_store_tools):
    for sched in all_schedules({"A": 2, "B": 2}):
        tools = make_store_tools()
        a, b = agent("A", "plan", "x"), agent("B", "plan", "y")
        Harness(tools, [a, b]).run(list(sched))
        final = tools.read_state("plan")["value"]
        committed = [x.name for x in (a, b)
                     if not x.log[-1]["result"].get("rejected")]
        # The invariant: the stored value belongs to the last COMMITTED write,
        # and every non-committed writer was told so.
        assert final == {"A": "x", "B": "y"}[committed[-1]], sched

Notice what's asserted. It isn't "the result is ship friday." It's an invariant that holds in every schedule: whatever is in the store was written by an agent that was told its write succeeded. That is the definition of no lost update, and it survives you changing the agents, the values, and the order. With three agents and three steps the count is 1,680, which is still milliseconds because nothing is calling a model. Past that, sample schedules with a fixed seed, and print the seed on failure so any red run can be replayed exactly.

Add a positive control. Before you trust this test, run it against the BAD signature, the one with no expected_version. It must fail. If your test passes against the broken tool, it isn't testing what you think, and you've learned that before shipping rather than after.

Test 2: goal drift is a ledger property, not an output property

Goal drift is the hardest of the three to test through behavior, because the symptom is a plausible answer to a subtly different question. You can't write an assert on "plausible." But the tool-design post gave you something checkable: every constraint on the origin task must be carried verbatim or waived with a reason. That is a partition, and a partition can be asserted.

The test drives a handoff chain with scripted paraphrase pressure. Each hop's script tries to drop or reword a constraint, the way a summarizing agent does, and the assertion is that the tool refuses.

ORIGIN = [
    {"id": "c1", "text": "Do not change the public API response shape."},
    {"id": "c2", "text": "No new network calls from the hot path."},
]

def lossy_hop(drop=None, reword=None):
    def step(h):
        carried = [dict(c) for c in ORIGIN if c["id"] != drop]
        if reword:
            for c in carried:
                if c["id"] == reword:
                    c["text"] = "Keep the API mostly stable."   # a paraphrase
        return h.tools.delegate(
            subtask="implement cache layer", origin_task_id="t-1",
            constraints=carried, acceptance_criteria=[], waived_constraints=[],
        )
    return step

def test_silent_drop_is_rejected(delegate_tools):
    a = ScriptedAgent("planner", [lossy_hop(drop="c2")])
    Harness(delegate_tools, [a]).run(["planner"])
    r = a.log[0]["result"]
    assert r["rejected"] and "c2" in r["error"]

def test_paraphrase_is_rejected(delegate_tools):
    a = ScriptedAgent("planner", [lossy_hop(reword="c1")])
    Harness(delegate_tools, [a]).run(["planner"])
    assert a.log[0]["result"]["rejected"]

The second test is the one people skip, and it's the interesting one. A completeness check that only compares constraint ids passes a reworded constraint without a murmur, because the id is still there. The tool has to compare the text against the origin ledger byte for byte. If test_paraphrase_is_rejected passes on your first try, I'd go look for why, because most first implementations of this check fail it.

Then test the chain, not just the hop. Drift compounds, so run five hops where each one carries the previous hop's output, and assert on the final ledger:

def test_five_hop_chain_preserves_ledger(delegate_tools):
    hops = [ScriptedAgent(f"hop{i}", [carry_forward_verbatim]) for i in range(5)]
    h = Harness(delegate_tools, hops)
    h.run([f"hop{i}" for i in range(5)])
    final = delegate_tools.ledger("t-1")
    assert [c["text"] for c in final.constraints] == [c["text"] for c in ORIGIN]

An assertion on the ledger is also the cheap version of what the observability post called a constraint-survival probe, with the difference that it runs in CI with no model in the path.

Test 3: context drift needs a correction injected mid-run

For context drift the test has to change the world while an agent is holding the old copy. The harness needs one more primitive, an event that fires between steps:

class Harness(Harness):
    def run(self, schedule, events: dict[int, Callable] | None = None):
        events = events or {}
        for i, name in enumerate(schedule):
            if i in events:
                events[i](self)            # runs BEFORE step i
            self.agents[name].advance(self)

Now the $32-credit scenario from the context-drift post becomes a deterministic test. A responder reads the refund policy, the policy is corrected, and the responder sends a message drafted against the old version:

def test_send_against_superseded_policy_is_refused(support_tools):
    def read_policy(h):
        r = h.tools.get_objective("ticket-9", agent_id="responder")
        h.scratch["policy"] = r
        return r
    def send(h):
        return h.tools.send_customer_message(
            "ticket-9", "We've credited $32.",
            policy_version=h.scratch["policy"]["version"])

    responder = ScriptedAgent("responder", [read_policy, send])
    h = Harness(support_tools, [responder])

    h.run(["responder", "responder"],
          events={1: lambda h: h.tools.correct_objective("ticket-9", "Credits capped at $20.")})

    result = responder.log[-1]["result"]
    assert result["rejected"] is True
    assert "capped at $20" in result["current_policy"]
    assert support_tools.outbox == []          # nothing reached the customer

The last assert is the one that carries the test. Not "the tool returned a rejection," but "the outbox is empty." A rejection that something downstream ignores is still a leak, and checking the side-effect channel directly is what makes this test hard to fool.

A second test covers the other half of the design: correction fan-out. Two agents read, a third corrects, and the test asserts the holder set contains exactly the two readers. A holder set that misses someone is a stale agent nobody will ever notify.

What to keep out of the suite

Don't assert on model output in the coordination tests. There's a place for evals on whether agents choose well under contention, and evaluating your evals is the caution about how easily those mislead. But the tool-boundary guarantee is deterministic, so test it deterministically. A flaky test that sometimes passes on a real model teaches the team to rerun red builds.

Don't treat schedule coverage as a vanity number. "We test 6 interleavings" means little. The useful question is whether there is a schedule that violates your invariant and isn't in your set. For small N, enumerate. For large N, seed and sample, and keep the seeds of anything that ever failed as permanent regression cases.

Don't let the harness diverge from production tools. The scripted agent should call the real tool functions against a real (in-memory) store, not a mock that returns what you expect. A mock of write_state that implements the version check is a test of your mock. If the production store is a remote service, run the same suite against a local instance of it nightly.

Pair it with the production signal

These tests prove the guard exists. They don't prove it's the only path. The production counterpart is the rejection rate from the instrumentation post: a rising count of rejected writes means contention is growing, and a count stuck at exactly zero for a crew that has several writers is suspicious, not reassuring. Zero rejections can mean perfect coordination, or it can mean a code path that bypasses the guarded tool. A CI test can't tell you which. A metric that was nonzero last month and is zero now can.

The ordering I'd follow: write the invariant first (no lost update, ledger is a partition, nothing is sent on a superseded basis), write the schedule that violates it, confirm the test fails against the unguarded tool, then confirm it passes against the guarded one. A coordination fix without a test that failed first is a fix you can't tell from a coincidence, and a crew's failure modes are exactly the kind that look like coincidence until they don't.

title: How I built an MCP server that lets AI agents run my API tests
description:
I built HTTP Forge because I was tired of maintaining Postman collections by hand. Every time a route changed, a DTO gained a field, or an auth header moved, the collection went stale — and nobody trusted it enough to keep it updated.

The second problem was more interesting: I wanted an AI agent to be able to drive the whole lifecycle — discover endpoints, generate tests, run them, read the report, diagnose failures, and fix stale assertions. Not just "write me a test" in a chat window, but actually operate the tool.

That meant building an MCP server.

This is the story of how it works, what I got wrong, and the transcript of an agent running a real test lifecycle.

Why MCP?

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way to expose tools to an AI agent. Instead of every agent vendor inventing its own plugin format, the agent discovers a server, lists its tools, and calls them with JSON arguments.

For a testing tool, that's a natural fit. A test run is a sequence of well-defined operations:

  1. List collections.
  2. Run a request or suite.
  3. Read the results.
  4. Explain a failure.
  5. Rewrite a stale assertion.
  6. Re-run.

Each of those is a tool. The agent doesn't need to know how HTTP Forge stores collections on disk — it just needs a stable contract.

The architecture

HTTP Forge has three consumers: a VS Code extension, a CLI, and an MCP server. They all share the same core engine, @http-forge/core, which is now open source (MIT).

The important constraint: core cannot import vscode. That forced a ports-and-adapters design. The core defines interfaces; the extension and CLI inject platform services (file system, workspace state, secret storage).

The MCP layer sits on top of core like this:

flowchart LR
    ext["VS Code extension"]
    cli["CLI"]
    mcp["MCP server"]

    core["@http-forge/core"]
    dispatch["dispatchGenericTool()"]

    subgraph handlers["Tool handlers"]
        inspection["inspection"]
        execution["execution"]
        discovery["discovery"]
        suite["suite"]
        environment["environment"]
        ai["AI"]
    end

    ext --> core
    cli --> core
    mcp --> core
    core --> dispatch
    dispatch --> inspection
    dispatch --> execution
    dispatch --> discovery
    dispatch --> suite
    dispatch --> environment
    dispatch --> ai

The dispatcher is deliberately small. Each tool lives in a handler module, and the registry assembles them:

const ALL_HANDLERS: McpToolHandler[] = [
  ...inspectionHandlers,
  ...executionHandlers,
  ...collectionHandlers,
  ...requestHandlers,
  ...discoveryHandlers,
  ...suiteHandlers,
  ...aiHandlers,
];

function buildRegistry(): Map<GenericToolName, McpToolHandler> {
  const registry = new Map();
  for (const handler of ALL_HANDLERS) {
    for (const name of handler.toolNames) registry.set(name, handler);
  }
  return registry;
}

Adding a tool means adding a handler — not editing the dispatcher. That Open/Closed boundary kept the MCP layer maintainable as it grew past 60 tools.

The tool surface

The MCP server exposes tools in a few groups:

  • Inspection — list_collections, list_requests, get_request, get_run_summary, get_failed_requests.
  • Execution — run_request, run_folder, run_collection, run_suite.
  • Discovery — create_request_from_endpoint, generate_test_suite, suggest_workflow, check_drift.
  • AI — suggest_assertions, explain_failure, heal_assertions, generate_scenarios.
  • Suites and environments — create/update nodes, select environments, set variables.

Two design choices matter a lot:

1. Execution is synchronous by default, async on request. A small suite returns its result inline. A large suite can be started with async: true, returning a runId that the agent polls with get_run_status.

2. Outputs are bounded. MCP responses go into an LLM context window. The server truncates large bodies and offers include fields (perRequest, failedOnly, consoleOutput) so the agent asks for detail only when it needs it.

A real lifecycle transcript

Here's what an agent actually does with the server. I've trimmed the outputs for readability.

Step 1 — Discover endpoints from source 

{
  "tool": "create_request_from_endpoint",
  "arguments": {
    "path": "./backend",
    "collection": "user-service",
    "endpointId": "POST /users"
  }
}

The agent gets back a created request plus provenance — framework, source file, confidence. No OpenAPI spec required.

Step 2 — Generate a suite 

{
  "tool": "generate_test_suite",
  "arguments": {
    "path": "./backend",
    "collection": "user-service",
    "suiteName": "smoke-tests"
  }
}

The generator creates one request node per endpoint and asserts the discovered status code. Generated nodes carry ai_generated: true and derived_from: <endpointId> so drift detection can find them later.

Step 3 — Run it 

{
  "tool": "run_suite",
  "arguments": {
    "suite": "smoke-tests",
    "environment": "staging",
    "include": ["failedOnly"]
  }
}

{
  "runId": "run-20261030-141501",
  "status": "completed",
  "allPassed": false,
  "failedRequests": [
    {
      "name": "Create User",
      "status": 500,
      "assertions": [
        { "name": "Status is 201", "passed": false, "actual": 500 }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Step 4 — Diagnose 

{
  "tool": "explain_failure",
  "arguments": {
    "runId": "run-20261030-141501",
    "request": "Create User"
  }
}

The response includes the full request, the response, every assertion result, any script errors, and a plain-English diagnosis. In this case: the staging database was down, not a test bug.

Step 5 — Heal a stale assertion

Now suppose the API legitimately changed: Create User used to return 201, and now returns 200. The test is stale, not the server.

The agent calls:

{
  "tool": "heal_assertions",
  "arguments": {
    "collection": "user-service",
    "request": "Create User",
    "runId": "run-20261030-141501"
  }
}

The server returns the current script and the last observed response:

{
  "task": {
    "currentScript": "pm.test('Status is 201', () => pm.response.to.have.status(201));",
    "lastResponse": { "status": 200, "body": { "id": "u1", "name": "Alice" } },
    "instructions": [
      "Rewrite the script to match the observed response",
      "Call set_request_script with the new script"
    ]
  }
}

The agent then rewrites and saves:

{
  "tool": "set_request_script",
  "arguments": {
    "collection": "user-service",
    "request": "Create User",
    "phase": "post-response",
    "script": "pm.test('Status is 2xx', () => pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.be.oneOf([200, 201]));\npm.test('Returns an id', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.have.property('id'));"
  }
}

And re-runs the suite. Green.

Assertion healing: why it's safe

The scary part of AI-driven testing is an agent silently weakening your assertions to make tests pass. I designed heal_assertions to avoid that:

  • It's advisory. The tool returns a task describing what to compare; the agent writes the new script.
  • The agent must explicitly call set_request_script to persist it. Every change is a normal script edit in the collection, visible in git.
  • The prompt instructs the agent to keep valid assertions and only fix stale ones.
  • There's no "auto-confirm" path. A human can review the diff like any other code change.

The goal is not "agent makes tests green." It's "agent proposes a fix you can review in the same way you'd review a PR."

Lessons learned

Error messages are prompts. When an agent calls run_request with a collection name that doesn't exist, a bare not found is useless. Returning the available names — Available: user-service, billing-service — lets the model self-correct in one turn. I rewrote most error paths for this.

Tool names must survive real IDs. MCP tool names have provider length limits, and HTTP Forge IDs embed human-readable names. I added deterministic short hashing for long IDs, with readable slugs where possible. The model picks tools by description, so short names don't hurt discovery.

Determinism matters. Discovery output is sorted by method, path, and file. No timestamps inside endpoint records. When the agent diffs two scans, noise kills the signal.

Token budget is a feature. Async runs, include filters, and body truncation aren't optimizations — they're what make the server usable with a 200k-token context.

Keep core UI-free. Because MCP, CLI, and the extension share the engine, a bug fixed in one is fixed everywhere. The vscode-free boundary is the reason that works.

Try it

If you want to play with the same lifecycle without wiring up a backend:

npm install -g @http-forge/cli
http-forge launch --examples

That clones a sample workspace with pre-built requests, environments, and suites, then opens it in VS Code. You can run a suite, break an assertion on purpose, and watch the explain/heal flow.

  • HTTP Forge for VS Code: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=henry-huang.http-forge
  • Open-source core: https://github.com/hsl1230/http-forge.core

If you're building your own MCP server, the two things I'd steal are the per-tool registry and the "errors as prompts" habit. They made the difference between a demo and something an agent can actually use.

title: API alerting best practices: what to page on for a Node API
description:
Your phone buzzes at 3am: CPU over 80% on one instance. You look, nothing is wrong for users, and you go back to sleep a little less willing to trust the next alert. A week later a real outage pages nobody, because the alert that mattered did not exist. API alerting best practices come down to one rule: page on symptoms users feel (errors, latency, the API not answering), send everything else to a ticket or a dashboard, and require every page to be actionable.

For a Node API run by a team of 1 to 20, that means four or five alerts, not forty. Here is which ones, how to keep them quiet, and working instrumentation and alert rules.

What should you alert on for an API?

The Google SRE book's guidance is to alert on symptoms rather than causes. For an HTTP API the symptom list is short:

Alert Condition (example) Page or ticket
Error rate 5xx above 2% of requests for 5 minutes, at least 50 requests Page
Latency p95 of key endpoints above 2x normal for 10 minutes Page
Down External check fails from 2+ locations for 3 minutes Page
Running out Disk, connection limit or quota will run out within hours Page if hours, ticket if days
TLS certificate Expires in under 14 days Ticket

Replace the example numbers with values from your own baseline. The structure matters more than the thresholds: ratios instead of counts, a minimum volume, and a duration.

API alerting best practices: what not to page on

  • CPU or memory percentage. High CPU with normal latency is a cost question, not an emergency.
  • A single 500. One error is a log line. Many errors are a rate.
  • Raw 4xx counts. Clients send bad requests; a 4xx spike is often a scanner or a broken client release. Ticket it, or route it to a security review.
  • One process restart. Page on restarts only if they cause errors users see, which the error-rate alert already catches.
  • A dependency's latency alone. If the vendor's slowness hurts your users, your own latency alert fires.

Causes like these belong on a dashboard you open when a symptom alert fires. Event loop lag is a good example: a vital diagnostic, a poor page.

How to reduce alert noise

Use rates and minimum volumes

Five errors out of ten requests at 4am is 50%, and it may be one confused client. Require a minimum request count before an error-rate alert can fire.

Add a duration

Use a for window (5 to 10 minutes) so a spike during a deploy does not page. Short, real outages are still caught by the external "down" check.

Alert on the routes that matter

Exclude /health, webhooks you ignore and admin routes from latency alerts, or alert per group of routes. One slow export endpoint should not page as "API slow".

Consider burn rate once you have an SLO

If you define an availability target, alerting on how fast you burn the error budget (fast burn pages, slow burn tickets) replaces fixed thresholds well. The SLOs and error budgets post covers how to set one up without much ceremony.

How to instrument a Node API for alerting

A request histogram labeled by route and status class is enough for every alert above. With prom-client and Express:

import express from 'express';
import client from 'prom-client';

const httpDuration = new client.Histogram({
  name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
  help: 'HTTP request duration',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status_class'],
  buckets: [0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5],
});

const app = express();

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const end = httpDuration.startTimer();
  res.on('finish', () => {
    end({
      method: req.method,
      route: req.route?.path ?? 'unmatched', // the pattern, not the raw URL
      status_class: `${Math.floor(res.statusCode / 100)}xx`,
    });
  });
  next();
});

app.get('/metrics', async (req, res) => {
  res.set('content-type', client.register.contentType);
  res.send(await client.register.metrics());
});

Label by route pattern, never by raw URL, or every user ID becomes a new time series. Note that req.route holds only the last matched path segment in nested routers; prefix it with req.baseUrl if you mount routers.

Then the alert rules, in Prometheus format:

groups:
  - name: api
    rules:
      - alert: ApiHighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{status_class="5xx"}[5m]))
            / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])) > 0.02
          and sum(increase(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])) > 50
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: page }
        annotations:
          summary: "5xx rate above 2% for 5m"
          runbook: "https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/api-errors"
      - alert: ApiSlowCheckout
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (
            rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"/checkout.*"}[10m]))) > 1
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: page }

The same logic works in Grafana Cloud, Datadog, New Relic or your platform's built-in alerting; the names change, the structure does not. For the "down" alert, use an external uptime check against a real endpoint, not just /health (see health checks that tell the truth).

Who gets paged on a small team?

  • Solo developer: pages go to your phone, so be strict. Three alerts: error rate, latency on your most important route, and down. Everything else goes to email.
  • Team of ~10: a weekly on-call rotation, one channel for pages and another for tickets, and a 15-minute review every week: for each page, was it real, and did someone need to act? Delete or downgrade any alert that fails twice.

Every page should include what fired, the current value, a link to the dashboard and a runbook link with the first three things to check. A runbook can be five lines.

If you only do one thing

  • Delete or downgrade every page that is a cause (CPU, memory, single errors) rather than a symptom.
  • Make sure three pages exist: 5xx rate, p95 on key routes, and external "down".
  • Give each a minimum volume and a duration.
  • Review pages weekly and delete the ones nobody acted on.

FAQ

What is the difference between a symptom alert and a cause alert?

A symptom alert fires on what users experience, such as errors or slow responses. A cause alert fires on something that might lead to that, such as high CPU. Page on symptoms and use causes for diagnosis.

Should I alert on p95 or p99 latency?

For paging, p95 over several minutes is steadier and harder to trip with a handful of slow requests. Watch p99 on dashboards and for tickets, especially on low-traffic routes.

How many alerts should a small API team have?

Few enough that every page gets acted on. For a single Node API, three to five paging alerts covering errors, latency, availability and capacity is a reasonable start.

Doing this with ApiTraffic

Alerts tell you something is wrong; the next ten minutes are spent working out what. If you would rather not build that investigation tooling yourself, ApiTraffic records every request and response, with route patterns and tags.

  • Search status_code >= 500 for the alert's time window to see the failing requests themselves, with bodies and headers (credentials masked by default).
  • tag:userId == "1042" AND status_code >= 400 shows whether one customer is behind the spike (tags and dimensions).
  • Endpoint details show p50, p95 and p99 per endpoint, and Regressions flags endpoints whose p95 rose after a recorded deploy event.

Start free and see every request your API handles: apitraffic.io

title: The managed Postgres bill nobody puts on the pricing page
description:
Suppose you move your database to a managed Postgres plan. Twenty-five dollars a month, no patching, a dashboard with a restore button. Compared to the VPS you were going to run yourself, it looks like the responsible choice.

Then you read the pricing page properly, all the way down, and find the line that changes the comparison: point-in-time recovery, billed at $100/month per 7 days of retention, on top of the plan.

That is not a hosting cost. That is a different product, priced like insurance, and it is the one thing a self-hosted pgBackRest gives you for the price of a cron job.

The comparison everyone makes

Prices read from the providers' own pages on 2026-10-29, before tax:

Option What it is Monthly
OVHcloud VPS-1 2 vCores, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB NVMe, daily backup €4.49
Supabase Pro 8 GB disk, $10 compute credit covering one Micro instance $25
Supabase PITR add-on 7-day retention +$100

On RAM per euro, the VPS wins by roughly a factor of twenty. A Supabase Micro instance is 1 GB of RAM for $25. A 4 GB VPS is four euros and change.

So the easy conclusion is "managed is a rip-off". That conclusion is wrong, and it is wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with RAM.

What you are actually buying

Five things, none of which appear in the spec column:

  1. Backups someone else scheduled.
  2. Point-in-time recovery — if you pay the line above.
  3. Major-version upgrades someone else ran first.
  4. Failover, on the tiers that include it.
  5. A connection pooler in front of a database that does not enjoy thousands of connections.

If you can do 1 through 3 reliably, self-hosting wins on money and you should close this tab. If you cannot, the managed price is not hosting. It is insurance, and insuring a database is cheaper than losing one.

The calculation nobody does

Write your hourly rate down first. Then:

self-hosted = VPS + (hours of database work × your rate)
managed     = plan + (hours of migration and plumbing × your rate)

A 4 GB VPS is €4.49. The managed plan is $25. The gap is about €20 a month — half an hour of a freelance rate. If self-hosting costs you more than thirty minutes a month in patching, backup checks and the occasional restore rehearsal, you are subsidising the server with your evenings.

That arithmetic flips at the first incident. An unrehearsed restore is not thirty minutes. It is a night, and sometimes a customer.

The one question that decides it

Not "which is cheaper". This one:

Have you restored from your own backup in the last 90 days, and did you time it?

If yes, self-hosting is a defensible engineering choice and you can stop paying for a dashboard.

If no, you do not currently have a backup strategy. You have a backup job whose success you have never verified, and the managed plan is the cheaper way to fix that today.

The full comparison, with the Neon per-CU maths, the migration path in both directions and the checklist I would run before choosing:
Managed PostgreSQL vs PostgreSQL on a VPS

title: Reproducing a flaky network in Linux namespaces with netem
description:
Faking a flaky network takes one Linux box. You need three network namespaces, a veth pair on each side of the middle one, and tc netem on the egress of the middle hop. No VMs and no spare hardware. Everything below runs as root and leaves nothing behind once you delete the namespaces.

This post is the recipe and the measurement method. We use the same setup in our lab to put a VPN client under impairment and watch what it reports. Here the setup is the subject, and any program that sends packets will do.

What we are building

Three namespaces in a line:

client  --  mid  --  server

mid forwards packets and is the only place where we break things. The client and server never know. That matters, because a test that touches the endpoints directly measures your test, not the path.

Build the topology 

for n in c m s; do ip netns add $n; ip -n $n link set lo up; done

ip link add c0 netns c type veth peer name m0 netns m

# second pair, server side
ip link add s0 netns s type veth peer name m1 netns m

for spec in c:c0:10.10.1.2 m:m0:10.10.1.1 m:m1:10.10.2.1 s:s0:10.10.2.2; do
  set -- ${spec//:/ }
  ip -n $1 addr add $3/24 dev $2 && ip -n $1 link set $2 up
done

# routes, then let the middle namespace forward
ip -n c route add default via 10.10.1.1 && ip -n s route add default via 10.10.2.1 && ip netns exec m sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

Check that the path works before you break anything:

ip netns exec c ping -c 3 10.10.2.2

If that fails, stop here. Every later result depends on a clean baseline, and a typo in a route will look exactly like packet loss.

Record a baseline first

Run each measurement once with no impairment and keep the output. When a number looks odd under fault, the baseline tells you whether the fault or the machine produced it.

We use two tools. ping gives a per-packet view of delay and loss. iperf3 gives sustained throughput.

ip netns exec s iperf3 -s -D
sleep 1
ip netns exec c iperf3 -c 10.10.2.2 -t 10 --json > baseline-iperf.json
# and the per-packet view
ip netns exec c ping -c 50 -i 0.2 10.10.2.2 > baseline-ping.txt

The veth pair is fast, so the baseline will be limited by your CPU and not by any link. That is fine. You are measuring change against yourself, never against an absolute figure.

A logger that does not lie

Summary output from ping hides the shape of a failure. A path that drops every packet for three seconds and then recovers can show the same loss percentage as a path that drops one packet in twenty. Those are different problems.

So log each probe on its own line, with a timestamp:

ip netns exec c bash -c '
while true; do
  t=$(date +%s.%N)
  if ping -c1 -W1 10.10.2.2 >/dev/null 2>&1; then r=ok; else r=fail; fi
  echo "$t,$r"
  sleep 0.2
done' > probe.csv &
echo $! > probe.pid

One row per probe means you can line the log up against the moment you applied each impairment. Write the time you applied it into a second file. Do this by hand if you must, but do it every time.

Impairment one: delay and jitter

Apply netem on the egress of m1, the interface facing the server:

ip netns exec m tc qdisc add dev m1 root netem delay 80ms 20ms

That adds a base delay with random variation around it. Note that netem acts on outgoing packets only. A single qdisc on m1 delays the forward direction. To delay the return path as well, add a matching qdisc on m0. Without it, only the forward leg is delayed, so a ping's round trip grows by the configured delay once, not twice.

Change values in place with change, not add:

ip netns exec m tc qdisc change dev m1 root netem delay 200ms 50ms

Remove it with:

ip netns exec m tc qdisc del dev m1 root

Impairment two: random loss 

ip netns exec m tc qdisc add dev m1 root netem loss 5%

Random loss is the gentle case. Real networks tend to lose packets in bursts. netem's optional correlation value does little to produce real bursts, so use its Gilbert-Elliott model instead:

ip netns exec m tc qdisc change dev m1 root netem loss gemodel 1% 20%

The first number is the chance of moving from a good state into a bad one, the second the chance of moving back. Every packet in the bad state is dropped, so this loses about 5% of packets on average, in runs of about five. Compare the two runs in your probe log. The count of failed probes may be similar, but the runs of consecutive failures will not be. Whatever you test, test it against both shapes. Retransmission logic that copes with scattered loss can struggle with a burst.

Impairment three: a narrow link

Netem has a rate option, but a token bucket filter gives you more honest queueing behaviour. Put netem under it if you want delay as well:

# remove the loss qdisc from the previous step first
ip netns exec m tc qdisc del dev m1 root
ip netns exec m tc qdisc add dev m1 root handle 1: tbf rate 5mbit burst 32kbit latency 400ms
# netem hangs off the bucket as a child
ip netns exec m tc qdisc add dev m1 parent 1:1 handle 10: netem delay 40ms

Now run iperf3 again and compare it with the baseline file. Throughput should settle close to the configured rate. If it does not, check that you applied the filter on the interface the traffic actually leaves through.

Impairment four: the path that silently shrinks

This one deserves its own section, because it is the hardest to spot from the endpoints.

A packet with the don't-fragment bit set that is too big for a hop should trigger an ICMP "fragmentation needed" message back to the sender. The sender then lowers its packet size. If that message never arrives, the sender keeps sending large packets that vanish. Small packets still pass. Pings work, the connection opens, and then anything bulky stalls.

Reproduce it in two steps. First, shrink the MTU on the far-side interface:

ip -n m link set m1 mtu 1400

Second, drop the ICMP errors that the middle hop would generate. Save this as drop-icmp.nft:

table inet t {
  chain out {
    type filter hook output priority 0;
    ip protocol icmp icmp type destination-unreachable drop
  }
}

Load it inside the middle namespace:

ip netns exec m nft -f drop-icmp.nft

Now compare a small probe with a large one:

# small probe
ip netns exec c ping -c 3 -M do -s 100 10.10.2.2
# large probe
ip netns exec c ping -c 3 -M do -s 1472 10.10.2.2

The first succeeds. The second gets no answer and no error message either. That silence is the whole point. A program that only checks whether the host answers will report a healthy path while real traffic goes nowhere.

To undo it, delete the nft table and set the MTU back to 1500:

ip netns exec m nft delete table inet t && ip -n m link set m1 mtu 1500

Reading the log

When a run is over, stop the logger and look at three things in probe.csv.

First, the time from the moment you applied an impairment to the first failed probe. Second, the longest outage. Third, the time from the moment you removed the impairment to the first success. Recovery time is the number people forget to measure, and it often tells you more than the failure itself.

This short awk script covers the second item:

awk -F, '$2=="fail"{if(!n)s=prev; n++; next} {if(n){d=$1-s; if(d>m)m=d} n=0; prev=$1} END{if(n){d=$1-s; if(d>m)m=d}; print m+0}' probe.csv

It prints the longest outage in seconds, measured from the last successful probe before the failures to the first success after them. It takes the duration from the timestamps, not from a count of rows, because a failed probe waits up to a second for its reply on top of the 0.2 second sleep. A probe cycle then takes about 1.2 seconds, so say in your notes that the figure is only as fine as that. The script assumes the first row is a success, which the baseline ping gives you.

What this tells you and what it does not

This is a lab. Namespaces on one machine share a clock and a CPU, so timing under heavy load will wobble. Netem's delay and loss are statistical models, not recordings of any real network. Run each condition several times and keep every log, because a single run can mislead you. We publish no results here for that reason: the useful part is the method, and your numbers will depend on your hardware.

It also tests one direction of cause at a time. Real faults combine. Add delay and loss together, then add the narrow link, and look again. The interactions are often where the surprises are.

If you test software that reports its own view of the connection, line its reports up against the probe log. In our lab we do this with a VPN client, and the useful question is whether what the client says matches what the probe log shows. When the two disagree, one of them is wrong, and the log is the easier one to audit.

Clean up 

kill $(cat probe.pid)
ip netns pids s | xargs -r kill
for n in c m s; do ip netns del $n; done

Deleting the namespaces removes the veth pairs and every qdisc with them.

Checklist

  • Build the path, then ping it before breaking anything.
  • Record a baseline for every tool you plan to use.
  • Log one line per probe, with a timestamp.
  • Note the time you apply and remove each impairment.
  • Impair both directions when you mean a round trip.
  • Repeat each condition and keep every log.
  • State your method next to every number you share.

This article was created with the help of AI.

title: Why Cheaper Tokens Fail to Cut the Inference Bill
description:
On October 29, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index updated its leaderboard. Google took the first position with Gemini 4 Carbon, pushing past the frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic that had led the benchmark for most of the year. Within hours of the ranking shift, OpenAI cut the API price of its workhorse mid-tier model by fifty percent.

Cutting nominal token rates in half looks like an immediate windfall for downstream engineering teams. If input and output tokens cost half as much, a team spending twenty thousand dollars a month on model calls should expect their next invoice to drop toward ten thousand dollars. In production software systems, monthly API expenditure rarely follows rate-card deflation.

Engineering budgets clear completed, verifiable outcomes. A production workflow requires an agent to parse customer intent, call external tools, validate a strict JSON schema, and write a clean database update. The clearing price of that unit of work depends on the entire execution trace, not the single-turn token rate.

When token tariffs fall, application behavior changes immediately. Cheaper tokens trigger standard economic demand elasticity. Lower marginal costs encourage developers to expand system prompts, preserve deeper conversational history, and add automated self-critique loops. An application that previously ran a single-turn prompt consuming fifteen hundred tokens gets redesigned into a four-turn agentic pipeline consuming eight thousand tokens. The engineering team justifies the added context because each individual token costs half as much, yet the total token volume across the task quadruples. The gross bill increases even as unit rates fall.

The larger operational cost sits in error distributions and retry cascades. Mid-tier models carry higher failure rates on complex structured outputs than flagship checkpoints. Suppose a frontier flagship completes a five-step tool-calling workflow with a ninety-five percent success rate on the first attempt, while a discounted mid-tier model succeeds eighty percent of the time.

In a multi-turn architecture, a failure on step three does not terminate cheaply. The model generates partial code or an invalid schema, the validation harness throws an exception, and the orchestrator triggers an automatic retry. That retry passes the entire prior conversation history back into the model, doubling the cumulative context window. If the retry fails a second time, a standard production fallback routes the accumulated context to the flagship model to finish the task.

The arithmetic of that fallback flips the intended savings. An engineering team running one thousand multi-step tasks pays for the initial turns on the discounted model, pays again for the expanded tokens generated during failed retry loops, and finally pays the full premium rate for the flagship fallback. When a task requires three corrective turns and an emergency escalation, the completed transaction costs more than routing the request directly to the expensive model from the start.

OpenAI chose to slash prices on its mid-tier model rather than its flagship because the two tiers serve distinct competitive functions. Frontier reasoning remains scarce, preserving its pricing power. Mid-tier models represent high-volume utility pipelines where developers build automated customer support, extraction microservices, and internal tooling.

By cutting mid-tier pricing by fifty percent, the lab builds an economic barrier around existing developer workflows. Migrating an enterprise application to Google Cloud to take advantage of Carbon requires rewriting system prompts, re-validating structured tool schemas, and conducting regression testing across internal test fixtures. That migration costs developer hours and introduces production risk. Offering a fifty percent discount removes the economic incentive for engineering teams to leave, protecting the provider's query volume while commoditizing the tier directly below the frontier.

The price war also compresses the margins of third-party inference providers and smaller hosting startups. Hyperscalers and well-capitalized foundation labs can absorb narrow gross margins on mid-tier inference by amortizing compute clusters across massive shared infrastructure and private financing. Independent hosting platforms that lease GPU clusters at market rates cannot match fifty percent cuts without operating at a cash loss.

Evaluating model infrastructure by dividing gross invoice spend by raw token volume treats every generated token as productive work. When tokens leak into conversational drift, schema validation errors, and defensive fallback invocations, those cycles represent straight capital waste. Measuring the realized cost per successful task outcome reveals whether a fifty percent rate reduction actually lowers monthly compute expenditure or simply subsidizes inefficient multi-turn loops.

Originally published at https://deanlee.info/essays/why-cheaper-tokens-fail-to-cut-the-inference-bill/

title: I got tired of production incidents caused by bad config, so I built a scanner
description:
How a 3 AM Kubernetes incident led me to build StackGuard, an open-source tool that scans your infra config and scores it before it reaches your production server.

It was 3 AM on a Tuesday. My phone was buzzing.

Our API pods were getting OOMKilled in a loop. Users were seeing 502s. The Slack channel was lighting up. I SSHed into the cluster, ran kubectl describe pod, and there it was:

Last State: Terminated
Reason:     OOMKilled

No resource limits. Someone had deployed a new service to production with no memory limits set. The container ate through the node's memory and took down three other pods with it.

The fix took two minutes. Adding resources.limits.memory: 512Mi to the deployment manifest. The incident took four hours.

That wasn't the first time something like this happened. A month before, a Terraform apply had gone through with an S3 bucket set to public-read. Nobody caught it in code review. Three weeks before that, a Dockerfile was running as root in production because nobody had added a USER directive.

Every single one of these was a known best practice. Every single one was missed because humans are bad at catching config mistakes in YAML files at 4 PM on a Friday.

The tools I tried

I looked at what was out there. There are great tools, don't get me wrong. But here's what I kept running into:

Scattered coverage. One tool does Terraform. Another does Kubernetes. A third does Dockerfiles. Now I need three tools in my CI pipeline, three sets of configuration, three different output formats.

No single number. Every tool gives me a list of findings. Some runs produce 47 warnings. Are we getting better or worse? Is this deploy safer than the last one? I had no way to answer that without reading every line.

Plugin SDKs and policy languages. I just wanted to write a rule that says "if this field has this value, that's bad." I didn't want to learn Rego or write a Go plugin.

I wanted one tool. One command. One score. One CI step. And rules that are just YAML.

So I built it

StackGuard is a single Go binary that scans your infrastructure config, Dockerfiles, Compose files, Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Terraform, GitHub Actions, Jenkinsfiles, Ansible playbooks, and nginx configs against a set of rules and gives you a production-readiness score out of 100.

$ stackguard scan .

examples/dockerfile/Dockerfile
  ✗ A stage pins only a channel tag, with no digest      DOCK_IMG_002 · line 1
  ⚠ The final image sets no USER, so it runs as root      DOCK_SEC_002 · line 8

Score: 81/100  1 error · 3 warnings · 0 info

That's it. No daemon. No config file required. No cloud service. It reads your files, evaluates 563 built-in rules, and prints what's wrong.

The things I actually care about

A score, not a wall of text. Every error costs 10 points, every warning costs 3, every info costs 1. Your score is 100 minus the deductions. You can gate your CI on it: --min-score 80. Now you have a number that trends over time.

Rules are YAML, not code. Here's a real rule:

id: K8S_SEC_001
title: Container runs as root
severity: ERROR
category: security
target: kubernetes
message: The container is explicitly configured to run as UID 0
query:
  path: containers[*]
  where:
    path: sc.runAsUser
    equals: 0

No Go. No Rego. No plugin SDK. Drop a YAML file in a directory and it loads on the next scan. If your org has a convention say, every Helm chart must set podDisruptionBudget you write a rule in 10 lines and it's enforced from that point on.

Nine targets, one command. I got tired of wiring up separate tools for each config format. StackGuard detects file types automatically. Point it at a repo and it figures out what's a Dockerfile, what's a Helm chart, and what's a Terraform module. One scan . covers the whole stack.

It fits in CI in two lines.

- name: StackGuard
  run: |
    stackguard scan . \\
      --fail-on error --min-score 80 \\
      --format sarif --output stackguard.sarif

- uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
  with:
    sarif_file: stackguard.sarif

The SARIF output means findings show up as annotations in your PR diff. Reviewers see the issue right next to the line, not buried in a CI log.

What it actually catches

Here are real categories of things StackGuard flags across different targets:

Security:

  • S3 buckets with public ACLs
  • Containers running as root
  • Secrets hardcoded in environment variables
  • SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0 in security groups
  • No network policies in Kubernetes

Reliability:

  • No resource limits on containers
  • No health checks in Dockerfiles
  • No PodDisruptionBudget for deployments
  • RDS instances without deletion protection
  • No retry configuration in CI workflows

Operational:

  • Unpinned image tags (:latest)
  • No .dockerignore file
  • Missing worker_connections in nginx
  • No log rotation configured
  • Jenkins pipelines without timeout

It's not trying to be a vulnerability scanner. It's checking the boring stuff that causes incidents at 3 AM the missing limits, the unpinned images, the defaults nobody changed.

How it works under the hood

The pipeline is straightforward:

  1. Discovery walks the paths you give it and classifies files by type.
  2. Parsers turn each file into a normalized resource tree. Rules never touch raw text.
  3. Engine evaluates compiled rules against those resources. Queries and regexes compile once before any file is read.
  4. Reporters emit findings in your chosen formats console, JSON, SARIF, HTML, or CSV.

A file that won't parse becomes a diagnostic, not a crash. One bad YAML file doesn't hide findings from the other 200 files in your repo.

The stuff I learned building it

Start with the output. I designed the terminal output first, then built backwards. If the output isn't useful at a glance, nobody will use the tool. The score was the first thing I implemented before the engine, before the parsers.

Embedded rules need to be opinionated. Early on I shipped with very conservative rules. Nobody complained, but nobody used it either. The tool became useful when I made the rules match what actually causes incidents, not what's theoretically incorrect.

YAML rules were the right call. I almost built a Go plugin system. I'm glad I didn't. The people who write infrastructure config are the same people who should write the rules for it. They know YAML. They don't necessarily know Go.

Scoring is surprisingly motivating. Teams that adopt StackGuard start treating the score like a game. "We were at 72 last sprint, we're at 84 now." That never happened with a flat list of warnings.

Install and try it 

# Homebrew
brew install nexutils/tap/stackguard

# Go
go install github.com/nexutils/StackGuard/cmd/stackguard@latest

# Then just
stackguard scan .

Point it at any repo that has infra config. It takes about 2 seconds for a typical project.

The project is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. We just shipped v0.2.0 with CSV output, a WASM playground, repo metadata in reports, and Homebrew/Scoop install.

If you've been bitten by a production incident that was caused by a config file someone didn't review carefully enough, I built this for you. Give it a try and let me know what you think.

title: Custom root pools and proxy trust after CVE-2026-111943
description:
Custom root pools and proxy trust after CVE-2026-111943

Custom certificate authorities are common in private APIs, internal service meshes, and enterprise TLS inspection. CVE-2026-111943 forces teams to look at those trust designs because a locally trusted CA can still lead to a chain containing one of the eight compromised eMudhra intermediates.

The flaw is in Go's crypto/x509 verification code. The Go vulnerability database lists affected versions before go1.26.10 and from go1.27.0-0 before go1.27.3. Mozilla reported that private keys for eight eMudhra intermediates were compromised and could be used for fraudulent HTTPS certificates. The Go fix adds a denylist based on SHA-256 hashes of certificate Subject Public Key Info values and filters out chains that contain a blocked certificate.

A trusted root is not the final answer

Certificate verification answers a chain-building question and a policy question. The chain must reach a root that the verifier trusts. The policy must also decide whether each link is acceptable. A custom root can satisfy the first part while doing nothing about a compromised intermediate later in the path.

The Go patch applies its negative decision after chain construction. A chain can be valid in the sense that signatures resolve to a configured root, while still being unacceptable because an intermediate key is on the blocklist. Applications and tests should treat CertificateInvalidError with NoValidChains as the expected result when such a chain is presented.

This distinction affects incident handling. Adding another root, changing the operating system trust store, or copying a CA file into a container does not remove the Go behavior introduced by the patch. A workaround that disables verification would weaken the application and should not be used to make a failing connection appear healthy.

Where enterprise PKI breaks

Organizations often insert an interception proxy between a Go application and an external service. The proxy generates a leaf certificate and signs it with an internal intermediate. If that intermediate or an upstream link is tied to a compromised key, a patched Go client will reject the chain. The application owner may see a general handshake failure while the network team sees a valid proxy certificate.

The same pattern can occur in private service meshes when a trust bundle is out of date or a synthetic chain is assembled by hand. Before changing application code, capture the presented chain and compare each SPKI hash with the Go denylist. If the chain uses a blocked key, replace the intermediate and distribute the new trust path. A new root alone may not be enough if the old intermediate remains in the served chain.

Third-party TLS inspection needs an explicit compatibility test. Deploy the patched binary against the same proxy configuration used in production, then verify that ordinary internal endpoints still validate. If a blocked certificate appears, obtain a clean replacement chain from the inspection platform's owner. Record the replacement date and the new SPKI values so that another team does not reintroduce the old chain from a cached configuration.

Do not confuse trust stores

Go may use the host trust store on some platforms and a custom pool supplied by the application on others. The review should identify which behavior each binary uses. It should also determine whether an embedded CA bundle, container image, operating-system package, or application configuration supplies roots. These are different sources of trust, and updating one does not imply the others changed.

The patched toolchain is still the necessary control. A binary built with an affected Go release can continue to accept a blocked chain even if the surrounding system trust store is current. A binary built with go1.26.10, go1.27.3, or a later patched release carries the new chain filter in its standard library.

Inventory and rollout

Locate Go binaries that use private roots for authentication or proxy traffic. Rebuild them with a patched supported toolchain and test against controlled certificate chains. Do not use live banking, identity, or customer endpoints to exercise the rejection path. A test harness with generated certificates is enough to prove the behavior.

For internet-facing assets, a ZoomEye search for app="Go" returned 260,278 fingerprint matches at the recorded time. Those assets are not known to be vulnerable or to use a custom root. The count is useful only as a broad starting point for ownership discovery.

The decision to record

The PKI owner should state whether any active proxy or internal service presents a chain with one of the eight blocked intermediates. The application owner should state which Go build is deployed and whether testing reached the expected rejection path. Security should confirm that no team bypassed verification to restore connectivity. These three records close the loop between CA replacement, code patching, and operational trust.

References

  • CVE-2026-111943 record
  • Go vulnerability database GO-2026-6809
  • Go issue 82345
  • Upstream fix commit
  • Mozilla security notice
  • CERT-BUND advisory source

title: عالم بوكيمون العربي: نبحث عن ملاحظات على تجربة البداية في لعبة متصفح
description:
نشارككم من فريق عالم بوكيمون العربي النسخة العربية من مشروعنا: لعبة تقمّص أدوار من صنع المعجبين تعمل من المتصفح. نريد عرض تجربة البداية على مطوري ألعاب الويب واللاعبين الناطقين بالعربية، وجمع ملاحظات عملية تساعدنا على تحسينها.

ما الذي يمكن تجربته؟

يمكن بدء التجربة كضيف واختيار بوكيمون البداية، ثم استكشاف العالم ثلاثي الأبعاد وجمع البوكيمون وتدريب الفريق وخوض المعارك. توجد أيضًا أنظمة للتبادل والتربية وفقس البيض. اللعب الأساسي مجاني، مع إعلانات ومشتريات اختيارية.

اختبار صغير يمكن لأي مطور تكراره

عند تجربة واجهة لعبة بلغة مختلفة، من المفيد فصل الخطوات إلى مهام قصيرة بدل الاكتفاء بسؤال «هل أعجبتك اللعبة؟». هذه مهام نقترح تجربتها في نسختنا:

  1. ابدأ كضيف وحدّد رفيق البداية: هل تعرف أين تضغط وما الذي سيحدث بعد الاختيار؟
  2. انتقل إلى العالم وحدّد أول هدف لك: هل تساعدك القوائم على معرفة الخطوة التالية؟
  3. جرّب من شاشة هاتف ومن شاشة كمبيوتر: هل تستطيع قراءة الأزرار والوصول إلى الخيارات المهمة؟
  4. انتبه إلى مزج العربية مع أسماء البوكيمون والنصوص الإنجليزية: هل ترتيب النص واضح؟

هذه أسئلة للاختبار وليست نتائج نَدّعي أننا حققناها. ما زالت بعض النصوص بالإنجليزية، ونرحّب بأمثلة محددة على المواضع التي تحتاج إلى تحسين.

كيف ترسل ملاحظة مفيدة؟

اذكر الجهاز والمتصفح، والخطوة التي حاولت تنفيذها، وما توقّعته، وما ظهر فعليًا. إذا وجدت مشكلة في الواجهة، أرفق لقطة شاشة خالية من معلوماتك الشخصية. لا تنشر كلمة المرور أو بيانات حسابك في التعليقات.

جرّب النسخة العربية على pokemonar.net، ثم شاركنا في التعليقات: ما أول نقطة احتجت عندها إلى توضيح؟ وأي رفيق بداية اخترت؟

هذا مشروع معجبين مستقل وغير رسمي، غير تابع لـ Nintendo أو The Pokémon Company أو Game Freak. تمت الاستعانة بالذكاء الاصطناعي في إعداد صياغة هذه الدعوة، وراجعنا وصفها وروابطها وصورها قبل النشر.
