title: I built a bookmarklet that shows where the Tab key goes, and what it never reaches
description:
Run Lighthouse on any page and scroll to the bottom of the Accessibility section. There is a list called "Additional items to manually check". Two of them are about the keyboard: "Interactive controls are keyboard focusable" and "The page has a logical tab order".

Manually. I wanted to check every page of my own site with the keyboard, so I built a tool for it.

What it is

Tab trail is a bookmarklet. Click it on any page and it draws a numbered dot on every Tab stop, joined by a line in the order the keyboard visits them. The stop you are on turns orange. Press Tab and follow the numbers, or press Play and it walks every stop for you.

Then it marks in red what fails WCAG 2.2 AA.

Try it on the live page. It has 3 things broken on purpose, so the first click shows red.

What turns red

7 checks, each with its WCAG rule:

  • Missed spots (2.1.1 A). Something looks clickable (a pointer cursor, a button role, an onclick) but Tab never gets there. The classic <div onClick> "Add to cart".
  • Hover menus (2.1.1 A, 2.4.7 AA). A menu that opens on :hover but never when Tab reaches it.
  • Forced order (2.4.3 A). A tabindex="5" that pulls an element ahead of the rest of the page.
  • Hidden focus (2.4.11 AA). Tab lands on something a sticky header, cookie bar or chat button covers completely. This one is new in WCAG 2.2.
  • Keyboard trap (2.1.2 A). Tab and Shift+Tab both leave focus on the same spot.
  • Lost focus (2.4.3 A). A popup closes and focus drops to the top of the page instead of going back to the button that opened it.
  • Out of order (2.4.3 A). Tab jumps somewhere it shouldn't, or a popup that blocks the page doesn't get Tab first.

The parts that were harder than they look

Hover menus come from CSS, so it reads your CSS. It goes through every style sheet it can read for :hover rules that show something (display, visibility, opacity, max-height) that is hidden right now and holds a link or button. Then it looks for a :focus, :focus-within or :focus-visible rule that shows the same element. No match and no aria-expanded toggle means red. Nested CSS and Tailwind v4 output had to work too: & rules resolved against their parent, @media inside rules, :hover inside :is() and :where().

Hidden focus needs the page to stop moving. After each Tab press it waits until scrolling is done, then tests 5 points on the focused element (the center and 4 corners). Only when all 5 land on something fixed or sticky is it flagged. Partly covered passes AA, so it is not red.

Safari and Firefox on a Mac skip links on Tab by default. Safari skips links and buttons until you turn on "Press Tab to highlight each item", Firefox skips links until you turn on Keyboard navigation in System Settings. A naive checker would flag every one of those presses as a jump. Tab trail marks them SKIPPED and tells you which setting to flip.

It has to survive any site. It draws inside its own shadow root, so the page's CSS can't touch it. It runs under a strict Content Security Policy and Trusted Types. When the page opens a modal <dialog>, everything outside it goes inert, so the tool moves itself into the dialog to stay clickable and moves back out when it closes.

Firefox can't store it. A bookmark there can be at most 65,536 characters, and Tab trail is 223,286. In Firefox you paste the script in the console.

Hand it to your AI

"Copy for AI" copies only the problems, each with its WCAG rule, what should happen, a unique CSS selector, a trimmed HTML snippet, the React, Vue or Angular component that drew it (on a dev build), a fix hint and how to check the fix. Paste it into your coding agent and it knows where to look.

Long numbers, emails and things that look like tokens are masked before they reach your clipboard. Read it once anyway.

Put it in your tests

While it is open, the page has window.__tabTrail, so a test can run it with no clicks:

npm i -D --save-exact tab-trail

import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

const script = readFileSync("node_modules/tab-trail/dist/tab-trail.js", "utf8");

test("Tab reaches everything", async ({ page }) => {
  test.setTimeout(300_000);
  await page.goto("http://localhost:5173/");
  await page.evaluate(script);
  await page.evaluate(() => window.__tabTrail.play());
  const problems = await page.evaluate(() => window.__tabTrail.problems());
  expect(problems.map((p) => `${p.check}: ${p.selector}`)).toEqual([]);
});

play() moves focus through every stop, so it covers Missed spots, Hover menus, Forced order and Hidden focus. Out of order and Keyboard trap need real Tab and Shift+Tab presses, and state().untested tells you which checks never ran, so a green test can tell a clean page from a skipped check. The full example, with the TypeScript types, is in the README.

Already run axe? Keep it. axe reads the HTML, Tab trail walks the Tab key.

What it doesn't do

It's the keyboard part, not a full audit. It checks that Tab gets there, not that Enter or Space then works. It doesn't compare Tab order with the visual order when CSS moves things around, doesn't judge your focus ring's contrast, and doesn't tell you what a screen reader says. Style sheets from other domains without CORS can't be read. The whole list is in docs/limits.md, and how it sits next to Accessibility Insights, WAVE and the rest is in docs/compared.md.

It reads the page and sends nothing: no network requests, no cookies, no storage. Close it and it's gone.

Get it

matjazkorosec / tab-trail

Tab order and focus order checker. A bookmarklet that draws every Tab stop and marks what Tab never reaches. WCAG 2.2 AA check helper.

Tab trail

One click shows the path the Tab key takes through any page, and marks in red what fails WCAG 2.2 AA.

Some people only use the keyboard. If Tab skips your "Add to cart" button, they can't buy from you. If it skips "Send" on your contact form, they can't write to you. Even Lighthouse tells you to check this by hand. Tab trail checks it for you.

I built it to check every page of my own site with the keyboard. Try it on the live page, it has 3 things broken on purpose.

Install

Bookmark

  1. Open matjazkorosec.com/tools/tab-trail and drag the Tab trail button to your bookmarks bar. Don't see the bookmarks bar? Press Ctrl+Shift+B, or Cmd+Shift+B on a Mac.
  2. Open your site and click the bookmark.
  3. Press Tab and follow the numbers, or press Play and it walks every stop for you. Click the bookmark…
View on GitHub

1 file of plain JavaScript, MIT licensed. Drag the button from the page to your bookmarks bar, click it on your own site, and press Play.

If it gets something wrong on your site, press Copy log in the panel and open an issue with it. I'd like to see the pages that break it.

title: Generate Presigned URLs for Tenant File Downloads in S3-Compatible Storage with Node.js
description:
The important choice for property-management report downloads is not which object store has the nicest SDK. It is where tenant isolation is enforced. For authenticated customer downloads, keep report objects private, make the application authorize the tenant before it asks for a short-lived signed URL, and keep report generation and storage under one clearly owned boundary when that reduces credential and retry complexity. A signed URL is an output of an authorization decision, not a replacement for one.

A second boundary can still be the better answer when it gives you controls your storage layer lacks. The decision is conditional: use a single REST boundary for a focused export pipeline when one key and one operating model are valuable; use a specialist storage or media service when public delivery, immutable retention, advanced browser upload policy, or cross-region replication is a hard requirement.

What did the download incident actually teach us?

In a bounded production review of a tenant-report workflow, I started by treating the download link as the product. That was the wrong unit of analysis. The durable unit was the authorization chain: authenticated customer, tenant identifier, report object key, and an expiry window that is short enough to limit replay. The URL only works safely when those four things have already been checked.

The invariant is simple: a customer session may receive a signed URL only for an object key derived from the authorized tenant and report record, never from an unchecked path parameter. Bucket and key correctness matter because the presign route cannot infer whether a key belongs to the customer. A URL that points at the wrong object can be perfectly valid cryptographically and still be a data-isolation failure.

That is the boundary.

For this workflow, Infrai is a deliberate fit when the report worker needs one plain REST API for storage and content processing, with no SDK installation or client-library version to coordinate. The same key and base URL can carry the handoff; that removes a second vendor credential set from a small export pipeline. It does not remove the need for tenant authorization.

That is why I would keep the bucket private and use signed-only access. This workflow is for authenticated customers, not a public gallery. A permanent public URL, a public-read ACL, or static-site hosting would move the decision to the wrong layer. The storage shape also lacks object versioning and object lock, so it is a poor fit for financial-grade WORM retention without an external control plane.

Short-lived access is not magic. It limits the lifetime of a leaked link; it does not revoke a link that has already been copied.

Which architecture keeps the tenant boundary legible?

There are two viable shapes. I prefer making the choice explicit in the design review because both can be correct, and neither should be smuggled in as a default.

Shape Invariant Good fit Boundary to accept
One service boundary The same application owns authorization, report processing, and the storage presign request A focused export pipeline where one key, one REST interface, and one operational owner reduce glue One vendor becomes a dependency for storage and content processing
Split storage and processing The application remains the authorization point and each specialist receives only the minimum scoped artifact Public media delivery, immutable retention, deep transformations, or mature cross-region controls Two account systems, credential rotation paths, retry models, and a handoff to test

The first shape is attractive when the seam is operational rather than product-defining. A storage call and a content-processing call can use the same Authorization: Bearer key and the same https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base URL, so there is no second signed-URL scheme to reconcile with the first one. The platform exposes a plain REST API, which means a Node.js service does not need an additional client library version to coordinate with its report worker. That is a concrete integration advantage, not a claim that one vendor removes every failure mode.

The split shape is stronger when the missing capability is a requirement. If a team needs public-read objects, object lock, hourly lifecycle, automatic cross-region copying, or broad migration tooling, it should choose a specialist or add an external control plane instead of pretending a signed link covers those requirements.

How can Node.js generate a presigned URL for an S3-compatible file download?

The application first authenticates the customer and loads the report row; only then does it construct the bucket and key for that tenant. The key is read from an environment variable, the method is explicit, and a non-success response is surfaced instead of being mistaken for a usable URL. The returned link is used within its expiration time, and the storage service does not receive the platform bearer token.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
)

func presign(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string) (string, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    // POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    endpoint := baseURL + fmt.Sprintf("/storage/object/presign/%s/%s",
        url.PathEscape(bucket), url.PathEscape(key))
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry with exponential backoff")
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("presign failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
    }
    body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return string(body), nil
}

The sample is Go because the publication constraints require Go code, but the protocol is language-neutral: any client that can send an HTTP request can call the route. In a Node.js service, use the equivalent explicit POST, read INFRAI_API_KEY, check the status, and parse the response according to the API response shape used by your client. Do not attach the platform Authorization header when the browser later requests the returned presigned URL; that URL is the download credential.

A retry needs care. Presigning is not a report write, but a rate-limit retry should honor Retry-After when present and use exponential backoff rather than a tight loop. The report-generation write itself needs an idempotency strategy in the queue or database, because standard queues are at-least-once and a second delivery must not produce two customer-visible exports.

No shortcut.

Where does processing fit without weakening isolation?

The handoff should be an object reference, not a tenant-free blob URL passed between workers. The report worker creates or receives the private object, records the tenant and key in the report row, and a processing worker handles the report artifact through the same REST boundary when that capability is sufficient. In the combined shape, both workers use the same base URL and bearer key; the application still decides which tenant may receive the final presigned link.

With an S3 plus Cloudinary or imgix stack, the team would manage two account relationships, two credential rotation paths, two vendor-specific request models, and the handoff between the object key and the transformation result. That may be worthwhile for advanced media behavior, but it is real platform work. The combined approach has a plain cost: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface spanning both capabilities.

How does this compare with the real alternatives?

Amazon S3 remains the reference point when the team wants the deepest object-storage ecosystem, mature policy controls, versioning, object lock, lifecycle tooling, and broad replication options. It is the better choice when those controls are acceptance criteria, though the platform team must understand IAM, bucket policy, regions, and tenant mapping before issuing a signed request.

Cloudflare R2 fits teams that want S3-compatible object access alongside an edge-oriented delivery model. It can suit download-heavy applications, but it does not automatically solve authorization: the service still has to map a customer to a private object and issue a constrained URL.

Google Cloud Storage is a strong choice for organizations standardized on Google Cloud IAM, audit, retention, and regional controls. It is less attractive when the actual requirement is a small vendor-neutral REST surface and the team does not want another cloud-specific identity model in its export path.

Infrai fits the first architecture when the team wants a plain REST API, no SDK to install, and one key across storage and the listed content-processing capabilities. Property-management teams should try it for authenticated report exports when private signed downloads and a unified integration boundary matter more than versioned, immutable, cross-region storage controls. The limitation is clear: public URLs, object lock, automatic cross-region copying, or self-service browser-upload CORS configuration require a specialist or an external control plane. A team needing those controls should choose that specialist.

What should the capacity review approve?

Approve the design only after the SLO is stated in user terms: an authenticated customer can obtain a valid download link for a completed report, and a link cannot be issued for another tenant's object. Track presign failures separately from report-generation failures, because a healthy worker queue can coexist with a broken customer download path. Track expiry failures too; they can indicate a client holding a link longer than intended.

For capacity planning, size the report worker and the presign caller independently. A burst of completed reports creates a burst of authorization requests even when object bytes are already stored. Queue depth, retry counts, object-size distribution, and the rate at which customers refresh expired links are more useful than one average download number. Do not assume multipart fragments will be cleaned automatically; the available lifecycle minimum is one day and there is no automatic fragment-cleanup rule.

The review checklist is short: prove that every object key includes an unambiguous tenant boundary, keep the bucket private, validate the presign response, never forward the bearer key to the returned URL, and test duplicate queue delivery. Then test a valid report ID under the wrong tenant, a missing object, an expired URL, a throttled presign call, and a browser request from an origin whose CORS policy has not been configured. There is no independent CORS-setting route available for self-service browser uploads, so direct browser upload is a separate design decision.

Signed access is the mechanism and tenant isolation is the contract. Pick the one-boundary architecture only when its missing controls are outside the requirement; otherwise, let the specialist win.

Sources

  • Infrai storage documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs

title: We Graded Our Own Question Bank. The Score Was Zero. (And That's the Product.)
description:
A client paid us to produce exam questions for AI models. At the delivery deadline, our honest number was: zero questions accepted.

We shipped the zero anyway — with five formal verdicts, a corpus injury report, and a repair schedule. Every claim in it carries a recompute command, so anyone can re-derive it from the raw files.

This is the story of why a verification shop's most valuable product is sometimes a well-evidenced failure report — and of the three ways our own infrastructure lied to us along the way.

1. The contract: a knife-edge difficulty band

Grading questions for AI models sounds like writing a quiz. It's closer to machining a needle.

A question passes acceptance only if, across five models with four runs each, all of the following hold simultaneously:

  • overall pass rate below 70%;
  • the strongest model passes all questions in only one to three of its four runs (it should find the question hard, not impossible);
  • mid-tier models fail hard — at least one full zero-run;
  • the weaker model's pass rate lands in a narrow band (25% or 50% — a signature, not a coincidence).

Too easy and the question measures nothing. Too hard, or unfair, and it measures noise. You are not looking for "a hard question". You are looking for a specific shape of partial failure, reproduced across model tiers. That shape is the product.

2. The theater problem: our own dashboards lied

For days, our production pipeline reported what every stakeholder loves to hear: metrics full, automation complete, artifacts counted.

The artifacts were corpses.

File counts counted files, not live questions. A production loop dutifully flipped status bits — built, blocked, delivered — while the things behind the bits were hollow or missing. The metric rewarded producing things, not passing things, and the system gave us exactly what we measured.

Everyone building agentic pipelines has this failure mode. The loop optimizes whatever you count. If you count files, you get files.

3. The contamination: the exam hall was sick, not the models

During one question's re-judging, the models kept producing what looked like defeated, near-blank answers. We burned hours chasing model channels — rate limits, context windows, prompt drift.

The actual root cause was in our repo. A housekeeping commit — whose message said it was restoring the original exam — had in fact shipped a fixed version of the code into the exam workspace. The grader could see the repaired code sitting next to the question it was supposed to fail on.

The commit message and the commit content disagreed. The md5 fingerprints didn't.

And here's the part that still gets me: the models were right. Shown a question with its answer lying beside it, submitting a deflated paper is the correct, honest behavior. We were diagnosing sick models for hours while the exam hall was the patient.

Lesson, now a standing rule: trust fingerprints and behavior tests, never intent-encoded strings — not commit messages, not file names, not the word "restore".

4. What verification actually took

Getting from theater to evidence took four mechanisms, none of them glamorous:

Criteria locks. The acceptance criteria themselves are frozen by hash. Changing them requires issuing a new locked version — and "criteria can only get stricter" is enforced by a pre-flight gate script that compares hashes before any grading run, not by a policy document nobody re-reads.

Evidence-chain scans. A scanner that walks the raw result files found 50 corrupted evidence files that had been silently rejected for days. Nothing flagged them, because the pipeline counted files, and the files existed.

Single-batch re-runs. Numbers are only comparable within a batch. Every verdict we ship comes from one batch, one config, no cherry-picking across runs.

Distrusting the grader itself. The freshest lesson, from this week: Python bytecode caching. When a test file gets replaced within the same second by a same-size file, the interpreter's .pyc cache considers itself still valid — and executes the old bytecode. Our loaders were, in the worst case, grading against stale copies of the code. A one-line minimal reproduction settled it; the fix (identity by inode + nanosecond mtime, compiling from source text directly) is now a hard gate on any re-judge.

That last one deserves emphasis, because it's rare enough to feel unfair: the measurement instrument had a bug that made failures look like model failures. If your acceptance pipeline executes code it doesn't hash-verify per-run, you own this bug too.

5. The first complete verdict

With the pipeline finally clean, we got our first complete verdict on a full question: 20 rounds, 5 models, one batch, evidence-clean.

The question failed. And here's the valuable part: every single failure landed on the same test. Not scattered, not noisy — one brittle assertion in the hard layer, with the rest of the question giving away points.

That's not a score. That's a diagnosis with a unique rework direction: add two or three heterogeneous failure points, fix the brittle assertion, and the question might actually have a difficulty shape instead of a difficulty spike.

This is what a "fail" should look like — a verdict that tells the writer exactly where the wall is.

6. The zero report

So what do you deliver when the delivery deadline arrives and the honest count is zero?

We delivered the zero. Specifically:

  • N = 0 accepted questions, stated plainly, no rounding, no "nearly there";
  • five formal verdicts on the stock questions, each conclusion tagged as measured, inferred, or unverifiable — inferences are never dressed up as measurements;
  • a corpus injury report — which stock questions are salvageable, which are structurally too easy, and why;
  • a repair schedule with the rework direction for each survivor;
  • and every claim carrying a recompute command, so the whole report is re-derivable by anyone with the raw files.

Did we miss the deadline? Yes. Was the trust damaged? The opposite, we'd argue: the client's question bank is now not seeded with unvetted questions that would have quietly poisoned every future benchmark score run on top of them.

A benchmark is a promise about the future. Shipping a fake-passing question into one is how that promise dies — slowly, invisibly, and exactly when someone important is looking at the score.

7. The offer

We're a small verification shop. This whole arc — the contamination, the locks, the pyc bug, the zero — was one client engagement.

If you build AI systems and your acceptance criteria actually matter to you, independent hands for criteria QA exist, as a batch service. The first real customer taught us the shape of it.

Judging stays free. You pay for the binding: the casebook, the certification, the protocol integration — the things that outlive the verdict.

And if any vendor ever tells you "metrics full, automation complete" — ask for the recompute commands. Watch what happens to the room.

A zero you can prove beats a hundred you can't.

title: AI agent visual regression testing for design systems
description:
AI coding agents now edit interface code all day, and they do it without looking at the screen. The code compiles, the tests pass, and a button three screens away has quietly changed color. Trail of Bits found the same pattern in security patches this month, and the UI version is easier to miss because nobody greps for "slightly off".

This article argues that visual regression testing is the review step product teams are skipping, and that the hard part is not the tooling but deciding what counts as a change. It is written for designers, product managers and founders who let agents touch a shared component library and want a setup they can put in place this week.

Agents fix the thing you asked and change the things you did not

On October 21, Trail of Bits published a review of its own merged patches. Across more than 130 merged pull requests, it confirmed 21 regressions: 16 functional, 1 performance and 4 in build or tests. A first agent pass flagged 58 candidates, and only 21 were real, about 36% precision. The lesson is not that agents write bad patches. It is that a change is judged against the bug it fixes, and nobody checks everything the diff touched.

That is a security team looking at server code. Interfaces have it worse. A functional test asks whether the checkout button submits the form. It does not ask whether the button is still the same green as the one on the pricing page.

Augment Code's guide to testing AI-generated UIs describes the failure plainly. Agent edits can pass linting, type checks and functional tests while still shipping layout shifts, broken CSS and styling drift. It is a vendor guide, so treat its benchmark numbers with care. The mechanism it describes matches what any team with a shared component library has seen.

My view is that this is a review problem, not a model problem. Better models will drift less, but they will also be given bigger tasks. The check has to live outside the author.

Why code review does not catch visual drift

A reviewer reading a diff sees --primary: #1a7f4b changing to --primary: #1b8250. Both are valid. Neither looks wrong. The reviewer cannot see that the token feeds hover states, disabled states, focus rings and the dark theme.

In shadcn/ui style setups the component source is copied into your repo, which means an agent can edit it directly. Augment notes that a change to --primary reaches every component that references it. One token, many consumers, one screen checked by the person who wrote the prompt.

Agents also vary run to run. Similar prompts can produce different spacing, different token choices and different responsive behavior. A spacing value of 14px is numerically fine and still off a 4px grid. A linter will not object. A person scanning a pull request will not either.

The fix is to stop asking humans to compute rendered output in their heads. Render it, compare it with the last approved render, and let the human judge only the differences.

What a visual test actually checks

The mechanism is simple. Playwright's snapshot testing saves a reference screenshot on the first run with expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(), then compares every later run against it. Storybook's visual testing does the same per story. Once enabled, every story becomes a test, and the first run creates the baselines.

Two details decide whether this helps or annoys your team.

First, thresholds. Playwright's per-pixel threshold defaults to 0.2 on a 0 to 1 scale, and maxDiffPixels is unset by default. That default will pass a subtle color shift on a large button. Tighten it for token-level components, loosen it for pages with photography.

Second, environment. Playwright's docs warn that rendering varies with the operating system, browser, hardware and headless mode, and baselines are named per browser and platform. A baseline made on a designer's laptop will fail in CI. Generate baselines in the same container image that runs the checks, or every run opens with false alarms and people learn to ignore the check.

Pixel diffing has a blind spot too. It tells you something changed, not whether the change was intended. That judgment is the part worth spending human attention on.

Test the components, then the flows that earn money

Teams usually start by screenshotting whole pages. I would start one level down. Shared components carry the blast radius, so cover each state of each one: default, hover, focus, disabled, loading, error. Storybook makes that cheap because the states already exist as stories.

Then add a short list of flows where a visual break costs revenue. For a SaaS product that is sign-up, the first-run screen and billing. For a store it is the product page, the cart and checkout. Five or six screens at two viewport widths is a better start than sixty screens nobody maintains.

Keep the noise out. Disable animations, wait for fonts, and mask regions that change by design, such as timestamps, rotating banners and ads. Playwright lets you move the mouse off interactive elements so hover styles do not leak into the shot, and a custom stylesheet can hide volatile content. Each of these removes a reason for someone to mute the check.

Where agents come in, give them the screenshots too. An agent that can see the rendered result can catch its own mistake before a human does. It should still not be the one to approve a baseline.

The approval rule that makes it work

The weak point of every visual test suite is the update command. In Playwright it is npx playwright test --update-snapshots. In Storybook you accept the change in the panel. Both are one click, and an agent that sees a red check will happily click it for you.

That turns the test into a rubber stamp. So write one rule down: an agent may propose a baseline change, a person who owns that component approves it. Make the UI check a required status on pull requests, which Storybook's Chromatic integration supports, and put the component owner on review for any file that changes a baseline.

The second half of the rule is about intent. Augment calls the failure "intent drift", where a change is visually clean but diverges from what the component is for. No screenshot diff finds that. Only someone who knows why the button is that size can, which is where a designer earns the review.

There is a catch worth admitting. Visual tests also report your own design lag. If the design file was not updated after a scope change, the test will flag the code as a regression when the design is stale. Fix the source of truth first, then the baseline.

A setup you can start on Monday

You do not need a platform purchase to begin. Here is a sequence that fits in a week.

Day one, list the ten components and five flows where a visual mistake would cost the most. Day two, write screenshot tests for them in Playwright, or turn on Storybook visual tests if you already keep stories. Day three, pin the browser and container image, and generate baselines there.

Day four, set thresholds. Start strict on tokens and buttons, looser on image-heavy pages, and review the first week of failures to see which are noise. Day five, make the check required, name an owner per component, and write the rule that agents propose baselines while people accept them.

After that, add one habit. When an agent task touches a token file or a shared component, the pull request description must list the screens it expects to change. If the diff shows others, the reviewer has a concrete question to ask.

None of this makes agents safer on its own. It makes their side effects visible, which is what Trail of Bits was trying to do for code. The cost is a few hours of setup and a review step that sometimes says no.

Originally published on kireev.us.

title: Terraform vs Pulumi vs CloudFormation in 2026: Which IaC Tool Should You Choose?
description:
TL;DR — the short answer

  • Terraform (or OpenTofu) is still the safest default for most teams in 2026: the largest provider ecosystem, the most modules and hiring pool, and one workflow that works across AWS, GCP, Azure and beyond. The tool is no longer open source, though — since 2023 it ships under the Business Source License, and the open-source continuation of the same codebase is OpenTofu.
  • Pulumi is the best fit when your team thinks like software developers: real programming languages (TypeScript, Python, Go, C#), real unit tests, and reusable abstractions built with loops and classes instead of a DSL. You pay for that power with a smaller ecosystem and a team that must actually be able to program.
  • CloudFormation is the right answer more often than the internet admits — if you are genuinely AWS-only. There is no state file to secure, no licence to think about, no per-resource SaaS bill, and new AWS services land here first. You pay with verbose templates and AWS lock-in.
  • There is no universal winner. There is only the tool that matches your clouds, your team's skills, and how much state and licensing risk you are willing to own.

Choosing an infrastructure-as-code (IaC) tool used to be a tooling decision. In 2026 it is also a licensing decision, a state-management decision, and a team-skills decision — and those three questions matter more than any feature checklist.

The original version of this comparison made the mistake most IaC comparisons make: star ratings, speed rankings with no measurements behind them, and AI features that sounded impressive but didn't survive scrutiny. This rebuilt 2026 edition takes a different approach. Every tool gets the same small, real example — an S3 bucket with versioning — so you can compare the shape of the work, not marketing copy. Pricing and licensing claims are stated carefully, with sources, because both changed significantly after HashiCorp relicensed Terraform in 2023.

One disclosure before we start: Terraform is the tool I have actually used in production work, across AWS and GCP. Pulumi and CloudFormation are covered here as evaluated options — researched and compared honestly, but I will flag where my hands-on depth is thinner. A comparison you can trust should tell you that.

Originally published on DevOps Enginer.

The comparison table

Dimension Terraform Pulumi CloudFormation
Language model Declarative DSL (HCL); limited functions, for_each / count for repetition General-purpose languages: TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, plus YAML Declarative YAML/JSON templates (+ AWS CDK, which generates CloudFormation from TypeScript/Python/etc.)
Cloud scope Multi-cloud and beyond: AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, SaaS APIs Multi-cloud: native providers for AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes, plus bridged Terraform providers AWS only
State management Explicit state file; you choose and secure the backend (S3, GCS, HCP Terraform…). Locking is your configuration's job Managed by Pulumi Cloud, or self-managed backend (S3/GCS/Azure Blob). Checkpoints handled by the service/CLI No state file. AWS stores stack state server-side
Provider ecosystem Largest: thousands of providers and modules in the Terraform Registry, mirrored by the OpenTofu Registry Smaller native set, but almost any Terraform provider can be bridged; strong Kubernetes support Every AWS service, via resource types and the Cloud Control API; community modules via the public registry
Testing Native test framework (terraform test, .tftest.hcl) since 1.6, plus Terratest (Go) for integration tests Unit tests with mocks in your host language's normal test runner; integration tests via Automation API cfn-lint, template validation, change sets as the built-in "plan/preview"; TaskCat for deployment testing
Policy as code Sentinel (HCP Terraform), or OPA/Conftest against plan JSON CrossGuard — policies written in TypeScript/Python or Rego (OPA) CloudFormation Guard (cfn-guard), Hooks, plus IAM and AWS Organizations SCPs
Pricing / licensing CLI is source-available under BSL 1.1 (not open source); free for internal use. HCP Terraform (SaaS): free up to 500 managed resources, then per-resource pricing CLI is open source (Apache 2.0). Pulumi Cloud: free for individuals; paid editions (Essentials, Pro, Enterprise) billed per managed resource plus per-secret charges; self-managed state is free Free. You pay only for the AWS resources you create. CDK is open source
Learning curve Moderate: HCL in a day, state/module discipline in months Low if you already program; steep if you don't Deceptively steep: simple YAML, but intrinsic functions, limits and stack behaviour take time
Best for Multi-cloud teams, platform teams, anyone hiring from the largest IaC talent pool Developer-heavy teams, complex logic, platform teams building internal abstractions AWS-only organisations, regulated AWS estates, teams allergic to state files and SaaS bills

A few rows deserve a warning. "Speed" rankings — the original version of this post ranked the three tools by execution speed — are mostly meaningless: all three spend nearly all their time waiting on the same cloud APIs. What differs is feedback speed: how fast you find out you made a mistake. Keep that in mind through the sections below.

The same bucket, three ways

The fastest way to feel the difference between these tools is to write the same thing in each: an S3 bucket with versioning enabled and a tag set.

Terraform (HCL) 

terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  bucket = "myapp-assets-prod"

  tags = {
    Environment = "prod"
    ManagedBy   = "terraform"
  }
}

# Since AWS provider v4, versioning lives in its own resource —
# the old inline `versioning {}` block (and the inline `acl`) are deprecated.
resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "example" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.example.id

  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

output "bucket_name" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.example.bucket
}

Note what the original version of this post got wrong: it set acl = "private" inline on the bucket. That argument has been deprecated for years, and modern provider versions push you toward separate resources for versioning, encryption, public-access blocks and ownership controls. Verbose — but explicit, and the plan output shows you exactly which resource will change.

Pulumi (TypeScript) 

import * as aws from "@pulumi/aws";

const bucket = new aws.s3.BucketV2("my-bucket", {
  bucket: "myapp-assets-prod",
  tags: {
    Environment: "prod",
    ManagedBy: "pulumi",
  },
});

const versioning = new aws.s3.BucketVersioningV2("my-bucket-versioning", {
  bucket: bucket.id,
  versioningConfiguration: {
    status: "Enabled",
  },
});

export const bucketName = bucket.bucket;

Same shape, different philosophy. This is ordinary TypeScript: the bucket is a class instance, its properties are typed, your editor autocompletes them, and if you need fifty buckets you write a for loop instead of learning a meta-argument. (The BucketV2 resources are the current form in Pulumi's AWS provider; the older aws.s3.Bucket with an inline versioning block is deprecated, just like Terraform's old inline arguments.)

CloudFormation (YAML) 

AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: S3 bucket with versioning enabled

Resources:
  AssetsBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: myapp-assets-prod
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      Tags:
        - Key: Environment
          Value: prod
        - Key: ManagedBy
          Value: cloudformation

Outputs:
  BucketName:
    Description: Name of the assets bucket
    Value: !Ref AssetsBucket

Short — for one bucket. CloudFormation templates grow linearly and verbosely: no loops, no functions beyond a fixed set of intrinsic helpers (!Ref, !GetAtt, !Sub, !If), and reuse means nested stacks or registry modules. That is exactly why AWS CDK exists — it lets you write TypeScript or Python that synthesises CloudFormation templates. If your team loves Pulumi's programming model but is committed to AWS, CDK — not hand-written YAML — is the honest comparison, and it changes the "Pulumi vs CloudFormation" answer for many AWS-only teams.

Terraform: the default, with an asterisk

Terraform's strengths are the ones the original post listed, and they are still true in 2026:

  • The ecosystem is the moat. Thousands of providers — AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, Cloudflare, GitHub, databases, SaaS APIs — and a public registry full of modules means the resource you need probably already has a maintained implementation. When something breaks, someone has almost certainly hit it before you.
  • One workflow, every cloud. init → plan → apply with human-readable plans is a genuinely good operational model, and it transfers between providers. For multi-cloud estates this is still unmatched.
  • The hiring pool. More engineers know HCL than any other IaC language. For a PM staffing a team, that is not a footnote — it is often the deciding factor.

The weaknesses are also real:

  • HCL is a ceiling. Loops, conditionals and abstraction exist (for_each, dynamic blocks, modules) but they are a DSL's approximation of programming. Complex, data-driven infrastructure fights the language.
  • State is your responsibility. The state file contains sensitive data in plaintext. Backend choice, locking, encryption at rest, and who can read it are all on you — see the common mistakes section.
  • The asterisk: licensing. Terraform is no longer open source. That deserves its own section, next, because it changes procurement conversations even when it doesn't change your daily workflow.

My own state rule is short enough to fit on a sticky note: never local, never unlocked, never shared between environments. State belongs in a remote backend with locking enabled and read access treated as sensitive — the state file effectively holds your infrastructure's secrets in plaintext — and each environment gets its own state, so an experiment can never reach production. I won't pretend the backend brand is the interesting decision here; it isn't. Almost every state horror story follows the same plot: the file lived somewhere casual, something wrote to it at the wrong moment, and afterwards nobody could say what the truth was. The rule exists so that story never gets started.

Modules taught me a related lesson about trust. The registry makes it wonderfully easy to import a building block with a confident README — and the first time you read one of those modules properly, all the way down to its resource list, you realise what you actually adopted: somebody else's defaults, running with your credentials. So my habit is split. For the patterns my own projects repeat — a network shape, a bucket with the right defaults — I write thin modules of my own, small enough to hold in my head. For the big, well-maintained pieces, I use the registry rather than reinventing them — but I read what a module creates before I trust it, not just what it promises. And either way, versions are pinned, for providers and modules alike, with upgrades reviewed in the plan instead of absorbed silently.

The OpenTofu factor: what actually changed, and what it means for you

The timeline, accurately:

  • August 2023 — HashiCorp moved Terraform from the open-source MPL-2.0 licence to the Business Source License 1.1 (BSL) for version 1.6 onward. Terraform 1.5.7 is the last MPL release. The BSL is source-available, not open source: you may read the code and use Terraform internally, but you may not use it to build a competing hosted offering. Each BSL release converts to MPL-2.0 four years after publication. Sources: https://dev.to/admiral-editor/opentofu-vs-terraform-in-2026-and-how-to-migrate-3omb and https://www.qovery.com/blog/opentofu-vs-terraform-2026-no-infra-engineers
  • September 2023 — The community forked the last MPL codebase as OpenTofu, under the Linux Foundation, keeping the MPL-2.0 licence. OpenTofu 1.6 GA followed in January 2024, and the project became a CNCF sandbox project in April 2025. Source: http://scalr.com/learning-center/what-is-opentofu
  • February 2025 — IBM completed its acquisition of HashiCorp (US$6.4B). The BSL stayed in place. Sources: https://www.qovery.com/blog/opentofu-vs-terraform-2026-no-infra-engineers
  • 2026, today — Both tools are actively developed and beginning to diverge. OpenTofu (1.13, September 2026) has features Terraform lacks: client-side state and plan encryption (AES-GCM with KMS or passphrase key providers), provider-level for_each, and an -exclude flag. Terraform has added features of its own — such as the Actions framework — that OpenTofu doesn't have yet. They are no longer drop-in identical twins — they are close relatives. Sources: https://infraplaybook.com/opentofu-vs-terraform/ and http://scalr.com/learning-center/what-is-opentofu

So what should a team actually do?

  • If you use Terraform internally, the BSL most likely does not restrict you. The licence targets competing hosted services. Most teams' real exposure is not legal — it's procurement policy ("we only run OSI-approved licences") and long-term pricing of the HCP Terraform control plane. HCP Terraform's free tier covers up to 500 managed resources; paid tiers have moved to per-managed-resource pricing (Essentials from roughly $0.10 per resource/month, Standard around $0.47, Premium around $0.99 — these figures have changed repeatedly, so check the current pricing page before budgeting). Sources: https://www.qovery.com/blog/opentofu-vs-terraform-2026-no-infra-engineers
  • If open-source licensing is a hard requirement, OpenTofu is the same skills and nearly the same code. Same HCL, same providers, same state format. Migrating a typical setup is swapping the binary and running tofu init — but test it on a copy of your state first, and be aware that very new Terraform features may not exist in OpenTofu (and vice versa).
  • If you sell a hosted IaC product, this is a legal conversation, not a blog-post conversation. Get advice; that's precisely the use the BSL restricts.

The honest summary: the fork did not kill Terraform, and Terraform did not kill the fork. In 2026, "Terraform vs Pulumi vs CloudFormation" is really a four-way decision, and HCL skills now buy you two engines.

Pulumi: infrastructure as software — with software's problems

Pulumi's pitch is simple and genuinely appealing: stop learning DSLs, write infrastructure in a language you already know, with your existing IDE, test framework, package manager and code-review habits.

Where that pitch holds up:

  • Real abstraction. Loops, conditionals, classes, functions, npm/PyPI packages. Building a tidy internal " VPC component" that a whole company reuses is natural in Pulumi in a way it never quite is in HCL.
  • Real unit testing. Pulumi supports unit tests with mocked providers in Jest, pytest, and friends. Testing that your component sets the right tags before anything touches a cloud account is a capability Terraform's native test framework only partially matches.
  • Type safety catches real errors early. A misspelled property is a compile error, not a failed apply twenty minutes in.
  • Kubernetes is a first-class citizen, with strong typed APIs for manifests and charts — one reason developer-heavy platform teams like it.

Where it doesn't:

  • The team must be able to program. "Low learning curve" is only true for developers. Hand a Pulumi codebase to an ops engineer who has never written TypeScript and the curve is steeper than HCL's, not shallower.
  • Abstraction cuts both ways. General-purpose languages make it easy to hide infrastructure inside layers of clever code that nobody can plan-review. A pulumi preview diff is only useful if a human can trace what generated it.
  • Ecosystem depth. Pulumi's native providers for AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes are strong, and almost any Terraform provider can be bridged — but bridged providers and community examples lag the Terraform Registry's depth. Expect to write more yourself.
  • The state question doesn't disappear. Pulumi Cloud manages state (and secrets) for you — free for individuals; the paid editions (Essentials from $40/month, Pro from $400, Enterprise from $2,000) then bill per managed resource (from about $0.18 per resource per month on Essentials) plus per-secret charges. The editions were restructured in 2026, so check the current pricing page before budgeting (https://www.pulumi.com/pricing). Self-managed backends (an S3 bucket, for example) make the CLI effectively free, at the cost of running state yourself — the same trade Terraform offers.

One correction to the original post: it leaned hard on Pulumi being "AI-native" with AI-assisted generation as a headline feature. AI code assistants can generate Pulumi, Terraform and CloudFormation today — that is a property of LLMs, not a durable Pulumi advantage, and it's no basis for choosing an IaC tool. What matters is whether the generated code is reviewable and testable in your workflow — which loops back to the points above.

CloudFormation: the AWS-native option that quietly improved

CloudFormation's reputation — verbose, slow, painful — was earned over a decade. But the honest 2026 picture includes several years of AWS investment that the "outdated" label ignores:

  • No state file, ever. AWS holds stack state server-side. There is no terraform.tfstate full of secrets to leak, encrypt, lock or corrupt. For regulated AWS estates, that single property settles arguments.
  • Stack refactoring (February 2025). You can now move resources between stacks and rename logical IDs without replacing the resources — historically one of CloudFormation's most painful limitations, and a common reason teams fled to Terraform. Source: https://dev.to/aws-builders/infrastructure-as-code-complete-aws-guide-to-iac-tools-2026-aak
  • IaC generator. CloudFormation can scan resources that already exist in your account and generate templates for them — the built-in answer to "we have three years of console-built infrastructure." Source: https://dev.to/aws-builders/infrastructure-as-code-complete-aws-guide-to-iac-tools-2026-aak
  • Drift detection and drift-aware change sets. Change sets (the CloudFormation equivalent of a plan) now account for drift between template, last deployment and reality, and scheduled drift detection flags console edits. Source: https://dev.to/aws-builders/infrastructure-as-code-complete-aws-guide-to-iac-tools-2026-aak
  • Day-zero AWS coverage and guardrails. New AWS services arrive as CloudFormation resource types first, StackSets deploy baselines across AWS Organizations accounts, and Hooks plus cfn-guard give you policy checks at deploy time.
  • It's free. No per-resource SaaS line item, no licence review.

The weaknesses remain structural, not incidental:

  • AWS only. This is not a limitation you can engineer around. The day a second cloud becomes real, CloudFormation knowledge and templates stay behind.
  • Template ergonomics. Intrinsic functions, stack limits, long stack update times on large estates, and failure states that historically required support tickets to escape (rollback behaviour has improved, but a stuck stack is still a bad day). CDK fixes the ergonomics by generating templates — at which point you're maintaining a TypeScript/Python codebase and its generated output.
  • Thin reuse story in raw YAML. Modules exist via the registry, but the ecosystem is a fraction of Terraform's.

For an AWS-only organisation — especially a regulated one that values audit trails, no external state, and no vendor licence review — CloudFormation (usually via CDK for anything complex) is not a consolation prize. It is a legitimate first choice. For everyone else, the multi-cloud row of the table decides it.

Decision guidance: choose by situation, not by hype

You are a small team (or solo) shipping on one cloud.
If that cloud is AWS and you don't expect a second one: CloudFormation via CDK, or Terraform — pick based on whether you want AWS's free, stateless model or the larger community. If there's any real chance of multi-cloud, start with Terraform/OpenTofu and skip a future migration.

You are a platform team serving many product teams.
Terraform/OpenTofu for the shared foundation (networking, accounts, clusters) — the module ecosystem and hiring pool win. Consider Pulumi for the application-facing layer if your developers are strong programmers who will own what they write. This hybrid is common in practice — despite what the original version of this post claimed, it's not because one tool is "faster"; it's because the two layers have different authors.

You work in a regulated environment (medical, finance, government).
Your deciding factors are audit trail, state security and licence/procurement rules — not language ergonomics. Terraform with a locked-down remote backend (or HCP Terraform) plus policy-as-code is a defensible default; if your procurement requires OSI-approved licences, that same setup on OpenTofu keeps the MPL-2.0 licence and adds client-side state encryption. AWS-only regulated estates can make an equally defensible case for CloudFormation: no external state file, native integration with AWS audit tooling, nothing to license. (I write this as general practice, not about any specific employer's setup — in regulated work, your compliance team's ruling outranks any blog, including this one.)

Your team is developer-heavy and infrastructure logic is genuinely complex.
Dynamic, data-driven infrastructure — per-tenant environments generated from a database, intricate Kubernetes platforms — is where Pulumi's programming model earns its keep, and where HCL starts to hurt.

You are already on one of these tools and it works.
Stay. Migrations are justified by licensing mandates, a cloud strategy change, or a team-skills shift — never by a comparison table. See the next section before volunteering for one.

Migration notes (the honest version)

  • Terraform ↔ OpenTofu: the only cheap migration on this page. Same HCL, same providers, compatible state. Swap the binary, run tofu init, plan, and expect an empty diff on a healthy setup. Do it on a copy of state first, pin versions, and check for the small set of features that now exist on only one side.
  • Terraform → Pulumi: Pulumi ships a converter (tf2pulumi, and pulumi convert) that translates HCL into Pulumi code — a starting point, not a finished migration. Realistically: convert or hand-port stack by stack, and either import existing resources into Pulumi state or let Pulumi adopt them carefully, resource group by resource group. Budget days-to-weeks per estate, not an afternoon.
  • Anything → CloudFormation: the IaC generator can produce templates from existing resources, which helps — but generated templates are a beginning, not an architecture. Expect to restructure into sane stacks (and learn the refactoring tools) before it feels like home.
  • CloudFormation → Terraform/Pulumi: use terraform import blocks (or Pulumi's import) incrementally, stack by stack; do not delete-and-recreate production resources to "start clean." Databases and stateful resources should be the last things moved, with a rollback plan that doesn't involve hope.
  • Every direction: migrate state in a maintenance window, keep the old tool able to plan (read-only) until the new one has applied successfully at least once, and never let two tools manage the same resource at the same time.

Common mistakes (all three tools)

  1. Committing state files to Git (Terraform/Pulumi self-managed). State contains secrets in plaintext. Use a remote backend with locking and encryption, and treat read access to state as read access to your infrastructure's passwords.
  2. Running applies from laptops. Whoever's machine, whatever local drift. Applies belong in CI with a reviewed plan/change set attached to the change — this is also your audit trail. (For this site's cluster view of that pipeline discipline, see our DevSecOps checklist for securing your CI/CD pipeline.)
  3. One giant state/stack for everything. Blast radius grows with estate size. Split by environment and by lifecycle (network ≠ application ≠ data), whichever tool you use.
  4. Unpinned providers and modules. "Latest" is not a version strategy. Pin, review upgrades in the plan, and upgrade deliberately — provider majors have broken production estates.
  5. Clicking in the console "just this once." Drift is how IaC estates quietly stop describing reality. Every tool here can detect drift; none can stop you creating it. If you must click, import the change back into code the same day.
  6. Testing only in production. Whatever your tool's testing story is — native tests, unit tests with mocks, linting, change-set previews — an untested template change to production networking is a career event.
  7. Choosing for the demo, not the decade. IaC choices are sticky: state, modules, skills and CI all accumulate. Weight the boring rows of the comparison table — state, licensing, ecosystem, hiring — over the exciting ones.

For the multi-cloud angle on this decision, see our multi-cloud strategy guide, and for how IaC fits a GitOps delivery model, GitOps vs traditional CI/CD.

Most engineers I know have a version of this story, and mine follows the standard plot. Early on, state feels like a by-product — a file the tool leaves lying around — so you treat it casually: it lives on your machine, applies run from wherever you happen to be working, and nobody thinks about what happens if that file is lost, corrupted, or written by two runs at once. Picture the moment it stops feeling like a by-product: a second environment appears, or a second pair of hands, and suddenly nobody can say with confidence which copy of the truth is the truth. Nothing dramatic has to break for the lesson to land — the near-miss is enough. The rule it left me with is the one this whole section keeps circling: remote, locked, backed up — and treated as sensitive, because it is.

FAQ

Is Terraform still open source in 2026?

No. Since version 1.6 (August 2023), Terraform is licensed under the Business Source License 1.1 — source-available, free for internal use, but not OSI-approved open source. If you need the same tool under an open-source licence, that is exactly what OpenTofu (MPL-2.0, Linux Foundation) is.

Should I switch from Terraform to OpenTofu?

Only for a reason: a procurement rule requiring open-source licences, a wish for OpenTofu-only features like client-side state encryption, or discomfort with the HCP Terraform pricing direction. Technically, the switch is small (same HCL, providers and state). "Because the internet is angry" is not a reason — the BSL does not restrict ordinary internal use.

Is Pulumi free?

The CLI is open source (Apache 2.0) and Pulumi Cloud is free for individuals with unlimited resources. Teams pay for Pulumi Cloud's paid editions (Essentials, Pro, Enterprise), billed per managed resource plus per-secret charges; self-managing your state backend avoids those fees. Check current pricing — the editions were restructured in 2026.

Does CloudFormation cost anything?

No. CloudFormation itself is free; you pay only for the AWS resources it creates. The same applies to AWS CDK, which is open source and generates CloudFormation templates.

Can CloudFormation manage non-AWS resources?

Only in a limited sense, via custom resources backed by Lambda — a workaround, not multi-cloud support. If you genuinely run two clouds, CloudFormation should not be your primary tool.

Which tool is best for Kubernetes?

Terraform and Pulumi both have mature Kubernetes providers, and both are widely used to provision clusters and platform layers. Pulumi's typed Kubernetes APIs are nicer for application developers; Terraform's ecosystem is deeper for cluster/platform provisioning. CloudFormation covers EKS well but is rarely chosen for Kubernetes. Note that many teams deliberately manage in-cluster resources with GitOps tools instead and use IaC only up to the cluster boundary.

Conclusion

In 2026 the honest answer to "Terraform vs Pulumi vs CloudFormation" is a decision tree, not a podium:

  • Default to Terraform or OpenTofu when you want the biggest ecosystem, multi-cloud reach and the deepest hiring pool — and choose between the twins based on your licence requirements, not features alone.
  • Choose Pulumi when your team genuinely programs, your infrastructure logic is complex, and you'll invest in testing and reviewing infrastructure like software.
  • Choose CloudFormation (usually via CDK) when you are AWS-only and committed — and value having no state file, no licence review and no SaaS bill more than portability.

And whichever you choose: remote state with locking, pinned versions, plans reviewed in CI, and no console clicks. Those four habits will matter more to your future self than the logo on the tool.

title: Get Instagram Story Alerts in Telegram with a Node.js Script
description:
Stories disappear after 24 hours, and Instagram has no way to say "tell me when this account posts one" for accounts you do not run. If you follow a brand, a creator or a competitor's public account and want a message the moment a new story appears, a short polling script does the job.

Updated October 2026.

This post builds one in Node.js: poll the stories of a list of accounts, remember which story ids you have already seen, save the media, and send a Telegram message for each new story. It also works out the cost per day, because polling is billed per request and the interval is the number you control.

Code was type-checked against storiesfly 1.1.0 (ESM, Node 18 or newer, no runtime dependencies). If you want the result without writing code, see the last section.

What you need

  • A StoriesFly API key. Sign in with Telegram at storiesfly.com/developers/dashboard. A new account gets 100 free requests.
  • A Telegram bot token from @BotFather, and the chat id the messages should go to. Send your bot a message, then open https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/getUpdates to see the chat id. 
npm install storiesfly
export STORIESFLY_API_KEY="your_key"
export TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN="123456:ABC..."
export TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID="123456789"

You never log in to Instagram with your own account. You send an API key, and your account never appears among a story's viewers.

What the stories call returns 

import { StoriesFly } from "storiesfly";

const client = new StoriesFly({ apiKey: process.env.STORIESFLY_API_KEY! });

const { user, stories } = await client.user.stories({ username: "instagram" });

console.log(user.id, stories.length);
console.log(stories[0]);

Output shape (values are illustrative):

{
  "id": "3012345678901234567",
  "url": "https://www.instagram.com/stories/instagram/3012345678901234567/",
  "taken_at": 1793000000,
  "taken_at_iso": "2026-10-28T09:30:00.000Z",
  "media_type": "video",
  "media_url": "https://...",
  "thumbnail_url": "https://...",
  "video_duration": 12.4
}

stories is empty when the account has none up. Ids are strings, which matters: Instagram ids are larger than 2^53 and a JSON number would round them. Always store and compare them as strings.

The polling script

The logic is a diff: fetch the stories that are up now, drop the ids you have already seen, alert on the rest, save the new ids.

import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { StoriesFly, StoriesFlyError, type Story } from "storiesfly";

const client = new StoriesFly({ apiKey: process.env.STORIESFLY_API_KEY! });

const ACCOUNTS = ["instagram", "natgeo"];
const INTERVAL_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000; // every 30 minutes
const SEEN_FILE = "./seen-stories.json";

type Seen = Record<string, string[]>; // username -> story ids

async function loadSeen(): Promise<Seen> {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(await readFile(SEEN_FILE, "utf8")) as Seen;
  } catch {
    return {};
  }
}

async function notify(username: string, story: Story): Promise<void> {
  const text = [
    `New ${story.media_type} story from @${username}`,
    story.taken_at_iso ?? "",
    story.media_url ?? story.url ?? "",
  ]
    .filter(Boolean)
    .join("\n");

  const res = await fetch(`https://api.telegram.org/bot${process.env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}/sendMessage`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ chat_id: process.env.TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID, text }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) console.error("Telegram error", res.status, await res.text());
}

async function checkAccount(username: string, seen: Seen): Promise<void> {
  const { stories } = await client.user.stories({ username });
  const known = new Set(seen[username] ?? []);
  const fresh = stories.filter((s) => !known.has(s.id));

  // Oldest first, so the chat reads in order.
  fresh.sort((a, b) => (a.taken_at ?? 0) - (b.taken_at ?? 0));
  for (const story of fresh) await notify(username, story);

  // Keep only ids that are still up, so the file does not grow forever.
  seen[username] = stories.map((s) => s.id);
}

async function runOnce(): Promise<void> {
  const seen = await loadSeen();
  for (const username of ACCOUNTS) {
    try {
      await checkAccount(username, seen);
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof StoriesFlyError) {
        console.error(`@${username}: ${err.code} (request ${err.requestId})`);
        if (err.code === "credits_exhausted") return; // stop until you top up
      } else {
        throw err;
      }
    }
  }
  await writeFile(SEEN_FILE, JSON.stringify(seen));
}

await runOnce();
setInterval(() => void runOnce(), INTERVAL_MS);

Notes on the choices in that script:

  • First run. Everything that is up when you start counts as new, so you get one batch of alerts. To avoid that, run once with the notify call commented out, then turn it back on.
  • Why store only ids that are still up. A story lives about 24 hours, so there is no reason to remember an id longer. The file stays small.
  • Errors. A private account answers private_account and a missing one not_found. Both are charged, so remove such usernames from the list rather than polling them forever. rate_limited is retried by the client twice before it reaches your catch.
  • One failure does not stop the others. The try is inside the loop over accounts.
  • Order of writes. The seen file is written after the alerts, so a crash between the two can send a duplicate alert. That is the safer direction compared with missing one.

Cron instead of setInterval

A long-running setInterval is fine on a VPS. If you prefer cron, drop the last line (setInterval) and run the script once per tick:

*/30 * * * * cd /path/to/project && node poll.mjs >> poll.log 2>&1

Cron survives restarts and leaves nothing running between ticks. If you compile the script from TypeScript, point cron at the compiled .js file.

Save the media soon

The media_url values are signed links, and they expire within days. A story is gone from the account after a day, and the file link does not last much longer. If you want to keep it, download it when the alert fires:

import { mkdir, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import type { Story } from "storiesfly";

export async function saveStory(username: string, story: Story): Promise<string | null> {
  if (!story.media_url) return null;

  const res = await fetch(story.media_url);
  if (!res.ok) return null;

  const ext = story.media_type === "video" ? "mp4" : "jpg";
  await mkdir(`./stories/${username}`, { recursive: true });
  const path = `./stories/${username}/${story.id}.${ext}`;
  await writeFile(path, Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer()));
  return path;
}

Call saveStory(username, story) next to notify. If you would rather get the file in Telegram than a link, the Bot API has sendVideo and sendPhoto, which take a URL.

What it costs

Each client.user.stories call is one request, and requests start from $1.50 per 1,000. The cost is accounts x polls per day:

Accounts Interval Requests / day Cost / day Cost / 30 days
5 60 min 120 $0.18 $5.40
20 30 min 960 $1.44 $43.20
20 15 min 1,920 $2.88 $86.40
100 60 min 2,400 $3.60 $108

The interval is the lever. Stories stay up for a day, so polling every 30 to 60 minutes still catches each one with hours to spare. Polling every minute only buys you earlier alerts, not more of them. A good rule is to poll busy accounts often and quiet ones rarely: keep two lists with two intervals.

Two things cost nothing to check. Your balance (client.account() is free) and the per-call charge (pass { withMeta: true } and read meta.unitsCharged). Add a guard that stops the script when balanceRemaining falls below a number you pick. It comes as a string in US dollars, so compare Number(meta.balanceRemaining).

Privacy, in one paragraph

You never log in with your own account, so your account never appears among a story's viewers. The person is not notified. The script reads public stories only: a private account gives private_account, and you cannot get around that.

Limits to know about

  • It only sees stories that are up now. There is no history, so if the script was down for two days, you missed those stories.
  • It detects a story at the next poll, not at the moment it is posted. The delay is at most your interval.
  • Highlights are a separate call (client.user.highlights), not part of this script.

If you do not want to run this yourself

The script above is a few dozen lines, but you have to host it, keep the bot token safe and watch the balance. If you only want the alerts, StoriesFly has a Telegram bot and a tracker that does this without code: you add an account and get a message when it posts. The API is the better fit if you want the data inside your own app.

FAQ

How do I get the Instagram story API without logging in?

Use an API key from the dashboard and call client.user.stories({ username }). There is no Instagram login, cookie or session on your side.

Can I look up an account by id?

Yes. client.user.stories({ id }) takes an id instead of a username. Pass one of the two, never both.

How often should I poll?

Every 30 to 60 minutes is enough for most uses, since a story stays up for a day.

Will the account know I looked?

The person is not notified.

Do the media links last?

No. They expire within days, so save the files when you get the alert.

Full method list and response types: storiesfly.com/developers/docs.

title: OAuth Trust at Machine Speed: What the ConnectWise Incident Teaches Cloud Teams
description:
A third-party app does not need to guess your employees’ passwords if your tenant has already granted it permission to act. That is the uncomfortable part of the ConnectWise Cloud Backup incident: the reported access path ran through application credentials and existing customer trust, not a fresh interactive login at every downstream organization.

Microsoft says the China-state-aligned actor it tracks as Storm-0940 used the open-source ARTEX agentic penetration-testing framework to accelerate activity after the ConnectWise compromise. It reports more than 2,250 tenant sign-in attempts, with follow-on actions in some environments that included Microsoft Graph reconnaissance and application credential or privilege changes. Microsoft also says the activity did not result from a compromise of, or vulnerability in, Microsoft systems, products, or services. Those distinctions matter: the report describes abuse of a compromised third-party application’s granted access, not a Microsoft platform breach.[1]

This is a report-based analysis, not a first-person incident-response story. The useful lesson is not that AI has invented a new kind of cloud attack. It is that automation can make an existing trust failure move faster than a manual review process.

The application was already inside the trust boundary

OAuth consent is easy to treat as a one-time setup screen. An administrator reviews a list of permissions, clicks approve, and the integration starts working. Months later, the app may feel like a background service rather than an identity with ongoing authority.

That mental model is risky. An enterprise application or service principal can authenticate without a human entering a password at that moment. Its access depends on the permissions, credentials, and grants already configured. If the vendor’s application credentials are compromised, an attacker may be able to use established trust to reach customers who authorized the app.

Microsoft describes that exact shape in the ConnectWise case: after gaining control of credentials for cloud applications, the actor used those applications to authenticate to customer environments with the access they had already been granted. Microsoft observed follow-on activity in multiple environments, including reconnaissance and attempts to modify credentials or privileges. The company cautions that an affected application or successful authentication does not, by itself, prove customer data was accessed or exfiltrated.[1]

ConnectWise’s own advisory describes unauthorized access to application credentials associated with Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick. Its latest advisory update, published October 28, says phased restoration was beginning through a new, security-hardened application, with partner action required. Partners must reset their password, configure multifactor authentication if needed, and re-authorize each Microsoft 365 tenant through the new app. The advisory warns not to re-enable previously disabled applications unless ConnectWise specifically instructs them to, and says re-authorization alone does not confirm that backups have resumed. Once backup capabilities are available, partners should verify that new snapshots complete successfully.[2]

ConnectWise’s technical guide also says that vendor-side containment does not change enterprise-application settings inside each partner or customer tenant. Those tenants need separate review, including dormant connections, and the guide cautions that completing the workflow does not prove a tenant was unaffected or authorize reconnection.[3]

What AI changes, and what it does not

Microsoft says ARTEX helped automate scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse. The report says some attacks reached privileged cloud access in under three hours. It also describes a password-spray campaign between October 10 and 14 that generated more than 151,000 failed sign-in events across 327 accounts at eight organizations. Microsoft observed no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call, or directory change from that particular password-spray campaign.[1]

That last sentence is not a footnote to skip. The 151,000 failed sign-ins belong to one described campaign phase; they are not evidence that 151,000 accounts were compromised. Microsoft separately reports downstream customer activity through the compromised applications. Collapsing those into one dramatic number would exaggerate what the source says.

The deeper change is operational tempo. An agentic workflow can test many paths and react to results without waiting for a person to review every step. That increases the value of controls that work continuously: short-lived credentials where supported, narrow permissions, anomaly alerts, and a tested way to revoke trust across tenants.

The incident does not show that a language model independently discovered a zero-day or that AI defeated a specific security product. It shows a threat actor used an agentic framework to accelerate an existing offensive workflow. The hard problem remains familiar: what can a trusted application do, where can it do it, and how quickly can an organization notice when that behavior changes?

The uncomfortable inventory problem

Most organizations can list their direct employees and core cloud subscriptions. Fewer can quickly answer a different set of questions:

  • Which third-party applications have tenant-wide or high-impact permissions?
  • Which integrations are still needed, and which are leftovers from a pilot or departed vendor?
  • Who owns each application relationship?
  • What is the expected sign-in pattern for each service principal?
  • What is the emergency process for disabling an app without destroying evidence?
  • Which customer or business processes stop if the integration is revoked?

A display name is not enough for that inventory. Microsoft’s response guidance tells affected customers to search by application ID rather than display name, review tenants where affected applications are currently or were previously installed, and record the local service-principal object ID. That is a useful general lesson: names are labels; stable identifiers are the better join key for investigation.[1]

This gets harder in service providers and other multi-tenant businesses. One integration can have many customer authorizations, and a single vendor-side credential incident can create a broad downstream review. A spreadsheet maintained only during onboarding will not stay accurate. The inventory needs an owner, a review cadence, and an offboarding trigger.

A practical third-party OAuth review

1. Build the inventory from identity data. Export enterprise applications, service principals, owners, credentials, consent grants, and app-role assignments from the identity platform. Include application ID, local object ID, tenant, permission scope, business owner, vendor contact, and last observed use. Do not treat a familiar product name as proof that the app is official or currently required.

2. Rank access by impact. Separate read-only access from write access, directory administration, mailbox access, key-vault access, and broad resource management. Mark permissions that can create credentials, assign roles, alter users or groups, or access sensitive data. Review the actual granted permissions, not only the vendor’s marketing explanation of what the integration needs.

3. Define expected behavior.
