title: Serverless vs Containers (2026): How to Choose for Cost, Scale and Speed
description:
Introduction: in 2026, it is rarely either/or

Should you build on serverless, or on containers?

It is still one of the most argued questions in cloud architecture — because the answer decides your cloud bill, how much infrastructure your team has to run, how fast you can ship, and how painful your system is to change later.

You will hear the two standard arguments:

"Serverless is simpler — no servers, no clusters, no ops."

"Containers are more flexible — portable, predictable, and built for complex systems."

Both are true — for different workloads. And in 2026 there is a third point that matters more than either argument: the line between the two has blurred. You can now run a container and pay for it in a serverless way, scaling to zero, with no cluster to manage. For a lot of teams, that middle option is the right starting point, and the old binary debate misses it.

So this guide does not crown a winner. It gives you:

  • A clear comparison of cost, performance, scaling, operations, security, and lock-in
  • A 7-question decision framework you can run any workload through
  • Workload-by-workload recommendations
  • The hybrid patterns most production systems end up with

Most of my own project work sits closer to containers — including the 3D portfolio behind this site — because I like controlling the runtime and deployment shape. Serverless still gets a fair hearing here: for event-driven and spiky workloads, it often wins.

Originally published on DevOps Enginer.

The short story that explains most real systems

Imagine two teams — these are illustrative scenarios, not specific companies:

Team A is small and building a new SaaS product. Speed matters most, traffic is unknown, and nobody wants to run infrastructure. They start serverless — functions behind an API, a managed database, object storage, and an event bus — and ship quickly.

Later, one part of the system becomes a problem: a long-running, steady-traffic workload that is always busy. On a pay-per-request model it never gets a chance to be cheap, and they want more control over its runtime. They move that workload — not the whole system — to containers.

Team B is larger and needs consistency: an internal platform, custom networking, and long-running services with predictable performance. They build on containers and Kubernetes.

Later, they notice a different problem: a pile of small, spiky, event-driven jobs — webhooks, file processing, scheduled clean-ups — that are a poor use of an always-on platform. They move those jobs to serverless.

Notice the pattern: neither team "switched sides". Each moved individual workloads to the model that fit them. That is what mature architectures look like.

TL;DR — the decision in 30 seconds

If your workload is mainly… Start with
Event-driven, spiky, unpredictable, or very low traffic Serverless functions
A normal API/web service and you want low ops without function constraints Serverless containers (e.g. Cloud Run, Fargate, Azure Container Apps)
Long-running, steady, high-volume, or latency-sensitive Containers (managed Kubernetes or a container platform)
GPU-heavy, custom-runtime, or needs special networking Containers
A mix of the above (most real systems) Hybrid: containers for the core, serverless for events and glue

Rule to remember: choose per workload, not per company.

What "serverless" actually means in 2026

"Serverless" does not mean there are no servers. It means you do not provision, patch, or pay for idle servers — the provider runs the infrastructure, scales it, and bills you for use.

Today it covers several different things, and mixing them up causes bad decisions:

1. Functions-as-a-Service (FaaS)

Small units of code that run in response to an event: an HTTP request, a file uploaded, a message on a queue, a schedule.

  • Examples: AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions
  • You get: automatic scaling, pay-per-invocation style billing, minimal operations
  • You accept: execution limits set by the provider, less control over the runtime environment, and a design built around events and managed services

2. Serverless containers

You ship a normal container image, but the platform runs it serverlessly — scaling (often to zero), load balancing, and billing based on the resources your container actually uses while handling requests.

  • Examples: Google Cloud Run, AWS Fargate (with ECS), Azure Container Apps
  • You get: your own runtime and dependencies, longer-running requests than a function typically allows, no cluster to manage
  • You accept: platform-specific configuration, and cold starts when the platform scales from zero

This category is the biggest change to the old debate. A lot of "serverless vs containers" is now really "functions vs serverless containers vs Kubernetes".

3. Serverless back-end services

Managed services you build on rather than run: serverless databases, object storage, queues, event buses, and authentication.

  • Examples: Amazon DynamoDB, Aurora Serverless v2, Google Firestore, Amazon S3, Amazon SQS / EventBridge, Azure Cosmos DB
  • These combine with both models above. Using Lambda does not force you into any one database, and Kubernetes does not prevent you using a serverless database.

4. Edge functions

Small functions that run close to the user, typically for request/response customisation, redirects, header/security logic, A/B routing, or light personalisation.

  • Examples: Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda@Edge, Vercel Edge Functions
  • These are a complement to a main back end, not a replacement for one.

What "containers" means in 2026

A container packages your code with its runtime and dependencies so it runs the same way on your laptop, in CI, and in production. That consistency — not Kubernetes itself — is the core value.

In practice, "containers" can mean three levels of control and responsibility:

Level What you run What you manage
Serverless containers A container on a fully managed platform Your image and its settings
Managed Kubernetes EKS, GKE, AKS (often with an autopilot/autoscaling mode) Your workloads; the provider manages much of the control plane and node lifecycle
Self-managed Kubernetes Your own clusters, on cloud or on-premises Almost everything, including upgrades and control-plane reliability

Supporting tools you will commonly see around Kubernetes include cluster/node autoscalers (for example Karpenter), GitOps controllers (for example Argo CD), and infrastructure-as-code tools. They reduce operational effort — they do not remove it.

What containers give you, at every level:

  • Full control over runtime, libraries, and system packages
  • Predictable, always-warm performance once the service is running
  • Portability of the workload format (an OCI container image) across providers and on-premises
  • A natural fit for long-running services, streaming, WebSockets, and background workers
  • GPU and custom-hardware options on the platforms that offer them

The full comparison

Factor Serverless functions Serverless containers Containers on Kubernetes
Unit of deployment A function A container image A container image, orchestrated as services
Scaling Automatic, per event/request Automatic, based on concurrent requests; can scale to zero Autoscaling of pods and nodes; you configure the policies
Idle cost Near zero when unused Near zero if scaled to zero You pay for the cluster/nodes that stay up
Cold starts Possible on new execution environments Possible when scaling from zero No cold start for already-running replicas
Long-running work Constrained by provider execution limits Better suited than functions; still check platform limits Best fit — services run indefinitely
Runtime control Lowest — provider-defined environment High — your image Highest — your image plus platform/network control
Operations burden Lowest Low Highest — upgrades, capacity, networking, platform skills
Portability / lock-in Highest lock-in — events, triggers and managed services are provider-specific Medium — the image is portable, the platform config is not Lowest at the workload level; your surrounding platform tooling may still be provider-specific
Observability Many small units; needs disciplined logging/tracing from day one Similar to a normal service Familiar service-level logs/metrics, but a larger platform to observe
Best at Events, glue, spiky and low-volume work APIs and services for small-to-mid teams Core platforms, steady scale, special requirements

Performance and cold starts

A cold start is the delay when a platform has to prepare a new execution environment before your code runs. It affects functions and any platform that scales to zero.

Practical guidance — without magic numbers:

  • Cold-start impact depends on runtime, package size, memory allocation, and whether the function is attached to a VPC. Heavy runtimes and large dependency bundles are usually slower to start than small, lean ones.
  • If a user-facing API has a strict latency budget, measure cold starts with your code in your region. Do not copy numbers from another article (including the previous version of this one).
  • Mitigations exist (smaller packages, keeping dependencies lean, provisioned/pre-warmed capacity where the provider offers it), but pre-warming usually reintroduces cost — it is a trade-off, not a free fix.
  • Always-on container replicas avoid cold starts for the traffic they are already handling. That is one reason latency-critical core APIs often stay on containers.

Scaling

  • Functions scale by creating more concurrent executions in response to events. That is excellent for bursts, but account/provider concurrency limits exist — check them, and request increases before a launch that depends on them.
  • Serverless containers scale by adding container instances based on concurrency. Tuning the requests-per-instance setting is your main performance/cost lever.
  • Kubernetes scales in two layers: pods (via the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, or event-driven autoscalers such as KEDA) and nodes (via a cluster autoscaler). You get more control, and more things to configure and test.

Cost: a method, not a myth

The original version of this article gave monthly totals for 10M and 200M requests. Those numbers are removed here, because a responsible cost comparison depends on at least: region, average request duration, memory allocated, concurrency pattern, data-transfer, load-balancer and logging costs, and how much of the day the system is idle. Any single total hides those assumptions.

Use this method instead:

Step 1 — Estimate your serverless cost shape

Function cost ≈ (number of invocations × price per invocation)
              + (invocations × average duration × memory allocated × price per GB-second)
              + API/front-door, database, storage, queue and log costs

Step 2 — Estimate your container cost shape

Container cost ≈ (compute that must stay running, 24×7 or your peak window)
               + load balancer + cluster management (if any)
               + storage, database, data-transfer and log costs
               + the engineering time to run the platform   ← do not leave this out

Step 3 — Ask the three questions that actually decide it

  1. What is my idle ratio? If the workload is idle most of the day, paying per use usually wins. If it is busy around the clock, always-on capacity usually wins.
  2. How spiky is it? Sharp, unpredictable spikes favour platforms that scale automatically without pre-provisioned capacity. Flat, predictable load favours containers you can size and discount.
  3. What does operating it cost in people time? A small team's scarcest resource is attention. A theoretically cheaper Kubernetes setup that consumes a day a month of maintenance may be the more expensive option in reality.

Step 4 — Run both numbers for your real workload in your provider's official pricing calculator, with your region and your measured duration/memory, and record the date and assumptions next to the result. Prices change; an undated cost comparison ages badly.

Operations and team skills

  • Functions push you toward many small deployable units and managed services. Deployment is easy; governing dozens of functions, their permissions, and their observability takes discipline.
  • Kubernetes gives you a standard platform for many services, at the price of needing platform skills: upgrades, node management, ingress, certificates, policies, and incident response for the platform itself.
  • Serverless containers sit between the two, which is why they are a sensible default for a small team that wants its own runtime without running a cluster.

Security: shared responsibility, different surface

  • With serverless, the provider patches and isolates the underlying runtime. Your main risks move upward: over-permissive permissions on a function, insecure event inputs, and secrets handling.
  • With containers, you additionally own image hygiene: base-image patching, vulnerability scanning, least-privilege Kubernetes RBAC, network policies, and keeping node/cluster versions current.
  • In both models: give every unit the least permissions it needs, keep secrets in a managed secrets store (never in code or plain environment files committed to a repo), and log enough to investigate an incident.

Portability and lock-in

Be precise about what is portable:

  • A container image is portable. The platform around it — autoscaling config, ingress, identity integration, service mesh, storage classes — often is not fully portable.
  • Function code is often simple; the triggers, event schemas, IAM model, and managed services around it are provider-specific.
  • Lock-in is not automatically bad. Using a provider's managed services is often exactly why a small team can ship. The mistake is taking on lock-in accidentally, without noticing which parts of your system would be hard to move.

The decision framework: 7 questions

Run each workload through these questions in order. The first clear "yes" often settles it.

1. Is it triggered by an event, and does it finish quickly?

Examples: a file is uploaded and needs a thumbnail/resize; a payment webhook arrives; an order event triggers a confirmation email.

→ Yes: serverless functions first. This is the workload functions were designed for.
→ No, it runs continuously: go to question 2.

2. Does it need to run for a long time, hold connections open, or keep state in memory?

Examples: WebSocket servers, streaming consumers, long batch jobs, game servers, anything holding long-lived connections.

→ Yes: containers. Functions are built for short, stateless executions, and provider limits will fight you.
→ No: question 3.

3. Is traffic steady and substantial for most of the day?

→ Yes: containers (or serverless containers with a minimum number of warm instances) — always-on capacity generally suits always-on load, and you avoid paying per request at volume.
→ Traffic is low, spiky, or unpredictable: serverless — paying for idle capacity is the cost you are trying to avoid.

4. Do you need a custom runtime, system libraries, or a GPU?

→ Yes: containers. You control the image, so you control the stack.
→ No strong requirement: either model works; decide on the other questions.

5. How much platform work can your team actually absorb?

Be honest. Count the people, not the job titles.

→ No dedicated platform capacity: serverless or serverless containers. Running Kubernetes well is a real job.
→ You already have (or are deliberately building) platform skills: Kubernetes becomes a reasonable long-term investment.

6. How tight is the latency budget, and can it tolerate an occasional cold start?

→ Strict, consistent latency: containers with warm replicas, or a serverless setup you have measured and tuned yourself.
→ Ordinary API latency targets: either model can work — measure a prototype instead of guessing.

7. How much does portability matter for this specific workload?

→ A genuine multi-cloud / on-premises requirement: containers, with provider-specific services kept at the edges.
→ Single-cloud is an accepted strategy: use the provider's managed services freely and save the engineering time.

Scoring shortcut

Give one point to serverless and one to containers for each question that points that way. A workload that scores heavily one way is an easy call. A workload that scores close to even is your serverless containers candidate — that middle option exists precisely for it.

Workload-by-workload recommendations

Workload Recommended starting point Why
Webhooks and third-party integrations Serverless functions Event-driven, bursty, short
Image / file processing on upload Serverless functions Triggered by storage events, parallel, short
Scheduled jobs and clean-ups Serverless functions (scheduled trigger) Runs briefly, then should cost nothing
New product / MVP API Serverless containers, or functions Low ops, real runtime, room to grow
Steady production API at real volume Containers, or serverless containers with warm instances Predictable cost and latency
WebSockets / real-time / streaming Containers Long-lived connections and in-memory state
Background workers and queue consumers Either — containers for constant load, functions for spiky queues Decide on the queue's shape, not the label
Data pipelines / ETL Either — managed/serverless services for spiky jobs, containers for long heavy jobs Duration and data volume decide
ML / AI inference Containers for model serving you control; managed/serverless endpoints for occasional inference Check current GPU/endpoint options per provider before deciding
Edge logic (redirects, headers, geo routing) Edge functions Latency is about distance to the user
Internal platform for many teams Containers on Kubernetes Standardisation and control are the product

Practical examples

These are illustrative patterns. Test any code in your own account before using it.

Example 1 — Event-driven file processing with a function

Pattern: a user uploads a file to object storage → the upload event triggers a function → the function processes the file → it writes the result back to storage and/or updates a database record.

Why serverless fits: the work only exists when a file arrives, each file is independent (so it parallelises naturally), and you pay nothing between uploads.

Handler sketch (Python-style pseudocode — adapt to your provider's event format):

import json

def handler(event, context):
    # 1. Read the object details from the storage event
    record = event["Records"][0]
    bucket = record["s3"]["bucket"]["name"]
    key = record["s3"]["object"]["key"]

    # 2. Do the smallest useful unit of work
    #    e.g. read the object, create a thumbnail / extract metadata, write the result

    # 3. Return a clear result for logging/retries
    return {"status": "processed", "bucket": bucket, "key": key}

Design notes worth teaching your readers:

  • Make the handler idempotent — events can be delivered more than once.
  • Keep the function small and single-purpose; put shared logic in a library, not in a mega-function.
  • Send failures to a dead-letter queue so a bad file does not disappear silently.

Example 2 — A long-running API in a container

Pattern: a normal web API packaged as a container, deployed to a container platform or Kubernetes, behind a load balancer, with replicas for availability.

Why containers fit: the service is always on, latency should be consistent, and you choose the runtime, framework and system dependencies.

Minimal Dockerfile sketch (adapt the base image and start command to your app):

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

Design notes:

  • Run as a non-root user in the image, and pin your base image version — then update it on a schedule.
  • The app must handle a shutdown signal gracefully, so the platform can replace instances without dropping in-flight requests.
  • Externalise configuration; do not bake environment-specific values or secrets into the image.
  • Add a health/readiness endpoint — every container platform and Kubernetes rely on it for safe rollouts. That is exactly the self-healing behaviour covered in the companion post linked below.

Example 3 — The hybrid most systems end up with 

                        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   Users ──────────────▶│  CDN + Edge functions        │
                        │  (redirects, headers, cache) │
                        └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                       │
                        ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
                        │  Core API — containers        │
                        │  (always-on, steady traffic)  │
                        └──────┬───────────────┬───────┘
                               │               │
                  ┌────────────▼───┐   ┌───────▼──────────────┐
                  │ Queue / Event  │   │ Managed database &   │
                  │ bus            │   │ object storage       │
                  └──────┬─────────┘   └──────────────────────┘
                         │
              ┌──────────▼────────────────────────┐
              │ Functions — webhooks, file jobs,  │
              │ notifications, scheduled tasks    │
              └───────────────────────────────────┘

Reading the diagram: containers carry the predictable core; functions carry the irregular edges; managed services carry the state. Most architecture arguments disappear once you assign each workload its own place like this.

Migration paths (you are not locked into your first answer)

From serverless toward containers — common triggers: a workload outgrows execution limits, a service is busy all day and per-request billing stops making sense, or you need runtime control. The practical path is usually: containerise that one service, put it behind the same API/front door, and move traffic gradually. You do not need to migrate the whole system.

From containers toward serverless — common triggers: a platform is oversized for the actual workload, small event-driven jobs are wasting always-on capacity, or the team's maintenance burden is larger than the value it creates. The practical path is: peel off the smallest, most event-shaped jobs first (webhooks, scheduled tasks, file processing).

Either way: move one workload at a time, keep the old path available until the new one has handled real traffic, and compare the actual bill and latency before and after — with dates and assumptions recorded.

Common mistakes to avoid

  1. Choosing for the whole company instead of per workload. This single decision causes most of the pain described in this article.
  2. Comparing only the compute line of the bill. Load balancers, logs, data transfer, and engineering time frequently matter more.
  3. Copying cost or cold-start numbers from articles (including old versions of this one). Measure your own workload; prices and platforms change.
  4. Building a "serverless monolith" — one giant function containing the whole application. You get the constraints of functions and the coupling of a monolith at the same time.
  5. Running Kubernetes because it is the industry default, before you have the traffic, team size, or platform need to justify operating it.
  6. Ignoring observability until the first incident. Distributed systems — functions especially — need structured logs, correlation IDs, and tracing from the first deployment, not after.
  7. Treating lock-in as either irrelevant or fatal. Know which parts of your system are provider-specific, and make that a conscious trade, not a surprise.

Final verdict

Containers give you control, consistent performance, portability of the workload format, and a home for long-running, custom, or hardware-specific work.

Serverless gives you simplicity, automatic scaling, low idle cost, and the smallest possible operations burden.

Serverless containers give a growing number of teams the workable middle: their own container, without the cluster.

The teams that get this right are not the ones that picked the "winning" technology. They are the ones that can answer, for each workload: What triggers it? How long does it run? How steady is its traffic? And who is going to operate it?

Answer those four questions honestly, and the serverless-versus-containers decision mostly makes itself.

My default today is hybrid thinking with a container lean: containers for the main application I need control over, serverless for small event-driven pieces around it.

Related guides

  • GitOps vs traditional CI/CD pipelines — how deployment automation changes once you have many small functions or many container services to ship.
  • how self-healing infrastructure works in Kubernetes — what those health checks and probes make possible on the container side.

FAQ

Is serverless cheaper than containers?

It depends mainly on how busy the workload is. Serverless is usually cheaper for low, spiky, or unpredictable traffic because you pay little or nothing when it is idle. Containers are usually cheaper for steady, high-volume workloads because you are paying for capacity that is actually being used. Always model your own duration, memory, and traffic pattern in your provider's pricing calculator rather than trusting a generic comparison.

What is a cold start, and should I worry about it?

A cold start is the extra delay when a platform must prepare a fresh execution environment before handling a request. It matters for latency-sensitive, user-facing APIs and much less for background jobs, webhooks, and scheduled tasks. If it might matter for you, measure it with your real code — its size depends on runtime, package size, and configuration.

Can I run containers in a serverless way?

Yes. Services such as Google Cloud Run, AWS Fargate, and Azure Container Apps run your container image, scale it (often to zero), and bill based on use, without you managing a cluster. For many APIs this is the best starting point: your own runtime, low operations, and a straightforward path to Kubernetes later if you outgrow it.

Is Kubernetes the same thing as containers?

No. Containers are the packaging format. Kubernetes is one way to orchestrate containers at scale — scheduling, scaling, networking, and self-healing them across machines. You can run containers productively on much simpler platforms and never operate Kubernetes yourself.

Does serverless mean no DevOps?

No. It removes server and cluster management, but you still own deployment pipelines, permissions, observability, cost control, and incident response. The work changes shape; it does not disappear. If anything, having more, smaller units makes good automation and discipline more important, not less.

Which is better for a startup or a small team?

Start with the lowest-operations option that fits the workload: functions for event-driven pieces, and serverless containers for your main API. Add Kubernetes when you have a specific reason — scale, custom platform needs, or a team that can operate it well — not as a default.

Can I mix serverless and containers in one system?

Yes, and most production systems do. A common pattern is containers for the core, always-on services, functions for events, webhooks and scheduled jobs, and managed services for data and storage. Choose per workload.

How do I avoid vendor lock-in?

Keep the parts that are most likely to move in portable forms (for example, a container image for your main service), use provider-specific services consciously where their convenience is worth it, and document which components would need work to migrate. Complete portability usually costs more engineering time than it saves; informed lock-in is a legitimate strategy.

title: Shipping AI-assisted migrations without a big-bang PR
description:
I asked an agent once to “migrate our data-fetching layer to the new client.” It came back with a 90-file PR, green CI, and a cheerful summary. I still couldn’t ship it. Reviewers bounced it. Rollback was a fantasy. Two weeks later we finished the same migration in six small PRs and nobody hated us.

AI is great at the mechanical parts of a migration. It is terrible at deciding how much to change in one go. Big-bang PRs feel fast because the agent can rewrite overnight. They are slow in calendar time because humans cannot review, stage, or revert them safely. Here’s how I run AI-assisted migrations so each slice is mergeable.

Why big-bang migrations fail even when CI is green

A migration PR is not a refactor. You are changing a contract: old API → new API, old store → new store, class components → hooks, CSS modules → something else. The failure modes are different:

  • Review theater — nobody can hold 90 files of “same behavior, different shape” in their head.
  • Hidden coupling — the agent updates call sites the tests don’t cover; production finds them.
  • No rollback story — reverting means undoing half the app at once, so you don’t revert; you hotfix forward.
  • Mixed intents — rename + API swap + “while I’m here” type tightening in one diff. You can’t bisect.

Green unit tests only prove the files the agent touched still pass their suites. They do not prove the migration is safe to flip for every route.

Slice by surface, not by “finish the migration”

I never prompt “migrate everything to X.” I pick a surface: one route group, one feature module, one package boundary. Example:

## Migration slice: settings routes only
Scope: `src/app/settings/**` and colocated tests/fixtures
Goal: replace `legacyFetch` with `apiClient` for settings pages
Out of scope: billing, onboarding, shared hooks used outside settings
Stop if a shared helper needs a signature change — list it, don’t chase it

That stop rule is the whole game. Migrations explode when the agent follows an import into shared land and “fixes” the shared helper for everyone in the same PR.

A useful heuristic: one PR should be reviewable in under fifteen minutes, and should have a clear “if this breaks, revert this PR” story. If the diff needs a guided tour, it’s too big.

Keep each PR reviewable (same rules as agent refactors)

I reuse the same three gates I use for agent-driven refactors:

  1. One intent — migrate call sites or change the shared client or delete the old path. Not all three.
  2. Narratable diff — PR description is 3–5 bullets a human wrote, not the agent’s essay.
  3. Contract-preserving tests — same public behavior asserted, preferably same test names where they still fit.

Order matters. I usually land the new client / adapter behind a flag or unused export first (tiny PR), then migrate one surface to call it (small PR), then delete the old path when the last surface is gone (delete PR). Agents love to do all three. I don’t let them.

Fixture and golden snapshots before you rewrite

Before the agent touches production code, I ask it to freeze the old behavior with fixtures or golden snapshots the new path must match.

// golden: settings profile payload shape (capture once from staging)
export const settingsProfileGolden = {
  id: "u_123",
  displayName: "Ada",
  prefs: { theme: "system", digest: "weekly" },
} as const;

Then the migration PR gets a dual assertion:

it("matches legacy settings profile contract", async () => {
  const fromLegacy = await legacyFetchSettingsProfile(userId);
  const fromNew = await apiClient.settings.profile(userId);
  expect(fromNew).toEqual(fromLegacy);
  expect(fromNew).toMatchObject(settingsProfileGolden);
});

If the new client “improves” the shape (renames a field, drops a null), the golden fails on purpose. That’s the point. Migrations should not silently change contracts unless the PR title says so and the changelog mentions it.

For UI migrations, I do the same with screenshot or DOM snapshots on the critical screens of that surface only — not the whole app. Whole-app visual baselines are how you get 400 flaky diffs and merge with eyes closed.

Feature flags and dual-write windows

For anything with side effects (writes, analytics, billing-adjacent), I want a dual-write or flag window, not a hard cutover in the same PR as the rewrite.

Pattern I prompt for:

1. Add `useNewSettingsClient` flag (default off) — no call-site changes yet
2. Behind the flag, call apiClient; else legacyFetch
3. Log mismatches for 48h on staging (read path) before enabling for one cohort
4. Separate PR to default the flag on for settings only
5. Separate PR to delete legacy path once flag is 100% and mismatch log is empty

The agent can implement step 1–2 in one PR if the diff stays small. Steps 3–5 stay human-scheduled. “AI finished the migration” is not the same as “we flipped traffic.”

If dual-write is too heavy (pure read UI, no durable state), a flag still buys you a one-line rollback without reverting a giant commit.

The rollback story has to fit in a sentence

Before I merge a migration slice, I write the rollback out loud:

  • Flag off — preferred. Instant. No git archaeology.
  • Revert this PR — only if the PR is small and doesn’t leave the shared client half-deleted.
  • Forward fix — last resort; means the slice was too big or mixed with unrelated cleanup.

If the honest answer is “we’d have to revert six stacked PRs and redeploy shared types,” the slice was wrong. Split again.

What belongs in the agent prompt vs the human checklist

Agent prompt (mechanical):

  • Exact file fence and stop rule
  • Old symbol → new symbol mapping
  • “Do not change public types unless listed”
  • “One commit; do not delete the old path in this PR”
  • “Update colocated tests only; do not invent new e2e coverage”
  • “After edits, run: pnpm test settings and paste the summary”

Human checklist (judgment):

  • [ ] Diff is one surface and one intent
  • [ ] Golden / fixture still asserts the old contract (or intentional change is named)
  • [ ] Flag or dual-write path exists if writes/side effects are involved
  • [ ] Rollback sentence is written in the PR body
  • [ ] Shared helpers outside the fence were not rewritten “for convenience”
  • [ ] Delete-the-old-path is a future PR, not hidden in this one
  • [ ] I actually opened the critical route in the browser once

I keep that checklist in the PR template. The agent doesn’t get to mark it done for me.

A concrete prompt template I reuse 

You are migrating ONE surface. Do not finish the whole migration.

Surface: src/features/settings/**
Replace: legacyFetch(path) → apiClient.request(path) for settings modules only
Rules:
- Do not edit files outside the surface + their colocated tests
- Do not change apiClient’s public types
- Do not delete legacyFetch
- Do not rename symbols unrelated to the fetch swap
- Keep existing test names; update implementations to hit apiClient via the test double
- Stop and list paths if a shared helper under src/lib/** must change

When done:
1. Summarize files touched (bullet list)
2. Paste test output for the settings package
3. Propose the NEXT surface only — do not start it

That last line matters. Agents love to keep going. Your job is to end the turn.

What “done” looks like for a migration program

Done is not “the agent said migration complete.” Done looks like:

  • N small merged PRs, each with a rollback sentence
  • Old path deleted in a dedicated PR after traffic is off it
  • Goldens either retired (contract intentionally changed) or still green
  • No “temporary” dual code left rotting for months without an owner

AI shortens the typing. It does not shorten the need for staged cutovers. If you let it ship a big-bang PR, you didn’t save time — you borrowed it from the next outage.

Slice the surface. Freeze the contract. Flag the cutover. Keep the delete for last. Then let the agent type.

title: Building a CMS Theme: Templates, Components, and Styles
description:
A maintainable CMS theme does more than make a homepage look good. It presents real content consistently across page types, adapts when an editor writes a longer heading, and remains understandable to the people who must update it later.

This article looks at templates, reusable components, styles, and release checks as general concepts. The examples are deliberately platform-neutral: a real CMS determines its own package format, template API, and asset-loading rules. Check the documentation for the specific version before using them in a project.

Establish the boundary first

A CMS typically supplies or stores content; the presentation layer decides how to display it. A post title, service description, or contact detail is content. The structure, typography, and spacing that present those values belong to the theme's design.

The exact boundary differs between systems. Before building, ask what happens to important information if the theme changes. A form's appearance may belong in the theme while its processing belongs elsewhere, depending on the platform and extension. Avoid locking essential business behavior into presentation code merely because it was convenient during the first build.

Start by listing actual page types: perhaps a homepage, service listing, service detail, article listing, article, search results, and error page. Include only the scenarios the project needs. For each, write down required fields, optional fields, and the empty state.

Make templates reflect page responsibilities

A shared site shell can contain navigation, the main content area, and a footer. A post template can add a heading, metadata, and article content. A listing template can present a collection of cards and pagination when appropriate.

Extract shared elements so that changing navigation does not require editing every page separately. Avoid the opposite extreme: a single universal file with a maze of unrelated conditions can be difficult to review. Divide templates around meaningful differences in content and behavior.

Do not assume that directories or functions from one CMS apply to another. Verify how the chosen system registers themes, supplies data, loads assets, handles module output, and updates packages. Build in a separate test environment with non-sensitive sample data and a verified recovery plan for the production site.

Design components for variation

A component is a reusable piece with a purpose and a defined set of inputs. A service card might require a title and description while allowing an optional image and link. Decide what happens when the image is missing or the title is unusually long before placing the component across several templates.

Here is a plain HTML card. It is not an API example; replace the illustrative URL with a real route in your project.

<article class="service-card">
  <h2 class="service-card__title">Website design</h2>
  <p>We plan page structure and presentation.</p>
  <a class="service-card__link" href="/contact">
    Discuss your project
  </a>
</article>
~~~

The following independent CSS gives it a basic presentation and a visible keyboard-focus state:

~~~css
.service-card {
  padding: 1.5rem;
  border: 1px solid #b7ccd5;
  background: #f5fafc;
  color: #173544;
}

.service-card__title {
  margin: 0 0 0.75rem;
  font-size: 1.25rem;
}

.service-card__link {
  display: inline-block;
  color: #164a61;
  text-decoration: underline;
}

.service-card__link:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
~~~

The sample colors are illustrative. Test the actual design's contrast and focus appearance, including secondary text and controls. Do not remove a focus indicator without providing an equally understandable replacement.

## Treat dynamic output according to context

Once values come from editors or storage, use the escaping and sanitization facilities provided by the platform. HTML text, attribute values, URLs, and JavaScript contexts have different requirements. Escaping a string for HTML text alone does not make it a safe URL or a safe script fragment.

Validate allowed URL schemes and decide how trusted editorial HTML is handled. Review the platform's security guidance rather than assuming a theme engine's behavior from a different CMS. Keep secrets and production customer data out of demonstration fixtures.

## Build responsive behavior around content

On a narrow viewport, a group of cards may need one column; on a wider one, it can use additional columns when the content has room. Test the widths between your named breakpoints as well as familiar devices. Overflow and awkward wrapping often appear in those intermediate ranges.

Use semantic headings and controls for their actual purpose. Check reading order, labeled form inputs, keyboard operation, zoomed text, and visible focus. Provide useful alternative text for meaningful images and avoid repeating nearby text for purely decorative imagery.

Keep image dimensions and asset sizes appropriate to the page. Remove duplicate libraries and measure the actual result on a representative device and connection. A new theme alone cannot promise a particular performance score or search ranking.

## A release checklist

Before handing the theme to a client, test a deliberately varied set of content:

1. Open each required page type, follow navigation and links, and check empty states.
2. Try short and long titles, lists, tables, optional images, and missing fields.
3. Check narrow and wide layouts, keyboard navigation, focus visibility, and enlarged text.
4. Review the handling of untrusted output and the compatibility of required extensions.
5. Re-test after an update in a safe environment; document account ownership, deployment, backups, and a verified rollback or recovery procedure.
6. If distributing a theme package, test it on a clean installation of the supported CMS version rather than assuming your development environment's settings exist elsewhere.

A theme is ready for handoff when the team can explain how to maintain it as well as how it looks.

## Follow the project

Morlix CMS is under development. Its closed beta has not started; applications from web studios are being collected for future approval. The public-release target is March 11, 2027, and is not a guarantee. Follow updates in the [Morlix CMS Telegram channel](https://t.me/morlix_cms).

Read the [original Russian article](https://morlix.ru/blog/razrabotka-temy-dlya-cms-shablony-komponenty-i-stili) for the related discussion and checklist.

---

title: Moving Marketplace Listing Pages From Microdata to JSON-LD
description:
If your product pages were built a few years ago, there's a good chance their structured data is written in Microdata: itemscope, itemtype and itemprop attributes spread through the HTML. It works, but it's tied to the template. Every time someone redesigns a component, the markup can quietly break.

JSON-LD keeps the same information in one <script type="application/ld+json"> block, separate from the layout. Google supports all three formats (JSON-LD, Microdata and RDFa) and says they're equally fine when the markup is valid, but it recommends JSON-LD where your setup allows, as the easiest to implement and maintain at scale and the least prone to errors.

On a marketplace, where listing pages are generated from seller data you don't fully control, that maintainability matters even more. Here's how we're approaching the move.

1. Before: what Microdata looks like on a listing page

A typical Microdata listing mixes the markup into the visible HTML:

<div itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Product">
  <h1 itemprop="name">Canon EF 50mm f/1.8 STM Lens</h1>
  <img itemprop="image" src="/img/listing-123.jpg" alt="Canon EF 50mm lens">
  <div itemprop="offers" itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Offer">
    <span itemprop="priceCurrency" content="USD">$</span>
    <span itemprop="price" content="89.00">89.00</span>
    <link itemprop="availability" href="https://schema.org/InStock">
    <link itemprop="itemCondition" href="https://schema.org/NewCondition">
  </div>
</div>

It's valid, but the structured data now depends on the exact nesting of divs. Move the price into a different component during a redesign, and price can end up outside its Offer without anyone noticing.

2. After: the same data as JSON-LD 

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Product",
  "name": "Canon EF 50mm f/1.8 STM Lens",
  "image": ["https://www.example.com/img/listing-123.jpg"],
  "description": "Canon EF 50mm f/1.8 STM lens, new in box.",
  "brand": { "@type": "Brand", "name": "Canon" },
  "offers": {
    "@type": "Offer",
    "url": "https://www.example.com/listing/123",
    "price": "89.00",
    "priceCurrency": "USD",
    "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock",
    "itemCondition": "https://schema.org/NewCondition",
    "seller": { "@type": "Person", "name": "example_seller" }
  }
}
</script>

The page's HTML can now change freely, as long as the JSON-LD still describes what the buyer sees.

3. Generate it on the server from your listing model

Hand-writing JSON inside a template is how bugs creep back in. Build it from the same listing object that renders the page, and serialize it with a real JSON library.

![Five steps to generate JSON-LD for a listing page: listing model, map values, serialize, escape, embed and test]

In a Java stack, for example, with Jackson:

Map<String, Object> offer = new LinkedHashMap<>();
offer.put("@type", "Offer");
offer.put("url", listing.getCanonicalUrl());
offer.put("price", listing.getPrice().setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP).toPlainString());
offer.put("priceCurrency", "USD");
offer.put("availability", listing.isSold()
        ? "https://schema.org/SoldOut"
        : "https://schema.org/InStock");
offer.put("itemCondition", conditionUrl(listing.getCondition()));
offer.put("seller", Map.of("@type", "Person", "name", listing.getSellerName()));

Map<String, Object> product = new LinkedHashMap<>();
product.put("@context", "https://schema.org");
product.put("@type", "Product");
product.put("name", listing.getTitle());
product.put("image", listing.getImageUrls());
product.put("description", listing.getShortDescription());
product.put("offers", offer);

String json = objectMapper.writeValueAsString(product);

Two details in that snippet are there on purpose:

  • Price as a plain decimal string, with no currency symbol or thousands separator, and the currency in priceCurrency as an ISO code such as USD.
  • Availability follows the listing's real state. On a marketplace, listings sell out constantly. Marking a sold item InStock sends buyers to a dead end and breaks the rule that markup must match the page.

4. Escape seller-written text before it goes into a script tag

This one is specific to marketplaces and other user-generated content. Listing titles and descriptions are written by sellers. If a title ever contains </script>, unescaped JSON-LD can close your script tag early, which breaks the page at best and opens an injection hole at worst.

A JSON library escapes quotes and backslashes, but it doesn't make text safe inside HTML. Escape <, > and & as Unicode escapes after serializing:

String safeJson = json
        .replace("<", "\\u003c")
        .replace(">", "\\u003e")
        .replace("&", "\\u0026");

The output is still valid JSON, and parsers read it exactly as before.

5. Map conditions explicitly

Sellers describe condition in their own words; schema.org has a fixed list. Use an explicit mapping rather than passing seller text through:

static String conditionUrl(Condition c) {
    switch (c) {
        case NEW:         return "https://schema.org/NewCondition";
        case REFURBISHED: return "https://schema.org/RefurbishedCondition";
        case USED:        return "https://schema.org/UsedCondition";
        default:          return null; // omit rather than guess
    }
}

If you can't map a value confidently, leave the property out. A wrong condition is worse than a missing one.

6. Name the actual seller, and check what you're eligible for

On a marketplace, the person selling the item usually isn't the marketplace itself. Schema.org's Offer has a seller property, so the markup can say who the seller is.

This also matters for what Google can show. Google's merchant listing documentation says the "merchant has to be the seller of the product in order to be eligible for merchant listing experiences." Read that section carefully against your own setup before expecting merchant listing features. Product markup is still useful for describing the page accurately, but don't assume every rich result applies to a marketplace listing.

7. Remove the Microdata when the JSON-LD goes live

Running both formats for the same product on one page makes it easy for the two to disagree, especially on price and availability. Switch one template at a time, and remove the old itemprop attributes in the same release.

8. Validate before and after

  • Rich Results Test on a sample of listing URLs, including sold, used and multi-image listings, not just the tidy ones.
  • URL Inspection in Search Console to see the page as Google renders it.
  • Search Console's structured data reports after release, to catch errors that only show up across thousands of pages.

Keep in mind that valid structured data makes a page eligible for rich results; it doesn't guarantee them.

Checklist

  1. Generate JSON-LD on the server from the listing model, with a JSON library.
  2. Price as a plain decimal string, currency as an ISO code.
  3. Availability and condition reflect the real listing; omit values you can't map.
  4. Escape <, > and & in the serialized JSON.
  5. Use seller for the actual seller, and check merchant listing eligibility rules.
  6. Remove the old Microdata in the same release.
  7. Test sold, used and edge-case listings, then watch Search Console.

Moving to JSON-LD isn't a ranking trick. It's a way to describe every listing accurately and keep it accurate as the site changes, which matters more the more listings and sellers you have.

FAQ

Is JSON-LD better than Microdata for SEO?

Google treats all three formats as equally valid when the markup is correct. It recommends JSON-LD because it's easier to implement and maintain at scale and less prone to errors.

Can I use JSON-LD and Microdata on the same page?

You can, but describing the same product twice makes it easy for the two to disagree. When migrating, remove the Microdata in the same release that adds the JSON-LD.

What should availability be when a listing has sold?

Use a value that matches the page, such as https://schema.org/SoldOut, rather than leaving InStock in place.

Disclosure: written by the TrueGether team. TrueGether is one of the eBay alternatives built for independent sellers, with listing pages across categories from electronics to collectibles.

title: Designing progress for slow jobs: what a video-to-notes pipeline taught me about failure states
description:
Disclosure: I'm the maker of FrameNotes, the tool used as the example here. This post is about a design decision, not a feature tour.

Most web requests finish before the user notices them. A video conversion doesn't. Upload, frame analysis, audio extraction, transcription through a third-party provider, then building several export files: that's a long-running job with several ways to fail, and some of those failures happen in services you don't control.

My first version of FrameNotes handled this the lazy way: one spinner and a "Processing..." label. People refreshed the page, re-uploaded the same file, and reported "it's broken" when it was simply on step three. This is what I changed.

1. Split the job into stages the user can see

Instead of one opaque job, the pipeline reports four named stages:

  1. Upload: the browser sends the file. There is no server task yet.
  2. Visual extraction: detect meaningful visual changes, drop near-duplicate frames.
  3. Transcription: extract audio, send it to the speech-to-text provider, align segments to frames by timestamp.
  4. Export: build HTML, Markdown ZIP, DOCX, PDF, and presentation-style HTML.

Each stage reports a status and a percentage. The point isn't precision. It's that when something stalls, the user and I both know where.

A simplified sketch of the status payload (illustrative, not the exact production schema):

{
  "task_id": "abc123",
  "stage": "transcribing",
  "progress": 60,
  "status": "running",
  "error": null
}

2. Make the task survive a refresh

Once the upload completes, the API returns a task ID and processing continues as a background job. The frontend stores recent task IDs in localStorage, so after a refresh it can query their status again instead of starting over. Simplified sketch:

const KEY = "recentTasks";

function rememberTask(id) {
  const ids = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY) || "[]");
  localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify([id, ...ids.filter(x => x !== id)].slice(0, 10)));
}

async function restoreTasks() {
  const ids = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY) || "[]");
  return Promise.all(ids.map(id => fetch(`/api/tasks/${id}`).then(r => r.json())));
}

There's one honest caveat I put in the UI: don't close the page during the initial upload, because until the upload finishes there's no server task to restore. Saying that clearly helped more than any clever retry logic.

3. Fail with a message, never with made-up output

The hardest rule to keep: if transcription fails, show an error. Don't fill the gap with placeholder or generated text. A note tool that quietly invents a transcript is worse than one that fails.

The failure causes I actually see, and the message each one maps to:

Cause What the user sees
File above the beta limit (30 min / 500 MB) Limit message before processing starts
Damaged or unsupported media stream Upload/processing error at stage 1–2
No usable audio track Transcription-stage error
Provider quota or availability issue Transcription-stage error, retry later
Too little visual change Note with few frames, explained, not padded

4. Show limits before the job, not after

Accepted formats (MP4, MOV, AVI, MKV) and size/length limits are shown at upload time. Rejecting a file in one second is kinder than rejecting it after a long wait.

What I'd do earlier next time

  • Design the status model before the pipeline, not as a patch after.
  • Treat every external dependency (here, the speech-to-text provider) as a stage that can fail on its own.
  • Write the error copy at the same time as the happy path.

If you're building anything with slow background jobs, such as media processing, imports, or report generation, I'd love to hear how you handle progress and recovery. And if you want to see the stages in action on a short video of your own, the tool is at framenotes.org.

Written by Mary, the maker of FrameNotes.

title: Architecting an Air-Gapped Local RAG Pipeline: SQL Server to ChromaDB
description:
The cloud-hosted GenAI honeymoon is officially hitting reality for enterprise IT infrastructure.

If your data engineering pipelines are currently streaming relational company data through international cloud API endpoints, you are actively introducing two major operational liabilities:

  1. Volatile, USD-denominated token billing structures impacting tight operational budgets.
  2. Complicated legal vulnerabilities surrounding cross-border data residency and compliance laws like POPIA.

Most beginner tutorials show you how to parse a static PDF. In the real world, enterprise context is locked inside structured relational database tables.

Here is a look at the production architecture required to build a completely air-gapped, zero-cost local pipeline.

Why Local-First is a Mandatory Enterprise Starting Line

  • **Traditional cloud-hosted RAG frameworks present structural vulnerabilities. A hardened enterprise architecture must enforce three strict constraints:

  • Financial Zero-Baseline: Running inference and local embeddings completely on-premise results in exactly $0 (R0) in recurring cloud API token overhead.

  • Absolute Air-Gapped Compliance: Ensuring data processing stays entirely resident on native client hardware mitigates corporate firewall data-bleed and leak vectors.

  • Isolated Relational Staging: Messy database schemas and unoptimized text inputs must be refactored inside a dedicated sandbox before hitting vector indexes.

The Production Blueprint Architecture

To safely move production database rows into high-performance vector retrieval space, the pipeline is split into five distinct functional layers:

Phase 1: Hardened Data Extraction
A robust ingest engine requires SQLAlchemy connection pooling and memory-protected server-side streaming cursor extraction. This safeguards production SQL Server instances from memory exhaustion when pulling massive transactional logs.

Phase 2: Staging & Cleanse
Programmatic, regex-driven data isolation and automated schema refactoring ensure messy table constraints are coerced into standardized layouts inside a local staging environment.

Phase 3: Algorithmic Chunking
Standard character splitting breaks semantic meaning. This layer implements sliding-window character text chunking utilizing precise word boundary detection to preserve mathematical metrics and relational logic.

Phase 4: Vector Synchronization
Data changes over time. The pipeline maps data locally to an offline HNSW vector database (ChromaDB) paired with an MD5 incremental delta synchronization engine to only update modified database rows.

Phase 5: Local LLM Execution Layer
Access control is maintained via security-gated metadata role filters and strict context-band system prompts wired directly into a local, zero-cost Ollama runtime.

Open-Source Scaffold & Production Blueprint

title: TanStack Redact: Ship Less React Without Touching Your React Code
description:
I've been doing frontend for about twelve years, and a big part of that has been fighting bundle size. Code splitting. Lazy routes. Swapping heavy date libraries for lighter ones. Hunting down that one dependency that pulls in all of lodash. A Webpack 4 to 5 migration done with codemods because doing it by hand across a big codebase wasn't realistic.

But there was always one chunk of the bundle nobody touched: React and React DOM themselves. You just accepted that cost. It was the floor.

TanStack Redact just lowered the floor. And the reason I think it matters isn't the clever engineering behind it (though there's plenty of that). It's how useful it is on day one.

What Redact actually is

Redact is a smaller, React-compatible runtime for the browser. You add one plugin to your build config, and your existing React imports, components, hooks and third-party libraries run on Redact in the browser instead of React DOM.

That's the whole pitch. No new API to learn. No import { h } from 'somewhere-else'. No rewriting components. Your app code stays exactly the same.

It started as Tanner Linsley's experiment on his personal site and tanstack.com, where it's been running in production since April 2026. It stuck, other people started using it in production too, and on October 26 it shipped as 0.2.0 with stable integrations for TanStack Start, Vite, Vinext and Next.js (both App Router and Pages Router).

The usefulness is the headline

Most performance wins come with a migration cost. Move to a new framework, adopt a new rendering model, rewrite your state layer, retrain the team. The win is real, but you pay for it in weeks.

Redact flips that. Here's a plain Vite + React app:

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
import { redact } from '@tanstack/redact/vite'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), redact()],
})

And TanStack Start:

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import { tanstackStart } from '@tanstack/react-start/plugin/vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
import { redact } from '@tanstack/redact/vite'

export default defineConfig({
  ssr: { noExternal: true },
  plugins: [tanstackStart(), react(), redact()],
})

For Next.js there's a withRedact wrapper from @tanstack/redact/next (the docs have the exact setup).

That's it. Install, add a line, build, measure.

Think about what this means in a real team:

  • No refactor PR. Your diff is a config file and a package.json line. Easy to review, easy to reason about.
  • Rollback is trivial. Remove the plugin and you're back on React. That makes it a low-risk experiment instead of a bet-the-quarter decision.
  • Your ecosystem comes with you. Component libraries, form libraries, query libraries — they keep importing react and just get Redact in the browser.
  • Nobody has to learn anything. New hires still write React. Your docs, your Storybook, your patterns all stay valid.

I've led teams where the right performance move was blocked purely because it meant touching hundreds of components. A tool that gives you the win without that cost is the kind of thing that actually gets adopted.

The numbers

The TanStack team built the same small app with React and with Redact in each framework, then added up the gzip size of all emitted client JS and CSS:

Framework React Redact Saved
TanStack Start 109.3 KB 62.3 KB 47.0 KB (43.0%)
Vite 68.3 KB 20.1 KB 48.1 KB (70.5%)
Vinext 138.1 KB 98.8 KB 39.3 KB (28.5%)
Next.js 175.6 KB 139.9 KB 35.7 KB (20.4%)

Those are the default builds. If you turn off optional features your app doesn't use, Start drops to 59.8 KB and a client-only Vite app goes down to 12.6 KB.

The team is upfront that these are whole-build totals for a small sample app, so your percentages will vary. The benchmark source is public if you want to reproduce it. I appreciate that honesty — it's rare in launch posts.

Why do 35–48 KB of gzip matter? Because that's JavaScript every user downloads, parses and executes before your app becomes interactive. On a fast laptop on fiber, sure, you won't notice. On a mid-range Android phone on a patchy mobile connection — which is a huge share of real users in markets like India — that's a noticeable chunk of your load budget, and it's coming out of the one dependency you thought you couldn't shrink.

It's not a toy React

My first worry with any "React but smaller" project is: what breaks? A counter demo working proves nothing. Real apps lean on hydration, Suspense, transitions, forms, error boundaries, and a pile of framework internals.

Redact supports JSX, hooks, context, refs, memo, lazy, portals, error boundaries, streaming SSR and hydration. Pending transitions, form actions and optimistic state are covered too.

What gave me more confidence is how they test it. The compatibility suite runs real browser journeys in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit: retained layouts, back/forward navigation, redirects, canceled navigation, Server Actions, pending forms, optimistic updates, uploads, streamed Suspense, and Fast Refresh that keeps state across edits. That's the stuff that actually breaks in production.

And you don't lose your tooling: React DevTools still works for inspection, editing and commit profiling in development.

Server Components stay with React

This is a really smart design call. With Next.js and Vinext, Redact doesn't try to replace everything. React still does server rendering and Server Components. The framework still owns routing, caching and Server Action transport. Redact picks up in the browser, hydrates the HTML, and runs your client components.

So you're not swapping out your framework's server story. You're only swapping the part that ships to your users' devices. That keeps the blast radius small, and it's exactly where the bytes matter.

Go smaller if you want to

For Start and Vite you can tune what's included:

// Start: keep hydration and router features, drop what you don't use
redact({
  features: {
    activity: false,
    fragmentRefs: false,
    portal: false,
  },
})

// Vite: a client-only app with no optional features
redact({ preset: 'nano' })

The default is a sensible "full" preset, and the docs recommend starting there and only disabling features after checking what your app (and its dependencies) actually use. Next.js and Vinext use the full runtime so framework features keep working.

"Why not just use Preact?"

Fair question, and the Redact team answers it directly: Preact is smaller. But Redact keeps more of the modern React behavior your app may depend on, like pending transitions, deferred results and form actions. If you're on a modern React stack and you don't want to discover compatibility gaps one bug report at a time, that matters more than the last few kilobytes.

The honest tradeoff

Redact renders synchronously. No time slicing, no interruptible renders. Suspended transitions, pending forms and optimistic state still work, but a genuinely heavy render can block input while it runs.

For a lot of apps, that's fine. Marketing and content sites, docs, ecommerce storefronts, typical CRUD dashboards, embedded widgets — most of their renders are small, and the bundle savings are pure win.

Where I'd be careful: screens that render huge trees in one go, or code that relies on useTransition to keep typing responsive during an expensive update. The TanStack team says the same thing: try it against your busiest screens first. Their compatibility guide spells out the boundaries clearly.

That's not a knock on Redact. It's a clear, documented choice, and it's the reason the runtime can be this small.

Why I'm a fan

What I like most is the attitude behind it. This isn't "React is bad, switch to X." Tanner is explicit that he still believes in React and wants it to keep growing. Redact is just another runtime option inside the React ecosystem for people who want to keep their components and ship less.

That's the kind of tool I want more of: respects the code you already have, gives you a real win, tells you the tradeoff upfront, and lets you walk back with one line if it doesn't fit.

If you have a React app on Vite, TanStack Start or Next.js, the cheapest experiment you'll run this month is:

  1. pnpm add @tanstack/redact
  2. Add redact() (or withRedact) to your config
  3. Build, compare your bundle, click through your heaviest screens

Worst case you learn something about your app. Best case you delete tens of kilobytes from every page load without changing a single component.

Links

  • Launch post: https://tanstack.com/blog/introducing-tanstack-redact
  • Docs: https://tanstack.com/redact/latest
  • Compatibility guide: https://tanstack.com/redact/latest/docs/compatibility
  • GitHub: https://github.com/TanStack/redact
