title: I Rebuilt My Website So People Step Into It, Not Scroll Past It
description:
TL;DR: An immersive website uses layered images, motion, and interactive elements to turn passive scrolling into active exploration. I rebuilt julianneagu.com this way, and it loads in 750 KB on phones while staying fully SEO-friendly. This guide walks through what immersive means, how it differs from classic and 3D sites, and when it makes sense for your business.

Most websites get scrolled past in three seconds. I rebuilt my own site so people step into it instead. The immersive version of julianneagu.com uses layered depth, moving water, lights you can switch on, and product scenes you tap through. It feels 3D, but it is not. It is built like a normal web page, so it loads fast and search engines can read every word.

This is what an immersive website is, how it works under the hood, and who it is for. I built the site, so this is written by the person who made it. That is also why it says plainly what it cannot do.

What an immersive website actually is

An immersive website is a site you step into instead of scrolling past. Instead of one long page of blocks, it moves you through a story scene by scene, with depth, motion, and things to tap. Visitors explore rather than skim.

The immersive version of julianneagu.com sits next to a classic version and a full 3D version. You can switch between them with a button at the top. They are three different levels, not three names for the same thing.

What makes it immersive, not just animated:

  • Layered depth. The room, the window, the lake, and the sky are separate layers that move at different speeds as you scroll. That movement creates the feeling of depth without a 3D engine.
  • Living details. Only the water moves, with ripples, mist, the odd shooting star, and a signature that writes itself. The trees, railings, and dock stay still.
  • Things to do. Tap a light to open a product. Open the monolith to see everything at once. Flip a switch to light the room.
  • A story, not a list. The page walks from the window, down the stairs, along the dock, to the products, the way of working, and the contact details.

An immersive website uses layered images that move at different speeds, real animated water, lights you switch on, and product scenes you tap through. It feels 3D, but it is not 3D: it is built like a normal web page.

The honest way to describe the immersive style is that it feels 3D but loads like a normal site. If a page needs a camera that flies through a true 3D space, that is the 3D version, which is heavier and needs more from the phone.

Classic vs immersive vs 3D websites

I now run three versions of the same site. They are not interchangeable. Each one is built for a different goal and comes with different trade-offs.

Feature Classic Immersive 3D
Feels like A normal website Walking through a film Flying through a 3D world
Built with A normal page Layered images and motion (2.5D) A real 3D engine (WebGL)
Speed on phones Fastest Fast Heaviest
Best for Most businesses Brands and founders who want to stand out Showpiece launches and portfolios
Images needed Photos and screenshots A set of custom scenes 3D scenes and textures

The immersive version loads in approximately 750 KB on phones. That is fast enough for Google's Core Web Vitals, which I covered in detail in my website guide best practices. The classic version is lighter. The 3D version is heavier and needs a stronger device.

A walk through the immersive site, scene by scene

The window and the numbers

A point of light opens into a room with a glass window over a lake. My signature writes itself on the glass. Scroll, and you pass through the window onto the balcony, where the headline appears. Then you move down the stairs as the numbers count up: 1000+ domains, 500+ AI tools, and 300+ apps.

Each number is a line of real HTML text. Search engines can read it. Screen readers can speak it. That is the difference between an immersive site and a video.

The monolith: every light opens a product

Lights float around a tall monolith by the water. Tap one and a card opens for that product. Tap the monolith and it opens up into five product screens at once, so a visitor sees everything I offer in one move, then closes it again with one tap.

This is where the immersive approach does something a classic page cannot. Instead of listing five products in a row, the monolith turns the list into a moment. You tap it. It opens. You remember it.

The same monolith scene works on desktop. The lights are bigger. The tap becomes a click. The layout adjusts, but the experience stays the same.

Switch it on

A dark room with a light switch. Flip it and the room lights up. It is a small moment, but it turns a line of text, "every product starts as an idea in the dark", into something the visitor does with their own finger.

This is the kind of interaction that makes an immersive site worth the effort. A visitor who flips a switch remembers the brand behind it.

How I work, and the contact

Eight stages float over the lake, from finding the gap to launching the product. They slide past as you scroll. The walk ends at the contact section, so the last thing a visitor sees is how to start.

The structure is intentional. The page does not dump everything at once. It walks the visitor through the story, step by step, scene by scene. That is what "immersive" means in practice.

How I built it, in plain words

There is no 3D engine on the immersive page. It is a normal web page with a few tricks.

Custom scene images

Each scene is a set of pictures made for this site: the room, the balcony, the stairs, the dock, the monolith, and the stages over the lake. I drew them in Photoshop, exported them as layered images, and placed them in the page.

Sticky scenes

Each scene stays in place while you scroll. The scroll position moves the layers, the text, and the wipes between scenes. This is what creates the feeling of depth.

The technique is called parallax scrolling. Different layers move at different speeds. The sky moves slower than the lake. The lake moves slower than the dock. Your brain interprets that as depth.

Water that moves on its own

The water is drawn live on a canvas. A mask for each picture marks where the water is, so only the water ripples and everything in front of it stays still.

Here is how it works in code:

``javascript
const canvas = document.getElementById('water-canvas');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
let animationFrame;

function drawWater() {
// Clear the canvas
ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);

// Draw ripple effect using sine wave
const time = Date.now() * 0.001;
for (let y = 0; y < canvas.height; y += 2) {
const offset = Math.sin(y * 0.05 + time) * 2;
ctx.fillStyle = 'rgba(100, 150, 200, 0.3)';
ctx.fillRect(offset, y, canvas.width, 2);
}

animationFrame = requestAnimationFrame(drawWater);
}

// Stop drawing when off screen
const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
if (!entries[0].isIntersecting) {
cancelAnimationFrame(animationFrame);
} else {
drawWater();
}
});

observer.observe(canvas);
``

The water only draws when it is on screen. When you scroll past it, the animation stops. That saves battery and keeps the page fast.

Real text

Headlines and copy are normal HTML text, not words baked into pictures. That means search engines can read them. Google can index them. Screen readers can speak them.

This is the single most important SEO decision in an immersive site. If you bake the text into the images, you lose search traffic. Keep it as HTML, and you keep everything.

For more on how this fits into broader SEO strategy, see my step-by-step SEO best practices guide.

Speed was the rule from the start

Phones get smaller copies of every picture. Images below the screen load only when needed. The moving water stops drawing when it is off screen.

In my tests, the page needs about 750 KB to open on a phone. That is fast enough to pass Google's Core Web Vitals, which measure loading speed, visual stability, and responsiveness.

Here is what that looks like in practice:

  • Images: Each scene has a desktop version (1920px wide) and a mobile version (750px wide). The page serves the right one based on screen size.
  • Lazy loading: Images below the fold do not load until you scroll near them.
  • Canvas optimization: The water animation uses requestAnimationFrame, which syncs with the browser's refresh rate and stops when the tab is not visible.

The immersive version of julianneagu.com requires approximately 750 KB to load on phones, fast enough to pass Google's Core Web Vitals.

Why a business would want an immersive website

People explore instead of skimming. Each scene gives a reason to keep scrolling, so more of the page actually gets seen. A classic page loses half its visitors before they reach the second screen. An immersive page keeps them moving.

It is remembered. A visitor who opens a monolith or switches on a light remembers the brand behind it. Memory is the start of trust, and trust is the start of a sale.

It explains, not just lists. The scene-by-scene format suits a story: who you are, what you make, how you work. A list of features does not stick. A walk through a world does.

It still converts. The basics of a good page still apply: a clear headline, one main action, and an easy way to get in touch. An immersive site keeps every one of them. I walk through the full conversion framework in my guide to landing page best practices.

When an immersive website makes sense

An immersive website is not for everyone. It makes sense for:

  • Brands and founders who want to stand out. If your business depends on being remembered, immersive design is a tool that works.
  • Products with a story to tell. If you need to explain how something works, why it exists, or what problem it solves, a scene-by-scene format does that better than a list.
  • Portfolios and showpiece launches. If the site itself is part of the pitch, immersive design shows what you can do.

It does not make sense for:

  • Large shops with hundreds of products. The format works for a few products, not a catalog.
  • Blogs or news sites. Text-heavy sites need speed and simplicity, not animation.
  • Daily-use utility sites. If people visit your site five times a day to check a number or fill a form, they do not want to walk through a story.

An immersive website makes people explore instead of skim, increasing engagement and memory retention.

I built the immersive version of my site because my business is building products and helping others build theirs. The site itself is proof of what I do. If your business does not need that proof, a classic site is faster to build and faster to load.

What it cannot do

An immersive site cannot replace a classic site for most businesses. It is slower to build, harder to update, and heavier on the browser than a normal page. It also does not work well for content that changes often. If you post new articles every week, you do not want to rebuild a scene every time.

It also does not work for complex user flows. If your site has a multi-step signup, a checkout process, or a dashboard, those pieces stay classic. Immersive design is for the front door, not the whole house.

What I learned building it

Building an immersive site taught me three things:

  1. Motion is cheap. Custom scenes are expensive. The code for parallax scrolling is simple. The hard part is making the scenes worth scrolling through.
  2. Real text beats everything. Baking text into images kills SEO, accessibility, and translation. Keep it as HTML, even if it takes more work to position.
  3. Speed is a feature, not a constraint. Every optimization I made, from lazy loading to canvas pausing, made the site faster and better. Speed does not fight design. It sharpens it.

I documented the full build process on my YouTube channel, where I walk through the code, the design decisions, and the mistakes I made along the way.

Final thought

An immersive website is a middle ground between a classic page and a full 3D experience. It feels richer than a normal site, but it loads fast and works on phones. It is best suited for brands, founders, and businesses with stories to tell.

If your business depends on being remembered, an immersive site is worth the effort. If it does not, a classic site is faster to build and easier to maintain. Both are valid choices. The key is knowing which one serves your goal.

title: Updating an Android app without the Play Store: a manifest, an APK and a read-only share
description:
We hand out Android tablets to people who use our app in the field. Most of the devices are ours, nobody signs in with a personal Google account, and we do not want the app in a public store. Still, when a release is mandatory, every tablet has to pick it up, and whoever publishes the release should not need a developer's laptop and an adb cable.

This article describes how we update the app without a marketplace: a small JSON manifest, a single APK, two authenticated endpoints on the backend, and a publishing path built on a read-only NFS share and a WebDAV folder. I keep the hostnames and paths generic on purpose.

Why the app is not in a store

The app is built for police forces. It is part of a service we provide to them under contract, and it works together with our backend. A listing in a public store would put the APK within reach of anyone, and anyone who holds a copy can decompile it.

Keeping the file out of a public listing does not make reverse engineering impossible. It narrows who can get the file in the first place. The real boundary stays on the backend, where every call is authenticated and scoped to a tenant.

Some customers also want to use tablets they already own, which we do not manage. That rules out the approach of enrolling devices in a management system of our own, so we deliver the update ourselves.

What I wanted from the design

The fleet is small and known. Updates can be mandatory. The tablets already log in to our backend and carry a JWT, so the backend is the one place every device is willing to talk to. Adding a public static web server just for APKs would mean a second thing to secure, so I decided against it and let the backend serve the files.

I also wanted the publishing side to be boring. One person uploads two files and the tablets do the rest.

Two files, one version at a time

The share contains exactly two files: a manifest and the APK. There is no version history and no per-device targeting.

{
  "version": "1.4.2",
  "force": true,
  "note": "Mandatory update with fixes for the inspection form.",
  "size": 48213377,
  "sha256": "9f2c...e41a"
}

The manifest has no URL field. An earlier idea was to put the download URL in the manifest, so the APK could carry its version in the file name. I dropped it. With a fixed file name, the manifest cannot point the app anywhere: the app downloads from the backend it is logged in to, and the file is always the same one. Having one fixed name was also easier to explain to the person who publishes.

size and sha256 describe the APK. The app uses them to check that the download is complete before it tries to install anything.

What happens on the tablet

After login the app calls GET /api/app-version and compares the version in the manifest with the one it is running. If the manifest is newer and force is true, the app blocks the normal screens until the update is installed. If force is false, it offers the update and lets the user postpone.

The download is GET /api/app-apk, with the same bearer token as every other call. The response carries Content-Length, which is what lets the app draw a real progress bar with percentage and megabytes. When the file is complete, the app compares size and sha256 with the manifest and hands the APK to the Android package installer.

Android puts two conditions on this. The first is that the app needs the "install unknown apps" permission, which since Android 8 is granted per app, so someone has to allow it once on each tablet. The second is that an update must be signed with the same key as the installed version and must have a higher versionCode.

The signature check is the real safety net. Whoever can write to the share cannot make a tablet install an APK signed with a different key. They could still make every tablet download a file, so the write credential deserves care, and the signing key stays off the server entirely.

The two endpoints

Both endpoints sit behind the same middleware as the rest of the API: JWT validation and the tenant header. Both read from a directory given by one environment variable, APP_RELEASES_PATH, so no path is hard-coded.

/api/app-version returns the manifest as it is, or a 404 if the file is missing. /api/app-apk streams the APK with Content-Type: application/vnd.android.package-archive, Content-Length and a Content-Disposition header, or a 404.

Where the files live

The backend runs in a container on one machine, while the people who publish upload to another. I wanted a path between the two that the backend can only read.

On the file server, the directory is exported over NFSv4, read-only, to the private network of the application nodes. It is a dedicated export. The account that can write through WebDAV only ever reaches this directory and nothing else on the server.

# /etc/exports on the file server
/export/releases   10.0.0.0/16(ro,sync,no_subtree_check)

On the backend node the export is mounted read-only, and the container gets the same directory as a read-only bind mount at the same path:

# /etc/fstab on the backend node
fileserver:/releases  /mnt/releases  nfs4  _netdev,auto,nofail,noatime,ro,tcp  0 0

# docker-compose.yml
volumes:
  - "${APP_RELEASES_PATH:-/mnt/releases}:${APP_RELEASES_PATH:-/mnt/releases}:ro"

The default value after :- makes the compose file start even when the variable has not been set yet. If the mount is missing, the directory on the host is empty and the endpoints answer with an error. I accepted that: the container still starts and the failure is visible.

The directory is owned by the web server user, with mode 0755 for the folder and 0644 for the files. The backend reads them as "other", so there is no need to line up user ids across machines.

Publishing with WebDAV

The WebDAV folder is served by the Apache that already runs on the file server, with mod_dav and a dedicated account.

Alias /releases /srv/releases
<Directory /srv/releases>
    Dav On
    Options -Indexes
    AuthType Basic
    AuthName "Releases"
    AuthUserFile /etc/apache2/htpasswd_releases
    <RequireAll>
        Require method GET HEAD OPTIONS PUT MOVE DELETE PROPFIND
        Require user publisher
    </RequireAll>
</Directory>

Two details are worth explaining. Require method sits inside a RequireAll because several Require lines at the same level are combined with OR, so a bare method restriction next to Require user would let any authenticated user use any method. And the folder is never listed publicly: there is no directory index, and every request needs credentials.

A plain PUT is not atomic, and an APK is tens of megabytes. The backend can start reading a file that is still being written. So each file is uploaded under a temporary name and then renamed with MOVE, which is a rename on the same filesystem. The order matters too. The APK goes first and the manifest last, because the manifest is what the tablets read to find out that a new version exists.

BASE=https://files.example.com/releases

curl --netrc-file ~/.netrc -T app.apk "$BASE/app.apk.tmp"
curl --netrc-file ~/.netrc -X MOVE "$BASE/app.apk.tmp" \
     -H "Destination: $BASE/app.apk" -H "Overwrite: T"

curl --netrc-file ~/.netrc -T version.json "$BASE/version.json.tmp"
curl --netrc-file ~/.netrc -X MOVE "$BASE/version.json.tmp" \
     -H "Destination: $BASE/version.json" -H "Overwrite: T"

In my tests the PUT answered 201, the MOVE answered 201 for a new file and 204 when it overwrote one, and a wrong password gave 401. The credentials live in a .netrc file with mode 600, so the password never appears on the command line or in the shell history.

I wrapped the four commands in a small script for Linux and one for Windows. It checks every status code, deletes the .tmp file if a step fails, and at the end downloads both files again to compare their sha256 with the local ones.

Two limits I know about

Between the MOVE of the APK and the MOVE of the manifest there are a few seconds in which the new APK sits next to the old manifest. A tablet that starts a download in that window sees a sha256 that does not match and discards the file. It tries again at the next check, which is acceptable for a fleet that checks at every login.

The other limit is that a release cannot be rolled back on devices that have already installed it, because Android refuses to install an APK with a lower versionCode. The share keeps a single version, so a bad release is fixed by publishing a new build with a higher version, and the previous APK has to be kept by whoever builds it.

There is also no staged rollout. Every tablet that checks after the manifest is replaced gets the new version, and for this fleet I prefer that to the extra machinery.

title: Agent‑safe change delivery on Oracle: discovery, online mechanics, idempotent migrations, and provable rollbacks
description:
This is article 7 of 8 in my Oracle AI Database Skills series.

Agent-assisted database changes need discovery, preview, approval, bounded execution, and independent verification. Reversibility must be established for the exact change and database release; an online operation is not automatically a safe rollback path. 

Key Takeaways

  • The safety net is the process, not the model. Discovery before proposal, preview before apply, session-scoped verification before broad exposure, and a prepared rollback path — these steps protect against risk regardless of how confident the assistant sounds.
  • Invisible indexes let you test the impact of a change in one session before committing it to all queries. A reversible setting can reduce risk, but the rollback procedure and any concurrent changes still need validation.
  • Liquibase updateSQL and Flyway dry-run output play the same role as SHOWSQL for migrations: they show exactly what SQL would execute before anything changes, giving a human an explicit approval moment.
  • DBMS_REDEFINITION and Edition-Based Redefinition support different online-change patterns. Validate eligibility, cutover, and rollback behavior for the specific feature, release, and change; do not assume a universal rollback window.

Change is where ambiguity turns into outages. If you let an assistant propose schema or index changes on Oracle Database, slow the work down just enough to make it safe. The pattern across this series is route → act → trust: route proposals through Oracle Database Skills so the assistant performs discovery and establishes intent; act only through a bounded, inspectable MCP surface (SQLcl MCP, where MCP is Model Context Protocol—locally, or a managed MCP in Autonomous AI Database when available); and deliver changes with Oracle‑native online and editioning mechanics, inside a migration workflow that’s idempotent on rerun and leaves a trail you can prove later.

This piece shows that posture in motion. We’ll take one additive change an assistant proposes, preview it, apply it safely, verify it helped, and capture the evidence—with a rollback ready if it didn’t.

Governed Oracle Database change workflow with MCP enforcement, validation, evidence capture, and rollback controls.

Version scope and expectations

Most examples target Oracle Database 19c and later. We rely on invisible indexes and session testing via the OPTIMIZER_USE_INVISIBLE_INDEXES parameter (settable at the session or system level) as documented in the 19c Database Reference. For index maintenance, we use online index rebuilds where the 19c SQL Language Reference documents them for your index type and release (ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD ONLINE). For structural table changes under DML load, we point to DBMS_REDEFINITION (19c PL/SQL Reference). For view/package evolution, we use Edition‑Based Redefinition (EBR). Migration previews use Liquibase or Flyway state tables and dry‑run modes. Evidence and rollback rely on session tagging, SQLcl MCP logging, and (optionally) Unified Auditing.

If you’re on Oracle Database 26ai or Autonomous AI Database, you can also evolve vector indexes with a build‑new → validate → drop‑old pattern and measure recall/latency with DBMS_VECTOR. Always confirm exact syntax and capabilities for your Release Update (RU) and service tier.

  • ALTER INDEX (ONLINE for REBUILD): 19c SQL Language Reference
  • OPTIMIZER_USE_INVISIBLE_INDEXES: 19c Database Reference
  • Managing invisible indexes: 19c Admin Guide
  • DBMS_REDEFINITION: 19c PL/SQL Reference
  • CREATE VECTOR INDEX, VECTOR_DISTANCE, DBMS_VECTOR: 26ai docs
  • SQLcl MCP restrict levels, tools, monitoring: 25.x SQLcl docs
  • Liquibase and Flyway: vendor docs

Why agent‑safe change matters most

Assistants are good at pattern matching; they are bad at implicit context. Database change has a lot of implicit context: constraints you can’t see from one table, write paths you forgot exist, and optimizer behavior that swings when you add the “perfect” index. The way to make an assistant useful here is to force it to surface what it thinks it knows before it acts. That’s what Oracle Database Skills are for: schema discovery, intent disambiguation, destructive‑operation guards, and idempotency patterns live right next to delivery mechanics—migrations, online operations, EBR, and testing—so the work becomes a sequence you can reason about, not a free‑form prompt.

The assistant can still draft the change. Your job becomes review and control: you see the SQL (Article 5’s SHOWSQL discipline), you preview the migration (dry run), you apply through a constrained channel (MCP), and you verify impact before broad exposure (invisible index testing, or EBR for code). When that loop is the norm, teams stop arguing about whether to “let the model write DDL” and start shipping low‑risk improvements steadily.

Safety before execution: discovery, intent, and rerunnable SQL

Change work starts with a map. If the assistant suggests an index for DOCUMENTS, its first step isn’t to create it; it is to list what already exists and establish the blast radius.

Oracle Database safety gates for governed schema changes and migration execution.

Inventory what’s there (use USER_* views in‑schema; ALL_*/DBA_* if querying across schemas):

SELECT index_name, visibility, status
FROM   user_indexes
WHERE  table_name = 'DOCUMENTS';

Also list indexed columns so you don’t reinvent an existing index:

SELECT index_name, column_name, column_position
FROM   user_ind_columns
WHERE  table_name = 'DOCUMENTS'
ORDER  BY index_name, column_position;

If the assistant claims “add an index to speed source and published date filters,” make it specify the target predicates and expected plan effect. If it can’t state the WHERE clause and the rows accessed in plain terms, it doesn’t understand the workload yet. Article 6 showed why this matters: you don’t expose a new index broadly until you’ve seen it influence a plan the way you expect.

For DML, destructive‑operation guards are non‑negotiable. Updates and deletes happen only with a WHERE clause you can count. Preview the scope:

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM   documents
WHERE  source = 'kb'
AND    published >= DATE '2025-01-01';

Oracle doesn’t enforce WHERE clauses on UPDATE/DELETE; enforce guardrails in tooling (preview gates) and code review.

Reruns should be safe by default. On the data side, MERGE turns brittle “insert then update” sequences into idempotent steps:

MERGE INTO config t
USING (SELECT 'max_connections' AS key, '100' AS value FROM dual) s
ON (t.key = s.key)
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.value = s.value
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (key, value) VALUES (s.key, s.value);

On the DDL side, migration tools carry the idempotency for you with state tables and checksums. Liquibase tracks applied changeSets in DATABASECHANGELOG and coordinates with DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK, and Flyway uses flyway_schema_history. Crucially, both can emit exactly what they would execute. Liquibase’s updateSQL and Flyway’s dryRunOutput are the human gate that pairs well with Article 5’s SHOWSQL: you inspect the proposed SQL first, then approve the apply.

Preview‑gate example (Liquibase):

# Print the SQL that would run, without changing the database
liquibase --changelog-file=changelog.xml updateSQL

# Example output (truncated)
-- Changeset 20250108-idx-docs:1
CREATE INDEX docs_src_pub_idx ON documents(source, published) INVISIBLE;
-- Changeset 20250108-config-merge:2
MERGE INTO config ...

Liquibase prints the SQL it would execute against the current database state, based on DATABASECHANGELOG and checksums.

Alternatively, with Flyway (Teams/Enterprise for dry‑run variants):

# Generate a dry-run script of pending migrations
flyway -locations=filesystem:sql -dryRunOutput=preview.sql migrate

dryRunOutput is not available in Community; use Teams/Enterprise for dry‑run script generation.

From preview to apply: bounded MCP, not ad‑hoc credentials

Once you’ve reviewed a change, you still need a controlled way to act. That’s the MCP layer: the SQLcl MCP Server locally, or a managed MCP experience in Autonomous AI Database if your tier and RU expose one.

SQLcl MCP exposes a deliberately small tool surface—connect, disconnect, list saved connections, run SQL—over a stdio server. In the 25.3 docs, Level 4 is the most restrictive. Check your installed version’s “Restrict levels” page for the default, and keep the highest level practical in shared environments. The recommended posture is to use pre‑saved least‑privilege connections; restrict levels can be configured to disallow ad‑hoc credentials and keep the tool surface small. The server tags sessions (V$SESSION.MODULE and .ACTION) and writes activity to DBTOOLS$MCP_LOG once used, so DBAs can see who did what and when. This is what “bounded action” looks like: the assistant can only do the few things the server allows, with least privilege and a record behind it. See “Using the SQLcl MCP Server,” “Restrict levels,” and “Monitoring” in the SQLcl docs for the precise tools, defaults, and logs for your version.

Bounded MCP action surfaces for governed Oracle Database access and auditing.

If your Autonomous AI Database service and RU expose a managed MCP endpoint (see your service’s Help Center “Use MCP Server” page), you can integrate assistant actions with database identity, network controls, and auditing. Capabilities and APIs vary by service tier and RU; verify availability and procedures in your tenancy documentation. If a managed MCP endpoint isn’t available for your tier/RU, use the SQLcl MCP Server approach above.

Reduce blast radius with Oracle’s online mechanics

Not every change needs a window. Oracle has first‑party features for evolving structures while the system stays available.

Structural changes under write load use DBMS_REDEFINITION. The flow is predictable—eligibility check, start, copy dependent objects and constraints, sync the interim table, finish, and clean up—and the documentation spells out object and LOB rules per release (19c PL/SQL Reference).

Bounded MCP action surfaces for governed Oracle Database access and auditing.

A compact, typical plan:

  • Eligibility (choose key strategy; use CONS_USE_PK when a primary key exists, or CONS_USE_ROWID otherwise—confirm constraints and object types supported in your version):
BEGIN
  DBMS_REDEFINITION.CAN_REDEF_TABLE(
    uname        => 'APP_OWNER',
    tname        => 'ORDERS',
    options_flag => DBMS_REDEFINITION.CONS_USE_PK
  );
END;
/
  • Create interim table with desired structure (required unless supplying a column mapping to START_REDEF_TABLE):
-- Example: like-for-like copy you will later adjust as needed
CREATE TABLE app_owner.orders_int
AS SELECT * FROM app_owner.orders WHERE 1=0;
  • Start:
BEGIN
  DBMS_REDEFINITION.START_REDEF_TABLE(
    uname     => 'APP_OWNER',
    tname     => 'ORDERS',
    int_table => 'ORDERS_INT'
    -- , col_mapping => '...'  -- use when structures differ
  );
END;
/
  • Copy dependents (constraints, triggers, indexes, grants) and track errors:
DECLARE
  v_errs PLS_INTEGER;
BEGIN
  DBMS_REDEFINITION.COPY_TABLE_DEPENDENTS(
    uname            => 'APP_OWNER',
    tname            => 'ORDERS',
    int_table        => 'ORDERS_INT',
    num_errors       => v_errs,
    copy_triggers    => TRUE,
    copy_constraints => TRUE,
    copy_indexes     => TRUE,
    copy_statistics  => TRUE
  );
END;
/
  • Sync:
BEGIN
  DBMS_REDEFINITION.SYNC_INTERIM_TABLE('APP_OWNER', 'ORDERS');
END;
/
  • Finish and swap:
BEGIN
  DBMS_REDEFINITION.FINISH_REDEF_TABLE('APP_OWNER', 'ORDERS');
END;
/
  • Cleanup: reconcile stats/grants, then drop interim artifacts as appropriate.

LOBs, materialized view logs, row movement, and editioning interactions have version‑specific rules - confirm them in your release documentation before use.

When your change is in editioned code rather than the table itself, Edition‑Based Redefinition lets you run two versions at once and cut over on your terms. Tables are not editioned, so the safe pattern is to shield them behind editioning views and synonyms, evolve the views or packages in a child edition, test in that edition, then switch references.

Prerequisites (typically applied by a DBA):

  • System privileges: CREATE ANY EDITION (to create editions), DROP ANY EDITION (to retire), and the ability to ALTER USER ... ENABLE EDITIONS.
  • Object privileges in the target schema to create editioning views and editioned synonyms.

Build‑plan: EBR cutover (compact)

Oracle Database edition-based redefinition workflow for online application upgrades and cutover.

  • Enable editions for your user:
ALTER USER app_owner ENABLE EDITIONS;
  • In ORA$BASE (or your current default edition), create an editioning view to shield the underlying table. The view name is editioned; the table is not:
CREATE EDITIONING VIEW ev_orders AS
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_ts, status
FROM   orders;
  • Create a child edition:
CREATE EDITION app_v2 AS CHILD OF ORA$BASE;
  • Test in the child edition and evolve the API surface:
ALTER SESSION SET EDITION = app_v2;

-- Evolve API in the child edition (example: add a computed projection)
CREATE OR REPLACE EDITIONING VIEW ev_orders AS
SELECT order_id,
       customer_id,
       order_ts,
       status,
       CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_cancelled
FROM   orders;
  • Cutover: change which edition clients use (via connection‑level edition, services, or app routing). Keep ORA$BASE as a rollback window.
  • Rollback: switch sessions back to the previous edition while you investigate; retire the old edition once stable.

EBR timeline

Oracle Database edition-based redefinition workflow for online application upgrades and cutover.

Indexes get two useful mechanics. First, invisible indexes let you test plan influence without affecting other sessions. You can create a new index INVISIBLE or set an existing index invisible, then in your session enable it:

ALTER SESSION SET optimizer_use_invisible_indexes = TRUE;

If plans improve (verified via EXPLAIN PLAN and DBMS_XPLAN, and ideally timed execution), you can make the index visible for everyone. Second, ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD ONLINE is documented in 19c for supported index types, letting DML continue during maintenance with some restrictions. Note the careful wording: in 19c the ONLINE clause is documented for REBUILD; do not assume CREATE INDEX ONLINE for B‑tree indexes unless your exact release and index type say so.

Oracle Database index rollout workflow using invisible indexes, validation, and controlled cutover.

The same mindset for vector and relational indexes

Oracle Database 26ai adds native vector indexes—HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) and IVF (Inverted File)—and vector distance operators. The safe evolution pattern is the same as for relational indexes: build a tuned index in parallel, validate it with representative queries, then drop the old one after a soak period.

-- Check your exact RU/service tier for required/optional clauses and defaults.
-- HNSW example (common defaults shown; tune per workload)
CREATE VECTOR INDEX docs_hnsw_new
ON documents(embedding)
ORGANIZATION HNSW
DISTANCE COSINE;

-- IVF example (parameter defaults vary by RU)
CREATE VECTOR INDEX docs_ivf_new
ON documents(embedding)
ORGANIZATION IVF
DISTANCE COSINE;

If your RU requires additional parameters (e.g., neighborhood or partition knobs), supply them as documented; prefer a build‑new → validate → drop‑old evolution unless your docs explicitly state online/rebuild semantics. Validate using workload queries or DBMS_VECTOR advisers/accuracy checks, watching both recall and latency.

Proving what happened—and preparing to undo it

If an assistant participates in change, you need clean answers to who did what and how to reverse it. Start by tagging sessions at the application level:

BEGIN
  DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO.SET_MODULE('mcp-agent','index-additive-change');
END;
/

DBAs can then look in V$SESSION for that module/action pair, and SQLcl MCP adds its own evidence in DBTOOLS$MCP_LOG with each tool‑mediated request. With Unified Auditing enabled, you can go further: define policies for specific DDL or DML and query UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL to show who executed which statement and when. Access to dynamic performance views or audit trails depends on privileges; if your role is narrower, MCP logs still give you a reliable record. If you lack access to V$SESSION, ask a DBA to expose a filtered view you can query.

Rollback should be proportional to the change. For an index, the fastest backout is to mark it invisible; the hard backout is to drop it. For redefinition or EBR, the rollback is to keep the original structure or edition until final cutover and switch back if something misbehaves. For migrations, Liquibase can roll back by tag/changeSet/date when you’ve authored rollbacks (for supported change types); Flyway supports undo with authored scripts (Teams/Enterprise editions). The operative word is “authored”: write the backout path when you write the forward path.

Oracle Database governance and rollback workflow for MCP-driven schema and vector index changes.

A quick Unified Auditing check (if enabled and you have privileges):

SELECT event_timestamp, dbusername, action_name, object_schema, object_name, sql_text
FROM   unified_audit_trail
WHERE  action_name IN ('CREATE INDEX','ALTER INDEX','DROP INDEX')
AND    object_schema = 'APP_OWNER'
ORDER  BY event_timestamp DESC
FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;

Mini‑demo: propose, review, apply, verify, prove

Let’s run one small, additive change that an assistant proposes. We’ll add a composite index to speed a common filter on DOCUMENTS. The mechanics are deliberately conservative: INVISIBLE first, session‑level test, then visible or back out.

Governed Oracle Database change workflow with MCP, plan verification, and rollback readiness.

Prerequisites for this demo:

  • Oracle Database 19c or later.
  • Privileges: CREATE INDEX on DOCUMENTS owner; ALTER SESSION; EXPLAIN PLAN; EXECUTE on DBMS_XPLAN and DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO.
  • Access to V$SESSION requires SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE or equivalent; if not available, rely on DBTOOLS$MCP_LOG for evidence.
  • SQLcl MCP Server running with a pre‑saved least‑privilege connection to the target schema.

1) Preflight discovery. If an assistant suggests an index, ask it to verify there isn’t already one that covers the same columns:

SELECT index_name, visibility, status
FROM   user_indexes
WHERE  table_name = 'DOCUMENTS';

SELECT index_name, column_name, column_position
FROM   user_ind_columns
WHERE  table_name = 'DOCUMENTS'
ORDER  BY index_name, column_position;

(Outside the owner schema, use ALL_INDEXES/ALL_IND_COLUMNS.)

2) Proposal. The assistant drafts an index for source and published. Keep it INVISIBLE so only a session that opts in can use it:

CREATE INDEX docs_src_pub_idx
ON documents(source, published)
INVISIBLE;

3) Apply through a bounded surface. Approve the statement and run it via SQLcl MCP’s SQL tool using a least‑privilege, pre‑saved connection. Configure restrict levels to keep the tool surface small and auditable; MCP logs the call and tags the session automatically in V$SESSION (subject to your privileges).

4) Test before broad exposure. Enable invisible indexes only in your session and check plan shape and timing:

ALTER SESSION SET optimizer_use_invisible_indexes = TRUE;

EXPLAIN PLAN FOR
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM   documents
WHERE  source='kb'
AND    published >= DATE '2025-01-01';

SELECT plan_table_output
FROM   TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY());

For final validation, prefer executed plans via DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR with ALLSTATS LAST after running the query, as EXPLAIN PLAN can differ from runtime under binds or adaptive features. If PLAN_TABLE isn’t present in your schema, either create it (DBA task) or use DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR, which doesn’t rely on PLAN_TABLE.

Also capture actual timings on representative data:

-- Show the last executed statement's plan with runtime stats (if available)
SELECT *
FROM   TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR(NULL, NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));

If the plan and timings improve, make the index visible:

ALTER INDEX docs_src_pub_idx VISIBLE;

5) Evidence. Tag the module/action explicitly and pull recent MCP entries:

BEGIN
  DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO.SET_MODULE('mcp-agent','index-additive-change');
END;
/

-- Evidence in V$SESSION (requires privileges)
SELECT module, action
FROM   v$session
WHERE  module = 'mcp-agent';

-- Evidence in MCP logs (column names can vary by version)
-- DESCRIBE DBTOOLS$MCP_LOG;
SELECT *
FROM   DBTOOLS$MCP_LOG
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;

-- If you need ordering, first identify a timestamp or sequence column via DESCRIBE/USER_TAB_COLUMNS,
-- then apply ORDER BY accordingly.

If logs appear empty, run a simple MCP run-sql request and retry—the log table populates after the first tool interactions. Querying V$SESSION requires SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE or equivalent; if you don’t have it, rely on MCP logs and application‑level evidence or ask a DBA to expose a filtered view.

6) Rollback if needed. If the index hurts a minority of queries or adds unacceptable write overhead, back it out quickly:

ALTER INDEX docs_src_pub_idx INVISIBLE; -- tactical backout
-- or
DROP INDEX docs_src_pub_idx;            -- hard revert

That’s the loop: propose through discovery, preview the SQL, act through MCP, verify locally via INVISIBLE, and record the proof.

Delivery mechanics that hold up in real pipelines

The same loop translates cleanly to CI/CD and change boards. Migration tools handle state and retries; MCP provides execution discipline; Oracle features reduce blast radius.

In practice, you keep DDL/DML changes in version control and insist on previews. Liquibase’s updateSQL prints exactly what would run for a given changelog; Flyway’s dryRunOutput does the same for pending migrations. Checksums and state tables prevent accidental reruns. Avoid hand‑run DDL outside the tool, which can desynchronize history tables from reality. For table changes that must happen while writes continue, DBMS_REDEFINITION is the predictable route; for code and view evolution, EBR gives you reversible cutovers. For online index maintenance, REBUILD ONLINE helps keep writes flowing, while INVISIBLE indexing keeps tests local until you’re ready.

Testing belongs inside this posture, not as an afterthought. For PL/SQL and schema‑anchored behavior, utPLSQL lets you write fast, repeatable tests and run them in CI. When you’re changing query paths, pair DBMS_XPLAN plan displays with simple timing harnesses and capture them in artifacts the same way you capture dry‑run SQL. This is how agents and humans occupy the same workflow: the agent proposes, the pipeline proves.

A short view for migration leads

If you’re modernizing a system or switching database platforms, treat “agent‑safe change” as the daily rhythm and migrations as a route through it. The sequence has four stages:

1 — Assess. Inventory every object by type and complexity before writing a single migration script. Oracle’s skills repo includes a migration-assessment.md skill that routes this step. In practice, complexity falls into three tiers: simple objects (tables with standard types, views, sequences) that translate with minimal manual effort; moderate objects (stored procedures, triggers, basic PL/SQL packages) that need construct-by-construct review; and complex objects (advanced types, Java stored procedures, database links, Oracle-specific partitioning strategies, or heavy use of DBMS_* packages) that require hands-on expert review. An assistant can draft the inventory query and score the tiers—your job is to sanity-check the classification before committing to a timeline.

A useful starting inventory:

SELECT object_type, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM   all_objects
WHERE  owner = UPPER(‘<SOURCE_SCHEMA>’)
GROUP  BY object_type
ORDER  BY cnt DESC;

2 — Translate with source-specific guidance. Each source platform has predictable problem areas. For PostgreSQL migrations, the most common friction points documented in migrate-postgres-to-oracle.md are: sequence syntax (SERIAL → GENERATED AS IDENTITY), BOOLEAN columns (Oracle has no native BOOLEAN in SQL prior to 23ai; the standard convention is NUMBER(1,0) with a CHECK (col IN (0,1)) constraint), RETURNING clauses (Oracle restricts RETURNING INTO to PL/SQL blocks, requiring application refactoring), ILIKE (rewrite as UPPER(column) LIKE UPPER(pattern) with a supporting function-based index), and DATE semantics (Oracle's DATE stores time-of-day, so equality filters like WHERE created = DATE '2024-01-15' silently miss rows that have a non-midnight time component). An assistant loaded with migrate-postgres-to-oracle.md from the skills repo can flag these automatically when reviewing source DDL—but always verify the translation with a human before running it in staging.

3 — Pilot additive changes in staging. Before cutover, run a representative subset of translated objects through the full discovery → preview → bounded apply → verify loop described above. This is where invisible indexes, preview-gate SQL, and DBMS_REDEFINITION earn their keep. Focus on the moderate and complex tiers first; the simple tier can usually be scripted and batch-applied. Confirm that application queries return the same results on Oracle as they did on the source—row counts, join shapes, and date arithmetic are the usual suspects for silent semantic differences.

4 — Cutover and verify. Keep ORA$BASE or a pre-cutover schema snapshot available as a rollback window. Use Liquibase or Flyway changelogs so the migration state is recorded and reruns are safe. After cutover, run your standard smoke tests plus any Oracle-specific validation queries you assembled during assessment. Tag the migration session with DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO so post-cutover audit queries can isolate migration activity from normal application traffic.

By the time you’re scheduling the production cutover, the mechanics should be boring. The assistant can draft scripts and surface incompatibilities; your tooling and Oracle’s online features make the process predictable and reversible.

What to remember—and what’s next

Agent‑safe change is not a bet on model intelligence; it’s a bet on process. Force discovery before action. Require a previewed SQL artifact. Act only through a bounded server with least privilege. Use Oracle’s online and editioning features to keep availability high. Tag sessions, log activity, and keep a rollback path that matches the change. When you operate this way, you can accept more assistant help without accepting more risk.

In Article 8 we’ll close the loop with governance: identity and least privilege, policy, VPD, data redaction, and Unified Auditing as a procedural trust layer around the same route → act → trust loop.

 Sources and further reading

  • SQLcl MCP Server: tools, restrict levels, monitoring and logs
  • Online operations and index behavior (19c)  ALTER INDEX (ONLINE for REBUILD)  OPTIMIZER_USE_INVISIBLE_INDEXES  Managing invisible indexes
  • DBMS_REDEFINITION (19c)
  • EBR (editions and editioning views)  Start with the SQL Language Reference (CREATE EDITION; ALTER SESSION SET EDITION) and the Edition‑Based Redefinition Guide for your release (19c/23ai/26ai).
  • Vector indexing and functions (26ai)  CREATE VECTOR INDEX  VECTOR_DISTANCE  DBMS_VECTOR
  • Migrations tooling  Liquibase  Flyway
  • Evidence and auditing  DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO: PL/SQL Packages and Types Reference (match your version)  Unified Auditing and UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL: Oracle Database Security Guide (match your version)
  • Series continuity  Article 5 (Select AI, AI Profiles, SHOWSQL) and Article 6 (index and vector evaluation) provide the inspection and evaluation habits used here.

Notes on differences across releases and editions

  • Index ONLINE semantics: In Oracle 19c, ONLINE is documented for ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD for supported index types with restrictions; check your exact RU and index type. Do not assume CREATE INDEX ONLINE for B‑tree indexes in 19c.
  • Invisible indexes: Controlled by OPTIMIZER_USE_INVISIBLE_INDEXES at the session/system level. Validate on your target RU.
  • Vector indexes: 26ai introduces HNSW and IVF; confirm syntax and capabilities for your RU/tier. Prefer build‑new → validate → drop‑old unless your docs state otherwise.
  • SQLcl MCP: Tools and restrict‑level defaults are versioned. Verify the tool list and defaults for your installed SQLcl version.

What belongs in the rollback acceptance check? 

Test the undo procedure before broad exposure and specify what happens to writes made after the change. Record edition, feature, and tooling restrictions. A reversible index setting, an online table redefinition, and an application migration have different rollback semantics and should not share a blanket safety claim. 

Continue the implementation: The trust layer for enterprise AI on Oracle: prove identity, scope, policy, and evidence for every assistant action. Use the validation described above as the acceptance check for your next step.

title: Java Interview Questions for Experienced Developers: 10 Code Review Tasks
description:
These ten Java snippets look like code from a normal pull request, and each one hides a bug that breaks production.

When I conducted Java interviews, code review tasks were the best way to start a real conversation. A candidate can memorize what a HashMap does. Applying it to strange code is a different skill, and it shows the level faster than 100 questions about theory.

The tasks go from Java core to Spring Boot. I built every snippet on Spring Boot 4.1.1 (Hibernate 7.4.5, Jackson 3.1.5) and Java 21, and checked the main bugs with unit tests that reproduce them.

How to run a code review interview

Share the code and ask one question: “What’s wrong with it?” Don’t tell the candidate how many problems there are. Watch which problem catches their eye first and how they rank them. Then ask the follow-up questions from each task.

# Task Topic
1 Remove a user from a list Collections, strings
2 Seats as HashMap keys equals and hashCode
3 Visit counter in a Spring service Threads
4 Report with a parallel stream Streams
5 Login check SQL injection, passwords
6 Token authenticator JWT, Jackson
7 Password change Spring transactions, proxies
8 Wallet entity and service Spring Data JPA
9 SMS after shipping Side effects, idempotency
10 A cleanup job with a green test Testing

Java core

Task 1. Remove a user from a list 

public class UserCleanup {

    public static List<String> removeUser(List<String> users, String userToRemove) {
        for (String user : users) {
            if (user == userToRemove) {
                users.remove(user);
            }
        }
        return users;
    }
}
  1. If the caller passes a list from List.of, remove throws UnsupportedOperationException. The method signature promises nothing about mutability.
  2. Removing inside a for-each loop throws ConcurrentModificationException on the next iteration. Remove the second-to-last element and nothing throws: the loop just stops and never checks the last element.
  3. The == operator compares references. It works in a unit test because string literals are interned, and fails for a name that came from a request or a database.
  4. The method changes the caller’s list and returns it, so the return value hides a side effect.
  5. A null list throws NullPointerException.

A version that leaves the input alone and compares values builds a new list:

public class UserCleanup {

    public static List<String> withoutUser(List<String> users, String userToRemove) {
        return users.stream()
                .filter(user -> !Objects.equals(user, userToRemove))
                .toList();
    }
}

Follow-up questions: What changes if the input is a LinkedList? What does removeIf do differently from removing in a loop?

Task 2. Seats as HashMap keys 

public class Seat {

    private String row;
    private final Integer number;

    public Seat(String row, Integer number) {
        this.row = row;
        this.number = number;
    }

    public void moveTo(String row) {
        this.row = row;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Seat other && row.equals(other.row) && number == other.number;
    }
}
  1. equals without hashCode. Two equal seats get different identity hash codes, so a HashMap never finds a booking by a new Seat object, and a HashSet keeps both.
  2. The number is an Integer compared with ==. Integer.valueOf caches values from -128 to 127, so seat 127 equals seat 127, and seat 128 doesn’t equal seat 128.
  3. A seat with a null row throws NullPointerException from equals.
  4. moveTo changes a field that takes part in equality. Add the missing hashCode and a moved seat gets lost inside a HashSet, because it sits in the bucket of its old hash.

A record gives equals and hashCode over immutable components:

public record Seat(String row, int number) {
}

Follow-up questions: Why does a record need no hand-written hashCode, and when would you still write one? What breaks if a subclass adds a field and overrides equals?

Task 3. Visit counter in a Spring service 

@Service
public class VisitCounter {

    private final Map<String, Integer> visits = new HashMap<>();

    public void visit(String page) {
        Integer count = visits.get(page);
        visits.put(page, count == null ? 1 : count + 1);
    }

    public int visits(String page) {
        return visits.get(page);
    }
}
  1. A Spring service is a singleton, so every request thread shares one HashMap. HashMap isn’t thread-safe, and concurrent puts can lose entries.
  2. Get, then put, is check-then-act. Two threads read 5 and both write 6. Swap in a ConcurrentHashMap and the update still gets lost: a thread-safe map doesn’t make two calls atomic.
  3. visits throws NullPointerException for a page nobody opened, because a null Integer is unboxed to int.
  4. The page comes from the request. Every new query string adds a key that nothing evicts, so the map grows until the heap runs out.

Atomic per-key updates fix the race:

@Service
public class VisitCounter {

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> visits = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void visit(String page) {
        visits.computeIfAbsent(page, key -> new LongAdder()).increment();
    }

    public long visits(String page) {
        LongAdder count = visits.get(page);
        return count == null ? 0 : count.sum();
    }
}

The fix still counts per instance: three pods keep three counters. The keys still need a limit, for example only known routes.

Follow-up questions: Is a synchronized method enough? When is LongAdder better than AtomicLong?

Task 4. Report with a parallel stream 

public class ReportService {

    public List<MemberSummary> summarize(List<Member> members) {
        List<MemberSummary> summaries = new ArrayList<>();
        members.parallelStream().forEach(member -> {
            if (member.inactive()) {
                members.remove(member);
            } else {
                summaries.add(MemberSummary.from(member));
            }
        });
        return summaries;
    }
}

This method can throw four exception types. While every member is active and the list is short, it usually works, so it can live in production for a long time.

  1. ConcurrentModificationException. The stream iterates members, and remove changes the same list. The spliterator checks the modification count after its traversal and throws.
  2. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, or summaries that silently go missing. Pool threads call add on one unsynchronized ArrayList at the same time.
  3. UnsupportedOperationException when the caller passes List.of or any unmodifiable list.
  4. NullPointerException for a null list.

The method also changes the caller’s list, and a failure leaves it half changed. Parallel forEach doesn’t keep the order, and parallelStream adds overhead with nothing measured to justify it.

public class ReportService {

    public List<MemberSummary> summarize(List<Member> members) {
        return members.stream()
                .filter(member -> !member.inactive())
                .map(MemberSummary::from)
                .toList();
    }
}

Follow-up questions: Which thread pool runs a parallel stream? When does parallelStream help?

Security

Task 5. Login check with JdbcTemplate 

@Repository
public class LoginRepository {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;

    public LoginRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    public boolean canLogin(String username, String password) {
        String sql = String.format(
                "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE username = '%s' AND password = '%s'",
                username, password);
        Integer count = jdbc.queryForObject(sql, Integer.class);
        return count > 0;
    }
}

Only 3 out of 10 candidates found the critical issues in this task during my interviews.

  1. SQL injection. String.format doesn’t escape anything. The first line as a username logs in without a password. The second line as a password logs in as anyone: 
admin' --
' OR '1'='1

Passwords are stored as plain text, because the query compares the raw input with the column. One database leak, and every password is out, including the ones people reuse on other sites.

No validation. A null username becomes the text “null” in the query. Blank input goes straight to the database too.

COUNT(*) greater than zero hides duplicates. Nothing in this code notices two rows for one username.

A common follow-up: would plain JDBC fix it? No. Statement with concatenation has the same hole. Parameters fix it, whether you use JdbcTemplate or JPA:

@Repository
public class LoginRepository {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;

    public LoginRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbc, PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }

    public boolean canLogin(String username, String password) {
        List<String> hashes = jdbc.queryForList(
                "SELECT password_hash FROM users WHERE username = ?", String.class, username);
        return hashes.size() == 1 && passwordEncoder.matches(password, hashes.get(0));
    }
}

The column now holds a BCrypt hash, and the encoder compares the input with it in Java. Declare a BCryptPasswordEncoder bean, because Spring Boot doesn’t create one.

Follow-up questions: Why should password hashing be slow? Where else can user input reach SQL (ORDER BY, LIKE patterns)?

Task 6. Token authenticator 

@Slf4j
@Service
public class TokenAuthenticator {

    private final ApiClientRepository clients;

    public TokenAuthenticator(ApiClientRepository clients) {
        this.clients = clients;
    }

    public Optional<ApiClient> authenticate(String token) {
        log.info("Authenticating token {}", token);
        String[] parts = token.split("\\.");
        ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
        Map<String, Object> header = mapper.readValue(decode(parts[0]), Map.class);
        Map<String, Object> claims = mapper.readValue(decode(parts[1]), Map.class);
        log.debug("Token signed with {}", header.get("alg"));
        return clients.findByLogin((String) claims.get("sub"));
    }

    private static byte[] decode(String part) {
        return Base64.getDecoder().decode(part);
    }
}
  1. The signature is never checked. A token with a random signature passes, and so does a token with the header alg set to none. Anyone can write any subject.
  2. No expiration check. A token stolen a year ago still works.
  3. The full token goes to the INFO log, so anyone who reads logs can reuse it.
  4. A new ObjectMapper on every call. The mapper is expensive to build and thread-safe to share. During a load test I once saw a flame graph where 70% of CPU time was spent creating object mappers.
  5. Map plus casts. A numeric subject throws ClassCastException at runtime.
  6. JWT parts are base64url. The basic decoder rejects the – and _ characters, so some valid tokens fail with IllegalArgumentException.
  7. A string without dots throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, an unhandled exception instead of a clean 401.

Don’t parse tokens by hand. Spring Security’s resource server checks the signature and the expiration. It checks the issuer too once you set it below. The Boot 4 starter replaces the deprecated spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server, and start.spring.io adds it when you pick OAuth2 Resource Server:

<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>

// build.gradle.kts
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server")

# application.properties
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=https://auth.example.com

When code needs JSON, inject the JsonMapper that Spring Boot 4 configures for Jackson 3 instead of building a new one.

Follow-up questions: What does the alg header change? Why is a symmetric key risky when many services verify tokens?

Spring and Spring Data JPA

Task 7. Password change 

@Service
public class PasswordService {

    @Autowired
    private AppUserRepository users;
    @Autowired
    private AuditLogRepository auditLogs;

    public void updatePassword(Long userId, String oldPassword, String newPassword) {
        AppUser user = users.findById(userId).get();
        saveAuditLog(userId, "PASSWORD_CHANGE");
        user.setPassword(newPassword);
        users.save(user);
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void saveAuditLog(Long userId, String action) {
        auditLogs.save(new AuditLog(userId, action, LocalDateTime.now()));
    }
}

This task got the most reactions of all my interview posts on LinkedIn. The problems, from critical to minor:

  1. Anyone can change anyone’s password. oldPassword is never checked, and the user id comes from the caller instead of the security context.
  2. The new password is stored as plain text and never validated. A blank password passes.
  3. The audit row is saved first and committed on its own. When the update fails (for example, a null password hits a NOT NULL column), the audit log says the password changed.
  4. REQUIRES_NEW does nothing here. updatePassword calls saveAuditLog on this, not through the Spring proxy, so no new transaction starts. Called from another bean, the same method does get its own transaction.
  5. updatePassword has no transaction. The read and the write run in two separate repository transactions.
  6. Field injection hides dependencies from the constructor and makes the class harder to test.
  7. findById(…).get() throws NoSuchElementException with the message “No value present”, without the id.
  8. The action is a free string, and LocalDateTime.now() takes the server’s time zone.

A fixed version takes the user from the security context and checks the old password with PasswordEncoder before it stores a hash of the new one. The change and its audit row commit together in one transactional method. The bean gets its repositories through the constructor.

Follow-up questions: Which annotations work through the same proxy? Why can’t a private method be transactional?

Task 8. Wallet entity and service 

@Data
@Entity
public class Wallet {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String owner;
    private double balance;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.ORDINAL)
    private WalletStatus status;
    private String createdAt;
}

public interface WalletRepository extends JpaRepository<Wallet, Long> {

    @Modifying
    @Query("update Wallet w set w.status = :status")
    int setStatusForAll(WalletStatus status);
}

@Slf4j
@Service
public class WalletService {

    private final WalletRepository wallets;

    public WalletService(WalletRepository wallets) {
        this.wallets = wallets;
    }

    public void rename(Long id, String owner) {
        Wallet wallet = wallets.findById(id).get();
        wallet.setOwner(owner);
    }

    @Transactional
    public List<Wallet> freezeAll() {
        wallets.findAll().forEach(w -> log.info("Freezing wallet of {}", w.getOwner()));
        wallets.setStatusForAll(WalletStatus.FROZEN);
        return wallets.findAll();
    }
}
  1. rename does nothing. Outside a web request, findById runs in its own short transaction and returns a detached entity, so setOwner changes only an object in memory.
  2. freezeAll returns stale data. The bulk update goes straight to the database and skips the persistence context. The second findAll returns the same managed wallets, still ACTIVE, while the table says FROZEN.
  3. Lombok @data builds hashCode over every field, including the id. save sets the id on the same object, and a wallet put in a HashSet before saving can’t be found after.
  4. ORDINAL stores the position of the constant: FROZEN is 1. Add a constant in the middle of the enum and old rows change meaning.
  5. A double balance drifts: three deposits of 0.1 don’t add up to 0.3.
  6. IDENTITY ids turn off JDBC insert batching in Hibernate, because Hibernate has to run each insert at once to learn its id. More on batching in my Spring Data JPA batch insert article.
  7. createdAt is a String: no time zone, and text sorting breaks on the first different format.

Fixes for the entity: getters and setters instead of @data, EnumType.STRING, BigDecimal, Instant, and a sequence. rename needs @Transactional; dirty checking then saves the change without a save call. The bulk update needs a transaction and a cleared persistence context:

public interface WalletRepository extends JpaRepository<Wallet, Long> {

    @Transactional // a write needs a transaction, whoever calls it
    @Modifying(flushAutomatically = true, clearAutomatically = true) // fresh reads after the update
    @Query("update Wallet w set w.status = :status")
    int setStatusForAll(WalletStatus status);
}

Follow-up questions: What does dirty checking need to work? What does open-in-view hide in a case like rename?

Task 9. SMS after shipping 

@Service
public class ShippingNotifier {

    private final SmsGateway sms;
    private final NotificationRepository notifications;

    public ShippingNotifier(SmsGateway sms, NotificationRepository notifications) {
        this.sms = sms;
        this.notifications = notifications;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void onOrderShipped(OrderShipped event) {
        String messageId = sms.send(event.phone(), "Your order is on the way");
        notifications.save(new Notification(event.orderId(), messageId));
    }
}

A real case cost a company $2,000 in duplicate SMS messages: a Kafka consumer sent the SMS and then did one more write. This snippet has the same shape.

  1. @Transactional doesn’t make the flow atomic. The SMS goes out first, then the insert fails, the transaction rolls back, and the customer already has the message.
  2. No idempotency. Kafka delivers at least once, so the same event can arrive again after a timeout or a rebalance. The second delivery sends a second SMS and then fails on the unique order id, and a retrying consumer can repeat that.
  3. The transaction holds a pooled database connection during the HTTP call to the SMS provider. A slow provider can drain the pool for the whole service.

A safer shape: save a pending notification with the order id as the idempotency key. Send the SMS after the commit, from an outbox table or an AFTER_COMMIT listener. Mark it sent, and only then acknowledge the Kafka offset.

Follow-up questions: What happens if the service crashes after the SMS but before it marks the notification sent? Where does the consumer acknowledge the message?

Task 10. A cleanup job with a green test

This one is close to a bug I shipped myself: the test for a scheduled @Modifying query was green, and in production the job silently did nothing.

@Component
public class SessionCleanup {

    private final LoginSessionRepository sessions;

    public SessionCleanup(LoginSessionRepository sessions) {
        this.sessions = sessions;
    }

    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 * * * *")
    public void removeExpired() {
        sessions.deleteExpired(Instant.now());
    }
}

public interface LoginSessionRepository extends JpaRepository<LoginSession, Long> {

    @Modifying
    @Query("delete from LoginSession s where s.expiresAt < :now")
    int deleteExpired(Instant now);
}

@DataJpaTest
@Import(SessionCleanup.class)
class SessionCleanupTest {

    @Autowired
    SessionCleanup cleanup;
    @Autowired
    LoginSessionRepository sessions;

    @Test
    void removesExpiredSessions() {
        sessions.save(new LoginSession(Instant.now().minusSeconds(60)));
        cleanup.removeExpired();
        assertThat(sessions.count()).isZero();
    }
}

The test is green. In production the job throws InvalidDataAccessApiUsageException caused by TransactionRequiredException on every run, and the scheduler only logs it.

  1. Spring Data JPA applies no transaction to your own query methods. A @Modifying query needs one, and the scheduler calls removeExpired without it.
  2. @DataJpaTest wraps each test in a transaction. The test borrows that transaction, and production has none.

The fix puts the transaction on the write:

public interface LoginSessionRepository extends JpaRepository<LoginSession, Long> {

    @Transactional // the scheduler calls it without a transaction
    @Modifying
    @Query("delete from LoginSession s where s.expiresAt < :now")
    int deleteExpired(Instant now);
}

The bigger fix is in the tests. Run integration tests with @SpringBootTest and without @Transactional on test classes. An ArchUnit rule can fail the build when someone adds @DataJpaTest or @Transactional to an integration test again.

Follow-up questions: Which repository methods are transactional by default? How else can a test transaction hide a bug?

Spring Boot good practices to ask about

Tasks 5, 7, 8 and 9 break at least one of these, and a candidate can explain them without any code.

  1. Constructor injection. Required dependencies are final, and a unit test can build the class without Spring.
  2. HTTP stays in the controller layer. Services throw domain exceptions such as UserNotFoundException, and a @RestControllerAdvice maps them to responses.
  3. Turn on Problem Details for errors. It is off by default: 
# application.properties
spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true

Return DTOs, not entities. An entity leaks internal fields such as a password hash, and lazy associations fail after the transaction closes.

Turn off open-in-view. Spring Boot 4.1 still turns it on by default and only logs a warning. It keeps the database session open while the response renders and hides lazy loading problems:

# application.properties
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

# application.properties
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

Validate input at the edge with Bean Validation on request DTOs, then trust the types inside.

Tokens and secrets never go in the URL. Query parameters end up in access logs and proxy logs.

Every write that a client or a broker can retry needs an idempotency key.

Which of these tasks would you give a candidate first, and which bug did you miss on the first read?

At the end

If you like this post, follow me on LinkedIn for new code review tasks. More on entities and transactions: Spring Data JPA guide.
