title: React Pull to Refresh in a PWA Without Fighting the Browser
description:
TL;DR

A React pull to refresh that holds up in a PWA needs four things: overscroll-behavior-y: contain on the scroller so Chrome does not reload the page, a touchmove listener added with { passive: false } because React's onTouchMove is passive and Safari on iOS ignores overscroll-behavior for its own refresh, a rubberband curve instead of a linear drag, and a refresh button for people who cannot drag. Pick an indicator that matches the platform (iOS spokes that move the list down, or a Material ring that floats over it) and fire one haptic tick at the threshold as an extra, never as the only signal. The Pro Wingo UI Pull To Refresh does all of this in one component.

A React pull to refresh looks like forty lines of touch handlers until it runs in a phone browser. Chrome on Android and Safari on iOS have their own pull to refresh that reloads the page, React registers onTouchMove as passive so preventDefault() does nothing, and a list that follows the finger one to one feels wrong on a phone. This guide fixes each one for a PWA, with the raw pattern and the Wingo UI Pull To Refresh that packages it.

Why does a PWA need its own pull to refresh?

Because the browser's version reloads the document, and once the app is installed it may not exist at all. A reload runs every script again and drops all in-memory state: fetched data, an open sheet, the scroll position of a nested list. A data refresh only refetches the list. And a web app added to the iPhone home screen opens in standalone mode, without Safari's toolbar or its pull to refresh (our React PWA install prompt tutorial covers how people get it there). Discourse shipped a theme component to add one back; its December 2024 announcement opens with "Pull to refresh is a huge gap in iOS PWA."

Ready-made packages are thin. As of October 2026, a search for pull to refresh react pwa still puts @patlux/react-pull-to-refresh (last published November 2018) and react-js-pull-to-refresh (last published August 2022) near the top, next to React Native packages that do not run in a browser. Android calls the gesture swipe to refresh, so a React swipe to refresh component is the same thing under another name.

How do you stop the browser's own pull to refresh?

Set overscroll-behavior-y: contain on the element that scrolls: html when the window scrolls, the container otherwise. That one line is the whole overscroll-behavior pull to refresh fix in Chrome, which has supported the property since Chrome 63; contain keeps the overscroll glow and none removes it too. Per MDN, contain "disables native browser navigation, including the vertical pull-to-refresh gesture".

Safari is the exception. It has supported the property since Safari 16 (caniuse), but WebKit bug 275947, filed in June 2024 and still open when we checked in October 2026, reports that neither none nor contain turns off Safari's pull to refresh on iOS. What works there is JavaScript: once a touch at the top moves down, call preventDefault() on its touchmove, so the page does not scroll, bounce or start Safari's refresh under the finger.

That is where React gets in the way. The React 17 changelog lists "Keep onTouchStart, onTouchMove, and onWheel passive." A passive listener cannot cancel the event, so onTouchMove={(e) => e.preventDefault()} is silently ignored. Attach the listener yourself, on the scroller:

// React registers onTouchMove as a passive listener, so preventDefault() inside it is ignored.
// attach it yourself, on the scroller (on document, every scroll on the page would wait for this handler)
export function attachPull(scroller: HTMLElement, onPull: (dy: number) => void, onRelease: () => void) {
  let startY: number | null = null;
  let pulling = false;

  const start = (event: TouchEvent) => {
    pulling = false;
    startY = event.touches.length === 1 && scroller.scrollTop <= 0 ? event.touches[0].clientY : null;
  };
  const move = (event: TouchEvent) => {
    if (startY === null) return;
    const dy = event.touches[0].clientY - startY;
    if (!pulling && dy < 0) {
      // the finger went up first: a normal scroll, hand it back
      startY = null;
      return;
    }
    pulling = true;
    event.preventDefault(); // allowed because the listener is not passive
    onPull(Math.max(0, dy));
  };
  const end = () => {
    if (pulling) onRelease();
    startY = null;
    pulling = false;
  };

  const previous = scroller.style.overscrollBehaviorY;
  scroller.style.overscrollBehaviorY = "contain";
  scroller.addEventListener("touchstart", start, { passive: true });
  scroller.addEventListener("touchmove", move, { passive: false });
  scroller.addEventListener("touchend", end);
  scroller.addEventListener("touchcancel", end);
  return () => {
    scroller.style.overscrollBehaviorY = previous;
    scroller.removeEventListener("touchstart", start);
    scroller.removeEventListener("touchmove", move);
    scroller.removeEventListener("touchend", end);
    scroller.removeEventListener("touchcancel", end);
  };
}

Call it from a useEffect and return its cleanup. Write dy to a motion value or a ref, not to state, or every touchmove re-renders the list. It is a skeleton. The Wingo UI component adds what it misses: it waits 8px before deciding whether a touch is a pull, drops gestures that are more sideways than down, cancels on a second finger (a pinch is never a pull), and never starts in an input, inside [data-no-pull], in a horizontal scroller or in a nested list that is not at its own top.

How much resistance should a pull to refresh have?

Resistance that grows the further the finger goes, so the list slows down smoothly instead of following one to one into a hard stop. react-simple-pull-to-refresh, the most recently released web package we looked at (1.3.4, January 5, 2026, MIT, React 16.10 to 19), divides the finger travel by a resistance prop (default 1) and clamps it at maxPullDownDistance (default 95px): a linear pull into a wall. With no dependencies, it is a fair pick for a prototype.

A native list follows a curve. The rubberband helper in Wingo UI's lib/motion uses an iOS-style one, (1 - 1 / (x * 0.55 / d + 1)) * d, where x is the finger travel past the 8px slop and d the scroller height (480px at least, so a short box resists like a phone-sized one). On a 480px scroller with the defaults, 100px of finger travel moves the list 49px, 200px moves it 89px, the refresh arms at 72px (threshold) after about 154px, and the list never passes maxPull (128px). The pull lives in a motion value, so a touchmove never re-renders your list; React state changes only when the phase does (pulling, armed, refreshing, done).

A release before the threshold springs back with the finger's velocity. A release past it parks the list at the threshold while onRefresh runs (500ms at least, so the spinner never flashes), then shows a check, or an alert when the promise rejects, for doneDuration (600ms) before the list glides back. Under reduced motion the list jumps to each resting point instead of springing.

Arrow, iOS spokes or a Material ring: which indicator should you use?

Match the platform most of your users hold, and decide whether the content should move. The three variants of the component:

variant The list While pulling While refreshing Good fit
arrow (default) moves down an arrow that turns at the threshold a spinner neutral apps on both platforms
ios moves down 12 spokes that draw one by one the spokes spin in 12 steps, like UIRefreshControl iPhone-first apps
material stays put a floating circle whose ring fills a spinning ring in the circle Android-first apps, image grids, virtual lists

size sets the glyph to 20, 24 or 28px (the Material circle to 36, 40 or 44px), tone colors it (neutral by default), and showLabel adds a line that reads Pull to refresh, Release to refresh, Refreshing…, then Updated. Under reduced motion the spokes spin at half speed.

Live demo: Pull To Refresh. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Pull the inbox down with a finger, or scroll up past the top on a trackpad: the spokes draw as you pull, the label flips to Release to refresh at the threshold, and new messages land on top). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Pull To Refresh docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add pull-to-refresh

Here is a full inbox screen with the iOS variant around the List. scroll="self" makes the component the scroll container, with overscroll-behavior-y: contain on itself. With the default scroll="parent" it watches the scroller you pass or provide, else the nearest scrolling ancestor, else the window, and sets the property there while it is mounted and enabled.

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { RotateCw } from "lucide-react";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { List, type ListItemData } from "@/components/ui/list";
import { PullToRefresh, type PullToRefreshApi } from "@/components/ui/pull-to-refresh";

type InboxProps = { initial: ListItemData[]; load: () => Promise<ListItemData[]> };

export function Inbox({ initial, load }: InboxProps) {
  const [items, setItems] = useState(initial);
  const [api, setApi] = useState<PullToRefreshApi>();

  return (
    <div className="flex h-dvh flex-col">
      <header className="flex h-14 shrink-0 items-center justify-between px-4">
        <h1 className="text-lg font-semibold">Inbox</h1>
        {/* the same refresh for keyboards, switch access and mouse users */}
        <Button variant="ghost" size="icon" radius="full" aria-label="Reload" onClick={() => void api?.refresh()}>
          <RotateCw />
        </Button>
      </header>
      <PullToRefresh
        scroll="self"
        variant="ios"
        shortcut="shift+r"
        className="min-h-0 flex-1"
        setApi={setApi}
        onRefresh={async () => setItems(await load())}
        labels={{ refreshing: "Checking for mail…", done: "Up to date", error: "Could not check for mail" }}
      >
        <List variant="plain" items={items} />
      </PullToRefresh>
    </div>
  );
}

The indicator spins until the onRefresh promise settles; a rejection shows the error state. Pass refreshing when the app starts a reload on its own, and disabled while the user edits or filters: turning it on mid-pull springs the list back without refreshing.

How do you add a haptic tick to a pull to refresh?

Fire one short tick when the pull crosses the threshold, the moment letting go starts to mean refresh; never on every frame or on release. The component calls haptic("medium") from the haptics helper when the pull arms and haptic("error") when a pulled refresh fails. haptics={false} turns both off, and configureHaptics({ enabled }) is the app-wide switch.

Treat the tick as a bonus, because support is uneven. As of October 2026, caniuse lists navigator.vibrate in Chrome for Android and Samsung Internet, removed from Firefox in version 129 and never in Safari. On iPhone the helper clicks a hidden <input type="checkbox" switch> from script to play the system tick; the switch arrived in Safari 17.4, and WebKit's announcement does not mention a haptic, so nothing promises it will last. ios-haptics, built on the same trick, said in its June 2026 README (version 3.1.1) that it "only works on ios 17.4 to 26.4, as apple patched it in ios 26.5". Its September 2026 release (3.2.0) forwards the user's own tap to the switch as a trusted click instead, which suggests a click from script no longer plays. A pull never produces a tap, so expect the tick to stay silent on iOS 26.5 and later, and never put information in it that the indicator does not show.

Vibration also needs sticky user activation, and touchmove is not an activation event (touchend, a finger's pointerup, mousedown and keydown are). If a pull is the first thing someone does on a fresh page, that tick is silent; haptic() returns false instead of letting Chrome log a blocked call. Our Web Vibration API guide covers the rest of the platform gap and a setting that turns haptics off.

How do you make a custom pull to refresh accessible?

Give the same refresh a button, a key and an announcement, because a pull is a dragging movement. WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.5.7 (level AA) exempts the browser's own drag to refresh, since the user agent provides it, but applies once your content implements its own, so you need a single-pointer alternative. Android's swipe to refresh guide asks the same of native apps: a refresh action in the app bar's overflow menu, for people who use a keyboard or a D-pad.

The component has a path for each input. setApi hands you { refresh() }, which runs exactly what a pull runs (indicator, promise, done state), so a header button and a pull never drift apart; a call during a running refresh returns the running promise. shortcut binds a key such as shift+r. A polite live region announces Refreshing…, then Updated or the error, and the root carries aria-busy meanwhile. On a laptop, scrolling up once more at the very top with a trackpad or wheel pulls (wheel, on by default; momentum that carries a scroll to the top never does), and pullWithMouse lets a mouse drag pull, for kiosks. The header button in the inbox example uses the Button's size="icon", which is 40px with a mouse and 44px on touch screens, the size the minimum touch target guide recommends.

Live demo: Pull To Refresh. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (With a mouse, drag the list down (pullWithMouse is on in this demo); on a phone, pull it. The ring fills while the rows stay put, and the Reload button in the header runs the same refresh without a gesture). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Pull To Refresh docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add pull-to-refresh

How do you use pull to refresh with a long virtualized list?

Let one element scroll and share it, so both components watch the same scroll position. The Virtual List with scroll="window" follows the nearest ScrollContainerProvider, and Pull To Refresh with its default scroll="parent" does too:

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { ListItem } from "@/components/ui/list";
import { PullToRefresh } from "@/components/ui/pull-to-refresh";
import { VirtualList } from "@/components/ui/virtual-list";
import { ScrollContainerProvider } from "@/hooks/use-scroll-state";

type Order = { id: string; customer: string; city: string; total: string };

type OrdersProps = {
  orders: Order[];
  hasMore: boolean;
  reload: () => Promise<void>;
  loadPage: () => Promise<void>;
};

export function Orders({ orders, hasMore, reload, loadPage }: OrdersProps) {
  // one element scrolls, and both components follow it through the provider
  const [scroller, setScroller] = useState<HTMLDivElement | null>(null);

  return (
    <div ref={setScroller} className="h-dvh overflow-y-auto">
      <ScrollContainerProvider value={scroller}>
        <PullToRefresh variant="material" onRefresh={reload}>
          <VirtualList
            aria-label="Orders"
            scroll="window"
            items={orders}
            renderItem={(order) => <ListItem id={order.id} title={order.customer} description={order.city} value={order.total} />}
            hasMore={hasMore}
            onLoadMore={loadPage}
          />
        </PullToRefresh>
      </ScrollContainerProvider>
    </div>
  );
}

Use the material variant here. The Virtual List measures where it starts inside the scroller with getBoundingClientRect(), which counts transforms, and it measures again when its size changes. The arrow and ios variants hold the rows 72px down with a transform while onRefresh runs, which is exactly when new rows arrive. The material ring floats over rows that never move. For the other end, loadMode="pull" on the Virtual List loads the next page when the user pulls past the last row and lets go.

Which pull to refresh pitfalls show up in production?

Check these five before you ship, whether you use our component or your own React pull to refresh component:

  • A sticky or translucent header over the list. The indicator hides under it. indicatorOffset moves its resting line down by the header's height.
  • A pull during the bounce at the top. On iOS the scroll position goes negative while the list bounces past the top, so a strict scrollTop === 0 check refuses pulls that start then. Treat anything at or below 0 as the top.
  • A fixed bar inside the pulled content. The arrow and ios variants move the content with a transform, and a transformed element becomes the containing block of its position: fixed children, so a tab bar or floating button rendered inside rides down with the pull. Render fixed bars outside the component.
  • Nested pull to refresh areas, such as a feed inside a tab of a page that refreshes. The inner one should win; the component makes the outer one ignore the gesture.
  • A refresh that never ends. If onRefresh hangs, so does the spinner. Put the timeout on the request, for example fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) }), not on the indicator: the rejection then shows the error state and the indicator tells the truth.

For the rest of the mobile layer (bottom sheets, safe areas, dvh, tab bars), read the guide to mobile-first React components or browse Mobile UI in React.

What should you install next?

If your list already exists, wrap it. npx wingo-ui@latest add pull-to-refresh copies the component into your project with the Spinner and the hooks and helpers it imports (haptics, motion, scroll state, shortcuts), and installs motion and lucide-react. Pull To Refresh, List and Virtual List are part of Wingo UI Pro, so sign in first with npx wingo-ui@latest login; the Spinner it uses is free.

Components in this post

  • Pull To Refresh (Pro): Pull a list down past its top to reload it, with rubberband resistance, an arrow, iOS spokes or a Material ring, and a haptic tick. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add pull-to-refresh
  • List (Pro): Rows on a page for settings, contacts, inboxes and orders: iOS grouped panels, selection, row menus, swipe actions and drag to reorder. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add list
  • Virtual List (Pro): Long and endless lists at 60fps: thousands of list rows virtualized, sticky group headers, infinite loading and scroll restoration. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add virtual-list
  • Haptics (Pro): Haptic feedback for the web in one call: short vibration ticks on Android and the system tick on iPhone, silent everywhere else. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add haptics

FAQ

How do I disable the browser's pull to refresh in Chrome?

Set overscroll-behavior-y: contain on the element that scrolls, which is the html element when the window scrolls. Use none instead to remove the overscroll glow as well. Chrome has supported the property since version 63.

Does overscroll-behavior stop pull to refresh in Safari on iOS?

Not reliably. Safari has supported the property since version 16, but WebKit bug 275947, open since June 2024, reports that it does not turn off Safari's own pull to refresh. Call preventDefault in a non-passive touchmove listener once the gesture is a pull.

Why does preventDefault not work in onTouchMove in React?

Since React 17, onTouchStart, onTouchMove and onWheel are registered as passive listeners, and browsers ignore preventDefault in a passive listener. Attach the listener yourself with addEventListener and { passive: false } in an effect, on the scrolling element.

Is a custom pull to refresh accessible?

Only with an alternative. WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (level AA) exempts the browser's own drag to refresh but covers one you build, so add a refresh button or shortcut that runs the same reload and announce the result in a live region.

Is the Wingo UI Pull To Refresh free?

No. It is a Pro component, like the List, the Virtual List and the haptics helper it pairs with; the Spinner it uses is free. With a Pro account signed in through npx wingo-ui@latest login, npx wingo-ui@latest add pull-to-refresh copies the component and everything it imports into your project.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: React Pull to Refresh in a PWA Without Fighting the Browser. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Prerendering a React SPA for SEO (and the OG-tag gotcha I hit)
description:
In my last post I said my biggest regret was not starting with SSR or prerendering. This is the follow-up: what I did about it.

Here's the problem. A React single-page app sends every visitor the same index.html: a <div id="root"></div> and a script tag. The content only appears after JavaScript runs.

Google can run JavaScript, but it does so later and less reliably. LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Slack and most other link-preview bots don't run it at all. They read the raw HTML and stop.

For ResumeOrbitz, which is a free resume builder that lives on organic search, that meant every page looked identical to a crawler. Same title, same description, almost no text.

What prerendering actually does

Prerendering means running your app once at build time, for every route, and saving what the browser sees as a real HTML file. No server, no framework migration. You keep your SPA and get static HTML on top.

The pipeline is short:

  1. vite build produces the normal SPA in dist/.
  2. The script copies dist/index.html to app-shell.html: a pure client-side shell for routes that shouldn't be prerendered (dashboard, editor).
  3. It starts Vite's preview server on dist/ and launches headless Chromium with Playwright.
  4. For each route in sitemap.xml, it loads the page, waits for React and react-helmet to finish, and grabs the full HTML.
  5. It writes each page as a flat file: /templates becomes dist/templates.html.
  6. Netlify serves those files directly. Protected routes fall back to app-shell.html.

The result on ResumeOrbitz: all 105 sitemap routes now arrive with their real content, title and meta tags in the first response.

My setup: one Playwright script, run after the build

Everything lives in scripts/prerender.mjs. npm's pre/post hooks wire it in, so a plain npm run build does all three steps:

"prebuild": "tsx scripts/generate-sitemap.ts",
"build": "vite build",
"postbuild": "node scripts/prerender.mjs"

The sitemap is generated first, and the prerender reads its routes straight from it, so the two can never drift apart:

function getRoutesFromSitemap() {
  const xml = readFileSync(join(root, 'public/sitemap.xml'), 'utf8');
  const matches = [...xml.matchAll(/<loc>https:\/\/resumeorbitz\.com([^<]*)<\/loc>/g)];
  return matches.map((m) => m[1] || '/');
}

The core loop, trimmed:

for (const route of routes) {
  await page.goto(`${base}${route}`, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });
  await page.waitForSelector('#root > *', { timeout: 10_000 });
  await page.waitForTimeout(800); // let react-helmet commit its head tags

  // (the OG-tag fix goes here, see below)

  const html = '<!doctype html>\n' +
    (await page.evaluate(() => document.documentElement.outerHTML));

  if (route === '/') homepageHtml = html;   // write the homepage last
  else writeFileSync(outputPathFor(route), html);
}
writeFileSync(join(distDir, 'index.html'), homepageHtml);

Four lessons hide in those few lines:

  • A fixed wait beat a smart one. I first polled until the DOM stopped changing. It sometimes "settled" in the pause before Helmet's effect even started, and saved pages without their tags. A plain 800 ms wait has been reliable.
  • page.content() drops tags. It silently left out some of Helmet's injected <script> tags, including JSON-LD schema. Reading document.documentElement.outerHTML gets everything.
  • Write the homepage last. The preview server falls back to index.html for any route without a file yet. Overwrite it early, and later pages without their own SEO head inherit the homepage's canonical URL and FAQ schema.
  • Flat files, not folders. dist/templates/index.html makes Netlify 301-redirect /templates to /templates/, which then disagrees with the canonical tag. dist/templates.html serves at the exact sitemap URL.

The gotcha: two sets of OG tags, and the wrong one wins

Prerendering worked. View-source showed real content. Then I looked closer at the <head> and found every page carried two og:title tags: the homepage's, and its own.

The cause was in index.html. Like most SPAs, mine had a static block of social tags so that something showed up when people shared links:

<!-- Open Graph / Social sharing -->
<meta property="og:type" content="website" />
<meta property="og:title" content="ResumeOrbitz - Build a Resume That Gets You Hired" />
<meta property="og:description" content="Create a professional, ATS-friendly resume..." />

React-helmet doesn't replace those tags. It adds its own per-page tags further down the <head>. So every prerendered page ended up with two og:title tags: the generic one first, the correct one second.

Browsers don't care. Link-preview bots do, and many of them simply take the first tag they find. Left alone, every page on my site would have told LinkedIn it was the homepage.

The fix: strip the static OG and Twitter tags during prerendering, once Helmet's per-page tags are in place. The template keeps its defaults for the non-prerendered fallback, but every prerendered page has exactly one set of tags: its own.

await page.evaluate(() => {
  document
    .querySelectorAll(
      'meta[name="description"]:not([data-rh]), ' +
      'meta[property^="og:"]:not([data-rh]), ' +
      'meta[name^="twitter:"]:not([data-rh])'
    )
    .forEach((el) => el.remove());
});

Helmet marks every tag it adds with data-rh, so anything without it is a static leftover. app-shell.html keeps its defaults because it's copied before this runs.

If you view-source a ResumeOrbitz page today, you can still see where the bug was. The <!-- Open Graph --> and <!-- Twitter Card --> comments are there, with nothing underneath, and the real tags sit lower down, marked data-rh="true".

Check your own site in 2 minutes

You don't need any tools beyond a terminal:

# 1. Does the raw HTML have real content, or an empty root?
curl -s https://yoursite.com/some-page | grep -o '<h1[^>]*>[^<]*'

# 2. How many og:title tags does the page ship? It should be exactly 1.
curl -s https://yoursite.com/some-page | grep -c 'property="og:title"'

Then paste a URL into LinkedIn's Post Inspector. It shows exactly what LinkedIn's bot reads, and refreshes its cached preview while it's at it.

If check 2 returns 2, you have the same bug I had.

What I'd tell past me

If you're starting a content-heavy React app today, pick a framework with SSR or static generation from day one. If you're already deep into a Vite SPA like I was, a prerender script is a good middle path: one file, no rewrite.

Just check your <head> after you do it. The page can look perfect in the browser while every share bot reads the wrong tags.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of ResumeOrbitz, the site used as the example here.

Over to you: did you go SSR or prerender for your React app? And did the OG tags bite you too?

title: I changed the rows. PostgreSQL's statistics still remembered them.
description:
The table had zero canary rows. Its planner statistics still named the canary.

That is the result of a small PostgreSQL test I built after reading the Anonymizer 3.3 security release. The release describes several fixes, including an issue involving authentic values left in statistics after static masking.[1] I wanted to make the underlying metadata surface visible without pretending to reproduce the extension's vulnerability.

So I used plain PostgreSQL 16.11, a disposable cluster and 100 synthetic rows. No extension. No real personal data. Just a deliberately memorable string: SYNTHETIC_CANARY.

After UPDATE, the current table returned zero matches for that string. pg_stats.most_common_vals still included it. After ANALYZE, that field described the replacement value instead. 🐤

Original figure from the executed synthetic example. This demonstrates ordinary statistics refresh behavior, not an Anonymizer CVE reproduction or secure erasure.

Put a recognizable value in the room

I made the canary common enough to appear in the most-common-values list: 80 rows contained it and 20 contained ordinary.

Run the following only in a new disposable database you own. The table name must be unused. It intentionally disables autovacuum for this one teaching table so automatic statistics refresh does not race the observation; that setting is not a production recommendation.

CREATE TABLE canary_demo (label text)
WITH (autovacuum_enabled = false);

INSERT INTO canary_demo
SELECT CASE WHEN i <= 80
            THEN 'SYNTHETIC_CANARY'
            ELSE 'ordinary' END
FROM generate_series(1,100) AS s(i);

ANALYZE canary_demo;

Here is the inspection query, repeated at each stage:

SELECT most_common_vals::text, most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats
WHERE schemaname = 'public'
  AND tablename = 'canary_demo'
  AND attname = 'label';

Its first result:

most_common_vals             | most_common_freqs
{SYNTHETIC_CANARY,ordinary}   | {0.8,0.2}

Those are actual values, accompanied by their observed frequencies in this tiny example. “Statistics” does not mean the field can contain only an aggregate such as a count. The documented view includes most-common values and can also include histogram boundaries.[2]

Change every row, then ask two different questions

Next I replaced every label:

UPDATE canary_demo SET label = 'masked';

SELECT count(*)
FROM canary_demo
WHERE label = 'SYNTHETIC_CANARY';

The count was 0. Repeating the statistics query still returned:

{SYNTHETIC_CANARY,ordinary}|{0.8,0.2}

Both answers can be true. The row query asks about visible table contents. The statistics query asks about a stored description collected earlier.

That distinction is the entire trap. Checking only the transformed rows demonstrates the transformation's effect on those rows. It does not enumerate every representation of the old data elsewhere in the database system.

The complete SQL script includes the stage labels and both inspections. With psql connected to your own disposable database, it can be run as:

psql -X -A -F '|' -f demo.sql

The script sets ON_ERROR_STOP, so an error stops execution rather than letting later output look like a successful sequence. It creates its table directly and leaves it available for inspection in your disposable database. Do not point it at a shared application database.

Refresh the description

Finally:

ANALYZE canary_demo;

The statistics query then returned:

{masked}|{1}

ANALYZE collects planner statistics from table contents.[3] In this example, refreshing them changed the visible most-common-values list to the replacement label. PostgreSQL normally uses automatic analyze as tables change; deliberately suppressing that for this table made the intermediate state easy to observe.

I ran the example in a separate temporary cluster with no TCP listener, then stopped and removed that cluster. The first attempt found client utilities without a matching server binary; switching to an already installed complete PostgreSQL 16.11 distribution allowed the real run to finish. There is no simulated SQL output in the figure.

Access matters as much as storage

This test inspected statistics as the database owner. It does not demonstrate an unprivileged reader bypassing permissions.

The documented pg_stats view restricts visibility according to table read permissions.[2] If a system introduces masked roles, security views or extension-managed policies, its effective access model needs its own verification. Merely observing a value as an owner is not evidence that every application role can see it.

That is one reason I am keeping the release claim and the mechanism demo separate. Anonymizer's release identifies its affected surfaces and upgrade guidance. My plain SQL test explains how an old value can remain in a statistics description; it does not validate the extension patch, determine affected installations or reproduce the reported exploit.

If you use Anonymizer, follow its release and upgrade instructions rather than treating this toy as a remediation recipe.[1][4]

What I would add to a masking check

For a controlled synthetic test, I would first identify the intended reader role and the surfaces it should be allowed to inspect. Then I would seed distinctive values and check those surfaces after transformation: the visible rows, permitted statistics, derived tables, caches and exports that actually exist in that system.

A negative row query is a useful check. It is simply narrower than a claim that the old value has disappeared everywhere.

Nor does the final ANALYZE result establish secure erasure. This example says nothing about old tuple storage, WAL, replicas, backups, logs or snapshots. Rebuilding a planner description is not a general deletion guarantee.

The smallest useful takeaway is therefore a test question: after changing the rows, which stored descriptions and downstream copies still need inspection? Here, one extra query found the gap immediately.

References and figure

  1. PostgreSQL Anonymizer 3.3 security release.
  2. PostgreSQL 16: pg_stats.
  3. PostgreSQL 16: ANALYZE.
  4. Anonymizer upgrade documentation.

SQL, synthetic data and the state diagram are original. Counts and labels come from the completed PostgreSQL run.

AI disclosure

AI was used to draft the article.

title: Role of JavaScript in Web Development
description:
JavaScript is one of the most important programming languages used in modern web development. It plays a crucial role in making websites interactive, dynamic, and user-friendly. While HTML provides the structure of a webpage and CSS handles its design and appearance, JavaScript adds functionality and enables users to interact with different website elements.


From displaying interactive menus and animations to developing complex web applications, JavaScript has become an essential technology for creating modern digital experiences.

  1. Making Websites Interactive

One of the primary roles of JavaScript is to make websites interactive. It allows developers to create elements that respond to user actions, such as clicking buttons, submitting forms, scrolling pages, and selecting options.

For example:

Displaying pop-up messages.

Creating dropdown menus.

Validating forms before submission.

Showing and hiding website content.

These features improve user engagement and make websites easier to navigate.

  1. Dynamic Content Updates

JavaScript allows developers to update website content without reloading the entire webpage. Using the Document Object Model (DOM), developers can modify HTML elements, change text, update images, and adjust styles dynamically.

For example, an e-commerce website can instantly update the shopping cart quantity when a customer adds a product.

  1. Form Validation

JavaScript helps validate user input before sending information to the server. It can check email formats, passwords, phone numbers, and mandatory fields.

This reduces unnecessary server requests and helps users correct errors immediately. However, server-side validation is also necessary for security and data accuracy.

  1. Asynchronous Communication

JavaScript supports asynchronous communication through technologies such as Fetch API and AJAX. These technologies allow websites to exchange data with servers without refreshing the entire page.

For example:

Loading new posts on social media.

Displaying live search suggestions.

Updating weather information.

Fetching product details from an online store.

This makes websites faster and provides a smoother browsing experience.

  1. Developing Modern Web Applications

JavaScript is widely used to develop complex web applications. Popular frameworks and libraries such as React.js, Angular, and Vue.js help developers build scalable, reusable, and efficient user interfaces.

These technologies are commonly used in:

E-commerce platforms.

Social networking websites.

Online banking applications.

Content management systems.

Business dashboards.

  1. Server-Side Development

JavaScript is not limited to frontend development. With Node.js, developers can also use JavaScript on the server side.

It helps build APIs, handle database operations, manage authentication, and process application requests. This allows developers to use a single programming language across both frontend and backend development.

  1. Improving User Experience

JavaScript enables features such as animations, interactive maps, sliders, real-time notifications, and multimedia controls. These functionalities make websites more engaging and improve the overall user experience.

title: How I Am Training AI Directly on Devices (Without Stealing User Data 🚀)
description:
Hey Dev.to family! Let us be real: privacy regulations are putting a massive squeeze on traditional AI architectures. If your game plan is still "just send all raw user inputs to a centralized cloud AI server," you are basically one data leak away from some heavy compliance fines. Today, we are talking about how to train models directly on your users’ devices using Next.js and secure Rust aggregators, without ever seeing their private data.

Machine learning has officially hit a regulatory wall. In 2026, pushing raw user data to centralized cloud inference servers violates stringent US data privacy laws and enterprise compliance standards. To survive in the modern ecosystem, US engineering teams are pivoting entirely to Federated Learning. The architectural paradigm has flipped. The machine learning model now travels to the data, not the other way around.

If you are building artificial intelligence products on the Next.js App Router, you can no longer pipe user inputs to a centralized Python backend. You must orchestrate local inference and distributed training directly at the edge, utilizing WebGPU in the client and memory safe Rust aggregators on your server.

How do you implement Federated Learning at the edge using Next.js?

In a federated architecture, the Next.js frontend acts as an autonomous training node. Instead of sending sensitive user metrics to the server, the browser downloads a lightweight, quantized base model. It then trains this model locally on the user's private device using WebGPU for hardware acceleration.

Only the calculated weight updates (the gradients) are sent back to your server via Next.js Server Actions. This guarantees zero knowledge of the underlying raw data.

  • Local Compute orchestration: Next.js Client Components load ONNX or WebAssembly compiled models and execute training steps utilizing the client GPU.
  • Secure Transport: React Server Components receive the encrypted gradient updates via strictly typed Zod payloads.
  • Differential Privacy: The client injects mathematical noise into the gradients before transmission to prevent reverse engineering of the local dataset.

Why are US tech giants relying on Rust for secure gradient aggregation?

When tens of thousands of Next.js clients push gradient updates simultaneously, the backend must merge these mathematical tensors without blocking the main thread or dropping data. Python is too slow and resource intensive for this scale of synchronous high frequency I/O.

Modern US engineering teams rely on Rust to handle gradient aggregation. Rust provides fearless concurrency and memory safety, allowing you to lock and update global model weights across highly concurrent distributed systems without race conditions.

Below is an architectural concept of how a Rust microservice safely aggregates incoming local gradients into a global model.

use ndarray::Array1;
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};

// 2026 FAANG Standard: Memory safe gradient aggregation in Rust
pub fn aggregate_gradients(
    global_weights: Arc<Mutex<Array1<f32>>>,
    local_gradients: Vec<Array1<f32>>,
    learning_rate: f32,
) -> Result<(), String> {
    // Acquire a safe lock on the global model parameters
    let mut weights = global_weights.lock().map_err(|_| "Mutex poisoned")?;

    for gradient in local_gradients {
        // Enforce strict dimensionality checks to prevent runtime memory panics
        if weights.len() != gradient.len() {
            return Err("Tensor dimension mismatch detected".to_string());
        }

        // Apply the distributed local gradients to the global model
        for i in 0..weights.len() {
            weights[i] -= learning_rate * gradient[i];
        }
    }

    Ok(())
}

This Rust binary runs as a high performance sidecar to your Next.js application, consuming payloads from a Redis queue and outputting a newly optimized global model every few minutes.

What is the impact of privacy first ML on US engineering salaries?

The era of the basic LLM wrapper developer is over. The 2026 US job market heavily filters out software engineers who only know how to make external API calls to OpenAI. The real capital is flowing to AI Systems Engineers.

Companies like Apple, Meta, and top tier health tech startups require engineers who can build distributed machine learning pipelines. If your portfolio demonstrates that you can orchestrate WebGPU training in Next.js and write memory safe gradient aggregators in Rust, you are bridging the rarest gap in modern tech. Hiring managers are routinely offering total compensation packages exceeding $400k for builders capable of architecting compliant, privacy preserving artificial intelligence at scale.

FAQs:

1. What is Federated Learning and why is it required in 2026?
Federated Learning is a machine learning technique where a model is trained across multiple decentralized edge devices holding local data samples, without exchanging the raw data. It is required to comply with strict US data privacy regulations and enterprise security standards.

2. How does Next.js handle local machine learning training?
Next.js acts as the client orchestration layer. It delivers quantized models to the browser and utilizes WebGPU to leverage the local machine's graphics card, executing complex matrix multiplications without relying on a cloud server.

3. Why use Rust instead of Python for backend aggregation?
When thousands of clients upload gradient updates simultaneously, the backend requires high performance concurrency. Rust provides memory safe multithreading and blazing fast execution speeds, easily outperforming Python for handling massive, parallel tensor merges.

What do you all think?

Are you exploring Federated Learning or are your datasets still firmly tied to the cloud? Have you tried offloading training steps to client-side GPUs using WebGPU in Next.js? Let us know in the comments below, and do not forget to follow for more US tech market insights!

title: Building a Reusable WebGPU & Rust Engine: Part 5 — Implementing Lighting Systems
description:
It’s time to bring depth and atmosphere into our scene through Dynamic Lighting. In a typical rendering pipeline, lighting also works closely with shadows.

The light types I am aiming for are:

  • Point Light
  • Directional Light
  • Spot Light
  • HDRI Light Analytical lights (point, directional, and spot) use uniform buffer data. In contrast, HDRI lighting is image-based (IBL) and requires a cubemap texture (texture_cube<f32>) and sampler rather than a standard uniform buffer.

Rust Implementation: lighting.rs
In lighting.rs, we create a unified structure to upload the light parameters to the GPU:

  • light_type (identifying which mode to evaluate)
  • direction
  • inner_cone and outer_cone (for spot light boundaries)
  • color, rangle, intensity (basic things about light)

Just like we did for the depth buffer and post-processing passes, we create a GPU buffer to hold the light information, construct a bind group layout and bind group, and instantiate the light controller in the scene.

WGSL Shader Computation: shader.wgsl
Next, we update the fragment shader to compute illumination based on the active light_type:

  • Directional Light->> Provides incoming light ray directions (vector L) uniformly everywhere across the scene, independent of position.
  • Point Light->> Computes the direction from the fragment's world position toward the light position (vector L). It uses an inverse-falloff calculation to dim the light over distance, using clamp to avoid infinite brightness when objects get too close.
  • Spot Light (Cone Light)->> Calculates the dot product between the light vector vector L and the negative spot direction to get the cosine of the angle. This angle is then compared against the cosine of the inner and outer cone limits to smoothly attenuate the beam.

Diffuse Shading & Material Interaction
To calculate diffuse shading, we compute the dot product between the surface normal vector and the light direction vector, clamping negative values to zero.
Finally, lighting interacts directly with materials. When returning the surface color, we combine all terms together by multiplying:
Final Color = Base Color * Light Color * Light Intensity * Diffuse * Attenuation

Image-Based Lighting (HDRI) and PBR Integration
An HDR image is loaded as an environment texture and mapped using spherical coordinates to project across the scene. However, real-time renderers do not use random sampling at runtime to compute the light. Random sampling is meant for offline path-tracers and causes heavy frame lag and noise.
Instead you prefilter once into:

  • A diffuse irradiance cubemap that supplies smooth ambient light from all directions.
  • A pre-filtered specular cubemap that stores reflections blurred across different roughness levels.

HDRI requires a Physically Based Rendering (PBR) workflow to look correct. Without physical material properties like roughness, metallic values, and viewing-angle Fresnel reflection, an HDR image merely acts as a flat ambient tint:

  • Roughness determines which blurred reflection level is sampled.
  • Fresnel calculates how reflective the surface becomes at grazing angles.
  • Metallic controls whether the surface reflects dielectric colors or tinted metallic highlights.

Floating-Point Texture Pipeline Setup
Standard textures clip brightness values at pure white (1.0). Because HDR images store illumination values far higher than 1.0, precision must be maintained throughout the pipeline:

  1. The HDR texture is uploaded using a high-precision 16-bit floating-point format (Rgba16Float).

  2. The offscreen scene texture and the 3D scene pipeline color target format are also set to Rgba16Float instead of the default window surface format. This prevents bright HDR highlights from clipping during the lighting pass.

  3. The post-processing pass reads this 16-bit floating-point scene texture, applies tone mapping to compress the high range down to displayable limits, and outputs the final color to the standard screen format.

Next PBR implementation:

  • F0 = mix(vec3(0.04), base_color.rgb, metallic)
  • Fresnel (Schlick)
  • GGX normal distribution
  • Smith geometry

Because covering the full pipeline takes significant space, we will wrap up analytical lighting and basic PBR here, and continue with Image-Based Lighting (IBL) environment integration in the next part!

Load the HDRI+PBR texture working together

title: Neon Realtime vs Supabase Realtime
description:
Neon shipped Realtime on October 15, 2026. You subscribe to a SQL query, and Neon keeps the result up to date as the data changes. Neon hasn't published latency numbers yet, so I measured it.

I compared it with polling, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and both flavors of Supabase Realtime, on 10,000 and 1,000,000 rows. Everything ran on October 28, 2026 in Frankfurt.

TL;DR

Median time from UPDATE to an up-to-date result on the client, at 10k and 1M rows:

  • Neon Realtime: 40–46 ms for filters, joins and top-10 queries. That's one network round trip from my laptop. The change usually arrived within 8 ms of the write's commit ack.
  • Supabase Broadcast: 58–60 ms on a plain filter. Joins and top-10 need a refetch, so 108–115 ms.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: 70–244 ms. Every change costs a second query.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: 328–434 ms, and 1.1 s for the aggregate at 1M rows.
  • Polling every second: 414–546 ms, change or not.
  • The large aggregate used more bandwidth. At 1M rows, Neon still had the lowest latency at 179 ms, but re-sent the full 1,000-group result: ~111 KB per change.
  • Scale-to-zero still works. The compute suspended with a subscription open and stayed suspended for the 10 minutes I watched. The subscription stayed live and got the next write.

What Neon Realtime does

Your server defines the query and seals it into a token that expires after 60 seconds. The browser subscribes with that token over a WebSocket. Neon sends the full result once, then only the changes.

// Server: the query and its parameters stay on your side
import { createRealtime, rawSql } from "@neon/realtime/server";

const realtime = createRealtime({ secret: process.env.NEON_REALTIME_SECRET, db: "neondb" });
const sealed = await realtime.seal({
  query: rawSql("SELECT id, name, score FROM players WHERE team_id = $1", [teamId]),
});
// send `sealed` to the browser

// Browser
import { createRealtimeClient } from "@neon/realtime/client";

const client = createRealtimeClient({ url: NEON_REALTIME_URL });
const subscription = client.subscribe(sealed);
subscription.onChange(({ data }) => render(data));

The client asks your server for a fresh token before the old one expires. The React bindings and QueryRefreshController do that for you.

Limits in the beta:

  • Queries: read-only and deterministic, so no now() or gen_random_uuid(). Joins, aggregates, ORDER BY … LIMIT, subqueries and window functions are supported.
  • Tables: every table needs a primary key.
  • Auth: no row-level security yet. You authorize when you seal the query.
  • Regions: four AWS regions (us-east-1, us-east-2, eu-central-1, ap-southeast-1).
  • Price: Realtime is free during the beta. Compute and egress are billed as usual.

The setup

  • Neon: 0.25 CU (1 GB RAM), Postgres 18.6, aws-eu-central-1.
  • Supabase: Nano instance (0.5 GB RAM, shared CPU), Postgres 17.11, eu-central-1.
  • Client: my laptop, about 40 ms round trip from Frankfurt. That round trip is the floor for every number below.

Both are the smallest compute on their platform. The Supabase project was on the Free plan. The Neon project sat in my Launch-plan org, but Neon's Free plan runs the same 0.25 CU with the same 5-minute scale-to-zero, and the whole benchmark used 0.43 CU-hours of the 100 a month it includes.

The Postgres versions were the defaults. Neon created the project on Postgres 18. Hosted Supabase tops out at 17.11 as of this writing.

The table is players(id, name, team_id, score) with 1,000 teams. Each write is UPDATE players SET score = $1 WHERE id = 1 over an open direct connection. Then I timed how long the subscriber took to see the new score.

Five ways to keep a query live:

  1. Neon Realtime: subscribe to the SQL query.
  2. Supabase Broadcast: a trigger calls realtime.broadcast_changes() into a private channel. Supabase recommends it "for scalability and security".
  3. LISTEN/NOTIFY on Neon: a trigger sends NOTIFY, and the app re-runs the query.
  4. Supabase Postgres Changes: subscribe to row changes on players.
  5. Polling on Neon: re-run the query every second.

The four queries:

  • Filter: the players in one team. 10 rows at 10k, 1,000 rows at 1M.
  • Join: the same players joined with teams.
  • Aggregate: player count and top score for every team (1,000 groups).
  • Top 10: the 10 highest scores across all players.

With both Supabase methods, the client applies the changed row itself for the filter. A change event alone can't update a join, an aggregate or a top 10, so for those the client refetches the query over the REST API.

How I measured
  • One Node process runs the writer and the subscriber, so both timestamps come from the same clock.
  • Write to screen is the time from sending the UPDATE until the subscriber's copy of the result contains the new score. It includes any refetch the method needs.
  • 5 warm-up writes, then 100 writes per cell with a random 250–750 ms gap. Timeout 10 s. Nothing timed out.
  • The Supabase refetches query views through supabase-js, with RLS on and a public read policy.
  • Bytes per change are the WebSocket bytes received plus the size of any refetched result.
  • One writer, one subscriber. I didn't test fan-out to many subscribers.

Write to screen

The differences come down to how many trips a change takes to reach the screen:

  • Neon Realtime: the change arrived between 2 ms before and 8 ms after the writer got its commit ack. So it's as fast as the network allows. The exception is the aggregate at 1M rows (next section).
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: the notification arrives about as fast as Realtime, then the query runs a second time. At 1M rows the filter returns 1,000 rows (64 KB), so it climbs to 159 ms.
  • Supabase Broadcast: the event arrived ~57 ms after the write in every cell. The REST refetch added 50–70 ms, and ~740 ms for the aggregate at 1M rows.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: the event alone took 315–384 ms. Supabase's docs say it processes changes on a single thread and checks RLS for every subscriber, and that it "does not scale as well" as Broadcast.
  • Polling: on average you wait half the interval, plus the query. It also runs 86,400 queries a day per client, even when nothing changes.

Getting the first result after subscribing took 0.4–0.8 s on Neon Realtime and 0.8–1.4 s on Supabase Broadcast, including the WebSocket handshake.

At 1–2 writes a second, the write itself took ~40 ms with every method. A live query didn't slow down the writer.

p50 / p95 tables (ms)
10,000 rows
Method Filter Join Aggregate Top 10
Neon Realtime 40 / 56 40 / 48 44 / 51 42 / 123
Supabase Broadcast 58 / 62 110 / 122 125 / 196 108 / 125
LISTEN/NOTIFY 84 / 90 83 / 87 128 / 207 85 / 315
Supabase Postgres Changes 371 / 569 397 / 619 418 / 642 368 / 615
Polling every 1 s 484 / 724 534 / 731 546 / 700 498 / 708

1,000,000 rows

Method Filter Join Aggregate Top 10
Neon Realtime 44 / 52 41 / 54 179 / 191 46 / 74
Supabase Broadcast 60 / 249 115 / 132 793 / 856 110 / 121
LISTEN/NOTIFY 159 / 176 145 / 155 244 / 269 70 / 74
Supabase Postgres Changes 328 / 540 418 / 626 1129 / 1293 434 / 633
Polling every 1 s 542 / 723 495 / 740 517 / 732 414 / 709

Bytes per change

For filters and joins, Neon sends only the changed row, ~0.4 KB per change, whatever the table size. A refetch downloads the whole result again: 64–73 KB per change at 1M rows.

The large aggregate exposes Neon's bandwidth tradeoff. At 10k rows, each change arrived as a ~0.4 KB delta. At 1M rows the engine switched to re-sending the full 1,000-group result: ~111 KB and 179 ms per change. That's more than twice the data transferred by a refetch. Neon's docs warn that "complex queries add write-processing latency, especially on larger datasets."

Top 10 re-sends the full result on every change too, but that's only 1.8 KB.

Supabase's aggregate refetch took ~740 ms after the event at 1M rows. Part of that is the Nano instance: the same query took ~200 ms on Neon's 0.25 CU. Bigger Supabase compute would help.

Scale to zero

Neon suspends a compute after 5 minutes without queries. I opened a Realtime subscription while the compute was suspended, then left it alone (twice). For comparison, I did the same with a plain LISTEN connection.

  • The subscription woke the compute: first result in 1.3–2.5 s.
  • The compute suspended anyway, 5.3–5.4 minutes later, with the subscription open.
  • It stayed suspended. In the second run I watched for 10 more minutes. The compute never woke, though the subscription's token renewed every minute.
  • The subscription stayed live. A write to the sleeping database woke it (ack in 917–965 ms, most of it connecting), and the subscriber had the change 9–48 ms after the ack.
  • LISTEN didn't block suspension either, but Neon terminated the connection after 5 min 18 s (57P01). The registration is gone, notifications sent before you reconnect are lost, and reconnecting wakes the compute again.

So an open dashboard tab doesn't keep the database billing. Polling does, because it never stops querying.

Caveats

  • One subscriber and one writer at 1–2 writes a second. Fan-out and heavy write load are untested.
  • Every number includes a ~40 ms round trip from my laptop. A server in the same region would see lower numbers everywhere.
  • Supabase's Nano has half the RAM of Neon's 0.25 CU and a shared CPU. That affects refetch-heavy cells, not event delivery.
  • Neon Realtime is a beta. Neon says the protocol isn't stable yet.
  • One run per configuration, on one day.

Which one should you use?

  • Neon Realtime: live results of real queries (lists, joins, leaderboards, per-user views) on Neon. Watch large aggregates, and authorize at seal time until RLS lands.
  • Supabase Broadcast: you're on Supabase and the client can apply the changed row itself.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: any Postgres, a small result, and you're fine with a refetch per change. On Neon, reconnect after the compute suspends.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: prototypes. Supabase itself points you to Broadcast.
  • Polling: when a few seconds of delay is fine and the database is awake anyway.

Sources

Checked October 28, 2026.

  • Neon: Realtime launch, overview, how it works, queries, subscribing, compute lifecycle, LISTEN/NOTIFY guide
  • Supabase: subscribing to database changes, Postgres Changes, changelog
  • Charts: rendered from the raw results with Pele

title: Smell-checking AI-suggested React hooks before you merge
description:
AI is weirdly confident about React hooks. Ask for “extract the data fetching into a custom hook” and you’ll get something that looks idiomatic: useSomething, a useEffect, a couple of useMemos, maybe a useCallback for good measure. Types pass. The demo works once. Then you merge and discover the effect fires twice on every keystroke, or the cleanup never ran, or the hook is just a wrapper around three lines that didn’t need a name.

I treat AI-suggested hooks like AI-suggested refactors: useful drafts, not mergeable by default. Here’s the smell checklist I run before I accept the branch.

Smell 1: useEffect dependency lies

The model loves this pattern:

useEffect(() => {
  fetchUser(userId).then(setUser);
}, []); // "run once on mount"

Except userId changed three routes ago, and the effect still holds the first id. Or the opposite lie:

useEffect(() => {
  analytics.track("view", { id: item.id });
}, [item]); // object identity thrash

Every parent re-render invents a new item object, so “track once” becomes “track forever.”

What I check: for every useEffect, I ask “what should actually retrigger this?” If the answer is “once,” I want an explicit id/primitive in the deps, or an abortable fetch keyed by that id — not an empty array with a closed-over value. If the answer is “when X changes,” I want X to be a stable primitive or a memoized value I trust, not a fresh object from JSX.

Smell 2: unstable callbacks as dependencies

Classic AI move: wrap a handler in useCallback, then put that callback in another hook’s deps… while the callback itself depends on props that change every render.

const onSave = useCallback(() => {
  save(formState);
}, [formState]); // formState changes constantly

useEffect(() => {
  window.addEventListener("keydown", onSave);
  return () => window.removeEventListener("keydown", onSave);
}, [onSave]); // rebinds every keystroke of formState

useCallback didn’t stabilize anything. It just moved the thrash one layer down.

What I check: if a callback is only a dep because another effect needs it, I prefer reading the latest value from a ref, or narrowing the callback’s deps to the primitives it actually needs. “Add useCallback” is not a fix by itself.

Smell 3: derived state stuffed into useState

The agent sees fullName used in three places and invents:

const [fullName, setFullName] = useState("");
useEffect(() => {
  setFullName(`${first} ${last}`);
}, [first, last]);

That’s derived data. It doesn’t need state. It needs:

const fullName = `${first} ${last}`;

Or a useMemo if the derivation is actually expensive (it almost never is for string concat).

What I check: any useState + useEffect pair that only syncs from other props/state is guilty until proven otherwise. AI does this a lot because “state” feels like the React vocabulary for “a value I can name.”

Smell 4: missing cleanup (or fake cleanup)

Fetch-in-effect without abort. Subscriptions without unsubscribe. setTimeout without clear. The demo looks fine because you never navigate away mid-request.

useEffect(() => {
  let cancelled = false;
  load(id).then((data) => {
    if (!cancelled) setData(data);
  });
  return () => {
    cancelled = true;
  };
}, [id]);

That’s the minimum. Better: AbortController so the network work actually stops. AI often ships the happy path only.

What I check: every effect that starts async work, timers, or listeners must have a cleanup that matches. I also watch for “cleanup” that only sets a flag but still lets expensive work continue — fine for setState races, not fine for upload loops.

Smell 5: over-abstraction into useX

Not every three lines deserve a hook.

function useIsOpen(initial = false) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(initial);
  return { open, open: () => setOpen(true), close: () => setOpen(false) };
}

Cute. Also a digression in code review. Custom hooks earn their name when they encapsulate a non-obvious contract: syncing with a store, coordinating multiple effects, sharing behavior across distant components. “Boolean with open/close” is just state.

What I check: would I explain this hook in a PR description without sounding silly? If the hook exists only so the component file is shorter, I inline it. AI loves extracting; I love deleting.

Smell 6: stale closures dressed as “helpers” 

function useSearch(items: Item[]) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const filter = () => items.filter((i) => i.name.includes(query));
  return { query, setQuery, results: filter() };
}

Looks fine until filter gets passed to a child as a callback and the child memoizes it, or until someone moves filter into a useEffect with []. Closures over items and query go stale in ways that are hard to see in a generated diff.

What I check: values computed from props/state should either be plain expressions in render, or memoized with the right deps — not casually closed over inside nested functions the agent plans to “reuse.”

Smell 7: “just add another useMemo”

When something re-renders too often, the model’s first instinct is memoization:

const sorted = useMemo(() => [...items].sort(byName), [items]);
const visible = useMemo(() => sorted.filter(isVisible), [sorted, isVisible]);
const rows = useMemo(() => visible.map(toRow), [visible]);

Three memos, still thrashing if items is a new array every parent render. Memo is a tax you pay after you’ve fixed identity and state shape — not a perfume you spray on the smell.

What I check: before accepting a memo, I ask what identity is unstable upstream. Fix that first. Keep useMemo for real work (big lists, expensive pure transforms), not for obj.a + obj.b.

Smell 8: hooks that hide side effects

The scariest AI hooks look pure in the name and impure in the body:

function useCartTotal(cart: Cart) {
  useEffect(() => {
    localStorage.setItem("cart-total", String(cart.total));
  }, [cart.total]);
  return cart.lines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.price, 0);
}

Callers think they’re reading a number. They’re also writing storage. Side effects buried in “getter” hooks are how you get “why did navigating to settings clear my draft?” bugs.

What I check: naming. useX that returns data should not silently write, fetch, or mutate globals. If it does I/O, the name should say so (usePersistCartTotal) and the call site should look intentional.

My merge gate (short version)

Before I merge an AI-touched hook, I want yes on all of these:

  1. Deps match the real trigger (no empty-array lies, no object thrash)
  2. No useState for values that are pure derivations
  3. Async / listeners / timers have matching cleanup
  4. The hook earns its name (shared or non-obvious contract)
  5. No drive-by useMemo / useCallback pile-on
  6. Side effects are obvious from the name and the call site

If two or more fail, I don’t “tweak the hook.” I ask the agent for a smaller change: inline the logic, or rewrite the effect with an explicit contract in the prompt.

Prompt that produces fewer smelly hooks

When I do want a custom hook from the model, I fence it:

Extract a hook only if the behavior is reused or the effect graph is non-trivial.

Prefer derived values over syncing state in effects.

Every useEffect must list real deps and a cleanup.

Do not add useMemo/useCallback unless you can point to a measured or structural reason.

No hidden I/O in hooks named like getters.

That doesn’t make the model perfect. It makes the first draft close enough that the smell checklist is a quick pass instead of a rewrite.

Hooks are easy to generate and expensive to debug after merge. Five minutes of smell-checking beats an afternoon of “why does this fire twice in Strict Mode only on the settings page.”

title: React: carga rápida sin saltos ni confusión
description:
Un estado de carga parece una pieza pequeña de la interfaz. Sin embargo, decide si una persona entiende lo que ocurre o pulsa el botón varias veces. En un formulario de registro, por ejemplo, la espera puede incluir una petición, una validación y la llegada de un email. Si cada paso cambia el layout, el producto se siente lento aunque la red no sea el principal problema.

Mi regla práctica es esta: una carga debe conservar el espacio, explicar el siguiente paso y tener una salida clara si algo falla. No hace falta una animación espectacular. Hace falta que el diseño, React y la accesibilidad cuenten la misma historia.

El problema no es esperar, es no entender la espera

Un patrón bastante común muestra un spinner después de pulsar “Continuar”. El botón desaparece, aparece un texto debajo y, unos milisegundos después, todo vuelve a su sitio. Ese salto visual aumenta la sensación de inestabilidad y puede hacer que alguien pulse otra vez.

También hay otro fallo: usar el mismo estado para “estamos comprobando”, “se envió el email” y “no pudimos completar la acción”. Son situaciones diferentes. El usuario necesita saber si debe esperar, revisar su bandeja o corregir un dato.

En flujos de QA aparecen búsquedas como tempmailso, temp mail so y hasta el typo tempail. No son estados de la interfaz, claro, pero sirven para recordar que la parte de email tiene varios pasos. El frontend no debería presentar todos como un simple “cargando”.

Un estado de carga que conserva el layout

Primero defino un contrato pequeño para el componente:

  • idle: el formulario acepta interacción.
  • loading: la petición está en curso y la acción se puede bloquear.
  • success: la operación terminó y se explica qué hacer ahora.
  • error: hay un mensaje útil y una acción para intentarlo de nuevo.

El espacio reservado es importante. En vez de insertar un aviso que empuja el formulario, dejo un contenedor con una altura mínima. Así, el botón y los campos no bailan cuando cambia el mensaje. Es una decisión de CSS, pero mejora el rendimiento percibido sin fingir que la operación terminó antes.

Un componente sencillo puede ser suficiente:

type Status = "idle" | "loading" | "success" | "error";

type StatusMessageProps = {
  status: Status;
  message?: string;
};

export function StatusMessage({ status, message }: StatusMessageProps) {
  if (status === "idle") return <div className="status-space" aria-hidden="true" />;

  return (
    <p
      className={`status status--${status}`}
      role={status === "error" ? "alert" : "status"}
      aria-live={status === "error" ? "assertive" : "polite"}
    >
      {message}
    </p>
  );
}

El estado idle conserva el hueco, mientras que los demás estados ofrecen información. En una aplicación real, evitaría que message sea una cadena genérica como “Error”. El texto debería decir qué pasó y cuál es la siguiente acción, por ejemplo: “No recibimos respuesta. Intenta de nuevo en unos segundos”.

React y CSS para feedback accesible

El atributo aria-busy puede indicar que una región está siendo actualizada. No lo pondría en toda la página: prefiero aplicarlo al bloque que realmente cambia.

<section aria-busy={status === "loading"} aria-labelledby="signup-title">
  <h2 id="signup-title">Crear cuenta</h2>
  <EmailForm disabled={status === "loading"} />
  <StatusMessage status={status} message={message} />
</section>

Para el estilo, una reserva mínima y una animación discreta suelen bastar:

.status-space {
  min-block-size: 2.75rem;
}

.status {
  min-block-size: 2.75rem;
  margin-block: 0.75rem 0;
  padding: 0.65rem 0.8rem;
  border-radius: 0.4rem;
}

.status--loading {
  color: #394150;
  background: #f1f4f8;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .status {
    animation: none;
  }
}

Hay un detalle que se olvida facil: el contraste y el foco. Un color amarillo claro puede verse “amable” en el diseño, pero no comunica nada si el texto se pierde. También conviene revisar el flujo con teclado y con un lector de pantalla; el spinner por si solo no explica el progreso.

Cuando el proceso depende de varios eventos, una evidencia separada ayuda al equipo. Por ejemplo, puedes guardar un recibo de email para pruebas automatizadas y conectar ese resultado con el estado visible. Si el backend necesita aislamiento entre entornos, revisa también el patrón de emails aislados por rama de desarrollo.

Medir la experiencia sin inventar precisión

No mediría solo el tiempo hasta que desaparece el spinner. Una vista más util es registrar:

  1. cuánto tarda en aparecer el primer feedback;
  2. cuánto tiempo permanece cada estado;
  3. cuántas veces se repite la acción;
  4. cuántos errores terminan en reintento o abandono.

Estas señales ayudan a separar un problema de backend de uno de comunicación. Si la respuesta llega rapido pero muchas personas repiten el clic, quizá el botón no muestra suficiente confirmación. Si el estado de error aparece sin una acción clara, el tiempo de red no cuenta toda la historia.

Checklist antes de publicar

  • ¿El layout conserva el espacio durante la carga?
  • ¿El botón tiene foco y queda deshabilitado solo cuando corresponde?
  • ¿El mensaje diferencia espera, éxito y error?
  • ¿Un lector de pantalla recibe el cambio sin demasiados anuncios?
  • ¿La interfaz funciona con teclado y con prefers-reduced-motion?
  • ¿El test cubre una respuesta lenta y un reintento?

Q&A rápido

¿Siempre necesito un skeleton?

No. Un skeleton funciona cuando conoces la forma del contenido que llegará. Para una acción breve, un mensaje estable y un botón con estado claro suele ser más honesto.

¿Debo mostrar porcentaje de progreso?

Solo si puedes calcularlo de forma fiable. Un porcentaje inventado crea más dudas. Para una petición de email, “Comprobando el envío” puede ser mejor que avanzar de 10% a 90% sin evidencia.

¿Qué aporta CSS al rendimiento?

No reduce por sí solo el tiempo del servidor, pero puede evitar saltos, repintados innecesarios y confusión. Esa combinación hace que la interfaz parezca más rapida y, sobre todo, sea más entendible.
