title: The GBase Database Reliability Blueprint: Integrating Deployment, Development, and Performance Governance
description:
Enterprise database reliability cannot be achieved through a single installation procedure or monitoring command. It emerges from the coordination of deployment quality, architectural design, SQL development, operational diagnostics, and controlled change management.

GBase Database teams can use a unified reliability framework to connect these disciplines.

1. Establish deployment integrity

A reliable environment begins with verified software packages, compatible operating systems, valid licenses, and controlled installation procedures.

uname -m
df -h
sha256sum gbase-installer-package.tar.gz

The checksum should be compared with the trusted value supplied for the official package.

2. Design the right architecture

For distributed deployments, document node responsibilities, communication paths, storage requirements, and failure scenarios before installation.

Avoid copying a topology from another environment without confirming product version, workload, and supported architecture.

3. Develop SQL for predictable behavior

Production SQL should be readable, parameterized, and tested against realistic data volumes.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM customer_orders
WHERE created_at >= DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id;

Validate date syntax and supported functions against the target GBase product and release.

4. Make diagnostics part of daily operations

Use product-specific tools to establish health baselines.

For GBase 8s:

onstat -

For supported GBase 8a cluster deployments:

gcadmin showcluster

Combine database-level diagnostics with operating-system metrics and application monitoring.

5. Govern operational changes

Changes to SQL, configuration, node roles, and cluster modes should follow a documented process:

  • Record the current state.
  • Assess business and technical impact.
  • Test in a representative environment.
  • Obtain required approval.
  • Execute during an appropriate window.
  • Verify the outcome.
  • Preserve the change record.

6. Measure reliability continuously

A practical reliability scorecard can include:

Dimension Example indicator
Availability Service uptime and connection success
Performance Query latency and throughput
Capacity Storage and resource utilization
Integrity Constraint and validation failures
Recovery Tested recovery objectives
Change quality Failed changes and rollback frequency

Metrics should be defined consistently and interpreted in the context of application service requirements.

Conclusion

The GBase Database reliability blueprint connects deployment integrity, distributed architecture, SQL quality, operational diagnostics, and change governance into one lifecycle. This integrated approach helps organizations move beyond successful installation toward databases that are measurable, maintainable, and ready for enterprise workloads.

title: GBase Database Change Management: Controlling Configuration, SQL, and Cluster Operations
description:
Database changes are unavoidable as applications evolve. However, uncontrolled changes to SQL, installation settings, licenses, or cluster operating modes can introduce risks that are difficult to diagnose.

A formal change-management process helps GBase Database teams balance delivery speed with operational stability.

1. Classify database changes

Different changes require different levels of review.

Change category Example
Installation Package or release upgrade
Configuration Instance or resource settings
SQL Schema and query modifications
Security Account or permission changes
Cluster Node maintenance or mode transition
Infrastructure Storage and network modifications

2. Establish a pre-change baseline

Before executing a change, record the current state.

For GBase 8s, an instance status snapshot may include:

onstat -

For a supported GBase 8a cluster, administrators may inspect:

gcadmin showcluster

The relevant commands depend on the product being operated.

3. Define the change record

Every production change should include:

  • Business reason.
  • Technical scope.
  • Target GBase product and version.
  • Expected impact.
  • Execution procedure.
  • Validation steps.
  • Rollback or recovery plan.
  • Responsible approver and operator.

4. Validate SQL changes

A schema modification should be tested with representative application operations.

For example:

ALTER TABLE customer_profile
ADD COLUMN account_status VARCHAR(20);

Before deploying a change like this, verify syntax and compatibility for the target GBase product. Also assess application dependencies, existing data, locking behavior, and migration duration.

5. Verify after execution

Do not close a change merely because the command completed.

Check:

  1. The database remains available.
  2. The intended schema or configuration is present.
  3. Application transactions work correctly.
  4. Performance remains within expected limits.
  5. Logs contain no unexpected errors.
  6. Monitoring reflects the expected state.

Conclusion

Disciplined change management protects GBase Database environments from avoidable operational disruption. Baselines, approvals, controlled execution, and post-change validation make database changes more transparent and easier to audit.

title: Delete Confirmation Dialogs: Show the Exit Path in Your Public SaaS Demo
description:
A useful public demo of a delete confirmation dialog should show which item will be affected, what deletion means, and how someone leaves without deleting anything. Record the safe exit as well as the final action. A screenshot of a red button cannot show whether backing out preserves the work or whether the interface tells the truth about recovery.

For a developer building a SaaS in public, this gives founder peers a concrete interaction to review. It also exposes questions that belong in implementation checks rather than a discussion about button color. Use prepared data and a suitable test environment for the demonstration.

The project-deletion flow below is fictional. It is a review method, not a report of testing an actual product. No action in a demo should affect real customer work, and a simulated result should be labelled as simulated.

Define exactly what the delete action affects

Imagine a small planning app with projects and tasks. Its current design allows the owner to delete a project. Before asking anyone to review the dialog, the developer needs to know whether this also removes tasks, attachments, shared access, or references elsewhere in the app.

Write that behavior in ordinary language. If the implementation archives a project and permits restoration, describe that behavior. If it permanently removes the project, do not borrow reassuring language from an archive flow.

The interface and the underlying behavior must agree. A dialog that says “Remove from this view” creates a different expectation from one that says “Delete this project and its tasks.” Changing the label alone cannot resolve an uncertain backend operation.

Keep the review scoped to one action. Deleting a task, leaving a shared project, and deleting a whole workspace can have different consequences. A public demo becomes hard to assess when it switches between those operations without explaining the difference.

Start the recording before the dialog opens

Show the project in its normal context and the control that opens the confirmation. A viewer should be able to tell which project the action concerns before reading the dialog.

In the fictional app, use a prepared project with a neutral name and sample tasks. Say that the data is prepared for the demo. Don't include real project names or customer material merely to make the recording look realistic.

Open the dialog and pause long enough for someone to read it. Avoid editing out the transition if that hides where focus goes or makes it unclear whether the dialog has already performed the action.

Ask a reviewer what they think has happened so far. They may interpret opening the dialog as the deletion itself, especially if the background item disappears early. That is a specific point to investigate rather than a general verdict on whether the design looks modern.

Make the target and consequence visible together

A generic “Are you sure?” prompt asks the person to remember the action and its scope. In the example, the dialog can name the prepared project and explain the actual consequence beside the final button.

Use only information the application can support. If the dialog displays a task count, check that the count refers to the affected tasks under the current conditions. A convincing number that is stale or calculated from another scope can make the prompt less trustworthy.

Don't add a list of alarming consequences simply to make the interaction feel serious. Name the consequences that actually apply. The point is to help someone decide, not to create a dramatic warning around every small action.

A peer review question can be direct: “Which item do you think will be removed, and what else do you expect to happen?” The answer reveals the viewer's interpretation before you explain the intended one.

Record the path that keeps the project intact

First demonstrate backing out. Use the non-destructive control, then show the original project and its tasks still present. If the interface offers more than one way to dismiss the dialog, inspect those paths separately.

The label for leaving should fit the operation. A dialog about cancelling a scheduled job can make “Cancel” ambiguous. In your own flow, check whether a reader can distinguish cancelling the dialog from performing the action described in it.

A visible return to the project is stronger evidence for this one path than simply closing the modal. It still does not prove that every dismissal path is safe. Keyboard input, clicking outside, navigation, or a connection problem may exercise different behavior.

Keep those unresolved paths in the review notes. Public feedback can help identify the questions; implementation checks establish what the actual system does. Do not describe an untested path as safe because the main recording ended well.

Review keyboard and assistive-technology behavior separately

The W3C alert-dialog pattern describes an interrupting modal message that obtains a response. It explains the role, label and description relationships, and warns that marking a dialog modal must match how it actually behaves.

This guidance is useful when reviewing a confirmation, but a video of the screen cannot establish that its semantics work. Inspect the dialog's accessible name and description, focus behavior, available controls, and the return from dismissal in the actual implementation.

Use the appropriate dialog pattern for the interaction rather than adding an alert role for emphasis. A semantic label is not decoration. It communicates behavior to software and people using assistive technology.

Report the checks you performed and the ones you did not. A short public clip may show a keyboard path while leaving screen-reader behavior for a separate check. That is a useful bounded artifact without claiming that the whole application meets an accessibility standard.

Show completion without implying an undo that does not exist

Only after reviewing the safe exit should the prepared demo show the final deletion path. Reopen the dialog for the same prepared project, confirm the action, and show the resulting state.

If the system supports restoration, demonstrate the actual supported restoration route in another bounded sequence. If it does not, say that clearly. Do not put an “Undo” control into a mockup and present it as proof that recovery works.

Check what a person sees if completion is uncertain. A slow response, repeated click, or stale list can leave the interface out of step with the operation. Those questions may need a separate test rather than a longer public recording of the happy path.

The completion message should describe the operation you can verify. A disappearing card alone does not tell you whether related data was removed, access changed, or the backend accepted the action exactly once.

Ask peers one question about the decision

Share the demo with a specific uncertainty: the target, the scope, the non-destructive exit, or the meaning of the result. Asking “Any thoughts?” invites people to review a different problem from the one you need to resolve.

Buildside is the community context here. Uriel Bitton builds and runs Buildside, which is this article's publisher relationship. Wherever you request feedback, give peers enough task context to judge the interaction without assuming they know the implementation.

A peer may understand the dialog perfectly and still lack the customer's workflow. Another may point out a risk you had not considered. Treat each response as a scoped observation or suggestion, then decide which question needs further evidence.

Don't turn agreement about the wording into proof that accidental deletion will never occur. Clear communication and reliable behavior are both part of the interaction, and each needs appropriate checks.

Keep a review record that survives the next redesign

Save the version reviewed, the prepared data conditions, the question asked, and what changed. Attach the relevant recording or screenshots to your own development notes so a later visual redesign does not lose the reasoning.

For the fictional project flow, the record might say that the dialog now names the project and that the recorded safe exit returns to the intact task list. It should separately list any unresolved recovery or keyboard question.

A follow-up build-in-public update can show the specific revision and the behavior verified. Avoid claiming a drop in user mistakes unless you have measured that outcome under a suitable method.

The useful public artifact shows a real choice with an understandable consequence and exit. That gives other founders a precise way to help and gives the developer a concrete interaction to revisit as the product changes.

title: Why Netflix Won't Write to Two Databases at Once: Change Data Capture Explained
description:
Zero results. Ana, a production coordinator at Netflix Studios, saved a new film called Night Train a minute ago, and search can't find it. The movie database has it. The search index has never heard of it.

Ana is our example, but the gap is one Netflix's engineers wrote about. Most engineers reach for the obvious cure: when you save the film, write it to both places. That cure is exactly how this happens. Netflix's engineers wrote down why it fails, and then they turned down the textbook answer too: one transaction across both databases.

So how do you keep two databases in agreement, when you can't write to both at once? The animated version:

The second write fails

Ana's film is one row, film 8812, in MySQL, the database that owns the truth. Search runs on a second store, Elasticsearch. Netflix's engineers call the store that owns the truth the primary store, and a search index like this a derived store.

The obvious code does a dual write: save the row to MySQL, then send the same film to Elasticsearch.

  • The second write can fail: a timeout, a deploy, a node restarting. MySQL says Night Train exists, search says it doesn't, and nothing notices.
  • Flip the order and you get the opposite bug: search shows a film the database never saved.
  • Even when both writes succeed, two editors renaming the film at the same moment can land in a different order in each store. Now they disagree for good.

The repair job becomes the system

So teams add a repair job that re-reads the database and patches search. Netflix's engineers list the costs: custom work nobody can reuse, stores wrong until it runs, and load on the primary. Netflix's movie search team lived a version of this, polling other services for changes on a timer even when nothing had changed; Netflix says it quickly grew very complex and hard to maintain.

The real problem fits in one sentence: no single write can land in two different databases at once.

The textbook cure doesn't fit

The textbook answer is a distributed transaction: one commit that lands in every store, or in none. The common standard is XA: each store first promises it can commit, and only then does anyone commit.

But if the app dies between the promise and the commit, the stores are left waiting; Netflix's post points out that XA blocks in exactly that case. And Elasticsearch doesn't support XA, or any transaction that spans different kinds of store. A transaction across two stores is only as strong as the weaker one.

The outbox: one database, one transaction

What if the whole transaction stayed inside one database? Add a second table to MySQL, a change log, and write to it in the same transaction as the film. Night Train's row and a note saying "film 8812 was created" commit together or not at all. A worker polls the table, sends each note to Elasticsearch, and removes it once every store has it.

This is the outbox pattern, and it works: if the worker crashes, the note simply waits. But Netflix runs services in many languages, and every one would need the same outbox library behaving the same way. And MySQL can't put a schema change, like adding a column, inside a transaction.

Read the database's own diary

Every serious database already keeps a change log. MySQL keeps one called the binlog, for its replicas; Postgres has its write-ahead log. Read through the replication interface, every committed insert, update and delete comes out, in commit order.

Change data capture (CDC) means reading that log and turning every committed change into an event. Ana's save becomes one event: create, film 8812, Night Train. Her app now writes to MySQL, and only MySQL. A rolled-back transaction is never a committed change, so search can't show a film that was never saved.

Netflix's Delta pipeline

Netflix built this as a platform called Delta:

  1. The Delta-Connector reads MySQL's log in real time.
  2. Each change goes onto a Kafka topic in Keystone, Netflix's streaming platform.
  3. A Delta application on Apache Flink picks up the event and enriches it by calling the deal, talent and vendor services.
  4. The finished document lands in Elasticsearch. Netflix describes the whole trip as nearly real-time.

The polling system is gone: search updates when something actually changes, and only then.

The log forgets

Transaction logs are trimmed after a while, so a brand-new search index needs a full copy of the table, a dump. Netflix tried Maxwell, SpinalTap, Yelp's MySQL Streamer and Debezium; for dumps, each had at least one deal-breaker. Some stop reading the log until the dump finishes. Others lock the table, and then Ana can't save anything.

DBLog, Netflix's framework, copies the table in chunks sorted by primary key, and fences each chunk with watermarks:

  • Write a low watermark: an update to a tiny table of its own, which shows up in the log.
  • Select the chunk into memory, then write a high watermark.
  • If a row in the chunk was edited in the log between the two marks, drop it from the copy. The copy might be stale; the log can't be.

The log only pauses briefly, and no table is locked. The rule fits in one line: when the copy and the log disagree, the log wins.

Don't lose it in the pipe

Netflix's messaging had been tuned for availability over durability, so a lagging broker could take over as leader and events could be lost. For Delta, Netflix built a dedicated Kafka cluster: unclean leader election off, a replication factor of 3 (up from 2), acks = all with at least 2 in-sync replicas (up from 1), and brokers that reattach their old disk so catch-up drops from hours to minutes.

The gap that always closes

Delta is eventually consistent: for a moment after Ana saves, MySQL knows about Night Train and search doesn't yet. The difference from dual writes is that the gap closes on its own. If a screen must confirm a save instantly, read it from MySQL; search is for finding things. The outbox still earns its place for events the table can't express, like "deal approved", in one service and one language.

Takeaways

  • No single write can land in two databases at once, so dual writes drift.
  • XA blocks on failure, and Elasticsearch can't join it.
  • The outbox works inside one service; CDC works for every service.
  • DBLog copies a live table without locks: when the copy and the log disagree, the log wins.
  • In an interview: one store owns the truth, and every other store is built from its log.

Watch the full breakdown: https://youtu.be/VNz614qTxAs

Sources: Netflix TechBlog, "Delta: A Data Synchronization and Enrichment Platform" and "DBLog: A Generic Change-Data-Capture Framework" (2019). Ana, Night Train and film 8812 are illustrative.

More breakdowns like this: https://systemdesignlab.in

title: How I Split an Avatar Pipeline Between v1 and v2
description:
The gdenticon Refactoring Log — Part 2

The part that actually needed refactoring

gdenticon v1 could already generate avatars as a Go package. It had mirrored grids, pattern filtering, and deterministic colour selection. Judged only by the result, it was not an unusable release.

Its use was still centred on Go code and local PNG files. Callers assembled the settings themselves and passed them to Save for disk output. Later, I wanted gdenticon to work as a standalone tool, produce several image formats, and send the same avatar to memory, an HTTP response, or another destination. The original API was no longer a comfortable fit for those uses.

I could have kept extending the old structure, but each change spread beyond one layer. WritePNG did more than encode PNG: it accepted the original identifier and called Generate internally. The outer Save function then handled content hashing, filename selection, and persistence. Adding SVG or JPEG would either duplicate a similar entry point or make Save responsible for a growing set of formats and output rules.

That became the reason to start v2. Before adding more features, I needed to split the fixed path into three steps: produce a reusable avatar, choose an encoding, and let the caller choose the destination.

v1: a Go package that eventually reached Save

v1 had no CLI. Callers first assembled a model.Image in Go:

img := model.Image{
    GridSize:  5,
    ImageSize: 256,
    Mirror:    true,
    Hash:      gdenticon.SHA256,
}

That value mixed two kinds of settings. Grid, mirroring, digest, and colours described how to generate the avatar. ImageSize and Format described how to encode it.

They then called:

path, err := gdenticon.Save(id, img, "")

Save called WritePNG, and WritePNG called Generate. The complete path looked like this:

Go caller
  → model.Image
  → Save
  → WritePNG
  → Generate
  → encode PNG into bytes.Buffer
  → derive a filename from the bytes
  → write the file

The path worked, but it left several problems for the next round of changes.

The problem was not PNG; it was the cost of adding another encoder

The v1 model.Image reserved names for SVG, PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, and WEBP. Those constants were placeholders for future output work. They did not mean every format was implemented, and their presence was not a refactoring argument.

The architectural problem was the call direction. Save called WritePNG, and WritePNG triggered Generate. Continuing with the same design would either create parallel entry points such as WriteJPEG(id, img) and WriteSVG(id, img), or turn Save into a dispatcher that still owned generation and persistence.

Both approaches could work. Neither made an encoder independently replaceable. Every new format would still touch the original input, generation settings, and file policy. That was the signal to change the boundary.

WritePNG knew about input, generation, and encoding

The v1 WritePNG accepted the original identifier and the complete model.Image, not an avatar that had already been generated:

func WritePNG(w io.Writer, id string, img model.Image) error {
    icon, err := Generate(id, img)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return png.Encode(w, raster(icon, img.ImageSize))
}

PNG output became another entry into the generation pipeline. A caller that already had an Icon had no common Write function to continue with. Every additional encoder would also need a decision about generation and size validation.

The core package also owned the filesystem

Save selected the temporary directory, created the gdenticon folder, derived a content-based filename, and wrote the file. That was convenient for callers that wanted a local file, but it was not a natural policy for every use case.

An HTTP response, an object-storage upload, or an in-memory result does not need a directory or filename. Once local persistence became the default endpoint, other callers had to bypass Save and reconstruct the path themselves.

The full encoded image was buffered first

To derive a filename from the output, v1 encoded the complete PNG into a bytes.Buffer:

var buf bytes.Buffer
if err := WritePNG(&buf, id, img); err != nil {
    return "", err
}

path := filepath.Join(dir, fileName(buf.Bytes()))
if err := os.WriteFile(path, buf.Bytes(), 0o644); err != nil {
    return "", err
}

A default-sized avatar is small, so this was not an immediate failure. It did mean that saving waited for the full encoding, then read the same bytes for hashing and disk output. That path was worth removing before considering larger batches.

I am not attaching a performance number to this structural change. Without a benchmark, less buffering is not evidence of a measured speedup. What can be stated is that the new save path no longer requires the core package to retain the complete encoded image.

The v2 goal: separate three different jobs

The issue was not the number of files or how the folders looked. Three different jobs had become one fixed route:

  1. derive an avatar from the input;
  2. encode that avatar as an image format;
  3. decide where the encoded image belongs.

v2 gives each job a boundary:

GenerateOptions
  → Generate
  → Icon
  → Write(io.Writer)
  → file, memory, HTTP response, or object storage

The pattern algorithm remains inside Generate. PNG, SVG, and the other encoders belong to Write. Directories, cache entries, and replacement policy move to the filesystem package. The CLI composes those parts without moving its persistence decisions into the core package.

Split generation settings from encoding settings

v2 removed the separate model package and moved its public types into gdenticon. More importantly, the old model.Image became two option types.

GenerateOptions contains the values needed to derive a logical avatar:

type GenerateOptions struct {
    GridSize   int
    Mirror     bool
    Style      PatternStyle
    Digest     DigestFunc
    Foreground ColorFunc
    Background color.Color
    Format     Format
}

WriteOptions contains values used during encoding:

type WriteOptions struct {
    Size        int
    JPEGQuality int
}

Format remains on GenerateOptions and Icon so the generated value carries the encoder selected for the next stage. Pixel-size validation is delayed until Write. SVG does not need to satisfy raster-size constraints, while PNG and JPEG do.

The point is not the extra struct. Generation no longer has to carry every rule imposed by an encoder.

Make Icon the real intermediate value

v2 Generate produces an Icon and stops:

icon, err := gdenticon.Generate(id, opts)

Icon stores the grid, filled cells, colours, and target format. It describes the avatar without being an image file:

type Icon struct {
    GridSize   int
    Filled     []bool
    Background color.Color
    Foreground color.Color
    Format     Format
}

v1 already had an Icon; the concept itself is not new. The change is that encoders now consume this value directly instead of accepting an identifier and regenerating it.

This also marks the limit of the architectural refactoring. Hash-derived entropy, mirrored grids, density limits, four-connected-component filtering, and colour selection already existed in v1. v2 largely kept that core while changing how the surrounding code reaches and leaves it.

There is still room to optimise the algorithm, but changing it at the same time as the output pipeline would make the source of any improvement harder to measure.

Use one Write entry for every format

The encoding API is now:

func Write(w io.Writer, icon Icon, opts WriteOptions) error

Write selects PNG, SVG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, or TIFF from icon.Format. Callers no longer need one public function per encoder or the original identifier.

The io.Writer boundary is the more important part. The core package writes encoded bytes without creating or closing a file. The destination can be:

  • a bytes.Buffer in memory;
  • an http.ResponseWriter;
  • an os.File;
  • an object-storage upload stream;
  • an io.MultiWriter with several destinations.

Multi-format support is therefore part of the real output path rather than a list of constants. The CLI now exposes --format, and that choice reaches the shared Write function.

Move persistence out of the core package

v2 removed Save from the core package and introduced pkg/gdenticon/file for directories, temporary files, replacement, and content-addressed caching.

The CLI composes encoding and caching like this:

entry, err := iconfile.PutCacheEntry(
    dir,
    icon.Format.Extension(),
    0o644,
    func(w io.Writer) error {
        return gdenticon.Write(w, icon, gdenticon.WriteOptions{Size: f.size})
    },
)

The filesystem layer supplies a writer. PutCacheEntry uses io.MultiWriter to stream the encoding into a temporary file and SHA-256 at the same time, without first retaining the complete image in memory.

Cache hits, concurrent creation, and Windows replacement behaviour belong here. They matter to the CLI but are not identicon-generation rules. A caller that only needs bytes in memory can ignore this package completely.

Introduce the CLI in v2.0.0

v1 was primarily a Go package. v2.0.0 introduced the CLI, which had to translate command-line strings into GenerateOptions and WriteOptions before joining the new generation, encoding, and filesystem pipeline.

v2.0.0 supports both direct generation and an interactive mode, so main chooses how input is collected:

func runProgram(args []string, stdin io.Reader, stdout, stderr io.Writer) int {
    if interactiveRequested(args) {
        return runInteractive(stdin, stdout, stderr)
    }
    return run(args, stdout, stderr)
}

Interactive mode does not duplicate option parsing or generation. It passes the arguments following generate through the same Cobra command tree and records the result through a callback. Direct and interactive requests share the same path after input collection.

Usage errors still return 2 with command help, while runtime failures return 1 with their cause. Interactive mode keeps the session alive and changes only how the same errors are presented.

This work is far from the avatar algorithm, but it keeps the newly added terminal state and session management out of the package that generates images.

The current v2 request path

Running:

gdenticon alice@example.com --grid 7 --format svg

now follows this route:

main
  → choose direct or interactive input
  → validate and translate CLI options
  → Generate an Icon
  → Write the selected format to an io.Writer
  → store or reuse a content-addressed file
  → print the final path

Compared with v1, the pattern algorithm has not been wrapped in additional layers. The responsibilities around it are simply clearer:

  • Generate does not own image size or a file path;
  • Write does not regenerate the avatar or select a destination;
  • the filesystem package does not know about digests or grids;
  • the CLI only connects user input to those capabilities.

That is the main v1-to-v2 refactoring. It does not prove a speedup by itself, but it creates places where later changes can be measured and replaced independently.

What remains open

Separating generation, encoding, and persistence leaves plenty of work inside avatar generation itself.

The current algorithm turns a digest into a renewable bitstream, generates a mirrored grid, and rejects candidates that are too empty, too full, or too fragmented using density and four-connected components. That core idea already existed in v1; v2 did not replace it wholesale.

The next questions are more specific: which calculations can be removed, whether candidate scoring should change, where the grid and raster paths allocate unnecessarily, and what each change does in a benchmark. Until those measurements exist, I will not present an architectural cleanup as a performance result.

Next

The next part will move inside Generate, starting with how digest bits reach the mirrored grid and how balanced filters candidates, then identifying the parts that still have room for optimisation.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/hourinX/gdenticon

title: Building a Reliable GBase Database Operations Runbook: From Health Checks to Incident Recovery
description:
A database platform is only as reliable as the procedures used to operate it. Even a correctly installed GBase Database environment needs consistent health checks, diagnostic practices, and incident-response workflows.

An operations runbook converts individual administrator knowledge into a repeatable team capability.

1. Define routine health checks

A useful daily checklist should cover:

  • Database service availability.
  • Cluster health where applicable.
  • Storage capacity.
  • CPU and memory trends.
  • Error logs and failed operations.
  • Application connection success.
  • Backup execution and verification.

For GBase 8s, administrators can begin with:

onstat -

For supported GBase 8a cluster environments, a cluster status check may include:

gcadmin showcluster

These commands apply to different GBase product families and should not be treated as interchangeable.

2. Standardize incident classification

A runbook should distinguish several common incident categories:

Availability incidents: Database services cannot be reached or are not in the expected state.

Performance incidents: Queries or applications experience abnormal latency.

Capacity incidents: Storage, memory, or other resources approach operational limits.

Configuration incidents: Recent changes cause unexpected behavior.

Deployment incidents: Installation, license, or initialization steps fail.

3. Collect evidence before making changes

During an incident, capture the current state before restarting services or changing configuration.

date
hostname
df -h
free -m

Then collect product-specific diagnostics and relevant database logs.

Preserving the initial state helps teams understand what happened and reduces the risk of losing useful evidence.

4. Define escalation and recovery criteria

A good runbook should specify:

Item Required definition
Severity Business impact and scope
Owner Responsible technical team
Evidence Logs, metrics, and command output
Escalation When specialist support is required
Recovery Approved and tested procedure
Closure Verification and incident report

5. Improve the runbook after each incident

After recovery, document the root cause, contributing factors, corrective actions, and preventive measures. Convert repeated manual checks into approved automation where appropriate.

Conclusion

A GBase Database operations runbook creates consistency across routine maintenance and unexpected incidents. By standardizing health checks, evidence collection, escalation, and recovery verification, organizations can improve operational visibility and reduce dependence on individual expertise.

title: Designing a Zero-Config create-app CLI for Monorepos
description:
• Why 'Convention over Configuration' Is Non-Negotiable for DX
  • How to Architect a 'create-app' CLI: Templates, Presets, and Plugins
  • Wiring into a pnpm + Turborepo Monorepo Without Surprises
  • Make Configs Ejectable — But Safe, Reversible, and Auditable
  • Testing, Documentation, and One-Command Onboarding Workflows
  • Practical Blueprint: Checklists, Scripts, and Example Files

Scaffolding production apps inside a monorepo is a systems problem, not a styling problem: the CLI you ship either accelerates every engineer or becomes the next tech debt item. A well-designed create-app CLI for a pnpm/ Turborepo workspace must be deterministic, discoverable, and ejectable on demand without wrecking the monorepo's assumptions.

The pain is obvious in real teams: ambiguous workspace resolution, a developer who can’t start the server in < 60s, CI jobs that rebuild what everyone else already built, and a one-off forked config copy that nobody wants to maintain. Those symptoms mean the CLI and templates are leaking complexity into every team instead of reducing it.

Why 'Convention over Configuration' Is Non-Negotiable for DX

The single best lever you have for developer velocity is reducing decisions. A zero-config experience that gets you to a working dev server, type checks, lint, and tests in under a minute removes the friction that causes context switches.

  • Make the monorepo layout a convention: apps/* for deployable apps and packages/* for shared libs. This simple split unlocks tooling heuristics and predictable turbo behavior.
  • Provide sane defaults for bundler and dev server (e.g., Vite-based HMR, SWC/esbuild for transforms), but implement them as opinionated presets that the CLI applies silently for first-time users. Defaults are the on-ramp; presets are the escape hatch.
  • Treat CI parity as a first-class requirement: install with pnpm in CI using --frozen-lockfile and cache the pnpm store to keep installs reproducible and fast.

Conventions should be explicit and documentable in the templates/presets so engineers understand the behavior and can opt into change when necessary.

How to Architect a 'create-app' CLI: Templates, Presets, and Plugins

Your CLI is a product. Build it in composable pieces so the DX team and feature teams can evolve independently.

Core components

  • Templates — file trees (optionally Git or tarball URLs) that define folder structure, package.json scripts, and example code.
  • Presets — declarative composition documents (JSON/YAML) that select template + opinionated settings (lint rules, test config, tsconfig extends).
  • Plugin model — small packages that mutate the generated project (add Storybook, Tailwind, or a feature flag SDK) without changing the CLI binary.

Minimal file layout

packages/create-app/
  templates/
    web-next-ts/
      files...
  presets/
    web-next-ts.json
  plugins/
    plugin-eslint/
      index.js
  bin/
    create-app.ts

Plugin contract (example)

export type Plugin = {
  id: string
  apply: (ctx: { dest: string; answers: Record<string, any> }) => Promise<void>
  // optional capability metadata:
  requires?: string[]
}

Boot sequence (high-level)

  1. Discover workspace root and detect pnpm + turbo presence.
  2. Resolve preset with cosmiconfig-style lookup: preset in root, then workspace-level defaults, then builtin preset.
  3. Merge preset -> template -> local overrides deterministically (deep-merge with arrays replaced).
  4. Materialize files, run pnpm install in the created workspace package, and register tasks in existing turbo.json (or prompt to add them). Use turbo gen/generators where appropriate for monorepo-aware generation.

Example CLI skeleton (TypeScript / Node)

#!/usr/bin/env node
import { cosmiconfig } from 'cosmiconfig';
import { copyTemplate } from './utils/fs';
import enquirer from 'enquirer';

const explorer = cosmiconfig('createApp');
const result = await explorer.search(process.cwd());
const preset = result?.config?.preset ?? 'web-next-ts';

const name = await enquirer.prompt({ type: 'input', name: 'name', message: 'App name' });
await copyTemplate(`templates/${preset}`, `apps/${name.name}`);
// run pnpm install inside the new package, register turbo tasks, etc.

Why a plugin surface (practical): plugins let infra own the common DX (HMR, dev scripts, shared lint rules) while teams install optional capabilities as maintainable packages—no CLI churn. Use a plugin manifest and load order: project-local plugins override org-level plugins, and core plugins come last. The oclif plugin model is a proven pattern for this kind of extensibility.

Wiring into a pnpm + Turborepo Monorepo Without Surprises

Monorepos win when dependency resolution and build orchestration are predictable. That means the CLI must be workspace-aware and conservative about changing hoisting/installation behavior.

Key pnpm facts to encode into the CLI

  • A workspace requires a pnpm-workspace.yaml at the root. Use it to declare apps/* and packages/*.
  • Use the workspace: protocol for strict local linking so the workspace never silently resolves to a registry version. This removes surprising mismatches.
  • Control hoisting when necessary with hoistPattern, publicHoistPattern, and shamefullyHoist. These settings solve ecosystem edge cases (native modules, Metro bundler, some serverless hosts) and must be surfaced as a knob, not a default change.

Sample pnpm-workspace.yaml

packages:
  - 'apps/*'
  - 'packages/*'

Turborepo integration rules

  • Detect or add turbo.json entries and set packageManager: "pnpm" and pnpmWorkspaceFile fields when integrating generated apps so turbo can compute correct hashes for caching.
  • Prefer adding pipeline entries at the root with dependsOn rules like "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"] } so turbo schedules library builds before apps automatically.

Example turbo.json fragment

{
  "packageManager": "pnpm",
  "pnpmWorkspaceFile": "pnpm-workspace.yaml",
  "pipeline": {
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"] },
    "test": { "dependsOn": ["build"] }
  }
}

Enforce dependency boundaries

  • Use Turborepo's boundaries and/or an ESLint ruleset (e.g., eslint-plugin-boundaries or Nx's enforce-module-boundaries) to prevent implicit cross-package imports that break caching and incremental builds. This keeps turbo's task graph sane and cache-friendly.

Make Configs Ejectable — But Safe, Reversible, and Auditable

Engineers must be able to own their app's config, but ejection is a one-way escalation unless you design for reversibility and traceability.

Patterns to implement

  1. Config resolution chain (non-destructive, default-first)

    • Use cosmiconfig semantics so a create-app.config.js or create-app property in package.json overrides presets, but defaults remain provided by the CLI package. This provides a safe override mechanism without immediate file churn.

  2. Soft-eject (recommended default)

    • Materialize organizational defaults into a hidden directory like .create-app/ within the new package. The runtime tooling prefers ./create-app.config.* in the project root if present, else falls back to .create-app/ and then to the packaged preset.
    • Record metadata in .create-app/EJECT-META.json with sourcePreset, cliVersion, and ejectedAt so downstream automation can reason about divergence.

  3. Hard-eject (explicit, guarded)

    • Implement an explicit --eject command that:
      • requires a clean Git working tree,
      • writes a full copy of configs to project root (.vscode/, config/, scripts/),
      • adds a sentinel in package.json such as "createAppEjected": { "version": "1.2.3" },
      • commits the changes for traceability or prompts a pre-made commit message.
    • Mirror create-react-app's model: make it explicitly destructive and one-way unless the CLI provides a revert command that uses the recorded EJECT-META to restore the packaged baseline. The CRA eject behavior and one-way warning are instructive here.

Example eject precondition pseudo:

# in bin/create-app-eject.sh
if [ -n "$(git status --porcelain)" ]; then
  echo "Please commit or stash changes before running eject."
  exit 1
fi
# then copy files and write EJECT-META.json

Safety checklist for ejections

  • Require git status --porcelain clean.
  • Write EJECT-META and patch package.json with an ejectedBy entry.
  • Optionally create a revert-eject script that re-applies the packaged presets if available (best-effort only).
  • Never mutate other workspace packages during eject.

Important: Treat eject as privileged workflow — gate with CI checks and a human review for large repos.

Testing, Documentation, and One-Command Onboarding Workflows

A create-app flow must produce not only code but the signals (tests, docs, lint) that keep the app healthy.

Testing strategy to scaffold

  • Unit: vitest or jest with a standard test script.
  • Integration/E2E: playwright or cypress scaffolded with a sample spec and CI job.
  • Per-package test orchestration: expose test scripts and let turbo run turbo run test --filter=<app> so only affected packages run on change. turbo caching will make reruns fast.

Example turbo.json pipeline (test & lint)

{
  "pipeline": {
    "lint": {},
    "test": { "dependsOn": ["^test"] },
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"] }
  }
}

CI + caching (practical)

  • In CI, set up pnpm via the official action, cache the pnpm store (or rely on setup-node cache: "pnpm"), then run pnpm install --frozen-lockfile. This keeps CI deterministic.
  • Connect turbo remote cache (Vercel Remote Cache or a self-hosted implementation) so CI and developers share artifacts. This reduces wasted CPU across the org.

Sample GitHub Actions install snippet

- uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
  with:
    version: 10
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: '20'
    cache: 'pnpm'
- run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
- run: pnpm -w build # or turbo run build

(Adapt keys to your lockfile and store path caching strategy.)

Documentation & onboarding

  • Auto-generate a concise README for the created app that lists one-command dev start (pnpm dev), how to run tests, how to eject, and where infra-owned configs live.
  • Provide a GETTING_STARTED.md in the root of a new app with the steps: pnpm install, pnpm dev, pnpm test. Make sure those are validated by the scaffold CI for every new template.

Practical Blueprint: Checklists, Scripts, and Example Files

This section is an implementable checklist and minimal code you can paste into your monorepo to get a safe, zero-config create-app UX.

Operational checklist for infra (what to commit into packages/create-app)

  • Templates for each preset (web-next-ts, spa-react-vite, etc.).
  • presets/*.json documenting scripts, devServer, eslintrc, tsconfig.extend.
  • plugins/ implementing apply() to mutate generated projects.
  • bin/create-app binary that:
    1. Validates clean repo (or warns).
    2. Resolves preset via cosmiconfig fallback to builtin.
    3. Copies files and rewrites package.json.name.
    4. Calls pnpm install in the new workspace package.
    5. Optionally runs turbo gen or updates turbo.json pipeline.

Quick example: presets/web-next-ts.json

{
  "name": "web-next-ts",
  "template": "templates/web-next-ts",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "next dev",
    "build": "next build",
    "test": "vitest"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "typescript": "^5.0.0",
    "vitest": "^0.30.0"
  }
}

Eject modes (quick comparison)

Mode What gets copied Reversible Suitable for
Extend-only (default) none (uses presets) Yes (always) Most teams
Soft-eject .create-app/ with metadata Yes (delete folder) Teams that want safe local overrides
Hard-eject Full config to repo root One-way unless tracked Teams taking full ownership of build config

Sample package.json scripts the CLI should create for an app

"scripts": {
  "dev": "turbo run dev --filter=@repo/my-app...",
  "build": "turbo run build --filter=@repo/my-app...",
  "test": "turbo run test --filter=@repo/my-app..."
}

Quick operational checklist for maintainers

  1. Publish or pin create-app package version in monorepo devDeps.
  2. Keep presets/ and plugins/ under version control and instrument a test that bootstraps a template and runs pnpm install && pnpm dev.
  3. Add a turbo CI job that exercises a generated sample app to catch regressions.

Closing

A zero-config create-app for a pnpm/Turborepo monorepo is not magic — it’s a discipline: explicit workspace wiring, deterministic template materialization, and a careful eject story that gives control without destroying the shared factory floor. Build the CLI as composable templates + presets + a small plugin surface, encode the monorepo conventions into the tool (not into every developer's head), and make ejection a traceable, auditable operation so ownership can shift cleanly when it must. The result is consistent, auditable, and fast DX that scales with the organization.

Sources:
pnpm Workspaces - How pnpm defines workspaces and the workspace: protocol; guidance for pnpm-workspace.yaml usage.

pnpm Workspace Settings (hoisting) - hoist, hoistPattern, publicHoistPattern, and related hoisting configuration for pnpm workspaces.

Configuring turbo.json (Turborepo) - turbo.json fields like packageManager, pnpmWorkspaceFile, and pipeline configuration.

Generating code (Turborepo) - Turborepo generators, turbo gen, and Plop-based custom generators integration.

Caching (Turborepo) - Local and remote caching behavior, and Remote Cache usage for speeding local and CI builds.

Create React App: Available Scripts (eject behavior) - Explanation of npm run eject and the one-way nature of ejecting a scaffolded app.

cosmiconfig (GitHub) - Standard config discovery and loader behavior (used for preset/config resolution patterns).

oclif Plugins - Plugin architecture and resolution patterns for building extensible CLIs.

pnpm Continuous Integration - Recommended CI patterns for pnpm (install flags, caching strategies, setup actions).

title: Why a Search Box Shrinks to 2px When You Add container-type
description:
You add one line of CSS to a search form. Then the form is gone.

Well, not gone. DevTools says it is 2px wide. That is just its left and right border.

The line is container-type: inline-size. The plan was simple: the form should switch from a stacked layout to a side-by-side layout when it has room. Instead, it has no room at all.

We rebuilt this bug on a test page to measure it. In our tests it came down to one rule, so let us look at that rule.

The setup

Here is a cut-down version of the page. A header bar holds a logo on the left and a search form on the right.

<header class="toolbar">
  <div class="logo">Logo</div>

  <form class="search">
    <div class="search-inner">
      <input type="search" placeholder="Search">
      <button>Go</button>
    </div>
  </form>
</header>

.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.search {
  container-type: inline-size; /* new: this is what breaks it */
  border: 1px solid #333;
}

.search-inner {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 0.5rem;
}

@container (min-width: 30rem) {
  .search-inner {
    flex-direction: row;
  }
}

Before the container-type line, the form was as wide as its input and button. After it, the form measured 2px in Chrome 156 (we checked with getBoundingClientRect()). The input and button spilled out over the edge.

What went wrong

A query container has a deal with the browser. The browser agrees to work out the container's width without looking at its children.

The browser needs that deal. Your @container rules change the children. If the children could also change the container's width, the two would keep changing each other forever.

MDN puts it like this for inline-size:

"The inline size of the element can be computed in isolation, ignoring the child elements"

Now look at the toolbar again. The search form is a flex item. It has no width and no flex-grow. So how wide is it? As wide as its content.

But the browser just promised to ignore the content. So the content counts as zero. All that is left is the border: 1px on each side, 2px total.

MDN says the same thing in plain words:

"The container size has to be set by context, such as block-level elements that stretch to the full width of their parent, or explicitly defined. If a contextual or explicit size is not available, elements with size containment will collapse."

So the rule to remember is short. A container must get its width from outside, never from inside.

Places where width comes from inside

These are the spots where an element sizes itself to its content. A container in any of them will collapse.

  • A flex item in a row with no width, flex-basis or flex-grow. (Our bug.)
  • A child of a column flexbox that uses align-items: center.
  • An element with width: fit-content or width: max-content.
  • Floats, inline-block elements and absolutely positioned boxes with no width.
  • A grid item that is centered with justify-self: center.

We tried the first three in Chrome 156. All three came out 2px wide, which was just their borders. The same form inside a column flexbox with the default align-items: stretch was full width, as expected.

Fix 1: Let the flex item grow

In a flex row, give the container a share of the free space.

.search {
  container-type: inline-size;
  flex: 1 1 20rem;
}

Now the width comes from the toolbar, which is outside. In our test the form filled the rest of the 1000px toolbar, and the @container rule switched the layout to a row. When we made the page 400px wide, it switched back to a column. That is the behavior the form was meant to have from the start.

Fix 2: Give it a real width

If you don't want it to grow, set a width that does not depend on the children.

.search {
  width: min(100%, 32rem);
  container-type: inline-size;
}

min() picks the smaller value. On a wide screen the form is 32rem. On a small screen it can't get wider than its parent. Either way, the number comes from outside the form.

Fix 3: Move the container up one level

Sometimes you can't touch the width of the element. Maybe it comes from a shared component.

In that case, make a different element the container. Pick an ancestor that already stretches, like a plain block div. Then query that one.

<div class="search-area">
  <form class="search">...</form>
</div>

.search-area {
  container: search-area / inline-size;
}

@container search-area (min-width: 30rem) {
  .search-inner { flex-direction: row; }
}

The container shorthand sets a name and a type at once. The name lets your @container rule target this exact box, even if other containers sit around it.

One thing to keep in mind: an @container rule styles the container's descendants, not the container itself. So put the container one level above the element you want to change.

A trap with container-type: size

size is stricter than inline-size. It ignores the children for the width and the height.

.preview {
  container-type: size;
  width: 400px;
}

This box has a width, but no height. In our test it came out 400px wide and 0px tall, so its text spilled out.

If you need size, give the box a height that does not come from its content. A fixed height works. So does aspect-ratio:

.preview {
  container-type: size;
  width: 400px;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
}

That gave us a 400 by 225 box. For most layouts, though, inline-size is all you need.

Find collapsed containers in one go

Paste this in the DevTools console. It lists every container on the page that is less than 10px wide.

for (const el of document.querySelectorAll('*')) {
  const type = getComputedStyle(el).containerType;
  if (type !== 'normal' && el.getBoundingClientRect().width < 10) {
    console.warn('Collapsed container?', el, type);
  }
}

normal is the default value of container-type, so anything else is a container. On our test page this found all three broken forms and none of the fixed ones.

In Chrome DevTools, the Elements panel also puts a container badge next to query containers. That makes them easy to spot.

Browser support

MDN marks container-type as Baseline widely available and says "It's been available across browsers since February 2023." Our own tests ran in Chrome 156 only. We did not test Firefox or Safari this time, so please check the layout there too.

The short version

Adding container-type tells the browser to size the box without its children. If the box was relying on its children for its width, it shrinks to its borders. Give the width a source from outside: flex-grow, an explicit width, or a stretching parent that acts as the container instead.

Sources

  • MDN, container-type: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/container-type
  • MDN, CSS container queries: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries
  • MDN, Using CSS containment: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Using_CSS_containment
  • Chrome DevTools, Inspect CSS container queries: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/css/container-queries
  • CSS Conditional Rules Module Level 5, container queries (W3C): https://www.w3.org/TR/css-conditional-5/

title: GBase Database Installation Troubleshooting: A Systematic Method for Resolving Deployment Failures
description:
Installation failures are often described as a single problem, but their underlying causes can be very different. A GBase Database deployment may fail because of package incompatibility, missing operating-system dependencies, license validation, filesystem permissions, or incorrect environment configuration.

A structured troubleshooting process helps administrators identify the failing layer instead of repeatedly rerunning the installer.

1. Classify the failure

Start by identifying when the failure occurs:

Installation stage Common investigation area
Package extraction Archive integrity and permissions
Installer startup OS compatibility and dependencies
License validation License file and deployment authorization
Instance initialization Configuration and storage
Service startup Ports, environment, and runtime logs
Application connection Network and database availability

2. Check package and operating-system compatibility

Collect basic host information:

uname -a
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release
df -h

Confirm that the GBase package supports the operating system release and processor architecture.

3. Inspect permissions and paths

Installation accounts need appropriate access to the installation directory and required storage locations.

id
ls -ld /opt
ls -ld /opt/gbase

Avoid solving permission problems by applying unrestricted permissions across the filesystem. Grant only the access required by the installation procedure.

4. Review license-related failures

When license validation fails, check:

  • Whether the correct license file was supplied.
  • Whether the file is readable by the installer or database account.
  • Whether the license matches the intended product and environment.
  • Whether validity and deployment conditions are satisfied.

Do not modify license contents to bypass validation.

5. Preserve diagnostic evidence

When an installation fails, capture:

  • The complete installer error message.
  • Relevant installation logs.
  • Operating system and architecture.
  • GBase product and version.
  • The step where the failure occurred.
  • Recent configuration changes.

Redact passwords, license secrets, and sensitive infrastructure details before sharing logs.

Conclusion

GBase Database installation troubleshooting becomes more efficient when failures are classified by deployment stage. Package validation, environment checks, license verification, permission review, and log analysis provide a repeatable framework for resolving installation problems.

title: A combo editor where every tile is a word someone says out loud
description:
I work on FightNome, so this is about our own app.

FightNome is a pad-work trainer for boxing, Muay Thai, kickboxing and MMA. A recorded voice calls strikes on the beat of the music and you throw them with the phone in your pocket. In an earlier post I wrote about timing those voice files against the beat. This one is about the screen where people build the combos, which turned out to be the harder design problem.

A tile is a sound first

On most workout screens a tile is a picture with a label. Ours is a promise about what you'll hear later, with nobody looking at the phone. So every tile carries two things: the strike (what you do) and the callout (the exact word the coach says).

Those two are often different. A hook can be called "hook", "lead hook", "rear hook", "three" or "four". An uppercut can be "upper", "lead upper", "rear upper", "five" or "six". Kicks get the most options, 17 words such as low, mid, high, teep, calf, switch and their lead and rear versions. Every preset has its own recorded sample bundled in the app, so picking a word never means falling back to a synthetic voice.

Keeping strike and word apart matters because gyms don't agree on vocabulary. One coach calls a cross "two", another says "cross", a Muay Thai coach may want "rear" in front of most things. The combo underneath stays the same and only the words on top change.

The tile menu

Tapping a tile opens a short menu:

  • Quick Strike ×2 makes the strike take half of its beat window, and the tile gets a ×2 badge.
  • Edit Callout changes the word, from the presets for that strike.
  • Replace with Strike swaps the strike and keeps its place in the sequence.
  • Rearrange puts the grid into jiggle mode so you can drag tiles around.
  • Remove from Sequence deletes it.

The list is short on purpose. Every extra option is one more thing to explain to someone who may already have wraps on.

Pauses are tiles too

The palette starts with Pause, then Jab, Cross, Hook, Upper, Body, Kick, Elbow, Knee, Slip and Pivot. Putting the pause in the same grid as strikes keeps the rhythm visible. A pause is a beat where the coach says nothing, and it can be cut to half a beat. Real pad work has gaps for resetting and defending, and a combo with no pauses would be one long burst.

Section settings

Combos live inside sections. Each section has a duration in 5-second steps, an intensity (half time, normal time, double time), a switch for the backing track and tick, and a preview button. If you turn on tempo control in Settings, there's also one tempo slider for the whole workout. Workouts run at 90 BPM by default.

Generating a combo

There's a generate button that rolls a fresh combo. It uses Apple Intelligence on devices where that's available and the app's own combo grammar everywhere else. The grammar is the interesting part: rules for which strike can follow which are easy to write and much harder to make feel like something a coach would actually say.

Combo vs reaction

The same screen has a mode switch. Combo mode is a scripted sequence the coach calls on the beat. Reaction mode is random calls you react to. The tile grid is what you edit for combo mode.

Open question

The thing I'm least sure about is discoverability. Long-press menus are familiar on iOS, but a plain tap opening a menu seems easier when your hands are taped. If you've designed for people using a phone with gloves or wraps on, I'd like to hear what worked.

If you want to try it

FightNome is on the App Store (iOS 26 and up) and Google Play. It's a paid subscription, and only the yearly plan has a 3-day trial. More at https://fightnome.app.

title: Safe Runtime Mode Transitions in GBase 8a: A Database Operations Playbook
description:
Database maintenance sometimes requires changing a cluster's operating mode. Such changes must be treated as controlled operational procedures because an incorrect transition can affect application access and workload availability.

In supported GBase 8a environments, administrators may use cluster management commands to inspect cluster state and perform mode transitions.

1. Understand the operational objective

Before changing a mode, clarify:

  • Why the transition is required.
  • Which applications and users may be affected.
  • Whether active workloads must be drained.
  • Whether the cluster is healthy.
  • How the previous operating state can be restored if necessary.

Do not initiate a mode transition simply because a command is available.

2. Inspect cluster state first

A cluster status check may use:

gcadmin showcluster

For an environment using a virtual cluster, the following form may be supported:

gcadmin showcluster vc vc1

Review the output and confirm that the cluster is in an expected state before proceeding.

3. Execute the planned transition

For supported GBase 8a releases, a normal-mode transition may use:

gcadmin switchmode normal

A virtual-cluster-specific form may be available:

gcadmin switchmode normal vc vc1

These are release-dependent examples. Verify command syntax, required permissions, supported source states, and maintenance requirements before execution.

4. Verify the result

After the operation, inspect the cluster again:

gcadmin showcluster

Then perform application-level checks:

  • Confirm that expected database services are available.
  • Test representative read and write operations.
  • Review database and cluster logs.
  • Check application connection pools.
  • Confirm that monitoring reports a healthy state.

5. Make the procedure reversible

A production runbook should document the approved transition path, expected output, responsible operator, maintenance window, and recovery procedure.

Never assume that a reverse command is safe or supported in every cluster state.

Conclusion

GBase 8a mode management should be approached as a controlled database change. Pre-change health checks, documented execution steps, and post-change verification reduce operational risk and help protect application continuity.

title: SQL Development for GBase Database: From Reliable Queries to Production-Ready Data Access
description:
SQL is the foundation of enterprise database development. Yet production-ready SQL requires more than correct syntax. Developers must consider data integrity, query behavior, transaction boundaries, and compatibility with the target database product.

GBase Database development benefits from a disciplined approach that connects application requirements with database-level reliability.

1. Write queries with explicit intent

Avoid retrieving unnecessary columns when an application needs only a small subset of data.

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    order_status,
    created_at
FROM customer_orders
WHERE order_status = 'PENDING';

Explicit column selection improves readability and reduces unnecessary data transfer.

2. Use parameters in application code

Applications should bind user-supplied values rather than concatenate them into SQL strings.

sql = """
SELECT order_id, order_status
FROM customer_orders
WHERE customer_id = ?
"""

cursor.execute(sql, (customer_id,))

The exact placeholder style depends on the GBase driver and DB-API implementation being used. Confirm the supported syntax in the relevant driver documentation.

3. Protect data changes with transactions

Related updates should be treated as one logical operation.

BEGIN WORK;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE account_id = 1001;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 100
WHERE account_id = 1002;

COMMIT WORK;

If an operation fails, the application should follow the transaction and rollback behavior supported by its GBase product and driver.

4. Validate data before insertion

Constraints and application-level validation work together to protect data quality.

CREATE TABLE customer_profile (
    customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    customer_name VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(200),
    created_at DATE
);

The example illustrates basic constraints. Data types, identity definitions, and additional constraint syntax should be checked against the specific GBase product and version.

5. Measure query behavior

A query that works correctly with a small test dataset may behave differently at enterprise scale.

Evaluate:

  • Filter selectivity.
  • Join conditions.
  • Index or distribution design where applicable.
  • Data volume.
  • Concurrent workload.
  • Execution-plan behavior supported by the target product.

Conclusion

Effective GBase Database development combines readable SQL, parameterized application access, transaction discipline, and data-quality controls. These practices help developers build applications that remain maintainable as workloads and data volumes grow.

title: Thiết kế danh mục cây cảnh: checklist cho website bán hàng nhỏ
description:
Bài toán: đưa danh mục cây cảnh lên web mà vẫn dễ dùng

Một website bán cây cảnh có những yêu cầu giống nhiều cửa hàng trực tuyến khác: người dùng cần tìm được sản phẩm, xem thông tin rõ ràng và liên hệ hoặc đặt hàng. Tuy nhiên, dữ liệu sản phẩm cây xanh có vài điểm riêng. Cùng một tên cây có thể có nhiều kích thước hoặc loại chậu; ảnh cần thể hiện tương quan với đồ vật xung quanh; và thông tin ánh sáng, nước tưới nên được trình bày sao cho khách không phải đoán.

Bài viết này là một checklist triển khai cho nhà phát triển làm website thương mại điện tử nhỏ. Các ví dụ là mẫu minh họa, không khẳng định một website cụ thể đang dùng công nghệ hoặc đã đáp ứng các tiêu chí bên dưới.

1. Xây dựng cấu trúc dữ liệu trước giao diện

Trước khi tạo component, hãy xác định những trường tối thiểu: tên sản phẩm, đường dẫn, mô tả, ảnh, trạng thái còn hàng và giá nếu cửa hàng thực sự công bố giá. Với cây cảnh, bạn có thể bổ sung chiều cao ước tính, loại chậu, nhu cầu ánh sáng và lưu ý chăm sóc. Những thông tin thay đổi theo lô hàng nên có cách cập nhật rõ ràng thay vì hard-code vào giao diện.

Đừng gộp tất cả chi tiết vào một đoạn mô tả tự do nếu người dùng cần lọc hoặc so sánh. Tuy nhiên, cũng không cần tạo hàng chục trường bắt buộc ngay từ đầu. Chọn các trường có người chịu trách nhiệm cập nhật và tạo giá trị cho người mua; dữ liệu thiếu nên được hiển thị là chưa có thông tin thay vì tự suy đoán.

Một mô hình minh họa đơn giản:

{
  "name": "Cây cảnh để bàn",
  "slug": "cay-canh-de-ban",
  "image": "/images/cay-canh-de-ban.webp",
  "light": "Ánh sáng gián tiếp",
  "potDiameterCm": 12,
  "availability": "in_stock"
}

Đơn vị kích thước cần nhất quán. Nếu chiều cao phụ thuộc từng cây, mô tả đó là khoảng ước tính và bổ sung ảnh thực tế khi có thể. Tránh tạo thuộc tính khẳng định tác dụng sức khỏe hoặc môi trường nếu cửa hàng không có căn cứ phù hợp.

2. Thiết kế danh mục theo nhu cầu tìm kiếm

Danh mục nên phản ánh cách khách chọn hàng: cây để bàn, cây nội thất, chậu hoặc tiểu cảnh. Có thể bổ sung bộ lọc theo khoảng giá, kích thước và điều kiện ánh sáng khi dữ liệu đủ tin cậy. Trên màn hình nhỏ, bộ lọc cần dễ mở, dễ đóng và hiển thị số điều kiện đang áp dụng.

Mỗi thẻ sản phẩm nên có ảnh, tên, thông tin giá hoặc cách liên hệ và một đường dẫn rõ ràng đến trang chi tiết. Nếu sản phẩm có nhiều biến thể, hãy làm rõ biến thể nào đang được hiển thị. Đừng dùng màu sắc làm dấu hiệu duy nhất cho tình trạng còn hàng; nên có thêm nhãn văn bản.

Một ví dụ có thể tham khảo về nhóm sản phẩm và danh mục là Tiểu Mộc Cát. Khi dùng một website làm ví dụ thiết kế, hãy kiểm tra thực tế và ghi rõ đâu là quan sát, đâu là đề xuất; không nên xem mọi tính năng trong checklist này là tính năng website đó đã triển khai.

3. Ảnh sản phẩm: nhanh, rõ và có ngữ cảnh

Ảnh cần đủ rõ để người mua nhìn thấy hình dáng cây và chậu. Nên có ít nhất một ảnh chính nhất quán và, nếu có điều kiện, một ảnh cho thấy kích thước tương đối trong không gian. Với cây sống, màu sắc và hình dáng có thể thay đổi; phần mô tả cần nói rõ ảnh mang tính minh họa hay là ảnh của cây được giao.

Về hiệu năng, tạo nhiều kích thước ảnh và chọn kích thước phù hợp với vị trí hiển thị. Dùng width và height hoặc aspect-ratio để giảm xê dịch bố cục. Chỉ dùng lazy loading cho ảnh ngoài vùng nhìn ban đầu; ảnh chính ở đầu trang nên được ưu tiên tải. Văn bản alt cần mô tả nội dung hữu ích của ảnh thay vì nhồi từ khóa.

4. Thông tin chăm sóc và quy trình liên hệ

Trang chi tiết nên trả lời những câu hỏi thực tế: cây đặt ở đâu, cách kiểm tra độ ẩm trước khi tưới, kích thước ước tính và loại chậu đi kèm. Nếu cửa hàng giao cây, cần trình bày rõ khu vực phục vụ, thời gian dự kiến và chính sách xử lý khi sản phẩm gặp vấn đề. Các thông tin đó phải được xác nhận bởi cửa hàng, không tự phát minh từ giao diện mẫu.

Nút liên hệ cần có nhãn dễ hiểu và hoạt động bằng bàn phím. Khi dùng biểu mẫu, chỉ thu thập dữ liệu cần thiết và giải thích mục đích sử dụng. Nếu mở ứng dụng nhắn tin ngoài, hãy cho người dùng biết trước và kiểm tra trải nghiệm trên cả điện thoại lẫn máy tính.

5. HTML ngữ nghĩa và khả năng truy cập

Dùng một tiêu đề chính mô tả trang, sau đó tổ chức nội dung bằng các tiêu đề cấp thấp hơn. Các nút thực hiện hành động nên là <button>; đường dẫn điều hướng nên là <a>. Nhãn biểu mẫu phải liên kết với trường nhập và thông báo lỗi cần mô tả cách khắc phục.

Kiểm tra thứ tự tab, trạng thái focus và độ tương phản của chữ. Đừng ẩn toàn bộ thông tin quan trọng trong ảnh. Nếu có carousel, người dùng cần dừng chuyển động và điều khiển bằng bàn phím. Những kiểm tra này có thể thực hiện thủ công trước khi bổ sung công cụ tự động.

6. Kiểm thử trước khi phát hành

Tạo một bộ dữ liệu thử có sản phẩm đủ thông tin, sản phẩm thiếu ảnh và sản phẩm hết hàng. Kiểm tra lọc danh mục, đường dẫn bị thiếu, trạng thái rỗng, hình ảnh tải chậm và hiển thị ở các kích thước màn hình khác nhau. Đảm bảo thay đổi nội dung không làm mất bố cục hoặc tạo liên kết hỏng.

Cuối cùng, đo hiệu năng bằng dữ liệu thực, kiểm tra trên thiết bị di động và theo dõi phản hồi của người dùng. Với một cửa hàng nhỏ, một danh mục rõ ràng, hình ảnh nhất quán và thông tin được cập nhật thường xuyên có thể mang lại nhiều giá trị hơn việc bổ sung các tính năng phức tạp nhưng ít được sử dụng.

title: Data Types in Java
description:
What is a Data Type?

A data type tells Java what kind of value a variable can store, such as numbers, decimal values, characters, or text.

Every variable in Java must have a data type before we can use it.

Example:

int age = 25;
String name = "John";
double salary = 25000.50;

Types of Data Types in Java

Java data types are divided into two categories:

  1. Primitive Data Types
  2. Non-Primitive Data Types

1. Primitive Data Types

Primitive data types are the basic data types available in Java. They store simple values directly.

Java provides eight primitive data types.

Integer Types:

Data Type Size Description
byte 8 bits Small whole numbers
short 16 bits Short-range integers
int 32 bits Commonly used for integers
long 64 bits Large whole numbers

Floating-Point Types:

Data Type Size Description
float 32 bits Decimal values
double 64 bits More precise decimal values

Other Types:

Data Type Size Description
char 16 bits Stores a single character
boolean JVM-dependent Stores true or false

Example:

int age = 25;
long population = 8000000L;

float price = 99.5f;
double salary = 25000.75;

char grade = 'A';
boolean isPassed = true;

Default Values of Primitive Data Types

When primitive variables are declared as class fields without assigning values, Java provides default values.

Data Type Default Value
byte 0
short 0
int 0
long 0L
float 0.0f
double 0.0d
char '\u0000'
boolean false

2. Non-Primitive Data Types

Non-primitive data types are used to store references to objects rather than directly storing simple values.

Some common examples are:

String

A String is used to store a sequence of characters (text).

String name = "Java";

Array

An array is used to store multiple values of the same data type in a single variable.

int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40};

Class and Object

A class is a blueprint used to create objects. An object is an instance of a class.

Creating a Class:

class Student {
    String name;
    int age;
}

Creating an Object:

Student s1 = new Student();

s1.name = "John";
s1.age = 22;

Here, Student is the class, and s1 is the object created from that class.

Default Value of Non-Primitive Data Types

The default value of a non-primitive reference variable is null when declared as a class field without an assigned value.

Example:

class Student {
    String name;
    int age;
}

Here, the default value of name is null, and the default value of age is 0.

Note: Java provides default values for class fields, but local variables must be initialized before they are used.

title: Variables and Objects in Java
description:
What is a Variable?

A variable is a named memory location used to store data in a program.

Syntax:

dataType variableName = value;

Example:

int age = 25;
String name = "John";
double salary = 25000.50;

Rules for Creating Variables

  • Names can contain letters, digits, _ and $.
  • A variable name cannot start with a digit.
  • Spaces are not allowed.
  • Java keywords cannot be used as variable names.
  • Variable names are case-sensitive (age and Age are different).
  • Use meaningful names and follow camelCase.

Types of Variables in Java

Java has three types of variables:

  1. Local Variables
  2. Instance Variables (Non-static)
  3. Static Variables

1. Local Variables

Declared inside a method, constructor, or block.

  • Accessible only within that method or block.
  • Must be initialized before use.
  • Do not receive default values. 
void display() {
    int age = 25;
    System.out.println(age);
}

Here, age is a local variable.

2. Instance Variables (Non-static)

Declared inside a class but outside methods and constructors.

  • Each object gets its own copy.
  • Can have different values for different objects.
  • Receive default values if not initialized. 
class Student {
    String name;
    int age;
}

Here, name and age are instance variables.

3. Static Variables

Declared inside a class using the static keyword.

  • Only one shared copy exists for the class.
  • All objects share the same variable.
  • Can be accessed using the class name. 
class Student {
    static String college = "ABC College";
}

Here, college is a static variable shared by all Student objects.

Remember: Instance variables belong to objects, whereas static variables belong to the class.

What is an Object?

An object is an instance of a class.

A class is a blueprint used to create objects.

Every object has three characteristics:

  • State: Properties or data (model, price).
  • Behavior: Actions (drive, brake).
  • Identity: Distinguishes one object from another.

Creating a Class and Object

Let's understand this with a simple Car example.

Example:

public class Cars {

    String model;  // Instance variable
    int price;     // Instance variable

    void drive() {  // Instance method
        System.out.println("Car is driving...");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Cars myCar = new Cars();  // Object creation

        myCar.model = "XUV";
        myCar.price = 600000;

        myCar.drive();  // Method calling
    }
}

Output:

Car is driving...

Understanding the code:

  • Cars – Class name.
  • model and price – Instance variables.
  • drive() – Instance method (non-static).
  • new Cars() – Creates an object.
  • myCar – Reference variable that refers to the object.
  • myCar.drive() – Calls the object's method.
