title: Hệ Thống Unicode (Unicode System) Trong Java
description:
Unicode là gì?

↳ Unicode là một chuẩn mã hóa ký tự được sử dụng rộng rãi trong ngành công nghệ máy tính. Mục tiêu của Unicode là cung cấp một cách thức thống nhất và duy nhất để biểu diễn các ký tự từ tất cả các ngôn ngữ viết trên thế giới.

↳ Unicode sử dụng hệ thập lục phân (hexadecimal) để biểu thị các ký tự. Ví dụ, giá trị 0x0041 tương ứng với ký tự Latin A.

↳ Lý do ban đầu cho việc sử dụng 16 bit để mã hóa ký tự trong Unicode là vì các máy tính thời điểm đó chủ yếu là máy tính 16 bit.

Ảnh mô tả xử lý mã hóa ký tự trong java

Unicode và Java

↳ Khi ngôn ngữ lập trình Java được phát triển, chuẩn Unicode đã được chấp nhận và kiểu dữ liệu char được định nghĩa là kiểu 16 bit, có thể lưu trữ các ký tự trong phạm vi từ 0x0000 đến 0xFFFF.

↳ Tuy nhiên, mã hóa 16 bit chỉ hỗ trợ tối đa 2^16 (65,536) ký tự, không đủ để chứa tất cả các ký tự trên thế giới. Do đó, chuẩn Unicode đã được mở rộng lên 0x10FFFF, hỗ trợ hơn một triệu ký tự.

↳ Vấn đề đặt ra là không thể thay đổi định nghĩa của một ký tự trong Java từ 16 bit sang 32 bit vì điều này sẽ khiến hàng triệu ứng dụng Java hiện có không còn hoạt động bình thường.

Thuật ngữ trong Unicode

↳ Ký tự (character): Là đơn vị nhỏ nhất của văn bản, mang ý nghĩa ngữ nghĩa. Ví dụ: a, b, c, $, €, こんにちは (konnichiwa).

↳ Bộ ký tự (character set): Là tập hợp các ký tự có thể được sử dụng bởi nhiều ngôn ngữ. Ví dụ: Bộ ký tự Latin được sử dụng bởi tiếng Anh và hầu hết các ngôn ngữ châu Âu, trong khi bộ ký tự Hy Lạp chỉ được sử dụng bởi tiếng Hy Lạp.

↳ Bộ ký tự mã hóa (coded character set): Là bộ ký tự trong đó mỗi ký tự được gán một số duy nhất.

↳ Điểm mã (code point): Là giá trị được sử dụng trong bộ ký tự mã hóa. Một điểm mã là kiểu dữ liệu int 32 bit, trong đó 21 bit thấp hơn biểu thị giá trị điểm mã hợp lệ và 11 bit cao hơn bằng 0.

↳ Đơn vị mã Unicode (Unicode code unit): Là giá trị char 16 bit. Ví dụ: Chuỗi "abc" tiếp theo bởi ký tự Deseret LONG I (ký tự này được biểu diễn bằng hai giá trị char). Chuỗi đó chứa bốn ký tự, bốn điểm mã nhưng có tới năm đơn vị mã.

↳ Ký hiệu Hexa (hexadecimal): Để biểu diễn một ký tự trong Unicode, giá trị hexa được thêm tiền tố U+.

↳ Phạm vi điểm mã Unicode hợp lệ: Là từ U+0000 đến U+10FFFF. Giá trị điểm mã cho ký tự Latin A là U+0041. Ký tự € (đại diện cho đơn vị tiền tệ Euro) có giá trị điểm mã U+20AC. Ký tự đầu tiên trong bảng chữ cái Deseret, LONG I, có giá trị điểm mã U+10400.

Bảng dưới đây hiển thị giá trị điểm mã cho một số ký tự:

Ký tự

Điểm mã Unicode

Hình tượng

Latin A

U+0041

A

Latin ß (sharp S)

U+00DF

ß

Hán tự Đông (Đông)

U+6771

東

Deseret, LONG I

U+10400

𐐀

↳ Ký tự bổ sung (supplementary character): Là ký tự nằm trong phạm vi từ U+10000 đến U+10FFFF.

↳ Mặt phẳng đa ngôn ngữ cơ bản (Basic Multilingual Plane - BMP): Là tập các ký tự từ U+0000 đến U+FFFF.

Tiềm hiểu rõ hơn về hệ thống Unicode trong Java: Tại đây

title: Still Renewing Tomcat and Spring Boot Certificates by Hand? How to Automate Renewal and Deployment
description:
With Nginx, a renewed certificate is two PEM files and a reload. Tomcat and Spring Boot usually load a keystore instead (.jks or .p12), so each renewal also means downloading the Tomcat-format certificate from your CA or cloud console, or running openssl pkcs12 or keytool to build a keystore yourself, then replacing the old file and restarting the app. That's fine once a year. Public certificates issued today are already capped at 200 days, the cap drops to 100 days on March 15, 2027, and to 47 days on March 15, 2029. At that point you are doing it roughly every month.

This post covers how to automate renewal for Java apps: first check whether the app loads the certificate at all, then the Tomcat and Spring Boot settings that matter, the three errors that most often break a certificate swap, and two ways to automate the whole thing: a Certbot hook you maintain yourself, or LapseZero as a hosted service.

Check where HTTPS terminates

Many Java apps sit behind Nginx, HAProxy or a cloud load balancer that handles TLS, while Tomcat listens on plain HTTP on port 8080. In that setup the certificate has nothing to do with Java. Renew it the way you would for Nginx or the load balancer and skip the keystore work.

To check: in Tomcat, look for a Connector with an SSLHostConfig in conf/server.xml. In Spring Boot, look for server.ssl in application.yml, application.properties or the startup arguments. If neither is there, the Java app usually doesn't load a certificate. The rest of this post assumes it does.

Tomcat

Since Tomcat 8.5 (including 9, 10 and 11), TLS settings go in an SSLHostConfig inside the Connector:

<Connector port="8443" protocol="org.apache.coyote.http11.Http11NioProtocol" SSLEnabled="true">
  <SSLHostConfig>
    <Certificate certificateKeystoreFile="/opt/tomcat/ssl/tomcat.p12"
                 certificateKeystorePassword="changeit"
                 certificateKeystoreType="PKCS12" />
  </SSLHostConfig>
</Connector>

For automation, four attributes on Certificate matter:

  • certificateKeystoreFile is where the renewed keystore has to be written.
  • certificateKeystorePassword has to match the password the new keystore is built with.
  • certificateKeystoreType defaults to JKS when omitted. Use PKCS12 and set it explicitly.
  • certificateKeyAlias is left out above. Without it, Tomcat uses the first key it reads from the keystore, which is the simplest option when the keystore holds a single certificate.

You can also skip keystores. Tomcat 8.5 and later read PEM files directly through certificateFile, certificateKeyFile and certificateChainFile. There is no need to switch an existing keystore setup to PEM just to automate it; both work.

Once the file is replaced, Tomcat has to load it. A restart is the simplest way, and HTTPS is down while it runs: on a small test VM, a normal Tomcat 10.1 restart took HTTPS offline for about 7 seconds. To avoid the gap, the Manager app has an sslReload command that re-reads the certificate and key files without re-parsing server.xml:

curl -fsS -u deployer:password "http://localhost:8080/manager/text/sslReload" | grep -q '^OK'

This needs the Manager app deployed and a user with the manager-script role. When the reload fails, Manager answers with text starting with FAIL and curl still exits 0, so the grep is what turns a failed reload into a non-zero exit code.

Spring Boot

Spring Boot runs an embedded Tomcat and reads the certificate from its own configuration:

server:
  port: 8443
  ssl:
    key-store: file:/opt/app/ssl/app.p12
    key-store-type: PKCS12
    key-store-password: changeit

This works the same in Spring Boot 2.7 and 3.x. Watch the file: prefix. A lot of tutorials use classpath:keystore.p12, which bundles the keystore into the jar. Then a new certificate means a new build and a new release, and nothing on the server can replace it. Move the keystore out of the jar and point key-store at an absolute file: path before automating anything.

Spring Boot also accepts PEM files: server.ssl.certificate for the chain and server.ssl.certificate-private-key for the key.

From Spring Boot 3.2 you can swap certificates without a restart. Define the certificate as an SSL bundle with reload-on-update enabled and Spring Boot watches the files in the background, reloading them when they change:

spring:
  ssl:
    bundle:
      jks:
        web:
          reload-on-update: true
          keystore:
            location: file:/opt/app/ssl/app.p12
            password: changeit
            type: PKCS12
server:
  ssl:
    bundle: web

The bundle type is called jks, but it holds PKCS12 files too; type decides. server.ssl.bundle can't be combined with server.ssl.key-store and the other keystore properties, so remove those when you switch. On versions before 3.2, a restart is the only option. Spring Boot also starts slower than plain Tomcat: on the same test VM, a minimal Spring Boot 3.5 app was unreachable over HTTPS for about 15 seconds during a restart, and real applications usually take longer.

Three errors that break a certificate swap

The alias doesn't match

Many Tomcat guides create the keystore with keytool -alias tomcat and set certificateKeyAlias="tomcat" (or server.ssl.key-alias: tomcat in Spring Boot). Build the renewed keystore with a different tool and the alias may change. On the next start the app fails with:

java.io.IOException: Alias name [tomcat] does not identify a key entry

You won't see this while the app is running, because it keeps the old certificate in memory. It shows up on the first restart after renewal, when the app refuses to start. Either build the new keystore with the same alias (openssl pkcs12 -export -name tomcat), or, if the keystore only ever holds one certificate, remove the alias from the config.

The password doesn't match

The new keystore's password has to equal certificateKeystorePassword or server.ssl.key-store-password. Otherwise startup fails with:

Failed PKCS12 integrity checking

A JKS file from a CA or cloud console sometimes has a key password that differs from the keystore password, which shows up as certificateKeyPassword in Tomcat or server.ssl.key-password in Spring Boot. In a generated PKCS12 file both passwords are the same, so remove that setting or set it to the keystore password.

The restart succeeds and the app is down

This is the one that slips through. Most systemd units for Java apps use Type=simple, where systemctl restart returns as soon as the process starts, long before Java loads the certificate. With a wrong alias or password, systemctl restart still exits with 0. Tomcat keeps running without its HTTPS connector; Spring Boot exits a few seconds later. Your deploy script sees a successful command and moves on while the service is down.

So the restart step should only succeed once HTTPS actually answers, and fail otherwise:

#!/bin/sh
# Usage: restart-and-wait.sh <service> <https-port>
set -eu
systemctl restart "$1"
for attempt in $(seq 1 30); do
  if curl --insecure --fail --silent --max-time 1 "https://127.0.0.1:$2/" >/dev/null; then
    exit 0
  fi
  sleep 1
done
echo "$1 did not become HTTPS-ready" >&2
exit 1

--insecure is only there because this is a local liveness check. Replace / with a path in your app that returns 200 without a login.

The first time you automate this, also check file permissions. The Java process usually runs as a non-root user, and it has to be able to read the newly written keystore.

Doing it yourself with a Certbot deploy hook

If Certbot issues the certificate on the same server, put the conversion, the swap and the restart in a deploy hook. Certbot runs it after each successful renewal and passes the certificate directory in RENEWED_LINEAGE:

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -in "$RENEWED_LINEAGE/fullchain.pem" \
  -inkey "$RENEWED_LINEAGE/privkey.pem" \
  -name tomcat -passout file:/etc/tomcat/keystore.pass \
  -out /opt/tomcat/ssl/tomcat.p12.new
mv /opt/tomcat/ssl/tomcat.p12.new /opt/tomcat/ssl/tomcat.p12
/usr/local/bin/restart-and-wait.sh tomcat 8443

acme.sh doesn't set RENEWED_LINEAGE. Use --install-cert to choose where the full chain and private key are written, point the script at those paths, and run it through --reloadcmd.

For one app on one server, that's enough. With more servers and apps, a few things are left to you:

  • Recovery: if the restart fails, the old keystore has already been overwritten. Keep a backup and restore it on failure, or the app stays down until someone fixes it.
  • Distribution: the renewed certificate only exists on the machine where Certbot runs. For several servers you either run Certbot and the hook on each one, or copy the certificate over and run the same steps everywhere.
  • Alerts: Certbot doesn't notify anyone by default. A failed hook only shows up in its log, so nobody knows unless someone reads it.

Deploying to Java apps with LapseZero

LapseZero is a hosted service that issues certificates, renews them before they expire and deploys them to servers and cloud services. The certificates are free DV certificates with wildcard support, validated over DNS with either a DNS provider API key or a single CNAME record. Nothing needs to be migrated: the first deployment writes the new certificate to your existing keystore path.

A Java server is set up once. Add a deployment target, choose Server, pick Tomcat or Spring Boot, and fill in three fields:

  • Certificate Path: the keystore path from your config, without the file: prefix for Spring Boot.
  • Keystore Password: the same password as in your config. If your config sets a key alias, enter that alias too.
  • Post-deploy Command: the restart-and-wait.sh script above.

LapseZero connects over SSH or through a deployment agent that needs no inbound port. Private keys and passwords are stored encrypted.

From then on, every renewal builds a new PKCS12 file, writes it to the same path and runs your command, and the three errors above stop being your problem. The keystore is built with your password and alias, so they match. If the command fails, for example because the app isn't serving HTTPS within 30 seconds, LapseZero puts the old keystore back and runs the command again, so the app keeps the old certificate and the notification tells you it was rolled back. Add the app's HTTPS address under Live check and each deployment also confirms the new certificate is actually being served.

For an app on several servers, add one deployment target per server with the same settings. The Nginx, load balancer or cloud services in front of it get the same certificate from the same place, with no hook script to maintain on every machine.

The free plan covers 3 domains and 5 deployment targets with no time limit, enough to try it on one or two servers. One domain on six servers is past the free plan; Starter is $3/month for 10 domains and 20 deployment targets.

title: Lazy Loading Strategies
description:
Alright, gather 'round, tech enthusiasts and web wizards! Today, we're diving deep into a concept that can make your websites feel like a superhero – Lazy Loading Strategies. Ever visited a website that felt zippy and responsive, even with a ton of images and content? Chances are, they were harnessing the power of lazy loading.

Think of it like this: you're at a buffet, and you don't want a plate piled high with everything you might potentially eat. You want to grab what you're craving right now, and then maybe go back for more later. Lazy loading is the digital equivalent for your website's resources. It's all about being smart, efficient, and making your users happy.

So, let's get this party started!

The Lazy Loading Lowdown: Why We Should Care

Introduction: More Than Just a Buzzword

Lazy loading isn't just some trendy tech term; it's a fundamental optimization technique that can dramatically improve your website's performance, user experience, and even its search engine rankings. In a nutshell, lazy loading is a design pattern that defers the loading of non-critical resources until they are actually needed by the user.

Why is this so important? Well, in the digital age, speed is king. Users are impatient. If your website takes too long to load, they'll bounce faster than a superball on a trampoline. Lazy loading tackles this by only fetching what's immediately visible on the screen, making that initial load lightning-fast.

Imagine a webpage with a dozen high-resolution images. If all of them are loaded upfront, the user has to wait for all those hefty files to download before they can even see the first piece of content. With lazy loading, only the images in the viewport (the part of the screen the user can see) are loaded initially. As the user scrolls down, more images are loaded on demand. It's like a magical unveiling, keeping things snappy and engaging.

Prerequisites: What You'll Need to Know (No Superpowers Required!)

Before we dive headfirst into the exciting world of lazy loading implementation, let's ensure you've got the basic toolkit. Don't worry, no advanced degrees in rocket science are needed here!

  • Basic HTML, CSS, and JavaScript Knowledge: You should be comfortable with the building blocks of the web. Understanding how to structure content with HTML, style it with CSS, and add interactive elements with JavaScript is key.
  • Understanding of Web Performance Metrics: Familiarity with concepts like "time to first byte" (TTFB), "Largest Contentful Paint" (LCP), and "First Contentful Paint" (FCP) will help you appreciate the impact of lazy loading.
  • Familiarity with the DOM (Document Object Model): Knowing how to select and manipulate elements in the HTML document using JavaScript is crucial for implementing many lazy loading techniques.
  • A Willingness to Experiment: The best way to learn is by doing! Don't be afraid to try things out and see what works best for your specific project.

The "Why": Unpacking the Glorious Advantages

So, what's in it for you and your users? The benefits of lazy loading are pretty compelling:

  • Blazing Fast Initial Load Times: This is the headline act. By delaying the loading of non-essential assets, your initial page load becomes significantly quicker. This leads to a better user experience and reduced bounce rates.
  • Reduced Bandwidth Consumption: Users, especially those on mobile devices with limited data plans, will thank you. Lazy loading means they only download the content they actually interact with, saving them precious data.
  • Improved SEO (Search Engine Optimization): Search engines like Google favor fast-loading websites. Improved performance can lead to better search rankings, attracting more organic traffic to your site.
  • Enhanced User Experience: A snappy website is a pleasant website. Users are more likely to engage with your content, explore more pages, and convert if they don't have to wait around for things to load.
  • Lower Server Load: By reducing the number of resources served at once, you can alleviate some of the pressure on your web server, especially during peak traffic times.

The "But": Acknowledging the Potential Pitfalls

As with any powerful tool, there are a few things to keep in mind. Lazy loading isn't a silver bullet for every situation, and it does come with its own set of considerations:

  • Potential for Jankiness (if not implemented correctly): If the lazy loading implementation is clumsy, users might experience noticeable "jumps" or delays as content appears. This can be jarring.
  • Accessibility Concerns: Ensure that any content loaded lazily is still accessible to screen readers and assistive technologies. Proper ARIA attributes are your friend here.
  • SEO Indexing Challenges (for older methods): Historically, some search engine crawlers might have struggled to find and index lazily loaded content. However, modern crawlers are much better at this.
  • JavaScript Dependency: Most lazy loading techniques rely on JavaScript. If a user has JavaScript disabled (though this is increasingly rare), the lazily loaded content won't appear.
  • Complexity in Implementation: While there are user-friendly solutions, building a robust lazy loading system from scratch can add a layer of complexity to your development process.

The "How": Diving into Lazy Loading Strategies

Now for the juicy part – how do we actually do this? We'll explore a few popular and effective strategies.

1. The Native Browser Approach: loading="lazy"

This is the modern, elegant solution. The HTML <img> and <iframe> elements now support a loading attribute. Setting it to "lazy" tells the browser to defer the loading of these resources until they are close to entering the viewport.

Advantages:

  • Zero JavaScript Required: This is the biggest win! It's built directly into the browser, making it incredibly lightweight and performant.
  • Browser Handles the Logic: You don't need to write any complex JavaScript to detect when an element is visible. The browser does all the heavy lifting.
  • Great Fallback: If a browser doesn't support this attribute, it will simply load the image normally, providing a seamless experience.

Disadvantages:

  • Limited Browser Support (Historically): While support is now widespread, older browsers might not understand this attribute.
  • Only for <img> and <iframe>: Currently, it's limited to these two elements. For other assets like background images or JavaScript-loaded content, you'll need other methods.

Code Snippet:

<img src="path/to/your/image.jpg" alt="A descriptive alt text" loading="lazy" width="600" height="400">

You can also apply it to <iframe> elements:

<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/your-video-id" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen loading="lazy"></iframe>

Tip: Always provide width and height attributes for your images. This helps the browser reserve space for the image before it loads, preventing layout shifts (CLS - Cumulative Layout Shift).

2. The JavaScript Intercept Method: Intersection Observer API

This is a powerful and efficient JavaScript API that allows you to asynchronously observe changes in the intersection of a target element with an ancestor element or with the viewport. It's the go-to for more complex lazy loading scenarios beyond just <img> and <iframe> tags.

Advantages:

  • Highly Performant: It's designed specifically for this purpose and is much more efficient than traditional scroll event listeners.
  • Versatile: Can be used to lazy load images, iframes, videos, or even entire sections of your webpage.
  • Control Over Thresholds: You can define exactly when you want an element to be considered "visible" (e.g., when 50% of it is in view).

Disadvantages:

  • Requires JavaScript: If JavaScript is disabled, this method won't work.
  • Slightly More Complex to Implement: You need to write some JavaScript code.

Code Snippet:

Let's lazy load an image using Intersection Observer.

HTML:

<img data-src="path/to/your/image.jpg" src="path/to/placeholder.gif" alt="A descriptive alt text" width="600" height="400" class="lazy-load">

Notice the data-src attribute. This is where we store the actual image URL. The src attribute holds a placeholder or a low-quality image that loads immediately. The lazy-load class will be used by our JavaScript.

JavaScript:

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  const lazyImages = document.querySelectorAll(".lazy-load");

  const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries, observer) => {
    entries.forEach(entry => {
      if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        const lazyImage = entry.target;
        lazyImage.src = lazyImage.dataset.src; // Set the real image source
        lazyImage.removeAttribute("data-src"); // Clean up the data attribute
        lazyImage.classList.remove("lazy-load"); // Remove the class

        // Optional: Add a class to indicate the image has loaded if you want to add animations
        // lazyImage.classList.add("loaded");

        observer.unobserve(lazyImage); // Stop observing this image once loaded
      }
    });
  });

  lazyImages.forEach(image => {
    observer.observe(image); // Observe each lazy image
  });
});

In this example:

  • We select all elements with the lazy-load class.
  • We create an IntersectionObserver.
  • When an element becomes visible (entry.isIntersecting), we swap the src with the data-src.
  • We then remove the data-src attribute and the lazy-load class.
  • Finally, we stop observing the image because its job is done.

3. The Scroll Event Listener (The Older Way)

Before the loading="lazy" attribute and IntersectionObserver became mainstream, the common approach was to use scroll event listeners. You'd attach a listener to the window.scroll event and, within the handler, check if elements were in the viewport.

Advantages:

  • Works in Older Browsers: This method has been around for a long time and is well-supported.
  • Full Control: You have complete control over when and how elements are loaded.

Disadvantages:

  • Performance Intensive: Scroll events fire very frequently. If your scroll handler is not optimized, it can lead to performance issues, especially on complex pages.
  • Can be Tricky to Optimize: You often need to implement throttling or debouncing to prevent the handler from running too often.
  • More Code: Generally requires more JavaScript code compared to the other methods.

Code Snippet (Simplified Example):

HTML:

<img data-src="path/to/your/image.jpg" src="path/to/placeholder.gif" alt="A descriptive alt text" width="600" height="400" class="lazy-load-scroll">

JavaScript:

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  const lazyImages = document.querySelectorAll(".lazy-load-scroll");
  const viewportOffset = 200; // Load images when they are 200px from the bottom of the viewport

  function loadLazyImages() {
    lazyImages.forEach(image => {
      const rect = image.getBoundingClientRect();
      if (rect.top >= 0 && rect.bottom <= window.innerHeight + viewportOffset) {
        image.src = image.dataset.src;
        image.removeAttribute("data-src");
        image.classList.remove("lazy-load-scroll");
      }
    });
  }

  // Initial load check
  loadLazyImages();

  // Throttle the scroll event for better performance
  let throttleTimer;
  window.addEventListener("scroll", () => {
    if (throttleTimer) {
      clearTimeout(throttleTimer);
    }
    throttleTimer = setTimeout(() => {
      loadLazyImages();
    }, 100); // Adjust the delay as needed
  });
});

In this example:

  • getBoundingClientRect() gives us the position of the image relative to the viewport.
  • We check if the image is within the viewport (plus our viewportOffset).
  • We also implement a simple throttling mechanism using setTimeout to limit how often loadLazyImages is called.

4. Lazy Loading Background Images and CSS

Lazy loading images directly embedded in HTML is straightforward. But what about background images defined in CSS? This requires a different approach.

Strategy: You can use JavaScript to dynamically apply styles with background images only when the element is in the viewport.

HTML:

<div class="lazy-background" data-bg-image="path/to/your/background.jpg"></div>

CSS:

.lazy-background {
  /* Placeholder styles */
  background-color: #eee;
  height: 300px;
  width: 100%;
  background-size: cover;
  background-position: center;
}

.lazy-background.loaded {
  /* Remove placeholder styles once loaded */
  background-color: transparent;
}

JavaScript (using Intersection Observer):

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  const lazyBackgrounds = document.querySelectorAll(".lazy-background");

  const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries, observer) => {
    entries.forEach(entry => {
      if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        const lazyBg = entry.target;
        const imageUrl = lazyBg.dataset.bgImage;

        if (imageUrl) {
          lazyBg.style.backgroundImage = `url('${imageUrl}')`;
          lazyBg.classList.add("loaded"); // Add class to remove placeholder styles
          lazyBg.removeAttribute("data-bg-image");
          observer.unobserve(lazyBg);
        }
      }
    });
  });

  lazyBackgrounds.forEach(bg => {
    observer.observe(bg);
  });
});

This approach dynamically sets the backgroundImage style property.

Beyond Images: Lazy Loading Other Assets

While images are the most common use case, lazy loading isn't limited to them. You can apply similar principles to:

  • Iframes: As shown with loading="lazy" or Intersection Observer.
  • Videos: Load the <video> element and its source only when the user is about to play it or when it enters the viewport.
  • JavaScript Modules: Use dynamic import() statements to load JavaScript code only when it's needed. This is particularly useful for code-splitting and reducing the initial JavaScript payload.

Example of dynamic JavaScript import:

// When a button is clicked, load a specific module
document.getElementById('load-extra-features-button').addEventListener('click', async () => {
  try {
    const extraFeatures = await import('./extra-features.js');
    extraFeatures.init(); // Call a function from the loaded module
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Failed to load extra features:', error);
  }
});

Tools and Libraries to Help You Out

While building your own lazy loading solutions is educational, there are excellent libraries that simplify the process and offer advanced features:

  • Lozad.js: A lightweight and performant lazy loading library that uses Intersection Observer.
  • vanilla-lazyload: Another popular and robust vanilla JavaScript solution.
  • AOS (Animate On Scroll): While primarily for animations, it often incorporates lazy loading principles.
  • Web Components: Custom elements can encapsulate lazy loading logic, making it reusable.

Conclusion: Embracing Efficiency for a Better Web

Lazy loading is a powerful weapon in your web development arsenal. It's about being mindful of user experience, bandwidth, and server resources. By adopting smart lazy loading strategies, you can transform a sluggish website into a high-performing, engaging platform that users will love.

Whether you opt for the simplicity of native loading="lazy", the versatility of IntersectionObserver, or the robustness of a dedicated library, the core principle remains the same: load what's needed, when it's needed.

So, go forth and implement lazy loading! Your users, your servers, and even Google will thank you for it. Happy optimizing!

title: How I built 14 accessible Next.js apps with Claude Code
description:
AI code generators write broken accessibility by default, but not because LLMs are incapable of writing semantic HTML. The issue is that an LLM does not know when it has produced inaccessible code, and most developers do not verify what it outputs.

I built 14 production Next.js applications with Claude Code over the last six months. Every single one passes WCAG 2.1 Level AA across roughly 350 unique screens, using Next.js 16, Tailwind CSS 4, and shadcn/ui. Every app passes axe-core with zero critical or serious violations.

This worked because I set up a verification workflow that catches Claude's mistakes the same way you would catch a junior engineer's mistakes.

The myth about AI and accessibility

The common claim on developer forums is that AI code generators cannot produce accessible code because LLMs hallucinate ARIA attributes and ignore semantic HTML.

That is half true. LLMs do hallucinate ARIA attributes. Claude has generated role="container" (which does not exist) and aria-pressed="yes" (which should be "true") right in front of me. I have watched it output buttons as divs, form inputs without labels, and contrast ratios failing at 2.1:1.

The flaw in the argument is the conclusion. AI generates broken code, but so do humans. Experienced developers catch their own mistakes because they review their work against a checklist and run automated tooling. Most teams using AI skip both.

The solution is not to stop using AI. It is to enforce a repeatable review discipline.

Step 1: Start with an accessibility-first system prompt

Claude Code follows the priorities defined in your system prompt. If you omit accessibility requirements, the model optimizes for visual layout and generation speed.

I add this block to CLAUDE.md in every project before asking Claude to write code:

# Accessibility requirements (NON-NEGOTIABLE)

Every component you write must pass WCAG 2.1 AA. Specifically:

1. Use semantic HTML before reaching for ARIA. <button> not <div onclick>.
   <nav> not <div role="navigation">. <main> not <div id="main">.

2. Every interactive element must work with keyboard alone. Tab to focus,
   Enter/Space to activate, Esc to close. Test by mentally walking through
   the tab order.

3. Every form input must have an associated <label>. Placeholders are
   not labels.

4. Color contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI
   components. Use the design tokens from globals.css; do not invent
   new colors.

5. Focus indicators must be visible against every background the
   component can sit on. Ring-2 with offset, never ring-1 with opacity.

6. Status changes must be announced to screen readers via aria-live
   or role="status". Toasts use sonner with role="status".

7. Never use color alone to convey meaning. Always pair color with
   icon or text.

8. Modals trap focus, return focus to trigger on close, close on Esc.
   Use shadcn Dialog (built on Radix), not custom implementations.

9. Touch targets are at least 44x44px on mobile. Use min-h-11 on tap
   targets that look smaller.

10. Test the following before marking anything complete:
    - Tab through every interactive element
    - Resize browser to 320px wide (no horizontal scroll)
    - Toggle dark mode (contrast still passes)
    - Run the page through axe DevTools (zero criticals)

Claude still makes mistakes with this in place, but they happen far less often, and the model fixes them faster when reminded of its own rules.

Step 2: Use shadcn/ui as the base instead of custom components

shadcn/ui wraps Radix UI primitives. Radix handles focus management, keyboard navigation, ARIA attributes, and screen reader announcements out of the box.

Whenever a screen needs a button, modal, dropdown, dialog, or popover, use the shadcn implementation. Never let Claude build a custom modal or dropdown from scratch. It will eventually drop the focus trap or miss the aria-expanded attribute.

Step 3: Run axe-core on every screen

After Claude generates a screen, run axe DevTools on the rendered page. It takes a few minutes and catches roughly 60% of automated accessibility issues.

To automate this in your test suite, use @axe-core/playwright:

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test"
import AxeBuilder from "@axe-core/playwright"

test("dashboard has no a11y violations", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/dashboard")
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(["wcag2a", "wcag2aa", "wcag21a", "wcag21aa", "wcag22aa"])
    .analyze()

  expect(results.violations).toEqual([])
})

When this test fails, copy the exact violation details back into Claude Code and tell it to fix them. Claude is bad at preventing violations on the initial generation, but it is reliable at fixing them when given the exact failing rule.

Step 4: Run a manual keyboard test

Static tools miss dynamic interaction bugs. A screen can pass axe-core while remaining unusable without a mouse. For every screen:

  1. Navigate to the page.
  2. Press Tab repeatedly through every interactive element.
  3. Check that the tab order follows the visual reading order.
  4. Trigger actions using only the keyboard: Enter or Space for buttons, arrow keys for menus, Esc to dismiss overlays.
  5. Watch for elements that trap focus inappropriately or drop focus entirely.

This takes about 90 seconds per view and catches broken dialog traps or menus that fail to focus their first item on open.

Step 5: Run a screen reader smoke test

Turn on VoiceOver on macOS (Cmd+F5) or NVDA on Windows and walk the main user flow. Check three things:

  • Meaningful labels: every interactive item announces a clear label, not just "button" or "edit text".
  • Dynamic updates: loading spinners, form error states, and success toasts trigger announcements.
  • Headings: the hierarchy is logical, starting with one h1, followed by h2 sections, without skipped levels.

Step 6: Test color contrast across all themes

shadcn relies on CSS custom properties for theming. A color pair that passes contrast in light mode can easily fail in dark mode.

The most frequent regression is muted-foreground placed on top of muted backgrounds. Check every theme permutation explicitly.

Common Claude mistakes and the fix prompts

Across hundreds of generated screens, Claude repeatedly falls into the same specific traps:

1. Clickable divs

Claude will build a card as a <div> with an onClick handler. It looks right visually, but screen readers and keyboards ignore it.

Prompt: "Make every clickable card a <button> or wrap it in a <Link> from next/link, never a div with onClick."

2. Skipped heading levels

Claude often puts an <h1> on the title and jumps immediately to <h3> for cards to match visual styling, violating WCAG 1.3.1.

Prompt: "Heading levels must be sequential. After h1, the next level can only be h2. After h2, only h2 or h3. Never skip a level."

3. Placeholders instead of labels

Inputs will get placeholder="Email address" with no <label> element. Once the user types, the placeholder disappears, and screen readers lose context.

Prompt: "Every form input must have a <label> element associated via htmlFor. Use the shadcn <Label> component. The placeholder is for example text only, never as the label."

4. Custom modals without focus traps

If Claude writes a modal without Radix primitives, tabbing escapes the overlay into background elements.

Prompt: "Always use the shadcn <Dialog> component for modals. Never build a custom modal. Radix Dialog handles focus trap, focus return, and Esc-to-close correctly."

5. Silent asynchronous updates

Claude generates a "Saving..." text label on submit, but omits an announcement region.

Prompt: "Status messages must be in a region with role='status' or aria-live='polite' so screen readers announce them. For toast notifications, use sonner which handles this automatically."

6. Relying purely on color

Inputs fail with a red border alone, without an error message or icon, which violates WCAG 1.4.1.

Prompt: "Status indicators must combine color, icon, and text. Failed inputs need a red border AND an error message AND an aria-invalid attribute. Successful submits need a green icon AND text AND a status announcement."

7. Hallucinated ARIA

Claude writes attributes that do not exist in the WAI-ARIA specification, such as aria-tooltip or aria-hidden="yes".

Prompt: "Pay especially close attention to attribute names and boolean values. Ensure every ARIA attribute matches the W3C specification exactly."

What cannot be delegated to Claude

Claude Code handled the bulk of the initial markup, but specific tasks required manual implementation:

  • Recharts SVGs: Chart graphics have no accessible fallback out of the box. You must write visually hidden <table> summaries alongside each chart so screen readers can consume the underlying dataset.
  • Dynamic announcement copy: Specific announcements like "Filter applied, showing 47 results" get missed by LLMs unless explicitly requested.
  • Physical screen reader listening: No automated tool replaces testing an interface with VoiceOver or NVDA to verify the spoken reading order.

This is a shorter version of a guide I wrote at Frontkit Studio. The full post has the complete walkthrough.

title: A JWKS cache keyed on the token, not on a timer
description:
A key set cached for fifteen minutes stays correct right up to the moment the issuer rotates. An issuer signs with a new key as soon as it publishes it, so a resource server waiting out its TTL turns away every token minted in the gap: good signature, trusted issuer, correct audience, 401. What the cache needs is a second trigger with nothing to do with age, a token naming a key id the cache does not hold, and once you add that trigger the hard decisions move somewhere new.

I have been verifying bearer tokens since 2018, in production systems where money moves, and this is the failure that never turns up in staging. Rotations are rare, on the issuer's side they are instant, and the symptom is a few minutes of 401s that stop by themselves before anyone has finished reading the logs. The code below comes from mcpaudience, a small Go package that does the resource-server half of MCP authorization, and the key set lives in jwks.go.

The timer answers a question nobody asked

A TTL answers one question: how old is my copy of the key set. The question a verifier actually has is whether that copy contains the key this token names. Those two questions agree nearly all of the time and come apart during exactly one event, a rotation. The issuer publishes rsa-2 and starts signing with it right away, and my cached copy, eight minutes old and perfectly fresh by its own accounting, holds only rsa-1.

So this is not a TTL cache. The lookup takes the kid first and the clock second:

func (j *JWKS) Key(ctx context.Context, kid string) (crypto.PublicKey, error) {
    if err := j.checkURL(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    // The lock is held across the fetch, so a burst of requests arriving on a
    // rotation makes one request at the issuer rather than one each.
    j.mu.Lock()
    defer j.mu.Unlock()

    cached, known := j.keys[kid]
    if known && !j.stale() {
        return cached, nil
    }
    if err := j.refresh(ctx); err != nil {
        if known {
            // An issuer being unreachable is not evidence that the key it
            // published stopped being its key. Tokens still expire on their own.
            return cached, nil
        }
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("no key for kid %q: %v", kid, err)
    }
    if key, ok := j.keys[kid]; ok {
        return key, nil
    }
    if reason, ok := j.skipped[kid]; ok {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("the key set lists kid %q but it cannot be used: %s", kid, reason)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("no key for kid %q in the key set at %s", kid, j.URL)
}

The fast path is those first four lines: a kid I hold, in a set that is not stale, answered out of memory with no network at all. Everything after that is the rotation path. CacheFor is still there and still forces a refetch at fifteen minutes by default, but its job has shrunk to housekeeping, eventually noticing keys the issuer took away. It is not what makes rotation work any more.

About the mutex: it is held across an HTTP request, not only around the map. That serializes verification for the length of one fetch, which sounds expensive until you price the alternative: a rotation throws off a burst of unknown-kid lookups that all arrive together, and with no lock each one of them opens its own connection to the issuer. One bounded wait is cheaper than a herd I caused myself. Bounded is doing real work in that sentence, because the default client carries a ten second timeout and the response body is read through io.LimitReader up to maxKeySetBytes, so a hanging or endless issuer cannot sit on the lock forever.

A fetch the caller can trigger needs a floor

This is the part that makes the unknown-kid trigger more than a one-line change. The kid comes out of the token header, and the token header is attacker-controlled. If an unknown kid means a fetch, then a stream of tokens carrying invented kids means a fetch each, and my resource server turns into a small load generator aimed at my own authorization server. That server is shared infrastructure: the amplification takes out the login flow, not just my service.

So refresh refuses to run twice inside MinRefresh, thirty seconds by default, and it records the attempt before it tries:

func (j *JWKS) refresh(ctx context.Context) error {
    now := j.now()
    if since := now.Sub(j.attempted); !j.attempted.IsZero() && since < j.minRefresh() {
        return fmt.Errorf("the key set was fetched %s ago and is not fetched again more than once every %s",
            since.Round(time.Second), j.minRefresh())
    }
    j.attempted = now

    body, err := j.get(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    keys, skipped, err := parseKeySet(body)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("%s: %v", j.URL, err)
    }
    j.keys, j.skipped, j.fetched = keys, skipped, now
    return nil
}

func (j *JWKS) minRefresh() time.Duration {
    if j.MinRefresh > 0 {
        return j.MinRefresh
    }
    return 30 * time.Second
}

j.attempted = now sits above j.get, and that is the line I would get wrong if I were writing this in a hurry. Record the attempt only on success and a down issuer means the floor never engages, so every single request retries: the floor would hold exactly when nothing needed holding, then disappear during the outage, when hammering a sick issuer is at its worst. Note too that j.fetched moves forward only on success, so a failed attempt limits retries without making a stale set look fresh. Two timestamps doing two different jobs, and collapsing them into one is tempting and wrong.

The behaviour is cheap to pin down in a test, and this is the one I would write first:

// Refetching on an unknown kid is free traffic at the issuer unless it is rate
// limited: invented key ids must not become one request each.
func TestAnUnknownKeyIDIsNotAFetchPerToken(t *testing.T) {
    s := newSigner(t)
    issuer := newKeyServer(t, rsaJWK("rsa-1", &s.rsaKey.PublicKey))
    v := keySetVerifier(&JWKS{URL: issuer.url, MinRefresh: time.Minute, Now: func() time.Time { return now }})

    for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
        _, err := v.Verify(context.Background(), s.sign(t, "RS256", "invented", goodClaims()))
        if !errors.Is(err, ErrBadSignature) {
            t.Fatalf("err = %v, want ErrBadSignature", err)
        }
    }
    if got := issuer.count(); got != 1 {
        t.Errorf("the issuer was asked %d times for a key id it never published, want once", got)
    }
}

The injected Now is what makes this testable without sleeping. A key set cache is almost all clock-dependent logic, and a clock you cannot set is a cache you cannot test.

Unknown is three answers, not one

After a successful refresh there are three distinct reasons the kid is still not usable, and the tail of Key keeps them apart. The key is present: return it. The kid is in skipped, meaning the issuer did publish it but parseKeySet dropped it and remembered why: an HMAC or none alg, an RSA modulus under 2048 bits, a curve that is not P-256, a kty of oct. That refusal says so, with the reason attached. Only a kid the issuer has genuinely never published comes back as "unknown".

Two lines of distinction there save an hour of somebody's day. "Unknown kid" sends an operator off to the issuer to check whether the key was published, and the issuer answers yes, it is right there in the document. "The key set lists kid rsa-3 but it cannot be used: RSA modulus is 1024 bits" sends them straight to the right place. A set with no usable key in it is an error rather than an empty cache, and the previous keys stay put, since a malformed publish should not take verification down.

The fetch is a trust boundary too, and the cheapest guard sits at configuration time:

func (j *JWKS) checkURL() error {
    raw := strings.TrimSpace(j.URL)
    if raw == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("no key set URL configured")
    }
    parsed, err := url.Parse(raw)
    if err != nil || !parsed.IsAbs() || parsed.Host == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("key set URL %q is not an absolute URL", j.URL)
    }
    if parsed.Scheme != "https" && parsed.Hostname() != "localhost" && parsed.Hostname() != "127.0.0.1" {
        return fmt.Errorf("key set URL %q must use https: a key set an attacker on the path can replace verifies the attacker's tokens", j.URL)
    }
    return nil
}

The error message is the argument. Nothing else in a verifier counts for much if the document that supplies the public keys can be swapped in transit.

Availability over freshness, stated out loud

The last branch is the one worth arguing about. When the refresh fails and the kid was already held, the cached key verifies the token anyway. My reasoning: an issuer being unreachable is not evidence that the key it published stopped being its key, and the tokens it signed expire on their own. Refusing every request while the issuer is down converts a brief issuer blip into a total outage of my service, and it buys no security, since nothing about an HTTP 503 says anything about a public key.

The cost is real and I will name it. A key the issuer deliberately removed keeps verifying tokens until the next successful fetch. If a signing key leaks and the issuer pulls it from the document, my server honours it for as long as the issuer stays unreachable. That is the trade, and I think it is only acceptable because a key set was never a revocation mechanism: pulling a key does not invalidate the already-issued tokens signed with it either. If you need revocation that takes effect now, you need token introspection, and then you are making a request per token with its own failure policy instead of pretending a cached document can do that job.

Note that the fallback applies only to a kid already held. An unknown kid during an outage gets the error, because there is nothing to fall back to and guessing would mean picking some other key out of the set.

One more detail decides what the client sees. The verifier resolves a kid against its configured Keys first and the fetched KeySet second, so a fetched key never overrides a pinned one, and every key-set failure comes back wrapped in ErrBadSignature:

func (v *JWTVerifier) key(ctx context.Context, kid string) (crypto.PublicKey, error) {
    if key, ok := v.Keys[kid]; ok {
        return key, nil
    }
    if v.KeySet == nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: no key for kid %q", ErrBadSignature, kid)
    }
    if strings.TrimSpace(kid) == "" {
        // Without a kid there is nothing to look up and nothing to rotate; a
        // verifier that guesses picks the wrong key the first time one is added.
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: the token names no kid, so no key can be chosen", ErrBadSignature)
    }
    key, err := v.KeySet.Key(ctx, kid)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", ErrBadSignature, err)
    }
    return key, nil
}

The wrapping is a deliberate answer to a question that comes up in review: should "I could not reach the issuer" be a 500? It should not. The client's situation is identical either way, the token it presented did not verify and its move is to go get a new one, and a 500 invites it to retry that same token against a server it has just been told is broken. A token with no kid at all is refused for the same reason it cannot be rotated: there is nothing to look up, and a verifier that guesses picks wrong the first time the issuer adds a second key.

What I would do differently

The rate limit is global, not per kid. An attacker spraying invented kids can burn the one allowed attempt in an interval and delay the refetch that a genuine rotation needs by up to MinRefresh. With a thirty second default that window is small and the failure heals itself, so it is a defensible shape for a small package. In a system where I controlled both ends, I would keep a per-kid negative cache next to the floor, so a kid that was already refused and is already absent from a freshly fetched set does not spend the shared attempt at all.

I would also not leave the outage recovery passive. As it stands, the last good set returns to normal only when some request happens to arrive with a kid that is unknown or a set that has gone stale. A background refresh attempt during a known-failed state would shorten the window in which a removed key stays live, which is the one cost of the availability trade.

And I would instrument skipped and attempted. Both are facts about the issuer that nothing else in the system knows: a key published but unusable, and a refetch declined by the floor. They stay invisible until someone reads a 401 and starts guessing...

The shape that matters generalizes past JWKS. When a cache's correctness depends on an external event rather than on elapsed time, the trigger belongs with the event and not with the clock, and the moment that trigger becomes reachable by an untrusted input, it needs a floor that counts failures.

Originally published on polycratia.com — where I write about payment systems, crypto rails and marketplace backends.

title: Your AI agent skips steps. Give it a todo list.
description:
You give an agent a real job: "audit these ten endpoints, fix the auth bug in each, run the tests, write up what changed."

It starts well. Six endpoints fixed, some tests run, a tidy summary. The last four endpoints? Never touched.

No crash. No error. It just lost track.

If you've built anything agentic, you've seen this. Here's a small tool that fixes most of it, and how we run it in ByteChef, an open-source workflow automation and AI agent platform built on Java and Spring.

Why agents drop steps

Language models pay less attention to whatever sits in the middle of a long context. As an agent works, its context fills with tool calls and results, and the original plan drifts into that middle zone.

The Spring AI team covered this in their TodoWrite post and borrowed the fix from Claude Code: don't keep the plan in your head. Write it down as a checklist and keep it current.

The TodoWrite tool

TodoWriteTool lives in the spring-ai-agent-utils library. The model sees a tool called TodoWrite. Every call sends the whole list, and each item has three fields:

  • content - the task as an instruction: "Update the Spring Boot version"
  • activeForm - the same task while it runs: "Updating the Spring Boot version"
  • status - pending, in_progress or completed

One rule does most of the work: only one task can be in_progress at a time. The tool rejects a list with two tasks in progress and tells the model to finish the current one first. That forces the agent to work in order instead of starting everything at once.

A few more details from the tool's instructions:

  • Use it for jobs with 3+ distinct steps, not for single simple requests. The agent decides when a job needs a plan.
  • Only mark a task completed when it's fully done. If tests fail or the work is partial, keep it in_progress.
  • If something blocks a task, add a new task for the blocker.

Why writing it down works

A checklist only helps if the agent keeps reading it. That's the real trick.

Each TodoWrite call carries the full current list in its arguments. During a run, the agent's tool-calling loop keeps every tool call and result in the conversation. So whenever the model picks its next step, the latest list is right there: three done, one in progress, six pending.

The plan can't fall out of attention because it gets written again on every update.

Spring AI vs. ByteChef setup

In plain Spring AI, you wire this up yourself: add the tool to a ChatClient, configure MessageChatMemoryAdvisor and ToolCallAdvisor so tool messages actually reach the model, and add chat memory if you want follow-ups.

In ByteChef, the AI Agent component already runs the tool-calling loop and keeps tool messages in the conversation. The Todo Write Tool is one element you drop into the agent's Tools slot. Here's the entire wrapper:

TodoWriteTool todoWriteTool = TodoWriteTool.builder()
    .build();

return ToolCallbackProvider.from(ToolCallbacks.from(todoWriteTool));

That's it. The library does the work, the AI Agent provides the loop.

Spring AI ByteChef
Add the tool In code, on a ChatClient Todo Write Tool element on an AI Agent
Tool messages reach the model Configure advisors Built into the agent loop
Chat memory Add it yourself Add a Chat Memory element

Same tool, same three statuses, same one-in-progress rule.

Try it: a Spring Boot 4 migration planner

Spring Boot 4 migrations are a good stress test. Lots of small steps (Java version, dependencies, Jakarta changes, config properties, tests), and skipping one is easy.

The Spring Boot 4 migration planner template is three steps:

  1. New Chat Request - a message arrives in the workflow chat.
  2. AI Agent - an Anthropic model, Chat Memory for follow-ups, and the Todo Write Tool.
  3. Reply - the answer goes back to the chat.

The system prompt does the rest:

You are a senior Java engineer. For any request with 3 or more distinct
steps, first create a todo list with the TodoWrite tool. Keep exactly one
task in_progress at a time, mark each task completed as soon as it is done,
and update the list after every step. Finish with a short summary.

To run it:

  1. Import the template into a project.
  2. Add your Anthropic connection to the model under the AI Agent.
  3. Open the workflow chat and ask for something multi-step, like: "Plan and walk me through migrating a Spring Boot 3.5 service on Java 17 to Spring Boot 4."

Before answering, the agent calls TodoWrite with a plan. Exact tasks depend on the model, but expect something like:

[ ] Upgrade the service to a supported Java version
[ ] Update the Spring Boot version and the dependency BOM
[ ] Fix renamed and removed configuration properties
[ ] Update tests and run the build
[ ] Summarize the changes

Here's the first TodoWrite call from a real test run, from the AI Agent's Logs tab. One task in progress, the rest pending:

Then it works through the list one task at a time, calls TodoWrite after each step, and ends with a summary. The Agent Playbook in the editor shows every update as a tool-call card, so you can watch the list change.

If the agent skips the list on a big job, make the request more explicit about its steps or tighten the system prompt.

Why it earns its place

It looks almost too simple to matter. On long tasks it's one of the most useful tools you can give an agent:

  • It fights lost-in-the-middle by design. The plan is rewritten on every update, so no step quietly disappears.
  • One task in progress keeps the agent focused. It finishes what it started instead of leaving half-done work.
  • It makes the work visible. You see what's done and what's next. That's the fastest way to check the agent understood the job.

It also pairs well with the other agent utils: File System, Shell, Grep and Glob tools give an agent hands. The todo list gives it a plan to use them on.

Wrapping up

The tools that make agents reliable are rarely the flashy ones. TodoWrite is a checklist, but one the agent writes itself and re-reads at every step. That's exactly what a long task needs.

Got an agent that drops steps on long jobs? Import the migration planner template, add your Anthropic connection, and give it a ten-step job.

This is Part 3 of our AI Agentic Patterns series. Part 1 covered Agent Skills. If you like where ByteChef is going, a star on GitHub helps a lot.

title: J'ai créé 5 outils web gratuits, sans inscription : voici ce que j'ai appris
description:
Depuis quelques mois, je développe sous le nom Maketru de petits outils web gratuits. Chacun répond à un besoin précis. Pas de compte à créer, pas d'abonnement : on ouvre la page et ça marche.

Les 5 outils

  • DocSlice permet de fusionner des PDF, d'en découper, et d'extraire ou de supprimer des pages. Tout se fait dans le navigateur : les fichiers ne sont jamais envoyés sur un serveur. C'était ma première motivation, parce que la plupart des outils PDF en ligne téléversent vos documents.
  • SolarPulse est un simulateur de panneaux solaires. Il estime la production photovoltaïque et les économies pour une maison en France, en Suisse ou au Luxembourg.
  • WaterPulse est un calculateur de cuve de récupération d'eau de pluie. Il dimensionne la cuve à partir de la surface du toit, de la pluviométrie et des besoins en eau.
  • ChronoPulse regroupe un minuteur, un chronomètre et un compte à rebours en ligne, simples et lisibles.
  • FacturePulse compare les logiciels de facturation électronique, pour aider les entreprises françaises à se préparer à l'obligation.

La technique

Les sites sont faits en React avec Vite et hébergés sur Firebase Hosting. Comme une application monopage est mal lue par les moteurs de recherche, j'ai ajouté un prérendu : chaque page est générée en HTML statique au moment du build, avec son titre, sa description et ses données structurées. Pour DocSlice, toute la manipulation des PDF se fait côté client, ce qui évite d'avoir un serveur et protège la confidentialité.

Ce que j'ai appris

  • Un outil qui fait une seule chose bien est plus facile à expliquer et à référencer qu'une grosse application.
  • Le référencement d'une application monopage demande du travail dès le départ : prérendu, sitemap, une page par intention de recherche.
  • Supprimer l'inscription réduit énormément la friction pour l'utilisateur.

Vos retours m'intéressent beaucoup : qu'est-ce qui vous manque dans ces outils, ou quel outil aimeriez-vous voir ensuite ?

title: How I Built UAE Gratuity and Overtime Calculators That Follow the Actual Rules
description:
Most salary calculators I tried had the same problem: you type a number, you get a number, and you have no idea how it was calculated. That is fine for a rough guess. It is not fine when the number is someone's end-of-service gratuity or overtime pay.

So when I built the UAE tools on Toolkit Studio, I started from the rules first, and the UI second.

The rules I coded, not guessed

For UAE gratuity, the calculation follows Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021. The daily wage is basic salary divided by 30. The entitlement is 21 days of basic salary for each year of service for the first five years, and 30 days per year after that. Partial years are calculated pro-rata, and the total is capped at two years of basic salary.

For overtime, the hourly rate is basic salary divided by 30, divided by 8. Daytime overtime is paid at 1.25x that rate, and night overtime (10 PM to 4 AM) plus rest-day work is paid at 1.5x.

These are estimates for planning, not legal advice. The pages say that clearly, and they link to the idea of checking the official MOHRE guidance for a real case. A calculator that pretends to be a lawyer is worse than no calculator at all.

Why the UAE weekend mattered

The UAE weekend has been Saturday and Sunday since January 2022. That small fact changes a date calculator too. My date difference tool already counted Monday to Friday as business days, which is also the UAE working week. When I added the UAE guides, I wrote that out in plain words instead of leaving it as an assumption in the code. If a rule affects the answer, it should be visible on the page.

The other two tools in the set

The AED converter uses the fixed peg of 3.6725 AED per US dollar, and lets the user edit the USD to INR rate instead of hard-coding a rate that goes stale. The Dubai salary calculator starts from a simple fact: Dubai has 0% income tax, so gross pay equals net pay, and then it compares that with a taxed-abroad figure so the user can see the difference in numbers, not in slogans. The example on the page uses AED 25,000 per month net in Dubai, AED 300,000 per year, and AED 18,750 per month abroad at a 25% tax rate, for an annual difference of AED 75,000.

How it is built

All four tools are client-side React components in a Vite app, with no signup and no backend. The same shared tool UI is reused, and each page is prerendered with its own guide and FAQs, so the explanation and the calculator live on the same page. That was a deliberate choice: if the formula is the point, the formula should not be hidden behind a second click.

The hardest part was not the maths. It was resisting the urge to add more inputs. Every extra field makes the tool look powerful and makes the user less likely to finish it. I kept the inputs to the ones the rule actually needs: basic salary, years of service, and for overtime, the hours and when they were worked.

What I would do differently

I would write the worked example first, before the component. On the first version of one page, the example and the live tool used different example numbers, and that kind of mismatch is exactly what makes a user stop trusting a calculator. Now the example on the page is the same example the tool would produce.

Try the tools here: Toolkit Studio — the UAE calculators are the gratuity calculator, the overtime pay calculator, the AED currency converter, and the Dubai salary calculator.

What rule-based calculator have you built where the rule itself was the hardest part to get right? I would like to hear how you handled it.

title: Ask the User Before You Act: Human-in-the-Loop Questions for AI Agents with Spring AI
description:
Every agent builder knows this failure mode. You give the agent a task, "plan our team offsite", and it just runs. It picks a city. It picks a budget. It picks the one week half the team is on holiday. Now you're not reviewing a plan. You're undoing one.

The Spring AI team put it well in their AskUserQuestionTool post: the AI makes assumptions, and each assumption creates rework. Their fix is a tool that flips the default. The agent asks first, and acts only once it has real answers.

ByteChef is an open-source workflow automation and AI agent platform built on Spring AI, so it runs the same tool. In Part 1 we gave agents know-how with skills. In this part we teach them to ask.

TL;DR: The Ask User Question Tool lets a ByteChef AI Agent stop and ask the user 1 to 4 multiple-choice questions before it acts. In a deployed chat, the workflow suspends for up to 30 days and resumes when the answers arrive. No thread is held while it waits. Try it with the offsite planner template.

The example: an offsite planner that asks first

The template has three steps:

  1. New Chat Request - a message arrives in the workflow chat.
  2. AI Agent - the Chat (stream) action with an Anthropic model, Chat Memory, and the Ask User Question Tool in its Tools slot.
  3. Reply - the plan goes back to the chat.

The system prompt does the real work:

You plan team events. Never guess requirements. Before you plan anything,
call the AskUserQuestionTool once with three or four multiple-choice
questions covering budget, dates, team size and location. Offer 3 or 4
concrete options per question. After the answers arrive, produce a
one-page plan.

Two rules matter here:

  • "Never guess requirements" tells the model that asking is expected, not a failure.
  • "Call the tool once" stops it from asking one question at a time and dragging the conversation out.

What the model actually sees

The tool comes from Spring AI's spring-ai-agent-utils toolkit. The model sees a tool named AskUserQuestionTool that takes 1 to 4 questions. Each question has:

  • header - a short label, 12 characters max, like "Budget"
  • question - the question itself
  • options - 2 to 4 choices, each with a label and a description
  • multiSelect - for questions where more than one answer fits

For the offsite planner, a call looks roughly like this:

{
  "questions": [
    {
      "header": "Budget",
      "question": "What's the total budget for the offsite?",
      "multiSelect": false,
      "options": [
        { "label": "Under $5k", "description": "Local venue, day trips" },
        { "label": "$5k to $15k", "description": "Nearby city, one night" },
        { "label": "$15k+", "description": "Travel, multiple nights" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "header": "Dates",
      "question": "Which week works best?",
      "multiSelect": true,
      "options": [
        { "label": "Mid May", "description": "Before summer holidays" },
        { "label": "Early June", "description": "Good weather, busier venues" },
        { "label": "September", "description": "After holidays, everyone back" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The model writes these itself, from the user's request and your system prompt.

In plain Spring AI you'd also write a question handler: the code that shows the questions and collects the answers. On a console, that's reading a line from stdin. In a real product, the user might answer in ten seconds or tomorrow, from a different device. That gap is what ByteChef fills.

What happens when the agent asks

When the agent calls the tool, ByteChef sends the questions to the chat as an ask_user_question event. The chat renders each question with its header and a numbered list of options. You answer by typing, so you can pick an option or write your own answer.

Here's a real test run. Asked to plan a two-day offsite, the agent sent four questions instead of a plan:

What happens next depends on where the chat runs.

In a deployed workflow, the questions come with a resume URL and the workflow suspends. It isn't holding a thread. The run is persisted and can wait up to 30 days. When you answer, the chat posts to the resume URL, and the AI Agent picks up exactly where it stopped, with your answers as the tool result, and streams the plan back.

In the editor's test chat, there's no resume URL. The questions still show, but the agent is told to end its turn and read the answers from your next message. Because the template has Chat Memory, the agent still sees its own questions when your answer arrives, so it behaves the same.

This suspend/resume mechanism is the same one behind ByteChef's Approval component. Waiting for someone to approve and waiting for someone to answer are the same problem: a run that has to stop, wait for days, survive a restart, and continue on an outside signal.

Two limits worth knowing:

  • The tool needs the Chat (stream) action. With the non-streaming Chat action there's no way to deliver the questions, so the agent is told to proceed on its best judgment and state its assumptions.
  • If the questions can't be delivered, the agent gets the same instruction. It never waits for answers nobody can see.

Try it in 4 steps

The template needs only an Anthropic connection.

  1. Import the template. Open Plan a team offsite with an agent that asks before it plans and add it to a project.
  2. Connect the model. Add your Anthropic connection to the model under the AI Agent.
  3. Test it in the editor. Open the chat and write "Plan an offsite for my team." You should get 3 or 4 questions back instead of a plan. Reply with your choices in one message and the agent writes the plan.
  4. Deploy it. Deploy the project, open Chats in the Automation sidebar, and pick the workflow. Now the run really pauses while it waits for you.

Thanks to Chat Memory, you can ask for changes afterwards, like "move it to September", without starting over.

Why asking first matters

It's tempting to treat clarifying questions as polite extras. For agents, they're closer to a correctness tool:

  • They prevent rework. A wrong guess costs the failed step, the tokens spent getting there, and the turns you spend correcting it. One round of questions is cheaper.
  • They're a natural human-in-the-loop gate. For anything that matters, like spending money, emailing a customer, or deleting records, "ask before acting" is the safe default.
  • They don't tie anything up. A deployed run actually suspends. The agent can wait days without holding a worker.

Spring AI vs. ByteChef: what you get for free

The Spring AI post ends where a library ends: here's the tool, write a handler. Here's what ByteChef adds on top:

Plain Spring AI ByteChef
You implement the question handler Built in
A console handler blocks the current thread Deployed workflow suspends up to 30 days and frees the worker
Getting questions to a UI is your job Streamed to the chat, run resumes when the answer is posted back
Adding the tool means code and config One tool on the AI Agent

The question format, the library, and model portability stay the same. The template uses Claude, but the tool works with any model provider ByteChef supports.

Wrapping up

The most useful agent behaviors are often the boring ones. "Ask before you assume" isn't flashy, but it's the difference between an agent whose work you undo and one whose work you can trust.

Import the offsite planner template, add your Anthropic connection, and ask it to plan your next offsite. Then add the Ask User Question Tool to your own agents wherever a guess would be expensive.

If you like where this is going, a star on GitHub helps a lot.
