title: RAG Pipelines: Why Your Chatbot Hallucinates and How to Fix It
description:
Ask a chatbot a question about your own documentation and it answers confidently, fluently, and sometimes completely wrong. The model is not broken. It is doing exactly what it was trained to do: produce plausible text. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, exists to change the job from "produce plausible text" to "answer from these documents." When RAG works, hallucinations drop sharply. When it fails, it usually fails in one of a handful of predictable places, and each one is fixable.

What RAG actually is

A RAG pipeline has four stages, and the model is only the last one. First, your documents are split into chunks. Second, each chunk is converted into a vector embedding, a list of numbers that captures its meaning. Third, at query time, the user's question is embedded the same way and the nearest chunks are retrieved. Fourth, those chunks are pasted into the model's prompt and the model answers from them.

Documents -> chunks -> embeddings -> vector store
Question -> embedding -> top-k chunks -> prompt + model -> answer

Most teams obsess over the model and neglect the first three stages. In practice, retrieval quality decides answer quality. A model given the right three paragraphs answers correctly. A model given the wrong three paragraphs answers confidently and wrong, because nothing in its prompt tells it otherwise.

Failure 1: chunks that destroy meaning

The most common RAG bug is chunking by fixed size with no respect for structure. A 500-token window that cuts a table in half, splits a function from its explanation, or separates a warning from the procedure it warns about produces chunks that are individually meaningless. Retrieval then returns fragments, and the model stitches fragments into fiction.

Fix it by chunking on structure: split by headings, by function, by paragraph, and keep small overlaps between adjacent chunks so context survives the boundary. Overlap of 10 to 20 percent is a reasonable starting point. Then read retrieved chunks for real queries and judge them by eye: would a human given only these chunks answer correctly? If not, the chunking is wrong, not the model.

Failure 2: retrieval that returns the wrong neighbors

Vector similarity is not relevance. A question about "refunds for annual plans" can retrieve a chunk about "refunds for monthly plans" because the words are close, while the chunk about annual plans sits just outside the top-k cutoff. Pure vector search also misses exact terms: a product code, an error string, a person's name.

The standard fix is hybrid retrieval: combine vector search with keyword search, typically BM25, and merge the results. The vector search catches paraphrases; the keyword search catches exact terms. Reranking the merged set with a small cross-encoder model before handing it to the generator is the second upgrade, and it is usually the highest-return change in the whole pipeline.

# Hybrid retrieval in sketch form: keyword hits plus vector hits, reranked.
keyword_hits = bm25_search(query, top_n=20)
vector_hits = vector_search(embed(query), top_n=20)
candidates = dedupe(keyword_hits + vector_hits)
ranked = cross_encoder_rerank(query, candidates)[:5]
answer = llm.generate(prompt_with(ranked))

Failure 3: prompts that invite invention

Even with perfect retrieval, a prompt that says "answer the question" invites the model to fill gaps from its training data. The fix is boring and effective: instruct the model to answer only from the provided context, and to say it does not know when the context does not contain the answer. "I don't know" is a feature, not a failure, and teams that treat it as one will keep shipping hallucinations.

Add citations to the output: require the model to quote or reference the chunk each claim comes from. Citations do two jobs at once. They let users verify answers, and they make hallucination visible during evaluation, because an uncited claim is a claim the pipeline cannot defend.

Failure 4: never measuring anything

The deepest RAG failure is building the pipeline and never evaluating it. Without a test set of real questions with known-good answers, every change is a guess. Build a set of 50 to 100 questions your users actually ask, with the correct answer and the source document noted. Then measure: how often does retrieval return the right chunk, and how often does the final answer match? Most teams discover that retrieval, not generation, is the bottleneck, and that a week of chunking and reranking work beats a month of model tuning.

Evaluation also catches data drift. Documents change, products rename, policies update. A chunk store built from last quarter's documentation answers last quarter's questions. Rebuild embeddings when source documents change, version the index, and re-run the test set after every rebuild. A RAG system without a refresh process is a snapshot pretending to be a service.

The honest summary

Hallucination in a RAG system is usually a retrieval failure wearing a model's clothes. Chunk on structure, retrieve with hybrid search, rerank before generating, prompt for grounded answers with citations, and measure against real questions. None of that is glamorous, and all of it is the difference between a chatbot that helps and one that confidently misleads. The model is the last 10 percent of the system. The pipeline is the other 90, and it is where the work belongs.

When RAG is the wrong tool

Not every question-answering problem is a RAG problem, and forcing it causes a different class of failure. If the answer requires computation, aggregation, or live data, retrieval cannot help. "How many open tickets do we have?" is a database query, not a document lookup, and a RAG pipeline that retrieves a stale wiki page about ticket counts will answer confidently and wrong. Route those questions to tools: let the model call a function that queries the live system, and reserve RAG for knowledge questions with stable, document-backed answers.

The same logic applies to questions with a single authoritative answer that changes often. Prices, quotas, and policy thresholds belong in a structured store queried at answer time, not in embeddings rebuilt nightly. A useful rule: if the answer would change between index rebuilds, do not put it in the index. Put a pointer in the index and fetch the value live.

Finally, respect the case where the honest answer is that no document covers the question. A RAG system that always answers, even when retrieval returns nothing relevant, is a hallucination machine with good branding. Build the abstention path deliberately: when the best retrieved chunk scores below a threshold, say so, and offer the closest related topic or a human contact. Users forgive "I don't know" far faster than they forgive a wrong answer delivered with confidence.

Start with one pipeline, not ten

If your team is new to RAG, resist the urge to build one pipeline per department. Build one pipeline for one well-understood document set, with a test set of real questions and a named owner for the index. Run it for a month, fix the chunking problems you find, add hybrid retrieval and reranking, and only then expand. A single pipeline that answers correctly teaches the organization what good looks like. Ten pipelines built at once teach it that RAG is unreliable, and that reputation is hard to reverse. Quality first, coverage second, always.

title: Building Multilingual Ecommerce Websites: Practical Lessons
description:
Building an ecommerce website for an international audience introduces challenges that go beyond translating website content.

Customers need to understand product information, navigate categories easily and feel confident when purchasing products online.

For developers and ecommerce businesses serving customers in Germany, localisation and user experience should be considered important parts of the development process.

Here are six practical areas to consider when building or improving an international ecommerce website.

1. Localise More Than Just the Language

A translated website is not necessarily a fully localised website.

Localisation can include:

  • German-language navigation
  • Clear product descriptions
  • Appropriate currency formatting
  • Familiar date and measurement formats
  • Local delivery information
  • Relevant customer support information

The objective is to make the shopping experience feel natural to the intended audience.

2. Build a Logical Product Taxonomy

International grocery stores often have products from several countries and food cultures.

A useful product taxonomy can organise products by:

  • Food category
  • Country or cuisine
  • Product type
  • Brand
  • Dietary characteristics, where verified

A well-designed taxonomy improves navigation and can also help search engines understand the relationship between website pages.

3. Improve Internal Search

Customers may search using different product names, spellings or languages.

An effective search system should consider:

  • Alternative product spellings
  • Brand names
  • Synonyms
  • Category filters
  • Relevant product suggestions

Search analytics can reveal what customers are looking for and which searches return poor results.

4. Make Product Pages Informative

A product page should answer the most important questions before a customer makes a purchase.

For grocery products, this might include:

  • Product name and brand
  • Net weight or quantity
  • Ingredient information
  • Preparation instructions
  • Storage instructions
  • Product images
  • Availability

Accurate product information is especially important for international products that customers may not recognise immediately.

5. Optimise Mobile Performance

Mobile shopping should be treated as a core requirement.

Developers can improve the experience by:

  • Compressing images
  • Reducing unnecessary JavaScript
  • Using responsive product grids
  • Improving page loading performance
  • Keeping navigation accessible
  • Simplifying checkout

Performance testing should cover product pages, category pages and checkout, not just the homepage.

6. Use Data to Improve Ecommerce Decisions

Analytics can help identify problems in the customer journey.

For example, high search usage with low product engagement may indicate that search results need improvement.

High cart abandonment may indicate friction during checkout or unclear delivery information.

Measuring these behaviours provides a more reliable basis for improvements than making design decisions based only on assumptions.

A Real-World Ecommerce Context

International grocery stores provide an interesting example of the importance of localisation and product discovery.

TargetMart.de focuses on international food products and grocery shopping in Germany.

Its international food selection provides a practical context for thinking about product categorisation, search functionality and making different cuisines easier to discover.

Conclusion

Building an ecommerce website for the German market requires attention to language, product organisation, accurate information, mobile performance and customer expectations.

The best approach is to treat localisation as part of the overall product experience rather than simply translating text.

For developers, these improvements can make ecommerce websites easier to navigate, understand and use.`

title: The migration that kept running after the rollback
description:
You push a deploy. The dashboard accepts it. Then nothing happens.

No error. No crash. No failed build log to read. Your live service keeps serving traffic happily, as if nothing is wrong. The deploy just sits in the queue, waiting for a worker that never picks it up.

That is what happened at Render on Wednesday, October 14, 2026. Between 12:12 and 15:08 PDT, builds and deploys across all regions failed to start, stalled, or were badly delayed, in two periods of impact totalling about 2 hours and 20 minutes. Live user services were not affected. Only the machinery that starts new work was stuck.

That split is the clue worth sitting with. When the thing that is already running works fine and the thing that starts new work does not, the problem is usually not the whole platform. It is in the path that new work takes, and in whatever that path shares with something else.

What happened, in order

Render runs an internal job scheduler. It coordinates builds, deploys, and other critical platform operations. On October 14, the team was rolling out improvements to how that scheduler distributes work, after a successful practice run in a test environment. The planned version upgrade included a database schema migration.

A schema migration is a change to the shape of a database: adding a column, changing a type, adding an index, that kind of thing. Some migrations are quick. Some need a lock on a table, which means other work on that table has to wait until the migration finishes.

This migration locked a large table and drove database CPU use to 100 percent. That database stores two kinds of thing: the scheduler's core job state, and secondary data used for search and reporting. With the database that busy, the scheduler could not read or write job state reliably. Builds and deploys stopped or slowed.

Here is the timeline from Render's postmortem, posted October 22, 2026. All times are PDT on October 14.

12:13: The upgrade starts, including the migration. Database load rises and builds and deploys stop starting.

12:24: Impact identified, incident escalated.

12:34: Engineers revert the upgrade and stop the client performing the migration.

12:37: The scheduler recovers. Builds and deploys resume, but slowly.

13:17: Engineers restart one unhealthy instance of the system to rebalance load. Database connections and errors increase. The second period of impact starts.

13:37: Free tier deploys are paused to reduce load.

13:49: Engineers find the migration still running on the database and terminate it.

14:16: The database is restarted. An attempt to add database capacity fails because of an error from the underlying cloud provider.

14:30: Builds and deploys start to recover, slowly, as the backlog is processed.

15:08: Deploy start times return to normal and database load returns to pre-incident levels.

15:18: Incident resolved.

Read that timeline again and notice the two moments that hurt most. The first is 12:34. The team reverted the upgrade and stopped the client doing the migration, and the system briefly looked better. The second is 13:49, more than an hour later, when they found the migration still running on the database.

Stopping the client did not stop the migration.

The lesson most people miss: a migration lives on the server

This is the part of the story that translates directly to your own work, even if you never run a platform like Render.

When you run a migration, you usually run a small program on your machine, or in CI, that sends a statement to the database and waits. It is easy to think of that program as the migration. It is not. The migration is the work happening inside the database. Your program is just the messenger waiting for an answer.

If you kill the messenger, the database may keep working. If you roll back the deploy that started it, the database may keep working. If you restart your app, the database may keep working. The statement you sent is still there, still holding its lock, still driving CPU up, until it finishes, or until someone kills it on the database side.

That is why the partial recovery at 12:37 is so instructive. Deploys resumed, but deploy start times were about 20 seconds instead of a few hundred milliseconds. That is not a healthy system. That is a system still carrying a heavy load it has not named yet. The migration was still running, quietly, underneath a recovery that looked good enough.

Then a well meaning restart at 13:17, meant to rebalance load, made things worse. Connections and errors rose, and the second, longer period of impact began. When a system is already struggling with a hidden load, adding a restart on top can tip it from slow to stuck.

There were two more unlucky breaks in this incident, and both are worth noting because they are the kind of thing you only discover when you need them. A pre-upgrade step to create a database clone for rollback could not be completed, because of an error from the underlying cloud provider. So a fast rollback was not available. Later, an attempt to add database capacity failed for the same kind of reason. Two escape routes, both blocked by the same dependency. If your rollback plan depends on a step that can fail, test that step, not just the plan that assumes it worked.

Three guards you can add this week

None of this requires a platform team. The guards below are for the database you already run. Render's postmortem does not name its database engine or the exact migration statement, so treat the code here as a general guard for your own migrations, not as a description of Render's setup.

1. Put a leash on every migration

A migration should never be allowed to run forever, holding a lock, while you wonder what happened. Set a lock timeout before you run DDL, which is the database term for statements that change schema. On Postgres, that looks like this:

SET lock_timeout = '30s';
SET statement_timeout = '10min';
ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS retry_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

A lock timeout says: if you cannot get the lock in 30 seconds, give up loudly instead of queueing behind everything else. A statement timeout says: if the whole statement takes longer than 10 minutes, stop it. The numbers are yours to choose. The point is that a migration fails fast and visibly, instead of succeeding slowly while it strangles the system. A failed migration you can see is better than a running migration you cannot.

If you use a migration tool, check whether it sets these for you. Many do not, by default. That one setting is the difference between a bad deploy you roll back in minutes and a bad afternoon you reconstruct from a timeline.

2. Kill it on the database side, and prove it is dead

When you stop a migration, do not trust the client. Check the database itself for long running statements, and terminate the one you mean to terminate. On Postgres, you can look like this:

SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS running_for, state, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
  AND query_start < now() - interval '5 minutes'
ORDER BY query_start;

pg_stat_activity is Postgres's view of what every connection is doing right now. pid is the process id of that connection on the database server. If you find your migration there after you stopped the client, terminate that process id on the database side, then run the query again and confirm it is gone. The second check matters. The Render timeline shows a gap of about an hour and a quarter between stopping the client and finding the migration still running. A check that takes thirty seconds would have closed that gap.

In Python, the same habit looks like this: never assume a cancelled task cancelled the work. If you cancel a migration runner, follow it with a check against the database before you declare the rollback done.

def migration_is_still_running(conn, needle):
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT pid, query FROM pg_stat_activity "
        "WHERE state = 'active' AND query ILIKE %s",
        ("%" + needle + "%",),
    ).fetchall()
    return rows

Pass in a distinctive fragment of the migration statement, and treat a non-empty result as "not rolled back yet". That is a small function, and it is the one Render's team would have wanted at 12:35.

3. Keep hot job state away from reporting data

The scheduler database held both core job state and secondary data for search and reporting. That is a quiet design choice with a loud failure mode. When one store does two jobs, a problem in the less important job can block the important one. A reporting query, a search index rebuild, or a migration on a shared table can all hold up the thing that actually starts your deploys.

You do not need to split the database on day one. But you can ask one question before your next migration: does this table also carry the state that decides whether work starts? If it does, that migration deserves a production sized test, a lock timeout, and a named person watching it. A practice run in a test environment passed for Render, and the migration still locked a large table in production. Test data is usually small. Production tables are not. A migration that is instant on a thousand rows can be a lock storm on millions. If you cannot test at production size, test at a size that at least makes the lock visible, and treat "it was fast in test" as weak evidence, not a guarantee.

Render's planned fixes point the same way: blue-green deploys for this component, so the system is not upgraded under load, cross-zone high availability for the database, and storage mechanisms better suited to the scheduler workload. Blue-green means running the new version alongside the old one and switching traffic over only when the new one is healthy, instead of upgrading the live system in place. That is a bigger change than a lock timeout, but it is the same idea at platform scale: never upgrade the only copy of a critical path while it is carrying traffic.

What to check before your next migration

Look at the last migration you ran, or the next one in your queue, and ask four questions.

First, if you stop the client mid-migration, what kills the statement on the database? If you cannot answer that, find the answer before the migration, not during the incident.

Second, what timeout bounds it? If there is none, add one.

Third, does the table it touches also hold the state that starts work? If it does, that migration is critical path work, whatever its size looks like in test.

Fourth, does your rollback depend on a step that can fail on its own, like a clone or a capacity increase? If it does, test that step separately, and have a second way back.

The Render outage did not come from a exotic bug. It came from an ordinary migration, on an ordinary upgrade, with a rollback plan that had a hole in it and a running statement nobody could see from the client side. That is what makes it worth learning from. Your next migration will also look ordinary, right up until it does not.

Sources: Render postmortem, "Builds, deploys, and queued deploys are not starting in all regions", October 14, 2026 incident, postmortem posted October 22, 2026, https://postmortem.io/incidents/render--2026-10-14--job-scheduler-schema-migration-builds-deploys/

When was the last time a migration surprised you, and did you check the database side before you called it rolled back?

title: Java Complete Beginner Blog: Theory + Technical + Real Understanding
description:
Java is a powerful, object-oriented programming language used to build applications that run on many devices and operating systems. This blog explains Java from the basics to constructors, OOP, loops, memory, and runtime concepts in a simple way, with code, output, and diagrams.

1. What Is Java?

Java is a high-level, object-oriented, platform-independent programming language. It was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems and first released in 1996 as JDK 1.0.

Java is used to build:
Android apps

  • Banking and finance systems
  • Web backend applications
  • Enterprise software
  • Cloud applications
  • Desktop applications

Java code is written in .java files, compiled into .class bytecode files, and executed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM).

Human-readable code  →  Bytecode  →  JVM  →  Output
     Main.java           Main.class              Hello World

2. Why Java?

Java is popular because it is:

  • Platform-independent: The same Java program can run on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
  • Object-oriented: Real-world things can be represented using classes and objects.
  • Secure: Java has strong memory management and runtime checks.
  • Stable: Large companies use Java for systems that must run for many years.
  • Job-friendly: Java is still widely used in backend, Android, banking, insurance, and enterprise development.
  • Community support: Java has huge documentation, libraries, frameworks, and learning resources.

3. Java History

Java was originally called Oak. Later, it was renamed Java and released publicly in 1996.

Year Java version Important point
1996 JDK 1.0 First public release oracle
1997 JDK 1.1 Improved event handling
2004 Java 5 Generics, enums, for-each loop
2014 Java 8 Lambda expressions, Streams
2018 Java 11 LTS version ops
2021 Java 17 LTS version ops
2023 Java 21 LTS version ops
2025 Java 25 Latest LTS version ops+1

Java 8, 11, 17, 21, and 25 are LTS versions, meaning Long-Term Support versions. Companies prefer LTS versions because they receive support and updates for a longer time.

4. What Is a Fortune 500 Company?

A Fortune 500 company is a company listed in the Fortune magazine’s annual list of the 500 largest United States companies by total revenue.
Examples include companies such as:

  • Amazon
  • Walmart
  • JPMorgan Chase
  • Google
  • Microsoft Many large companies use Java because their systems need stability, security, scalability, and long-term support. Java is especially common in banking, insurance, financial services, and government systems.

5. Do 90% of Companies Use Java?

No. The statement “90% of companies use Java” is not accurate.

Java is very widely used, but not by 90% of all companies. In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, about 29.4% of all respondents reported using Java. Java adoption is higher in large companies, banking, insurance, and government sectors.

So the correct way to write it in a blog is:
Java is used by millions of developers and many large enterprises, especially in banking, insurance, backend systems, and Android development. However, it is not correct to say that 90% of all companies use Java.

6. Is Java the Fastest Programming Language?

No. Java is not the fastest programming language in every situation.

Languages such as C, C++, Rust, and Zig are generally faster for raw, low-level performance because they compile more directly to machine code. However, Java is still very fast for real-world applications because the JVM uses JIT compilation to convert frequently used bytecode into optimized machine code while the program runs.

In one 2026 benchmark, Java completed the tested workloads close to C#, Go, and C-level performance, but it was not the overall fastest language.

Correct statement:
Java is not always the fastest language, but it is fast enough for most enterprise, backend, and Android applications.

7. Java Job Market

Java remains in demand, especially for:

  • Backend developer roles
  • Android developer roles
  • Full-stack Java roles
  • Software engineer roles
  • Enterprise application developer roles In 2026, Java is still used heavily in enterprise backend systems and cloud services. Large companies continue to hire Java developers because many existing business systems are built using Java.

Java skills that improve job opportunities:

  • Core Java
  • OOP
  • Collections
  • JDBC
  • Spring Boot
  • REST APIs
  • SQL and databases
  • Git
  • Maven or Gradle

8. Java Plays Well With Others

Java works well with other technologies:

  • Databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, MongoDB
  • Web: Spring Boot, REST APIs, JSON
  • Cloud: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud
  • Android: Android apps use Java or Kotlin
  • Build tools: Maven, Gradle
  • Version control: Git and GitHub Example: A Java backend application can receive a request from a website, read data from a MySQL database, process it, and return JSON data to the frontend.

9. String Types in Java

A String is a non-primitive data type used to store text.

String one = "hi";
System.out.println(one);

Output:
hi

String array

String[] playlists = new String[3];

playlists[0] = "songs1";
playlists[1] = "songs2";
playlists[2] = "songs3";

System.out.println(playlists[0]);

Output:
songs1

Here:

  • String[] means an array of String values.
  • new String[3] creates space for 3 String values.
  • playlists[0] accesses the first value because array indexing starts from 0.

10. Compile Time vs Runtime

This is one of the most important Java concepts.

Compile time
Compile time is when the Java compiler checks and converts your source code into bytecode.

javac Main.java

At compile time, Java checks:

  • Syntax errors
  • Missing semicolons
  • Wrong variable names
  • Wrong data types
  • Missing methods
  • Access modifier mistakes

Example:
int age = "twenty"; // Compile-time error
Error:
incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int

Runtime
Runtime is when the JVM actually executes the compiled bytecode.
java Main
At runtime, Java handles:

  • User input
  • File reading
  • Database connection
  • Network calls
  • Arithmetic errors
  • Null pointer errors
  • Garbage collection Example: 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        int b = 0;

        int result = a / b; // Runtime error
        System.out.println(result);
    }
}

Output:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
The code compiles successfully because the syntax is correct. But when the program runs, dividing by zero causes a runtime exception.

Diagram

Write code
   ↓
Compile time: javac checks syntax
   ↓
If no error → Main.class bytecode
   ↓
Runtime: JVM executes bytecode
   ↓
Output OR runtime exception

11. Class and Object

A class is a blueprint.
An object is a real instance created from that blueprint.

class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    void display() {
        System.out.println(name + " - " + age);
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student();
        s1.name = "Rakesh";
        s1.age = 20;
        s1.display();
    }
}

Output:
Rakesh- 20

  • Student is the class.
  • s1 is the object.
  • new Student() creates the object in heap memory.
  • s1.name accesses the object’s attribute.

12. Variables in Java

Local variable
A local variable is declared inside a method and can be used only inside that method.

void show() {
    int localNumber = 10; // Local variable
    System.out.println(localNumber);
}

Global variable
A global variable is declared inside a class but outside methods.

class Student {
    String name; // Global / instance variable
}

Static variable
A static variable belongs to the class, not to one object. All objects share the same static variable.

class College {
    static String collegeName = "ABC College";
}

Non-static variable
A non-static variable belongs to each object separately.

class Student {
    String name; // Each object has its own name
}

Example:

class Student {
    static String collegeName = "ABC College";
    String name;

    Student(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student("Arun");
        Student s2 = new Student("Priya");

        System.out.println(s1.name);
        System.out.println(s2.name);
        System.out.println(Student.collegeName);
    }
}

Output:Arun
Priya
ABC College

13. Methods
A method is a block of code that performs a specific task.

returnType methodName(parameters) {
    // method body
}

Example:

public class Main {
    static int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int result = add(5, 3);
        System.out.println(result);
    }
}

Output:
8

Method return type

  • int: Returns an integer.
  • String: Returns text.
  • void: Returns nothing. 
static String getName() {
    return "Arun";
}

14. Static Method vs Non-Static Method

Static method
A static method belongs to the class. You can call it without creating an object.

class MathUtils {
    static int square(int number) {
        return number * number;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(MathUtils.square(5));
    }
}

Output:
25

Non-static method
A non-static method belongs to an object. You must create an object to call it.

class Student {
    void greet() {
        System.out.println("Hello Student");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        s.greet();
    }
}

Output:
Hello Student

15. Access Modifiers

Access modifiers control who can access a class, method, or variable.

Modifier Access level
public Accessible everywhere
private Accessible only inside the same class
protected Accessible in the same package and subclasses
default Accessible only in the same package 
public class Student {
    private int marks = 90;

    public int getMarks() {
        return marks;
    }
}

Here, marks is private, so another class cannot directly access it. But it can access it through the public method getMarks().
This is called encapsulation.

16. this Keyword

this refers to the current object.

class Student {
    String name;

    Student(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

Here:

  • name inside Student(String name) is the parameter.
  • this.name is the object variable.
  • this.name = name; assigns the parameter value to the object variable.

17. super Keyword

super refers to the parent class.

class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    void sound() {
        super.sound(); // Calls parent class method
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog d = new Dog();
        d.sound();
    }
}

Output:
Animal makes sound
Dog barks

18. new Keyword

The new keyword creates an object in memory.
Student s1 = new Student();

  • Student is the class.
  • s1 is the reference variable.
  • new allocates memory.
  • Student() calls the constructor.

19. Constructor in Java

A constructor is a special method used to initialize an object. It has the same name as the class and has no return type.

class Student {
    String name;

    Student(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

When is a constructor used?
A constructor is used when an object is created.
Student s1 = new Student("rakesh");
Here, Student("rakesh") calls the constructor and sets the name immediately.

Why use a constructor?
Without a constructor:

Student s1 = new Student();
s1.name = "Arun";

With a constructor:
Student s1 = new Student("Arun");
The constructor makes object creation cleaner and safer.

Default constructor
If you do not write any constructor, Java automatically provides a default constructor.

class Student {
    String name;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student(); // Default constructor
    }
}

Empty constructor
An empty constructor is written by the programmer but has no code inside.

class Student {
    Student() {
        // Empty constructor
    }
}

Difference:

  • Default constructor: Automatically provided by Java when no constructor is written.
  • Empty constructor: Manually written by the developer with no statements inside.

Constructor overloading
Constructor overloading means having multiple constructors with different parameters.

class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    Student() {
        this.name = "Unknown";
        this.age = 0;
    }

    Student(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = 0;
    }

    Student(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student();
        Student s2 = new Student("Arun");
        Student s3 = new Student("Priya", 21);

        System.out.println(s1.name + " " + s1.age);
        System.out.println(s2.name + " " + s2.age);
        System.out.println(s3.name + " " + s3.age);
    }
}

Output:
Unknown 0
Arun 0
Priya 21

20. Destructor in Java

Java does not have a destructor like C++.
Instead, Java uses the Garbage Collector to remove unused objects from memory.

Student s1 = new Student();
s1 = null; // Object becomes unused

Later, the Garbage Collector may remove that unused object automatically. You normally do not need to manually destroy objects in Java.

21. Method Overriding

Overriding means a child class provides its own version of a parent class method.

class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes sound");
    }
}

class Cat extends Animal {
    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Cat meows");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal a = new Cat();
        a.sound();
    }
}

Output:
Cat meows

We use overriding when a child class needs different behavior from the parent class.

22. Interface in Java

An interface is a contract. It defines what a class should do, but not always how it should do it.


interface Vehicle {
    void start();
}

class Car implements Vehicle {
    public void start() {
        System.out.println("Car starts with key");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Car car = new Car();
        car.start();
    }
}

Output:
Car starts with key

Why use an interface?

  • To achieve abstraction
  • To define common behavior
  • To support multiple inheritance of type
  • To make code flexible

Types of interface methods

interface Example {
    void normalMethod(); // Abstract method

    default void defaultMethod() {
        System.out.println("Default method");
    }

    static void staticMethod() {
        System.out.println("Static method");
    }
}

23. extends vs implements

Keyword Used with Purpose
extends Class Inherit from a parent class
implements Interface Implement interface methods 
class Animal { }

class Dog extends Animal { }

interface RunnableTask {
    void run();
}

class Task implements RunnableTask {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Task running");
    }
}

24. Lambda Function

A lambda function is a short way to write a method, especially for functional interfaces.

Normal way:

interface Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b);
}

class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Calculator c = new Calculator() {
            public int add(int a, int b) {
                return a + b;
            }
        };

        System.out.println(c.add(5, 3));
    }
}

Lambda way:

interface Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b);
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Calculator add = (a, b) -> a + b;
        System.out.println(add.add(5, 3));
    }
}

Output:
8

We use lambda functions to write shorter, cleaner code.

25. Memory Management: Primitive vs Non-Primitive

Primitive variables
Primitive variables store the actual value directly.
int a = 10;
Here, a stores 10 directly.

Non-primitive variables
Non-primitive variables store the reference or address of an object.
String name = new String("rakesh");
Here, name stores a reference to the String object in memory.

Primitive:
a → 10

Non-primitive:
name → String object in heap memory

26. Naming Variables

Use clear and meaningful names.

Good:

int studentAge;
String studentName;
double monthlySalary;

Bad:

int a;
String x;
double m;

Rules:

  • Class names start with a capital letter: Student
  • Variable and method names start with a small letter: studentName
  • Constants use capital letters: MAX_MARKS
  • Do not use reserved keywords as names.

27. Static Class Information

A static variable stores class-level information.

class School {
    static String schoolName = "Green School";
}

All objects share the same schoolName.

A non-static variable stores object-specific information.

class Student {
    String name;
}

Each student object can have a different name.

28. Operators and Comparison Operators

Arithmetic operators

int a = 10;
int b = 3;

System.out.println(a + b); // 13
System.out.println(a - b); // 7
System.out.println(a * b); // 30
System.out.println(a / b); // 3
System.out.println(a % b); // 1

Comparison operators

int a = 10;
int b = 20;

System.out.println(a == b); // false
System.out.println(a != b); // true
System.out.println(a > b);  // false
System.out.println(a < b);  // true
System.out.println(a >= b); // false
System.out.println(a <= b); // true

29. Reserved Keywords

Reserved keywords are special words already defined by Java.
Examples:

public, private, class, static, void, int, if, else, for, while, return, new, this, super, extends, implements

You cannot use them as variable names.
int class = 10; // Error

  1. Arrays An array stores multiple values of the same type. 
int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40};

System.out.println(numbers[0]); // 10
System.out.println(numbers.length); // 4

Enhanced for loop

int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30};

for (int number : numbers) {
    System.out.println(number);
}

Output:
10
20
30

31. Loops

while loop

int i = 1;

while (i <= 3) {
    System.out.println(i);
    i++;
}

Output:
1
2
3

do-while loop
A do-while loop runs at least once.

int i = 1;

do {
    System.out.println(i);
    i++;
} while (i <= 3);

Output:
1
2
3

for loop

for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

32. break and continue

break
break stops the loop.

for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i == 3) {
        break;
    }
    System.out.println(i);
}

Output:
1
2

continue
continue skips the current iteration.

for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i == 3) {
        continue;
    }
    System.out.println(i);
}

Output:
1
2
4
5

33. Taking User Input

Use the Scanner class.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);

    System.out.print("Enter your name: ");
    String name = scanner.nextLine();

    System.out.print("Enter your age: ");
    int age = scanner.nextInt();

    System.out.println("Name: " + name);
    System.out.println("Age: " + age);
}

}

Sample output:

Enter your name: Arun
Enter your age: 20
Name: Arun
Age: 20

34. Printing Object Attributes 

class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    Student(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }

    void printDetails() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student("rakesh", 20);
        s1.printDetails();
    }
}

Output:
Name: rakesh
Age: 20

  1. Random Numbers 
import java.util.Random;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Random random = new Random();

        int number = random.nextInt(10); // 0 to 9
        System.out.println(number);
    }
}

For a number from 1 to 10:
int number = random.nextInt(10) + 1;

36. printf

printf is used for formatted output.

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String name = "rakesh";
        int age = 20;
        double marks = 89.567;

        System.out.printf("Name: %s, Age: %d, Marks: %.2f%n", name, age, marks);
    }
}

Output:
Name: rakesh, Age: 20, Marks: 89.57

  • %s: String
  • %d: Integer
  • %.2f: Decimal number with 2 digits
  • %n: New line

37. substring

substring() extracts part of a String.

String name = "JavaScript";

System.out.println(name.substring(0, 4));

Output:
Java
Here, index 0 is included, but index 4 is not included.

38. Enhanced Switch

Modern Java supports enhanced switch syntax.

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int day = 2;

        String dayName = switch (day) {
            case 1 -> "Monday";
            case 2 -> "Tuesday";
            case 3 -> "Wednesday";
            default -> "Invalid day";
        };

        System.out.println(dayName);
    }
}

Output:
Tuesday

39. Types of Arguments

Formal parameters
Parameters written in the method definition.

static void greet(String name) {
    System.out.println("Hello " + name);
}

Actual arguments
Values passed while calling the method.
greet("rakesh");

Varargs
Varargs allows a method to receive any number of values.

static int sum(int... numbers) {
    int total = 0;

    for (int number : numbers) {
        total += number;
    }

    return total;
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(sum(1, 2));
    System.out.println(sum(1, 2, 3, 4));
}

Output:
3
10

40. Math Class

The Math class provides built-in mathematical methods.

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Math.max(10, 20)); // 20
        System.out.println(Math.min(10, 20)); // 10
        System.out.println(Math.sqrt(25));    // 5.0
        System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 3));   // 8.0
        System.out.println(Math.abs(-10));    // 10
    }
}

Output:
20
10
5.0
8.0
10

title: Construir un SaaS multi-tenant en Laravel: la serie que me habría gustado leer primero: 01 de 08
description:
Por qué escribo una serie sobre diseñar y entregar un SaaS multi-tenant en Laravel: qué haría distinto desde el primer día, qué cubre la serie, a quién va dirigida y cómo leerla.

Este es el artículo que habría querido leer antes de empezar a construir un sistema multi-tenant. Me habría ahorrado tiempo, mucho código reescrito y muchas horas migrando sistemas que ya estaban en marcha.

La mayoría de las decisiones caras en un SaaS multi-tenant son baratas el día uno y costosas el día cuatrocientos. Dónde vive el tenant en el schema, cómo una petición encuentra su empresa, qué sabe un job en segundo plano sobre para quién trabaja: cada una se puede resolver bien en una tarde al principio, o arreglar después con una migración, una reescritura y un deploy con los nervios de punta. Conozco el segundo camino porque lo he recorrido. Esta serie es lo que haría el primer día si empezara de nuevo, sabiendo lo que sé ahora.

Aquí va uno de esos caminos. Empecé multi-tenant, pero no multiusuario. Añadir el multiusuario después no fue una funcionalidad. Fue una reescritura que tocó todo el sistema. Y las guardas que mantienen los datos de un tenant lejos de otro no estaban tan bien construidas como debían. Los dos problemas están en los cimientos, y por eso el primer artículo de la serie trata de quién pertenece a qué empresa y cómo lo descubre una petición.

Qué es esta serie

Es un conjunto de decisiones con sus razones adjuntas, escrito para desarrolladores que ya construyen con Laravel y quieren diseñar y entregar un SaaS multi-tenant sin aprender las partes difíciles por el camino lento. Cada artículo sigue el mismo producto ficticio, una app de facturación donde el tenant es una Company, de modo que los ejemplos conectan de uno a otro.

No es una guía de paquetes, y no es un framework. No encontrarás una librería que instalar que te resuelva el tenancy. Encontrarás las piezas que creo que vale la pena construir tú mismo, por qué, y qué cuesta cada una. Donde una decisión es cuestión de criterio, lo digo.

Qué asume

Unas pocas elecciones están fijadas para que la serie pueda ir en profundidad y no en extensión:

  • Una aplicación Laravel y una base de datos, con una columna company_id en las tablas que pertenecen a un tenant. Si todavía decides entre un monolito modular y microservicios, esa es otra pregunta, y escribí sobre cómo abordarla en Monolito modular o microservicios: un marco para decidir sin dogmas.
  • Laravel 13 y PostgreSQL en los ejemplos, aunque casi todo aplica a otras versiones y a MySQL. El único artículo que depende de PostgreSQL lo dice desde el principio.
  • Un lector con algo de experiencia. No explico qué es un middleware ni una cola.

Lo que se deja fuera a propósito: una base de datos separada por tenant, el single sign-on y los detalles de cualquier proveedor de pagos concreto. Cada uno merece su propia serie, y ninguno es donde suele doler una primera versión.

Qué encontrarás

Estos son los artículos en el orden en que yo los leería. Cada uno se sostiene solo una vez que conoces el contexto del tenant del primero. Actualizo esta lista a medida que se publica la serie: un título con enlace ya está publicado, y un título sin enlace está por llegar.

  1. SaaS multi-tenant en Laravel: una base de datos, un global scope y las fugas que no detecta. El cimiento: cómo una petición encuentra su empresa, un scope que falla cerrado y lo que el scope todavía no ve.
  2. Adiós a los controladores gordos en Laravel: las Actions como hogar de la lógica de negocio. Dónde viven las reglas, para que un controlador, un comando y una API compartan una sola implementación.
  3. Data objects, Concerns y Events: el reparto de apoyo de una Action en Laravel. Qué alimenta a una Action, qué comparte y qué anuncia, con el contexto de tenant llevado a los listeners en cola.
  4. De la idea al primer cliente de pago: una hoja de ruta de entrega para un SaaS multi-tenant en Laravel. El orden del trabajo: muros antes que habitaciones, un slice temprano, límites de plan, webhooks de facturación y deploys seguros.
  5. Probar el aislamiento entre tenants en Laravel: tests de fuga, tests de guarda y lo que aún no detectan. Cómo demostrar, en cada commit, que una empresa no puede ver a otra.
  6. Observabilidad por tenant en Laravel: logs, métricas y errores por empresa. Cómo responder "¿qué le pasó a esta empresa?" sin ahogarte en datos.
  7. Row-Level Security en PostgreSQL: un segundo muro para una app Laravel multi-tenant. Una capa opcional a nivel de base de datos detrás del scope de la aplicación, y los casos en que vale su costo.

Cómo leerla

Dos hábitos ayudarán. Primero, trata el código como un punto de partida. Los fragmentos son pequeños a propósito, y no los he ejecutado contra tu schema, tus policies ni tu configuración de deploy. Segundo, presta atención a las secciones de costos. Cada patrón de aquí tiene un precio, y la pregunta honesta no es "¿es esto una buena práctica?" sino "¿vale la pena para mi equipo, a mi tamaño, este año?".

A veces la respuesta es que no. Una Action de paso, un Data object para dos argumentos o una política de base de datos para un prototipo son formas de gastar un esfuerzo que necesitabas en otro sitio.

Conclusión

Escribo esta serie porque el consejo más útil que puedo darle a mi yo del pasado es también el que la mayoría de los equipos oye demasiado tarde: decide los cimientos pronto, hazlos comprobables y mantén aburrido todo lo demás. Si estás a punto de empezar un producto multi-tenant, o estás lo bastante al principio como para que los cimientos aún puedan cambiar, empieza por el contexto del tenant. Todo lo demás de la serie se apoya en él.

title: International Ecommerce in Germany: Better Product Discovery
description:
`# International Ecommerce in Germany: Improving Product Discovery for Online Stores

Building an ecommerce website for an international audience introduces challenges that go beyond translating website content.

Customers need to understand product information, navigate categories easily and feel confident when purchasing products online.

For developers and ecommerce businesses serving customers in Germany, localisation and user experience should be considered important parts of the development process.

Here are six practical areas to consider.

1. Localise More Than Just the Language

A translated website is not necessarily a fully localised website.

Localisation can include:

  • German-language navigation
  • Clear product descriptions
  • Appropriate currency formatting
  • Familiar date and measurement formats
  • Local delivery information
  • Relevant customer support information

The objective is to make the shopping experience feel natural to the intended audience.

2. Build a Logical Product Taxonomy

International grocery stores often have products from several countries and food cultures.

A useful product taxonomy can organise products by:

  • Food category
  • Country or cuisine
  • Product type
  • Brand
  • Dietary characteristics, where verified

A well-designed taxonomy improves navigation and can also help search engines understand the relationship between website pages.

3. Improve Internal Search

Customers may search using different product names, spellings or languages.

An effective search system should consider:

  • Alternative product spellings
  • Brand names
  • Synonyms
  • Category filters
  • Relevant product suggestions

Search analytics can reveal what customers are looking for and which searches return poor results.

4. Make Product Pages Informative

A product page should answer the most important questions before a customer makes a purchase.

For grocery products, this might include:

  • Product name and brand
  • Net weight or quantity
  • Ingredient information
  • Preparation instructions
  • Storage instructions
  • Product images
  • Availability

Accurate product information is especially important for international products that customers may not recognise immediately.

5. Optimise Mobile Performance

Mobile shopping should be treated as a core requirement.

Developers can improve the experience by:

  • Compressing images
  • Reducing unnecessary JavaScript
  • Using responsive product grids
  • Improving page loading performance
  • Keeping navigation accessible
  • Simplifying checkout

Performance testing should cover product pages, category pages and checkout, not just the homepage.

6. Use Data to Improve Ecommerce Decisions

Analytics can help identify problems in the customer journey.

For example, high search usage with low product engagement may indicate that search results need improvement.

High cart abandonment may indicate friction during checkout or unclear delivery information.

Measuring these behaviours provides a more reliable basis for improvements than making design decisions based only on assumptions.

A Real-World Ecommerce Context

International grocery stores provide an interesting example of the importance of localisation and product discovery.

TargetMart.de focuses on international food products and grocery shopping in Germany.

Its product category structure and international food focus illustrate why ecommerce platforms need to make different cuisines and product types easy to discover.

Conclusion

Building an ecommerce website for the German market requires attention to language, product organisation, accurate information, mobile performance and customer expectations.

The best approach is to treat localisation as part of the overall product experience rather than simply translating text.

For developers, these improvements can make ecommerce websites easier to navigate, understand and use.`

title: Adding 8 working hours is harder than it looks
description:
A support desk in London works 09:00 to 17:00 on weekdays, with a lunch hour, and is closed on 25 and 28 December 2026. A ticket comes in at 16:30 on Christmas Eve with an 8-hour SLA. When is it due?

The answer is 09:30 on Wednesday 30 December. Getting there means skipping lunch hours, a weekend and two holidays, all in the desk's own time zone. That's business-time arithmetic, and it turns up everywhere: support SLAs, payroll and overtime, delivery ETAs that only count operating hours, staff rosters.

I built workclock, an open-source library for it: one Rust core, published for Rust, Python and JavaScript. This post walks through the cases that make the problem harder than it looks, and how workclock handles each one.

Why another library

I'd worked on this kind of problem before, with shifts that run past midnight. In Python, the usual library for it is businesstimedelta. Its last release, 1.0.1, came out in September 2019, and several of its bugs are still open. I wanted a maintained replacement that gets the edge cases right, and that existing code could move to without a rewrite.

The two questions

A business-time library answers two questions:

  • How much working time lies between two instants?
  • Which instant do you reach after adding or subtracting an amount of working time?

In workclock, a schedule is built from rules. Working-hour rules produce blocks of working time; breaks and holidays produce time off. The schedule's working time is the union of the working blocks minus the union of the time off. Every operation is defined on that set, so the order you list the rules in never matters, and overlapping rules never count time twice.

That definition sounds obvious. Most of the bugs below come from code that doesn't quite follow it.

Hard case 1: shifts that cross midnight

Take a 22:00 to 06:00 shift, Monday to Friday. Between Monday 22:00 and Tuesday 06:00 there are clearly 8 working hours.

businesstimedelta 1.0.1 counts 0. Adding 4 hours at Monday 22:00 lands on Wednesday 02:00 instead of Tuesday 02:00, and subtracting 4 hours from Tuesday 06:00 raises OverflowError.

workclock's rule: if a shift's end is at or before its start, the shift is overnight and the end falls on the next date. A shift belongs to the weekday it starts on, so a Friday 22:00 to 06:00 shift runs into Saturday morning, and no shift ends on Monday morning unless one starts on Sunday. A start equal to the end is a 24-hour shift. With that, the three answers above become 8 hours, Tuesday 02:00 and Tuesday 02:00.

Hard case 2: holidays

Holidays look like the easy part. Two open businesstimedelta issues say otherwise:

  • Once a query passes the last date in the holiday list, it raises TypeError (#8, #10).
  • When the holidays and the working hours use different time zones, it can loop forever (#9).

The second one is subtle. A holiday defined in UTC under a Los Angeles workday doesn't remove the Los Angeles day: it removes 16:00 the day before to 16:00 on the holiday. In workclock, each rule has its own time zone, and holidays default to the schedule's zone rather than UTC, which avoids that mismatch. Dates after the last holiday are simply ordinary days.

There's also a design question: what happens when an overnight shift runs into a holiday? workclock's answer is that a holiday removes calendar time, midnight to midnight, not whole shifts. A shift that crosses into a holiday loses only the part after midnight. Keeping it that simple keeps the rules independent of each other.

Hard case 3: daylight saving time

Working hours are wall-clock times ("09:00 to 17:00 in Europe/London"), but durations are elapsed real time. So a shift that spans a DST change is an hour shorter or longer than it looks. In America/New_York, a 22:00 to 06:00 shift is 7 hours on the night of Saturday 7 March 2026, when clocks jump forward, and 9 hours on the night of Saturday 31 October 2026, when they fall back.

DST also creates local times that don't exist and local times that happen twice. workclock resolves them with the same "compatible" strategy as jiff, RFC 5545 and JavaScript Temporal:

  • A time in the spring-forward gap moves forward by the length of the gap: 02:30, on a day when clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00, becomes 03:30.
  • A time in the fall-back overlap resolves to the earlier occurrence.

Following the same rule as those ecosystems means the three bindings agree with the date libraries people already use in each language. (businesstimedelta, through pytz's localize(), picks the later occurrence. That's one of the differences listed in the migration guide.)

A holiday on a DST transition day is still midnight to midnight, so it's shorter or longer than 24 hours by the size of the change.

Hard case 4: searches that never end

Ask for "8 working hours from now" on a schedule with no working time, and a naive implementation loops forever. In businesstimedelta, a rule with no working time hangs on addition.

In workclock every search is bounded. A schedule with no working time fails when it's built. add, sub and the period lookups stop with an error if they cross 366 days, plus seven days per holiday date, without finding working time. Library code doesn't panic: failures are errors, never hangs.

One smaller fix: between(a, b) is signed. If b is before a, the result is negative, the same as subtracting two datetimes (#12).

What it looks like

Here's the support desk from the top, in Python:

from datetime import date, datetime, time
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

from workclock import Break, Holidays, Schedule, WorkDay

london = ZoneInfo("Europe/London")
support = Schedule(
    [
        WorkDay(time(9), time(17)),  # Monday to Friday by default
        Break(time(12), time(13)),
        Holidays([date(2026, 12, 25), date(2026, 12, 28)]),
    ],
    time_zone=london,
)

opened = datetime(2026, 12, 24, 16, 30, tzinfo=london)
support.add(opened, hours=8)  # 2026-12-30 09:30, London time
support.between(opened, datetime(2026, 12, 29, 11, tzinfo=london))  # 2:30:00

The JavaScript package takes Dates or ISO 8601 strings, and durations in milliseconds:

import { Schedule } from "workclock";

const support = new Schedule({
  timeZone: "Europe/London",
  rules: [
    { type: "workday", start: "09:00", end: "17:00" },
    { type: "break", start: "12:00", end: "13:00" },
    { type: "holidays", dates: ["2026-12-25", "2026-12-28"] },
  ],
});

support.add("2026-12-24T16:30:00Z", 8 * 3_600_000); // Date 2026-12-30T09:30:00.000Z
support.between("2026-12-24T16:30:00Z", new Date("2026-12-29T11:00:00Z")); // 9000000 ms

If you have existing businesstimedelta code, most of it runs unchanged with one import change:

import workclock.compat as businesstimedelta

The businesstimedelta test suite runs against workclock.compat in CI, and MIGRATING.md lists where it intentionally differs.

One core, three languages

The core is written in Rust on top of jiff. Python gets it through PyO3 and JavaScript through WebAssembly, so all three languages share one implementation instead of three that drift apart. The Python wheels and the npm package bundle the IANA time zone database, so they don't depend on the system's tzdata.

Every rule is specified with examples in a design document. Each example has an ID and becomes a test in every binding it applies to, and each binding is checked against a brute-force reference implementation with property-based tests.

Speed

Correctness was the point, but the engine's design also makes it fast. It computes working time a week at a time, and a week with no DST change and no holiday near it is the same as the week before, so a long span adds the previous week's total instead of rebuilding it. The cost of a span depends on how many of its weeks hold holidays or DST changes, not on its length.

Medians from Python, in a GitHub Actions run on a GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner (AMD EPYC 7763, 4 cores), against businesstimedelta 1.0.1:

Case businesstimedelta 1.0.1 workclock Speed-up
One call, a 5½-hour span 169 µs 3.96 µs 43×
One call, a year with bank holidays 53 ms 85.4 µs 620×
1,000,000 pairs 9.9 min 2.13 s (between_many on NumPy arrays) 280×

To be fair to the standard library: for one short span, a loop written by hand with datetime and zoneinfo keeps up (4.01 µs), because most of workclock's call goes on converting datetimes into and out of Rust. workclock pulls ahead as spans get longer or calls are batched, and that hand-written loop handles only one fixed schedule, without overnight shifts or per-rule time zones.

Try it 

cargo add workclock jiff
pip install workclock
npm i workclock

workclock is pre-1.0, so the API may still change in a minor release.

  • Docs: workclock.karthik.nz/docs
  • Playground: workclock.karthik.nz/playground
  • Code: github.com/Karthik-beta/workclock

If you find a case it gets wrong, an issue on GitHub is the best place to tell me.

I'm Karthik Parameshwara, a software engineer in Bengaluru. More of my work is at karthik.nz.

title: Local-First DX — What Belongs in the Browser vs a CLI
description:
I keep two folders of “tools I actually use.” One is a terminal aliases file. The other is a browser bookmarks bar labeled local. Both claim to be local-first. They solve different jobs, and mixing them up costs me more time than picking the slower option on purpose.

This isn’t “CLI good, browser bad.” It’s a decision rule for frontend DX: when should this live in the tab, and when should it stay in the shell?

The false dichotomy

People talk like local tooling is one pile. It isn’t.

  • A CLI is scriptable, pipeable, and great at files that already live on disk. Agents love it. CI loves it. Diffs love it.
  • A browser-local tool is visual, drop-zone friendly, and great at blobs you don’t want to save as tmp-whatever-3.png forever. No install. No chmod +x. Close the tab and it’s gone.

Both can keep data off a third-party server. That’s the local-first part. The UX surface is what actually changes how you work.

Where I default to the CLI

I reach for the shell when most of these are true:

  1. The input is already a path — repo files, dist/, fixtures, screenshots in e2e/artifacts/
  2. I need to repeat it — same transform tomorrow, or in CI, or for every PR
  3. I want a pipe — rg → jq → script → commit message
  4. An agent will do it — coding agents are fluent with argv and stdout; they’re clumsy in a GUI
  5. Exit codes matter — green/red in CI beats “looks fine in the preview pane”

Examples that belong here for me:

  • Lint, typecheck, format, bundle-size budgets
  • Image optimization of a whole public/ folder
  • Converting a design-token JSON into CSS variables as part of build
  • Replaying a failing Playwright run with the same flags

If I have to teach a teammate (or an agent) a click path, I’ve already lost the CLI case.

Where I default to the browser

I open a local page / side panel when most of these are true:

  1. The input is a blob I don’t want on disk yet — paste, drag-drop, clipboard screenshot
  2. I need eyes — color, layout, chart shape, crop, “does this GIF feel right”
  3. One-shot — I’m not putting this in CI; I’m answering a Slack “can you check this file”
  4. Install friction would kill the job — non-dev collaborator, locked-down laptop, hotel Wi‑Fi where npm i is a joke
  5. The output is also a blob — download once, attach, done; no need for a long-lived path in the monorepo

Examples:

  • Quick HEIC / WebP peek before I decide whether to commit it
  • Charting a client CSV I’m not allowed to upload anywhere
  • Diffing two JSON pastes from support tickets
  • Checking contrast on a hex someone dropped in chat

If the “tool” requires me to invent a filename first, the browser usually wins.

The agent angle (this changed my defaults)

Coding agents flipped a few of my old habits.

Agents are excellent at CLI. They can run pnpm test, read the log, and try again. They are mediocre at “open this URL, drop a file, click Export.” So anything I want agents to own — refactors, migrations, CI gates — stays CLI-shaped.

But agents also create a lot of visual leftovers: screenshots, generated SVG, “try this CSS,” chart previews. Those leftovers are terrible as permanent repo files and fine as ephemeral browser transforms. I stopped asking the agent to curl a SaaS converter for those. I either keep a local browser tool bookmarked, or I ask the agent to write a small Node script if the job will recur.

Rule of thumb I use now:

If the agent should do it twice, make a CLI (or a script in the repo).

If a human needs to see it once, keep it in the browser.

A boring decision checklist

When I’m adding a new “helper” for the team, I ask:

Question Lean CLI Lean browser
Will CI run it? yes no
Is the primary input a disk path? yes no (paste/drop)
Is judgment visual? no yes
Should an agent own the loop? yes no
Do non-devs need it without Node? no yes
Is the artifact temporary? maybe usually

If the table splits 3–3, I build the CLI first and add a thin browser UI later only if humans keep bouncing off the flags. Flags are documentation; a drop zone is empathy. Both can exist — just don’t start with two surfaces.

Anti-patterns I’ve paid for

Electron for a one-button transform. Congrats, you shipped an OS update surface for a FileReader job.

“Just paste into this SaaS.” Local-first died the moment the paste left the machine. Browser-local and cloud-paste are not the same category.

CLI with no --stdin / no file args, only interactive prompts. Agents and CI choke. If it’s CLI, make it non-interactive by default.

Browser tool that quietly POSTs “for processing.” Read the network tab once. Local means the heavy work stays in-tab unless I opt in.

How I keep the split sane on a team

  • Repo scripts for anything that gates merges (package.json scripts, just, make — pick one).
  • A short internal doc titled “browser-local helpers” with 5–10 bookmarks, not 40. If it isn’t in the doc, it isn’t a team tool.
  • No duplicate truth — don’t maintain a CLI and a web UI that drift. Prefer one engine (shared WASM / shared Node package) and two thin fronts only when both audiences are real.
  • Name the constraint in the PR — “this is agent-facing → CLI” or “this is designer-facing → browser” stops bikesheds.

Takeaway

Local-first isn’t a single product category. It’s a privacy/ownership promise that still needs a surface.

Put repeatable, path-based, agent-friendly work in the CLI. Put visual, ephemeral, drop-zone work in the browser. Optimize for who (or what) will run the loop next — you once, CI forever, or an agent at 2 a.m.

The wrong surface doesn’t just feel awkward. It quietly pushes people back to uploading files to whoever’s landing page loaded first. Pick deliberately, and the local habit sticks.

title: Building Better Beauty Ecommerce Websites: Hair Care
description:
Building Better Beauty Ecommerce Websites: Product Discovery for Hair Care Stores

Beauty and hair-care ecommerce websites have unique product discovery challenges.

Unlike some general retail products, hair-care products are often selected according to individual preferences, hair texture, styling routines and specific product needs.

For ecommerce developers, this creates an opportunity to build more useful product catalogues, filters and educational content.

Here are seven practical considerations when developing a hair-care ecommerce website.

1. Organise Products Around Customer Needs

A hair-care store may offer shampoos, conditioners, oils, masks, styling gels and treatments.

Organising products into clear categories helps customers navigate a large catalogue.

Possible categories include:

  • Shampoo and cleansing products
  • Conditioners and leave-in treatments
  • Curl creams and styling products
  • Hair oils and serums
  • Hair masks and deep treatments
  • Hair colour products
  • Scalp-care products

Clear categorisation is one of the foundations of good ecommerce navigation.

2. Build Useful Product Filters

Customers may want to filter products according to their intended use.

Depending on the available product information, useful filters could include:

  • Product type
  • Brand
  • Hair texture
  • Styling purpose
  • Product size
  • Price range
  • Verified product characteristics

Filters should be based on accurate product data rather than unsupported marketing claims.

3. Write Detailed Product Descriptions

Beauty products often require more information than a simple product name.

A helpful product page should explain:

  • What the product is
  • Its intended use
  • Important ingredients
  • How to use it
  • Product size
  • Relevant warnings or precautions

Clear descriptions can help customers make more informed purchasing decisions.

4. Use High-Quality Product Images

Product images are particularly important in beauty ecommerce.

Customers often want to inspect packaging, product texture, colour and size before purchasing.

Developers should consider:

  • Consistent image dimensions
  • Optimised image formats
  • Descriptive alternative text
  • Responsive image delivery
  • Fast-loading product galleries

Image optimisation can improve both usability and website performance.

5. Create Helpful Educational Content

Educational articles can help customers understand products and develop better shopping habits.

Useful content topics include:

  • How to build a basic curly hair routine
  • Understanding shampoo and conditioner
  • How leave-in conditioners are used
  • Differences between curl creams and styling gels
  • How to read hair-care product ingredients
  • Choosing products according to hair texture

Educational content should provide practical information rather than simply repeating product descriptions.

6. Improve Related Product Recommendations

Relevant recommendations can make product discovery easier.

For example, someone viewing a shampoo might also be interested in a compatible conditioner.

Someone browsing curl creams may want to explore leave-in conditioners or styling gels.

Recommendations should be genuinely related to the products being viewed.

7. Make the Website Mobile Friendly

Beauty products are frequently discovered through mobile browsing and social content.

A good mobile shopping experience should include:

  • Readable product descriptions
  • Clear product images
  • Simple category navigation
  • Accessible filters
  • Easy-to-use shopping controls
  • A straightforward checkout process

Mobile usability should be tested across different devices and screen sizes.

A Practical Example in Hair-Care Ecommerce

Specialised hair-care stores demonstrate why product categorisation and educational content matter.

Haarplaneet.nl offers hair-care and beauty products, including shampoos, conditioners, styling products, treatments and products for curly and Afro-textured hair.

This type of product range illustrates why ecommerce websites benefit from clear product information and navigation designed around different customer needs.

Final Thoughts

A good hair-care ecommerce website should help customers understand products, explore relevant categories and find items that suit their personal routines.

For developers, improving product data, search, filtering, mobile usability and educational content can create a more useful shopping experience.

The goal is not simply to display more products. It is to make product discovery easier and help customers make informed decisions.`

title: Designing Empty States That Actually Help Users, Not Just Look Nice
description:
Designing Empty States That Actually Help Users, Not Just Look Nice

An empty cart, a zero-result search, an empty wishlist — these states get hit constantly, and most stores treat them as an afterthought: a generic illustration and a flat "nothing here" message, with no actual path forward offered.

🎯 The Missed Opportunity in Every Empty State

An empty search result is a moment where the visitor has clearly expressed intent (they searched for something) and gotten nothing back — the single highest-leverage place to suggest alternatives, correct an obvious typo, or surface popular items in the category they were searching.

🖼️ Beyond the Cute Illustration

A nice illustration is fine, but it's not the thing doing the work — a clear, specific action ("browse bestsellers," "try a broader search," "here's what's in your recently viewed") is what actually recovers an otherwise lost visitor from that dead-end moment.

🔍 Worth an Actual Audit

Most stores have never actually looked at what their zero-results search page or empty cart page says, because almost nobody intentionally designs them — they're whatever the theme shipped with by default. A ten-minute audit of every empty state on the site usually finds easy wins.

Originally published on the KLYX blog.
