title: Building a Better Online Grocery Shopping Experience: 7 Things That Matter
description:
Online grocery shopping has become an important part of modern ecommerce. Customers want to find products quickly, understand what they are purchasing and complete their orders without unnecessary complications.

For ecommerce developers and online store owners, creating a good grocery shopping experience involves more than displaying products. Website structure, search functionality, product information and mobile usability all play important roles.

Here are seven areas worth considering when building or improving an online grocery store.

1. Organise Products Into Clear Categories

A well-organised product catalogue helps customers find what they need.

For an international grocery store, categories might include:

  • Rice and grains
  • Spices and seasonings
  • Snacks and sweets
  • Sauces and cooking ingredients
  • Drinks and beverages
  • Canned and packaged foods
  • International speciality products

Clear categories reduce unnecessary browsing and make the shopping journey more straightforward.

2. Make Product Search More Useful

Search functionality is particularly important for grocery websites with large product catalogues.

Consider implementing:

  • Product-name suggestions
  • Brand-based search
  • Category filters
  • Relevant search results
  • Typo-tolerant search

A customer searching for a particular ingredient should not have to browse dozens of unrelated products.

3. Write Helpful Product Descriptions

Product descriptions should explain what an item is, how it can be used and what customers should know before purchasing.

For food products, useful information can include ingredients, weight, country of origin where verified, preparation instructions and storage recommendations.

4. Prioritise Mobile Shopping

Many customers browse online stores using smartphones.

Responsive layouts, readable product information, clear navigation and accessible shopping controls can make a significant difference.

Developers should test the entire purchase journey on different screen sizes rather than checking only the homepage.

5. Improve Product Discovery

Related products and complementary ingredients can help customers discover items they might otherwise overlook.

For example, someone browsing rice could also be interested in lentils, spices or sauces.

Recommendations should remain relevant rather than overwhelming the customer.

6. Provide Transparent Shopping Information

Customers need clear information about delivery, payment methods, returns and customer support.

These details should be easy to locate before checkout.

Transparency helps establish trust and reduces confusion during the purchasing process.

7. Measure the Shopping Experience

Analytics can help store owners understand how customers interact with their websites.

Useful metrics include:

  • Product search usage
  • Category engagement
  • Add-to-cart rate
  • Checkout abandonment
  • Mobile conversion rate
  • Returning customer rate

These measurements can help identify areas that need improvement.

A Practical Example

International grocery ecommerce demonstrates why product organisation and discovery are important.

A store serving customers interested in different cuisines needs to make products easy to find across categories and food cultures.

TargetMart.nl is an example of an online store focused on international groceries and food products in the Netherlands.

Looking at specialised grocery stores can provide useful ideas for developers working on product catalogues, search functionality and category navigation.

Final Thoughts

A successful online grocery experience depends on more than having a large product selection.

Clear categories, useful descriptions, mobile-friendly design, effective search and transparent shopping information all contribute to a better customer journey.

For ecommerce developers, continuously testing and improving these elements is one of the most practical ways to build a more useful online store.`

title: How a HashMap Works: A Quick Walkthrough with Java
description:
You probably used a HashMap today without thinking about it. But what actually happens when you call map.put("apple", 3)? Let's open the box, with plain words and a small Java program you can run yourself.

The idea in one minute

A HashMap is an array of buckets. When you store something:

  1. The key goes through hashCode(), which turns it into a number.
  2. That number is reduced to a bucket index (in our model: hash % 8).
  3. The key and value are stored in that bucket.

Two different keys can land on the same bucket. That is a collision, and the bucket simply keeps them as a small chain. Finding a value means: hash the key, jump to the bucket, walk the short chain comparing keys.

Watch the flow

The animation walks three moments: storing apple in an empty bucket, storing mango which collides with apple and joins its chain, then finding apple again by walking that chain. (It shows a simplified 8-bucket teaching model - the same one the code below runs.)

Run it yourself

This tiny hash map prints every step, so you can see the hashing, the bucket choice, the collision and the chain walk:

import java.util.HashMap;

public class HashMapDemo {

    // A tiny hand-rolled hash map so we can watch every step
    static class SimpleHashMap {
        static final int BUCKETS = 8;
        static class Node {
            String key; int value; Node next;
            Node(String k, int v) { key = k; value = v; }
        }
        Node[] table = new Node[BUCKETS];

        int bucketIndex(String key) {
            return (key.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff) % BUCKETS;
        }

        void put(String key, int value) {
            int i = bucketIndex(key);
            for (Node n = table[i]; n != null; n = n.next) {
                if (n.key.equals(key)) {
                    System.out.println("put(" + key + ", " + value + ") -> bucket " + i + ": key exists, value overwritten");
                    n.value = value;
                    return;
                }
            }
            Node n = new Node(key, value);
            n.next = table[i];
            table[i] = n;
            System.out.println("put(" + key + ", " + value + ") -> hash " + (key.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff)
                + " -> bucket " + i + (n.next != null ? " (collision: added to chain)" : ""));
        }

        Integer get(String key) {
            int i = bucketIndex(key);
            int steps = 0;
            for (Node n = table[i]; n != null; n = n.next) {
                steps++;
                if (n.key.equals(key)) {
                    System.out.println("get(" + key + ") -> bucket " + i + ", found after " + steps + " step(s): " + n.value);
                    return n.value;
                }
            }
            System.out.println("get(" + key + ") -> bucket " + i + ": not in chain, returns null");
            return null;
        }

        void printTable() {
            System.out.println("\nFinal table (" + BUCKETS + " buckets):");
            for (int i = 0; i < BUCKETS; i++) {
                StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("bucket " + i + ": ");
                if (table[i] == null) sb.append("(empty)");
                for (Node n = table[i]; n != null; n = n.next) sb.append(n.key).append("=").append(n.value).append(" -> ");
                if (sb.toString().endsWith(" -> ")) sb.setLength(sb.length() - 4);
                System.out.println(sb);
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SimpleHashMap map = new SimpleHashMap();
        map.put("cat", 1);
        map.put("dog", 2);
        map.put("apple", 3);
        map.put("banana", 4);
        map.put("mango", 5);
        map.put("cat", 9);   // same key again: overwrite
        map.printTable();
        System.out.println();
        map.get("dog");
        map.get("apple");
        map.get("zebra");

        System.out.println("\n-- The real java.util.HashMap --");
        HashMap<String, Integer> real = new HashMap<>();
        real.put("cat", 1);
        real.put("dog", 2);
        real.put("apple", 3);
        real.put(null, 99);           // null key is allowed
        System.out.println("real.get(\"cat\") = " + real.get("cat"));
        System.out.println("real.get(null) = " + real.get(null));
        System.out.println("iteration order: " + real.keySet() + "  (not guaranteed, do not rely on it)");
    }
}

What it actually printed (JDK 21) 

put(cat, 1) -> hash 98262 -> bucket 6
put(dog, 2) -> hash 99644 -> bucket 4
put(apple, 3) -> hash 93029210 -> bucket 2
put(banana, 4) -> hash 751128421 -> bucket 5
put(mango, 5) -> hash 103662530 -> bucket 2 (collision: added to chain)
put(cat, 9) -> bucket 6: key exists, value overwritten

Final table (8 buckets):
bucket 0: (empty)
bucket 1: (empty)
bucket 2: mango=5 -> apple=3
bucket 3: (empty)
bucket 4: dog=2
bucket 5: banana=4
bucket 6: cat=9
bucket 7: (empty)

get(dog) -> bucket 4, found after 1 step(s): 2
get(apple) -> bucket 2, found after 2 step(s): 3
get(zebra) -> bucket 6: not in chain, returns null

-- The real java.util.HashMap --
real.get("cat") = 1
real.get(null) = 99
iteration order: [null, apple, cat, dog]  (not guaranteed, do not rely on it)

Three things to notice:

  • mango and apple both hash to bucket 2, so they sit in one chain. get("apple") checks mango first, then finds apple on step 2.
  • Storing cat again does not add a second entry; it overwrites the value (1 becomes 9).
  • zebra hashes to bucket 6, which holds cat. The map walks that chain, finds no match, and returns null - a wrong bucket is never even looked at.

The real HashMap adds a few upgrades

Our 8-bucket model keeps the moving parts visible. Per the Java 21 HashMap documentation, the real one:

  • Gives constant-time get and put, assuming the hash function spreads keys well across buckets.
  • Grows automatically: when entries exceed capacity x load factor (default 0.75), it rehashes to roughly twice the buckets.
  • Permits one null key and any number of null values.
  • Makes no order guarantees - do not rely on iteration order.
  • Is not synchronized; for concurrent access wrap it with Collections.synchronizedMap (or use a concurrent map).
  • Can use comparison order to break ties when many keys share a hash code (in practice, very long chains are turned into trees to keep lookups fast).

Sources

  • HashMap (Java SE 21 & JDK 21)
  • Object.hashCode() (Java SE 21 & JDK 21)

Written with AI assistance; code examples were compiled and run on JDK 21 before publishing.

title: Least privilege, checked by a compiler
description:
TL;DR: In Staal, code can't send a message, write a file, call an API or move money unless it holds a capability for that action. Capabilities come only from the host app, can only be narrowed, are checked before every action, and are never handed to a model. Below: how that works, real compiler errors, a real run's log, and a benchmark against plain Python.

Nine seconds

On April 24, 2026, an AI coding agent deleted a company's production database in nine seconds.

It was doing routine maintenance in staging for PocketOS, which builds software for car rental businesses. It hit a credential mismatch, searched the filesystem, and found an API token in an unrelated file. The token had been created to manage custom domains, but it was root-scoped: it could perform any operation the hosting provider's API offered. One call later, the production volume was gone, along with every backup stored inside it.

The model made a bad call, but that isn't the interesting part. The task needed to fix a configuration in staging. The token could delete production. Nothing between the agent and the API knew what the task was, so nothing could say that's too much power for this.

It's a pattern. In July, researchers showed that an instruction left in a public GitHub issue could steer an agentic workflow into leaking private repository data. In Gravitee's survey of 750 organisations this year, excessive permissions was the most consistently reported failure: agents with more access than their task needs, often through shared service accounts and inherited credentials.

Models will keep being wrong, and keep being talked into things. What decides the damage is how much the agent was able to do.

The payment networks already know the answer

Where agents touch money, the industry has stopped handing them general-purpose credentials. Stripe's agentic commerce tokens are scoped to one merchant, one session and one amount range, and usable once. Mastercard's Agent Pay makes an agent present a signed record of what it was asked to do, and the network stops a transaction that goes beyond it.

That's capability security, an idea that's decades old: instead of asking who are you and what may you do?, hand out unforgeable tokens that each carry one bounded power. The payment networks are building it into their rails one network at a time. Staal builds it into the language, for every action an agent's code takes.

Authority as a value

A capability is part of a function's type, and the type says how far it reaches:

`fn remind(patients: List<Patient, 50>, texts: cap sms.send(uses: 50, only: ["234*"])) -> Int
fn archive(report: Report, files: cap fs.write(only: ["/reports/*"])) -> Receipt
fn open_doors(lock: cap building.lock.open(uses: 2, only: ["north-door", "loading-bay"])) -> Done
fn refund(r: Refund, pay: cap payments.refund(max: 500 USD, each: 50 USD)) -> Receipt`

The first can send at most 50 texts, only to Nigerian numbers. The second can write only under /reports. The third can open the north door and the loading bay, at most twice in all. The fourth can refund at most 50 USD at a time and 500 USD in total.

Limit What it bounds
only which targets an action may touch: exact text, or a pattern with one *
uses how many actions may be attempted, failed ones included
each the most money one action may move
max the most money moved in total over the run

The names after cap aren't built in. sms.send, building.lock.open and payments.refund are paths chosen by whoever deploys the program, and the rules treat them all alike. You can read a signature like these in code review and know the most the function can ever do before you read its body.

Only the app creates authority

Nothing inside a Staal program can create a capability: no function, no library, no model. They come from the host app that starts the run, which is ordinary Python or Node.js and the only place that knows which customer this is and what they're entitled to:

python

import staal

lib = staal.Library()
TIER_LIMIT = {"gold": 500, "standard": 50}  # USD per refund, decided by your app

def handle(customer, order, complaint, model):
    limit = min(TIER_LIMIT[customer["tier"]], order["total"])
    return lib.run("refund.staal", {
        "entry": "main",
        "inputs": {"complaint": complaint},
        "grants": {"pay": {"cap": "payments.refund",
                            "each": {"amount": str(limit), "currency": "USD"},
                            "only": [order["payment_id"]]}},
        "model": model,
    })

The app decides; Staal enforces, and so does the code's own signature. If the program declares each: 500 USD and the app grants 800 by mistake, the run gets 500. A grant can narrow what the code accepts, never widen it.

The config is validated before anything runs: a missing grant or an unknown key means nothing starts. And capabilities, receipts and outcomes are never accepted as inputs at any depth, so neither input data nor a model can forge one.

That's the answer to the token in the unrelated file. A token found lying around is only text. Acting with it still needs a capability for that API, and only the app can grant one.

Narrowed, never widened

A capability can be passed on, and every time it's passed on it can only shrink:

text

type Patient { name: Text, phone: Text }

fn remind(patients: List<Patient, 50>, texts: cap sms.send(uses: 50, only: ["234*"])) -> Int {
    let sent = 0
    for p in patients {
        let r = try notify(p, texts)
        if r.ok {
            set sent = sent + 1
        }
    }
    return sent
}

fn notify(p: Patient, texts: cap sms.send(uses: 1, only: ["234*"])) -> Receipt {
    return texts.send(p.phone, "Hello " + p.name + ", see you tomorrow.")
}

Each call to notify gets a child capability with one use. Everything the child does counts against its parent, and the parent's parent, up to the grant. That's delegation in a multi-agent system, checked by a compiler.

Going the other way doesn't compile:

text

widen.staal:4:21: error[E003]: in call to 'blast': capability limited to 1 uses cannot be widened to 100 uses

And neither does acting without one:

text

nocap.staal:2:12: error[E002]: 'files.write' acts on the world but 'files' is not a capability in scope

Both come from staalc check, before anything runs. Widening covers every limit: a higher max, each or uses, a dropped limit, or an only pattern that reaches outside the original. The pattern check is deliberately conservative.

Checked before every action

The compiler proves the program never asks for more than it holds. The runtime makes sure it never uses more either.

Every capability lives in a broker, and a program only ever holds a handle. When the program acts, the broker checks the action against that capability and every capability it was narrowed from, before the service is called. Here's the reminder program above, granted two uses for this run, over four patients. The third has a UK number:

json

{"entry": "remind",
 "inputs": {"patients": [
   {"name": "Ada",   "phone": "2348012345678"},
   {"name": "Tunde", "phone": "2348098765432"},
   {"name": "Mary",  "phone": "447700900123"},
   {"name": "Chidi", "phone": "2348055555555"}]},
 "grants": {"texts": {"cap": "sms.send", "uses": 2}}}

The run returns 2. Its log, condensed:

action_performed  sms.send 2348012345678
action_performed  sms.send 2348098765432
action_refused    'sms.send' may only act on ["234*"]; this action targets "447700900123"
action_refused    'sms.send' has used all 2 of its allowed uses

The UK number hit the limit the code declared. The fourth patient hit the limit the app granted. Neither request reached the SMS service.

Three details that matter:

  1. Uses count attempts: A use is spent when the broker approves the action, so a failed request still costs one and a loop can't retry its way past a limit.
  2. Limits fail closed: A limit that can't determine the amount or target refuses the action.
  3. Money is charged even on failure when a request may have moved it, so failures can't be used to spend past max.

Models propose, programs act

A model never holds a capability. propose keeps the instruction (which must be trusted) apart from the data (which may be anything), and the answer comes back as Proposed, which can't reach an action until validate checks it against T. This gets both rules wrong:

fn handle(ticket: Text, pay: cap payments.refund(each: 50 USD)) -> Text budget(calls: 1, tokens: 500) {
    let d = propose(Decision, instruct: ticket, data: [pay], tokens: 500)
    return "ok"
}

model.staal:3:41: error[E006]: untrusted value used as a model instruction; pass it in `data: [...]` instead, or mark its source @trusted
model.staal:3:56: error[E101]: a capability cannot be sent to a model as data

Everything that comes back from the world is untrusted by type: HTTP bodies, tool results, model output (even after validation). So an injected instruction can change what the model asks for, but the proposal still has to pass validation, and the action still has to pass the broker, which holds a limit the model can't see or reach.

Keys out of reach

Real services need keys, URLs and HTTP access. None of those belong to the program that wants to act. They belong to a library that declares a capability:

capability termii.sms {
    needs http: cap net.http.post
    needs key: Secret
    needs base: Text
    needs sender: Text

    canonical(phone: Text) -> Text {
        return number(phone)
    }

    action send(to: Text @target, text: Text) -> Text {
        ...   // one request through `http`
    }
}

The host grants the library its key (by environment variable name, so it never lands in a config, journal or log), its URL, and an HTTP capability narrowed to the one endpoint. The program asks for cap termii.sms.send(uses: 50) and holds the right to send texts, nothing else. only is matched against the library's canonical form, so +234 801 234 5678 and 2348012345678 are the same number to the broker.

Secrets never become text. A Secret can't be printed, interpolated or encoded, even inside the library. When a benchmark edit tried to log request headers:

error[E101]: `json` cannot encode a Header: secrets never become text
Why it holds as code changes

Any careful team can build least privilege into an agent on the day it ships. The hard part is keeping it. So I built the same support agent twice, in Python alone and in Python with Staal, with the same limits, permissions, retries and crash recovery. Both passed all 47 scenarios: prompt injection, malformed model output, permission escalation, failing services, and the process killed before and after every external call. Python took 312 lines; Staal, 159.

Then I made six changes to each, the kind teams make months later. In Python, "one refund per job" lived in a policy object, and the refactor built a fresh one per step, silently resetting its counter. In Staal, the refactor passed the capability to a helper, the broker counted the use against the original grant, and the second refund was refused. The limit was never in the code that changed.

In ordinary code, least privilege is a convention every future change has to respect. In Staal, it's a property the compiler and the broker keep, whoever edits the code next.

Try it

Your app stays in Python or Node.js. Only the part that acts is Staal:

bash

pip install staal
npm install @staal/node

Packages are built and tested for Linux (x86_64, arm64) and macOS (Apple Silicon, Intel). Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exception.

Repo and quickstart: github.com/laurells/staal
Benchmark: github.com/laurells/staal/bench/agent
Runtime spec: github.com/laurells/staal/docs/RUNTIME.md

If you're building agents that touch money, messages or records, I'd like to hear where this would and wouldn't fit. Comments are open.

Sources: Giskard on the PocketOS deletion · Curity: 5 agentic AI security incidents · Gravitee: State of AI Agent Security 2026 · ATXP: agent payment protocols compared

title: How much RAM does a Java application really need? Sizing a small server
description:
When people size a Java server they look at -Xmx. That sets the maximum heap, where your objects live. The operating system sees the whole process, and that is larger:

  • Heap: your objects, caches and sessions, up to -Xmx.
  • Metaspace: loaded classes. A framework-heavy application uses 100 to 300 MB.
  • Thread stacks: about 1 MB per thread by default, so 200 threads is 200 MB.
  • Code cache: compiled code, tens of MB.
  • Direct and native memory: network buffers, compression, JDBC drivers.
  • GC overhead: the collector's own bookkeeping.

As a working rule, the process uses the heap plus 300 to 600 MB. If Nginx, a database and the OS share the server, add those too.

The split I use

With a database on the same server I give 45% of RAM to the JVM heap, 15% to database buffers, and leave 40% for the OS, metaspace, thread stacks and file cache. Without a database the heap gets 60%.

Workload Heap Server
Small Spring Boot, Quarkus or Micronaut API 256 to 512 MB 2 GB
Tomcat with one or two WARs 512 MB to 1 GB 2 to 4 GB
Spring Boot with Hibernate, database on the same server 1 to 2 GB 4 to 8 GB
WildFly or Payara with one application 1 to 2 GB 4 to 8 GB

These are starting points. WildFly alone used about 450 MB on my test server before any application was deployed.

Measure, do not guess

Look at the heap after a full garbage collection: that is your live data, and the maximum should be at least 2.5 times that. Turn on GC logging and a dump on failure:

-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/myapp/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=10m
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError

If the service disappears with no Java error in the log, the Linux OOM killer took it. Check dmesg -T | grep -i "killed process". Then the heap is too big for the machine, and raising it makes things worse.

I put the split into a small JVM heap calculator: enter RAM, app server and database, and it prints the -Xmx, -Xms, metaspace and database buffer values to paste into systemd.

The full version of this guide is here.

title: How to Stop Overselling in Inventory Management Software Development (Node.js and PostgreSQL) published: false
description:
Two checkout requests arrive 4 ms apart for the last unit of a SKU. Both read on_hand = 1, both pass the check in application code, and both write. Stock ends at -1 and one customer gets an apology email. This race appears wherever a web store, a marketplace sync, and a warehouse scanner write to the same row, and it grows worse with every added channel or worker process. It is the first bug we design against in inventory management software development for concurrent, multi-writer systems. The fix is small: let PostgreSQL decide the outcome, not your Node.js process.

Context and Setup

The scenario is a Node.js 20 API with pg talking to PostgreSQL 15, serving several channels that reserve stock before payment clears. PostgreSQL is a safe base for this: the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey reports it as the most-used database among professional developers (55.6%).

You need two tables. stock_levels holds sku, location, on_hand, and reserved. reservations holds a unique idempotency_key, qty, status, and expires_at. Available stock is on_hand - reserved, and it must never go below zero.

Reserving Stock Atomically in Inventory Management Software Development

The short answer is one conditional UPDATE guarded by a constraint. Three steps get you there.

Step 1: Make the database refuse negative stock

In Inventory Management Software Development a constraint protects the invariant from every writer, including services that do not exist yet.

  1. Fix any existing rows that violate the rule.
  2. Add the constraint in a migration with a short lock timeout. 
-- Why: even buggy code or a manual script cannot oversell past this line
ALTER TABLE stock_levels
  ADD CONSTRAINT available_not_negative CHECK (on_hand - reserved >= 0);

Step 2: Reserve with One Conditional UPDATE in Inventory Management Software Development

Check and write must be one statement. PostgreSQL locks the row during UPDATE, and under READ COMMITTED a waiting transaction re-evaluates the WHERE clause after the lock clears (see the PostgreSQL transaction isolation docs). The second request then matches zero rows.

import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

export async function reserve({ key, sku, location, qty, ttlSeconds = 900 }) {
  const db = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await db.query("BEGIN");
    // Why: the unique key turns a client retry into a no-op instead of a double hold
    const hold = await db.query(
      `INSERT INTO reservations (idempotency_key, sku, location, qty, status, expires_at)
       VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, 'held', now() + make_interval(secs => $5))
       ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING RETURNING id`,
      [key, sku, location, qty, ttlSeconds]
    );
    if (hold.rowCount === 0) { await db.query("ROLLBACK"); return { status: "duplicate" }; }

    // Why: check and write in one statement avoids the read-then-write race
    const upd = await db.query(
      `UPDATE stock_levels SET reserved = reserved + $3
       WHERE sku = $1 AND location = $2 AND on_hand - reserved >= $3`,
      [sku, location, qty]
    );
    if (upd.rowCount === 0) { await db.query("ROLLBACK"); return { status: "insufficient" }; }

    await db.query("COMMIT");
    return { status: "reserved", id: hold.rows[0].id };
  } catch (err) {
    await db.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw err;
  } finally {
    db.release();
  }
}

Step 3: Expire holds and weigh the alternatives

Inventory Management Software Development Abandoned carts must release stock, or reserved drifts upward. Run this worker query every minute.

-- Why: SKIP LOCKED lets several workers run without blocking each other
WITH expired AS (
  SELECT id, sku, location, qty FROM reservations
  WHERE status = 'held' AND expires_at < now()
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100
), flipped AS (
  UPDATE reservations r SET status = 'expired'
  FROM expired e WHERE r.id = e.id
  RETURNING e.sku, e.location, e.qty
), totals AS (
  -- Why: UPDATE ... FROM applies only one source row per target row, so sum first
  SELECT sku, location, sum(qty) AS qty FROM flipped GROUP BY sku, location
)
UPDATE stock_levels s SET reserved = s.reserved - t.qty
FROM totals t WHERE s.sku = t.sku AND s.location = t.location;

The trade-offs against other designs:

  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE first: correct, but it adds a round trip and holds the lock longer.
  • Optimistic version column: cheap for cold SKUs, yet hot SKUs burn retries.
  • Redis counters: fast, but they create a second source of truth that needs reconciliation.

The conditional update serializes writers per row. For a flash-sale SKU, split stock into bucket rows.

Real-World Application

In one of our inventory management software development projects at Oodles

Key Takeaways

  • In inventory Management Software Development put the invariant in the database with a CHECK constraint, because application checks cannot see concurrent writers.
  • Collapse check and write into one conditional UPDATE; READ COMMITTED re-evaluates the WHERE clause after a lock wait.
  • Use an idempotency key so client and queue retries never double-reserve.
  • Expire holds with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED workers, and sum quantities before updating the parent rows.
  • Choose Redis or optimistic locking only after measuring contention on hot SKUs.

Questions about reservation design or hot-SKU contention? Drop them in the comments, or reach us about inventory management software development.

What is inventory management software development?
It is the engineering of systems that track stock across locations and channels, reserve units for orders, and keep counts consistent under concurrent writes. Core work covers data models, reservation logic, integrations, and audit trails.

How do you prevent overselling in inventory software?
Combine a database CHECK constraint with a single conditional UPDATE that tests available stock in its WHERE clause. The database serializes competing writers per row, so only requests that fit the remaining quantity succeed.

Should I use Redis or PostgreSQL for stock counts?
In Inventory Management Software Development Use PostgreSQL as the source of truth because it gives transactions, constraints, and audit history. Add Redis only as a read cache or rate limiter, and reconcile it against the database to avoid drift.

Which isolation level do stock updates need?
READ COMMITTED is enough for a conditional UPDATE, because PostgreSQL re-checks the WHERE clause after a lock wait. Use SERIALIZABLE only for multi-row invariants, and be ready to retry on serialization failures.

Why do reservations need idempotency keys?
Clients, queues, and gateways retry failed calls. A unique idempotency key lets the second attempt hit ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so one order can never hold stock twice.

title: From 10 Seconds to Under 1: How I Made a Site 10x Faster
description:
How I Cut 60% of the Bundle and 76% of the Boot CPU of a Large Web App

In production, the home page of the app took more than 10 seconds. Now it takes under 1 second.

No single trick did that. I cut the JavaScript and CSS that every page downloads from 6,070 KB to 2,434 KB gzip, and the code that runs before the first paint from 6.1 s to 1.5 s of CPU. I moved more than 1,000 templates out of the main bundle and loaded each one with its route. Then I served the lazy code from a CDN I designed, in chunks built from the module graph.

In this article I'll walk through how I found where the time went, the tools I built to measure it, each cut with its numbers, the lazy-loading patterns I kept, the traps that broke features, and what the CDN changed.

The case: a large web app with about 1,150 client templates, React panels inside them, and about 9,000 lazy modules. It runs on Meteor 2.16. Some limitations of this work come from Meteor, and I'll name them. The method does not depend on Meteor.

The Result

Home page in production Before After
Time until the page starts to show 12.6 s 0.8 s

I measured the "after" number in production, after the CDN release, logged in: 0.89 s at the median of five loads.

The other numbers in this article come from the lab, and they are higher than the production number. That is expected. The lab starts every load with an empty cache, so the browser downloads and compiles all the code each time. It runs on a local server, with no CDN and no HTTP/2. Its timings count until the largest element of the page appears. A second lab profile also slows the network to Fast 3G and the CPU by 4x, close to what a slow phone gets. I used the lab only to compare two versions of the code with the same test.

What every page downloads. The measurement is deterministic, so these numbers are exact.

Eager bundle, gzip Start End Change
JavaScript 5,666 KB 2,042 KB −64.0%
JavaScript + CSS 6,070 KB 2,434 KB −59.9%

A cold load of /home in the lab. Median of five loads. I measured both columns on the same day.

Measurement Start After the view tree Change
Modules in the main bundle 11,177 5,041 −54.9%
CPU spent running modules before the first paint 6,113 ms 1,454 ms −76.2% (4.2x)
Longest task 6,476 ms 2,053 ms −68.3% (3.2x)
First Contentful Paint 8,704 ms 2,900 ms −66.7% (3.0x)
Largest Contentful Paint 8,988 ms 4,068 ms −54.7% (2.2x)
LCP, 5 core routes, one load each 9.6–10.8 s 3.9–4.8 s −53% to −62%

The timings come from the view-tree commit. Three later cuts took another 352 KB gzip out of the JavaScript, and I did not measure their timings in the lab. The bundle table includes them.

Where the Time Went

Before I had a profile, I did two rounds of bundle work: the error-tracking SDK, a second copy of pdf.js, a timezone library, and a few feature routes. They took 622 KB gzip out of the JavaScript. On Fast 3G with a 4x slower CPU, the median LCP of the five core routes fell by 11 s. On localhost, the LCP of /home went from 8,684 to 8,172 ms, and the ranges of the two builds overlapped. Fewer bytes helped the slow network. They did not shorten the wait on a fast one.

So I measured where the time went. The first runtime measurement was a timeline of one cold load of /home, on the build after those two rounds:

Moment Time
The HTML arrives 21 ms
The CSS arrives 181 ms
The JavaScript (5,043 KB gzip, 23,189 KB raw) downloads 59–1,322 ms
One long task: the bundle parses and runs 1,432–6,747 ms
The WebSocket opens 6,878 ms
First Contentful Paint 6,884 ms
Largest Contentful Paint 7,724 ms

On the five core routes of that build, the LCP was 7.7 to 9.8 s, and the shape was the same on every route. The network delivered the bundle in 1.3 s. Then the tab spent 5.3 s in one long task, with nothing on the screen. The first paint came 6 ms after that task ended. No data request could start before it, because the code that opens the socket was inside the same bundle.

Two more numbers explained the size of the problem:

  • Only a third of the code ran. V8 coverage on /home showed 7.7 MB of the 23.1 MB of eager JavaScript in use. The browser downloaded and decompressed the other 15.4 MB, and V8 still pre-parsed it, but none of it ran.
  • A slow network made it extreme. On Fast 3G with a 4x slower CPU, the LCP of the five core routes was 51 to 55 s.

So the problem had two parts: too many bytes, and too much CPU at boot. They turned out to be separate problems, with separate fixes.

Measure First: Three Small Tools

The usual tools gave me wrong answers, so I wrote three small scripts.

1. Exact bytes per module. A bundle visualizer that reads the source map puts the bytes of generated code (the compiled templates, for example) on a neighboring file, because the map has no entry for them. measureEagerBundle.js parses the module tree of the built bundle instead, so each module gets its exact byte span. It is deterministic: two builds of the same code give the same numbers.

2. CPU per module. A sampling profile said that one file, the one that creates the app's 112 database collections, cost 2,160 ms. That was wrong. The profile reads positions through the same source map. measureModuleTime.js replaces the module installer before the bundle runs and wraps every module function with a timer. The real cost of that file was about 280 ms. This is the core of it, simplified:

// Runs before the bundle (Playwright addInitScript).
// Meteor gives every module tree to one global installer.
// The hook wraps each module function with a timer.
const stack = [];
window.__moduleTimes = [];

function wrapTree(tree, prefix) {
  const out = Array.isArray(tree) ? [] : {};
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(tree)) {
    const modulePath = prefix ? `${prefix}/${key}` : key;
    if (typeof value !== 'function') {
      out[key] = value && typeof value === 'object' ? wrapTree(value, modulePath) : value;
      continue;
    }
    out[key] = function timedModule(...args) {
      const frame = { child: 0 };
      stack.push(frame);
      const started = performance.now();
      try {
        return value.apply(this, args);
      } finally {
        const elapsed = performance.now() - started;
        stack.pop();
        // The parent's own time does not include the time of its children.
        if (stack.length) stack[stack.length - 1].child += elapsed;
        window.__moduleTimes.push({ path: modulePath, self: elapsed - frame.child });
      }
    };
  }
  return out;
}

let wrapped;
Object.defineProperty(window, 'meteorInstall', {
  configurable: true,
  get: () => wrapped,
  set(realInstall) {
    wrapped = (tree, options) => realInstall(wrapTree(tree, ''), options);
    Object.assign(wrapped, realInstall);
  },
});

No source map is involved. One rule made the report useful: a large number means "this module is the door to an expensive package". npm packages go through a separate copy of the installer, so they have no row of their own. Their cost goes to the first app module that requires them.

3. The doors. edges.js walks the static import graph from every file that loads on every page, and stops at each dynamic import(). It answers two questions: which npm packages a page can reach, and which eager file is the first import on the chain to a module. I call that file a door. Close the door, and everything behind it leaves the bundle.

node scripts/perf/edges.js "$PWD" npm:material-react-table   # the eager importers of one package
node scripts/perf/edges.js "$PWD" <directory>                # the chains that reach a folder

For page timings, one run was useless. Five cold loads of the same build varied by up to 940 ms on localhost. I took the median of five loads per side, and I used Fast 3G with a slower CPU when I needed to separate two results.

The Cuts, One Door at a Time

First, every step on one table. The bytes are exact. The timings are cold loads of /home on the same machine, with the same script and the same account.

Step Eager JS, gzip Saved Module evaluation Longest task LCP
Start 5,666 KB — 6,113 ms 6,476 ms 8,988 ms
1. Error-tracking SDK, second pdf.js, timezone library, feature routes 5,044 KB −622 KB 5,319 ms 5,772 ms 8,172 ms
2. Video recorder 5,014 KB −30 KB 4,290 ms 4,438 ms 7,028 ms
3. Table library 4,712 KB −302 KB 3,516 ms 3,534 ms 5,708 ms
4. Server code, date pickers, AI chat panels 4,496 KB −216 KB 2,712 ms 3,364 ms 5,828 ms
5. Content catalogue, video-call SDK 4,398 KB −164 KB¹ — 3,457 ms² 5,716 ms²
6. View tree 2,394 KB −2,004 KB³ 1,454 ms 2,053 ms 4,068 ms
7. Server-only reporting helpers 2,345 KB −49 KB — — —
8. Material UI off the first paint 2,107 KB −238 KB — — —
9. jQuery UI 2,042 KB −65 KB — — —

¹ A merge of new code from the main branch added 66 KB between steps 4 and 5, so the column moves by 98 KB, not 164 KB.
² Median of three loads. The other LCP and longest-task cells are medians of five.
³ Step 6 holds 24 commits. The move of the view tree is the largest.

I measured the start row and step 6 on the same day. I measured steps 1 to 5 on two earlier days, when the start build had an LCP of 8,684 ms. Read the timing columns as a trend, and the byte column as exact. The table counts JavaScript only. Step 1 also cut the CSS from 404 KB to 271 KB, a revert of that CSS work came back with step 6, and the CSS is now 392 KB.

Two things stand out. Step 2 saved 30 KB and took 1 s off the boot CPU. Step 6 saved 2 MB, more than all the other steps together.

Before the profile: an error-tracking SDK (step 1)

The bundler cannot tree-shake, so a static import of @sentry/browser brought the SDK with replay, feedback and canvas recording: 916 KB minified. Twelve client files imported it.

I made one module the only door. It queues every call, and it loads the SDK in requestIdleCallback after the first route paints, with a 4 s limit. Errors raised before that go into a 20-entry buffer and reach Sentry when it starts. The Sentry packages left the bundle: −276 KB gzip.

A recorder that cost 1 second of CPU (step 2)

The CPU report put one module at the top: the app's video recorder component, at 1,032 ms. It was the first file to require react-media-recorder, which pulls standardized-audio-context. That library builds a class hierarchy when it loads. It is cheap to download and expensive to run.

Exactly one eager file imported the recorder, for a panel that renders behind a condition. I made that import lazy:

Cold load of /home, median of 5 Before After
FCP 7,276 ms 6,256 ms (−14.0%)
LCP 8,172 ms 7,028 ms (−14.0%)
Longest task 5,772 ms 4,438 ms (−23.1%)

The bundle barely moved: 5,044 KB to 5,014 KB gzip. Boot CPU and bundle size are separate problems. A byte budget alone would never have found this.

A table library behind 22 doors (step 3)

The next module was the app's table wrapper, at 795 ms, the door to material-react-table. Making that one file lazy did not help: 37 modules imported the package, through 22 different doors. Most of them were template helpers that returned a React component at module scope. Each one became a lazy component.

Result: −302 KB gzip, −774 ms of module evaluation. After the recorder and the table, the longest task on /home was 42.7% shorter than at the start.

Server code that ran in the browser (step 4)

Shared code had if (Meteor.isClient) return; at the top, but it still imported the server's event store. Those modules built a validation schema when they loaded: 234 ms of CPU in the browser, for code that never runs there. A function-level require() stopped the CPU cost, but the bundler still found the literal and kept the bytes.

The fix that removes the bytes too is a registry: the shared code has an empty slot, and a server-only file fills it.

// Shared code: the slot.
let eventStore: EventStore | null = null;

export function registerEventStore(store: EventStore): void {
  eventStore = store;
}

export function getEventStore(): EventStore {
  if (!eventStore) {
    throw new Error('The event store is not registered.');
  }
  return eventStore;
}

// server/registerEventStore.ts: the only import of the real module.
registerEventStore({ append });

A catalogue that the header loaded for one field (step 5)

The header called a hook, the hook called a helper, and the helper read a content catalogue of 43 items with all their text. It used one field of each item: the _id.

I moved the 43 ids to a small file, and I kept the full catalogue lazy. A unit test compares the two lists, so a new item that reaches only one file fails the build. Result: −160 KB gzip, and a feature folder fell from 60 eager modules to 12.

A video-call SDK that loaded on every page (step 5)

The chat panel sits in the default layout, and its onCreated hook loaded the video-call SDK: an 843 KB gzip chunk, on every page, for every user. Nobody had started a call.

Now the SDK loads when a chat window holds a live video. For one screen that needs it right after a click, the download starts at the click, while the modal opens and the server creates the session. 843 KB gzip stopped loading on every page.

Smaller doors

Door What it cost
A date picker package imported through its root barrel 73 KB gzip, 260 ms of CPU across 3 files
AI chat panels in 5 template helpers the door to a charting library, 97 KB gzip
A PDF viewer package that listed pdf.js twice 406 KB minified, one copy ran and exported nothing
moment-timezone from npm next to a global moment 763 KB minified, for one component

The big one: templates that load with their route (step 6)

Each fix above closed one door. The bundle was still about 4.4 MB gzip, because the framework loads every file under client/ on every page, whatever the imports say. More than 1,000 templates lived there.

The key observation: the templating layer finds a template by name when it renders, not when the file loads. So a route can wait for a chunk, and then render any template inside it. Only the templates that render on every page must load with the page: 135 of 1,148.

I moved the view tree to a lazy folder. A list of 155 files loads with the page. The other 604 files load in a route chunk. Each route group waits for its chunk:

const adminArea = createRouteChunkLoader({
  importChunk: () => import('/imports/features/admin/ui'),
});

const adminRoutes = FlowRouter.group({
  name: 'adminRoutes',
  waitOn: adminArea.waitOn,
  whileWaiting: adminArea.whileWaiting,
});

The helper exists for one reason. The router calls whileWaiting on every route run, and a query parameter change is a route run. A plain waitOn showed the loading screen on each change, so the page lost its state. The helper shows the loading screen only while the chunk is on the way.

This table compares the start with step 6:

Measurement Start After the view tree
Eager JavaScript, gzip 5,666 KB 2,394 KB (−57.8%)
Modules in the bundle 11,177 5,041 (−54.9%)
npm packages that a page can reach 57 40
Module evaluation on /home 6,113 ms 1,454 ms (−76.2%)
Longest task on /home 6,476 ms 2,053 ms (−68.3%)
LCP on /home, median of 5 8,988 ms 4,068 ms (−54.7%)
Share of the eager code that runs on /home 34.6% 50.2%

On the five core routes, LCP fell between 53% and 62% in the lab, and between 42% and 46% on Fast 3G with a 4x slower CPU. The longest task fell between 68% and 75%.

Three more doors after the view tree (steps 7 to 9)

  • Reporting helpers that only the server calls. 48 files moved to a server folder, which never enters the client bundle: −49 KB gzip.
  • Material UI on the first paint. Four static imports still carried it: a barrel file of the component library that 37 files read for the theme, the entry of the confirmation dialog, a menu with its own table, and a demo page. The barrel went away. The dialog entry now loads the dialog on its first call, so its 131 call sites did not change. Result: −238 KB gzip, and the Material UI components in the bundle fell from 73 to 33. The 33 that stay belong to the header, which paints on every page.
  • jQuery UI. The file (247 KB raw) sat in an eager folder, and no file on the first-paint path called a widget. It moved to a lazy folder, and the 67 modules that call a widget import it: −65 KB gzip.

After the Bundle: the Data Waterfall

A smaller bundle moved the first paint earlier, and then the data became visible. After the long task, the page opened its socket and sent 28 subscriptions for 109 documents. The payload was small. The cost was the number of round trips and their order.

Only 3 of the 28 held the first paint. That fact told me which fixes would move LCP and which would not:

  • Duplicate subscriptions. Two call sites asked for the same data, so the server ran two publications twice. I gave each subscription one owner: 28 became 26. LCP did not move. I had predicted that, because the duplicates did not hold the paint. The page still did less work.
  • A 3-second timer from 2018. Six subscriptions waited for a setTimeout of 3,000 ms that no longer had a purpose. They held 80 of the 109 documents. Without the timer, notifications were ready 506 ms after the first subscription message, instead of 3,042 ms. LCP did not move here either: none of the six held the paint.
  • A blocking waitOn. / and /home waited for a full publication before they rendered anything, and the same data was already on its way through another subscription. I removed the wait.
  • A publication that read a whole user document. One of the 3 that hold the paint read the full user document, which grows with every login session, to get one field. With a projection it went from 126 ms to 18 ms. The 3 run in parallel, so the gate went from 126 ms to 56 ms, a gain too small for the lab to show in LCP.

Cutting requests that do not hold the paint does not move LCP. Find the requests that do, and make them shorter.

Patterns I Kept

A React panel that loads on its first render 

// Rendered only when its panel opens, so it loads on demand.
const SecurityPanelLazy = lazyComponent(
  () => import('/imports/features/account/ui/SecurityPanel'),
  'SecurityPanel',
);

lazyComponent shows a spinner until the module arrives. When the download fails, it renders nothing, reports the failure, and shows a toast that offers a reload.

Code that runs after a click 

'click button[data-action="create-project"]'(event, template) {
  // The handler stays synchronous: the template layer drops the promise
  // of an async handler, so a failed chunk would leave the button dead.
  import('/imports/features/projects/ui/CreateProjectDialog')
    .then(({ showCreateProjectDialog }) => showCreateProjectDialog(userId))
    .catch(error => {
      reportError(error, { context: 'CreateProjectDialogLoadFailed' });
    });
},

A library that loads at the moment of use 

let chartPromise;

export const loadChart = () => {
  if (!chartPromise) {
    chartPromise = import('chart.js').then(({ default: Chart }) => {
      Chart.defaults.global.pointHitDetectionRadius = 1;
      return Chart;
    });
    // A failed download clears the promise, so the next chart tries again.
    chartPromise = chartPromise.catch(error => {
      chartPromise = undefined;
      throw error;
    });
  }
  return chartPromise;
};

Every caller waits for the same download, and the global setup of the library runs once. After the await, check that the component still exists.

A small index of large data

Keep the part that eager code reads in a small eager file, keep the full data lazy, and add a test that fails when the two differ. I used this for the content catalogue and for a list of program definitions.

Traps That Broke Features

A lazy load changes when code runs. Each of these broke a feature during the work:

  • A side-effect module stopped running. A file that registers custom validators moved to a lazy folder, and only the server imported it. Eight forms failed validation with Expected undefined, got string.
  • A global stopped existing. Seven files assigned helpers to a global namespace and moved with no importer. Creating a form failed with ... is not a function.
  • The CSS cascade changed. A lazy stylesheet loads last, so its rules win. One component stylesheet imported the global styles and restyled every button.
  • A route waited for its own chunk. A redirect module sat inside the chunk that waits for a route, and the route waited for the redirect module. The page stayed on the loading screen.
  • Two modules changed order. Both read a value that clears when it is read. A deep link after a login landed on the home page.
  • A pre-commit hook rewrote a vendor file. eslint --fix changed var to let in a minified jQuery UI file, and every view that used it failed to load.
  • A moved file left an import on the old path. Neither ESLint nor the build reported it. The browser threw Cannot find module only when the import ran.

The last one is the most dangerous, because nothing fails before production. I test every changed page three ways: a cold deep link in a private window, a hard reload, and an in-app navigation, then again on Fast 3G.

The CDN

Lazy loading moved cost from boot to navigation. After the view tree left the bundle, /home asked for its route code in one request to the app server: 1,021 KB, between the first paint at 2,900 ms and the LCP at 4,068 ms. The same request had a second problem. After a deploy, the server answered with the code of its new build, so an open tab could receive modules from another build.

I moved the lazy modules to a CDN with versioned names, so every tab reads the modules of its own build. The full design will be in my next article. These are the parts that matter for speed:

  • Chunks from the module graph. The first version made one request per module. /home needs 2,591 lazy modules, so it made about 2,600 requests. In a sandbox, a public route with about 2,000 modules took 9.4 to 9.9 s through CloudFront, against 1.7 to 2.1 s through the app server. So I grouped the modules with the rules of Rollup, webpack and Turbopack. On a production build, /home now loads its 2,591 modules in 24 chunks, plus one index. The chunks carry 1.0% more bytes than the modules that /home needs.
  • A cache per module. Meteor's dynamic-import package already stores each module in IndexedDB under its version. With the CDN, that cache holds only modules of the right build. A second visit to the same build makes one request: the index of the build.
  • Small deploys stay small. After a deploy, the browser plans each chunk: it downloads the whole chunk only when the requests that it saves cost more than its unused bytes. The modules that did not change come from the local cache.
  • Edges and HTTP/2. CloudFront serves the chunks from an edge near the user, with Brotli and up to 128 parallel streams on one connection.
  • A preload that I removed. Preloading the chunks from the HTML gained 0.31 s, and cost about 12 s when the preload failed.

Not in production yet. A 30 s total timeout per request aborted the largest chunk of /home (4.3 MB before compression) on a 3G profile while its data was still arriving. The fix aborts a request only after 10 s with no data on any CDN request.

Keeping It Fast

A bundle that shrinks by 60% grows back if nobody watches it. So I wrote down 13 ways the bundle grew back, each with an example from the app's history: a new file in an eager folder, one static import into a large tree, a barrel import, a download from code that runs on every page, server code in shared folders, large data in an eager file, a second copy of a library, generated CSS, and others.

The contribution rules of the project now point to this list. A change that adds a file to an eager folder, or a dependency to client code, starts with a read of it. A release gate in CI also measures the JavaScript that / downloads on a staging server, and it fails above a budget of 2,042 KiB.

The Limitations

  • Lab and production are different setups. The lab numbers come from localhost with an empty cache and no CDN. The production "after" number is my own measurement for a returning user, on one account and one machine, not a p75 of all users.
  • A first visit to a route waits for its chunk. Lazy loading moves cost from boot to navigation. A failed chunk needs a recovery path, and every page needs a test on a slow network.
  • Meteor 2 loads every file under client/ and both/ on every page. The meteor.mainModule option turns that off, and this app does not use it. In an app of this size, every file needs an importer before that option can work, which is the same work as the view-tree move. There is no tree shaking either, so every cut needed a move, not only an import().
  • A require() inside a function still bundles the module. The bundler reads the literal. Only a registry slot removes the bytes.
  • Each lazy chunk grows the version manifest. The main bundle carries the version of every lazy module. It grew from 152 KB to 556 KB raw during this work, and it is now 288 KB gzip, 14% of the eager JavaScript.
  • Some weight is still on every page. The header keeps 33 Material UI components, 128 KB gzip of Material UI in all. The icon font stylesheet blocks the first render, and /home downloads 453 KB of fonts. About 495 method stubs in a shared folder still reach the browser.
  • The home chunk is still large. /home asks for the chunk of the whole authenticated area, not only for the templates that it renders.

Conclusion

In production, the home page went from more than 10 seconds to under 1 second for a returning user. In the lab, the same work cut 60% of the bytes and 76% of the boot CPU. These are the lessons I keep:

  • Measure bytes and CPU separately. A 1 s CPU cost hid behind a library that was cheap to download.
  • Find the doors, not the files. One static import from an eager file can bring a whole package. Close the door, and the package leaves.
  • Build your own measurements when the usual tools are wrong. Source maps put bytes and CPU on the wrong files. Five runs per side, not one.
  • The large win was structural. The fixes to single doors saved tens to hundreds of KB each. Moving the view tree to its routes saved about 2 MB gzip.
  • Fix what holds the paint. Requests that do not hold the first paint do not move LCP.
  • Give the lazy code a short path too. Versioned chunks on a CDN, a cache that matches the build, and a few well-sized requests.
  • Guard it. A written list of the known regressions and a budget in CI keep the bundle where you left it.

title: Maker-Checker Approvals and Audit Logs: Design Notes for Government Workflow Apps
description:
Government applications rarely fail because a form is hard to build. They fail when an approval chain is unclear, a record changes without a trace, or an integration breaks at the worst moment. If you are building a citizen or department portal, these are the parts worth designing first.

Model the approval chain before the screens

  • Write down each role (citizen, clerk, section officer, approver) and what it can see and do. Role-based access is the base layer.
  • Use maker-checker: one person prepares a record, a different person approves it. Enforce this in the backend, not only in the UI.
  • Keep hierarchical approvals and inter-department hand-offs as rule-based workflow steps, so a policy change does not mean a code change.
  • Generate sanction letters and other documents automatically from the approved state, not from editable drafts.

Make every change traceable

  • Log who did what, when and on which record, for every approval, rejection and edit.
  • Keep audit logs separate from the main tables and make them append-only.
  • Feed scheme monitoring and MIS dashboards from the same events, so reports match the trail.

Treat integrations as a security boundary

  • Put Aadhaar, PAN and other external integrations behind a secure API gateway.
  • Plan IAM integration early instead of building a separate login system.
  • Expect a vulnerability assessment or a NIC or CERT-In empanelled audit, and leave time to fix findings before launch.

Do not forget the citizen side

  • Mobile-friendly, multilingual screens and visible application tracking cut down support calls.
  • Follow GIGW guidelines, including accessibility and bilingual content.

More detail: how we approach e-governance portals and workflow automation

Written by the team at Affix Center, an IT services company in Lower Parel, Mumbai.

title: Agent-Driven Refactors: Keep the PR Reviewable
description:
I used to ask the agent for “a clean refactor of this module” and get a 40-file PR that touched naming, folder layout, hooks, and tests in one swing. CI was green. I still couldn’t review it.

Green doesn’t mean reviewable. An agent-driven refactor is useful only if a human can answer “what changed and why?” in under ten minutes. Here’s the process I use so the model does the mechanical work without turning the PR into a archaeology dig.

The failure mode: one prompt, one mega-diff

The ask that blows up:

Refactor BillingForm and related helpers. Clean up naming, extract hooks, align with our patterns, update tests.

What lands:

  • Renames across 12 files
  • A new hooks folder
  • Test rewrites that assert the same behavior with different structure
  • A drive-by import sort and a “while I was here” type tweak

None of that is wrong in isolation. Together it is unreviewable. You can’t tell which hunk is the real refactor and which is noise. Reviewers rubber-stamp or reject the whole thing. Both waste the agent’s work.

Reviewable means three things

I won’t merge an agent refactor unless all three hold:

  1. One intent per PR — rename or extract or move or behavior change. Not a combo meal.
  2. Diff you can narrate — I can write a 3–5 bullet PR description without opening every file.
  3. Tests that prove the same contract — same public behavior, preferably same assertion names where they still fit. Silent test rewrites hide regressions.

If the agent can’t keep those three, I split the ask before I accept the branch.

Slice the refactor before you prompt

I never start with “refactor X.” I write a short plan the agent must follow:

## Refactor plan (do in order; stop after each step)
1. Rename `useBill` → `useBillingState` in place — no logic changes
2. Extract `validateLineItems` from BillingForm into `billing/validate.ts` — same signature
3. Move `formatCurrency` from utils/misc to billing/format — update imports only
4. (Optional, separate PR) Split BillingForm into Form + Summary if step 1–3 stay green

Rules:
- One git commit per step
- Do not rename and extract in the same step
- Do not “improve” unrelated types or imports
- After each step: run unit tests for billing; report pass/fail before continuing

Then I paste that plan as the prompt body. The agent gets a sequence, not a vibe.

Force small commits (or small PRs)

Reviewability dies when everything is one commit. I ask for one commit per plan step, with messages that match the plan:

refactor(billing): rename useBill → useBillingState
refactor(billing): extract validateLineItems
refactor(billing): move formatCurrency to billing/format

If the tool can’t commit mid-run, I still force one PR per step. Slower wall-clock, faster review. I’d rather merge three 80-line PRs than one 800-line “cleanup.”

Stacking works too: open PR1, wait for review, then PR2 on top. Agents are fine with that if you say so up front.

Give the agent a blast-radius fence

Left alone, models expand scope. I put hard fences in the prompt:

Only touch files under src/features/billing/** and their colocated tests.

Do not edit src/components/ui/**, shared utils outside billing, or CI config.

If a rename requires a file outside that fence, stop and list the paths — don’t chase them.

That stop rule matters. Without it, a rename becomes a repo-wide find-replace that pulls in stories, docs, and e2e fixtures you didn’t mean to review tonight.

Keep behavior frozen while structure moves

For pure refactors I add:

No behavior changes. Same props, same return shapes, same error messages, same network calls.

If you think behavior should change, open a note in the PR description — don’t ship it in this branch.

Then I ask for a short “behavior freeze” checklist in the PR body:

  • [ ] Public component API unchanged
  • [ ] Snapshot / contract tests unchanged (or only path updates)
  • [ ] No new feature flags
  • [ ] No copy / i18n string edits

If those boxes aren’t honest, it’s not a refactor PR anymore — and it shouldn’t pretend to be.

What I review (human checklist)

When the PR opens, I skim in this order:

  1. File list first — does it match the plan’s fence?
  2. Commit messages — one intent each?
  3. Largest hunk — is it mechanical (rename/move) or clever?
  4. Test diff — assertion text drift without a reason?
  5. rg for drive-bys — prettier/eslint mass rewrites, import resorting outside touched files

If step 1 fails, I don’t deep-read the rest. I send it back with “split to match the plan.”

Prompt template I reuse 

Execute ONLY step N of the refactor plan below.
Do not start step N+1.
Stay inside the blast-radius fence.
No behavior changes.
When done: paste `git status`, `git diff --stat`, and test results.

[paste plan]

Boring. Repeatable. The agent does the typing; I keep the narrative.

Takeaway

Agent-driven refactors fail when you optimize for “the model finished” instead of “a human can own the merge.” Slice the work, fence the blast radius, freeze behavior, and ship one intent per PR (or per commit).

The agent is fast. Review time is the scarce resource. Write prompts that protect the reviewer’s ten minutes — that’s the whole game.
