title: How CSS Controls the Layout of a Webpage: A Beginner-Friendly Guide
description:
Have you ever looked at a webpage and wondered:

“How did they get everything to sit exactly there?”

The heading is at the top.

The navigation links are arranged neatly.

The cards sit beside each other.

The button is aligned with the text.

The sidebar stays where it belongs.

And on a smaller screen, everything rearranges itself instead of becoming a complete mess.

That isn't happening by accident.

CSS controls the layout. 💻

Many beginners first learn CSS as the language used to change colours, fonts, borders, and backgrounds.

That's certainly part of it.

But CSS does something much bigger.

It determines how elements are displayed, where they appear, how much space they occupy, how they align, and how they relate to other elements on the page.

Once you understand CSS layout, you're no longer simply styling individual elements.

You're learning how to make those elements work together as a webpage.

Let's break it down.

What Does CSS Layout Actually Mean?

Imagine you have these HTML elements:

My Website

Welcome to my website.

Learn More

HTML gives you the elements.

But HTML alone doesn't give you complete control over how those elements should be arranged visually.

CSS allows you to decide things such as:

  • Should elements appear on separate lines?
  • Should they sit beside one another?
  • How much space should exist between them?
  • Should they be arranged in rows or columns?
  • Should an element stay in a particular position?
  • Should a group of cards form multiple columns?
  • How should the layout change on smaller screens?

That's the world of CSS layout.

And one of the first concepts you need to understand is the display property.

  1. The display Property

The CSS display property determines how an element participates in the layout.

For example:

.container {
display: block;
}

Or:

.container {
display: flex;
}

Or:

.container {
display: grid;
}

These values can produce very different layouts.

That's why understanding display is essential.

Some of the most important display-related concepts for beginners include:

  • Block
  • Inline
  • Inline-block
  • Flex
  • Grid

Let's look at each one.

  1. Block Elements

Block elements generally begin on a new line and take up the available width of their parent container by default.

Common examples include:

Imagine writing:

Welcome

Hello there!

Learning CSS is fun.

These elements naturally stack vertically.

You can think of them like boxes being placed one underneath another.

[ Heading ]

[ Paragraph ]

[ Paragraph ]

This behaviour is useful for many parts of a webpage because content often needs to flow vertically.

However, sometimes you don't want everything stacked.

What if you want two elements beside each other?

That's where inline elements and other layout systems become useful.

  1. Inline Elements

Inline elements generally flow alongside other content instead of automatically starting on a new line.

Common examples include:


Link
Important

For example:

Visit our website to learn more.

The link doesn't automatically jump onto a new line.

It remains within the flow of the paragraph.

You can think of inline elements as content that naturally flows within a line.

This makes them useful for things such as:

  • Links
  • Emphasised text
  • Small pieces of content
  • Inline icons
  • Text-level elements

But there is another option when you want something to behave partly like an inline element and partly like a block.

  1. Inline-Block

inline-block combines some characteristics of inline and block behaviour.

For example:

.card {
display: inline-block;
width: 200px;
}

The elements can sit alongside one another, while still allowing you to control dimensions such as width and height.

You might use this for simple horizontal layouts.

However, modern CSS gives us much more powerful tools for layout.

Two of the most important are:

Flexbox

and

CSS Grid.

  1. Flexbox: Arrange Elements in a Row or Column

Flexbox is one of the most useful CSS layout systems beginners should learn.

It is designed primarily for arranging elements along one dimension.

That means you can work with:

  • A row
  • Or a column

For example:

.container {
display: flex;
}

Now the children of .container become flex items.

Instead of stacking vertically like normal block elements, they can be arranged horizontally.

Imagine:

[Card 1] [Card 2] [Card 3]

You can also change the direction:

.container {
display: flex;
flex-direction: column;
}

Now the items can stack vertically:

[Card 1]

[Card 2]

[Card 3]

Flexbox also gives you powerful alignment tools.

For example:

.container {
display: flex;
justify-content: center;
align-items: center;
}

This allows you to control how items are distributed and aligned within the container.

That's why Flexbox is commonly used for:

  • Navigation bars
  • Buttons
  • Toolbars
  • Card rows
  • Form layouts
  • Aligning content
  • Small component layouts
  1. CSS Grid: Rows AND Columns

Flexbox is excellent for one-dimensional layouts.

But what if you need to work with rows and columns at the same time?

That's where CSS Grid comes in.

For example:

.container {
display: grid;
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
}

This can create a three-column layout.

You might have:

[Card 1] [Card 2] [Card 3]

[Card 4] [Card 5] [Card 6]

Grid is particularly useful for:

  • Image galleries
  • Product cards
  • Dashboards
  • Website sections
  • Article layouts
  • Complex page structures

The important thing isn't to memorize every Grid property immediately.

Start by understanding the basic idea:

Grid gives you a system for arranging elements into rows and columns.

Flexbox vs Grid

Beginners often ask:

“Should I learn Flexbox or Grid?”

The answer isn't that one replaces the other.

They solve different layout problems and can be used together.

A simple way to think about them is:

Flexbox

Think:

One direction.

Row or column.

Grid

Think:

Two directions.

Rows and columns.

For example, you could use Grid for the overall structure of a dashboard and Flexbox inside individual cards.

CSS layout isn't about choosing one tool forever.

It's about understanding which tool fits the layout you're trying to create.

  1. CSS Positioning

Flexbox and Grid help you arrange elements within layouts.

But sometimes you need more specific control over an element's position.

That's where CSS positioning comes in.

CSS provides several positioning values, including:

  • static
  • relative
  • absolute
  • fixed
  • sticky

Let's briefly understand them.

position: static

This is the default positioning behaviour for elements.

The element remains in the normal flow of the document.

.element {
position: static;
}

Most elements behave this way by default.

position: relative

The element remains in the normal document flow but can be visually shifted from its normal position.

.element {
position: relative;
top: 10px;
}

Relative positioning is also commonly used as a reference point for absolutely positioned descendants.

position: absolute

An absolutely positioned element is removed from the normal document flow and positioned relative to an appropriate containing block.

For example:

.parent {
position: relative;
}

.child {
position: absolute;
top: 0;
right: 0;
}

This pattern is useful for things like:

  • Badges
  • Icons
  • Overlays
  • Decorative elements
  • Elements positioned within a component

position: fixed

A fixed element is positioned relative to the viewport.

For example:

button {
position: fixed;
bottom: 20px;
right: 20px;
}

This can be useful for elements such as floating controls that should remain visible while the user scrolls.

position: sticky

Sticky positioning combines aspects of relative and fixed positioning.

For example:

header {
position: sticky;
top: 0;
}

This can allow an element to remain in place as the user scrolls once a specified threshold is reached, subject to its containing context.

You've probably encountered sticky navigation on websites without realizing CSS was responsible.

CSS Layout Is About Relationships

Here's the bigger idea beginners sometimes miss.

CSS isn't only about individual elements.

It's about relationships between elements.

Imagine a webpage containing:

Header
↓
Navigation
↓
Main Content
↓
Cards
↓
Footer

You aren't only deciding what each individual element looks like.

You're deciding:

  • How wide it should be
  • Where it should sit
  • What it should align with
  • How much space surrounds it
  • How it interacts with neighbouring elements
  • How it responds when the available space changes

That's layout.

A Simple Real-World Analogy

Think about arranging furniture in a room.

HTML gives you the furniture:

🛋️ Sofa
🪑 Chairs
🪴 Plants
🖼️ Pictures
🗄️ Tables

CSS helps decide where everything goes.

Do the chairs sit beside the sofa?

Does the table sit in front of it?

Is there enough space between the furniture?

Should something stay against the wall?

Should everything rearrange when the room becomes smaller?

That's similar to what CSS does with elements on a webpage.

HTML gives you the objects.

CSS determines how those objects are presented and arranged.

Why display Matters So Much

You might see code like:

display: flex;

and think:

“Okay, it just puts things in a row.”

But there's much more to it.

Changing display can fundamentally change how an element's children participate in the layout.

For example:

.container {
display: block;
}

is very different from:

.container {
display: flex;
}

which is also different from:

.container {
display: grid;
}

This is why understanding layout systems is more useful than memorizing isolated CSS properties.

You need to understand the relationship between the parent and its children.

The Parent-Child Relationship

This is another important concept.

Consider:

One
Two
Three

Here:

.container is the parent.

The .card elements are children.

When you write:

.container {
display: flex;
}

you're primarily changing how those child elements are laid out within the container.

That's a powerful idea.

Instead of individually pushing every card around with random margins, you can often control the parent layout and let the children arrange themselves according to the layout system.

This leads to cleaner and more maintainable CSS.

Don't Use Margins to Solve Every Layout Problem

One common beginner habit is using margins for everything.

Something is too far left?

Add a margin.

Something is too low?

Add another margin.

Something isn't aligned?

Add more margin.

Soon you have:

margin-left: 37px;
margin-top: 14px;
margin-right: 22px;

And then changing one thing breaks three other things. 😭

Margins have their place.

But they shouldn't be your default solution to every layout problem.

Sometimes the real solution is:

  • Flexbox
  • Grid
  • gap
  • Alignment properties
  • Width constraints
  • The Box Model
  • Positioning
  • A better parent layout

The goal isn't simply to move an element until it looks correct.

The goal is to understand why it needs to be there.

CSS Layout and Responsive Design

Modern websites need to work across different screen sizes.

A layout that works on a desktop might not work well on a phone.

For example:

Desktop:

[Card] [Card] [Card] [Card]

Mobile:

[Card]

[Card]

[Card]

[Card]

CSS layout systems make these changes possible.

You can use Flexbox, Grid, media queries, flexible sizing, and other CSS techniques to create layouts that adapt to available space.

This is why responsive design shouldn't be treated as something you add at the very end.

You should think about how your layout behaves at different sizes while building it.

A Beginner-Friendly CSS Layout Roadmap

If you're just starting with CSS, you don't need to master everything at once.

A practical learning sequence could be:

Step 1: Understand normal flow

Learn how elements naturally appear on a page.

Step 2: Learn display

Understand block, inline, and inline-block behaviour.

Step 3: Learn the Box Model

Understand:

Content → Padding → Border → Margin

Step 4: Learn Flexbox

Practise:

  • flex-direction
  • justify-content
  • align-items
  • gap
  • Flex wrapping

Step 5: Learn Grid

Practise:

  • Columns
  • Rows
  • Gaps
  • Flexible tracks
  • Grid areas

Step 6: Learn positioning

Understand:

  • Static
  • Relative
  • Absolute
  • Fixed
  • Sticky

Step 7: Learn responsive layouts

Practise building layouts that adapt to different screen sizes.

This progression gives you a foundation before moving into more advanced CSS techniques.

Build Instead of Just Memorizing

One of the best ways to learn CSS layout is to build small projects.

Try creating:

Project 1: Navigation Bar

Use Flexbox to arrange links horizontally.

Project 2: Profile Cards

Use Flexbox or Grid to arrange multiple cards.

Project 3: Image Gallery

Use CSS Grid to create rows and columns.

Project 4: Dashboard

Combine Grid and Flexbox.

Project 5: Responsive Landing Page

Build a desktop layout and make it adapt to smaller screens.

Every project will expose you to different layout problems.

And those problems are where much of the real learning happens.

Don't Memorize CSS. Understand It.

You don't need to memorize every CSS property before you can build something useful.

Instead, develop the habit of asking:

What am I trying to arrange?

Then:

What layout system fits this problem?

For example:

Need a simple row?

→ Consider Flexbox.

Need rows and columns?

→ Consider Grid.

Need an element positioned relative to another?

→ Consider positioning.

Need to understand why an element starts on a new line?

→ Look at normal flow and display behaviour.

Need consistent space between layout items?

→ Consider gap.

This way of thinking is much more useful than randomly trying properties.

Final Thoughts

CSS is often introduced as the language that makes HTML "look good."

But that's only part of the story.

CSS also determines how the pieces of a webpage come together.

It controls:

Display → How elements participate in layout.

Block and Inline → How elements naturally flow.

Inline-block → A combination of inline flow with controllable dimensions.

Flexbox → Flexible one-dimensional layouts.

Grid → Two-dimensional rows and columns.

Positioning → More specific control over where elements appear.

And these systems don't exist in isolation.

They work together to create the layouts we interact with every day.

So when you're learning CSS, don't only ask:

“How can I make this element look better?”

Start asking:

“How should this element relate to everything around it?”

That's when you're no longer just styling a webpage.

You're learning how to build its layout. 💻

What CSS layout concept are you learning right now: display, Flexbox, Grid, or positioning?

title: Our machine-readable source of truth for colour holds 40 hex values and shares exactly one with the app: white
description:
docs/design-tokens.json opens like this:

"description": "Poppy, fresh-produce-energy design system for the Munchable gut-health app. Machine-readable source of truth; codegen'd into the RN theme."

114 lines, 48 hex values in it, 40 of them distinct. The design doc beside it is firmer:

The machine-readable source of truth is docs/design-tokens.json, which is codegen'd into the React Native theme. When the two disagree, the JSON wins and this doc is stale, fix it.

Open munchable.app and look at it. Cream background, cocoa text, caramel buttons. Then look at the JSON's palette: bg: #FBFDF6, primary: #0A8049. That is a white-green. The brand section calls for "vibrant greens, ripe fruit accents" and a farmers market on a sunny morning. The app has been a biscuit for months.

I compared the two palettes with a script instead of my eyes:

json hexes 40   package hexes 17
json ∩ package  1   ->  {'#FFFFFF'}

One colour in common, and it is white.

How to tell which file is real

Not by what it says about itself. By who imports it.

rg -n "design-tokens.json" --glob '!node_modules'
# docs/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md:6    the machine-readable source of truth sentence
# docs/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md:298  a line in the future-work list

Two hits, both in the prose document that calls it the source of truth. No build step, no script, no app. Line 298 is the giveaway, because it is in a list of future work:

Consume docs/design-tokens.json via codegen into a typed theme object

So the codegen the sixth line describes in the present tense is item one of the roadmap at the bottom. The file was authored as the output of a design exercise, the exercise produced a direction that got replaced, and because nothing ever imported it, nothing ever noticed. Its $schema points at https://munchable.app/schemas/design-tokens.v1.json, which answers 404. I checked that too.

The one that is real

packages/design-tokens/src/index.ts, 151 lines, 17 hex values, no platform in it at all. Its header explains why it is a package rather than a file in the app:

These values live in their own package because more than one surface has to look like the app. The reels render a phone running Munchable, and they used to carry a hand-copied mirror of apps/mobile/src/theme/tokens.ts: a copy drifts silently, so changing the caution colour or the "Can't assess" label in the app left the marketing videos showing the old one with no type error anywhere.

That is a package justified by an actual incident, not by symmetry. The marketing videos are Remotion compositions that render a phone running the app. When the app's colours moved, the videos kept rendering the old ones, and the only detector was somebody watching a video and squinting. Now both import the same object, and a renamed key is a type error in the video renderer.

Two consumers: the Expo app's theme module re-exports everything and adds what needs React Native (motion curves, shadows, the font family names Expo loads), and the video package's theme. One source, two surfaces, one of which is a video.

The colours themselves carry their contrast ratios in comments next to them:

bg: '#FFF8EC',        // cream
text: '#3B2314',      // cocoa · cream 13.9:1
textMuted: '#7F5F47', // warm brown · cream 5.5:1

and one of them carries a warning instead:

/** Pop colour (pink sprinkles). Decoration only: it fails contrast as text. */
accent: string;

A token whose doc comment says "do not put words on me" is doing more for accessibility than the audit that found it.

The third palette, which is the website

The site you are reading the links to is not a consumer of that package. app/globals.css declares 28 hex values of its own. 15 of them are the same strings as the package's, which is the brand surviving a copy by hand. 13 are the website's alone: deeper shades for hairlines and gradients, the kind of value a CSS file needs and a React Native StyleSheet does not.

So the honest count is three palettes: a fossil with no importers, a package with two, and a stylesheet that agrees with the package 15 times out of 28 because somebody was careful. You can see the result of the careful part on /recipes and /conditions, where the cards and the app's cards are the same cream and the same border.

The typography is half alive

This is the part I did not expect. The fossil's font families are still the app's font families: Outfit_700Bold for headings, Nunito_400Regular for body. Every size in it is wrong:

JSON shipping
display 40 / 44 32 / 38
h1 32 / 38 27 / 33
h2 26 / 32 21 / 27
title 20 / 26 17 / 23

Everything shrank, and a face the JSON has never heard of (Fredoka, for the wordmark and hero headlines only) was added. So the dead file is not uniformly dead. It is right about two font names and wrong about every number next to them, which is the worst possible state for a document people are told to trust when it disagrees.

What bypasses the palette

23 hex literals sit in the app's own source, outside the tokens. I expected sloppiness and found a pattern: almost all of them are in the camera chrome and in the SVG of the cookie mark.

The camera ones exist because the palette has no dark values. Munchable is light mode only, deliberately, and a viewfinder is the one screen that is mostly a dark photograph, so the scrims and the hairlines over it need colours the design system does not name. The cookie mark's are artwork, four flat fills inside one SVG that happen to be brand colours, which is a different kind of value from a semantic token.

Neither is an argument for leaving them there. Both are an argument that the tokens file is missing two named groups, which is a more useful conclusion than "developers hardcode colours".

The rule I would write down instead

A file is a source of truth when something breaks if it is wrong. The JSON could be deleted today and the app, the website and the videos would all render identically, which is the definition of not being one. The package cannot be edited without changing both the app and the videos, which is the definition of being one.

And the tie-break sentence in the doc, "when the two disagree, the JSON wins", is now the most dangerous line in the repository: a rule that points a future contributor at the green.

Compare for yourself. The app's palette is on munchable.app, and the 26-pixel cookie mark every one of those colours was lifted from is the first thing in the header on every page.

title: The Hidden Cost of Shopify Theme Bloat
description:
The Hidden Cost of Shopify Theme Bloat

Every theme accumulates cruft over time — sections added for a campaign that ended months ago, app blocks from apps that got uninstalled but left their code behind, CSS overrides nobody remembers the reason for. None of it feels urgent to clean up, and all of it compounds.

📥 How Theme Bloat Actually Accumulates

A seasonal campaign section gets added and never removed after the campaign ends. An app gets uninstalled but its theme snippet stays referenced. A CSS override from a one-off fix never gets cleaned up once the "real" fix ships. Each individual addition is small; the sum isn't.

💰 The Compounding Real Cost

Extra JavaScript and CSS slow down every single page load, not just the feature that needed it. Orphaned code becomes a liability during theme updates, since nobody remembers if it's safe to remove. New developers working in the codebase inherit confusion about what's actually load-bearing.

🧹 A Practical Approach to Cleanup

A quarterly audit — removing sections unused in the last publish, auditing for orphaned app snippets, and checking actual CSS/JS payload size against the previous quarter — catches this before it becomes a full theme rebuild. Small, regular cleanup beats an occasional massive one.

Originally published on the KLYX blog.

title: RepoDNA v1.4.5: Building Smarter Offline Repository Intelligence
description:
RepoDNA v1.4.5: Building Smarter Offline Repository Intelligence

Understanding a software repository is more than reading its README or scanning its directory structure.

Developers need to understand architecture, dependencies, historical changes, code quality signals, and the evidence behind technical conclusions.

That's why I've been building RepoDNA, an open-source, local-first repository intelligence and code archaeology platform.

Today, I'm sharing two stable releases:

RepoDNA v1.4.4 — October 28, 2026

RepoDNA v1.4.5 — October 30, 2026

Together, these releases represent another step toward more reliable, locally evaluated, evidence-driven repository analysis.

What is RepoDNA?

RepoDNA helps developers analyze software repositories and understand how their codebases work.

Its existing capabilities include:

  • Repository architecture and dependency analysis
  • Git history and code archaeology
  • Code quality and complexity signals
  • Security, testing, and documentation signals
  • Interactive analysis and Project DNA reports
  • CLI, desktop, browser, and CI workflows
  • Optional AI-assisted explanations

The central principle is simple: analysis should be supported by inspectable evidence.

v1.4.4: Introducing Native Evidence Intelligence

One of the most important additions in v1.4.4 is the optional native explanation provider.

Instead of requiring an external language-model API for every explanation, RepoDNA now supports an offline, keyless, built-in evidence digest.

This capability is extractive, meaning it works with evidence obtained from repository analysis rather than generating unrestricted natural-language responses.

The release also introduces a small CPU-only evidence-relevance ranker.

Developers can prepare labeled examples and train a local ranking checkpoint without downloading third-party model weights.

The trained ranker can optionally reorder the evidence selected for native explanations.

Better evaluation

v1.4.4 also introduced retrieval-quality measurements, including:

  • Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)
  • Precision@k
  • Recall@k
  • NDCG@k

The system compares trained ranking results against the original evidence ordering using repository-disjoint holdout data.

This gives developers a more useful way to evaluate whether local ranking is improving evidence retrieval.

Better findings review

The Findings interface now supports confidence-based filtering and expanded export capabilities.

Filtered findings can be exported in CSV, JSON, or Markdown formats.

These outputs help maintainers inspect findings, review supporting evidence, and incorporate the results into their own development workflows.

Additional improvements strengthen browser import safety, local API validation, package-release integrity, and reliability.

v1.4.5: Reproducibility and Evaluation

v1.4.5 builds on the native evidence-ranking foundation established in v1.4.4.

The focus of this release is not simply adding more ranking features.

It is making ranking behavior easier to reproduce, evaluate, and trust.

1. Deterministic local training

Training is designed to produce consistent outputs even when input dataset rows are shuffled.

The release strengthens validation of evidence identities and repository boundaries.

It also rejects unsafe or ambiguous training data, helping prevent misleading evaluation results.

2. Calibration diagnostics

v1.4.5 adds evaluation diagnostics including:

Brier score: Measures error in relevance probability estimates.

Binary log loss: Evaluates probability predictions against labeled relevance outcomes.

Calibration bands: Help examine whether estimated scores align with observed relevance frequencies.

These evaluate evidence-label relevance, not the factual accuracy of a generated answer.

3. Answerability threshold evaluation

The release introduces offline analysis of hypothetical answerability thresholds.

This helps explore how different thresholds would affect incorrect acceptance and missed answerable questions.

Importantly, these measurements are diagnostic. They do not automatically enable runtime abstention.

4. Stronger regression coverage

Additional tests cover training CLI behavior, checkpoint generation, deterministic output, file overwrite protection, and repository leakage prevention.

The objective is to make the native evidence-ranking system more predictable across supported development environments.

Why Local-First Matters

RepoDNA is designed around a local-first workflow.

Core repository analysis can be performed without uploading source code to a hosted analysis service.

The native extractive explanation capability does not require an external AI API key.

For developers working with internal projects, large codebases, or offline environments, those properties are particularly useful.

And because RepoDNA is open-source, developers can inspect the implementation and evaluate the results themselves.

How to Try RepoDNA

Option 1: Browser

Try the web application:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

Option 2: Install the CLI 

npm install --global @sanskarin/repodna

Then analyze a repository:

repodna analyze .

Option 3: Desktop

Download the latest release for Windows, Linux, or macOS from GitHub.

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.4.5

What's Next?

These releases strengthen the groundwork for continued development of native repository intelligence.

The focus remains on reproducible analysis, evidence quality, useful developer workflows, and transparent limitations.

RepoDNA is not trying to replace software engineers' judgment.

It is being built to help developers make better-informed decisions about their codebases.

Explore and Contribute

GitHub: https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA

Latest stable release: https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.4.5

Web application: https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

More projects: https://sanskarin.github.io/

If you're interested in developer tooling, repository analysis, Rust, or local-first software, I'd welcome your feedback and contributions.

RepoDNA — Understand your codebase. See its DNA.

title: Building Production-Ready Microservices in Go with GoFr: Zero-Config Observability, SQLite & Migrations
description:
Building Production-Ready Microservices in Go with GoFr: Zero-Config Observability, SQLite & Migrations

When building microservices in Go, developers often spend substantial time assembling boilerplate: wiring up OpenTelemetry tracers, configuring Prometheus metrics exporters, setting up structured JSON loggers with trace correlation, managing database connection pools, and building custom health check endpoints.

GoFr is an opinionated, developer-first Go microservices framework (listed on the CNCF Landscape) designed to eliminate this repetitive plumbing. With GoFr, out-of-the-box observability, configuration management, health probes, and datasource lifecycle handling work seamlessly from a single unified context.

In this tutorial, we will build a production-grade Task Management REST Microservice from scratch using GoFr, featuring:

  • Datasource integration with SQLite
  • Automated versioned schema migrations
  • Clean REST CRUD endpoints (POST, GET, PUT, DELETE)
  • Custom Prometheus business metrics
  • Zero-config health checks and OpenTelemetry tracing
  • End-to-end integration tests

Source Code: The complete, tested source code for this project is available on GitHub: manchitt/gofr-task-api.

1. Prerequisites & Project Setup

Ensure you have Go 1.26 or higher installed.

Create a new directory and initialize your Go module:

mkdir gofr-task-api && cd gofr-task-api
go mod init gofr-task-api
go get gofr.dev@latest

2. Configuration Management

GoFr follows 12-factor application principles, loading configuration automatically from environment variables or a configs/.env file.

Create configs/.env:

APP_NAME=task-api
HTTP_PORT=9000
METRICS_PORT=2121
DB_DIALECT=sqlite
DB_NAME=tasks.db

Notice what is happening here:

  • DB_DIALECT=sqlite informs GoFr's SQL datasource manager to initialize an embedded SQLite driver.
  • HTTP_PORT=9000 sets the REST API server port.
  • METRICS_PORT=2121 automatically exposes Prometheus metrics on a dedicated port.

3. Versioned Database Migrations

GoFr features a built-in migration system that tracks applied versions directly inside the datastore.

Create a migrations/ directory with two files:

migrations/1730300000_create_tasks_table.go 

package migrations

import (
    "gofr.dev/pkg/gofr/migration"
)

const createTasksTable = `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tasks (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    description TEXT,
    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    priority TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'medium',
    created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);`

func createTasks() migration.Migrate {
    return migration.Migrate{
        UP: func(d migration.Datasource) error {
            _, err := d.SQL.Exec(createTasksTable)
            return err
        },
    }
}

migrations/all.go 

package migrations

import (
    "gofr.dev/pkg/gofr/migration"
)

// All returns all migrations registered in chronological order.
func All() map[int64]migration.Migrate {
    return map[int64]migration.Migrate{
        1730300000: createTasks(),
    }
}

When the application boots, GoFr detects app.Migrate(migrations.All()), inspects the current database version table, and executes pending migrations before starting the HTTP listeners.

4. Building the Application (main.go)

Now let's build the core service in main.go:

package main

import (
    "database/sql"
    "errors"
    "fmt"

    "gofr-task-api/migrations"
    "gofr.dev/pkg/gofr"
    gofrHTTP "gofr.dev/pkg/gofr/http"
)

type Task struct {
    ID          int64  `json:"id"`
    Title       string `json:"title"`
    Description string `json:"description"`
    Status      string `json:"status"`
    Priority    string `json:"priority"`
    CreatedAt   string `json:"created_at,omitempty"`
}

func main() {
    app := gofr.New()

    // Register migrations
    app.Migrate(migrations.All())

    // Register Task REST endpoints
    app.POST("/tasks", createTask)
    app.GET("/tasks", listTasks)
    app.GET("/tasks/{id}", getTask)
    app.PUT("/tasks/{id}", updateTask)
    app.DELETE("/tasks/{id}", deleteTask)

    app.Run()
}

// createTask handles POST /tasks
func createTask(c *gofr.Context) (any, error) {
    var task Task
    if err := c.Bind(&task); err != nil {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorInvalidParam{Params: []string{"body"}}
    }

    if task.Title == "" {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorMissingParam{Params: []string{"title"}}
    }

    if task.Status == "" {
        task.Status = "pending"
    }
    if task.Priority == "" {
        task.Priority = "medium"
    }

    query := `INSERT INTO tasks (title, description, status, priority) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)`
    res, err := c.SQL.ExecContext(c, query, task.Title, task.Description, task.Status, task.Priority)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to insert task: %w", err)
    }

    id, err := res.LastInsertId()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to retrieve last insert id: %w", err)
    }
    task.ID = id

    // Increment custom Prometheus metric
    c.Metrics().IncrementCounter(c, "tasks_created_total")

    return task, nil
}

// listTasks handles GET /tasks with optional ?status= filter
func listTasks(c *gofr.Context) (any, error) {
    statusFilter := c.Param("status")

    var (
        rows *sql.Rows
        err  error
    )

    if statusFilter != "" {
        query := `SELECT id, title, description, status, priority, created_at FROM tasks WHERE status = ? ORDER BY id DESC`
        rows, err = c.SQL.QueryContext(c, query, statusFilter)
    } else {
        query := `SELECT id, title, description, status, priority, created_at FROM tasks ORDER BY id DESC`
        rows, err = c.SQL.QueryContext(c, query)
    }

    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to query tasks: %w", err)
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    tasks := make([]Task, 0)
    for rows.Next() {
        var t Task
        if err := rows.Scan(&t.ID, &t.Title, &t.Description, &t.Status, &t.Priority, &t.CreatedAt); err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to scan task: %w", err)
        }
        tasks = append(tasks, t)
    }

    return tasks, nil
}

// getTask handles GET /tasks/{id}
func getTask(c *gofr.Context) (any, error) {
    id := c.PathParam("id")
    if id == "" {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorMissingParam{Params: []string{"id"}}
    }

    var t Task
    query := `SELECT id, title, description, status, priority, created_at FROM tasks WHERE id = ?`
    err := c.SQL.QueryRowContext(c, query, id).Scan(&t.ID, &t.Title, &t.Description, &t.Status, &t.Priority, &t.CreatedAt)
    if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorEntityNotFound{Name: "task", Value: id}
    }
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to retrieve task: %w", err)
    }

    return t, nil
}

// updateTask handles PUT /tasks/{id}
func updateTask(c *gofr.Context) (any, error) {
    id := c.PathParam("id")
    if id == "" {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorMissingParam{Params: []string{"id"}}
    }

    var update Task
    if err := c.Bind(&update); err != nil {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorInvalidParam{Params: []string{"body"}}
    }

    query := `UPDATE tasks SET title = COALESCE(NULLIF(?, ''), title),
                               description = COALESCE(NULLIF(?, ''), description),
                               status = COALESCE(NULLIF(?, ''), status),
                               priority = COALESCE(NULLIF(?, ''), priority)
              WHERE id = ?`

    res, err := c.SQL.ExecContext(c, query, update.Title, update.Description, update.Status, update.Priority, id)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to update task: %w", err)
    }

    rowsAffected, err := res.RowsAffected()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if rowsAffected == 0 {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorEntityNotFound{Name: "task", Value: id}
    }

    return getTask(c)
}

// deleteTask handles DELETE /tasks/{id}
func deleteTask(c *gofr.Context) (any, error) {
    id := c.PathParam("id")
    if id == "" {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorMissingParam{Params: []string{"id"}}
    }

    query := `DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = ?`
    res, err := c.SQL.ExecContext(c, query, id)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to delete task: %w", err)
    }

    rowsAffected, err := res.RowsAffected()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if rowsAffected == 0 {
        return nil, gofrHTTP.ErrorEntityNotFound{Name: "task", Value: id}
    }

    return nil, nil
}

Key GoFr Concepts Highlighted:

  1. Uniform Handler Signature: func(c *gofr.Context) (any, error). Any returned struct is automatically marshaled into standard JSON response format {"data": ...}. Returning errors automatically responds with appropriate HTTP status codes (201 for created resources, 204 for deletes, 404 for missing entities, 400 for bad parameters).
  2. Context Propagation: Always pass c (*gofr.Context) to c.SQL.ExecContext and c.SQL.QueryContext. This preserves the OpenTelemetry active span across the database query.
  3. Built-in Error Types: GoFr provides rich standard HTTP error types like gofrHTTP.ErrorEntityNotFound, gofrHTTP.ErrorMissingParam, and gofrHTTP.ErrorInvalidParam.

5. Running and Testing the Service

Run the microservice:

go run main.go

Startup output:

{"level":"INFO","time":"2026-10-30T13:57:00+05:30","message":"Loaded config from file: ./configs/.env","gofrVersion":"dev"}
{"level":"INFO","time":"2026-10-30T13:57:00+05:30","message":"connected to 'tasks.db' database","gofrVersion":"dev"}
{"level":"INFO","time":"2026-10-30T13:57:00+05:30","message":"running migration 1730300000","gofrVersion":"dev"}
{"level":"INFO","time":"2026-10-30T13:57:00+05:30","message":"Migration 1730300000 ran successfully","gofrVersion":"dev"}
{"level":"INFO","time":"2026-10-30T13:57:00+05:30","message":"Registered HTTP server on port: 9000","gofrVersion":"dev"}
{"level":"INFO","time":"2026-10-30T13:57:00+05:30","message":"Starting metrics server on port: 2121","gofrVersion":"dev"}

Testing the Endpoints

1. Create a Task 

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:9000/tasks \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title": "Explore GoFr", "description": "Write article and run benchmarks", "priority": "high"}'

Response (HTTP/1.1 201 Created):

{
  "data": {
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Explore GoFr",
    "description": "Write article and run benchmarks",
    "status": "pending",
    "priority": "high"
  }
}

Notice the server log output automatically generated by GoFr for this request:

{
  "level": "INFO",
  "time": "2026-10-30T13:57:00+05:30",
  "message": {
    "trace_id": "5d4b8e169c116689518fab5029799c45",
    "span_id": "9af1f5a261da4ee6",
    "start_time": "2026-10-30T13:57:00+05:30",
    "response_time": 637,
    "method": "POST",
    "user_agent": "curl/8.7.1",
    "ip": "127.0.0.1:52000",
    "uri": "/tasks",
    "response": 201
  }
}

Every single request automatically gets a distributed trace_id and span_id without a single line of OpenTelemetry boilerplate!

2. Query Health Check (/.well-known/health) 

curl -s http://localhost:9000/.well-known/health | jq

Response:

{
  "data": {
    "name": "task-api",
    "status": "SUCCESS",
    "version": "dev",
    "details": {
      "sql": {
        "status": "UP",
        "details": {
          "host": "tasks.db",
          "database": "tasks.db",
          "stats": {
            "openConnections": 1,
            "inUse": 0,
            "idle": 1
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

GoFr automatically pings the database and reports pool statistics in the health probe!

3. Custom Prometheus Metrics

Check the metrics endpoint:

curl -s http://localhost:2121/metrics | grep tasks_created_total

Output:

# HELP tasks_created_total
# TYPE tasks_created_total counter
tasks_created_total{app_name="task-api"} 1

6. Writing Integration Tests

GoFr provides a dedicated testutil package that reserves ephemeral ports and manages server lifecycle for deterministic integration tests.

Create main_test.go:

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "testing"

    "github.com/stretchr/testify/assert"
    "github.com/stretchr/testify/require"

    "gofr.dev/pkg/gofr/testutil"
)

func TestMain(m *testing.M) {
    os.Setenv("GOFR_TELEMETRY", "false")
    m.Run()
}

func TestIntegration_TaskAPI(t *testing.T) {
    configs := testutil.NewServerConfigs(t)

    go main()
    testutil.WaitForHTTPServer(t, configs.HTTPHost)

    client := http.Client{}

    // 1. Create Task (201 Created)
    createBody := []byte(`{"title":"Write GoFr Tutorial","description":"Complete article for open-source contribution","priority":"high"}`)
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, configs.HTTPHost+"/tasks", bytes.NewReader(createBody))
    require.NoError(t, err)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    assert.Equal(t, http.StatusCreated, resp.StatusCode)

    var createResp struct {
        Data Task `json:"data"`
    }
    require.NoError(t, json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&createResp))
    assert.Equal(t, "Write GoFr Tutorial", createResp.Data.Title)
    taskID := createResp.Data.ID

    // 2. Get Task by ID (200 OK)
    req, err = http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, fmt.Sprintf("%s/tasks/%d", configs.HTTPHost, taskID), http.NoBody)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    resp, err = client.Do(req)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    assert.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)

    // 3. Delete Task (204 No Content)
    req, err = http.NewRequest(http.MethodDelete, fmt.Sprintf("%s/tasks/%d", configs.HTTPHost, taskID), http.NoBody)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    resp, err = client.Do(req)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    assert.Equal(t, http.StatusNoContent, resp.StatusCode)

    // 4. Verify Task is gone (404 Not Found)
    req, err = http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, fmt.Sprintf("%s/tasks/%d", configs.HTTPHost, taskID), http.NoBody)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    resp, err = client.Do(req)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    assert.Equal(t, http.StatusNotFound, resp.StatusCode)

    // 5. Verify Health Check (200 OK)
    req, err = http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, configs.HTTPHost+"/.well-known/health", http.NoBody)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    resp, err = client.Do(req)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    assert.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
}

Run the tests:

go test -v ./...

Output:

=== RUN   TestIntegration_TaskAPI
--- PASS: TestIntegration_TaskAPI (0.11s)
PASS
ok      gofr-task-api   0.764s

Conclusion

GoFr dramatically reduces boilerplate in Go backend engineering. In less than 150 lines of code, we built an end-to-end microservice with:

  • Fully automated SQLite migrations
  • Idiomatic REST endpoints
  • Automatic JSON structured logging with correlation IDs
  • Out-of-the-box OpenTelemetry tracing and Prometheus metrics
  • Production-grade health checks and pool monitoring

Check out the official GoFr documentation and repository to learn more:

  • Tutorial GitHub Repository: github.com/manchitt/gofr-task-api
  • Official Website & Docs: gofr.dev
  • GitHub Repository: github.com/gofr-dev/gofr
  • CNCF Landscape: CNCF App Definition and Development

title: How to Add a Border in CSS Without Changing Element Size
description:
Using CSS border is the standard way to outline an element. But it has a side effect that breaks layouts: borders add to the element's total width and height.

If you have a 100px wide div and add a 5px border, it suddenly becomes 110px wide. In a tight grid or flexbox layout, this causes elements to overflow or wrap unexpectedly.

You can fix this globally by setting box-sizing: border-box, but sometimes you need a border that doesn't take up any space at all, or you want multiple borders on a single element.

The solution is to use box-shadow.

The Problem with Borders

Here is a standard box:

.box {
  width: 100px;
  height: 100px;
  border: 2px solid blue;
}

Total width: 104px. Total height: 104px.

If you're positioning this element absolutely, or fitting it into a strict grid, those extra 4 pixels matter.

The Solution: Hard Box Shadows

A box-shadow is normally used for fuzzy drop shadows, but if you set the blur and spread values correctly, it acts as a solid border.

.shadow-border {
  width: 100px;
  height: 100px;
  /* x-offset | y-offset | blur | spread | color */
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 2px blue;
}

Total width: 100px. Total height: 100px.

Because shadows are drawn outside the box model and don't affect layout, the element's dimensions remain exactly 100x100.

The Inset Shadow

You can also use box-shadow to draw inside the element. Add the inset keyword.

.inner-shadow {
  box-shadow: inset 0 4px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15);
}

This creates a recessed, "pushed-in" look, useful for input fields or pressed buttons.

Layering Multiple Borders

The real power of box-shadow is that it accepts a comma-separated list. You can stack multiple borders on a single element.

.multi-border {
  box-shadow: 
    0 0 0 2px blue,
    0 0 0 4px red,
    0 0 0 6px green;
}

This creates three distinct borders without adding a single wrapper div.

Common Gotchas

  • Border Radius: Box shadows follow the border-radius of the element. If your element is round, your shadow borders will be round.
  • Clipping: If the parent container has overflow: hidden, the outer shadow borders will get clipped and disappear.
  • Accessibility: Focus states using box-shadow are fine visually, but make sure they are distinct enough for keyboard users.

Prototyping Visually

Writing shadow borders by hand is tricky. You have to guess the spread and offset values, and one typo makes the border look fuzzy instead of crisp.

If you want to design and test multi-layered borders using CSS box-shadow without altering the box model, I built a free CSS Shadow Borders Designer.

What it does:

  • Designs crisp, multi-layered borders using box-shadow
  • Previews them without altering DOM dimensions
  • Exports clean CSS instantly

Try it here

100% client-side. Nothing uploaded.

Do you use box-shadow for borders, or do you rely on border and box-sizing? Let me know in the comments.

title: Your RAG doesn't need a better embedding model. It needs better chunking.
description:
For the last week I've been running LongMemEval against Palace, a local memory store I build for coding agents. It's a single Rust binary with SQLite, BM25 and a small ONNX embedding model. No LLM sits anywhere in the write or recall path.

This post isn't about the final number. It's about what I learned getting there: which changes moved recall, which didn't, and how many of the improvements turned out to be plain bugs that only a benchmark run would surface.

Short version, so you can stop here if you want:

  • Swapping embedding models did nothing on this dataset. Every difference was 1 to 4 questions.
  • Chunking conversations the way the product actually stores them helped more than anything else.
  • The ranking gains were mostly bug fixes. A substring match, an overeager phrase rule, and a chunker that silently dropped text.
  • int8 models give different vectors depending on what else is in the batch. That one surprised me.

What's being measured

LongMemEval asks questions about a long chat history. In the s_cleaned split each question comes with a haystack of about 50 sessions (about 115k tokens), and somewhere in there are the sessions that hold the answer. 470 questions get scored; the 30 abstention questions are excluded, as usual.

I only measure retrieval: did the right session show up in the top K? The metric is recall_any@K at session granularity. That is not the same thing as the end-to-end QA accuracy many memory systems report, where an LLM reads the retrieved context and answers. Retrieval recall is an upper bound on what a reader model can do, and it's the part I control. So please don't line these numbers up against QA accuracy tables. They measure different things.

Setup for every run in this post:

  • Windows, 16 threads, CPU only
  • MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dim) unless stated otherwise, 512-token cap
  • Hybrid search: BM25 fused with cosine, plus the product's normal ranking boosts
  • No LLM at any stage: no extraction at ingest, no query rewriting, no answer generation

One number worth keeping in your head the whole way through: one question is 0.0021. On 470 questions, a "+0.4 points" improvement is two questions. I'll say how many questions a change moved wherever I can, because decimals make small things look bigger than they are.

Starting point: the number had drifted

Back in May the README said R@5 0.981. When I reran the same configuration in October, I got 0.977.

My first instinct was "noise, run it again." But there's no noise here. The retrieval is deterministic: fixed ONNX model, BM25, cosine, no sampling. A rerun gives the same 0.977 every time. So two questions had genuinely moved, and something in the code had moved them.

Since May, the ranker had grown a few extra boosts on top of the plain BM25/cosine fusion: coding-agent intent boosts, preference matching, recency. I diffed the per-question results against the May baseline and found the first culprit:

The query contained the word "latest". The intent classifier saw "test" inside it, decided this was a question about running tests, and lifted an unrelated drawer into the top five.

The fix was to match intent terms only at word starts (inflections still match). R@5 went from 0.977 to 0.979. The coding-agent eval didn't change.

Lesson one: a benchmark number in your README is a claim about your current code. If the ranker changes, the number has to be re-earned. Reproducing an old number is a good way to find out what broke.

The model swap that changed nothing

I had just added support for switchable embedding models, so the obvious question was whether a better model would help. I ran five of them through the same per-session configuration:

Model R@1 R@5 R@10 Ingest
minilm-l6-v2 (fp32) 0.889 0.977 0.991 508 s
minilm-l6-v2-q8 (int8) 0.891 0.977 0.991 355 s
bge-small (fp32) 0.898 0.972 0.985 920 s
bge-small-q8 (int8) 0.898 0.972 0.985 622 s
bge-base-q8 (int8, 768-dim) 0.887 0.970 0.979 1181 s

Every recall difference in that table is between 1 and 4 questions. BGE got a slightly better R@1, mostly on single-session-user questions, and paid for it with worse R@5 and R@10 on multi-session ones. Nothing beat MiniLM in a way I'd be willing to call real.

What was real was the speed. The int8 MiniLM gave the same recall with about 1.4x faster ingest. That made it the interesting option, not because it's smarter but because it's cheaper for the same answer.

Lesson two: on a retrieval benchmark, the embedding model was not the bottleneck. I'd assumed it would be. Twelve-layer models cost twice as much per embedding as six-layer ones, and on this data I got nothing back for it.

A detour: batching was slower than not batching

While sizing the model work I measured embedding throughput on real drawers and found something backwards: embedding one text at a time did 94 drawers/s, and batching made it slower. 69/s at batch 16, 53/s at 32, 42/s at 64.

The cause was padding. A batch gets padded to its longest text, so one long drawer makes every short drawer in the batch pay for its length. Sorting texts by length and capping batches at 8 took it from 29/s (the old batched path) to about 110/s.

Another detour: int8 vectors depend on their neighbours

Later, when I made the int8 model the default for new palaces, an existing test started failing. It checks that embedding a text in a batch gives the same vector as embedding it alone.

For fp32 the worst cosine between "batched" and "alone" was 0.999999. For int8 it was 0.976.

Dynamically quantized ONNX models compute their activation scales over the whole input tensor. That means the whole batch. Put a text next to a long, unusual neighbour and its vector shifts. For a memory store that's a real problem: the same sentence could land in a slightly different place depending on what else happened to be mined in the same call.

The fix: int8 models embed one text per call. That costs some of the speedup, but the q8 model still indexes faster than fp32 (150 vs 132 drawers/s on real palace drawers, about 1.7x on longer synthetic ones), and now a text's vector depends only on the text.

I wouldn't have found this without the switch, and I wouldn't have switched without the benchmark telling me q8 was "free."

Chunking: measure what you ship

The usual LongMemEval setup stores each session as one document. That's not how Palace stores conversations. When it mines a chat log it splits it into exchange pairs: one chunk per user turn plus the reply to it.

So the benchmark was measuring a configuration no user ever runs. I added a --chunking flag to the runner with three modes:

  • session: one drawer per session (the standard setup)
  • text: the generic paragraph chunker used for project files
  • exchange: each session goes through the exact normaliser and chunker that palace mine-convos uses

In the chunked modes a session ranks by its best chunk.

Chunking (q8) R@1 R@5 R@10 Drawers Ingest
session 0.891 0.979 0.991 22k 351 s
text 0.896 0.983 0.996 401k 1016 s
exchange 0.906 0.985 0.994 194k 1150 s

Exchange pairs won, and the biggest move was where I least expected it: single-session-preference R@1 went from 0.633 to 0.767. A preference (say, "I've been trying to cut down on caffeine") is usually one sentence buried in a long session about something else. As one big document, the session's embedding is dominated by everything else. As an exchange pair, the preference turn gets a vector of its own.

The text mode is a useful contrast. It has twice as many drawers as exchange and does worse. More, smaller chunks isn't the point. Chunks that follow the shape of the conversation are.

The chunker was dropping text

Wiring the real chunker into the benchmark turned up a bug in the product. The exchange chunker kept the user turn and the first 8 lines of the reply, and silently dropped the rest. Any long assistant answer lost everything after line 8.

Nobody had noticed because nothing ever compared mined conversations against the original. Running the real chunker over thousands of sessions with known answers did.

Replies are now kept whole. An exchange over about 2,000 characters continues in further chunks that each repeat the user turn, so the question context travels with every piece of the answer. Short sessions with fewer than three user turns fall back to paragraph chunks, the same as in the product.

Lesson three: benchmark the code path your users run, not a convenient stand-in. If I'd kept the one-document-per-session setup I'd have a slightly lower number and a chunker that was still eating replies.

Ranking: three general mechanisms and one bad rule

At this point I set myself a rule, which I'll quote because it shaped everything after it: "We're not tuning for the score, we're tuning for the output." LongMemEval is a proxy. Reading the misses to find general weaknesses is fine. Writing rules that fix specific questions isn't. Any change has to be a mechanism that would help a real palace, and has to be checked on data other than the data that inspired it before a number gets published.

With that in place, here's what changed in the ranker.

1. "should I" is not a convention question

Palace has an intent classifier, and questions that sound like project conventions ("should we use tabs?") get a boost toward convention-style drawers. The trigger included "should I".

One preference question in LongMemEval starts with "should I". The classifier filed it under conventions and boosted the wrong drawers. I narrowed the trigger. That question recovered, and R@1 on the coding-agent eval (a separate fixture, not LongMemEval) went up too.

2. Date-aware ranking

Temporal questions ("what did I buy two weeks ago?") were the category I most wanted to improve. In a live palace every drawer has a date, so a question that points at a time window should favour drawers from that window.

To make that testable the runner had to stop cheating in the other direction: every question is now asked on its own question_date, and every drawer is dated by its session. Relative dates like "10 days ago", "last Tuesday" or "in the past month" now resolve the way they would in a real palace.

The ranker parses those spans and gives drawers inside the window a small boost (weight 0.12). Two bugs came out while building it: spans like "two weeks" have to count in full rather than as a point, and "on Tuesday" in a sentence usually isn't a time reference at all, so that pattern is skipped.

Honest result: the temporal R@5 didn't move on s_cleaned. The three temporal misses that remain lose on topic, not on date. The gold chunk is from the right day and still scores below unrelated chunks from the same days. Date-awareness helps break ties; it can't rescue a chunk that doesn't look relevant. On larger haystacks, with many sessions per day, it's mostly a tie-breaker too.

I kept it anyway, because in a real palace "what did we decide last week" is a very common question, and the mechanism is right even when this dataset doesn't reward it much.

3. Sources that match in several places

When a session ranks by its best chunk, a session where three different exchanges match the question looks the same as a session where one does. That's throwing away evidence.

Now a drawer gets a small lift (weight 0.1) from the best other matching drawer from the same source. I picked the weight on a different split plus probes from a real palace, froze it, then ran s_cleaned once. 0.1 was best; 0.3 already hurt.

The bad rule I'm still carrying

In the interest of honesty: Palace's separate coding-agent eval is partly tuned. The ranker contains a handful of phrases copied from that eval's own questions. With them, the int8 model scores R@1 0.922 on it; without them, 0.902. The README says so and shows both. They have zero effect on LongMemEval and on real-palace probes, and I'm keeping them only until general mechanisms reach the same numbers.

I mention it because it's exactly the kind of thing that makes benchmark numbers meaningless if nobody discloses it, and it's very easy to do by accident.

Where it ended up

With exchange chunking, int8 MiniLM, and the ranking changes above, frozen before the run:

Configuration Model R@1 R@5 R@10
One drawer per session minilm-l6-v2 0.896 0.981 0.991
One drawer per session minilm-l6-v2-q8 0.898 0.981 0.991
Exchange pairs minilm-l6-v2-q8 0.915 0.987 0.996

Per question type (exchange pairs, q8):

Question type R@1 R@5
knowledge-update 0.958 1.000
multi-session 0.909 0.992
single-session-assistant 1.000 1.000
single-session-preference 0.767 0.933
single-session-user 0.984 1.000
temporal-reasoning 0.858 0.976

From the start of the week, exchange pairs went from 0.906/0.985/0.994 to 0.915/0.987/0.996. That's four more questions at R@1, one more at R@5. Per session, R@5 is back to 0.981, the May number, but now from code that's actually in the repo.

What's still weak

Preferences. Still the weakest category. "I prefer X" sentences rarely share words with the question that needs them ("what should I cook tonight?"), so BM25 can't help and a 384-dim embedding only partly can. Exchange chunking helped a lot. The rest probably needs something structural, not a new weight.

Temporal questions that lose on topic. As above. Not a date problem.

s_cleaned is near the ceiling. At R@5 0.987 the remaining misses are a handful of questions, and it's very easy to fit them by accident. That's why the source weight was picked elsewhere, and why I'm careful about reading much into the last few points. I've also been running the much larger m_cleaned split, where the numbers are lower and more informative. I'll write about it once I'm happy with what it says.

This is retrieval, not answers. The next honest step is running other memory systems through the same harness, so the comparison is like for like instead of across different metrics.

Things I'd tell myself a week ago

  1. Rerun your old numbers before chasing new ones. The drift pointed straight at a bug.
  2. Count questions, not decimals. One question is 0.0021 here. Most "improvements" are one or two.
  3. Benchmark the path you ship. The product's chunker beat the standard setup, and testing it found a bug that had been quietly dropping text.
  4. A bigger model isn't a free win. On this data it was slower and no better.
  5. Quantization has side effects beyond accuracy. int8 vectors depended on batch neighbours. A boring equality test caught it.
  6. Pick weights on data you won't report on, freeze them, then run once.
  7. Disclose the tuned bits. Even small ones, even in a separate eval.

Reproducing it

Everything here runs locally from the repo. The benchmark runner, the exact commands for each row, and the per-question outputs are in the benchmarks docs:

https://github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs

If you run it on different hardware or another split and get different numbers, I'd like to hear about it.

One question for you: has anyone else seen int8 or quantized embeddings drift depending on what else is in the batch? I'd love to know if it's just my setup.

title: Scroll anchoring is Baseline: content stops jumping
description:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

You're halfway down a page, an ad or a batch of new posts loads above you, and the paragraph you were reading slides off the screen. Since Safari 27, every major browser fights that jump for you. Scroll anchoring, and the overflow-anchor property that controls it, became Baseline on September 14, 2026.

What surprised me is how old this is: MDN's compatibility data lists Chrome 56 and Firefox 66. What was missing was Safari, and with it the iPhone.

What scroll anchoring does

The classic behaviour of a scroll container is to keep its scroll offset fixed. If something 300 px tall appears above what you're looking at, the offset stays the same, so everything you can see moves down by 300 px. The spec's introduction names the usual culprits: script inserting an ad iframe, or images without dimensions loading on a slow network.

Scroll anchoring flips that. The browser picks an anchor node inside the scroller, remembers where it is, and when a layout change moves it, adjusts the scroll offset by exactly the same amount. Your scroll position changes, but what you're looking at stays put.

That's what the demo above shows. Both panes are the same feed, the highlighted card is "where you are reading", and the dashed line marks where it was. Press "+ 3 posts above" or load the ad: on the left the card drops and the meter counts the pixels it moved; on the right the meter stays at 0 px and scrollTop grows instead. "Auto feed" keeps inserting posts every 1.4 seconds, which is the timeline-with-new-items situation where this matters most.

The code: it's on by default

There's nothing to turn on. The only CSS in the demo is the opt-out on the left pane:

.feed {
  overflow-y: auto; /* scroll anchoring applies here by default */
}

.bad .feed {
  overflow-anchor: none; /* the old behaviour: the content jumps */
}

overflow-anchor takes two values. auto, the initial value, makes an element eligible to be an anchor. none takes the element and its descendants out of anchor selection, and set on the scroller itself it disables anchoring for that scroller. The property doesn't inherit, but the spec notes you can't turn anchoring back on inside a none subtree, with one exception: a nested scroll container gets its own anchoring again unless it also says none.

How the anchor is chosen is worth knowing too. The spec's algorithm walks the scroller's children looking for a node that's fully visible, going deeper when a node is only partially visible, because deeper nodes are less likely to change internally. Elements with display: none, position: fixed, position: sticky or an absolute box positioned relative to something outside the scroller are skipped.

The fallback, if you need one

In browsers without native anchoring, the demo emulates it with the same idea in a few lines: note the reading card's position, insert the content, and compensate the difference.

if (!CSS.supports('overflow-anchor', 'auto')) {
  const before = reader.offsetTop;
  insertAbove();                                   // whatever adds content above
  feed.scrollTop += reader.offsetTop - before;    // put the reader back
}

offsetTop is relative to the feed because it has position: relative. I checked this snippet in Chromium with native anchoring switched off, and the card moved 0 px. Don't run it where anchoring is native: you'd compensate twice. In the demo, when the fallback is active, the right pane also gets overflow-anchor: none so only the script adjusts it.

Gotchas I hit or checked

  • Nothing happens at the very top. The spec says that if the scroller isn't scrolled away from its origin, no anchor is selected. I tested it: with scrollTop at 0, inserting a 50 px element above moved the content 52 px (the element plus its borders). That's deliberate: if you're at the top of a feed, you probably want to see the new items.
  • It only protects the anchor. While building the demo on a 375 px screen, the ad was first inserted between the visible top of the pane and the reading card. Following the spec's algorithm, the anchor is the first fully visible card from the top, which sat above the insertion point. That card stayed still, and my reading card got pushed down 150 px anyway. Correct per the spec, and a good reminder: anchoring compensates for changes above the anchor node, not for everything on screen.
  • Suppression triggers. If, within the same suppression window (roughly, the same turn of the event loop), something changes top/left/right/bottom, margin, padding, a width or height property, position or transform on the path between the anchor node and the scroller, the adjustment is cancelled.
  • It fires scroll events. The adjustment counts as a scroll, so scroll listeners will see it. MDN's guide says that if a page misbehaves with anchoring, the usual reason is a scroll listener that doesn't expect this extra scrolling, and that Firefox can highlight the chosen anchor with the layout.css.scroll-anchoring.highlight flag in about:config.
  • It doesn't replace reserving space. Setting width and height on images or a min-height on ad slots still prevents the shift in the first place, including at the top of the page where anchoring stays out of the way.

What to keep an eye on

  • Safari 27 in the wild. Baseline "newly available" means the latest versions support it, not that everyone has updated. Until older iPhones age out, Safari users on 26 and earlier still get the jump.
  • Feeds and chat UIs. Prepending older messages or new posts was a classic place for hand-written scrollTop fixes. Now that every engine anchors, those fixes can compensate twice, so it's a good moment to check if they're still needed.
  • The spec is still a draft. The suppression window, the slice of the event loop in which adjustments are batched, is only defined in this draft; the spec itself notes it should move into the HTML standard eventually.

Sources

  • overflow-anchor | MDN
  • Overview of scroll anchoring | MDN
  • CSS Scroll Anchoring Module Level 1 (Editor's Draft)

title: AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports Apache Iceberg table optimization in the US West (N. California) Region
description:
AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports automatic table optimization for Apache Iceberg tables in the US West (N. California) Region. Apache Iceberg is an open table format that delivers fast query performance over large tables in data lakes. With this launch, you can enable table optimization for individual tables or for all tables in your Data Catalog.

Apache Iceberg tables accumulate small files, snapshots, and unreferenced files with every write, which slows queries and increases storage costs over time. Table optimization continuously monitors your tables to compact small files in the background, remove snapshots that are past your retention settings, and delete unreferenced files that are no longer needed. You can monitor each run from the AWS Glue console, Amazon CloudWatch metrics, and logs.

You can enable table optimization using the AWS Glue console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. For the full list of Regions where table optimization is available, see Supported Regions for table optimizers. To learn more, see Optimizing Iceberg tables in the AWS Glue Developer Guide. To get started, visit the AWS Glue product page.

title: Mobile-First Responsive Design: A Practical Checklist
description:
A responsive website adapts its layout and interactions to the available space. Mobile-first is a way to build that behaviour: start with a usable narrow layout, then add enhancements as the viewport grows. It does not mean hiding essential information from desktop users or treating a phone as a scaled-down computer.

Start with the job, not the device

List what visitors need to accomplish: read an article, compare offers, submit a form or find contact details. On a narrow screen, order the content around that job. A decorative hero is secondary to a clear heading, useful context and the primary action.

Check the source order as well as the visual order. CSS can rearrange items visually while keyboard and assistive technology users encounter the document in a different sequence. Aim for an order that makes sense before applying layout changes.

Make the grid flexible

Give the main container a maximum width and flexible side margins. Start cards in one column and introduce more columns when the content has room. Here is a small example:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<section class="cards" aria-label="Features">
  <article class="card"><h2>First feature</h2><p>Useful details.</p></article>
  <article class="card"><h2>Second feature</h2><p>More details.</p></article>
</section>

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
.cards {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 72rem);
  margin-inline: auto;
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  gap: 1rem;
}
.card { min-width: 0; padding: 1.25rem; }
.card img { display: block; max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
@media (min-width: 48rem) {
  .cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr)); }
}

Place the viewport meta element in the document head. The breakpoint is an example, not a universal tablet boundary. Change the window width and select the point at which your actual content needs a different layout. Long links, tables and embeds can still overflow and need separate attention.

Design for touch and keyboard

A compact menu needs a clearly labelled control, a way to close it and a state that assistive technology can understand. Test focus visibility and keyboard navigation. Avoid making important actions available only on hover; touch users need a way to reach them too.

Leave enough space around controls so adjacent links are not easy to activate by mistake. Forms should have visible labels and clear errors. Verify that the submit action remains understandable after an error and that server-side validation handles the submitted values.

Treat media as content

Make images fit their containers without distortion. Write useful alternative text for meaningful images; decorative media should not repeat nearby content. If a design crops a picture, check whether the subject remains visible at different aspect ratios. Choose appropriately sized files while maintaining acceptable quality.

Video and scroll-driven effects need testing on real devices. Loading conditions, browser controls and autoplay behaviour can vary. Provide controls where needed, and avoid making the only way to understand essential content depend on sound or animation.

Tables, text and performance

Long headings and enlarged text expose fixed-height containers quickly. Test them before release, with sufficient contrast and a readable line length. A wide table may need a scrollable wrapper with a clear hint or an alternative presentation that preserves the relationship between headings and values. Do not silently hide information needed to make a decision.

Measure performance on your own pages. Large images, fonts and scripts can add significant cost on a slow connection. Reduce unnecessary resources and measure again; the result depends on the page, network and device.

A practical pre-launch checklist

  1. Test a narrow and a wide phone, a tablet and a desktop; resize between your chosen breakpoints.
  2. Check portrait and landscape, long headings and empty or error states.
  3. Look for page-wide horizontal scrolling, clipping and overlapping content.
  4. Complete the main journey using touch and keyboard, including form errors.
  5. Increase text zoom and check contrast, focus and reading order.
  6. Test media and loading on a constrained connection, preferably on real devices and browsers used by your audience.

Browser developer tools are useful for exploring many sizes, but a real device can reveal differences in gestures, keyboards and browser chrome. Fix the problems that block the main journey first, then recheck nearby widths.
