title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

Read more

title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is now available in Token Pass
description:
Token Pass now includes DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, alongside Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3, each accessed through its preferred provider, with more models to come. The DeepSeek model uses the latest weights (1017).

title: WebSocket support is now generally available
description:
WebSocket support in Vercel Functions is now generally available.

Since the public beta launched in late June, Vercel CDN has served 300 million WebSocket connections, and now serves 15 million per day.

Customers use WebSockets for AI chat, streaming, and realtime multiplayer apps. WebSockets also power AI Gateway's realtime models.

WebSocket connections follow the same limits and pricing as other Function invocations. With Active CPU pricing, CPU is billed only for the time spent processing messages.

Get started at the documentation.

Read more

title: Skipped monorepo deployments no longer count against limits
description:
Deployments that Vercel automatically skips in a monorepo no longer count against your deployment rate limits. Teams with monorepos now get more deployments from the same limits.

Vercel skips a project's deployment when its source code and internal dependencies haven't changed, using Turborepo's package graph and lockfile analysis to determine which projects a commit affects.

Skipping is enabled by default for new monorepo projects. You can turn it on for existing projects under Build and Deployment in the project's settings.

Learn more about skipping unaffected projects and deployment limits.

Read more

title: Routing Middleware now supports Python
description:
You can now write routing middleware in Python for FastAPI, Flask, Django, and other Python frameworks. It runs before requests reach your app, and can rewrite, redirect, or answer them.

To set it up, point the proxy entrypoint in vercel.toml at your proxy:

Your middleware is an ASGI or WSGI app that runs separately from your main app, with only the packages in the vercel.proxy dependency group of your pyproject.toml. Add the packages your middleware imports to that group:

The vercel-proxy package provides utilities for writing routing middleware on Vercel, including a Proxy app that routes requests by path:

Requests that match no route continue to your app unchanged.

For more information, see the Routing Middleware Python reference.

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available now in AI Gateway
description:
Kimi K3.1 Pro from Moonshot AI is now available on AI Gateway, along with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, a faster version for interactive use.

K3.1 Pro is the first model in Moonshot's K3.1 series. It builds on Kimi K3 with improvements in coding, 3D modeling, financial analysis, and agentic tasks, and keeps the 1M-token context window and image input.

For coding, K3.1 Pro handles work ranging from small fixes in an existing codebase to building a full project, including long agent runs with many steps. It builds front-end pages and interactive scenes with stronger typography and animation than earlier Kimi models. In finance, it can carry a task from start to finish, such as building a linked financial model with adjustable assumptions and scenarios, or writing research grounded in source documents. K3.1 Pro makes fewer factual errors than earlier Kimi models on difficult prompts.

Moonshot AI plans to release the model weights by November 4: support for more providers will follow.

Call either model through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. For Highspeed, use moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed in place of the model name below.

Use moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro as the model name:

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro or moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Kimi K3.1 Pro in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

title: Vercel CLI adds Spend Management
description:
You can now view and manage your team's Spend Management budget from the Vercel CLI. Run vercel budgets and you, or the scripts and agents you run, get back your current spend and the active budget.

View, set, and remove a budget

This is the same On-Demand Budget shown in your team's billing settings. Setting a budget does not stop usage on its own. The --pause flag pauses production deployments of all projects when spend reaches 100%.

List budget alert history

You can now see your budget alert history. Run vercel budgets alerts for the full log, filtered with --since, --until, --limit, and --json. A bare vercel budgets prints the three most recent alerts.

Managing budgets requires the Owner or Billing role. Spend Management is available at no additional cost to Pro teams and to Enterprise teams on the Flexible Commitment plan.

Full reference now available in the vercel budgets CLI reference. Read more about Spend Management.

Read more

title: Customizable widgets for project cards
description:
The Overview tab in the dashboard now lets you choose which metric appears on each project card.

Project cards used to show a fixed Real Experience Score in the top right, but not everyone on your team watches the same signal. You can now swap that slot for whichever metric matters for that project. A security-sensitive project can show firewall activity, while a marketing site project shows traffic.

Available widgets

  • Firewall: allowed requests, denied requests

  • Observability: alerts, edge requests, function invocations, error rate

  • Speed Insights: Real Experience Score, LCP, CLS

  • Web Analytics: visitors online, visitors, page views

Pick per project

Open the switcher in the top right of any project card. The menu shows the current value for each available metric. When you select one, your choice is saved for that project and follows your account across refreshes and devices.

Enable features from the card

If a project does not have a feature enabled, you can start the enable flow from the widget menu without leaving the Overview tab. This is available for Speed Insights Plus, Web Analytics, and alerts.

Get started

Open your team’s Overview tab and use the switcher on any project card.

Read more

title: Create custom monitors in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now create custom monitors to get alerts based on your Vercel Observability query results.

For example, you can track signals such as AI Gateway costs, Core Web Vitals and other performance metrics, Workflow and external API failure rates, or Vercel Sandbox CPU time.

Each monitor tracks a single metric, such as response time, or a ratio of two metrics, such as errors divided by total requests. Choose statistical anomaly detection or a fixed threshold, then configure the detection window, filters, and grouping.

To create a monitor, inspect a chart’s query in Observability, start from a preset, or open Settings > Alerts for your team.

You can also define a custom monitor in a JSON file and create it with vercel monitors add in the Vercel CLI. Run vercel monitors schema --type custom for the schema and examples.

Receive alerts through email, Slack, Vercel Inbox, push notifications, or team-level webhooks. You can also add context for Vercel Agent to use when investigating an alert.

Custom monitors are available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus, at $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Create a custom monitor or learn more in the configuration documentation.

Read more

title: HarnessAgent now supports image inputs for all harness adapters
description:
The AI SDK HarnessAgent layer now accepts image inputs across every harness adapter.

Pass images alongside text in the standard AI SDK message format: a content array mixing { type: 'text' } and { type: 'file' } parts.

Image input is processed by the harnesses' underlying vision models and supported across all available adapters: Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Cursor, Deep Agents, fx, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, OpenCode, Pi.

Read the HarnessAgent image inputs documentation to get started.

Read more

title: Vercel Agent sessions now cost 67% less
description:
Vercel Agent sessions in the dashboard and Slack now cost 67% less on average. We rebuilt how Agent manages context, reducing the tokens needed per session and improving prompt-cache reuse. These improvements are live and require no action.

What changed:

  • Workflow-based CLI skills: Updated Vercel CLI skills give agents clearer guidance for common workflows and error recovery. Other agents using these skills also benefit.

  • Incremental context management: Agent manages context more efficiently as conversations grow, including long Slack threads.

  • Improved prompt caching: Agent preserves more reusable context across turns so more of it can be read from the cache.

  • More efficient coding and planning: Updated guidance helps Agent plan changes and write code with fewer tokens.

Vercel Agent’s billing rates are unchanged. Paid sessions are billed at the model provider’s inference rates plus a Vercel Agent fee of $0.25 per million tokens. View usage and costs in the Agent section of your dashboard.

Read more

title: Vercel Agent can now validate alerts before paging
description:
Vercel Agent can now investigate alerts from Vercel monitors before they reach your paging system. With validation enabled for a webhook destination, only alerts Agent classifies as Critical are sent to it.

To enable validation:

  1. Open a monitor’s notification settings and create or link a webhook destination for your paging system, such as incident.io.

  2. Select Critical Only next to that destination.

You can also configure notification destinations with the Vercel CLI using vercel monitors notifications. Add --critical-only when linking or updating a webhook destination.

Agent checks logs and metrics to assess impact. For example, it can identify health-check errors that don’t affect customers or confirm sustained 5xx errors affecting checkout requests. You can also add context to each monitor to guide Agent’s investigation.

Alert validation is available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus. Observability Plus includes ten Agent investigations per billing cycle, with additional investigations billed separately. Custom monitors cost $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the alert webhook documentation.

Read more

title: Vercel Connect adds webhook triggers for more providers
description:
Vercel Connect now supports webhook triggers for Resend, X, Twilio, Notion, and Telegram.

Connect receives webhook events, such as Telegram bot messages or emails received by your Resend domain, and forwards them to an endpoint in your Vercel project. It verifies incoming requests and handles provider heartbeats and verification challenges for you.

To get started:

  1. Open Vercel Connect in the dashboard. Enable triggers when creating a connector for your provider or in an existing connector’s settings. Connect registers webhooks automatically for Resend and Telegram.

  2. For Twilio, Notion, and X, use the webhook URL from Connect and follow its instructions to complete setup in the provider’s settings.

  3. Add a trigger destination to choose the project and endpoint that should receive events.

You can turn triggers on or off later in the connector’s settings.

In the connector’s Observability tab, select Live to watch incoming trigger events.

These connectors join existing trigger support for Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, and Linear.

Learn more in the Connect triggers documentation.

Read more

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

Read more

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

Read more

title: Adding an AI Chatbot to a Website: 7 Things Developers Should Get Right
description:
Installing a chatbot is straightforward. Making it helpful, trustworthy, and maintainable is where the interesting work begins.

AI chatbots are becoming increasingly common on business websites.

But a successful chatbot needs more than a language model connected to a text box.

It needs useful knowledge, careful configuration, a good interface, and a fallback when automation cannot handle the request.

Here are seven important considerations when implementing an AI chatbot for a real business.

  1. Define What the Chatbot Should Answer

Begin by understanding the customer's requirements.

A retail website may need product and shipping answers.

An educational website may require course descriptions and admission information.

A service business might need to answer questions about pricing, availability, and operating hours.

Define these use cases before choosing a solution.

  1. Build Around Business Knowledge

An AI chatbot should use accurate business information.

Useful sources may include:

Product catalogs.

Website content.

Frequently asked questions.

Uploaded reference documents.

Company policies.

Without relevant information, a chatbot may produce responses that sound correct but aren't.

The objective is to ground answers in trustworthy material.

  1. Plan for Missing Information

What should happen when the assistant doesn't know the answer?

A useful solution should avoid inventing unsupported facts.

Instead, it can explain that the information isn't available and guide the visitor toward human assistance.

This is particularly important for pricing, inventory, service guarantees, and other business-specific claims.

  1. Keep Installation Simple

Many business owners don't want to build a custom frontend integration just to add chat support.

An embed snippet or a supported website plugin can simplify deployment.

MySampark, for example, provides a website chat widget that can be installed using a script snippet.

It also offers a WordPress integration.

The widget can be customized with brand colors, logo, and welcome messages.

  1. Design for Mobile Users

Website chat interfaces must work well across screen sizes.

A widget shouldn't obstruct important buttons, hide product information, or make navigation difficult.

Before deployment, test the chatbot on mobile and desktop layouts.

Check scrolling, message readability, input behavior, and the visibility of close controls.

  1. Provide Human Escalation

Even a well-configured assistant will encounter requests outside its knowledge.

Customers may need assistance with complex requests, sensitive complaints, or questions requiring judgment.

MySampark includes human takeover, allowing a team member to handle a conversation while AI responses are temporarily paused.

This is an important feature for real-world support workflows.

  1. Test Before Launch

Create a test set covering:

Common product questions.

Questions with missing information.

Similar or ambiguous product names.

Requests for human support.

Incorrect or outdated knowledge.

Mobile interface usability.

Repeated and unusual inputs.

Also review security, permissions, privacy notices, retention settings, and operational costs for any platform you integrate.

A chatbot isn't production-ready simply because it responds to "Hello."

Example: A Product-Aware Website Assistant

Consider an online clothing store.

A visitor asks:

"Does this jacket come in medium?"

A business-aware assistant can reference catalog information to answer if the necessary data exists.

If availability isn't known, the assistant should avoid guessing.

That distinction matters because a fluent answer isn't necessarily an accurate answer.

Using an Existing AI Chatbot Platform

Not every company needs to develop a complete chatbot infrastructure from scratch.

A hosted solution can be practical for teams that want to focus on their website or business rather than maintaining AI support systems.

MySampark combines a customizable website chat widget with business knowledge sources, human takeover, and a browser-based management interface.

It is one option for teams exploring this approach.

Conclusion

A useful AI chatbot isn't defined by how quickly it can generate messages.

It is defined by whether customers can trust the information and reach a person when required.

Start with accurate knowledge, keep the interface simple, and test real customer scenarios.

title: Database Migration Best Practices: How to Achieve Zero Downtime
description:
Changing a production database is rarely just a database operation. The application code running during the change may expect the old schema, while a newly deployed version may depend on a new one. Background workers, scheduled jobs, and older application instances can make the transition more complicated.

A migration that works perfectly in a development environment can still cause production errors if the application and database move to their new states at different times.

Zero-downtime database migration is about managing that transition so the service can continue handling requests while the schema and data evolve.

Why a single-step migration is risky

Imagine an application that stores a customer's name in a column called full_name. A team wants to replace it with separate first_name and last_name columns.

The simplest approach might be to rename the column, update the application code, and deploy everything together. But production systems often run multiple application instances. During a rolling deployment, old and new versions may operate simultaneously.

The old version expects full_name. The new version expects the two new columns. If the database changes before every old instance has stopped, some requests may fail.

A safer approach separates the change into smaller, backward-compatible steps.

Use the expand-and-contract pattern

The expand-and-contract pattern lets the database and application evolve over several releases.

  1. Expand the schema: Add the new columns without removing the existing column. The old application can continue using the old structure.
  2. Deploy compatible application code: Update the application to support the new schema. Depending on the change, it may temporarily read from the old column while writing to both old and new columns.
  3. Backfill existing data: Populate the new columns for existing records. For large tables, process data in batches rather than running one long operation that could create heavy locks or resource pressure.
  4. Verify consistency: Compare old and new values, check for missing data, and monitor errors. Do not assume the backfill succeeded simply because the job completed.
  5. Switch reads to the new structure: Once the new data is complete and verified, move application reads to the new columns. Keep compatibility for as long as older application instances or background jobs may still need the old schema.
  6. Contract the schema: Remove the old column only after the team has confirmed that no active code depends on it. This may happen in a later release.

The sequence matters. Each step should leave the system in a state that remains compatible with the application versions currently running.

Plan for data and locking risks

Schema changes can affect availability even when the application code is compatible.

Adding an index, changing a column type, or updating a large table may consume substantial resources or hold locks that delay normal queries. The impact depends on the database engine, table size, operation, and chosen migration method.

Before running a production migration, understand how the database handles the specific operation. Use online or concurrent operations where supported and appropriate. Test with realistic data volumes, monitor lock waits and query latency, and have a clear plan for stopping or resuming the migration safely.

For large data backfills, make the process restartable. Track progress, process bounded batches, and ensure rerunning a batch will not corrupt data or create duplicate side effects. These considerations also apply when modernizing the wider data architecture.

Rollback is more than reverting code

A common mistake is to assume that reverting the application version reverses the database change.

Once data has been written in a new format, the previous application may not be able to interpret it. A destructive schema change may also make recovery difficult if old data has already been discarded.

Before deployment, decide which steps can be reversed, which require a forward fix, and how data will be recovered if validation fails. Preserve the old schema until the new path is proven stable whenever practical.

A rollback plan should be tested, not just documented. For some migrations, restoring service safely may mean correcting the new schema rather than reversing it.

Make migration checks part of the delivery pipeline

Database migration best practices are easier to follow when the release process enforces them.

Use automated checks to verify migration scripts, test application compatibility with relevant schema versions, and confirm that deployment ordering is safe. Monitor application errors, query performance, replication lag where applicable, and data consistency during the rollout.

Not every database change can be completed without a brief interruption. The realistic goal is to choose a migration method that meets the service's availability requirements and makes any necessary maintenance window explicit.

A broader cloud transformation strategy can also account for infrastructure resilience and the operational requirements of evolving production systems. For teams working on data platforms, data engineering services provide further context on building and maintaining data solutions.

Treat schema changes as staged releases

A reliable zero-downtime database migration depends on compatibility, sequencing, data validation, and observability. The expand-and-contract pattern helps teams avoid forcing application code and database structure to change at exactly the same moment.

By treating schema evolution as a staged release rather than a single operation, teams can reduce deployment risk and keep production systems available while the underlying data model changes.

title: VITI Special Report: Why NIST is the World's Best Cookbook (And Why Your IT Kitchen is Still on Fire)
description:
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) is the undisputed gold standard of IT frameworks. CISOs love it. Auditors worship it. But there is a massive, elephant-sized problem in the room: NIST is just a piece of paper. It tells you exactly what to do, but leaves the how completely up to you.

VITI sat down to explore how Erkki Laine’s Business Impact Governance Framework (BIGF) takes the world’s most respected cyber frameworks and turns them from administrative Excel nightmares into ruthless, deterministic runtime code.

1. NIST CSF 2.0 and the "Govern" Trap

When NIST released the highly anticipated CSF 2.0, the biggest update was adding a new core function: Govern. The message was clear: cybersecurity risks must be managed as business risks.

The Reality: In most companies, adding "Govern" just meant setting up another steering committee and creating a new 106-row spreadsheet for auditors to check once a year.

The BIGF Solution: A framework taxonomy doesn't execute in production; code does. BIGF takes NIST’s "Target Profiles" and translates them into automated mathematical boundaries. It doesn't ask a committee for permission; it locks down the state machine.

2. NIST AI RMF: Asking Bots Nicely to Behave

NIST has also launched the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) and an AI Agent Standards Initiative. They are trying to create global rules for how autonomous AI bots should operate safely.

The Reality: Text-based guidelines do not stop AI agents. Telling a hallucinating LLM to "be trustworthy and secure" is like telling a toddler not to touch a hot stove via an email memo.

The BIGF Solution: BIGF provides the missing mathematical shield. In Laine's architecture, every NIST AI control is tied to cold logic and cryptographic proof chains. The AI bot cannot break the NIST safety model because the BIGF state machine drops the runtime gates (a 403 Hard Halt) before the AI even has a chance to hallucinate a bad decision.

The Cookbook vs. The Kitchen

Think of NIST as the world's best, Michelin-star culinary cookbook. It has all the recipes for perfect security. But to get actual food, you need a kitchen and a chef.

Without automation, your chef is an exhausted IT manager filling out compliance forms. BIGF is the automated robotic kitchen that executes the NIST recipes flawlessly, in milliseconds, without human error.

Here is how BIGF translates NIST consultant-speak into runtime reality:

NIST CSF 2.0 Function What NIST Asks For (The Theory) How BIGF Executes It (The Reality)
GOVERN Define risk strategy, policies, and responsibilities. Hardcodes risk thresholds directly into the architecture's mathematical parameters (B*S*T).
IDENTIFY Map critical digital assets and risks. Generates a real-time State Vector from dynamic system dependencies.
PROTECT Prevent and limit cybersecurity threats. Acts as an unbreakable 403 Hard Halt gate, instantly blocking unverified state changes.
DETECT Discover anomalies as quickly as possible. Real-time deterministic monitoring: detects instantly if any data stream deviates from the canonical truth.
RESPOND React to incidents in a controlled manner. Automates decision-making via "Authority Over Truth" – no slow crisis meetings required.
RECOVER Restore normal operations. Automatically routes resources to what is mathematically proven to be most critical to the business (BIA).

Stop the Governance Theatre

NIST gives you an incredibly elegant list of things that should be in order. But without a deterministic engine like BIGF running underneath, all that elegance just leaks away into corporate Governance Theatre—endless audits, subjective guesses, and manual approvals.

If you are still managing your NIST compliance with spreadsheets and dropdown menus, your kitchen is already on fire. You just haven't looked at the thermometer yet.

title: Workflows that survive a closed tab: durable waits with checkpoints and chrome.alarms
description:
"Browser automation dies when you close the tab" is the standard objection to running workflows in an extension. For a while it was true for AWFlow too: a workflow with a "wait 3 days, then check again" step only worked if you left a tab open for three days.

This post is about how runs can now pause for up to 30 days, survive a closed tab, a browser restart or an extension update, and resume where they stopped. It's the same mechanism that lets a run pause for a human approval.


Flip it. Save the run, let the browser wake it.

The constraint: MV3 has no long-lived process

In Manifest V3 the background is a service worker, and Chrome suspends it when it's idle. setTimeout(resume, 3 * DAY) is useless there: the worker is gone long before the timer fires. The page that runs the engine (the extension's app tab) can be closed by the user at any time.


Memory is the problem. The wait has to live somewhere else.

So a long wait has to be two things:

  1. a serialized snapshot of the run, stored somewhere that survives restarts, and
  2. a wake-up call that the browser itself owns.

In an extension, those are chrome.storage.local and chrome.alarms. If you want the bigger picture of what a browser can and can't do compared with a server, browser vs server automation covers it.

How a run pauses

Let a node ask to pause

Normally a node's execute() returns output. A node that needs to wait returns a suspend request instead:

type SuspendRequest = {
  resumeKey: string;              // filled in by the engine
  kind: 'approval' | 'timer' | (string & {});
  prompt?: string;                // shown in the "waiting" row
  meta?: Record<string, unknown>; // e.g. { resumeAt: 1735689600000 }
};

The engine spots it and throws a SuspendSignal to unwind the work queue back to the place where the queue and visited sets are in scope. That's where the checkpoint gets written. (One subtlety: the node runner's own catch must re-throw this signal instead of turning it into a node failure.)

Write a checkpoint that's actually resumable

My first version stored "which node paused, plus its input". It broke immediately on real workflows. A useful checkpoint needs everything the scheduler would need to continue as if nothing happened.


Peel it apart: five layers, each one needed to carry on.

Here is the shape in code:

const checkpoint = {
  resumeKey, workflowId, pausedNodeId, kind, meta,
  pausedInput,
  queue: queue.map(n => n.id),     // what was about to run
  visited: [...visited],
  wasVisited: [...wasVisited],     // see below
  nodeOutputs,                     // so downstream $('Node') references still resolve
  runVariables: runVariables.snapshot(),
  nodeExecutionCtx,                // per-node scratchpads: loop cursors, batch offsets
  parentLink,                      // a paused sub-workflow must still resume its parent
  createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
};

Two bugs taught me the less obvious fields:

  • Loops. An iterating Loop node is moved out of visited on each pass. If you only save outputs of visited nodes, a pause inside a loop body resumes with the loop's current item gone. Save outputs from visited ∪ wasVisited.
  • Batch cursors. A "Split in Batches" node keeps its offset in a per-node scratchpad. Capture the scratchpad of every node, not just visited ones, because the loop node is exactly the one that's been un-marked when you pause.

Serialize defensively, fail loudly

Node outputs are user-controlled (a Code node can return anything), so a BigInt or a circular reference would crash the run at the moment it tries to pause. So the checkpoint goes through a few guards before it is stored.


Save it under the run's resume key.

If the checkpoint can't be saved, the run fails loudly at that node. A pause that silently didn't persist would be the worst outcome: the user thinks it's waiting and nothing ever resumes it.

How it wakes up

For a timer suspend, saving the checkpoint also arms a one-shot alarm named after the resume key:

if (cp.kind === 'timer' && typeof cp.meta?.resumeAt === 'number') {
  chrome.alarms.create(`resume:${cp.resumeKey}`, { when: cp.meta.resumeAt });
}

In practice the app page asks the service worker to do it, because the worker owns the alarms API and the onAlarm listener. Here is the full round, from pause to resume.


The run carries on. Queue, visited sets, outputs and variables are rebuilt, and the next node runs.

The run saves itself

The engine writes the checkpoint before anything else happens.

It asks for a wake-up call

The app page messages the service worker, which owns the alarms.

The browser holds the alarm

A one-shot alarm named resume:<key> is set for the deadline.

Days later, it fires

The worker's onAlarm sees the resume: prefix: this is a parked run, not a scheduled workflow.

The worker opens the app

The engine lives in the app page, so the worker finds or opens that tab and passes the resume key.

The page loads the checkpoint

Everything the scheduler needs is read back from storage.

The run carries on

Queue, visited sets, outputs and variables are rebuilt, and the next node runs.

Re-arm the alarms you lost

Alarms don't survive everything. An extension update, for example, can clear them. So on startup the worker reconciles: list the timer checkpoints, list the existing alarm names, and create the missing ones.

function computeMissingResumeAlarms(checkpoints, existingAlarmNames) {
  const existing = new Set(existingAlarmNames);
  return checkpoints
    .filter(cp => cp.kind === 'timer' && typeof cp.meta?.resumeAt === 'number')
    .filter(cp => !existing.has(`resume:${cp.resumeKey}`))
    .map(cp => ({ name: `resume:${cp.resumeKey}`, when: cp.meta.resumeAt }));
}

It's a pure function, so it's trivially unit-tested, and it's the piece that makes the design trustworthy rather than "usually works". A deadline already in the past fires right away, so a laptop that was asleep through the deadline resumes as soon as the browser is back.


Missing alarms come back. Past deadlines fire right away.

Where the thresholds come from

  • Under 1 minute stays in memory. chrome.alarms doesn't fire reliably below about a minute, and a 5-second wait isn't worth a storage round-trip. Short waits stay plain timers.
  • Up to 30 days. An upper bound, so nobody schedules an alarm for 2031 by typo.
  • One pause per input, not per item. A Wait node pauses once for the whole batch. Per-item pauses can't be checkpointed cleanly. If you want per-item waits, wrap the step in a Loop.


Thirty days, with the tab closed and the browser restarted.

One mechanism, many kinds

Once the plumbing existed, other kinds came almost for free:

  • approval pauses until a person clicks approve. Because it's waiting on a human, the extension signals it: a badge, a sound, and an OS notification when the app isn't focused. It can even render the approval card on the web page you're on.
  • "Poll until" resumes on a timer, checks a condition, and if it's not met yet, suspends again. A resume that is allowed to re-suspend turned out to be the key primitive.
  • Sub-workflows pause with a parentLink, so the parent run continues once the child finishes.

The approval kind is the easiest to see in a real workflow. This docs example fills a web form from saved values, but stops before touching the page until you approve:


Run it. Every step shows what it did.

If page watching is your use case rather than forms, monitoring competitor prices shows the other side: a trigger that reacts when a page changes.

The honest limit

This is durable, not always-on. The alarm fires when the browser is running. If your laptop is off at the deadline, the run resumes when you next open Chrome, not at 3:00:00 sharp.


But it needs the browser running. Laptop off means it resumes later.

For "every 30 seconds, 24/7" you still want a server. For "wait until Thursday, check the price, ask me before buying", it's enough, and there's nothing to host.

title: Building a web studio's own site: Astro, one Cloudflare Worker route and a 199 KB homepage
description:
This month I started site-uri.ro, a small web studio in Romania that builds presentation sites and online stores for small businesses. Before showing anyone a portfolio, the studio's own site had to be the first proof: fast on a phone, easy to find, and boring to maintain.

Here is how it's built, with the parts of the code that matter.

Static output, one canonical URL per page

The whole site is Astro, built to plain HTML:

// astro.config.mjs
export default defineConfig({
  site: "https://site-uri.ro",
  trailingSlash: "never",
  build: { format: "file" },
  integrations: [sitemap({ filter: (p) => !p.endsWith("/404") })],
});

format: "file" writes /preturi.html, which is served at /preturi with no trailing slash. Every page has exactly one URL: the one in the sitemap, the canonical tag and the internal links. No redirect chains, nothing for Google to deduplicate.

No JavaScript framework ships to the browser. The pages carry three small inline scripts (the homepage animation, the mobile menu and the contact form) and zero .js files.

One Worker route, everything else is a file

The site runs on Cloudflare Workers with static assets. The Worker script only wakes up for one path:

// wrangler.jsonc
"main": "worker/index.js",
"assets": {
  "directory": "./dist",
  "binding": "ASSETS",
  "run_worker_first": ["/trimite"],
  "not_found_handling": "404-page"
}

/trimite is the quote form. Every other request is a static file served directly, without running any code.

A contact form with no database

The form posts JSON to the Worker, which sends it as an email through Cloudflare Email Routing (send_email binding) and stores nothing. Spam protection is two cheap traps instead of a CAPTCHA:

// From worker/index.js (comments translated)
// A hidden field a human never fills, and a form submitted less than
// 3 seconds after the page opened. Bots get a fake "ok" so they don't retry.
const openFor = Date.now() - Number(data.deschis ?? 0);
if (String(data.site_web ?? "") !== "" || !(openFor > 3000)) return reply(200, "ok");

The Worker also checks the Origin header, caps every field's length, and sets Reply-To to the visitor's email when they leave one, so answering a request is just pressing Reply.

Prices that can't go stale

Prices live in one TypeScript file. Pages never write a price by hand; they call a helper with the package name:

// Names translated from the Romanian original
export function price(s: Service, name: string): number {
  const p = s.packages.find((p) => p.name === name);
  if (!p) throw new Error(`Package "${name}" does not exist in ${s.slug}`);
  return p.price;
}

A typo in a package name, or a "from X" price that doesn't match any real package, stops the build. A title, a meta description or an FAQ answer can't keep advertising an old price after the price list changes.

The same idea applies to structured data: breadcrumbs (BreadcrumbList), the business (ProfessionalService) and the founder (Person, with sameAs links) are generated from the same data files the pages read.

The numbers

  • Homepage on a phone: 199 KB in total, including fonts and images (what a 375 px, 2x screen downloads).
  • 0 JavaScript files; 3 short inline scripts.
  • 0 accessibility errors from axe-core at the last check (27 October 2026).
  • Security headers (HSTS, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) in a _headers file.

The portfolio problem

A new studio has no clients, so the portfolio starts with six demonstration projects, each built end to end as if for a real client: a plumber, a dental clinic, a linen clothing shop, a guesthouse, a pottery studio and a real estate agency. For each one I first studied the top sites in that niche (what people search for, what information is missing, which structure works), then designed it with its own identity. They're clearly labelled as demos on the site.

You can see them at site-uri.ro/portofoliu.

Next up: the first real projects, and a write-up of how the real estate demo keeps its filters in the URL with about 2 KB of JavaScript.

If you build sites for small businesses: what do you ship by default, and what do you leave out?

title: Confirming an English word with Enter sent the chat
description:
The chat sends on Enter. Shift+Enter inserts a newline. With a Chinese IME, Enter is how you keep an English word you typed in that mode, instead of a converted candidate. The field still receives a keydown whose key is Enter. The handler called send, and the word went out as a message.

This is the textarea (or input) event, not a component API. compositionstart, compositionend, blur, and keydown are on the element. A React prop with the same name is just that listener.

isComposing on the keydown is enough in Chromium. The keydown that confirms the composition still has it set, so the handler can return and let the IME write the string. Safari runs the events the other way. compositionend happens first, and the Enter keydown after it already has isComposing false. A check that only reads the event treats that keydown as a normal send.

Keep a flag, set true on compositionstart. On compositionend, clear it with setTimeout(0), not in the listener itself. The Enter keydown is still on the stack when the timeout is queued, so the flag is true and the handler returns. The timeout runs after that turn. The next Enter is a separate keypress, and that one sends.

Leave keyCode === 229 out of the check. During composition, 229 means the key belongs to the IME. Some Android keyboards also report 229 for a plain Enter, and then Enter would never send. isComposing and the flag are the two signals.

compositionend does not always arrive. Switch input method, or leave the field mid-composition, and the flag can stay true. Enter then stops sending until some later composition ends. blur sets the flag false.

Returning early also skips preventDefault, so the IME can still commit the string. A Send button never hits keydown. A click sends whatever is already in the field. Characters still in the preedit are not in that value yet. After the composition ends, Shift+Enter inserts a newline, same as before.

The listeners 

const composingRef = useRef(false);

<textarea
  onCompositionStart={() => {
    composingRef.current = true;
  }}
  onCompositionEnd={() => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      composingRef.current = false;
    }, 0);
  }}
  onBlur={() => {
    composingRef.current = false;
  }}
  onKeyDown={(e) => {
    if (e.nativeEvent.isComposing || composingRef.current) return;
    if (e.key === 'Enter' && !e.shiftKey) {
      e.preventDefault();
      send();
    }
  }}
/>

Without React, add the same four listeners with addEventListener. Read event.isComposing on the keydown. The flag is the piece Safari needs, because isComposing is already false by the time that Enter arrives.

I dispatched the events on a live textarea. Enter during compositionstart did not call preventDefault. Enter in the same turn as compositionend did not either. After the timeout, Enter did.

title: How AI Is Changing Digital Marketing in 2026
description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the way businesses promote their products and services online. In 2026, AI has become an important part of digital marketing, helping businesses create content, understand customer behaviour, improve advertising campaigns, and deliver personalized experiences. From social media marketing to search engine optimization, AI-powered tools are changing how marketing strategies are planned and executed. Businesses can now use AI to save time, analyze information, and make better marketing decisions. Understanding how AI is changing digital marketing in 2026 is important for businesses that want to stay competitive and build a strong online presence. Working with the Best Freelance Digital Marketer in Perinthalmanna can also help businesses use modern digital marketing techniques effectively and achieve better results.

What Is AI in Digital Marketing?

AI in digital marketing refers to the use of artificial intelligence technologies to improve marketing activities and business performance. These technologies can analyze large amounts of information, identify patterns, generate content, and support marketing decisions. Instead of handling every task manually, marketers can use AI-powered tools to make their work faster and more efficient. For example, AI can help generate social media captions, suggest SEO keywords, analyze advertising performance, and create personalized email content. It can also help businesses understand what their customers are interested in and develop marketing strategies based on that information. In 2026, AI is becoming an important part of everyday marketing activities, but human creativity and decision-making remain essential.

How AI Is Changing Digital Marketing in 2026

AI is influencing almost every area of digital marketing. Businesses are using it to improve content creation, search visibility, social media engagement, paid advertising, customer communication, and data analysis. According to HubSpot's 2026 marketing research, marketers are increasingly using AI for content creation, media production, automation, and advertising optimization. This shows how AI is moving beyond simple experimentation and becoming part of regular marketing workflows. The main advantage is that businesses can complete certain tasks more efficiently while giving marketers more time to focus on strategy and creativity.

AI in Content Creation

Content creation is one of the biggest areas where AI is making a difference in digital marketing. Creating regular content for websites, blogs, social media platforms, and advertisements can take considerable time. AI-powered tools help marketers generate content ideas, prepare blog outlines, write captions, develop advertising headlines, and create different versions of marketing messages. Tools such as ChatGPT can support writing and brainstorming, while Canva AI can help with visual content creation. These tools make the content production process faster and provide new creative ideas. However, AI-generated content should always be reviewed and improved by a human. Adding personal experience, accurate information, brand identity, and a natural writing style helps make content more useful and engaging for the audience.

AI in Search Engine Optimization (SEO)

Artificial Intelligence is also changing how businesses approach Search Engine Optimization. Traditional SEO mainly focuses on keyword research, website optimization, quality content, and backlinks. These activities are still important, but AI-powered search experiences are changing how people discover information online. Users increasingly ask detailed questions through AI-powered search tools and expect direct, relevant answers. This means businesses need to create helpful, well-structured, and informative website content that clearly answers their audience's questions. AI tools can assist with keyword research, content planning, competitor analysis, website audits, and search intent analysis. Businesses should also pay attention to Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), which focuses on making content easier for AI-powered search and answer platforms to understand and reference. However, AI tools cannot guarantee better rankings. High-quality content, useful information, technical website performance, and a good user experience remain important parts of SEO.

AI in Social Media Marketing

Social media marketing is becoming more efficient with the support of artificial intelligence. Businesses need to publish regular content, communicate with followers, understand audience interests, and monitor performance across platforms such as Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and YouTube. AI tools can help marketers generate content ideas, write captions, prepare content calendars, suggest suitable posting times, and analyze audience engagement. They can also assist with creating images and short-form video concepts. This allows businesses to maintain a more consistent social media presence without spending too much time on repetitive tasks. However, successful social media marketing still requires creativity, original ideas, audience understanding, and genuine communication. Businesses should use AI as a supporting tool rather than depending on it for every post or interaction.

AI in Google Ads and Paid Advertising

AI is changing how businesses create, manage, and optimize paid advertising campaigns. Platforms such as Google Ads already use machine learning to support automated bidding, audience targeting, and campaign optimization. AI can help marketers analyze campaign data, identify performance patterns, test different advertising messages, and make adjustments based on available information. It can also support the creation of multiple headlines and descriptions for advertisements. These features help marketers manage campaigns more efficiently and understand which approaches may perform better. However, successful advertising still depends on choosing the right keywords, setting suitable budgets, creating relevant advertisements, and developing effective landing pages. Human monitoring is important to ensure that campaigns remain aligned with business goals and advertising budgets.

AI-Powered Personalization

Personalization is becoming an important part of modern digital marketing. Customers are more likely to engage with businesses when the content, offers, and messages match their interests and requirements. AI helps businesses analyze customer behaviour, preferences, previous interactions, and browsing patterns to create more relevant experiences. For example, an online shopping website can recommend products based on a customer's previous activity, while an email marketing campaign can send different messages to different audience groups. AI can also help businesses develop personalized advertisements and website experiences. This makes it easier to communicate with customers in a more relevant way. However, businesses must use customer information responsibly and respect privacy when applying personalization techniques.

AI Chatbots and Customer Support

AI chatbots are changing how businesses communicate with customers online. Instead of depending entirely on manual responses, businesses can use chatbots to answer common questions, provide service information, collect basic enquiry details, and guide visitors through their websites. These tools can help businesses respond to customers outside regular working hours and manage repeated enquiries more efficiently. For example, a cleaning service company can use a chatbot to answer questions about available services, collect customer contact details, and direct enquiries to its support team. AI chatbots can improve customer communication, but they should also provide a way for customers to contact a real person when they need personal assistance or have a more complicated issue.

AI in Data Analysis and Marketing Decisions

Understanding marketing performance is essential for business growth. AI-powered analytics tools can help marketers process large amounts of information, identify trends, and understand how customers interact with websites, advertisements, and social media content. Instead of reviewing every report manually, marketers can use AI-supported insights to identify areas that need improvement. For example, businesses can analyze website traffic, advertising conversions, customer engagement, and campaign performance to make more informed decisions. AI can also support predictive analysis by identifying patterns that may help businesses plan future marketing activities. However, marketers should verify the information and consider the business context before making important decisions based on AI-generated recommendations.

Popular AI Tools Used in Digital Marketing in 2026

Several AI-powered tools are helping marketers improve their daily activities. ChatGPT is useful for content ideas, blog outlines, marketing copy, and research assistance. Canva AI supports graphic design and visual content creation. Google Gemini can assist with research, writing, and brainstorming. Grammarly helps improve writing quality and clarity, while Semrush offers SEO research and website analysis features. Adobe Firefly provides AI-powered creative features for visual content. These tools can support different areas of digital marketing, but choosing the right tool depends on your business requirements, budget, and marketing objectives. Using too many tools without a clear strategy may create unnecessary work, so businesses should focus on tools that provide practical value.

Benefits of Using AI in Digital Marketing

AI offers several advantages for businesses and marketing professionals. It can reduce the time required for repetitive tasks, support faster content production, improve data analysis, and help businesses understand customer behaviour. It also makes it easier to test different marketing ideas and prepare personalized content for different audiences. Small businesses can benefit from AI because it provides access to tools that support activities such as content planning, customer communication, and advertising analysis. However, AI does not automatically guarantee business growth. Its effectiveness depends on how well businesses use the technology, the quality of the information provided, and the marketing strategy behind it.

Challenges of AI in Digital Marketing

Although AI provides many opportunities, businesses should also understand its limitations. AI-generated content can sometimes contain incorrect information, repetitive language, or ideas that lack originality. Depending too much on AI may also make a brand's communication feel less personal. Privacy and data protection are other important concerns, especially when businesses use customer information for personalization and advertising. In addition, AI tools cannot fully understand every business situation or replace human creativity, emotional intelligence, and strategic thinking. Marketers should review AI-generated content, verify important information, and ensure that all marketing activities follow relevant privacy and platform policies. A balanced approach that combines technology with human judgment is essential.

Will AI Replace Digital Marketers?

AI is changing the responsibilities of digital marketers, but it does not mean that human professionals are no longer needed. AI can support tasks such as content drafting, data analysis, keyword research, and campaign optimization. However, businesses still need professionals who understand customer behaviour, brand positioning, communication, creativity, and marketing strategy. A digital marketer must know how to select the right audience, develop effective campaigns, understand business goals, and evaluate results. In 2026, marketers who understand how to use AI tools effectively can improve their productivity and deliver more value to businesses. The future of digital marketing is likely to involve greater collaboration between human professionals and AI-powered technology.

Why Businesses Need an AI-Powered Digital Marketing Strategy

As digital platforms continue to evolve, businesses need marketing strategies that adapt to changing customer behaviour and technology. AI can support different marketing activities, but using tools without a clear plan may not produce meaningful results. Businesses should identify their target audience, understand their objectives, choose suitable platforms, and measure campaign performance regularly.
