  0.81  keep  Annual plans can be refunded in full within 30 days of purchase. After 30 days, the remaining months are prorated.
  0.06  drop  Refund requests are submitted from the billing page under Invoices.
  0.05  drop  Monthly plans can be cancelled at any time. The change takes effect at the end of the billing period.
  1 passage(s) passed to the chat model.

The sample doesn't use Context Focus yet. To try it, add a relevant_spans object to the request body, with mode set to enabled and a threshold and max_spans. Cohere's changelog shows the shape, and the spans come back in each result.

Final thoughts

The reranker is the cheapest quality step in a RAG pipeline. It doesn't write anything, and it doesn't need your whole index. You pass it the candidates your search already found, and it tells you which ones matter.

Start with Fast if you run many searches, and Pro for answers where the top passage has to be right. Whichever you pick, set the threshold on your own data, and build the "I do not know" path before you tune anything else. 🙂

Resources

  • Cohere-Rerank-V5-Pro-Fast-Csharp-Sample on GitHub
  • Cohere Rerank V5 is now available in Microsoft Foundry
  • Cohere Rerank 5 (Cohere blog)
  • Cohere Rerank v5 changelog
  • Cohere on Azure: reranking
  • Cohere-rerank-v5-pro in the Foundry catalog
  • Cohere-rerank-v5-fast in the Foundry catalog
  • Cohere Command A+ in Microsoft Foundry (previous post)

title: Supabase vs Firebase for Startups: An Honest Comparison
description:
Supabase vs Firebase comes down to one question: do you want a relational Postgres database with SQL, or a document database that syncs to clients with almost no setup? For most SaaS products with users, teams, billing and reports, Supabase is the safer long-term default. Firebase still wins for real-time, mobile-first apps where you want Google to run everything and your data is shaped like documents.

I've shipped production work on Firebase (Timegram, a time-tracking SaaS I built, runs on it) and I regularly work on Supabase apps, many of them generated by AI builders like Lovable. Below is how the two compare on the things that actually hurt later: data model, security, pricing, lock-in and hiring.

What is the difference between Supabase and Firebase?

Both are "backend as a service" platforms. You get a database, authentication, file storage, server functions and real-time updates without running your own servers. The difference is what sits in the middle.

  • Supabase is built on Postgres. Its docs describe each project as a full Postgres database rather than an abstraction over one, and Auth, Storage, Realtime and Edge Functions all hang off that database. You write SQL, use foreign keys and joins, and can add Postgres extensions such as pgvector for AI embeddings, PostGIS for maps and pg_cron for scheduled jobs.
  • Firebase is built around Cloud Firestore, a NoSQL document database from Google. Data lives in collections of documents, clients read and write directly through the SDK, and access is controlled by Firebase Security Rules. It plugs into the rest of Google Cloud (Cloud Functions, Cloud Storage, Analytics, Crashlytics, Cloud Messaging).

Neither is "better" in general. They suit different shapes of data and different teams.

Supabase vs Firebase at a glance

Supabase Firebase
Database Postgres (relational, SQL) Firestore (NoSQL documents)
Queries Joins, aggregates, views, full SQL Simple queries per collection; joins done in app code
Access control Postgres Row Level Security policies Firebase Security Rules
Pricing model Plan fee plus usage (storage, egress, MAU) Pay per document read, write and delete
Free tier 2 active projects, paused after a week of inactivity Daily free quota on reads, writes and storage
Self-hosting Possible (open source) No
Best fit SaaS, dashboards, B2B, reporting, AI features Mobile apps, chat, live collaboration, quick prototypes

Supabase vs Firebase pricing: what will you actually pay?

I checked both pricing pages in October 2026. Prices change, so confirm before you budget.

Supabase pricing

Supabase uses plans with included usage:

  • Free: $0. 500 MB database, 50,000 monthly active users, 5 GB egress, 1 GB file storage, 500,000 Edge Function invocations. You get two active projects, and free projects are paused after one week of inactivity.
  • Pro: from $25 a month. 8 GB database per project, 100,000 MAU, 250 GB egress, 100 GB file storage, 2 million Edge Function invocations, plus $10 of compute credits. Projects are never paused.
  • Overages on Pro: $0.125 per GB of database, $0.00325 per extra MAU, $0.09 per GB of egress, $0.0213 per GB of file storage.
  • Team: from $599 a month. Enterprise: custom.

A useful detail: the Pro plan has a spend cap switched on by default, so you won't get a surprise bill unless you turn the cap off.

Firebase (Firestore) pricing

Firestore charges per operation, not per plan. Google's Firestore pricing page lists a daily free quota of 1 GiB of stored data, 50,000 document reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes, plus 10 GiB of outbound transfer a month. Above that, in the Iowa (us-central1) location, you pay $0.03 per 100,000 reads, $0.09 per 100,000 writes and $0.01 per 100,000 deletes. Other regions are priced differently.

For sign-in, Google Cloud's Identity Platform pricing page lists email, phone, anonymous and social sign-ins as free up to 50,000 MAU, then $0.0055 per MAU up to 100,000. SAML and OpenID Connect (enterprise single sign-on) are free for only 50 MAU, then $0.015 per MAU. SMS for phone login is billed separately.

Which one is more affordable?

It depends on how your app reads data, not just how many users you have.

  • Firestore bills every document a query returns. A dashboard that loads 200 documents for every page view costs 200 reads each time. Listeners that re-run on every change add up fast. Badly structured Firestore apps are where surprise bills come from.
  • Supabase bills mostly for storage, egress and compute. A heavy SQL query costs CPU time, not per row returned, so read-heavy dashboards and reports are usually more predictable on a fixed plan.
  • For a small app with light traffic, both can stay free or close to it for a long time. Just remember the Supabase free plan pauses idle projects, which is fine for prototypes but not for a live product.

Is Supabase or Firebase better for a SaaS startup?

Ask what your data looks like six months from now.

A typical SaaS has organisations, users, roles, projects, invoices, subscriptions and audit logs, all linked to each other. That is relational data. In Postgres you model it with tables and foreign keys, and a report like "hours logged per client per month, grouped by team" is one SQL query. In Firestore you either duplicate data across documents so each screen can read it in one go, or you fetch several collections and join them in your code. Both work, but duplication means keeping copies in sync, and that is where bugs creep in.

Here is the same question asked both ways. In Supabase:

select c.name, sum(t.minutes) / 60.0 as hours
from time_entries t
join projects p on p.id = t.project_id
join clients c on c.id = p.client_id
where t.org_id = 'org_123'
  and t.started_at >= date_trunc('month', now())
group by c.name
order by hours desc;

In Firestore you would usually keep a running total on each client document and update it every time an entry is written, often from a Cloud Function:

// Illustrative: keep a per-client monthly total in sync on every new entry
export const onEntryCreated = onDocumentCreated(
  "orgs/{orgId}/entries/{entryId}",
  async (event) => {
    const entry = event.data?.data();
    if (!entry) return;
    const month = entry.startedAt.toDate().toISOString().slice(0, 7);
    const ref = db.doc(`orgs/${event.params.orgId}/clientTotals/${entry.clientId}_${month}`);
    await ref.set({ minutes: FieldValue.increment(entry.minutes) }, { merge: true });
  }
);

The Firestore version is fast and cheap to read, but you now have to handle edits, deletes and back-filling old data yourself. Every new report means another pre-computed total.

My rule of thumb:

  • Pick Supabase if your product is a B2B SaaS, has reporting or admin screens, needs complex permissions, or will add AI search with embeddings.
  • Pick Firebase if you're building a mobile-first or chat-style app, need offline sync on phones out of the box, already use Google Cloud, or your data really is a set of independent documents (user profiles, messages, feeds).

If you're still scoping your first version, this decision belongs in the planning stage of an MVP build, not halfway through development.

Supabase vs Firebase security: where do apps go wrong?

Both platforms let the browser or mobile app talk to the database directly. That's what makes them fast to build with, and it's also why security has to be done right on day one.

  • Supabase relies on Postgres Row Level Security (RLS). If a table is exposed and RLS is off, or the policies are too loose, anyone with your public anon key can read the data. This is the most common problem I find in apps built with Lovable and other AI tools. I wrote a full guide on it: Supabase RLS explained.
  • Firebase relies on Security Rules. The classic mistake is shipping with test-mode rules that allow all reads and writes, or rules that check a user is signed in but not that they own the document.

Check this before launch

Whichever you pick, test your access rules with a second, non-admin account. Try to read and change another user's data. If you can, so can anyone else.

Lock-in and switching later

Supabase is open source and the data sits in standard Postgres, so you can export it with normal Postgres tools or move to any Postgres host. That's a real advantage if investors or enterprise clients ask about vendor risk.

Firebase is a Google product with no self-hosted version. Moving away means rewriting data access code and reshaping documents into tables. Supabase publishes a migration path for this: community scripts that export each Firestore collection to JSON and import it as a Postgres table, flattening fields into text, numeric, boolean or jsonb columns. Nested arrays and objects need custom hooks or your own script to split into related tables, and each collection is migrated separately. It works, but plan time for the data modelling, not just the copy.

A quick decision checklist

  1. Write down your five main entities (users, orders, projects and so on) and how they link. Lots of links points to Supabase.
  2. List the reports and admin screens you'll need in year one. Cross-collection reports point to Supabase.
  3. Is it mostly a phone app that must work offline? That points to Firebase.
  4. Estimate reads per user per day. If a single screen loads hundreds of documents, model the Firestore cost before committing.
  5. Check if your team or future hires know SQL. Postgres skills are easy to find.
  6. Decide how much vendor lock-in you can accept.
  7. Whatever you choose, budget time to write and test RLS policies or Security Rules.

What this means for founders and app owners

If you're starting fresh, you can't really go wrong with either, as long as the data model fits the tool. The expensive mistakes come from forcing relational data into Firestore, or from launching a Supabase app with RLS switched off.

If you already have an app built with an AI tool and you're not sure whether the backend is set up safely or will scale, a production audit is the quickest way to find out what needs fixing before real customers arrive. And if you're planning a new product and want help choosing the stack, see how I approach MVP development.

Sources

  • Supabase pricing
  • Supabase docs: Database overview
  • Supabase docs: Migrate from Firestore to Supabase
  • Google Cloud: Firestore pricing
  • Google Cloud: Identity Platform pricing
  • Cover photo: Christopher Gower on Unsplash

Originally published on muhammadmoiz.dev. I'm Muhammad Moiz, a senior full-stack engineer building production apps with React, Next.js and Node.js. If you need a hand with your product, get in touch.

title: A Local-First VS Code Extension: No Git, No Telemetry, No Network, and It Works in Codespaces
description:
| SavePoint Diff runs entirely inside the extension host, so it works across local, SSH, WSL, containers, Codespaces, and vscode.dev.

Plenty of dev tools want an account, a network call, or a telemetry opt-out. I wanted the opposite for SavePoint Diff.

What "100% local" means here

  • Everything runs inside the VS Code extension host
  • No Git required
  • No telemetry
  • No network requests
  • No external services
  • The baseline is held in memory for the current window session and never touches disk

The only requirement is VS Code 1.60.0 or later.

Works where you work

Because there are no external dependencies, it behaves the same across:

  • Local folders
  • Remote-SSH
  • WSL
  • Dev Containers
  • GitHub Codespaces
  • Virtual filesystems like vscode.dev and github.dev

Make it yours

Everything is toggleable in settings:

{
  "savepointDiff.showAdded": true,
  "savepointDiff.showModified": true,
  "savepointDiff.showDeleted": true,
  "savepointDiff.showOverviewRuler": true,
  "savepointDiff.showBackgroundHighlight": false,
  "savepointDiff.enableRevertInHover": true
}

Prefer a subtle gutter only? Leave highlighting off. Want changed lines tinted too? Set showBackgroundHighlight to true. There's also a one-click status bar toggle (SavePoint: ON / OFF) if you want it out of the way temporarily.

Good to know

In Git repositories, VS Code's own editor-gutter "quick diff" colors are typically driven by Git's provider. SavePoint Diff's panel entry, badges, and diff view work independently alongside it, in Git and non-Git folders alike.

Try it 

ext install StayElite.StayElite-Savepoint-Diff

GitHub · MIT licensed · feedback and issues welcome.

title: Git seance: I let deleted functions speak from beyond the grave (with local Gemma)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every repository is a graveyard. Functions get written, argued over, shipped, and then one day a commit quietly removes them, and nobody says a word.

git seance holds the funeral they never got. It walks your git history, finds functions that were deleted and never came back, and lets one of them speak through a local Gemma model: who wrote it, when it was born, and the commit that killed it.

python git_seance.py --list path/to/repo                                   # visit the graveyard
python git_seance.py --summon set_http_proxy --ask "do you forgive them?" path/to/repo

My personal favourite:

python git_seance.py path/to/repo                        # summon a random ghost

It's a single Python file with zero dependencies (standard library only), and it understands Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Go and Rust definitions.

Demo

That's a real run on psf/requests, with gemma3:4b on my laptop's CPU through Ollama (long pauses trimmed). Its last 400 commits hold seven ghosts. The most tragic is set_http_proxy: 85 lines of carefully documented proxy handling, added to Session on 27 November 2020 and reverted the same day by its own author.

Here is what it said when I asked if it forgives them (another real run, unedited):

It's… strange, this quiet. A lingering echo of code, a phantom limb of functionality. I was a helpful thing, really. I took messy proxy strings – URLs, schemes, hostnames, ports – and neatly slotted them into the requests.Session object. I was born on November 27th, 2020, courtesy of Sylvain Marie. Then, poof. November 27th, 2020 again. […]

My advice to the living: don't prematurely prune your tools.

Code

DrunkWiz / git-seance

Talk to the functions your repo deleted. A stdlib-only Python CLI that lets dead code speak through local Gemma.

git seance

Commune with the code your repository buried.

git seance walks a repo's git history, finds functions that were deleted and never came back, and lets one speak from beyond the grave through a local open-weight model (Gemma 3 via Ollama by default): who wrote it, when, and the commit that killed it. With no model reachable it falls back to an offline "planchette" mode that only arranges the real facts.

One file, Python standard library only, no runtime dependencies.

A real run on psf/requests with gemma3:4b on a laptop CPU, long pauses trimmed.

Why an open model

Your git history is your team's private diary: names, dates, half-finished ideas, the commit messages people wrote at 2am. git seance reads all of it, so it should not have to leave your machine. With an open-weight model like Gemma running locally through Ollama, the whole seance happens on your laptop…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

Finding the dead. git log -p -U0 --no-merges gives every removed line in history. I parse the removed hunks, start a body at any line that looks like a definition (def, function, func, fn), and end it at the next definition at the same or lower indentation. That last rule came from a bug: the first version merged neighbouring deleted methods into one long ghost. In requests, initialize_options, finalize_options and run_tests were deleted from a setup.py command class together, and they kept coming back as a single conjoined spirit.

Making sure they're really dead. A function that was moved isn't a ghost. Before summoning, git grep -w checks the current tree for a definition with the same name. If one exists, the function just moved house.

Finding the birth certificate. Git's pickaxe (git log -S"def set_http_proxy") finds the commit that first added the function. My favourite bug lived here: requests later moved requests/ to src/requests/, and git's default history simplification hid every commit on the old path behind a merge. Every ghost was "born: unknown", and Gemma happily made up a birth story to fill the gap. --full-history brought the real birthday back.

Speaking. The facts (name, file, length, birth, death, the killing commit's message, the final source) go into a prompt along with a system prompt that tells the model to speak as the function, to be wistful and darkly funny but never cruel, and not to invent facts. The reply streams token by token from Ollama's /api/chat with nothing but urllib, typed out like a planchette moving. An OpenAI-compatible provider is there too, for anyone who'd rather point it at a gateway.

When the spirits won't come. If no model is reachable, planchette mode arranges the real facts into an epitaph with no AI at all. That came in handy: Ollama's CUDA runner crashes on my RTX 2060, so I added SEANCE_NUM_GPU=0 to run Gemma on the CPU. At 4B parameters, that's still fast enough.

Tests. A unittest suite covers the diff parser on a synthetic log, the dead-or-moved check on a throwaway repo, and both streaming providers against a fake model server on 127.0.0.1, so the tests never touch the network.

A ghost is an unreliable narrator, and I'd rather say so. The header line comes straight from git. Everything after it is Gemma, and despite the instructions it sometimes embellishes (in one run it insisted it had been reverted "twice"). --offline gives you only the facts.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because a git history is a diary. It holds names, dates, abandoned ideas, and commit messages written at the worst moments of people's weeks. A tool that reads all of that should not have to send it anywhere.

With an open-weight model like Gemma running locally, the whole seance happens on your own machine: no API key, no account, no bill, and it works on a private company repo or with no internet at all. I learned this the practical way. I first tried a hosted gateway, and its free tier wouldn't serve API calls without a key. Gemma 3 4B on Ollama just worked, on a laptop CPU, offline.

Open models also make the medium yours. You can read how it was made, swap it for a different one, or fine-tune it on your own team's commit messages. And open source is what gives the ghosts something to haunt: I could only summon set_http_proxy because requests keeps its whole history in the open.

My Agent Session

I built this with an AI coding agent (Claude Code). It ran the real seances against requests, tracked down the history-simplification and GPU bugs above, wrote the offline test suite, recorded the demo and helped draft this post. Every transcript and number here comes from an actual run.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos isn't about fearing the dead. It's about remembering them by name. Every deleted function was somebody's afternoon. git seance puts the name, the date and the author back on the gravestone, and lets the code say goodbye.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: the medium is gemma3:4b, running locally through Ollama.

title: How a Live Unsaved-Changes Diff Works in a VS Code Extension
description:
| Baselines, Myers line diffs, debouncing, undo/redo, and the edge cases behind SavePoint Diff's gutter markers.

I recently shipped SavePoint Diff, a VS Code extension that shows gutter markers for unsaved changes. Here's the design, in case you're thinking about building something similar.

The core idea: a baseline

Everything revolves around one string per file, the baseline, meaning the last saved content.

  1. File opens: capture its content as the baseline.
  2. Edit: diff baseline against the current buffer, then render the result as gutter decorations.
  3. Save: the baseline becomes the new content, and the markers clear.

The diff itself uses a small, well-established Myers line-diff library rather than anything custom.

Debouncing

Diffing on every keystroke is wasteful, so recalculation is delayed until typing pauses. The delay is configurable:

"savepointDiff.debounceMs": 150

Files above a size threshold skip live diffing entirely to protect performance (savepointDiff.maxFileSize, default 2,000,000 bytes).

Why undo/redo is free

Instead of tracking edits incrementally, the diff is always recomputed from baseline vs. current text. That means undo back to the saved state yields an empty diff, so markers vanish, and redo brings them back. There's no delta bookkeeping to corrupt.

Edge cases that bit me

The changelog lists a lot of these, but the interesting ones were:

  • CRLF and lone CR line endings need normalizing, or the diff lies.
  • Multi-change reverts: applying several edits must go in descending order, or earlier edits shift the ranges of later ones.
  • Revert File / external rewrites: if the file stops being dirty without a save, its content now matches disk, so the baseline re-syncs automatically.
  • Invalid settings: a bad maxFileSize (zero, negative, non-numeric) used to be able to silently disable diffing. It now falls back to the default.
  • Stale badges on hidden tabs needed explicit handling.

Savepoints are just a baseline move

The manual savepoint feature falls out of the design. It moves the baseline to the current in-memory content without writing to disk. No new machinery needed.

Takeaway

Recompute from two strings, resist clever incremental state, and spend your effort on the edge cases. The code is MIT licensed if you want to read it or contribute.

title: Local SEO Guide: How Businesses Can Improve Their Visibility in Local Search
description:
Local SEO Guide: How Businesses Can Improve Their Visibility in Local Search
Local SEO is an important strategy for businesses that want to attract customers from nearby areas. Whether you run a training institute, restaurant, retail store, or service-based company, appearing in local search results can help people discover your business. For digital marketing enthusiasts exploring a Digital Marketing Course in Thane West, understanding local SEO is also a valuable skill for building practical marketing knowledge.
What Is Local SEO and Why Does It Matter?
Local SEO is the process of optimizing a website and online presence to improve visibility in location-based search results. For example, when someone searches for "digital marketing institute near me" or "best training institute in Thane," Google displays relevant businesses based on location, relevance, and other ranking factors.

Unlike traditional SEO, local SEO focuses on attracting customers from specific geographical areas. It helps businesses connect with people who are actively looking for nearby products or services.
5 Effective Local SEO Strategies for Better Visibility

  1. Optimize Your Google Business Profile Google Business Profile is one of the most important tools for local SEO. It allows businesses to display essential information such as their address, phone number, website, business hours, photos, and customer reviews.

To improve your profile:

  • Add accurate business information.
  • Select relevant primary and secondary categories.
  • Upload genuine business photos regularly.
  • Update working hours and contact details.
  • Respond professionally to customer reviews.
  • Share relevant business updates. A complete and regularly maintained profile helps customers understand your business and makes it easier to discover.
  • Target Location-Based Keywords Keyword research plays an important role in local SEO. Businesses should identify search terms that include their services and target locations.

For example, a training institute can target phrases such as "digital marketing classes in Thane West" and "SEO training near me."

Include relevant keywords naturally in website titles, headings, service pages, and descriptions. Someone looking for a Digital Marketing Course in Thane West should be able to find relevant information without navigating through unrelated pages.

  1. Create Location-Specific Website Pages Creating dedicated location pages can improve your website's relevance for different service areas.

For example, a business serving Thane, Mumbra, Airoli, and Bhiwandi can create separate pages explaining its services in these locations.

Each page should contain unique information, relevant keywords, customer benefits, contact details, and useful content. Avoid creating multiple pages with nearly identical descriptions just to target different locations.

  1. Build Local Citations and Quality Backlinks Local citations are online mentions of your business name, address, and phone number. These listings can appear on business directories, industry websites, and local platforms.

Maintain consistent business information across relevant platforms. Additionally, build quality backlinks through guest articles, industry publications, and local business websites.

Focus on relevance and credibility instead of creating hundreds of low-quality backlinks. A few useful links from relevant websites can provide more value than spammy directory submissions.

  1. Collect and Manage Customer Reviews Online reviews influence how potential customers perceive a business. Encourage genuine customers to share their experiences after using your products or services.

Respond to both positive and negative reviews politely. Thank customers for positive feedback and address complaints with helpful solutions.

Never purchase fake reviews or offer incentives in exchange for positive ratings. Authentic customer experiences help build long-term trust.
Common Local SEO Mistakes to Avoid
Many businesses struggle with local search visibility because they overlook basic optimization practices.

Some common mistakes include:

  • Using incorrect business contact information.
  • Ignoring Google Business Profile updates.
  • Stuffing location keywords into website content.
  • Publishing duplicate location pages.
  • Building irrelevant or spammy backlinks.
  • Ignoring customer reviews.
  • Forgetting to optimize websites for mobile users. Regular monitoring and improvement can help businesses avoid these issues. Learn Local SEO and Build Practical Digital Marketing Skills Local SEO requires continuous learning, keyword research, content optimization, Google Business Profile management, and performance tracking. Understanding these concepts can help beginners develop useful digital marketing skills.

If you want to explore SEO, Google Ads, social media marketing, and other essential marketing concepts, consider learning through a structured Digital Marketing Course in Thane West.

to learn more about digital marketing training and practical learning opportunities.
Conclusion
Local SEO is not just about ranking higher on Google; it is about helping the right customers discover your business at the right time. By optimizing your Google Business Profile, targeting location-based keywords, creating useful website pages, earning relevant backlinks, and managing customer reviews, you can build a stronger local online presence.

title: Analyze what Xiaohongshu (RedNote) users say about a product with Claude and MCP
description:
Xiaohongshu (小红书, also called RedNote) is where a lot of Chinese shoppers go to review products before they buy, and to complain after. If you sell anything in China, or compete with someone who does, the notes and comment sections there tell you a lot. The trouble is that there is no public API to sign up for, and reading hundreds of Chinese comments by hand is slow.

In this post we'll connect Claude Code to a remote MCP server, ask it what Xiaohongshu users say about a product, and let it search notes, read their comments and summarize them. At the end there's a short Python version that calls the same HTTP API without an agent.

Disclosure: I build Qovia, the API and MCP server used here. It's a paid API with a free trial.

Step 1: add the MCP server to Claude Code

Get a key from the Qovia console, then add the server with one line:

export QOVIA_KEY=sk-qovia-...
claude mcp add --transport http qovia https://api.qovia.ai/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $QOVIA_KEY"

The server exposes only four tools, so it doesn't fill the model's context with a hundred tool definitions:

  • search_endpoints: find data endpoints by keyword or platform
  • get_endpoint: show an endpoint's parameters, a response example and the price
  • call_endpoint: run an endpoint and return data plus billing info
  • get_account: check your key's balance and rate limit

search_endpoints and get_endpoint are free and work without an API key, so you can let the agent explore the catalog before you spend anything. Only call_endpoint needs the key. Setup details are in the MCP docs.

Step 2: ask a question

Start claude and give it something like this:

Using the qovia MCP tools, find out what Xiaohongshu users say about
the Stanley Quencher tumbler. Search in Chinese, take the 5 most
commented notes from the past month, read the first page of comments
on each, and summarize: main praise, main complaints, recurring
questions, and anything about fakes or pricing. Quote a few comments
in Chinese with an English translation. Tell me how much the run cost.

Step 3: what the agent does

The agent doesn't need to know Qovia's catalog in advance. A typical run goes like this.

1. Find the endpoints. It calls search_endpoints with platform: "xiaohongshu". That lists the Xiaohongshu endpoints, including:

Endpoint id Path Price per call
raw.xiaohongshu.search GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/search $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.comments GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comments $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.note GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/note $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.comment_replies GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comment_replies $0.005

2. Read the parameters. It calls get_endpoint for the two it needs.

raw.xiaohongshu.search returns 20 notes a page:

  • keyword (required, up to 50 characters)
  • sort: general (default), latest, most_liked, most_commented or most_saved
  • note_time: all (default), day, week, month or year
  • note_type: all (default), video or image
  • page: from 1, up to 50; stop when has_more is false

raw.xiaohongshu.comments returns a note's first-level comments:

  • note_id (required, 24 hex characters)
  • sort: default (Xiaohongshu's own order, pinned and popular first, about 5 a page) or latest (newest first, 10 to 15 a page, without like counts)
  • cursor: pass back the previous page's cursor unchanged; stop when has_more is false

3. Fetch the data. It runs call_endpoint with something like:

{ "endpoint_id": "raw.xiaohongshu.search",
  "params": { "keyword": "斯坦利 保温杯", "sort": "most_commented", "note_time": "month" } }

Each note in the result carries its Xiaohongshu id in extra.source_id. Here is an abbreviated example of the structure, taken from get_endpoint's response example (not from a real run of this prompt):

{
  "page": 1,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "soc_xia_c79d099f083d",
      "platform": "xiaohongshu",
      "text": "真假摩可纳咖啡对比（一）…",
      "author": { "user_id": "5a916db4e8ac2b54e8b53aba", "nickname": "J*y" },
      "metrics": { "likes": 1205, "saves": 966, "shares": 287, "comments": 1570 },
      "extra": {
        "title": "真假摩可纳咖啡对比（一）",
        "source_id": "69f7dc410000000035021f62",
        "url": "https://www.xiaohongshu.com/explore/69f7dc410000000035021f62",
        "note_type": "image",
        "published_at": "2026-05-04T07:37:37+08:00"
      }
    }
  ],
  "has_more": true
}

It then passes each source_id as note_id to raw.xiaohongshu.comments. Again an abbreviated example structure from get_endpoint:

{
  "items": [
    {
      "cid": "6a17eab1000000002902f300",
      "text": "喝了晚上还能睡着怎么解",
      "likes": 1918,
      "reply_count": 62,
      "ip_location": "陕西",
      "created_at": "2026-05-28T15:11:45+08:00",
      "author": { "nickname": "肉*嘟" }
    }
  ],
  "total": 1072,
  "cursor": "6a1b938c000000002b025bef",
  "has_more": true
}

4. Summarize. With five searches' worth of notes and their comments in context, Claude groups the comments into themes, picks quotes and translates them. ip_location is handy if you want a rough regional split. Every call_endpoint result includes charged_usd, so the agent can add up the cost when you ask.

A run like the prompt above is about 6 calls: one search plus five comment pages, so roughly $0.03.

Tip: search in Chinese

Xiaohongshu users write in Chinese, and they rarely use a brand's English name. Searching Stanley finds far fewer notes than 斯坦利 or 斯坦利 保温杯. A few things that help:

  • Ask the agent to try two or three Chinese keywords: the Chinese brand name, the brand plus the product category, and any nickname people use.
  • Add words people use when they review: 测评 (review), 踩雷 (bad buy), 真假 (real vs fake), 平替 (cheaper alternative).
  • Use sort: "most_commented" to find the notes with the most discussion, and note_time to keep it recent.
  • Read comments with the default sort first. It puts the most-liked comments on top, which are usually the most representative.

The same thing in plain Python

If you want this as a scheduled job instead of a chat, call the HTTP API directly. Every endpoint returns the same envelope: data holds the result and meta holds billing info.

import os, requests

BASE = "https://api.qovia.ai"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['QOVIA_KEY']}"}
spent = 0.0

def get(path, **params):
    global spent
    r = requests.get(f"{BASE}{path}", headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    body = r.json()
    spent += float(body.get("meta", {}).get("charged_usd", 0) or 0)
    return body["data"]

notes = get("/v1/raw/xiaohongshu/search",
            keyword="斯坦利 保温杯", sort="most_commented", note_time="month")["items"]

rows = []
for note in notes[:5]:
    comments = get("/v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comments",
                   note_id=note["extra"]["source_id"])["items"]
    for c in comments:
        rows.append((note["extra"]["title"], c.get("likes"), c["text"]))

for title, likes, text in rows:
    print(f"[{likes}] {title} | {text}")
print(f"spent ${spent:.3f}")

From there you can hand rows to any LLM with a "summarize praise and complaints" prompt, or write them to a CSV.

Pricing and trial

  • New accounts get 50 trial calls, enough to run the example above several times.
  • You're charged only when a call returns data. Empty results and errors are free, including a search with no hits or a note with no comments.
  • Both Xiaohongshu endpoints used here cost $0.005 per call ($5 per 1,000).
  • Discovery (search_endpoints, get_endpoint) is always free and needs no key.

More in the docs, the Xiaohongshu API page and the Xiaohongshu MCP page. If you try it, I'd like to hear which product you looked up and what the comments said.

title: A/B Testing for Data Analysts: How to Interpret Results Without Making Common Mistakes
description:
Imagine you're working as a data analyst for an ecommerce company. The product team has redesigned the checkout page and wants to know whether the new version performs better.

They run an A/B test, collect the results, and send you the data. The new checkout has a higher conversion rate, and the p-value is below 0.05.

So, should the company roll out the new checkout to everyone?

Not necessarily.

This is where A/B testing becomes more than comparing numbers. A good analyst needs to understand how the experiment was conducted, whether the observed difference is reliable, and what the results actually mean for the business.

Let's walk through a practical example.

1. Start With the Right Question

Before analysing an A/B test, you need to understand what the experiment is trying to achieve.

Suppose the existing checkout page is performing poorly. The team believes a simplified design could help more visitors complete their purchases.

The business question is:

Does simplifying the checkout process improve purchase conversion rates?

From here, we can define two hypotheses:

  • Null hypothesis (H₀): There is no difference in conversion rates between the existing and redesigned checkout.
  • Alternative hypothesis (H₁): The conversion rates are different.

This gives the experiment a clear objective. Without a predefined hypothesis, it's easy to look at the results and create an explanation that fits whatever numbers appear.

2. Choose Metrics That Actually Matter

One common mistake in A/B testing is tracking dozens of metrics without deciding which one determines success.

For our checkout experiment, we could use:

Metric Type Example Why It Matters
Primary Purchase conversion rate Measures whether more visitors complete purchases
Secondary Checkout completion time Helps explain how the experience changes
Guardrail Refund rate Checks for potential negative consequences

The primary metric answers the main business question. Secondary metrics provide supporting information, while guardrails help detect problems that might otherwise go unnoticed.

For example, a redesigned checkout could increase purchases but also increase refunds. Looking only at conversion rates would give an incomplete picture.

3. Understand the Experiment Before Trusting the Results

Let's say the experiment randomly assigns 10,000 eligible visitors between two checkout experiences.

Each group receives 5,000 visitors.

Before calculating significance, an analyst should confirm that the experiment was implemented correctly.

Were users randomly assigned? Was conversion tracking working? Did both groups follow the same eligibility rules? Was the experiment allowed to run for its planned duration?

These questions matter because even a statistically significant result can be misleading when the underlying experiment has problems.

A particularly useful check is sample ratio mismatch, which occurs when the observed traffic allocation differs unexpectedly from the planned split.

If the allocation is wrong, investigate why before interpreting the outcome.

4. A Practical A/B Testing Example

Here are the hypothetical results from our checkout experiment.

Metric Control (A) Treatment (B)
Visitors 5,000 5,000
Purchases 400 460
Conversion rate 8.0% 9.2%

The new checkout performs better in the observed data.

But how much better?

Absolute Uplift

9.2% − 8.0% = 1.2 percentage points

Relative Uplift

(9.2% − 8.0%) / 8.0% × 100 = 15%

This means the treatment group had a 15% higher observed conversion rate relative to the control.

Now comes the important question: Could this difference reasonably be explained by random variation?

For these independent binary outcomes, an approximate two-sided two-proportion test produces:

  • P-value: 0.032
  • 95% confidence interval: Approximately +0.1 to +2.3 percentage points for the absolute difference

At a predefined 5% significance level, the result is statistically significant.

However, statistical significance doesn't guarantee that the improvement will be equally large in future traffic, nor does it prove that launching the change is commercially worthwhile.

5. A/B Testing Cheat Sheet: What Every Analyst Should Check

A reliable A/B test follows a structured process, from defining the business question to interpreting the evidence and recommending an action.

Use this infographic as a quick reference when reviewing experiments or preparing for data analyst interviews.

6. Statistical Significance vs. Business Significance

Consider two possible experiments.

In the first experiment, a change produces a statistically significant improvement, but the actual uplift is extremely small. Implementing it might require substantial engineering effort.

In the second, a change shows a promising improvement, but the confidence interval is wide because the experiment has limited data.

Neither situation can be judged using the p-value alone.

A data analyst should consider three questions:

1. Is the experiment trustworthy?

Check randomisation, tracking, sample size and stopping rules.

2. How large and uncertain is the effect?

Report the absolute difference, relative uplift and confidence interval.

3. Does the outcome justify a business decision?

Consider implementation costs, user experience and guardrail metrics.

The goal is not simply to find a winning variant. It's to make a decision supported by reliable evidence.

7. Common A/B Testing Mistakes

A/B testing is a powerful technique, but several mistakes can lead to incorrect conclusions.

Stopping the Test Too Early

Checking results repeatedly and stopping as soon as the p-value falls below 0.05 can inflate false-positive risk under conventional fixed-horizon testing.

Changing the Success Metric After the Experiment

Selecting whichever metric looks most favourable makes the analysis less reliable. Define the primary metric in advance.

Ignoring Confidence Intervals

A p-value alone doesn't explain how large the effect might be or how uncertain the estimate is.

Confusing Correlation With Causation

Valid random assignment supports causal inference, but implementation, eligibility and tracking problems can undermine that interpretation.

Ignoring Guardrail Metrics

An improvement in one metric should not automatically justify rollout if important business or user-experience metrics deteriorate.

Recognising these issues is just as important as knowing how to calculate statistical significance.

8. How to Explain A/B Testing in a Data Analyst Interview

A/B testing is also a useful topic to prepare for when interviewing for analytics roles.

Rather than simply explaining what a p-value means, demonstrate how you'd approach a real business problem.

For example, if an interviewer asks how you would test a new checkout design, explain the experiment in this order:

  1. Define the business objective and hypotheses.
  2. Identify the primary success metric and guardrails.
  3. Explain randomisation, sample size and duration.
  4. Validate tracking and experiment allocation.
  5. Compare conversion rates and quantify the effect.
  6. Interpret statistical significance and uncertainty.
  7. Recommend whether to launch, continue testing or investigate further.

This approach shows that you can connect statistical analysis with business decisions, rather than just apply a formula.

Final Thoughts

A/B testing is not just about identifying which version performs better. It's about understanding what the experiment can reliably tell you and using that evidence to make a better decision.

For data analysts, developing this skill means learning how to design experiments, choose meaningful metrics, interpret uncertainty and communicate findings clearly.

The next time you review an A/B test, don't stop at the conversion rate or p-value. Ask whether the experiment was valid, whether the effect matters and what the business should do next.

Want a Complete A/B Testing Reference?

Explore hypotheses, statistical significance, experiment planning, worked examples and common mistakes in the full PangaeaX guide.

Read More: A/B Testing Cheat Sheet for Data Analysts

title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Practical Case Study of Amazon EC2
description:
Introduction

Cloud computing has changed the way individuals and organizations access and manage computing resources. Traditionally, businesses had to purchase physical servers, storage devices and networking equipment before they could deploy applications. This required significant financial investment, technical expertise and continuous maintenance.

Today, cloud computing provides an alternative through different service models, one of which is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

This article explores the concept of IaaS, its features, benefits and challenges, using Amazon Web Services (AWS), particularly Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), as a case study.

1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud computing model that provides virtualized computing resources such as servers, storage and networking over the internet.

Instead of purchasing physical servers and installing them in an office or organization, users can rent computing resources from a cloud service provider.

The cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, including the servers, networking equipment and data centres, while customers manage their operating systems, applications and data.

For example, a business that wants to host a website does not necessarily need to purchase a physical server. It can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider and use it to host its website.

3. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is one of the major cloud computing platforms. One of its infrastructure services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2).

Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers, known as instances, that allow individuals and organizations to run applications in the cloud.

Rather than purchasing physical servers, customers can launch EC2 instances, select their preferred operating systems and configure the resources required for their applications.

How Amazon EC2 Works

Consider a university that wants to develop an online course registration system.

Traditionally, the university might need to purchase physical servers, install operating systems, configure networking and provide storage facilities before deploying the application.

With Amazon EC2, the university can:

  1. Create an AWS account.
  2. Select an appropriate virtual server (EC2 instance).
  3. Choose an operating system, such as Linux or Windows Server.
  4. Configure the server's computing capacity, including memory and processing power.
  5. Configure network access and security settings.
  6. Install and deploy the university's course registration application.
  7. Increase or decrease computing resources as the number of users changes.

For instance, during course registration periods, many students may access the system simultaneously. The university can increase its computing capacity to accommodate the increased demand and reduce it when traffic decreases.

This demonstrates how IaaS provides flexibility and scalability.

Important Components of Amazon EC2

Some important components include:

  • EC2 Instances: Virtual servers used to run applications.
  • Amazon Machine Images (AMIs): Templates containing the operating system and other configurations required to launch instances.
  • Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS): Provides persistent storage for EC2 instances.
  • Security Groups: Act as virtual firewalls that control network traffic.
  • Instance Types: Determine the computing resources available, including CPU, memory and networking capacity.

4. Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution

1. Reduced Hardware Costs

Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications.

2. Scalability

Computing resources can be increased or decreased depending on application requirements.

3. Flexibility

Users can select different operating systems, server configurations and storage options.

4. Faster Deployment

Virtual servers can be launched without waiting for physical hardware to be purchased and installed.

5. Remote Management

Administrators can manage their cloud infrastructure through AWS management tools and interfaces.

5. Challenges and Limitations of IaaS

Despite its benefits, IaaS also has some limitations.

1. Security Responsibilities: Although the cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, customers remain responsible for securing their operating systems, applications, access permissions and data.

2. Internet Dependency: Accessing cloud infrastructure generally requires a reliable internet connection.

3. Cost Management: Poor resource management can result in unexpected expenses, especially when unused resources continue running.

4. Technical Knowledge: Users need some knowledge of operating systems, networking, security and server administration to manage their infrastructure effectively.

6. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has transformed how organizations obtain and manage computing resources. It reduces the need for physical infrastructure while providing flexibility, scalability and faster deployment of applications.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how IaaS works by allowing users to rent virtual servers, configure their computing environments and deploy applications without purchasing physical servers.

For organizations such as universities, businesses and startups, IaaS provides an alternative to traditional infrastructure management.

As cloud computing continues to develop, understanding IaaS is important for students, developers and organizations interested in modern computing technologies.

References

  1. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

  2. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Amazon EC2?

  3. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). Amazon EC2 Documentation

title: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): An Investigation into Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2 and Its Application in Modern Computing
description:
Author: Nweibong Emmanuel Praise
Category: Cloud Computing
Case Study: Amazon Web Services – Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2)

Abstract

The increasing demand for digital services has made traditional computing infrastructure increasingly challenging for some organizations to maintain. Businesses, universities and other institutions require computing resources that can support their applications, store information and accommodate changes in user demand. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) provides an alternative by allowing organizations to access computing resources through cloud service providers without having to purchase and maintain all the physical equipment themselves.

This article examines Infrastructure as a Service, focusing on Amazon Web Services (AWS) Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) as a case study. It investigates the architecture, operation, major components, benefits and limitations of EC2. It also examines how the service could be applied in hosting a university student management portal.

  1. Introduction

Computing infrastructure plays an important role in the operation of modern organizations. Almost every institution that provides digital services depends on servers, storage systems, networking equipment and software platforms.

In the past, organizations generally had to acquire their own physical servers and establish server rooms or data centres before deploying applications. Apart from the initial cost of purchasing equipment, they also had to consider electricity, cooling, maintenance, security and the availability of qualified technical personnel.

These requirements can become difficult to manage, especially for small organizations and institutions with limited financial resources.

Cloud computing has introduced a different approach to managing these resources. Instead of purchasing all the required hardware, organizations can obtain computing resources from providers over the internet.

One of the service models responsible for this development is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). It provides access to virtual computing infrastructure while allowing customers to manage their operating systems, applications and other configurations.

To understand how this model works in a practical environment, this research uses Amazon EC2 as a case study.

  1. Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)

Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud computing service model in which a provider makes computing resources available to customers over the internet.

These resources typically include:

  • Virtual machines and processing power.
  • Storage systems.
  • Networking infrastructure.
  • IP addresses and network configurations.
  • Virtualized computing environments.

The major idea behind IaaS is that organizations can use computing infrastructure without necessarily owning the physical hardware.

For instance, consider a university that wants to develop an online platform for managing student records. Rather than purchasing a physical server, the university can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider and install the necessary software.

The university manages the operating system, application and database configurations, while the provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure.

According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), cloud computing provides convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort.

This definition helps explain why IaaS has become an important approach to delivering computing infrastructure.

  1. Technical Operation of IaaS

IaaS relies heavily on virtualization and resource management technologies.

Virtualization allows a physical server to provide multiple independent virtual computing environments. Each virtual machine receives allocated resources such as processor capacity, memory and storage.

A customer can configure these resources based on the requirements of the application being deployed.

The general operation involves the following stages:

Resource provisioning: The customer requests computing resources through the provider's management interface.

Virtual machine creation: The provider allocates resources and creates a virtual server using a selected machine image.

Configuration: The customer installs and configures the operating system, applications and other required software.

Deployment: The application is uploaded and made accessible through the network.

Monitoring and scaling: Resource usage is monitored, and additional capacity can be provisioned when necessary.

This arrangement gives customers control over their computing environments without requiring them to manage the physical servers.

  1. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS) Elastic Compute Cloud

Amazon Web Services is a cloud computing platform that provides infrastructure and other computing services to individuals and organizations.

One of its major infrastructure services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2).

Amazon EC2 provides on-demand computing capacity through virtual servers known as instances. These instances can be configured to run different operating systems and applications depending on the customer's requirements.

An organization can launch an instance, connect to it remotely, install its software and use it to host services.

4.1 Major Components of Amazon EC2

To understand EC2 as an IaaS solution, it is important to examine some of its major components.

a. EC2 Instances

An instance is a virtual server running within AWS infrastructure. Different instance types provide different combinations of processing power, memory, storage and networking capacity.

For example, a small web application may require fewer computing resources than a large enterprise application.

b. Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)

An Amazon Machine Image is a template used to launch EC2 instances. It contains information required to configure the instance, including an operating system and potentially preinstalled software.

This makes it easier to create servers without manually installing everything from the beginning.

c. Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS)

EBS provides persistent block storage that can be attached to EC2 instances. It is useful for storing operating system files, application data and other information that must remain available beyond the lifetime of an individual instance session.

d. Security Groups

Security groups function as virtual firewalls for EC2 instances. They control incoming and outgoing network traffic through configured rules.

For example, an administrator can allow web traffic through HTTP and HTTPS while restricting remote administrative access to approved IP addresses.

e. Regions and Availability Zones

AWS organizes its infrastructure into geographical Regions and Availability Zones.

Regions represent separate geographical areas, while Availability Zones are isolated locations within a Region.

Deploying application resources across multiple Availability Zones can help reduce the effect of an individual location failure.

These components demonstrate that EC2 provides more than just a virtual computer. It provides a configurable infrastructure environment for deploying and managing applications.

  1. Practical Application: Hosting a University Student Management System

To examine the practical usefulness of IaaS, consider a university that wants to deploy a student management system.

The proposed system will allow students to:

  • Log in to their personal accounts.
  • Register for courses.
  • Check examination results.
  • Download learning materials.
  • Receive announcements.
  • View academic information.

Lecturers will also be able to manage courses, record attendance and upload students' grades.

The university needs a server capable of running the application and handling requests from different users.

Proposed AWS EC2 Implementation

Stage 1: Provisioning the server

The university creates an AWS account and launches an EC2 instance.

Ubuntu Linux can be selected as the operating system because it supports the software technologies required by the application.

Stage 2: Installing the application environment

The administrator installs the necessary technologies, such as:

  • Python programming language.
  • Django web framework.
  • Nginx web server.
  • PostgreSQL database system.

Stage 3: Deploying the application

The student management system is uploaded to the EC2 instance and configured to run as a web application.

Stage 4: Configuring network access

The administrator configures the instance's security group to permit the required web traffic.

Administrative access, such as SSH, should be restricted to authorized IP addresses rather than exposed unnecessarily.

Stage 5: Connecting the database

The application is connected to a database where student records, courses, examination results and other academic information are stored.

For a more reliable production environment, the database can be hosted separately using a managed database service.

Stage 6: Monitoring performance

The university monitors the server's resource consumption and application performance.

If the number of users increases significantly during course registration or examination periods, additional computing capacity can be introduced.

This example demonstrates how an educational institution can use IaaS to deploy a real application without purchasing its own physical server infrastructure.

  1. Proposed System Architecture

The following architecture illustrates how the student management system could be deployed using AWS EC2.

   STUDENTS / LECTURERS
            |
            |
         INTERNET
            |
            |
      AWS CLOUD
            |
            |
      EC2 INSTANCE
            |
      NGINX SERVER
            |
            |
     DJANGO APPLICATION
            |
            |
      DATABASE SERVER
            |
            |
     ACADEMIC RECORDS

The architecture separates the different responsibilities of the system.

  • Users interact with the application through their web browsers.
  • AWS provides the cloud infrastructure.
  • EC2 provides the virtual computing environment.
  • Nginx handles incoming web requests.
  • Django processes application requests and business logic.
  • The database stores and retrieves academic information.

This is a proposed deployment architecture, not a report of an actual university system already running on AWS.

  1. Analysis of the Benefits of IaaS

The use of IaaS offers several advantages when compared with traditional infrastructure management.

7.1 Reduced Initial Investment

Organizations do not necessarily need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications.

Instead, they can obtain computing resources and pay according to the selected pricing arrangement.

7.2 Resource Scalability

One major advantage of EC2 is the ability to change computing capacity when application requirements change.

A university may initially use a small server but increase its capacity when more students begin accessing the portal.

AWS also provides Auto Scaling to help automatically adjust the number of instances based on configured conditions.

7.3 Greater Flexibility

Customers can select operating systems, instance types, storage configurations and networking arrangements according to their requirements.

This is particularly useful for developers who need different environments for testing and production.

7.4 Faster Deployment

Creating a virtual server can be faster than acquiring and installing physical hardware.

This allows organizations to develop and deploy applications without waiting for physical infrastructure procurement.

7.5 Geographical Availability

AWS provides infrastructure across different geographical Regions and Availability Zones.

Organizations can select suitable deployment locations and design systems that distribute resources across multiple locations.

  1. Limitations and Challenges of IaaS

Although IaaS provides important advantages, it is not without limitations.

8.1 Security Responsibilities

Using a cloud provider does not mean that the customer has no security responsibilities.

AWS protects the underlying physical infrastructure, but customers remain responsible for securing their operating systems, applications, access permissions and data.

This is known as the shared responsibility model.

8.2 Dependence on Internet Connectivity

Applications hosted in the cloud generally require internet connectivity to be accessed remotely.

In areas where connectivity is unreliable, users may experience difficulties accessing cloud-hosted applications.

This is an important consideration for organizations operating in regions where internet infrastructure is still developing.

8.3 Cost Management

Although IaaS can reduce initial infrastructure investment, operating costs can increase if resources are not properly managed.

Running unnecessary instances, storing unused data and transferring large volumes of information may result in additional charges.

Organizations therefore need to monitor their resource consumption.

8.4 Technical Expertise

Managing an IaaS environment requires knowledge of operating systems, networking, server administration and security.

An organization without qualified technical personnel may find it difficult to configure and maintain its infrastructure properly.

8.5 Service Availability

Cloud providers design their infrastructure for availability, but service interruptions can still occur.

Organizations should therefore consider backup arrangements, monitoring and recovery strategies when deploying important applications.

  1. Security and Management Considerations

Security is an important part of any IaaS deployment, particularly when applications contain sensitive information such as student records.

For an EC2-based student management system, the following measures should be considered:

  1. Use strong authentication and protect administrative credentials.
  2. Restrict SSH access to authorized users.
  3. Configure security groups to allow only necessary network traffic.
  4. Regularly update the operating system and installed software.
  5. Implement appropriate database access controls.
  6. Encrypt sensitive information where necessary.
  7. Maintain regular backups.
  8. Monitor system activities and resource usage.

These measures help reduce the risk of unauthorized access, data loss and service disruption.

  1. Comparison of IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

Cloud computing is commonly divided into three service models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

Feature| IaaS| PaaS| SaaS
Full meaning| Infrastructure as a Service| Platform as a Service| Software as a Service
Main provision| Computing infrastructure| Application development platform| Ready-to-use software
User control| High| Moderate| Limited
User manages| OS, applications and data| Applications and data| Mainly usage and data
Example| Amazon EC2| Google App Engine| Gmail

The main difference between these models is the level of management and control given to the customer.

IaaS provides greater control over the underlying computing environment, while PaaS reduces infrastructure management responsibilities for developers. SaaS provides complete applications that users can access without managing the underlying infrastructure.

  1. Other Providers of Infrastructure as a Service

Amazon EC2 is not the only available IaaS solution. Other major providers include:

Microsoft Azure Virtual Machines: Provides configurable virtual machines for running applications and operating systems.

Google Cloud Compute Engine: Offers virtual machines and computing resources through Google Cloud.

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: Provides computing, storage and networking resources for different workloads.

DigitalOcean Droplets: Provides virtual private servers commonly used by developers and small businesses.

Although these providers offer similar infrastructure capabilities, their pricing structures, available resources and management tools differ.

  1. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has changed how organizations acquire and manage computing resources. Rather than depending entirely on physical infrastructure, organizations can obtain virtual servers, storage and networking resources from cloud providers.

The examination of Amazon EC2 shows how IaaS can be used to create flexible computing environments for hosting applications. The proposed university student management system demonstrates how an institution can deploy its services, manage academic information and adjust computing resources according to user demand.

However, adopting IaaS requires careful consideration of security, internet connectivity, technical expertise and operational costs.

In conclusion, IaaS is a valuable approach to modern infrastructure management. Its usefulness depends not only on the capabilities of the cloud provider but also on how effectively the organization plans, configures and manages the resources it uses.

  4. Amazon Web Services. Security in Amazon EC2.
    https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-security.html

  5. Amazon Web Services. Shared Responsibility Model.
    https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/shared-responsibility-model/

    https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/what-is-amazon-ec2-auto-scaling.html

title: Logging AI tool usage without logging sensitive data
description:
When a team adds an AI feature, the first debugging instinct is to log everything: the full prompt, the full response, the user's message. It works. It also means your logs now hold a copy of every customer email, contract and support ticket that went through the feature, sitting in a system with weaker access controls than your database and a much longer memory.

You need logs. You need them to debug bad answers, answer audit questions and keep costs under control. You don't need them to be a second copy of your customers' data.

Here's a practical middle path.

Decide what the logs are for

Before writing any code, list the questions your logs must answer. For most small teams it's these:

  1. Debugging: which prompt version and model produced this answer, and did the call fail?
  2. Audit: who (which user or service) used the AI feature, when, and on what record?
  3. Cost: how many tokens did we use, by feature and by customer?
  4. Safety: did a call get blocked, filtered or flagged?

Notice that none of these needs the full text of the prompt or the response. That's the key idea: log metadata by default, and content only by exception.

The default log record

This is the record to write for every call:

import hmac
import json
import logging
import os
import time
import uuid

log = logging.getLogger("ai_usage")


FP_KEY = os.environ["AI_LOG_FP_KEY"].encode()   # random secret, not in code


def fingerprint(text: str) -> str:
    """Keyed, non-reversible fingerprint so identical inputs can be grouped."""
    return hmac.new(FP_KEY, text.encode("utf-8"), "sha256").hexdigest()[:16]


def log_ai_call(*, feature, prompt_name, prompt_version, model, actor_id,
                record_id, prompt_text, response_text, usage, status, started):
    # started: value of time.monotonic() taken before the call
    usage = usage or {}                      # failed calls often have no usage data
    call_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    log.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "ai_call",
        "call_id": call_id,
        "feature": feature,                  # e.g. "ticket_summary"
        "prompt": prompt_name,
        "prompt_version": prompt_version,
        "model": model,
        "actor_id": actor_id,                # internal user or service id, not an email
        "record_id": record_id,              # e.g. ticket id
        "input_chars": len(prompt_text),
        "input_fp": fingerprint(prompt_text),
        "output_chars": len(response_text or ""),
        "input_tokens": usage.get("input_tokens"),
        "output_tokens": usage.get("output_tokens"),
        "status": status,                    # "ok", "error", "blocked"
        "latency_ms": int((time.monotonic() - started) * 1000),
    }))
    return call_id

With this, you can trace any answer to a prompt version and a record, add up costs by feature, and see failure rates, all without storing a word of the customer's text.

A note on the fingerprint: a plain hash of short or predictable text (an email address, a yes/no answer) can be reversed by guessing, so the fingerprint is keyed with a secret (AI_LOG_FP_KEY), so it can't be checked by guessing without the key. The fingerprint is for grouping long, varied inputs ("were these two calls the same request?"), not for hiding identifiers. Identifiers like emails shouldn't go into it in the first place.

When you do need content: redact first

Sometimes you need to see what was sent, for example while fixing a specific bug. When that happens, log a redacted sample, not the raw text, and only when a flag is switched on.

A simple redaction pass catches the most common sensitive patterns:

import re

PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"\b(?:sk|pk|api|key|token|ghp|xox[bp])[-_][A-Za-z0-9_-]{12,}\b", re.I), "[SECRET]"),
    (re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+"), "[EMAIL]"),
    (re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?<![\w.])\+?\d(?:[\s()-]{0,2}\d){9,14}(?![\w.])"), "[PHONE]"),
]


def redact(text: str, limit: int = 500) -> str:
    for pattern, label in PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(label, text)
    return text[:limit]

Order matters: run the most specific patterns first. Secrets go before emails, cards and phone numbers, or a phone pattern can eat the digits in the middle of a key and leave the rest in the log.

import os

DEBUG_CONTENT = os.getenv("AI_LOG_CONTENT") == "1"

call_id = log_ai_call(...)  # same call as above

if DEBUG_CONTENT:
    log.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "ai_call_content",
        "call_id": call_id,
        "prompt_sample": redact(prompt_text),
        "response_sample": redact(response_text or ""),
    }))

Be honest about the limits. Regular expressions catch emails, phone numbers, card-like numbers and obvious keys. They won't catch names, many provider key formats (cloud access keys, bearer tokens), addresses, medical details or anything written in free text. That's why content logging stays off by default, is switched on for a short time for a specific problem, and is truncated. If your feature handles health, financial or legal information, don't log content at all; reproduce the problem with test data instead.

Keep content logs somewhere separate, for less time

Metadata and content have different risks, so treat them differently:

Metadata log Content sample log
Default Always on Off; switched on per incident
Who can read it Engineering and whoever handles costs A named few engineers
How long it's kept As long as your audit needs (agree this with whoever owns compliance) Days, not months
Where Your normal log system A separate log stream or index with its own access rule and expiry

Most log platforms let you route by a field (here, event) and set a separate retention period per stream. Use that, so content samples expire automatically and nobody has to remember to delete them.

Don't forget the other copies

Your own logs are only one place prompts end up:

  • The AI provider. Check their data retention and training settings for your account, and turn off anything you don't need. Write down what you chose and why.
  • Error trackers. Exception reports often capture local variables, including the prompt. Configure them to scrub request bodies and the variables that hold prompt text. Provider error messages sometimes echo part of the prompt too, so log the exception type (type(exc).__name__) and status code, not str(exc).
  • Analytics and tracing tools. If you trace requests end to end, make sure spans don't attach the full prompt as an attribute.
  • Chat and tickets. When someone pastes a "bad answer" into a team chat to discuss it, that's a copy too. Share the call_id instead, and look the details up where access is controlled.

What auditors usually ask

If you work with larger clients, sooner or later someone will ask how you control AI use. The metadata log answers most of it:

  • Which features use AI, and which models? (feature, model)
  • Who used them, on which records? (actor_id, record_id)
  • Can you show a change history for prompts? (prompt_version, plus your repository history)
  • How long do you keep AI-related data, and who can see it? (your retention table above)

Being able to answer those from a dashboard, rather than by searching raw text, is a good sign you've got the balance right.

A short checklist

  1. Write a metadata record for every AI call: feature, prompt version, model, actor, record, tokens, status, latency.
  2. Never put emails or other identifiers into actor_id or the fingerprint.
  3. Keep content logging off by default; when it's on, redact and truncate.
  4. Send content samples to a separate stream with short retention and narrow access.
  5. Review provider retention settings, error-tracker scrubbing and tracing attributes.
  6. Share call IDs in chat, not prompts.

Good AI logs tell you what happened without telling everyone what your customers said.

Ahmed Vaseer is Founder & CEO - Ingenious Concepts, an AI-first technology and digital growth agency. 80+ projects, ISO 27001 certified via Global CB.
