title: What I Learned From Integrating 3rd Party APIs
description:
I've worked with a lot of third-party APIs: telecom and messaging services, social media platforms, and a few others. This post is what I learned about keeping those integrations from breaking, in the order I ran into the problems.

I'm still not a pro, and I won't cover everything. This is just how I know it. I split it into three stages: novice, a little knowledge, and intermediate. Each stage starts with a problem the last one couldn't handle.

The short version

  • Always set a timeout. Retry only errors that can go away on their own, with backoff and jitter. Know when to give up.
  • Respect rate limits and 429 responses. Put work the user doesn't wait for on a queue.
  • Make repeated operations safe. Then add circuit breakers, fallbacks and dead letter queues if you need them.
  • Track latency, error rate and retries for each provider.
  • Don't build all of it at once. I start with timeouts, rate limits, queues and retries.

Stage 1: novice

My first integrations were simple. I called the API over HTTP, wrapped it in a try/catch, and logged the error if it failed. Nothing much. My error handling was basically console.error and hope.

try {
  const res = await fetch("https://api.provider.example/v1/messages", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Provider returned ${res.status}`);
  return await res.json();
} catch (err) {
  console.error("provider call failed", err);
  throw err;
}

It all looked good at first. Then the first real problem showed up.

Stage 2: a little knowledge

Timeouts

The problem was my API waiting on the external API. If the provider is slow or never answers, the request just sits there. It holds a connection and memory. Enough of those and my service runs out of resources, even though the problem is on someone else's server.

That's how I learned about timeouts. You set one (30 seconds, or whatever fits your use case) and throw an error when it passes. If a user is waiting, use a shorter one. A background job can wait longer.

const res = await fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000),
});

At first I thought a timed-out request meant the provider had done nothing. But a timeout only means I stopped waiting. The provider may have done the work and just answered too slowly. This causes trouble later, in stage 3.

Retries, and which errors deserve one

Next, my API felt unreliable. A user sent a request, the provider had a bad moment, and the user got an error. So I learned about retries. My first version retried every error.

That doesn't work either. Some errors go away on their own and some don't.

A transient error can go away: a timeout, a dropped connection, a 502 or 503. A non-transient error fails the same way every time: a 400 for a bad payload, a 401 for a wrong API key, a 404 for something that doesn't exist. Retrying those fixes nothing. A 401 doesn't turn into a 200 because you asked nicely five times. It just wastes calls and delays the real error.

Retry the first kind. Fail fast on the second.

A transient error doesn't always mean it's safe to retry. If a POST times out, the provider may have already done the work, and a retry could do it twice. I'll come back to this in stage 3.

Exponential backoff

I also found out that retrying too fast makes things worse. If the provider is struggling, hitting it again right away adds more load. So you wait between attempts, and you wait longer each time: 1 second, then 2, then 4, then 8. That's exponential backoff.

Jitter

Backoff caused its own problem. Say a thousand requests fail at the same moment. They all wait 1 second and retry together. They fail together, wait 2 seconds, and retry together again. It's like everyone redialing the same busy number at the exact same second. The provider gets hit in waves. This is called the thundering herd problem. With no quiet moment to recover, a small problem can get a lot worse.

The fix is jitter. Add some randomness to the wait so the retries spread out.

When to stop retrying

At first I didn't know you could drop a request. I thought I had to keep retrying until it worked, so my code was a loop with no exit.

Retrying forever is a bug of its own. The user is still waiting, your workers are busy, and the provider keeps getting hit. Drop the request when any of these is true:

  • The error is non-transient. A 400, 401 or 404 fails every time, so drop it right away.
  • You've tried enough times. Pick a number, like 4, and drop the request after that.
  • You've waited too long. Give the whole request a time limit, like 10 seconds, no matter how many tries it takes. A 30 second timeout with 4 tries can leave the user waiting about two minutes. Nobody waits that long.
  • The provider asks you to wait too long. If its Retry-After header says 5 minutes and you can only wait 10 seconds, drop it. Waiting won't help.

When you drop a request, still do something with it. If a user is waiting, tell them it failed and that they can try again. If it's background work, move the job to a dead letter queue (more on that below) so it isn't lost.

This code puts it all together: a timeout on every try, retries only for transient errors, backoff with jitter, the Retry-After header, and the rules for giving up.

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(
    public status: number,
    public retryAfterMs?: number,
  ) {
    super(`Provider returned ${status}`);
  }
}

// Timeouts, network failures, 408, 429 and some 5xx errors may be transient.
// Check your provider's docs. 400, 401, 404 and similar fail every time.
const TRANSIENT_STATUS = [408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504];

function isTransient(err: unknown): boolean {
  if (err instanceof HttpError) return TRANSIENT_STATUS.includes(err.status);
  // fetch throws a TypeError on network failures, but a bug in your code can too
  return err instanceof Error && (err.name === "TimeoutError" || err.name === "TypeError");
}

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function withRetry<T>(
  fn: (timeoutMs: number) => Promise<T>,
  maxAttempts = 4,
  budgetMs = 10_000,
): Promise<T> {
  const deadline = Date.now() + budgetMs;
  let lastErr: unknown;
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const timeLeft = deadline - Date.now();
    if (timeLeft <= 0) throw lastErr ?? new Error("Out of time"); // don't start another try
    try {
      // each try gets at most 3 seconds, and never more than the time left
      return await fn(Math.min(3_000, timeLeft));
    } catch (err) {
      lastErr = err;
      const backoff = Math.random() * 1000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1); // backoff + jitter
      const asked = err instanceof HttpError ? err.retryAfterMs : undefined; // from Retry-After
      const wait = asked ?? backoff;
      const outOfTime = Date.now() + wait >= deadline;
      if (attempt >= maxAttempts || outOfTime || !isTransient(err)) throw err; // drop it
      await sleep(wait);
    }
  }
}

const result = await withRetry(async (timeoutMs) => {
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    const seconds = Number(res.headers.get("Retry-After") ?? NaN);
    throw new HttpError(res.status, Number.isNaN(seconds) ? undefined : seconds * 1000);
  }
  return res.json();
});

This is a simple example to learn from, not code to paste straight into production. Change the number of tries, the waits and the time limit to fit your provider. Check its docs to see which errors it wants you to retry. Real code needs more care. For example, not every TypeError is a network problem, because a bug in your own code can throw one too. And POST requests are not always safe to retry (see stage 3).

Rate limits and 429

After that I ran into 429 Too Many Requests. It means I had sent more requests than the provider allows. That limit is called a rate limit. I retried harder, and it only made things worse. The provider was saying "slow down", and I answered by going faster.

So I learned about throttling. It means slowing yourself down, so you never go over the provider's limit. Use a limiter that caps how many calls you make each second or each minute. If you run more than one server, make them all share the same limiter. Otherwise each server counts on its own, and together they still go over the limit.

If a 429 still gets through, wait before you try again. Many providers send a Retry-After header. It tells you how long to wait. Use it instead of guessing.

Queues

Then I learned when to use queues. A lot of work doesn't need to happen while the user waits: sending emails or SMS, generating reports, and similar jobs. The request returns right away, and a worker calls the provider in the background.

This is where everything above came together for me. The worker handles the timeout, the retries with backoff and jitter, and the rate limit. You decide how many workers call the provider at once, so a spike of user requests doesn't become a spike of provider calls. If a job fails, the worker can retry it in the background. The user's request doesn't have to stay open while that happens.

Stage 3: intermediate

Duplicate operations

Retries can cause a new problem: doing the same thing twice. Take the timeout from earlier. The provider may have already sent the SMS and just answered too slowly. If you retry, the user gets two SMS.

It can also happen without a timeout. Many queues promise to deliver a job at least once. That means the same job can run more than once. A worker sends the SMS, then crashes before it marks the job as done. The queue doesn't know the SMS went out, so it gives the job to another worker. That worker sends the same SMS again.

So the next thing I learned was how to make an operation safe to repeat. The word for this is idempotent: doing it twice gives the same result as doing it once. Whenever you can, make queue jobs idempotent, especially jobs that call an outside service or change important data.

If the provider supports idempotency keys, use them. An idempotency key is a unique ID that you send with each request. When the provider sees the same ID again, it knows the request is a repeat and doesn't do the work twice. Not every provider supports this.

If yours doesn't, keep your own record of what you've already sent. Check that record before you retry. And if you don't know whether the first try worked, ask the provider for the status first.

I wrote more about this in my post on payment integrations, where a duplicate means a duplicate charge.

Circuit breakers and fallbacks

This is where I got more excited about system design. I'm still new to this part. I only know the basics, and I'm learning more in my free time. Even a basic understanding of circuit breakers and distributed systems helps, though.

Say a provider is down for ten minutes. Retrying every request against it wastes time and ties up your workers.

A circuit breaker counts recent failures. When they pass a threshold, it stops calling the provider and fails right away. After a cool-down, it lets a few test requests through. If they succeed, traffic starts flowing again.

A fallback decides what happens while the breaker is open. It could be a second provider, a cached answer, or a plain "try again later" message.

Dead letter queues

Some jobs still fail after every retry. Retrying forever is a waste, and dropping them loses data. So they go to a dead letter queue. It holds them while you find out why they failed. Then you fix the cause and replay them.

Observability

Then someone asked me how my system was performing, and I had no idea. My answer was basically a shrug. That's when I learned about observability. I started with three things: latency, error rates and retries.

Look at latency in percentiles like p95, not just the average. The average hides the slow requests. Rising latency often shows up before the timeouts do.

The error rate tells you when a provider has gone bad, and which errors it returns.

Retries hide failures from users. So a rising retry count is how you spot a struggling provider before anyone complains.

You don't need all of it at once

All of this took me a lot of time to learn, so I wouldn't build it all in one go. Pick what fits the integration and the tradeoffs you're willing to take. A small script that calls one API once a day probably doesn't need a circuit breaker.

I usually start with timeouts, rate-limit handling, queues and retries. I add the rest when the integration needs it.

I'm Nishant, a backend-focused full-stack developer from Nepal. The original of this post, and the products I build, are on my site.

title: Separate Customer Errors From Provider Errors
description:
Protecting customers and operations by separating product-safe failures from provider diagnostics.

External providers frequently return messages intended for merchant operators. Passing them directly to customers can expose credentials, account permissions, liquidity information, or internal provider restrictions.

Store two error representations:

PaymentFailure(
    customer_message="Unable to complete this transaction. Please try again later.",
    provider_code=response.code,
    provider_reason=response.message,
    provider_payload=sanitized_payload,
)

The customer message should be clear and actionable without revealing infrastructure details. Operations staff need the exact provider reason, request identifier, and sanitized response for investigation.

Apply this rule consistently across API responses, transaction details, push notifications, emails, logs, and staff dashboards. Mask account numbers and never log credentials or complete authorization tokens.

Error normalization also prevents one provider's vocabulary from leaking into the product. Customers should experience a consistent QuickerPay failure model even when the underlying payment rails differ.

Build a small error taxonomy

Map provider responses into internal categories such as invalid recipient, temporarily unavailable, insufficient platform funds, authorization failure, limit exceeded, and unknown provider error. Categories allow the product to choose consistent HTTP statuses and customer messages without depending on unstable provider wording.

Some errors are actionable for customers. An invalid account number can ask them to check the details. Others are operational and should use a neutral retry message. Never claim a refund unless the ledger confirms that a refund occurred.

Preserve diagnostics safely

Operations usually need the provider code, request identifier, endpoint operation, response status, and sanitized payload. They do not need secrets, authorization headers, complete account numbers, or personal identity data in general logs.

Use structured logging so incidents can be searched by internal transaction reference and provider attempt. Keep detailed payloads in access-controlled records with an appropriate retention policy.

Make notifications use the same mapping

It is easy to sanitize the API response while a background task later inserts the raw provider message into a push notification. Centralize customer-facing failure text and require notifications, emails, and transaction serializers to use it.

Do not destroy the original evidence

Normalization should add an internal category; it should not overwrite the original provider response. Provider details are essential for support escalation and reconciliation.

A mature error system serves three audiences at once: customers need clarity, operators need evidence, and engineers need enough context to diagnose systemic failures.

Implementation checklist

Create a provider-error registry with internal category, retryability, customer message, operator guidance, and alert severity. Unknown errors should fall back safely while preserving sanitized diagnostics. Review the registry as providers introduce new responses.

Test the complete communication chain. Confirm that raw messages cannot escape through serializer fields, background notifications, email templates, or staff-written resend actions. Add automated tests using realistic provider payloads containing sensitive-looking content.

The objective is not to hide every failure. It is to communicate what the customer can do while routing technical evidence to the people who can act on it.

Choose retry behavior deliberately

Retry policy should follow the failure category. A timeout after submission calls for a status lookup because the provider may already have accepted the transfer. A validation error should usually fail immediately because repeating the same request changes nothing. Rate limits call for delayed retries with jitter, while authentication failures should alert operators instead of generating more traffic. Persist the attempt count, next retry time, and last failure category so workers resume safely after a restart. After exhausting the retry budget, move the transaction into a visible review state rather than leaving it indefinitely in processing.

title: Build Recovery Paths Beyond Webhooks
description:
Recovering asynchronous payments safely when callbacks are delayed, duplicated, or missing.

Webhooks are asynchronous evidence, not guaranteed delivery.

They may arrive twice, arrive out of order, or never arrive. A reliable payment platform therefore needs several ways to discover the same final state:

  • verified webhook ingestion;
  • scheduled polling for processing transactions;
  • controlled staff status checks;
  • reconciliation against provider records; and
  • provider webhook replay where available.

Every path must converge on one idempotent update function:

def apply_provider_status(payment_id, event):
    with transaction.atomic():
        payment = Payment.objects.select_for_update().get(id=payment_id)
        target = normalize_status(event)
        transition_payment(payment, target, evidence=event)

The function should ignore regressions, recognize terminal states, and separate provider acknowledgement from local ledger settlement.

Polling should run in background workers with bounded retries and observable failure reporting. Staff tools should call the same service instead of directly editing statuses.

This design allows multiple imperfect signals to converge safely. Missing one callback no longer means leaving customer money permanently stuck.

Verify before processing

Webhook endpoints should authenticate the source using the provider's documented signature scheme. Verification must use the raw request representation required by that scheme, a constant-time comparison, and an acceptable timestamp window when timestamps are signed.

Return quickly after durable ingestion. Expensive business work belongs in a background job so temporary ledger or notification failures do not cause the provider to repeatedly deliver the same event while the request remains open.

Store the event before applying it

Persist a sanitized event record containing the provider event identifier, transaction reference, event type, received time, verification result, and payload fingerprint. A unique constraint on the provider event identifier makes duplicate delivery harmless.

The event record and transaction state serve different purposes. The event proves what arrived. The transaction represents the application's accepted financial truth.

Poll selectively

Polling every transaction forever wastes capacity and can hit provider limits. Poll only non-terminal transactions that have passed an appropriate delay, use exponential backoff, and stop after a defined recovery window. Separate “still processing” from “status check failed” so network problems do not become payment failures.

Manual status checks should enqueue the same background task where possible. That keeps staff requests responsive and prevents the dashboard from implementing a second reconciliation path.

Observe unresolved work

Track the age and count of processing transactions, polling failures, webhook verification failures, duplicate events, and transitions recovered without a webhook. Alert on growing queues rather than individual routine retries.

A webhook integration is complete only when the system also knows what to do when the webhook does not arrive.

Implementation checklist

Give every recovery mechanism clear ownership and limits. Define when polling begins, how often it retries, when staff intervention becomes available, and when an unresolved payment becomes a reconciliation exception. Record which signal caused the final transition.

Create operational views for aging processing transactions and failed status checks. Include a safe replay mechanism for individual transactions and controlled batches, with permissions and audit records.

Finally, simulate missing, duplicated, reversed, and out-of-order callbacks. A recovery path that has never been exercised is only a diagram. Reliable systems continuously prove that alternative paths converge on the same result.

title: Design Provider Switching Across the Whole Payment Flow
description:
Keeping every step of a payment flow on the same provider without changing the customer journey.

Adding a second payment provider is easy. Switching safely between providers is the real engineering problem.

A payout flow usually includes bank discovery, account validation, recipient storage, fee quotation, execution, status checks, webhooks, and reconciliation. If each layer selects its provider independently, the system can mix incompatible identifiers.

Resolve the provider once and pass the decision through the workflow:

provider = provider_router.resolve(country="NG", operation="payout")
bank = provider.get_bank(request.bank_code)
recipient = provider.resolve_account(bank, request.account_number)
result = provider.transfer(recipient, request.amount)

Provider-specific bank codes should remain provider-specific. Saved recipients should record which directory produced their details. Cached bank lists should also include the provider in their cache key.

The adapter boundary should expose business operations rather than raw HTTP endpoints. That keeps controllers and transaction services independent of provider response shapes.

The customer flow can then remain stable while operations change the underlying rail. A good provider switch should feel uneventful to users because the architectural work happened before the switch.

Define a business-facing provider interface

An adapter should expose capabilities such as list_banks, resolve_account, quote_fee, create_transfer, and get_transfer_status. It should not leak provider endpoint names or response formats into views and serializers.

Each adapter translates its provider's vocabulary into internal types. One provider may call a successful payout SUCCESSFUL; another may use COMPLETED. The rest of the application should receive one canonical status.

Capabilities also need to be explicit. A provider may support payouts but not collections, or support bank transfers in one country and mobile money in another. Routing should evaluate country, operation, currency, environment, and availability rather than relying on one global string.

Treat reference data as provider-owned

Bank codes are a frequent source of subtle failures. Two providers may use different identifiers for the same institution. Matching by a normalized name looks attractive, but names change, contain abbreviations, and are not guaranteed to be unique.

Store the provider alongside each bank and recipient record. Include it in cache keys. When the active provider changes, show recipients created for that provider or require revalidation before reuse. Do not rewrite the saved identifier because operations may later switch back.

Separate configuration from transaction history

Provider selection can change at runtime, but an existing transaction must remember which provider handled it. Copy the provider, rail, fee configuration, and relevant identifiers onto the transaction attempt. Historical transactions must remain explainable after configuration changes.

Design the fallback deliberately

Automatic fallback after an ambiguous timeout can create two payouts. Only retry through another provider when the first attempt is known not to have been accepted. Otherwise keep the transaction processing and reconcile it.

A safe provider abstraction makes switching easy, but it must never make duplicate money movement easy.

Implementation checklist

Inventory every provider-dependent operation before enabling a switch. Include reference-data caches, recipient favorites, scheduled tasks, webhook routes, status normalization, fee rules, staff actions, and finance reporting. Add provider identity to logs and transaction attempts so production behavior can be traced without exposing credentials.

Test each provider as a complete vertical flow rather than testing only its transfer call. Run bank discovery through final reconciliation using the same configuration production will use. Also test switching away and switching back; saved data must remain valid for its original provider.

The abstraction is complete when no downstream layer has to guess which provider owns a piece of data.

title: Model Payment Statuses as a State Machine
description:
Turning scattered payment updates into explicit, enforceable lifecycle rules.

A payment status is not an arbitrary label. It represents a position in a controlled financial lifecycle.

Real transactions can be pending, processing, completed, failed, expired, reversed, or refunded. Problems appear when API handlers, background workers, webhooks, and staff tools can assign these values independently.

Define the valid transitions instead:

TRANSITIONS = {
    "pending": {"processing", "failed", "expired"},
    "processing": {"completed", "failed"},
    "failed": {"refunded"},
    "completed": set(),
    "refunded": set(),
}

Route every change through one domain service. Inside a database transaction, lock the payment row, validate the transition, save the provider evidence, and apply any ledger effect exactly once. Emit notifications only after the database commit succeeds.

Terminal states need special protection. A delayed processing event must never move a completed payment backward. Likewise, two simultaneous success signals must not produce two credits.

State machines make those rules explicit, testable, and shared by every entry point. In payment infrastructure, that is far safer than treating status as a writable string.

Centralize transitions instead of centralizing status writes

A common first improvement is to create a helper that updates the status field. That reduces duplication, but it does not yet protect the lifecycle. The service must understand the meaning of each transition and the work attached to it.

Moving from processing to completed may release a hold, post a ledger entry, update a linked order, and schedule a notification. Moving from processing to failed may refund the sender. These are domain operations, not model assignments.

The transition service should accept evidence, not trust callers to supply a final state blindly. A provider adapter can normalize its response into a small internal event containing the provider reference, normalized status, event time, and sanitized payload. The transition layer then decides whether that evidence is newer, valid, and financially actionable.

Protect transitions from concurrency

Imagine a polling worker and webhook handler receiving success at nearly the same time. Both read processing; both decide to complete; both attempt to credit the recipient. A state-machine table alone does not prevent this race.

Use a database transaction and row-level lock. After acquiring the lock, re-read the current state and check whether the financial effect already exists. Back the ledger reference with a unique database constraint. Application checks explain intent; database constraints provide the final concurrency guarantee.

Keep transition history

The current state answers where the payment is now. It does not explain how it got there. Record transition history with the previous state, next state, source, actor, provider evidence, and timestamp.

This history makes support and reconciliation substantially easier. It also reveals operational patterns such as transactions repeatedly moving into manual review or providers producing late events.

Test the lifecycle as a graph

Useful tests cover more than successful examples. Verify every permitted edge, every rejected edge, terminal-state protection, duplicate success signals, late failure events, and concurrent completion attempts.

The strongest invariant is simple: regardless of event order or retry count, the transaction reaches one valid state and every financial effect occurs at most once.

Implementation checklist

Before shipping a lifecycle, document every state and transition, identify the service responsible for each edge, define terminal states, and specify the ledger effect attached to every financial transition. Add database constraints for unique effects and structured transition logs for investigation. Review all writers of the status field; ideally, none should remain outside the transition service.

Monitor invalid transition attempts as well. They often reveal late provider events, duplicate jobs, or an endpoint bypassing the domain layer. A state machine is valuable not only because it permits valid movement, but because it makes invalid movement visible.

The result is a payment lifecycle that remains understandable under retries, concurrency, and operational intervention.

title: How to Fix 401 Unauthorized Errors in an LLM API
description:
The Problem

401 Unauthorized is one of the most common first-day errors in any LLM API project. It's also the one that eats the most time, because the body says the same thing whether your key is wrong or just badly copied:

openai.AuthenticationError: Error code: 401 - {'error': {...'invalid api key'...}}

The confusing part: 401 doesn't mean your key is wrong. It means the server refused to accept your credentials as presented. That gap covers several very different causes. Here's the checklist I run through, in order of likelihood.

Quick Definitions: 401 vs 403 vs 429

Code Meaning Usual cause
401 Server didn't accept your credentials Key missing, malformed, or invalid
403 Credentials accepted, but you're not allowed Account state, permissions, regional restrictions
429 Too many requests Rate limits — retry with backoff, see my next post

If you're getting 403, this isn't your article — but the table above saves you an hour of debugging the wrong thing.

The Checklist

1. Is the key actually being sent?

With an SDK, an empty or misnamed environment variable silently produces "no key":

import os
key = os.environ.get("HEFUAI_API_KEY")
if not key:
    raise SystemExit("HEFUAI_API_KEY is not set — check .env and load_dotenv()")

With raw HTTP, the header must include the scheme, exactly once:

Authorization: Bearer sk-...

Authorization: sk-... (no Bearer) and Bearer: sk-... (schemes swapped) both produce 401 on many gateways.

2. Is there invisible whitespace in the key?

The cause that wastes the most time. Copying a key out of a dashboard or a chat message drags along a trailing newline or space:

key = os.environ["HEFUAI_API_KEY"]
print("leading/trailing whitespace:", key != key.strip())

Fix it at the source (your .env file), not with .strip() everywhere — but if the key comes from user input or a config system you don't control, strip it defensively.

3. Test the key independently of your app

Before you blame your framework, send one raw request. This isolates key validity from code:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  https://api.hefu.hk/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $HEFUAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "deepseek-v4-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}]}'
  • 200 → your key is fine; the bug is in your app (wrong env var name, dotenv not loaded, per-directory .env)
  • 401 → the key itself is the problem; continue to #4

4. Was the key rotated, revoked, or never saved correctly?

Keys get invalidated more often than people admit:

  • Someone on the team rotated the key "for security" and your deploy didn't get the memo
  • You regenerated the key while debugging and are now running two versions
  • The key was never fully copied in the first place

Worth knowing how your provider stores keys. For example, HefuAI shows the plaintext once at creation and never again — so if you didn't save it, regeneration is the only path, not "view it again." If a key might be compromised, revoke and rotate in the console rather than hoping it blows over.

5. Are you hitting the right base URL with the right key?

A subtle one: if your base_url points at a different gateway or vendor than the one that issued your key, you'll get a 401 that has nothing to do with the key's validity. Same class of bug: dev keys against prod endpoints. Print both, every time, during setup:

print("base_url:", client.base_url)
print("key prefix:", os.environ["HEFUAI_API_KEY"][:6] + "...")

Don't Retry a 401

A rookie mistake is wrapping everything in a retry loop. 401 is not transient — retrying the same credentials will fail the same way 100% of the time, and retrying can even trigger rate-limit lockouts. Handle it explicitly and fail fast:

from openai import OpenAI, AuthenticationError

try:
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-v4-flash",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}],
    )
except AuthenticationError:
    # stop the pipeline, alert a human, check the checklist above
    raise SystemExit("Auth failed — do NOT retry. Check key, header, base URL.")

Retry budgets belong to 429 and 5xx errors — that's the next post in this series.

Common Mistakes

  1. Debugging 403 problems as if they were 401 (see the table above — account state vs credentials).
  2. Hardcoding the key to "test quickly," then the hardcoded key rotates and prod breaks mysteriously.
  3. Sharing a screenshot of your terminal that contains the full key. Rotate immediately if this happens.
  4. Mixing two providers' keys and base URLs in the same .env file.

Next Steps

Once auth works, the next error you'll meet in production is 429 Too Many Requests. The next post covers rate limits, exponential backoff, and building retry logic that actually respects Retry-After headers.

Disclosure: this tutorial series uses HefuAI as its example gateway. All code patterns apply to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

title: Why Your Controller Feels Different on PC vs Console (and How to Test Both)
description:
If you have ever plugged a controller you love on console into a PC and thought "this feels wrong," you are not imagining it. The same pad can behave differently across platforms, and most of the time it is not broken — it is being read differently.

The first difference is the driver layer. On console, the system knows exactly which controller you have and applies its own deadzones and curves. On PC, Windows usually exposes the pad through XInput or DirectInput, and each game then adds its own layer on top. A stick that rests at a tiny offset might be hidden by the console's deadzone but show up plainly on PC, or the other way round.

The second difference is calibration. Consoles rarely let you calibrate a stick; PCs do, through Steam Input, DS4Windows, or the manufacturer's app. That is useful, but it also means a bad calibration can follow you from game to game until you reset it. If a controller suddenly feels off after you changed software, check calibration before you blame hardware.

So how do you tell which layer is lying to you? Test the controller outside any game. Connect it to a PC, open a browser tester, and watch the raw inputs: leave both sticks untouched for ten seconds and see whether either one reports movement on its own. That is your drift baseline. Then move each stick slowly in a full circle and watch whether the motion is smooth or jumps. Press every button and pull both triggers fully, checking that each one reaches its full value and returns cleanly to zero.

You can test your controller online for free (https://www.gamepadtesterpro.com) — no install, just the browser reading what the operating system reports. Do the same test with the pad wired and then over Bluetooth if you use both; a stick that only drifts on Bluetooth is usually a connection or battery issue, not a worn sensor.

If the raw test is clean but a game still feels wrong, the problem is almost certainly in that game's deadzone or sensitivity settings, or in a calibration profile. Raise the game's deadzone a notch, or reset the calibration profile and retest. If the raw test shows drift while the stick sits untouched, cleaning around the stick base sometimes helps, but persistent drift on a worn pad usually means the sensor module is tired — cleaning buys time, it does not restore a worn track.

One more practical habit: test a controller the day you buy it, used or new, and again after any repair. A two-minute baseline makes every later "is this getting worse?" question answerable instead of guesswork. Controllers wear gradually, and noticing a small change early is what keeps a minor annoyance from becoming a ruined ranked match.

title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon EC2.
description:
1. Introduction

Cloud computing has transformed the way businesses, institutions, and individuals access and manage computing resources. Traditionally, organizations had to purchase physical servers, storage devices, networking equipment, and other IT infrastructure to operate their applications and services. However, maintaining these resources could be expensive and time-consuming.

Today, cloud computing provides an alternative through different service models, including Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS).

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is one of the most important cloud computing models because it provides users with virtualized computing resources over the internet.

This article explores the concept of IaaS, its characteristics, benefits, and challenges, using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) as a practical case study.

  1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud computing model that provides virtualized IT resources such as servers, storage, networking, and computing power over the internet.

Instead of purchasing and maintaining physical hardware, users rent computing infrastructure from a cloud service provider and pay according to their usage.

The cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, including servers, data centres, and networking hardware, while customers manage their operating systems, applications, and data.

Key Characteristics of IaaS

Some major characteristics of IaaS include:

  • Virtualization: Physical computing resources are converted into virtual machines that multiple users can access.
  • Scalability: Users can increase or decrease computing resources depending on demand.
  • Pay-as-you-go pricing: Customers pay for the resources they consume.
  • Resource management: Users have control over operating systems, applications, and configurations.
  • Internet accessibility: Infrastructure can be accessed and managed remotely.
  • Flexibility: Users can select computing resources according to their specific requirements.
  1. Case Study: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2)

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is a cloud computing service offered by Amazon Web Services (AWS).

It is a practical example of Infrastructure as a Service because it allows users to rent virtual servers instead of purchasing physical computers and server equipment.

With Amazon EC2, developers and organizations can launch virtual machines, install operating systems, deploy applications, configure networks, and manage storage.

How Amazon EC2 Works

Amazon EC2 operates through virtualization technology.

Users access the AWS management console and select the computing resources they need. They can choose an operating system, processor capacity, memory, storage, and networking configurations.

Once configured, AWS provisions a virtual server known as an EC2 instance.

The user can then:

  1. Launch a virtual server.
  2. Select an operating system such as Linux or Windows.
  3. Install the required software and applications.
  4. Configure security and network settings.
  5. Store and manage application data.
  6. Increase or decrease computing resources when necessary.

This allows organizations to operate applications without owning physical server infrastructure.

  1. Major Features of Amazon EC2

Amazon EC2 provides several features that make it useful for businesses and developers.

  1. Virtual Servers

EC2 provides virtual machines that users can configure according to their computing requirements.

  1. Flexible Computing Resources

Users can select different combinations of processing power, memory, storage, and networking capabilities.

  1. Storage Integration

EC2 supports integration with Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS), which provides persistent storage for virtual servers.

  1. Security Management

Users can configure security groups, which function as virtual firewalls to control network traffic entering and leaving their instances.

  1. Scalability

Computing capacity can be increased or decreased depending on application requirements.

  1. Multiple Availability Locations

AWS provides different geographical regions and Availability Zones, allowing organizations to deploy applications across separate locations to improve resilience.

  1. Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution

Amazon EC2 offers several advantages.

Cost Reduction

Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers or maintain large server rooms. They can rent resources and pay according to their usage.

Scalability and Flexibility

Businesses can increase their computing resources during periods of high demand and reduce them when demand decreases.

Faster Deployment

Virtual servers can be created within minutes, allowing developers to deploy applications without waiting for physical hardware installation.

Reliability

Applications can be deployed across multiple Availability Zones to reduce dependence on a single location.

Remote Accessibility

Users can manage their cloud infrastructure from different geographical locations through the internet.

  1. Challenges and Limitations of Amazon EC2

Despite its advantages, Amazon EC2 has some limitations.

  1. Security Responsibilities: Although AWS protects its physical infrastructure, customers must secure their operating systems, applications, access permissions, and data.

  2. Internet Dependency: Accessing cloud resources requires a reliable internet connection.

  3. Cost Management: Poor resource management can result in unexpected expenses, especially when unused instances continue running.

  4. Technical Complexity: Managing virtual servers, networking, operating systems, and security configurations requires technical knowledge.

  5. Vendor Dependency: Organizations may become dependent on AWS services, making migration to another provider complicated.

  6. Practical Application of Amazon EC2

Consider a university that wants to develop an online student registration system.

Traditionally, the university would need to purchase physical servers, install operating systems, configure networks, and employ technical personnel to maintain the infrastructure.

Using Amazon EC2, the university can:

  • Launch a virtual server to host its registration application.
  • Install the required operating system and web server.
  • Deploy the student registration application.
  • Connect the application to a database service.
  • Configure security to protect student information.
  • Increase computing capacity during registration periods when many students access the platform.

This demonstrates how IaaS can help educational institutions reduce infrastructure costs, improve flexibility, and manage changing computing demands.

  1. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has become an important component of modern cloud computing because it provides flexible, scalable, and cost-effective computing resources.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how organizations can access virtual servers, storage, and networking resources without purchasing and maintaining physical infrastructure.

Although IaaS introduces challenges such as security responsibilities, internet dependency, and cost management, its benefits make it a valuable solution for businesses, educational institutions, developers, and other organizations.

As technology continues to evolve, IaaS will remain an important foundation for digital transformation and modern application development.

  1. References

  2. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)? https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/iaas/

  3. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Amazon EC2? https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html

  4. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). Amazon EC2 Documentation. https://aws.amazon.com/documentation-overview/ec2/

  5. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). AWS Shared Responsibility Model. https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/shared-responsibility-model/

title: Black Friday as a Distributed System: Amazon Monitoring with Three Data Pipes
description:
Data as of October 29, 2026. Black Friday is November 27, 2026. Cyber Monday is November 30, 2026. Twenty-nine days remain. Most Black Friday advice reads like a checklist: stock up, file deals, raise budgets. This post treats the season as something else entirely: a monitoring system with three data pipes, each with its own cadence, granularity, and alert conditions. If you build systems for a living, that framing will feel familiar. The season is a distributed system under load, and the teams that survive it are the ones whose observability holds up.

The core claim: polling frequency is the strategy

A dashboard you check once a day is not monitoring. It is a history book. During Black Friday week, sponsored slots change hands within hours, rival prices move intraday, and AI recommendations shift as listings change. A daily poll finds all of that out after the money is gone. The difference between the sellers who win the week and the ones who write postmortems about it is usually not budget or catalog. It is how often they look, how finely they slice what they see, and whether anything pages them when a signal crosses a line.

That claim has numbers behind it. Adobe's 2025 actuals for United States online shopping: Cyber Monday $14.25 billion, up 7.1%, the biggest single day of the year; Black Friday $11.8 billion, up 9.1%, a record; Cyber Week $44.2 billion, up 7.7%; mobile at 57.5% of Cyber Monday spending; electronics, apparel, and furniture together at 57% of online spend; the holiday season from November 1 to December 31 at about $257.8 billion, up 6.8%. Adobe's 2026 forecast pushes further: holiday season $275.1 billion, up 6.7%; Cyber Monday $15.1 billion, up 6.2%, the first single day over $15 billion; Black Friday $12.9 billion, up 9.2%; Thanksgiving $6.9 billion, up 8.5%; October online spend $95.8 billion, up 8%; AI traffic up 130%, with Thanksgiving up 159%, Black Friday up 95%, and Cyber Monday up 88%.

Two more data points explain why monitoring, not just marketing, is the bottleneck. Adweek, citing Adobe, reported AI-driven retail traffic on Black Friday 2025 up 805% year over year. Salesforce counted AI and agents influencing 20% of orders globally during Cyber Week, 17% in the United States, worth about $13.5 billion. A fifth of orders now pass through a recommendation layer that most sellers never test. If you are not re-testing that layer daily, you are not monitoring the storefront. You are monitoring four-fifths of it.

The system: three pipes, three stages

Design the season as three pipelines feeding one war room. The price pipe emits price, deal price, Buy Box ownership, follow-seller presence, and inventory state. The ad pipe emits sponsored product, sponsored brand, and video slot occupancy for core keywords. The AI pipe emits recommendation results for a fixed question set. Each pipe runs on a different schedule in each stage, and the schedule is part of the design, not an afterthought.

Stage 1: Warm-up (now to about November 19) Stage 2: Black Friday week (expected November 19–29, unconfirmed) Stage 3: Cyber Monday and after (November 30 to early December)
Price pipe Competitor price bands, coupon baselines, verifying whether strikethrough prices are real Final price, deal price, Buy Box ownership, follow sellers, inventory Price recovery rhythm and competitor stockout windows
Ad pipe Baselines for gift and event keywords, organic and ad positions Core keyword sponsored product, sponsored brand, and video slots, hourly and split by ZIP code Keyword-level share-of-voice review, cutting underperforming keywords
AI pipe A baseline set of questions, recording who gets recommended Daily re-tests, defending the recommended first screen Reviewing recommendation reasons and feeding them back into listing revisions

Stage one is about baselines. You cannot alert on a deviation if you never recorded normal. Collect competitor price bands and coupon baselines, record organic and ad positions for gift and event keywords, and build the AI question set with its first round of answers. Stage two is about cadence: hourly ad checks, daily AI re-tests, continuous price and Buy Box watches. Stage three is about review: share-of-voice accounting, price recovery tracking, and turning recommendation reasons into listing changes.

Cadence: hourly where slots move, daily where answers move

The cadence choices fall out of the physics of each pipe. Paid slots are auctions. They change hands intraday, and the October rehearsal proved how fast money concentrates: Prime Big Deal Days on October 6–7 drove United States online spending to $9.86 billion, up 8.5% year over year, with electronics 85% above the September average, toys 158% higher, and games 90% higher. Triple Whale's sample of about 2,000 brands showed Amazon ad spend during the event up 149% against the prior week, with returns concentrated on day one. An hourly poll during stage two is not gold-plating. It is the sampling rate the auction demands. Anything slower aliases the signal: you see the average, miss the swing, and misattribute the outcome.

AI recommendations move slower than auctions but faster than weekly reviews. A daily re-test of a fixed question set catches a rival's listing change, a new recommendation entrant, or a dropped first-screen placement within a day. The May 2026 shift, when Amazon replaced Rufus with Alexa for Shopping and moved AI answers into the main search bar, made this pipe structural. Recommendations are now part of the storefront surface, and an untested surface is an unmonitored one.

Price and inventory move on both timescales, which is why the price pipe runs continuously in stage two: final price, deal price, Buy Box ownership, follow sellers, and stock state are all state changes that should emit events, not rows in a nightly dump.

Granularity: ZIP codes and keywords, not national averages

The second design decision is resolution. A national average is a lossy compression, and during Black Friday week it compresses away exactly the signal you need. The baby products case below is the textbook example: United States East Coast and West Coast ad performance diverged so sharply that a national average hid the problem entirely. The fix was ZIP-code splits on the ad pipe and parallel tracking of hundreds of long-tail keywords. When you slice by ZIP code, a regional slot loss becomes visible while it is still recoverable. When you track long-tail keywords in parallel, a category-level average cannot hide a keyword-level collapse.

Apply the same thinking to the price pipe. Competitor price bands per region beat a single national price. Coupon baselines per listing beat a category coupon average. And on the AI pipe, keep the question set fixed across re-tests. Changing the questions between runs destroys comparability, which is the one property a monitoring system cannot afford to lose.

Alerting: triggers from real incidents

A monitoring system without alerts is a log file. Define triggers before the week starts, and tie each one to a named response. The incidents in the cases below suggest the starter set: a rival price move beyond your band, a Buy Box loss, a follow seller appearing on a core listing, a core keyword slot changing hands, a regional divergence beyond your threshold, and an AI recommendation dropping off the first screen. Each trigger needs an owner and a runbook step: reprice, shift spend, or revise the listing. Alerts that page nobody are worse than no alerts, because they teach the team to ignore the system.

Cost discipline belongs in the alerting design too. A vendor estimate, not official data, puts the 2025 Amazon average cost per click near $1.12, with the fourth-quarter peak at $1.35 to $1.45, and competitive categories reaching $2 to $6 or more on Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Per PPC Land's reading of Adobe's forecast, discount depth is expected to stay similar to last year, so the margin battle will be fought on detection speed and spend allocation, not on deeper cuts. An alert that fires when a keyword's spend crosses its conversion value is worth more than a bigger budget.

Test results: three systems already running

The three cases below come from Pangolinfo's customer page and are used with permission. Read them as test reports from production systems, not as marketing copy.

An apparel seller at $2.2 billion scale, with more than 30,000 SKUs, treated the price pipe as a data engineering problem first. Price, bestseller rank, and review fields were collected steadily, standardized JSON landed in the ERP within 2 days, the success rate ran over 99%, and the selection cycle compressed to 8 hours. The engineering lesson: a clean, typed feed into an existing system beats a prettier dashboard that nobody can query. JSON into the ERP meant every downstream decision, from selection to repricing, ran on the same data.

A baby products seller at $1.8 billion in gross merchandise volume built the ad pipe the hard way, after core keyword ad slots were taken by rivals and traffic fell with no alert. Hourly competitor ad monitoring, ZIP-code splits, and hundreds of long-tail keywords tracked in parallel delivered the numbers: competitor slot-grabbing detected 10 times faster, average cost per click down over 38%, daily ad spend down 60%. The engineering lesson is the combination. Hourly cadence without ZIP granularity would have averaged the regional signal away. Granularity without hourly cadence would have found the slot loss too late.

Sif, a traffic analytics platform serving thousands of sellers at more than 30 million requests a day, runs the whole system at a scale where small error rates become large absolute errors. Its sponsored product ad placement collection rate runs over 98%, and page-structure restoration accuracy runs over 99%. Its chief technology officer described Pangolinfo as the strongest technical partner they had worked with on collection quality, concurrency, and configuration flexibility, and said Sif has fully switched. At 30 million requests a day, collection quality, concurrency, and configuration flexibility are not feature bullets. They are the load-bearing walls.

Calendar as configuration

Treat the calendar as config with confidence flags, not as fixed constants. Prime Big Deal Days on October 6–7 is done; use it as rehearsal data. A listing freeze around November 9 is seller practice, not an Amazon rule. The deal submission deadline of November 13 is to verify; the earlier date was October 20, and Seller Central prevails. The Black Friday week start around November 19–21 is unconfirmed by Amazon; last year it ran November 20 to December 1. Thanksgiving on November 26 carries a $6.9 billion forecast with mobile share expected to reach 63%. Black Friday on November 27 is forecast at $12.9 billion. Cyber Monday on November 30 is forecast at $15.1 billion. One rule from PPC Land is worth encoding in your pricing logic: October event prices do not count toward the lookback period Amazon uses for Black Friday deal price caps, so October discounts do not automatically lower your Black Friday ceiling.

Build order: one pipe, this week

You do not need all three pipes on day one. Register at tool.pangolinfo.com, where the free tier is 60 credits/month, resets monthly, no credit card required. Run your core ASINs and target ZIP codes through the console and inspect the actual storefront price, ad slots, and inventory. Then pick one pipe first: price, ad, or AI, starting with whichever hurts most. Teams already running AI agents can call live Amazon data through MCP access with one configuration, and teams tracking the AI doorway can look at the Amazon Alexa API. Developer docs live at docs.pangolinfo.com.

Get one pipe emitting events this week, with a baseline, a cadence, and one alert that pages a human. Add the second pipe once the first one has survived a full week of runs. The season rewards systems that are already running when the surge arrives, not architectures that are still being drawn when it hits. Twenty-nine days is enough time to build the first pipe properly. Start with the one that hurts most. The first alert that pages a human is the moment the system stops being a document and starts being infrastructure.

Schema: what each pipe emits

If you were to model the three pipes as events, the shapes would look roughly like this:

price_event: { asin, price, deal_price, buy_box_owner, follow_seller, inventory }
ad_event: { keyword, zip_code, slot: "sp | sb | video", occupant }
ai_event: { question, recommended_asins, first_screen }

The point of writing the schema down is not the syntax. It is the discipline: every event carries the keys the alert logic needs. A price event without the Buy Box owner cannot trigger a Buy Box alert. An ad event without the ZIP code cannot reveal a regional loss. An AI event without the first-screen flag cannot distinguish a recommendation from a mention.

Failure modes

Monitoring systems fail in predictable ways, and the cases above name most of them. Daily-only polling aliases intraday swings: the October rehearsal concentrated spend and returns on day one, so a daily poll sees the average and misses the swing. National averages hide regional losses: the baby products case proved that a single country-level number can describe neither coast. Changing AI questions between runs destroys comparability, which is the one property the AI pipe cannot lose. Alerts without owners get ignored, which teaches the team to distrust the system itself. And no baseline means no deviation detection at all: without stage-one price bands, keyword positions, and AI answers, stage two has nothing to compare against, and every alert is either noise or hindsight. Design against these five failures first, and the rest of the system gets easier.

Built with Pangolinfo Amazon Scraper API — the live Amazon data feed behind the cases in this article.

title: Beyond OpenCV: Light-Weight Monocular Depth Post-Processing in Pure NumPy
description:
When building desktop or edge AI applications, the default instinct for many engineers is to run pip install opencv-python.

However, as your architecture matures toward lightweight, self-contained edge software (such as a PyQt6 GUI app running ONNX Runtime on CPU), third-party C++ wrappers introduce real operational friction:

  • Deployment Bloat: 40–50 MB binary wheels (opencv-python-headless on Linux/Windows x64) that expand desktop installers.
  • Cold-Start Latency: Shared C++ library initialization delays during application startup.
  • Dependency Conflicts: Threading and event-loop clashes with native Qt backends.

In our project — Hawk Eye, an industrial AI edge application for monocular tire tread depth assessment — we enforced a strict rule: Zero CV-specific external dependencies (no OpenCV, SciPy, or Scikit-Image). The pipeline relies strictly on PyQt6, ONNX Runtime, PIL, and pure NumPy.

In this article, we look at how we solve camera perspective tilt in monocular depth maps using simple vector operations in NumPy.

The Problem: Relative Depth and Perspective Distortion

Monocular depth estimation models (like U-Net architectures optimized for edge CPU) map 2D pixels to depth predictions Z_raw in range [0.0, 1.0].

In field diagnostics, handheld devices or smartphone cameras are almost never held perfectly parallel to the tire surface. A 5-degree perspective tilt creates an artificial linear gradient across the depth map, causing the model to mistake perspective for actual physical tread wear.

To fix this, we detrend the baseline reference plane using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) fitted via SVD.

The Mathematics of Plane Fitting: Why SVD over Normal Equations?

We model the background surface using a linear 3D equation:

Z(x, y) = a * x + b * y + c

Where (x, y) are spatial pixel coordinates, a, b are surface slopes, and c is the global baseline offset.

Given an ROI matrix Z_raw of size H x W, we set up an overdetermined linear system A * x = b.

Numerical Stability: SVD vs. Normal Equations

In textbook linear algebra, the analytical solution is written via Normal Equations:

x_opt = inv(A^T * A) * A^T * b

In production, forming A^T * A squares the dynamic range of pixel coordinates. For a 224x224 depth grid (N = 50,176 pixels, max coordinate x_max = 223), the condition number of A^T * A reaches 10^4 - 10^5. Explicit matrix inversion leads to numerical instability on low-precision CPU runtimes.

Instead, we use Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) via np.linalg.lstsq. SVD solves the system directly without forming A^T * A, avoiding matrix inversion instability.

Production Python Implementation

Below is the self-contained implementation written purely in NumPy. It fits a least-squares plane, subtracts perspective tilt, and uses percentile masking to prevent deep grooves from corrupting the surface fit.

 python
import numpy as np

def detrend_and_scale_depth(
    depth_raw: np.ndarray, 
    scale_3d: float = 1.80, 
    bias_mm: float = 0.0,
    groove_mask_percentile: float = 40.0
) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Removes camera perspective tilt using SVD Least Squares Plane Fitting
    and converts raw relative depth predictions into millimeter profile maps.

    Convention: Assumes Z_groove < Z_surface (lower relative height in depth_raw).

    Parameters
    ----------
    depth_raw : np.ndarray
        2D floating-point array (H, W) of relative predictions from ONNX U-Net.
    scale_3d : float
        Optics scale factor (mm per relative depth unit).
    bias_mm : float
        Systemic bias correction in millimeters.
    groove_mask_percentile : float
        Empirical threshold (40%) masking lower depth values (grooves) 
        during plane fitting to prevent fit sags.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        2D array (H, W) containing detrended physical tread depth in millimeters.
    """
    h, w = depth_raw.shape

    # 1. Generate 2D pixel coordinate grids
    grid_y, grid_x = np.indices((h, w), dtype=np.float32)

    x_flat = grid_x.ravel()
    y_flat = grid_y.ravel()
    z_flat = depth_raw.ravel()

    # Design matrix A: Shape (N, 3) where N = H * W
    A = np.column_stack([x_flat, y_flat, np.ones_like(x_flat)])

    # 2. Trimmed OLS: Mask out deep grooves to fit plane ONLY on top tread blocks
    threshold_val = np.percentile(z_flat, groove_mask_percentile)
    mask = z_flat >= threshold_val

    # 3. Solve for plane parameters [a, b, c] via SVD (lstsq)
    plane_params, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(A[mask], z_flat[mask], rcond=None)
    a, b, c = plane_params

    # 4. Reconstruct background trend plane across full ROI
    z_plane = (a * grid_x + b * grid_y + c)

    # 5. Detrend surface (Subtract baseline slope)
    z_detrended = depth_raw - z_plane

    # 6. Robust baseline shift (P05 percentile instead of min to reject noise)
    baseline_floor = np.percentile(z_detrended, 5)
    z_detrended -= baseline_floor

    # 7. Convert relative depth delta to physical millimeters
    depth_mm = (z_detrended * scale_3d) + bias_mm

    return depth_mm


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Simulate 100x100 tile with camera tilt + 2.0 unit groove (20% of area)
    y, x = np.ogrid[:100, :100]
    simulated_tilt = 0.05 * x + 0.02 * y
    simulated_groove = np.where((x > 40) & (x < 60), -2.0, 0.0)
    raw_input = simulated_tilt + simulated_groove

    # Process depth map
    depth_mm = detrend_and_scale_depth(raw_input, scale_3d=2.5)

    # Evaluation using P95 - P05 percentiles (Assumes groove area >= 5-10% of ROI)
    groove_depth = np.percentile(depth_mm, 95) - np.percentile(depth_mm, 5)

    print(f"Input Range (Tilted): [{raw_input.min():.2f}, {raw_input.max():.2f}]")
    print(f"Corrected Depth Range: [{depth_mm.min():.2f}, {depth_mm.max():.2f}] mm")
    print(f"Measured Groove Depth: {groove_depth:.2f} mm (Expected Synthetic: 5.00 mm)")

Expected Output 

Input Range (Tilted): [0.00, 6.93]
Corrected Depth Range: [0.00, 5.00] mm
Measured Groove Depth: 5.00 mm (Expected Synthetic: 5.00 mm)

Production Considerations & Limitations

While linear plane detrending is fast, edge deployment has specific constraints:

  1. Groove Fitting Bias (Trimmed OLS): Unmasked OLS fits the plane to all pixels. If an ROI contains deep grooves, the fitted plane sags downward. Our implementation uses a 40% threshold mask (groove_mask_percentile=40) to fit strictly to elevated tread blocks (valid for typical 15–35% groove occupancy).
  2. Extreme Camera Tilt: If perspective tilt across the ROI exceeds the total groove depth, global percentile thresholding bleeds across regions. For severe angles (>30 degrees), local block-based RANSAC or quadratic fitting z = a*x^2 + b*y^2 + c*x*y + d*x + e*y + f should replace global OLS.
  3. Local vs. Global Slope Removal: OLS removes all linear trends. This works well for measuring local groove depth relative to adjacent tread blocks, but intentional tire shoulder curvature will also be flattened.

Benchmark Results

Replacing external CV packages with vectorized NumPy operations yielded clear benefits in our PyQt6 runtime:

  • Execution Latency: 0.38 ms on a 224x224 depth ROI (median of 100 runs after 10 warm-up iterations on Intel Core i5-1135G7 @ 2.40GHz, OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, NumPy 1.26.4).
  • Package Footprint: Saved ~45 MB on Linux/Windows x64 installers by removing opencv-python-headless.
  • Thread Safety: Pure NumPy array operations run inside PyQt6 worker threads without GUI loop blocking.

Conclusion

Linear algebra operations in pure NumPy are often enough for edge post-processing without bundling full C++ vision frameworks.

While synthetic tests verify the math, production calibration against real physical depth gauges (e.g., Mitutoyo 571-201-30) remains necessary to establish the optics scale factor (scale_3d) for different smartphone camera modules.

By combining SVD plane fitting with percentile masking, we achieved stable profile extraction for Hawk Eye — completely independent of external computer vision packages.

title: WooCommerce to Shopify migration: building the redirect map with a small script
description:
When a WooCommerce store moves to Shopify, products and customers usually move without much trouble. URLs are where you lose traffic. WooCommerce lets the store owner shape permalinks. Shopify doesn't: product URLs always start with /products/ and collections with /collections/. So almost every indexed URL on the old store changes on launch day.

This post walks through how we build the redirect map: collect every old URL, translate the predictable ones with a script, review the rest by hand, then import the result into Shopify as a CSV.

1. Collect every URL that matters

Don't start from the product export alone. You want every URL that Google or a customer might still request:

  • the WooCommerce XML sitemaps (with Yoast or Rank Math that's usually /sitemap_index.xml; WordPress core serves /wp-sitemap.xml)
  • a crawl of the live site
  • top landing pages from Search Console (Performance → Pages, last 12 months)
  • URLs with backlinks, from whatever backlink tool you use
  • existing redirects stored in a WordPress redirect plugin, so you can chain them straight to the final Shopify URL

Put them all in one list and remove duplicates. Keep the query string out unless it actually changes the content.

2. Know the default mappings

Most WooCommerce stores use the default bases. Check Settings → Permalinks in WordPress first, because many stores change them.

WooCommerce URL Shopify URL
/product/blue-hoodie/ /products/blue-hoodie
/product-category/hoodies/ /collections/hoodies
/product-category/clothing/hoodies/ /collections/hoodies (no nesting in Shopify URLs)
/product-tag/sale/ /collections/sale or the closest collection
/2024/05/how-to-wash-wool/ /blogs/news/how-to-wash-wool
/about-us/ /pages/about-us

News is the default blog on Shopify, which is why posts land under /blogs/news/.

3. Translate the predictable ones

Here's the script we start from. It reads a list of old paths (one per line) and writes the two-column CSV that Shopify's URL redirect import expects: Redirect from and Redirect to. Anything it can't map goes to a review file.

import csv
import re
import sys
from urllib.parse import urlparse

# Adjust these to match Settings > Permalinks on the old store
PRODUCT_BASE = "product"
CATEGORY_BASE = "product-category"
TAG_BASE = "product-tag"
BLOG_HANDLE = "news"

KNOWN_PAGES = {"about-us", "contact", "shipping", "returns", "faq"}

def to_shopify(path: str):
    parts = [p for p in path.strip("/").split("/") if p]
    if not parts:
        return None  # homepage stays the homepage
    if parts[0] == PRODUCT_BASE and len(parts) >= 2:
        return f"/products/{parts[-1]}"
    if parts[0] == CATEGORY_BASE and len(parts) >= 2:
        return f"/collections/{parts[-1]}"  # flatten nested categories
    if parts[0] == TAG_BASE and len(parts) >= 2:
        return f"/collections/{parts[-1]}"  # only if you build that collection
    if re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}", parts[0]) and len(parts) >= 3:
        return f"/blogs/{BLOG_HANDLE}/{parts[-1]}"  # /2024/05/slug/
    if len(parts) == 1 and parts[0] in KNOWN_PAGES:
        return f"/pages/{parts[0]}"
    return None

def main(src, out_csv, review_txt):
    rows, review = [], []
    with open(src) as f:
        for line in f:
            url = line.strip()
            if not url:
                continue
            path = urlparse(url).path or "/"
            target = to_shopify(path)
            if target:
                rows.append((path, target))
            elif path != "/":
                review.append(path)
    with open(out_csv, "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["Redirect from", "Redirect to"])
        w.writerows(sorted(set(rows)))
    with open(review_txt, "w") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(sorted(set(review))))
    print(f"{len(rows)} mapped, {len(review)} to review")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:4])

Run it as python map_redirects.py old-urls.txt redirects.csv review.txt.

The script is deliberately dumb. It assumes the product slug stays the same on Shopify, which is the single most useful decision you can make during the migration: if blue-hoodie stays blue-hoodie, most of the map writes itself.

4. Review what the script couldn't map

The review file is where judgement comes in:

  • Flattened categories. Two nested categories with the same last segment (say /men/hoodies/ and /women/hoodies/) can't both become /collections/hoodies. Rename one collection and fix the row.
  • Tag archives. Only redirect a tag to a collection if you actually build that collection. Otherwise pick the nearest real collection.
  • Old campaign pages and attachments. Send them to the closest live page, not the homepage. Mass redirects to the homepage are a common reason for traffic drops after a move.
  • Changed slugs. If the client wants cleaner product handles on Shopify, map those rows by SKU from the product export rather than by URL.

5. Watch Shopify's redirect rules

From Shopify's URL redirect docs, three things trip people up:

  1. A redirect only fires if the old path is broken on Shopify. If something now lives at that path, the redirect is ignored.
  2. Standard plans hold up to 100,000 redirects, which is plenty for most stores.
  3. Some paths can't be redirected at all, including anything starting with /cart, /apps or /shop. WooCommerce's /shop/ page is the usual casualty, so link to /collections/all from the navigation instead.

Import the CSV under Content → Menus → URL redirects → Import, then spot-check a few dozen rows by hand.

6. Test it after launch

Recrawl your original URL list against the live Shopify domain. Every row should return one 301 hop to a page that returns 200. Then submit Shopify's sitemap.xml in Search Console. Because the domain doesn't change, you don't use the Change of Address tool. Google's site-move guidance is to keep redirects for at least a year.

FAQ

Can I keep /product/ URLs on Shopify?
No. Shopify fixes the /products/ and /collections/ prefixes. Keep the slug and redirect the old path.

Should every unmapped URL go to the homepage?
No. Map each one to its closest equivalent. Homepage redirects for unrelated pages tend to be treated like soft 404s.

When do I import the redirects?
Prepare and test them on the unpublished store, then import them before you switch the domain, so they work from the first request.

If you'd rather hand the whole move to a team that does this every month, that's what our Shopify migration service covers, from the URL audit to post-launch checks.
