title: Fast Isn't Free
description:
A team picks a workflow tool. It runs well in testing, so they ship it.

A year later, traffic is up. The bill is up even more.

Nobody planned for that, because nobody asked the right question at the start. Not "how fast is it?" but "what will it cost when we're ten times bigger?"

Turn speed into daily volume

Throughput numbers are usually quoted per second, which makes them hard to feel. A quick conversion helps: multiply transactions per second by 86,400, the number of seconds in a day.

  • 1,000 per second is about 86 million a day
  • 10,000 per second is about 864 million a day

Now compare that with what you really expect. A lot of teams find they need far less than they feared. Others find they need a lot more than they planned for. Either way, you can't judge a tool until you know your own number.

Watch how the cost grows

A tool can be fine at small volume and painful at large volume. Here's an illustration. Spending $20,000 a year for a few thousand transactions per second might be reasonable. If handling a bigger load pushed that to $200,000, the math changes. Those are example figures, not anyone's price list, but the shape is real: what matters is whether cost rises in step with traffic or faster.

Simple workflows that run at low volume can live happily with a modest setup. Complex, high-volume ones can't. And a setup that's fast but very expensive tends to be dropped once the bill gets attention.

When latency is the whole point

Some use cases don't give you time to wait. Payment processing, IoT data pipelines and AI-driven workflows are all situations where slow responses or low throughput cause real problems for users. If yours looks like that, test under load before you commit, not after.

What to ask before you choose

  • How many transactions per second can one instance sustain, and what did that test look like?
  • What happens when you need more? Do you add instances, and how does the price change?
  • Does the number come from a workflow like yours, or a simple one-step example?
  • What does it cost at your expected volume, and at ten times that?

Those four questions tell you more than any single benchmark.

For reference, Unmeshed reports up to 10,000 transactions per second on a single instance, which works out to nearly a billion a day, and says larger loads are handled by adding instances to the cluster. As with any vendor's numbers, test it against your own workflows. You can try Unmeshed and see how it behaves with yours.

title: JPEG vs WebP vs AVIF: A Practical Guide to Image Formats in 2026
description:
If you've ever stared at a Lighthouse report and wondered why your "Performance" score refuses to move, the answer is usually sitting right in front of you: the images. On a typical content-heavy page, images are often the heaviest assets on the page, and the single biggest lever you have is choosing the right format and the right compression settings.

Here's a practical, no-fluff guide to the three formats that matter in 2026 — JPEG, WebP, and AVIF — and how to actually use them.

What each format is actually good at

JPEG — the universal workhorse

JPEG has been around since 1992, and every browser made in the last quarter century supports it. It's a lossy format designed for photographs: it throws away subtle detail the human eye is unlikely to notice in order to shrink the file.

  • Best for: photos, hero images, and anything where you need a guaranteed fallback.
  • Strengths: universal support, simple, predictable.
  • Weaknesses: no transparency, and at small file sizes you start seeing blocky compression artifacts.

WebP — the modern default

WebP was introduced by Google and supports both lossy and lossless compression, plus transparency (alpha channel) and even animation. At a comparable visual quality, a lossy WebP is usually noticeably smaller than an equivalent JPEG.

  • Best for: the everyday format for most web images.
  • Strengths: good compression, transparency, very wide support.
  • Weaknesses: a tiny fraction of very old browsers still don't support it, so a fallback is prudent.

AVIF — the next-generation option

AVIF is based on the AV1 video codec and is the most efficient of the three. It handles both lossy and lossless, supports transparency, and does especially well with high-detail photos and even HDR content. At the same visual quality, AVIF files are often the smallest.

  • Best for: squeezing the most out of large photographic images and modern sites.
  • Strengths: excellent compression, modern feature set.
  • Weaknesses: encoding is slower, and support is newer than WebP — so you still want fallbacks.

Quick rule of thumb

Format Lossy / Lossless Transparency Typical use
JPEG Lossy No Universal fallback, photos
WebP Both Yes Default for most web images
AVIF Both Yes Best compression, modern browsers
PNG Lossless Yes Logos, screenshots, graphics

Notice I kept PNG in the table: for photos it's usually overkill, but for clean graphics, logos, and screenshots with sharp edges and text, a well-optimized PNG (or indexed-color PNG-8) is still the right tool.

How to use them in real markup

The cleanest pattern is the <picture> element, which lets the browser pick the first format it understands and falls back to JPEG if it understands none:

<picture>
  <source srcset="hero.avif" type="image/avif" />
  <source srcset="hero.webp" type="image/webp" />
  <img
    src="hero.jpg"
    alt="A mountain lake at sunrise"
    width="1600"
    height="900"
    loading="lazy"
  />
</picture>

The browser downloads only the first source it can decode, so you don't pay for the others. The plain <img> inside is what makes this work everywhere and keeps your alt text in one place.

Don't forget responsive sizes

Format is only half the battle. Serving a 3000px-wide hero to a phone on a cellular connection is wasteful no matter how well it's compressed. Use srcset to hand the browser appropriately sized options:

<img
  src="hero-800.jpg"
  srcset="hero-800.jpg 800w, hero-1200.jpg 1200w, hero-1600.jpg 1600w"
  sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
  alt="A mountain lake at sunrise"
  loading="lazy"
/>

Protect your LCP

For the single largest above-the-fold image (often the hero), a couple of small tweaks help the browser prioritize it:

<img src="hero.avif" alt="..." fetchpriority="high" />

And reserve space with width and height attributes so the layout doesn't shift while the image loads — that helps both performance and Cumulative Layout Shift.

Picking quality settings

Modern formats are forgiving, and most people over-estimate the quality they need. A sensible starting point:

  • JPEG: quality around 60–75
  • WebP: quality around 65–75
  • AVIF: quality around 45–55 (its scale behaves differently, lower numbers go further)

The right method is always the same: make a copy, try a few settings, and compare at 100% zoom. Push compression until you can just start to notice a difference, then back off one notch. The goal is the smallest file that still looks indistinguishable to a normal viewer — not the highest possible number.

A note on privacy

One detail people overlook: many online compressors upload your files to a server to process them, and some retain copies for a period. If you're handling confidential designs, client work, or personal photos, that's a real consideration. A browser-based compressor that runs entirely client-side (using WebAssembly) never uploads the file in the first place, which removes that class of risk entirely.

I've been building exactly this — Eltorin is a free image compressor that does all the processing locally in your browser with no uploads, no signup, and no artificial file-count or size quotas. It handles JPEG, PNG, WebP, and AVIF, and it's a handy way to experiment with the quality settings above without sending anything anywhere.

The takeaway

  1. Default to WebP, use AVIF for maximum savings on modern browsers, and keep a JPEG fallback.
  2. Use <picture> for format negotiation and srcset for responsive sizes.
  3. Reserve image dimensions, lazy-load below the fold, and mark your LCP image with fetchpriority="high".
  4. Tune quality by eye — the smallest file that looks identical is the winner.

Get the images right, and that stubborn performance score usually starts taking care of itself.

title: The 200 KB Trap in Browser Image Compression
description:
Three images. Three green “within limit” results. Zero files that met the upload rules I had written down.

The compressor was doing what it promised. My acceptance check was asking a different question.

For this experiment, I defined a hypothetical destination that accepts JPEG, exactly 600 × 800 pixels, at most 200,000 bytes. Then I ran three synthetic inputs through a browser compressor's “200 KB” preset and inspected the downloaded files with a separate image decoder.

Here is the result before we get to any code:

Downloaded result Encoded bytes Actual format Actual dimensions Meets that destination's rules?
Noisy PNG, compressed 179,501 PNG 199 × 265 No: wrong format and dimensions
Noisy JPEG, compressed 204,128 JPEG 600 × 800 No: 4,128 bytes too large
Small transparent PNG, unchanged 12,736 PNG 600 × 800 No: wrong format

This was a controlled acceptance test, not a story about a real application form rejecting a customer. The “200 KB” preset explicitly meant 200 × 1,024 = 204,800 bytes. It allowed proportional resizing, preserved PNG by default, and left an already-small input untouched. All three files satisfied that policy.

I maintain ToolKnit's browser image compressor, which is the tool used for this case study. That affiliation matters: this is an engineering explanation of its limits, not an independent product review. The small implementation below is a separate teaching example, not a copy of the production algorithm.

Actual tool output from synthetic fixtures. The table above uses independently parsed downloads rather than rounded UI values.

The useful lesson is that “make it smaller” and “make it acceptable” are different specifications. A quality slider cannot decide the second one for you.

Write the destination's rules before choosing an encoder

A file-size ceiling is one field in a larger contract:

const destination = {
  maxBytes: 200_000,
  mime: "image/jpeg",
  width: 600,
  height: 800,
  animation: "reject",
  transparency: "flatten-on-white-with-consent",
};

Some fields are machine-checkable. Others are product decisions. Flattening a transparent asset onto white changes its appearance; it is not a harmless technical default. A portrait that must remain 600 × 800 cannot quietly become 199 × 265 just because a smaller canvas produces fewer bytes.

Ask these questions before processing:

  1. Does the receiver require an exact format or merely an allowed set?
  2. Are width and height exact, maximums, or unconstrained?
  3. Is the limit per file, per archive, or for the whole request?
  4. Must transparency, animation, metadata or a particular color profile survive?
  5. What is allowed to change when those requirements conflict?

If the receiver says only “200 KB,” check its documentation or actual byte limit. 200,000 bytes and 204,800 bytes differ by 4,800 bytes. The second row in the table fits one and fails the other. Formatting a number as “199.3 KB” does not resolve that ambiguity.

Use the encoded Blob.size, which is measured in bytes. Do not compare the length of a base64 data URL, a rounded display string, or the original file's size.

Quality is an encoder input, not a byte budget

This looks plausible:

canvas.toBlob(onResult, "image/jpeg", 0.85);

But 0.85 means neither “keep 85% of the original bytes” nor “produce an image of a predictable size.” It is also not a portable perceptual-quality score across codecs and browsers.

I generated two 600 × 800 canvases: one with four flat rectangles, another with deterministic RGB noise. In the same browser, using the same JPEG quality parameter:

Synthetic input Dimensions JPEG quality argument Encoded bytes
Flat rectangles 600 × 800 0.85 7,221
RGB noise 600 × 800 0.85 344,122

The noise is deliberately difficult input, not a representative photo collection. This is evidence that the parameter does not enforce a budget; it is not a comparison of photo quality or a ranking of compressors.

There are two more API details worth making explicit:

  • toBlob() can return null through its callback. A completed callback is not necessarily a usable image.
  • An unsupported requested output format falls back to PNG. Naming the download result.jpg does not make those bytes JPEG.

My unsupported-type probe requested image/x-budget-lab-test; the returned blob was image/png. An encoder wrapper should reject that mismatch when the output type is a requirement.

PNG has another trap: the canvas quality argument is intended for formats with lossy compression. In this run, encoding the transparent PNG fixture at 0.1 and 0.9 produced 12,736 bytes each, with identical SHA-256 hashes. Moving that slider did nothing to this PNG. That exact hash equality is an observation from this browser, not a promise about every implementation.

A small bounded encoder that is allowed to say no

For a fixed-dimension JPEG destination, I prefer a small, explicit policy over silently shrinking the image until some file emerges.

The following function:

  • accepts an already-decoded canvas;
  • explicitly composites it onto white;
  • preserves the canvas dimensions;
  • tries six decreasing JPEG quality settings;
  • returns a success only after checking the actual encoded bytes;
  • returns a refusal when none of those candidates fits.

The white background must be an accepted product choice. This function is not appropriate when alpha or animation must be preserved. Its pixel ceiling is a scope limit for the example, not a guarantee that every device can safely process that input.

It preserves the dimensions you give it; it does not crop an arbitrary source into a 600 × 800 portrait. Prepare the required canvas dimensions first, using a crop or padding policy the destination permits.

// Teaching example: a fixed-dimension, explicitly white-matted JPEG policy.
// It is NOT ToolKnit's production implementation or an optimal codec search.
function encode(canvas, type, quality) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    canvas.toBlob(blob => {
      if (!blob || blob.size === 0) {
        reject(new Error('Encoder returned no bytes'));
      } else if (blob.type !== type) {
        reject(new Error(`Requested ${type}; received ${blob.type}`));
      } else {
        resolve(blob);
      }
    }, type, quality);
  });
}

async function fitJpeg(canvas, maxBytes, {
  qualities = [0.92, 0.82, 0.72, 0.62, 0.52, 0.42],
  signal,
} = {}) {
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(maxBytes) || maxBytes <= 0) {
    throw new RangeError('maxBytes must be a positive safe integer');
  }
  // Copy before awaiting: caller mutation must not change this run's policy.
  const candidates = Array.isArray(qualities) ? [...qualities] : [];
  if (candidates.length < 1 || candidates.length > 12 ||
      candidates.some(q => !Number.isFinite(q) || q < 0 || q > 1) ||
      candidates.some((q, i) => i > 0 && q >= candidates[i - 1])) {
    throw new RangeError('Use 1–12 strictly decreasing quality values in [0,1]');
  }
  const {width, height} = canvas;
  if (!width || !height || width * height > 4_000_000) {
    throw new RangeError('This example permits 1–4,000,000 pixels');
  }
  signal?.throwIfAborted();
  const opaque = document.createElement('canvas');
  opaque.width = width;
  opaque.height = height;
  const attempts = [];
  try {
    const ctx = opaque.getContext('2d');
    if (!ctx) throw new Error('Canvas 2D unavailable');
    ctx.fillStyle = '#fff';
    ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height);
    ctx.drawImage(canvas, 0, 0);
    for (const quality of candidates) {
      signal?.throwIfAborted();
      const blob = await encode(opaque, 'image/jpeg', quality);
      // toBlob itself is not abortable; do not publish a stale result.
      signal?.throwIfAborted();
      attempts.push({quality, bytes: blob.size});
      if (blob.size <= maxBytes) {
        return {ok: true, blob, width, height, quality, attempts};
      }
    }
    return {ok: false, reason: 'No candidate in this policy fits', attempts};
  } finally {
    opaque.width = opaque.height = 1;
  }
}

For the hypothetical destination at the start, pass destination.maxBytes, which is 200_000. Changing the displayed unit should never silently change that integer.

The distinction in the failure message is intentional: “No candidate in this policy fits”, not “This image cannot be compressed any further.” A lower quality value, different codec, different dimensions or different encoder might fit. Those are changes to the policy, and some may violate the destination's requirements.

The function returns the first fitting value in the ordered ladder. It does not claim to find an optimal quality setting. Binary search can reduce the number of probes under suitable assumptions, but the canvas API does not define a portable byte-size function that guarantees your preferred search strategy finds the global best candidate. Whatever search you use, verify the blob you actually return.

What happened when I ran it

Using the explicit budget 204_800 and the six settings shown above:

Fixture Preserved dimensions Outcome Bytes
Flat rectangles 600 × 800 Fits at 0.92 7,778
Transparent rectangles, white matte 600 × 800 Fits at 0.92 7,857
RGB noise 600 × 800 Fits at 0.52 190,797
Larger RGB noise 1200 × 1600 Refused after all six candidates Smallest attempted: 648,881

The large-noise refusal is a valid result. Returning a smaller canvas would produce a different kind of success, one the caller has not authorized here.

These tables use different source representations and search policies: the production JPEG path started with an already-encoded JPEG, while the teaching function started with a canvas. Their byte counts do not establish which compressor is better.

Likewise, 0.52 passing a byte check does not prove the result is visually acceptable. Fine text, facial detail and gradients still need review in the actual destination. Keep the source so that a rejected result can be regenerated from the original rather than recompressed repeatedly.

Check the exported artifact, not just the function's return value

For blobs produced by your own encoder, a useful second check is to decode the output and inspect what it actually contains:

async function checkGeneratedImage(blob, rule) {
  const problems = [];
  if (blob.type !== rule.mime) problems.push("output MIME differs");
  if (blob.size > rule.maxBytes) problems.push("byte limit exceeded");

  const bitmap = await createImageBitmap(blob);
  try {
    if (bitmap.width !== rule.width || bitmap.height !== rule.height) {
      problems.push("pixel dimensions differ");
    }
  } finally {
    bitmap.close();
  }
  return problems;
}

This is a convenience check for an application's generated output, not a security validator for arbitrary user uploads. A client-supplied MIME label or extension is untrusted. A server must independently enforce its byte limits, recognize and safely decode allowed formats, validate dimensions and apply its own resource limits. Client-side checks improve the experience; they do not replace that boundary.

For this article, I downloaded the generated files and opened them with Pillow, separately from the browser. The verification compared format, dimensions, byte count and SHA-256, then checked alpha and selected pixels. It caught a useful visual distinction: direct JPEG encoding of the transparent canvas produced a black corner in this browser, while the explicit white-matte path produced (255, 255, 255).

I also downloaded the compressor's ZIP. Its three members were byte-identical to the individual downloads, but the archive was 396,759 bytes. Every member being below 204,800 bytes does not make the archive below 204,800 bytes. A per-file budget and an attachment budget need separate checks.

Four boundaries that deserve their own decisions

Animation. Drawing a decoded image onto one canvas gives you a bitmap, not a frame-preserving animation pipeline. Decide whether to reject animation, retain the original or use a suitable animated codec pipeline. Do not silently discard the other frames and call that a successful compression.

Orientation and metadata. Define dimensions in the orientation the receiver uses. createImageBitmap() defaults to using image orientation metadata when present. Re-encoding also should not be treated as a general guarantee that all metadata or color information was preserved—or removed. Test the fields your workflow actually depends on.

Memory. A 6000 × 4000 RGBA bitmap contains 96,000,000 bytes of pixel data before additional buffers. Compressed file size is a poor proxy for that cost. Put limits on input bytes, dimensions, decoded work and retained outputs; process batches with bounded concurrency. This example starts after decoding, so it does not solve admission control for a malicious or enormous source file.

Stale work. Someone can choose a new file while the previous encode is still running. The abort checks above prevent an aborted result from being returned, but do not cancel an in-progress toBlob() operation. The caller must abort the old run and ensure only the current run can update the UI. “I clicked Cancel” and “the encoder stopped consuming resources immediately” are different claims.

If the page processes files locally, describe that claim narrowly. Local file processing does not imply that the website makes no network requests; loading assets and ordinary analytics are separate concerns. It also does not make a page appropriate for every confidential workflow.

Reproduce the interesting part

These are synthetic fixtures, so the central experiment does not require anyone's private photos. Run the encode and fitJpeg definitions above in a browser module, then add this fixture generator and probe:

Deterministic fixtures and reproduction code 
// Deterministic fixtures: deliberate test inputs, not customer photos.
function fixture(kind) {
  const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
  canvas.width = kind === 'large-noise' ? 1200 : 600;
  canvas.height = kind === 'large-noise' ? 1600 : 800;
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('Canvas 2D unavailable');
  if (kind === 'noise' || kind === 'large-noise') {
    const pixels = ctx.createImageData(canvas.width, canvas.height);
    let seed = 0x12345678;
    for (let i = 0; i < pixels.data.length; i += 4) {
      for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) {
        seed = (Math.imul(seed, 1664525) + 1013904223) >>> 0;
        pixels.data[i + c] = seed >>> 24;
      }
      pixels.data[i + 3] = 255;
    }
    ctx.putImageData(pixels, 0, 0);
  } else if (kind === 'alpha') {
    ctx.fillStyle = 'rgba(22,120,200,0.5)';
    ctx.fillRect(100, 100, 400, 600);
    ctx.clearRect(200, 200, 200, 400);
  } else if (kind === 'flat') {
    ctx.fillStyle = '#fff';
    ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 600, 800);
    ['#182434', '#4276ad', '#d58456', '#94b5a2'].forEach((color, i) => {
      ctx.fillStyle = color;
      ctx.fillRect(40, 40 + i * 180, 520, 120);
    });
  } else {
    throw new Error('Unknown fixture');
  }
  return canvas;
}

const measurements = [];
for (const kind of ["flat", "alpha", "noise", "large-noise"]) {
  const canvas = fixture(kind);
  const baseline = await encode(canvas, "image/jpeg", 0.85);
  const fitted = await fitJpeg(canvas, 204_800);
  measurements.push({
    fixture: kind,
    width: canvas.width,
    height: canvas.height,
    baselineBytes: baseline.size,
    fits: fitted.ok,
    quality: fitted.ok ? fitted.quality : null,
    resultBytes: fitted.ok ? fitted.blob.size : null,
  });
  console.log(kind, fitted.attempts);
  canvas.width = canvas.height = 1;
}
console.table(measurements);

The measurements here were collected on October 30, 2026, in a Windows Chromium-based browser reporting Chrome 156. Another browser or encoder version can produce different bytes. Reproduce the invariants—dimensions retained, returned type checked, successful blobs within the byte cap, explicit failure—not a claim that everyone should get the same JPEG hash.

The local harness also exercised invalid budgets, invalid quality ladders, a pre-aborted run, a one-byte refusal and unsupported-format fallback. Those checks supplement the downloaded-file verification; a green test count by itself would not establish visual quality, cross-browser compatibility or safe handling of arbitrary inputs.

The UI should report what it actually proved

Instead of showing one ambiguous “Success” badge, report the constraints independently:

Bytes:       179,501 / 200,000       PASS
Format:      PNG / JPEG required    FAIL
Dimensions:  199×265 / 600×800       FAIL
Decision:    Do not submit this file

Then offer choices that match the failed rule: select a permitted format, obtain a suitable original, accept a resize only if allowed, or explain that the current policy has no fitting candidate. Do not keep lowering quality when the failing field is the format.

The most useful compression result is not always the smallest file. It is a file whose properties match the destination—and a clear refusal when they do not.

Which constraint has caused the most surprises in your upload flow: bytes, dimensions, alpha, or the receiver's definition of “KB”?

Disclosure: I maintain ToolKnit. AI tools produced the draft, example code and cover illustration. The numerical results came from actual browser runs and separately parsed downloads; the cover is not experimental evidence.

title: 5 Node.js Background Job Queue Patterns: Delayed Retry Beyond Seven Days
description:
Short answer: for a background job queue, keep the long date in your database, wake a small scheduler on a short interval, and enqueue only the delayed retry work that is due. A queue's seven-day ceiling then becomes a dispatch detail instead of a business deadline. For a marketplace renewal reminder, that separation is the difference between “send on the contract date” and “hope a broker still remembers it.”

1. Pick the clock that owns the promise

Start with a decision table. The right row depends on the delivery guarantee you can actually explain to a buyer or seller.

Pattern Pick this when Guarantee you can defend Main cost
Queue delay only The reminder is due within the queue's supported window Best effort inside that window A long delay may be rejected or capped
Database ledger plus cron scan Dates can be weeks or months away At-least-once dispatch after a due record is visible You operate a scanner and an index
Partitioned time buckets You have very high volume and predictable dates At-least-once dispatch with bounded scan work More moving parts and rebalancing
Managed workflow timer You need durable timers and accept a platform dependency Provider-defined retry and timer semantics Less control over portability

For a marketplace, I pick the ledger plus cron scan when a renewal deadline is a contractual date. The queue still handles fast retries, but it no longer pretends to be a calendar.

2. What should a Node.js scheduler record before it enqueues?

Record intent before transport. A row such as renewal_id, due_at, state, attempts, and an idempotency key is enough to begin. Put a unique constraint on the business event, not on a generated timestamp. Two scheduler processes may observe the same row; only one should win the claim, and a second delivery must be harmless.

The flow is easier to reason about as a sentence: database is the calendar; cron is the doorbell; the queue is the conveyor belt; the worker is the hand that sends the reminder. If the doorbell rings twice, the hand still sends once.

Dates move.

That is why the ledger, rather than an in-memory timer, owns the promise. A renewal can be postponed, cancelled, or moved to a new seller account while the scheduler is asleep; the next scan reads the current truth.

Here is a deliberately small claim-and-enqueue loop. The SQL shape is illustrative; use the transaction and locking syntax your database supports.

type Renewal = {
  id: string;
  dueAt: Date;
  dispatchKey: string;
};

async function dispatchDueRenewals(now: Date, limit = 200): Promise<void> {
  const renewals: Renewal[] = await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const rows = await tx.query<Renewal>(
      `UPDATE renewal_reminders
       SET state = 'claimed', claimed_at = $1
       WHERE id IN (
         SELECT id FROM renewal_reminders
         WHERE state = 'pending' AND due_at <= $1
         ORDER BY due_at
         FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
         LIMIT $2
       )
       RETURNING id, due_at AS "dueAt", dispatch_key AS "dispatchKey"`,
      [now, limit]
    );
    return rows;
  });

  for (const renewal of renewals) {
    await queue.publish({
      type: 'renewal-reminder',
      renewalId: renewal.id,
      idempotencyKey: renewal.dispatchKey,
    });
  }
}

The claim is short-lived, so a crashed process leaves a visible recovery path: a reaper can return stale claimed rows to pending. That is an operational policy, not a hidden workaround. Set the cron interval from the promise you made. A five-minute scan cannot honestly promise second-level delivery.

3. How do delayed retry limits, cron enqueue, and Node.js failure modes fit together?

Separate two clocks: the business clock (due_at) and the retry clock (next_attempt_at). A failed send may retry in 30 seconds, then 5 minutes, while the renewal date may be 45 days away. Never encode that 45-day wait as one broker message when the broker documents a seven-day maximum for delayed messages.

The common failure is a “sleep until due” process. Deploys interrupt it. Autoscaling multiplies it. A daylight-saving transition can shift a local timestamp. Store UTC, convert only at the presentation edge, and test a date around both a month boundary and a DST change.

Keep the worker boring. It checks the idempotency key, loads the current renewal state, sends only when the reminder is still valid, and records the provider response. A cancellation after enqueue should suppress the send; a duplicate enqueue should produce one effect. Exactly-once delivery is a seductive label here—at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent effect is the tractable contract.

4. Which option is observable enough for a delivery guarantee?

Measure the path, not just the queue. Emit due_lag_seconds when a row is claimed, enqueue_lag_seconds when it reaches the queue, and send_lag_seconds when the worker finishes. Alert on age of the oldest pending row, claim-to-publish failures, and the count of stale claims. A queue depth of zero can look healthy while the database ledger is quietly aging.

Use a trace or correlation id that survives the cron process, publish call, and worker. Log the renewal id and dispatch key, but redact customer content. On-call needs one query that answers: was the reminder never claimed, claimed but not published, retried, or sent and later cancelled?

Make the dashboard tell the same story as the ledger. A useful panel shows the number of rows by state (pending, claimed, sent, cancelled) and a percentile for due lag. During an incident, compare those values with queue publish acknowledgements. If claimed rises while acknowledgements flatten, the fault is between the transaction and the broker. If acknowledgements rise but sent does not, inspect workers and provider responses. This sequence sounds obvious on paper, yet it is the difference between a focused rollback and restarting every consumer in the marketplace.

Three real tools illustrate different boundaries without deciding for you. Vercel Cron Jobs is an HTTP-triggered scheduler, so you still own the ledger and idempotency. Inngest documents durable function execution and retries, but adopting it makes its execution model part of your portability decision. BullMQ offers Node.js queue primitives, while a long delay still has to fit the deployment and storage assumptions behind that queue. Your guarantee comes from the whole path, not the logo on one component.

5. The catch: when should you choose something else?

The main limitation is the scan interval: this design is not suitable when a legal notice must arrive within a few seconds and a five-minute scan is unacceptable; use a timer system with a documented latency target and keep a durable audit record anyway. It is also a poor fit for millions of dates that change every second, where a bucketed scheduler or specialized workflow engine may reduce database contention.

The ledger adds schema, indexes, reaping, and an on-call page. That is the trade-off. I'm not sure a hosted timer gives you the portability your team wants, and your mileage will vary with its replay and cancellation semantics. Write those semantics into a test before migrating.

For the marketplace renewal case, the decision rule is simple: store the deadline durably, scan at a stated cadence, enqueue within the transport window, and make the worker idempotent. The seven-day limit is then a design input, not a surprise in production.

References

  • https://vercel.com/docs/cron-jobs
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date

Further reading

  • https://vercel.com/docs/cron-jobs
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/

title: Node.js SMS OTP 2FA for Property Reports — A Reliable Identity Handoff
description:
Short answer: To implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in Node.js, look up the user, send the OTP through the SMS API, persist its timestamp and attempt state, and validate it server-side before authorizing a property report.

A reliable OTP flow is a small state machine, not a single SMS call. For a property-management login that unlocks a generated report, keep the identity lookup and the SMS send on the same authenticated API boundary, persist the OTP attempt and its timestamp, and accept the code only inside a short server-side window.

The decision rule is straightforward: choose a combined identity-and-SMS surface when reducing credential handoffs matters more than having separate specialists; choose Auth0 or Clerk with Twilio Verify when their independent policy, channel, or operational controls are a hard requirement. The trade is one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Say that plainly before discussing convenience.

That is the whole decision.

What must remain true across the handoff?

The report attachment is downstream of authentication, so a successful SMS response is not proof that the user is allowed to read every report. The application still owns authorization for the property and report. The useful invariants are narrower:

  • The identity record selected for the login is the identity that receives the code.
  • The OTP attempt has a server timestamp, an expiration decision, and a bounded retry count.
  • A code is accepted once, only for the intended login attempt, and only after server-side validation.
  • Resending creates a new delivery attempt without turning an untrusted client into an unlimited SMS sender.

I initially treated delivery as the main reliability problem. The more dangerous failure boundary is earlier: if the identity lookup and the phone-number decision are separate, a perfectly delivered code can still be attached to the wrong account. Delivery reliability begins with a stable recipient.

For a Node.js service, the application can use one bearer key and one base URL for both capability groups. The same boundary is useful even when the report generator runs asynchronously: authenticate first, authorize the property, then create or fetch the report and send its attachment. Do not make the attachment path responsible for deciding who the user is.

How can I implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in a Node.js API?

The critical path has five transitions: identify the user, create an OTP attempt, deliver it, validate it, and authorize the report. Store the generated OTP with its timestamp in the application database; do not use the SMS provider as your session store. The preset time window belongs to the service policy, and the service must reject an old or already-consumed attempt even if the SMS arrived late.

The following Python example shows the Node.js API seam explicitly. It uses the same key and base URL for the identity lookup and the OTP request, checks status codes, and backs off on rate limits. The exact expiration duration and attempt schema are application policy, so they remain in the database layer rather than being guessed here.

import os
import time
import uuid
from typing import Any

import requests

BASE_URL = os.environ["BACKEND_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}


def request_with_backoff(method: str, path: str, **kwargs: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    headers = {**HEADERS, **kwargs.pop("headers", {})}
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            method,
            f"{BASE_URL}{path}",
            headers=headers,
            timeout=10,
            **kwargs,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("SMS API rate limit did not clear after retries")


def start_login(email: str, phone_number: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    identity = request_with_backoff(
        "GET",
        "/auth/user/get_by_email",
        params={"email": email},
    )
    user_id = identity["user_id"]
    return request_with_backoff(
        "POST",
        "/sms/otp",
        json={
            "phone_number": phone_number,
            "user_id": user_id,
            "idempotency_key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        },
    )

That code deliberately stops before report authorization. The application should save the returned OTP attempt identifier, its creation time, and its consumed state. On a missing message, the retry path is POST /v1/sms/resend/{id}; apply the same account, IP, device, and attempt limits to resend as to the initial request. A successful SMS response is a delivery request, not a completed second factor.

One implementation detail deserves more attention than it usually gets: retries. A network timeout after the provider accepted the request is ambiguous. A client-supplied idempotency key prevents the retry from becoming a second OTP attempt when the write operation supports that convention. It also gives the database a correlation value for the login attempt. Never solve a timeout by blindly sending another code.

The code is the easy part.

Which stack fits the reliability boundary?

The options are different shapes, so a feature-count comparison is misleading. This table compares the seam that matters for this workflow.

Option Identity-to-message boundary Main strength Boundary or cost in this design
Combined REST surface One key and base URL connect the identity lookup to SMS OTP Less credential and glue management between the two calls One vendor becomes a shared dependency and an outage surface; business-layer fraud controls still belong in the application
Auth0 + Twilio Verify Auth0 manages identity while Twilio Verify handles verification Separate specialists and mature independent product surfaces Two signups and two credential sets; the application owns the handoff, correlation, and failure policy
Clerk + Twilio Verify Clerk supplies the user/session side while Twilio supplies verification A hosted identity experience paired with a dedicated verification service Again, two providers and glue code; account linking and recipient ownership need explicit tests
Twilio Verify alone Verification is the center of the flow Direct focus on phone verification It does not replace the application’s property authorization or report ownership model

Auth0 and Clerk are reasonable choices when their identity lifecycle is already the system of record. Twilio Verify is reasonable when phone verification is an independently governed service. The combined route is a better fit when the team values a single REST contract and one credential boundary for the identity-to-message handoff, and accepts the concentration risk.

The comparison also exposes what this article does not promise. SMS remains a fallible delivery channel. There are no webhook events in these namespaces; events are pull-based, so real-time delivery orchestration is limited. Geographic fraud fences and per-country spend breakers must be built in the business layer. A retry route cannot repair a blocked destination, a compromised phone, or an attacker rotating numbers.

Infrai's relevant advantage is the single key and plain REST boundary: the identity store and SMS sender can share one credential and one base URL, so the handoff does not require a second vendor credential. That is useful for this workflow, but it is not a universal recommendation.

Not suitable? Choose Auth0 or Clerk with Twilio Verify when provider independence, a specialist verification policy, or an existing identity system matters more than the smaller credential surface. The limitation is concentration risk: one combined provider can make the integration simpler while making that provider a larger dependency.

What should the database and abuse controls record?

At minimum, an OTP-attempt row needs the user identifier, a delivery identifier, a timestamp, an expiration decision, a consumed marker, and a bounded failure count. Hashing the submitted code before storage is a sensible local control, but the important invariant is that validation is server-side and tied to the login attempt, not to an email address supplied again by the browser.

Rate-limit at several boundaries: account, source address, device signal, destination number, and resend history. Add anti-fraud checks before spending an SMS attempt. A single global counter is easy to bypass and can lock out an entire tenant; a single per-number counter misses distributed abuse. The policy should also distinguish a wrong code from an expired attempt, because the two signals lead to different user and security responses.

Keep the report workflow separate. After the OTP is accepted, check the authenticated user’s property permissions, generate the report, and send it as an email attachment. There is no hosted email OTP fallback here, so an email-code fallback would be an application-owned feature. There is also no SMTP relay, no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel to silently substitute when SMS is unavailable.

The longer failure chain is worth writing down because it is where a plausible implementation becomes an unsafe one. A user enters an email address, the service retrieves an identity, and the service chooses a phone number; that choice must come from the trusted identity record or an explicitly authorized profile change, not from a second browser field that happens to match the account. The OTP request then gets a server-owned attempt identifier. The database records when it was created, how many validation failures have occurred, whether it has been consumed, and which user and login context it belongs to. If the first request times out, the retry uses the same idempotency value where the write contract supports it. If the message is delayed, the validator checks the timestamp rather than trusting arrival order. If the user gets a new code, the old attempt must not remain a parallel path to success. After validation, the session still needs a property authorization check, because a valid second factor proves control of a phone, not ownership of every building or report visible in the application. Finally, the email attachment step must inherit the authorized report identifier, not accept an arbitrary report path from the client. Each boundary has a different failure response, which is why one generic “OTP succeeded” boolean is too coarse for an audit trail.

Scheduled email has no cancellation route in the stated surface, while SMS does have POST /v1/sms/cancel/{id}. That difference is operationally important: do not design a universal cancellation abstraction that implies both channels can be revoked. An architecture record should name the narrower guarantee instead.

Rejected option: two providers by default

The rejected default is to start with Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify simply because each name is familiar. That stack is valid, and sometimes preferable, but it adds two signups, two credential sets, a user-to-recipient mapping, retry correlation, and a policy for disagreements between identity status and verification status. None of those are impossible; they are just application work that must be tested around the exact failure boundaries.

A combined surface does not remove those tests. It moves the seam closer to the API boundary. For a property report, I would still test a delayed SMS, a duplicate submit, an expired code, a resend after a timeout, a user with several properties, and a successful OTP followed by a failed property authorization. The last case is the one that prevents authentication from being mistaken for authorization.

The decision is therefore conditional. Use the one-key handoff when a plain REST integration and a smaller credential surface are the priority. Use the split stack when provider independence or a specialist verification policy outweighs the glue code. In both cases, preserve the same local OTP state machine and the same property-level authorization check.

References

  • Auth0 documentation
  • Clerk documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • RFC 7489: DMARC

title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon Web Services (AWS)
description:
Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Exploring how cloud infrastructure works, how Amazon EC2 provides computing resources, and why businesses are adopting IaaS.
Written by: Ngombe Emmanuel Puwakeh
Cloud Computing | Academic Article

*Introduction
*Technology has changed the way individuals and organizations store information, develop applications, and manage their computing resources. In the past, businesses that wanted to operate their own digital systems often had to purchase physical servers, networking equipment, storage devices, and other hardware. They also needed dedicated spaces and technical personnel to install, maintain, and manage these resources.
Although this traditional approach provided organizations with control over their infrastructure, it also came with significant costs and maintenance responsibilities. As businesses expanded, managing these resources became increasingly difficult, especially when their computing requirements changed.
Cloud computing emerged as an alternative to this approach. Instead of purchasing and maintaining all their computing equipment, organizations can access computing resources through the internet whenever they need them.
One of the major service models that makes this possible is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).
This article explores the meaning of IaaS, how it works, its major components, and its importance in modern computing. It also examines Amazon Web Services (AWS), particularly Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), as a practical example of how IaaS is implemented.

*1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
*Infrastructure as a Service, commonly known as IaaS, is a cloud computing model that provides users with access to computing resources such as virtual machines, storage, and networking over the internet.
Rather than buying physical servers and other infrastructure equipment, users rent these resources from a cloud service provider. The provider manages the physical infrastructure, while customers configure and manage the virtual resources required to run their applications.
In simple terms, IaaS allows an individual or organization to rent computing infrastructure instead of owning it.
For example, a company that wants to host a website does not necessarily need to purchase a physical server. It can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider, install the required software, and make its website accessible to users through the internet.
IaaS is particularly useful because it gives organizations flexibility. They can increase or decrease their computing resources depending on their needs without having to purchase additional physical equipment.

*2. How Does IaaS Work?
*IaaS works mainly through virtualization technology.
Virtualization allows a physical computer or server to be divided into multiple virtual computing environments. Each virtual environment operates independently and can have its own operating system, allocated memory, processing capacity, and storage.
Cloud service providers operate large data centers containing physical servers, storage devices, and networking equipment. Through virtualization, they make these resources available to customers as services.
The process generally involves the following steps:

  1. A user selects a cloud service provider.
  2. The user chooses the computing resources required, such as CPU, RAM, storage, and networking.
  3. The provider allocates the requested resources through its cloud infrastructure.
  4. The user configures the virtual environment and installs the required operating system or software.
  5. The user deploys applications and manages the resources through an online interface or application programming interface (API).
  6. The provider maintains the underlying physical infrastructure. This arrangement allows users to concentrate on their applications without having to manage the physical servers on which those applications operate.

****3. Major Components of IaaS

Infrastructure as a Service consists of several important components that work together to provide computing resources.

**3.1 Computing Resources
**Computing resources provide the processing power required to execute applications and perform tasks. They include central processing units (CPU), random access memory (RAM), and virtual machines.
A virtual machine behaves like a physical computer but operates within a virtualized environment. Users can select different configurations depending on the type of workload they intend to run.

**3.2 Storage
**Storage allows users to save application files, databases, documents, backups, and other information.
IaaS providers offer different storage options depending on the purpose. These may include block storage, file storage, and object storage.
For example, a business hosting an online application may require storage for its application files and customer information.

**3.3 Networking
**Networking enables virtual machines and other cloud resources to communicate with one another and with external users.
It includes virtual networks, IP addresses, firewalls, routing, and other networking services.
Proper network configuration helps organizations control access to their resources and establish secure connections between applications.

**3.4 Virtualization
**Virtualization is one of the technologies that makes IaaS possible. It allows providers to allocate physical computing resources to multiple virtual environments.
Through virtualization, customers can access computing resources without directly owning or managing the physical machines.

***4. Difference Between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
*
**IaaS is one of the three commonly discussed cloud computing service models. The other two are Platform as a Service (PaaS) and Software as a Service (SaaS).
Although they all provide services through the cloud, they differ in the level of control and management offered to users.
Service model Description Example

  • IaaS Provides virtual computing infrastructure, including servers, storage, and networking. Amazon EC2 PaaS Provides a managed environment for developing and deploying applications. Google App Engine
  • SaaS Provides ready-to-use software over the internet. Gmail The major difference is the responsibility of the user. With IaaS, users have greater control over their virtual infrastructure and are responsible for managing their operating systems and applications. With PaaS, the provider manages more of the underlying environment, allowing developers to concentrate mainly on application development. With SaaS, users simply access and use an existing software application without managing its underlying infrastructure.

****5. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS)

**5.1 Introduction to AWS
**Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a cloud computing platform operated by Amazon that provides a wide range of cloud-based services to individuals, businesses, and government organizations.
AWS offers services covering computing, storage, databases, networking, security, analytics, and other areas of information technology.
One of its major computing services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud, commonly called Amazon EC2.
Amazon EC2 is a good example of Infrastructure as a Service because it allows customers to create and manage virtual servers in the AWS cloud without purchasing or maintaining physical server hardware.

**5.2 What Is Amazon EC2?
**Amazon EC2 is a cloud computing service that provides resizable computing capacity through virtual servers known as instances.
An EC2 instance functions much like a physical computer. Users can select the operating system, processing capacity, memory, and other configurations required for their applications.
For example, a developer building a web application can launch an EC2 instance, install a web server such as Apache or Nginx, upload the application files, and configure the server to receive internet traffic.
This makes it possible to host applications without setting up a physical server.

**5.3 Major Features of Amazon EC2
**Amazon EC2 provides several features that make it useful for individuals and organizations.
Virtual Server Instances
EC2 allows users to launch virtual servers according to their computing requirements. Different instance types provide different combinations of CPU, memory, storage, and networking capacity.
Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)
An Amazon Machine Image is a template used to launch EC2 instances. It contains the information required to create an instance, including an operating system and, optionally, additional software.
Storage
Amazon EC2 works with Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS), which provides persistent block storage volumes that can be attached to instances.
This allows users to store application data and other information separately from the temporary storage provided by certain instance types.
Networking
EC2 instances can operate within Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). This allows users to create logically isolated virtual networks and control how their cloud resources communicate.
Security Groups
Security groups act as virtual firewalls for EC2 instances. They allow users to specify which network traffic is permitted to reach their instances and which traffic can leave them.
Scalability
Users can increase or decrease computing capacity depending on their workload. EC2 can also be integrated with AWS Auto Scaling to adjust the number of instances according to defined conditions.

**5.4 How Amazon EC2 Works in a Real-World Situation
**Consider a small company that wants to launch an online shopping website.
Traditionally, the company might need to purchase a physical server, install an operating system, configure networking, and employ technical personnel to maintain the equipment.
With Amazon EC2, the process can be different.
First, the company creates an AWS account and accesses the EC2 service through the AWS Management Console.
Next, it selects an Amazon Machine Image containing a suitable operating system, such as Linux.
The company then chooses an instance type based on the expected workload and launches the virtual server.
After launching the instance, the company configures its network settings and security groups to control incoming and outgoing traffic.
It can then connect to the instance, install the necessary software, configure a web server, and deploy its shopping website.
Once the website is running, customers can access it through the internet.
If website traffic increases, the company can add more computing capacity using suitable AWS scaling services. When traffic decreases, it can reduce the resources being used.
This example demonstrates how IaaS makes computing infrastructure more flexible and accessible.

6. Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution
Amazon EC2 provides several benefits to organizations that need flexible computing infrastructure.

**6.1 Reduced Initial Hardware Costs
**Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications. They can rent computing resources and avoid some of the initial costs associated with establishing a traditional data centre.

**6.2 Flexibility
**Users can choose the computing configurations that match their applications. They can also change their infrastructure as their requirements develop.

**6.3 Scalability
**EC2 allows organizations to adjust computing capacity as demand changes. This is useful for websites and applications that experience different levels of traffic at different times.

**6.4 Faster Deployment
**Creating a virtual server can be much faster than purchasing, installing, and configuring physical hardware. This helps developers and organizations deploy applications more quickly.

**6.5 Different Pricing Options
**AWS provides different purchasing options for EC2, including On-Demand Instances, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, and Spot Instances.
These options allow customers to choose a pricing arrangement based on their expected usage and workload requirements.

**7. Challenges and Limitations of IaaS

**Despite its benefits, IaaS also presents some challenges that organizations should consider before adopting it.

**7.1 Internet Dependency
**Cloud infrastructure is accessed through networks. Poor internet connectivity or network interruptions can affect users' ability to access their cloud resources.

7.2 Security Responsibilities
Although AWS manages the underlying physical infrastructure, customers are still responsible for securing important parts of their cloud environments.
For example, EC2 users must manage their operating system updates, application security, access permissions, and security group configurations.
Incorrect security configurations can expose applications and data to unauthorized access.

**7.3 Unexpected Costs
**IaaS can reduce the need for large hardware investments, but it does not mean that cloud computing is always inexpensive.
If organizations fail to monitor their usage, they may accumulate unnecessary charges from running instances, storage, data transfers, and other services.

**7.4 Technical Knowledge
**Managing an EC2 environment requires knowledge of operating systems, networking, security, and server administration.
Organizations without the necessary technical expertise may find it difficult to configure and maintain their cloud infrastructure properly.

**7.5 Dependence on a Cloud Provider
**Relying heavily on one cloud provider can make it difficult to move applications and data to another platform.
Differences in services, configurations, costs, and application architecture can make migration complicated.

8. Security and the AWS Shared Responsibility Model
Security is an important consideration when using Infrastructure as a Service.
AWS uses a Shared Responsibility Model to explain the security responsibilities of the cloud provider and its customers.
Under this model, AWS is responsible for security of the cloud, while customers are responsible for security in the cloud.
AWS manages the physical data centres, hardware, networking infrastructure, and virtualization layer.
Customers, on the other hand, are responsible for areas such as their guest operating systems, installed applications, data, access permissions, and security configurations.
For example, when a company launches an EC2 instance, AWS manages the underlying physical server, but the company must ensure that the operating system is updated and that its security groups are properly configured.
This arrangement is important because using a cloud provider does not automatically guarantee that every application and every piece of customer data is secure.

9. Practical Applications of IaaS
IaaS is used in different areas of information technology.
Some common applications include:
Website and Application Hosting: Organizations can use virtual servers to host websites, web applications, and backend services.
Software Development and Testing: Developers can create separate environments for testing applications without purchasing additional physical computers.
Data Storage and Backup: Businesses can use cloud storage services to store important files, application data, and backup copies.
Business Applications: Organizations can run internal systems, databases, and enterprise applications using cloud infrastructure.
Data Processing: Companies can rent computing resources to process large amounts of information and perform computational tasks.
These applications show that IaaS is not limited to large companies. Small businesses, developers, educational institutions, and individuals can also benefit from cloud infrastructure.

  1. Practical Application of IaaS

  1. Personal Observation: The Importance of IaaS to Small Businesses in Cameroon In my opinion, Infrastructure as a Service can be particularly useful to small businesses in Cameroon that want to expand their operations through technology. For example, a small business that sells clothes, electronics, or other products online may want to create an e-commerce website but may not have enough money to purchase and maintain its own physical server. Using a service such as Amazon EC2 would allow the business to rent computing resources instead of investing heavily in physical hardware. It could start with a small server configuration and increase its resources as the number of customers and website visitors grows. This would help the business manage its expenses while still having access to the computing infrastructure needed to operate online. Another advantage is that the business would not have to worry about maintaining the physical server equipment itself. AWS manages the underlying cloud infrastructure, while the business concentrates on managing its website, applications, and customer information. However, businesses must also consider challenges such as internet connectivity, electricity availability, security configuration, and the cost of cloud services. These factors are important when deciding whether cloud infrastructure is suitable for a particular business. Overall, I believe IaaS presents an opportunity for small businesses in Cameroon to access modern computing infrastructure without necessarily making large initial investments in physical equipment.

12. Conclusion
Infrastructure as a Service has become an important part of modern cloud computing because it provides individuals and organizations with access to computing resources without requiring them to own and maintain all the physical equipment.
The case study of Amazon Web Services, particularly Amazon EC2, demonstrates how this model works in practice. Through EC2, users can launch virtual servers, configure their computing environments, manage storage and networking, and adjust their resources according to their requirements.
However, adopting IaaS also requires proper planning. Organizations must understand their security responsibilities, monitor their cloud expenditure, and ensure that their infrastructure is configured correctly.
Overall, IaaS provides a flexible approach to managing computing infrastructure. As organizations continue to develop digital services and applications, cloud infrastructure remains an important option for meeting changing technology requirements.

title: Building QiLoom: Calendar Conversion Is a Domain Modeling Problem
description:
I’m building QiLoom, a free website for Gregorian and Chinese lunar calendar conversion, birthday lookup, zodiac lookup, completed age, and family milestones.

The interesting engineering problem isn’t the date picker. It’s deciding exactly what a date represents.

A scope note before the technical discussion: I’m not publishing a framework, hosting, or dependency inventory here. The useful part of this write-up is the domain model and the implementation questions it creates, not an invented stack tour.

A calendar date is not automatically a timestamp

A birthday is usually a civil date, not an instant.

That distinction matters in JavaScript. Moving a date through UTC serialization and local rendering can introduce a day shift that has nothing to do with the calculation the user requested.

For this kind of tool, I favor reasoning about year, month, and day as explicit components. Time zones should enter the model only when the operation actually requires them.

Lunar dates need more than three numbers

A Chinese lunar date needs calendar context, including whether the month is a leap month.

Conceptually, the input looks more like this:

type LunarDate = {
  year: number;
  month: number;
  day: number;
  isLeapMonth: boolean;
};

This is an illustrative model, not an extract from the production code.

The important point is that dropping isLeapMonth can discard information. A UI that hides that distinction can make an otherwise plausible calculation ambiguous.

Similar-looking calculations need separate contracts

Completed age, elapsed days, and a baby’s hundredth day are different operations.

Completed age depends on whether the birthday has occurred in the reference year. Date intervals require an explicit inclusion convention. A milestone calculation needs to explain how the birth date is counted.

I’d rather have small, separately testable domain functions than one generic helper with a growing collection of boolean flags.

Test the boundaries, not just the happy path

The test cases I care about include lunar new year boundaries, leap months, Gregorian leap days, month transitions, and birthdays close to the reference date.

Round-trip conversion checks are useful too, but they should complement comparison against trusted calendar references—not replace it.

Try QiLoom and tell me which assumptions the interface should expose more clearly. I’m especially interested in how other developers communicate calendar conventions without overwhelming the form.

title: Break it before you merge it: introducing litmus-lite
description:
Several years ago, we started LitmusChaos with a simple belief: chaos engineering is not just for Ops. Litmus has since grown into a CNCF incubating project, and many SRE and platform teams use it to put chaos to work on Kubernetes.

But one moment kept nagging us. You are about to open a pull request. You added a retry, a timeout, maybe a fallback. You think it works. The honest way to find out is to make the dependency slow or flaky and watch, but that usually means a cluster, a platform team, or a throwaway script nobody will ever run again. So most of us skip it, and production runs the test for us.

So we built the other end of the loop, at the developer's desk.

litmus-lite is chaos testing for developers and their agents.

It is one static binary. You describe a failure and what must stay true, it injects the failure, watches your service, and tells you which of your statements held. No cluster, no control plane, no account.

From a sentence to a verdict

In Cursor (or any MCP client), you just ask:

Add 800 ms of latency to the checkout API for 12 seconds and tell me whether it copes and how fast it recovers.

The agent writes a *.chaos.yaml next to your service, validates it, runs it, and answers in terms of the hypotheses it wrote. The important part: the test is the file. Commit it, review it, change a number, and run it again without the agent. Every MCP tool is just a CLI command you could have typed.

It fits how developers already work

  • Tests live in your repo. A scenario sits beside the service it tests and goes through code review like any other test.
  • It runs where your tests run. In a terminal or in CI, with -junit for your test reporter. The exit code is the verdict: 0 every hypothesis held, 3 the run finished and one did not. That is a finding about your service, not a tool error.
  • CI setup is one command. litmus-lite ci github writes a workflow that validates every scenario on every push.
  • It can reach into your code. For Go services, a small failpoint package lets you put hooks in your own code. They stay dark until a scenario arms them, so you can fail "the charge step" and not just "the network".
  • You stay in control. An agent cannot grant itself destructive permissions. Loopback targets only, PIDs you name, -yes for anything irreversible, and every fault is rolled back on exit or Ctrl-C.

A verdict you can trust

There is no "resilience: 73" here. You state what must hold, such as error_rate < 15% or recovery <= 5s, and the run reports which statements held. No data counts as a failure, and a service that never came back fails as "not recovered".

Every run also writes one self-contained HTML report that puts the fault next to its impact, so you can see the failure land and the service recover (or not):

A real red run: the sample service has no fallback, and the report says so.

Under the hood there is plenty to break: HTTP latency, errors and timeouts through a built-in proxy, failpoints, process pause and kill, docker pause, CPU and memory pressure, and disk fill. Add a load generator (VegaLoad, k6 or your own command) when you want to see what real traffic felt during the fault. And there is no telemetry: by default, nothing leaves your machine.

Try it in five minutes 

# Grab a release: https://github.com/litmuschaos/litmus-lite/releases
litmus-lite init     # connects Cursor (MCP server + rules); other MCP clients work too

Then ask your agent for a failure. The quick start walks you through one green run and one red run against a sample service. The red one ends with a line I like a lot:

Hypothesis charge survives its own outage failed: error_rate < 5% (observed 100.00%).

A test that can fail, and tells you why in plain words, is the whole point.

Where this goes next

This is a start, not a finish. Directions we are excited about (ideas, not promises):

  • Richer probes: request headers and bodies, JSON assertions, TCP probes.
  • Per-probe hypotheses and breakdowns in the report.
  • A published container image, so a scenario can also run as an in-cluster Job.
  • More faults, driven by what you ask for, including reaching apps running in VMs and path to the bigger experiments on your Kubernetes clusters via the OG LitmusChaos!

Come build it with us

litmus-lite is Apache-2.0 and developed in the open, and the best time to shape it is now:

  • Try it on your own service and tell us what broke, what confused you, and what you wished it did. Open an issue.
  • Add a fault or a hub template. Faults are plugins, so adding one barely touches the engine. See CONTRIBUTING.
  • Improve the docs, or share the prompt that made your agent do something clever.
  • Say hi in #litmus on Kubernetes Slack.

Start here:

  • Overview: litmuschaos.io/litmus-lite
  • Docs: litmuschaos.github.io/litmus-lite
  • Code and releases: github.com/litmuschaos/litmus-lite

Chaos engineering began as a way for teams to build confidence in production. We would love litmus-lite to help it start a little earlier, at the developer's desk, with a sentence and a file. Pip is waiting.

Uma Mukkara and Karthik Satchitanand, co-creators of LitmusChaos
