title: Failed Payments, Grace Periods and Automatic Access Revocation in Telegram Communities
description:
Suppose a subscriber's renewal payment fails at 10:00 UTC. Your bot removes them at 10:01. Two hours later, a payment retry succeeds, but the subscriber is still banned.

The payment retry succeeded, but the access workflow never restored the subscriber's ability to rejoin.

This walkthrough shows how to keep paid time separate from grace, set a fixed recovery deadline, and recover when removal conflicts with a later payment.

The scope is a custom bot managing access to a private Telegram community. The timeline is illustrative, and the Python function covers the access decision only. A working integration still needs billing, event processing, and Telegram delivery checks.

Give grace its own deadline

Keep payment status, entitlement, and observed membership separate. In particular, use different fields for paid time and temporary access:

Application field Meaning
paid_through End of the period granted by confirmed payment
grace_until End of a separately authorized recovery window
renewal_enabled Whether future automatic renewal is enabled
desired_membership Whether the access policy currently permits membership
observed_membership Last known membership state in Telegram

These are application fields, not a provider's universal schema. Preserve the payment and subscription references that explain each grant.

A failed renewal does not erase a period already purchased. Grace does not turn an unpaid period into a paid one.

Keep the evidence behind each deadline. Support should be able to distinguish purchased time, a recovery allowance, and a delayed removal without reconstructing them from one status flag.

Define one policy before writing handlers

Suppose Maya's paid period ends on December 1, 2026, at 10:00 UTC. Her renewal fails at that boundary.

The example community gives existing subscribers a 72-hour recovery window. This duration is an illustrative policy choice, not a Telegram default or a recommended duration for every community.

The policy is:

  • Grace applies to an eligible renewal after a previously paid period, not to an unpaid first purchase.
  • Its deadline is the previous paid-period end plus 72 hours.
  • A repeated failure or notification does not restart the clock.
  • Canceling renewal before the due date preserves paid time but does not create a recovery window for a renewal that was never due.
  • If grace has already been promised, turning renewal off does not silently shorten that promise.
  • Refunds, disputes, and moderation restrictions have their own explicit rules.

Record the grace decision against a stable renewal identifier, such as a provider invoice ID, with a uniqueness constraint and policy version. Schedule reconciliation at the renewal boundary even if no failure webhook has arrived: retrieve the billing state and evaluate the eligible renewal before removing access.

Do not calculate grace_until = webhook_received_at + 72 hours. Anchor it to the previous paid-period end. In this example, that same preauthorized window covers eligible renewals awaiting verification. Keep paid_through unchanged and distinguish unknown billing state from confirmed failure. Repeated events cannot restart the window. If verification remains unavailable, alert operators before the deadline; any outage exception needs separate authorization and a recorded end time. Never create new grace from an old invoice after a newer renewal has settled.

Two possible outcomes

Time, UTC Successful recovery No recovery
Dec 1, 10:00 Renewal fails; grace ends Dec 4, 10:00 Same
Dec 2, 10:00 Another failure; original deadline remains Same
Dec 3, 09:00 Payment settles the Dec 1–Jan 1 renewal period; grant is recorded once Still unpaid
Dec 4, 10:00 New paid period permits access; old removal task is obsolete Temporary entitlement ends; removal is due

This timeline uses calendar-month website billing with an unchanged billing anchor. Map the actual period covered by the settled invoice item to the access grant. Do not award a full new month from the retry time. Plan changes and prorations need their own mapping.

Separate collection retries from access grace

There are three independent retry mechanisms:

  1. Collection retry: the payment system tries to collect money again.
  2. Webhook retry: the sender attempts to deliver a notification again.
  3. Access-task retry: your worker attempts the Telegram operation again.

Only the first can result in a new payment. The other two must not charge the customer or grant duplicate paid time.

Stripe's retry documentation describes configurable collection behavior. Some failures require customer action or a new payment method. Do not promise another automatic attempt merely because the account is overdue.

Collection can continue after grace ends. Define the late-payment outcome before launch. Record the period a late payment settles, and restore current access only if that period or another valid grant covers the present time. A payment on January 5 for December 1–January 1 is historical settlement, not a reason to unban the subscriber. Compensation for interrupted access is a separate policy.

Explain that possibility to subscribers. If your offer instead promises no further collection after access ends, align the billing configuration with that promise.

Translate provider signals into access decisions

For an independent website subscription using Stripe, a compact mapping is:

Signal Application action
invoice.payment_failed Identify the affected renewal; evaluate grace eligibility
invoice.payment_action_required Direct the customer to complete the required payment action
invoice.paid Validate the applicable invoice and subscription state; record the corresponding grant once
Subscription update or termination Reconcile billing and cancellation policy; recompute entitlement

Stripe's subscription webhook guide explains these events and statuses. past_due does not guarantee another collection attempt. An active subscription alone is not proof that every outstanding invoice was paid. Avoid treating either status as your complete access model.

Cancellation also needs interpretation: period-end cancellation differs from immediate termination. Preserve your paid-grant history rather than replacing it with one cancellation flag.

For digital purchases inside Telegram bots or Mini Apps, Telegram requires Stars, using XTR. An external provider integration is not a substitute for that in-app requirement.

For bot subscriptions, use subscription_expiration_date from a confirmed SuccessfulPayment to map the paid deadline. Recurring Stars periods currently use 30 days, so do not copy the calendar dates above. BotSubscriptionUpdated includes states such as failed and canceled; a failure signal does not grant paid time.

Native paid channel subscription links are a separate mechanism. This custom grace policy does not configure Telegram's native subscription behavior.

Make the access decision testable

This Python 3.10+ function evaluates approved deadlines for one subscription. The caller must validate payment evidence and authorize grace first; this function makes no provider or Telegram requests.

from datetime import datetime

def access_state(
    *,
    now: datetime,
    paid_through: datetime | None,
    grace_until: datetime | None,
    blocked: bool = False,
) -> str:
    for value in (now, paid_through, grace_until):
        if value is not None and value.utcoffset() is None:
            raise ValueError("Use timezone-aware timestamps")

    if blocked:
        return "blocked"
    if paid_through is not None and now < paid_through:
        return "paid"
    if grace_until is not None and now < grace_until:
        return "grace"
    return "expired"

The caller supplies only grace that the policy has already authorized. For a subscriber with multiple subscriptions or other grants to the same community, evaluate all valid grants before removing access. An expired subscription must not override another current grant. Apply a community-wide moderation block separately.

At exactly grace_until, this function returns expired, unless paid time or a block produces a different result. Store timestamps as instants, use UTC in logs, and show the customer an unambiguous deadline with a timezone.

The policy deadline is not a guarantee of second-precise removal. Scheduler frequency, queues, and API failures introduce enforcement delay. Record that delay rather than quietly extending the entitlement date to match it.

Treat revocation as durable work

Track removal as pending, confirmed, or failed. Mark it confirmed only after checking the Telegram result.

When the deadline passes, recompute eligibility and write a removal task durably. Commit the decision and task together—for example, through a transactional outbox—so a crash cannot lose the action between them.

Use authenticated webhook input, durable event storage, and atomic uniqueness checks. Stripe documents duplicate events and unordered delivery. A late failure must not undo a later settled renewal. Deduplicating event IDs also does not replace deduplicating the business grant.

A removal task should carry a membership key, entitlement revision, reason, and decision time. The worker loads the latest state before acting and skips obsolete work.

That check reduces errors but does not close the whole race: payment can arrive between the database read and the Telegram request. Coordinate grant and removal operations for each user–community pair. After uncertain or concurrent results, reconcile actual membership against the latest entitlement. A database transaction cannot include Telegram in the same atomic commit.

banChatMember requires bot administrator rights. In supergroups and channels, re-entry requires unbanning, and the documented revoke_messages value is always true. Test its message-deletion behavior against your discussion archive. On recovery, unbanChatMember with only_if_banned=true avoids removing an existing member. Unbanning does not automatically rejoin someone.

Lift only a ban your billing workflow owns. A new payment must not reverse an independent moderation decision. Then offer re-entry through your controlled admission flow, checking current entitlement again.

If removal fails, retain the original deadline and mark enforcement as pending or failed. Retry transient failures with backoff; escalate missing permissions. After a timeout, check the result before assuming the action never happened.

Tell the subscriber what to do

A recovery notice should identify the failed renewal, the exact access deadline, and the required action. For Maya, it could say:

Your renewal payment was unsuccessful. Access remains available until December 4, 2026, at 10:00 UTC while you resolve it. Open billing settings to update your payment method or complete authentication. We will confirm when payment succeeds.

Do not promise a scheduled charge unless the billing system confirms one. Use the appropriate secure billing flow rather than collecting card details in chat.

Send notices for meaningful transitions: entering grace, approaching its deadline, confirmed recovery, and actual removal. Deduplicate them so repeated webhooks do not produce repeated warnings. Cancel obsolete reminders after recovery, and keep payment support reachable after community access ends.

Removal stops future membership under this workflow; it cannot recall copies of content already saved by a subscriber.

Test the failure paths

Use a payment test environment and a private test community with ordinary member accounts. These are proposed integration checks, not claimed deployment results.

Scenario Expected outcome
First purchase fails No paid grant or renewal grace
Renewal fails before paid time ends Existing paid access remains; grace uses the original period boundary
Same renewal fails again One grace decision; unchanged deadline
Failure notification is delayed or verification is unavailable Scheduled reconciliation evaluates the preauthorized window; no deadline is reset from delivery time, and unresolved verification is escalated
Paid renewal is followed by an older failure Paid grant remains; no new grace or removal
Grace deadline is reached without recovery Entitlement expires; a durable removal task is created
Payment arrives while removal is pending Obsolete task is skipped, or the membership error is repaired
Payment settles after removal Re-entry is offered only if a valid grant covers now and no independent moderation block applies; settling an ended period alone does not restore access
Another valid grant exists No removal solely because this subscription expired
Bot loses removal permissions Entitlement remains expired; failed enforcement is visible to operators

Monitor expired-but-present memberships and entitled-but-banned accounts. For confirmed removals, measure enforcement lag from the applicable access deadline to confirmed removal, recording any authorized exception separately. Investigate task failures and distinguish voluntary departures from admission errors. Keep event and grant references in logs, excluding payment credentials and bot tokens.

Conclusion

An unsuccessful renewal starts a recovery workflow. Whether access continues depends on existing paid time and an explicit grace policy.

Keep the deadline fixed, record successful renewal once, and treat removal and re-entry as operations that can fail. That makes the system easier to explain to subscribers and easier to repair when billing and Telegram disagree.

title: Use Node.js Cron to Trigger Webhook Tasks for User Reminders (3 Boundaries)
description:
Short answer: let Node.js cron make a short request to a public webhook, then enqueue a compact reminder task for a worker. For a nightly e-commerce payment reconciliation, do not make the scheduled HTTP request own the reconciliation itself.

That shape gives a one-person SaaS a useful checkpoint: the job was accepted by the queue. The provider can be slow, the worker can restart, and the reminder can still be processed without stretching the scheduler request across the whole reconciliation.

I first thought the schedule should call the reconciliation code directly. I later found that the handoff, rather than the entire job, is the unit I can retry without creating duplicate work. This is a delivery decision, not a syntax decision.

How should cron trigger a webhook task for a user reminder?

Use three small boundaries:

  1. A Node.js cron job fires at the required time.
  2. A publicly reachable webhook validates the request and pushes a reminder task into the queue.
  3. A worker consumes the task, reconciles payment records, and writes an idempotent result.

The public endpoint matters. A cron task can call a public HTTP URL; it cannot reach a private laptop or an internal-only service. Keep that endpoint narrow and validate any destination or user-controlled URL instead of turning it into a server-side request proxy. The OWASP SSRF guidance is a good reference for that boundary.

Infrai fits this handoff when a solo operator wants one key and one bill across backend capabilities. The second advantage is one REST API for the workflow: plain HTTP works from any language or runtime, without an SDK. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the public discovery surface is available without a key: it exposes request schemas, response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That removes a concrete integration cost from the webhook-to-queue boundary. One platform covers multiple backend capabilities with consistent conventions, so switching vendors does not require changing the application interface. Its breadth is real: 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. Adjacent backend work can stay on the same interface instead of growing another credential and invoice boundary.

The cron request should finish quickly. The execution limit is 900 seconds, so a reconciliation that can exceed that belongs in the queue-and-worker path. The standard queue is at-least-once. A duplicate delivery is therefore normal, and the worker must make its database write idempotent using the reconciliation date, merchant, and provider transaction identifier.

Here is the smallest application-side version. It shows the scheduling and webhook handoff without inventing a provider-specific payload schema.

import cron from "node-cron";
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const webhookUrl = process.env.RECONCILIATION_WEBHOOK_URL;
if (!webhookUrl) throw new Error("RECONCILIATION_WEBHOOK_URL is required");

async function publishReminder(payload: unknown, idempotencyKey: string) {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(`queue publish failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const waitMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }
  throw new Error("queue publish retries exhausted");
}

async function triggerReminder() {
  const response = await fetch(webhookUrl, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      kind: "payment-reconciliation-reminder",
      reconciliationDate: new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10),
    }),
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`webhook failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
}

cron.schedule("0 3 * * *", () => {
  triggerReminder().catch((error) => {
    console.error("reconciliation trigger failed", error);
  });
});

createServer((request, response) => {
  if (request.method !== "POST" || request.url !== "/reconciliation-hook") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }

  // Validate authentication and parse the body before enqueueing this task.
  publishReminder({ reminder: "validated request body" }, "reconciliation:date:merchant")
    .then((result) => {
      response.writeHead(202, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
      response.end(JSON.stringify({ status: "accepted", result }));
    })
    .catch((error) => {
      console.error("queue publish failed", error);
      response.writeHead(500).end("queue publish failed");
    });
}).listen(8080);

In a real handler, the queue publish must use an idempotency key derived from the business job, not a random value generated on every retry. Store the response status and request identifier as a minimal execution log. Store the reconciliation result separately. A four-kilobyte run-history output limit is not a ledger.

Which queue shape fits delivery guarantees?

The alternatives are good at different boundaries.

Option Where it fits What remains yours
BullMQ A Node.js product that already runs Redis and wants familiar worker controls Redis operations, the public trigger, deployment, and idempotent reconciliation writes
Amazon SQS A system already operating inside AWS and using its queue control plane The cron-to-webhook path, consumer behavior, reminder delivery, and application-level deduplication
Temporal A workflow with durable orchestration, timers, retries, and multiple dependent activities More workflow infrastructure and a broader programming model than this one handoff needs

BullMQ is attractive when Redis is already a core dependency. SQS is the conservative choice for an AWS-native service. Temporal becomes more compelling when reconciliation grows into a workflow with branches or joins. None of those differences disappear because the trigger happens to be cron.

For a solo SaaS, I also count operating surface area as part of the effective cost. Infrai puts its backend capabilities behind one key and one bill, rather than making a small service collect credentials and invoices across many dashboards. Its public discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples, and the REST interface needs no SDK installation. That reduces the time spent guessing at an integration boundary. The scarce resource is revenue per hour, not another cron expression.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the cron-to-queue handoff when a public HTTPS endpoint is acceptable, one credential boundary matters more than owning every queue component, and a self-describing REST API reduces integration work. Its documented scheduling surface includes cron creation and its queue surface includes publishing; use the live discovery schema for the request fields. This is a fit for a short trigger and an idempotent worker, not for a private endpoint or a workflow engine.

What changes when the workload grows?

Keep the queue message small. The message body limit is 256 KB, delayed messages are limited to 7 days, and retention tops out at 30 days. Put a reconciliation identifier in the message and keep provider pages, raw responses, and audit state in the application database.

Do not assume a paused cron will backfill missed runs. It does not. Trigger timing also has second-level jitter, which is fine for a nightly check and wrong for a hard ledger-close deadline. There is no native debounce or throttle, and the cron expression does not support non-standard L extensions.

The queue is not a replay log. Acknowledgement deletes the message, and the standard queue provides at-least-once delivery. If the worker sends a reminder and then crashes before acknowledging, the same task can return. Make the reminder write and the reconciliation write safe to repeat.

At larger volume, I would add a dead-letter review process and alert on message age, not only message count. I would also separate “payment data reconciled” from “user reminder delivered.” Those states have different retry policies and should not share one boolean.

The practical rule is simple: schedule the handoff, queue the work, and make the consumer idempotent. If the system needs DAG orchestration, fan-out joins, replay, or a private network destination, choose the specialist whose boundary matches that requirement. A single API is not a reason to erase those constraints.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the cron enqueueing guide and use the live schema before wiring the handler.

References

  • OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Amazon SQS documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Infrai cron enqueueing guide

title: React vs Angular: Which Should Beginners Learn?
description:
Imagine a student three weeks into JavaScript. A friend says "learn React." A YouTube video says "Angular gets you hired in big companies." A college senior says "just pick one." The student closes the laptop and learns nothing that day.

If that sounds familiar, this guide is for you. It covers react vs angular for beginners, with real code, current data, and a clear rule for choosing.

Why this choice matters

Both tools build the part of a website that users see and click, called the frontend. Both are mature and used in real products, so neither is a "dead" option.

Still, the choice shapes your first six months. It decides what you read, which jobs you can apply for, and how fast you build your first project.

In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, React was used by 44.7% of respondents and Angular by 18.2%. The State of JavaScript 2025 survey reports that the front-end ranking stayed stable, and that React tops the list of developer pain points, partly because it is the most used tool.

Usage favors React, and complaints exist for both. The real question is which one fits you.

What React and Angular actually are

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. A library gives you tools for one job, and you choose the rest yourself, such as routing, forms, and data fetching.

Angular is a full framework from Google. A framework makes more decisions for you. Routing, forms, HTTP calls, and testing tools come in the box, and it uses TypeScript by default.

TypeScript is JavaScript with types. A type tells the code what kind of value to expect, like a number or a string. It catches many mistakes before you run the app.

React Angular
Type Library Full framework
Language JavaScript or TypeScript TypeScript
Built-in routing and forms No, you pick packages Yes
Setup choices Many Few
Template style JSX (HTML inside JavaScript) HTML templates with Angular syntax
Maintained by Meta and community Google

The learning curve for students with no experience

Is React easier than Angular? React is easier to start. Angular is easier to keep organized.

React has a small core: components, props, state, and hooks. You can build a working page in a day. The hard part comes later, when you must choose a router, a state tool, and a folder structure. Nobody tells you what is "correct," so beginners often feel lost.

Angular asks for more upfront. You meet components, services, dependency injection, TypeScript, and RxJS (a tool for handling streams of data) early. The first week feels heavy. After that, every Angular project looks similar, so you rarely wonder where things go.

Think of cooking. React hands you a knife and a pan. Angular hands you a full kitchen with a manual.

The same feature in both

Let's build one small feature twice: a course list with a search box. It shows how each tool handles state, which is data that changes while the app runs.

React version 

import { useState } from "react";

const courses = [
  { id: 1, title: "HTML Basics" },
  { id: 2, title: "JavaScript Basics" },
  { id: 3, title: "React Basics" },
];

export default function CourseList() {
  // "search" holds what the user typed. setSearch updates it.
  const [search, setSearch] = useState("");

  // Keep only courses whose title matches the search text.
  const visibleCourses = courses.filter((course) =>
    course.title.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase())
  );

  return (
    <section>
      <input
        value={search}
        onChange={(event) => setSearch(event.target.value)}
        placeholder="Search courses"
      />
      <ul>
        {visibleCourses.map((course) => (
          <li key={course.id}>{course.title}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </section>
  );
}

useState stores the search text. When it changes, React runs the component again and redraws the list. The key helps React track each list item.

Angular version 

import { Component, computed, signal } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-course-list',
  template: `
    <input #box (input)="search.set(box.value)" placeholder="Search courses" />
    <ul>
      @for (course of visibleCourses(); track course.id) {
        <li>{{ course.title }}</li>
      } @empty {
        <li>No courses found</li>
      }
    </ul>
  `,
})
export class CourseList {
  courses = [
    { id: 1, title: 'HTML Basics' },
    { id: 2, title: 'JavaScript Basics' },
    { id: 3, title: 'Angular Basics' },
  ];

  // A signal holds a value and tells Angular when it changes.
  search = signal('');

  // A computed signal recalculates only when its inputs change.
  visibleCourses = computed(() =>
    this.courses.filter((course) =>
      course.title.toLowerCase().includes(this.search().toLowerCase())
    )
  );
}

This uses current Angular features. The Angular signals guide explains signals, and the built-in @for and @if blocks replace the older *ngFor and *ngIf. Tutorials may still show the old syntax, so check the date of any course you follow.

Both versions do the same thing. React puts HTML inside JavaScript. Angular keeps the template separate and adds its own syntax. If JSX feels strange, Angular may feel safer. If decorators and extra structure feel heavy, React will feel lighter.

Starting a project today

The React team deprecated Create React App in February 2025 and now suggests starting new apps with a framework such as Next.js or React Router. For a first learning project, a simple Vite setup also works well:

npm create vite@latest my-first-app -- --template react
cd my-first-app
npm install
npm run dev

If a tutorial starts with npx create-react-app, skip it or expect differences.

Angular setup is shorter because the CLI makes the choices:

npm install -g @angular/cli
ng new my-first-app
cd my-first-app
ng serve

Angular wins on simplicity here. React gives you more freedom but asks for more decisions.

What each one teaches you

React teaches core JavaScript well. Components are mostly functions, and you use array methods like map and filter all the time. These skills transfer to almost any JavaScript job.

Angular teaches structure. You learn services, dependency injection, typed code, and testing patterns early. These habits help in large codebases and carry over to backend frameworks like Spring or .NET.

Neither choice wastes your time. Many developers learn the second tool in a few weeks once the first one clicks.

Which has more jobs in 2026, React or Angular?

Usage data points to more React openings. A tool used by 44.7% of surveyed developers will appear in more job posts than one used by 18.2%. I could not find a reliable public count of open roles for either tool, so I will not invent one.

Angular still has real demand. It is common in large companies, banks, and enterprise teams that want strict structure. Those jobs often face less competition from self-taught beginners.

You can check the market in ten minutes. Search "React developer" and "Angular developer" on LinkedIn, Naukri, and Indeed with your city and "fresher" as filters. Note the counts and the common skills listed. Live data beats any article.

React or Angular for a first job as a fresher in India

Freshers in India usually apply to two kinds of employers: product and startup teams, and large service companies.

Startups and product teams often lean toward React, since it pairs with Next.js and fits small teams. Large service companies and enterprise clients often run Angular for long projects, since its structure suits big teams.

So the best fit depends on where you want to apply. Look at 15 companies you would actually apply to. If most list React, learn React. If many list Angular, learn Angular.

Either way, job posts also ask for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Git, and REST APIs. A student who knows these well and has one real project beats a student who half-knows two frameworks.

A simple decision guide

Your situation Start with
You are new to programming and want quick wins React
You like clear rules and a fixed structure Angular
You want startup or freelance work React
You target enterprise or service company roles Angular
You already know TypeScript or Java Angular
You still cannot decide React

The last row is not a cop-out. When two options fit equally, pick the one with more tutorials and community help.

A four-week plan that works for either

  1. Week 1: JavaScript functions, arrays, objects, and fetch.
  2. Week 2: Core ideas of your chosen tool. For React: components, props, and useState. For Angular: components, signals, and templates.
  3. Week 3: Build the course list above, then add a form and fetch data from a free public API.
  4. Week 4: Add routing, deploy the project to a free host, and write a short README.

Avoid three common traps. Do not switch tools after ten days. Do not follow outdated tutorials. Do not skip JavaScript, because most "React is hard" stories are really "JavaScript is hard" stories.

The bottom line

For most beginners, React is the easier door to walk through. Its small core, large community, and wide job reach make the first months smoother. Angular is the better pick if you like structure, want enterprise roles, or already know TypeScript.

Both are safe, and both can get you hired if you build real projects. The framework you finish learning beats the framework you keep researching.

FAQ

Q1. Should I learn React or Angular first?

Ans. Most beginners should start with React because it has a smaller core and more learning material. Choose Angular first if you prefer strict structure or aim for enterprise jobs.

Q2. Is React easier than Angular for beginners?

Ans. React is easier to start. Angular takes longer at the beginning but gives you clear structure once you pass that hump.

Q3. Which has more jobs in 2026, React or Angular?

Ans. React has wider usage, so it likely appears in more job posts. Angular remains in steady demand at larger companies. Search job sites in your city to see real numbers.

Q4. Do I need TypeScript for React or Angular?

Ans. Angular requires it. React works with plain JavaScript, though many teams use TypeScript. Learn JavaScript first, then add TypeScript.

title: Google Considers 1,200 MW Data Center Campus on 1,000 Acres in Goochland, Virginia
description:
Google is weighing the purchase of a roughly 1,000-acre site in West Creek Business Park in Goochland County, Virginia, where it would build a 1,200-megawatt data center campus.

The company confirmed the plan following a news release from the county, marking the first time Google has been publicly linked to the proposed development. The project would further expand Google's data center footprint in Virginia, adding to its existing data center projects in the Richmond region and strengthening the state's position as a key market for US data center development. The proposed facility also reflects continued investment in US data center infrastructure as demand for AI and cloud computing capacity grows.

**Early Stage: Due Diligence, No Plans Filed
**Google is currently performing due diligence on the property. If it decides to proceed and buy the land, the next step would be site engineering to develop a site plan to submit to the county.
As of now, Google has submitted no plans, Goochland County Administrator Jeremy Raley said in an email Wednesday.

**By-Right Status Under the Technology Overlay District
**The site lies within the county's recently approved technology overlay district, known as the TOD, which means any data center project there would be a by-right use.
As a result, it would not need to go through the public hearing process.
The project site would bisect Route 288 north of Patterson Avenue. It is owned by an entity tied to Pruitt Associates and Riverstone Group, which control the bulk of the land in West Creek.
From Unnamed Filing to Named User
Wednesday's county release was the first time Google was associated with the proposal.
The project was first mentioned, without naming Google, in a State Corporation Commission regulatory filing dated July 14. That filing listed several potential data center campuses proposed by unnamed applicants for the eastern portion of Goochland.
Besides the 1,200-megawatt project now linked to Google, it included a 600-megawatt project that would rise on roughly 150 acres off Ashland Road and a 200-megawatt project east of Route 288 and north of Patterson Avenue.
All three developments are located in the TOD and an accompanying technology zone, which together span about 5 miles along Route 288, from Interstate 64 south to Patterson Avenue.
The TOD area is bordered to the west by Hockett Road and covers roughly 4,400 acres, about 3,500 of which are within West Creek and controlled by Pruitt Associates.
According to the July filing, the customer for the 1,200-megawatt campus had executed four ELOAs, or engineering letters of authorization, for the project.

Once an ELOA is issued, projects are placed in a project queue for Dominion Energy, where they can sit for years before a feasibility study is conducted on a site and a construction letter of authorization, or CLOA, is executed.

The filing did not identify the customer, but Google officials confirmed on Wednesday that the company was interested in that specific site.
County's Account of Its Contact with Google

The county's release laid out a timeline of its dealings with Google.
It begins with the Virginia Economic Development Partnership reaching out to the county in early 2024 to meet with a data center user and show them potential sites in Goochland County.

The county entered into a nondisclosure agreement with Google on Jan. 10, 2024, and county staff held one meeting with Google officials to discuss potential locations for a data center development on Jan. 30 of that year.
According to the release, after the meeting the VEDP told the county that Google was not interested and was not moving forward, and there was no further communication with Google at that time.

After last November's adoption of the TOD, however, Google re-engaged with the county and began due diligence on the West Creek site.
Because the county was already under the NDA from the earlier discussions, it did not enter into a new one, the release says.
In what the county described as an effort to provide transparency, it requested to be released from the NDA.
Both the county and Google agreed to the release on Tuesday, which prompted Wednesday's announcement of Google's involvement.

Neighboring Tuckahoe Tech Park Faces a Different Process
The potential Google site lies east of the proposed Tuckahoe Tech Park, which would rise within the county's TOD West area, a 900-acre tract where data centers require a conditional-use permit.

Denver, Colorado-based data center developer Tract is behind that project, which would need approvals through the public hearing process before it could move forward.

Lawsuit Over the TOD Awaits a Ruling
The announcement comes shortly after a recent hearing in a lawsuit that four Goochland residents have brought against the county.
The residents claim that supervisors and planning commissioners failed to clearly and lawfully explain their adoption of the TOD.

A hearing last Tuesday addressed the county's motion to dismiss the lawsuit, and that motion is under advisement by the judge in the case.

Building on Google's Chesterfield Presence
Google's efforts in Goochland would build on its existing data center plans in the Richmond region. The company has begun construction on a data center campus on a site of more than 300 acres at 2700 Bermuda Hundred Road in eastern Chesterfield County, next to Meadowville Technology Park.
It also has several other data center facilities planned for the western end of Chesterfield County.

title: I took SSH away from my agent. Then my own tool started lying to it.
description:
This spring I wrote twice about not giving Claude SSH access to my home server. The argument was simple: a shell is too sharp, so give the agent a narrow tool instead. Structured answers, bounded scope, nothing it can rm -rf.

I still believe that. But six months of running it taught me the half I'd skipped.

A narrow tool that says something false is just as dangerous as a shell. Maybe more, because nobody double-checks it.

When I read my own tool's output, I bring context. I know I ran docker kill ten minutes ago. I know that port has always belonged to that container. An agent has none of that. It reads the words and acts on them. Every sentence the tool prints becomes a decision somebody else makes.

Eleven days on a Raspberry Pi

Before calling HomeButler 1.0, I put it on a Raspberry Pi with three apps, a watch service and a daily report --json, and left it for eleven days. I wasn't looking for crashes. I was reading every line it said and asking: is this true?

The first day was humbling:

  • I ran docker kill on a container. HomeButler filed it as an OOM, confidence: high.
  • It recorded a restart that never happened.
  • It suggested a command that doesn't exist.

None of these were crashes. The code ran fine. It just said things nobody had told it. It saw exit code 137 and guessed. It saw a timestamp field and filled it in. Every guess was plausible, and plausible is the problem.

The fixes were mostly deletions. oom only when Docker actually sent an oom event. A start time only when something actually started. I ended up with one rule for the whole project:

Say only what the machine reported.

The quiet day

The worst one was the most boring. On the first day nothing changed, report --json said the comparison could not be made.

"No significant changes" had been filed under the same kind as "I couldn't compare." For a person, that's a typo. For an agent, it's the difference between "all good" and "go investigate." Empty lists were also coming back as null, which a script reads as "missing," not "nothing."

So now there's a word for each case, and they never overlap:

skipped   the comparison could not be made
[]        the comparison was made and found nothing

An all-clear the tool can't stand behind is worse than no answer at all.

"Completely removed"

After the soak, I was cleaning up the demo machine and ran install purge filebrowser. It said Completely removed.

filebrowser's database and settings were still sitting in two Docker volumes. They'd been left behind on the soak machine before that too, and I'd never noticed, because the tool told me it was done.

If an agent had run that purge for me, it would have reported back "done, everything's gone," and it would have been sincerely, confidently wrong. Now the answer lists what was actually left, under Removed, except:, with the volume names. A purge that really removed everything answers the same as before.

Read-only doesn't mean safe to read

Earlier this month I added homebutler mcp --max-risk read. An agent can look at the machine and change nothing. That felt like the finish line of the "no SSH" idea.

Then I found that one read tool, docker_top, returned each container's full command line. If you started something with --token=..., the agent got your token, in read-only mode.

"Read" described what a call does to the machine. I had been using it as if it also described what a call reveals. Those are different promises. docker_top now returns the process name, not its arguments, and the docs for every read tool say what it returns, not just that it changes nothing.

Year one

One more, because it's my favourite. For a while, every alert watch sent was dated:

0001-01-01 00:00:00

On every provider. Discord, Slack, all of them. It went unnoticed until I pointed a real webhook at the Pi.

Freezing the words

Once I started seeing output as something an agent acts on, versioning looked different too. An agent branches on gone, new, replaced. If one of those words quietly changes meaning, its decisions change without anyone touching a prompt.

So 1.0 came with a promise: a tool, a field, or a word an agent branches on doesn't change before 2.0. A golden test checks every tool's answer field by field, and the build fails if something drifts.

That's also why so many of the soak fixes shipped before 1.0. Freezing a shape that said the wrong thing would have frozen the lie.

What I'd tell myself in April

Taking the shell away was the right first step. It shrinks what an agent can do. It doesn't shrink what it can be told.

If you're building tools for agents, I'd start with three questions about every line your tool prints:

  1. Did the machine actually say this, or did my code infer it?
  2. Can "nothing happened" be told apart from "I couldn't check"?
  3. Would I be fine if the agent repeated this to me as fact?

Most of the bugs I fixed in the last six months failed one of those. None of them showed up as a failing test.

Try it

HomeButler is still a single Go binary. No daemon, no database.

brew install Higangssh/homebutler/homebutler
homebutler report
homebutler mcp --max-risk read   # for your agent

Repo: https://github.com/Higangssh/homebutler

Genuine question: what's the most confidently wrong thing a tool has told you about your own server? I'm collecting them, partly for test cases, partly for comfort.

This post was written with the help of AI. The incidents, the decisions and the numbers come from my own soak runs and the project's changelog.

title: AWS SAA-C03 Exam Guide 2026: Format, Domains and Study Plan
description:
AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) tests whether you can design solutions on AWS based on the AWS Well-Architected Framework. Here is how the exam works in 2026, the four domains and their weights, what each domain covers, who it is aimed at, how to keep the certification, and our suggested study plan.

Is SAA-C03 being replaced?

Not as far as AWS has said. AWS’s September 2026 certification update announced new versions of three exams: Machine Learning Engineer – Associate, Solutions Architect – Professional and Developer – Associate. It did not include Solutions Architect – Associate. As of 28 October 2026, the AWS exam guides index still lists SAA-C03, and the AWS Training and Certification blog has not announced a successor.

The only change AWS has announced is about language: the Italian version of the exam will be retired after 31 December 2026. The exam stays available in its other languages.

The format

Detail SAA-C03
Level Associate
Questions 65: 50 scored and 15 unscored
Time 130 minutes
Question types Multiple choice and multiple response
Passing score 720 on a scaled score from 100 to 1,000
Fee USD 150 (AWS notes that extra costs, such as foreign exchange, may apply)
Delivery Pearson VUE, at a test centre or online proctored
Validity 3 years

A multiple choice question has one correct answer and three incorrect ones. A multiple response question has two or more correct answers out of five or more options. Unanswered questions are scored as incorrect, and there is no penalty for guessing, so answer every question.

The 15 unscored questions are ones AWS is trying out for future use. They are not marked on the exam, so treat every question as if it counts.

The exam uses a compensatory scoring model. You need to pass the exam as a whole, not each domain. Your score report may show how you did in each section, but AWS advises caution when reading that section-level feedback.

The exam uses short names for some AWS services. A list of short names and full names is available through the Help button during the exam, and AWS suggests you look at it before exam day.

The four domains

Domain Weight
1. Design Secure Architectures 30%
2. Design Resilient Architectures 26%
3. Design High-Performing Architectures 24%
4. Design Cost-Optimized Architectures 20%

The weights are shares of the scored content, so a higher weight means more questions from that domain.

What each domain covers

This is our short summary of the task statements in the official exam guide. The guide itself has the full lists of knowledge and skills.

Design Secure Architectures (30%)

  • Secure access to AWS resources: IAM users, groups, roles and policies, least privilege and MFA, role switching and cross-account access, federation, and multi-account security with AWS Control Tower and service control policies.
  • Secure workloads and applications: VPC design with security groups, network ACLs, route tables and public and private subnets, plus services such as AWS WAF, AWS Shield, Amazon Cognito, Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Secrets Manager.
  • Data security controls: encryption at rest with AWS KMS and in transit with AWS Certificate Manager, key policies and rotation, backups and replication, and data retention and compliance.

Design Resilient Architectures (26%)

  • Scalable and loosely coupled designs: event-driven, microservice and multi-tier architectures, queues and publish/subscribe messaging, serverless with AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate, containers on Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, Amazon API Gateway, load balancing, caching and read replicas.
  • High availability and fault tolerance: designs across Availability Zones and Regions, Amazon Route 53, removing single points of failure, failover, and disaster recovery strategies from backup and restore to active-active, judged against RPO and RTO.

Design High-Performing Architectures (24%)

  • Storage: choosing between object, file and block storage, such as Amazon S3, Amazon EFS and Amazon EBS, for performance and growth.
  • Compute: EC2 instance types, Auto Scaling, Lambda sizing, containers, and decoupling so components scale on their own.
  • Databases: picking a database type and engine, such as Amazon Aurora or Amazon DynamoDB, read replicas, proxies and caching with Amazon ElastiCache.
  • Networks: subnet tiers and routing, load balancing, Amazon CloudFront, AWS Global Accelerator, and connections such as VPN, AWS Direct Connect and AWS PrivateLink.
  • Data ingestion and transformation: streaming with Amazon Kinesis, transfer with AWS DataSync, transformation with AWS Glue, data lakes, and analytics with Amazon Athena.

Design Cost-Optimized Architectures (20%)

  • Storage: storage tiers, S3 lifecycle rules, backup and archive choices, and the cheapest way to move data into AWS.
  • Compute: Spot Instances, Reserved Instances and Savings Plans, right-sizing instances, and choosing between Lambda, EC2 and Fargate.
  • Databases: cost-effective database services, backup and retention policies, and capacity planning.
  • Networks: NAT gateway choices, data transfer routes, VPC endpoints, AWS Transit Gateway and VPC peering, and Direct Connect versus VPN.

Cost tools such as AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets appear across this domain.

Recommended experience

The exam guide describes a target candidate with at least 1 year of hands-on experience designing cloud solutions that use AWS services. The exam page adds that people with 1 to 3 years of IT experience have prepared for and earned this certification as a starting point. If you have no IT work experience, AWS suggests earning AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner first.

Keeping your certification

The certification is valid for 3 years. To recertify, you can pass the latest version of the exam. Earning AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional also recertifies the Associate certification automatically.

Our suggested study plan

This is our suggestion, not AWS’s. It gives each domain time roughly in line with its weight, over eight weeks. Stretch it if you are new to AWS.

  1. Weeks 1–2: Secure architectures. IAM policies and roles, cross-account access, VPC security, and encryption with KMS and ACM.
  2. Weeks 3–4: Resilient architectures. Queues and events, serverless and containers, load balancing, multi-AZ and multi-Region designs, and the disaster recovery strategies.
  3. Week 5: High-performing architectures. Matching storage, compute, database and network services to performance needs, plus caching and data ingestion.
  4. Week 6: Cost-optimized architectures. Purchasing options, storage tiers and lifecycles, NAT gateway and data transfer costs.
  5. Weeks 7–8: Practice and review. Take timed practice exams, read every explanation, and go back to your weakest domain.

Throughout, build things in your own AWS account where you can. Many questions describe a scenario and ask for the most secure, most resilient or cheapest design, and hands-on practice makes those trade-offs easier to spot. AWS also lists an Official Practice Question Set and an Official Practice Exam on the exam page.

Confirm the latest details on AWS’s Solutions Architect – Associate page before you book.

I run ExamCrest, where this guide first appeared. Try free SAA-C03 practice questions: https://examcrest.com/exam/aws-saa-c03/free-questions?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=s-n2a-saa-c03

title: Waste Is an Output, Not a Subtraction: Modelling By-Products, Waste Streams and Licensed Collections in a Food ERP
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

Most production software models a batch as inputs in, one product out. Whatever doesn't make it into the finished-goods line is "loss", a single number that nobody can explain. In a food factory that number is made of very different things: rejects, line purges, bran, whey, pomace, film offcuts, chemical containers and effluent. Some of it is sold as feed, some goes to a licensed collector, some is hazardous. If the system can't tell them apart, nobody can manage them.

This post walks through how we think about modelling waste and by-product streams in an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa. The operational checklist behind it is in the original article.

What the domain rules say

The requirements read like a spec:

  • Codex CXC 1-1969 (9.2.1): waste "should be collected, disposed of by trained personnel and, where appropriate, disposal records maintained"; containers "for waste, by-products and inedible or hazardous substances should be specifically identifiable". Source
  • EAS 39:2001 (10.8): skips emptied "at least once per week", factory waste containers "emptied daily" and not mistakable for food containers. Source
  • Kenya's Sustainable Waste Management Act, 2022: segregate "non-hazardous waste into organic and non-organic fractions" (s.12); a private sector entity's annual monitoring report specifies "the actual quantities of waste generated by the entity" (s.19); waste goes to "a person who is licensed to transport and dispose of the waste". Source

Translated into engineering terms: every production output has a type, every waste movement has a stream, a quantity and a destination, and every collection points at a counterparty whose licence has an expiry date.

Outputs are typed, not leftover

The first design choice is to stop calculating waste as input - output. Declare it.

RecipeOutput     (id, recipe_id, item_id, output_type, expected_pct)
                 output_type IN ('primary','co_product','byproduct','waste')
ProductionOutput (id, run_id, recipe_output_id, qty_kg, recorded_at, recorded_by)

A recipe that turns 1,000 kg of maize into flour, bran and screenings says so up front. When the run closes, each output is weighed and recorded against the run. "Unexplained loss" becomes the residual after declared outputs, which is the number you actually want to drive towards zero.

By-products are items. Bran or whey that leaves the gate as feed gets an item code, a lot, a stock location and a dispatch record, exactly like finished goods. If a raw-material lot is later found to have a problem, the by-product lot is in the same trace.

Waste never enters saleable stock. A waste output posts to a waste location (or no stock at all), so it can't be picked, sold or counted as inventory value.

Streams, movements and collections 

WasteStream      (id, name, category, hazardous, container_spec, removal_frequency, owner_id)
                 category IN ('organic','plastic','general_dry','hazardous','effluent')
WasteMovement    (id, stream_id, source_run_id NULL, source_area, qty_kg, moved_at, moved_by)
WasteCollection  (id, stream_id, collector_id, qty_kg, collected_at, destination, document_ref)
Collector        (id, name, licence_no, licence_expires_on)

A few rules make this useful:

Category is fixed on the stream. Segregation at source maps one-to-one to streams. If organic and plastic are mixed in one stream, the report can't separate them later.

Block expired collectors. A collection against a collector whose licence_expires_on is in the past should fail validation, or at least raise an exception for the EHS lead. That turns a filing-cabinet check into a system rule.

Schedules generate tasks. removal_frequency on the stream creates cleaning-schedule tasks (empty line bins every shift, skip weekly). A missed task is a hygiene finding, not a surprise at audit.

The queries that matter

Monthly totals by category, which is close to what an annual monitoring report asks for:

SELECT ws.category, date_trunc('month', wc.collected_at) AS month, SUM(wc.qty_kg) AS kg
FROM waste_collection wc
JOIN waste_stream ws ON ws.id = wc.stream_id
GROUP BY ws.category, month
ORDER BY month, ws.category;

And the one production managers care about, waste as a share of output per product and shift:

SELECT pr.product_id, pr.shift, 
       SUM(po.qty_kg) FILTER (WHERE ro.output_type = 'waste') /
       NULLIF(SUM(po.qty_kg), 0) AS waste_share
FROM production_output po
JOIN recipe_output ro ON ro.id = po.recipe_output_id
JOIN production_run pr ON pr.id = po.run_id
WHERE pr.started_at >= now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY pr.product_id, pr.shift
ORDER BY waste_share DESC;

When waste share on one shift starts climbing, it's usually a yield, equipment or training problem showing up early, long before it shows up in the month-end cost.

Takeaways

  • Declare outputs on the recipe: primary, co-product, by-product, waste.
  • Treat by-products as stock items with lots, not as negative waste.
  • Model waste streams with a fixed category so segregation is reportable.
  • Put licence expiry on collectors and validate against it.
  • Measure waste where it is made, per run, not by subtraction at month end.

The full 10-step operational checklist, with references to Codex, EAS 39, Kenya's food hygiene regulations and the Sustainable Waste Management Act, is on the FactoraERP blog.
