title: How to check which AI crawlers actually hit a new WordPress site in week one
description:
A site goes live on Monday. On Friday the question arrives: have the AI crawlers found it yet? If the access log format was picked years ago to debug PHP, there is no answer in the file, and the first week is already gone.

Two decisions have to be made before the first request: capture enough per request, and be able to tie a user agent to an IP you can check. Everything below assumes a self-hosted WordPress site where you control the web server.

Set the log format before launch

nginx, in a file included from the http block:

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/aiwatch.conf
log_format aiwatch '$time_iso8601 $remote_addr "$http_user_agent" '
                   '$request_method $request_uri $status $body_bytes_sent '
                   '"$http_referer" $request_time';

access_log /var/log/nginx/aiwatch.log aiwatch;

Apache httpd:

LogFormat "%{%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z}t %a \"%{User-Agent}i\" %m %U %s %B \"%{Referer}i\" %D" aiwatch
CustomLog /var/log/apache2/aiwatch.log aiwatch

Put it at the server level, not inside one vhost, or the next site you add silently logs in the old format. Then check what logrotate does to that file: if it rotates weekly and compresses, copy week one somewhere before it is replaced.

The fields that change a decision

Field What it decides
time_iso8601 Contains the UTC offset. Without it, cross-checking hits against the moment you published or changed robots.txt is guesswork.
remote_addr Must be the client IP. Behind a CDN or proxy it is the edge, and your verification step will confirm the CDN as a crawler. Fix with set_real_ip_from plus real_ip_header for whatever header your edge sets.
http_user_agent Store it whole. Truncating to 60 characters drops the version and the +https://... info URL that operators put there on purpose.
status 200, 304, 403 and 429 mean four different things. A crawler getting 403 is a different problem from a crawler that never came.
body_bytes_sent A 200 with 0 bytes is a HEAD request or an empty body. A status-only report calls both a success.
request_uri Did it fetch /robots.txt first, and did it ask for /llms.txt at all.
request_time A crawler that times out on your slowest page may not come back for the rest of the site.

Count what actually arrived

The UA is field 2 when you split the line on double quotes, because the format wraps it in quotes.

LOG=/var/log/nginx/aiwatch.log

awk -F'"' '
{
  ua = tolower($2)
  if      (ua ~ /gptbot/)          c = "GPTBot"
  else if (ua ~ /oai-searchbot/)   c = "OAI-SearchBot"
  else if (ua ~ /chatgpt-user/)    c = "ChatGPT-User"
  else if (ua ~ /claudebot/)       c = "ClaudeBot"
  else if (ua ~ /claude-user/)     c = "Claude-User"
  else if (ua ~ /perplexitybot/)   c = "PerplexityBot"
  else if (ua ~ /perplexity-user/) c = "Perplexity-User"
  else if (ua ~ /ccbot/)           c = "CCBot"
  else if (ua ~ /bytespider/)      c = "Bytespider"
  else if (ua ~ /amazonbot/)       c = "Amazonbot"
  else if (ua ~ /applebot/)        c = "Applebot"
  else if (ua ~ /googlebot/)       c = "Googlebot"
  else next
  n[c]++
}
END { for (k in n) printf "%-16s %d\n", k, n[k] }
' "$LOG" | sort -k2 -nr

A zero column for a crawler is not yet evidence of anything. Read the days before you read the total.

To see whether a crawler walked the site in order, print the first hit per IP with the path it asked for:

grep -i 'gptbot' "$LOG" | awk -F'"' '{split($1,a," "); print a[1], a[2], $3}' | sort | head -20

With this format, $1 is timestamp + space + ip, and $3 is the request line (method, path, status, bytes). If robots.txt and the home page appear in that list before anything else, the crawl is behaving; if the first hit is a deep product URL, it came in through a link, not through your sitemap.

Verify the IP before you trust the user agent

A user agent is a string the client chooses. Anyone can send GPTBot. Forward-confirmed reverse DNS is the cheap check: resolve the IP to a hostname, resolve that hostname back, and require the original IP to appear in the result.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Forward-confirmed reverse DNS. Reads IPs from argv or stdin."""
import socket
import sys


def check(ip):
    try:
        host = socket.gethostbyaddr(ip)[0]
    except (socket.herror, socket.gaierror, OSError):
        return ip, None, False
    try:
        addrs = socket.gethostbyname_ex(host)[2]
    except (socket.gaierror, OSError):
        return ip, host, False
    return ip, host, ip in addrs


def main():
    ips = sys.argv[1:] or [line.strip() for line in sys.stdin if line.strip()]
    for ip in ips:
        addr, host, ok = check(ip)
        print(f"{addr}\t{host or '-'}\t{'confirmed' if ok else 'NOT confirmed'}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

chmod +x fcdns.py
awk -F'"' 'tolower($2) ~ /gptbot|claudebot|perplexitybot/ {split($1,a," "); print a[2]}' "$LOG" \
  | sort -u | ./fcdns.py

Confirmed PTR means the IP belongs to whoever controls that reverse zone. It does not prove the request came from the crawler you have in mind, so compare against the operator's published IP ranges where they publish one. A hit that fails both checks is an unknown client with a borrowed user agent, and it should not go into your report as a crawler visit.

Tokens you will never find in a log

Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended are robots.txt user-agent tokens, not strings any client sends. Requests from those operators show up as Googlebot and Applebot. So "did Google-Extended fetch my page" has no answer in the access log; the only thing you control is whether robots.txt permits that token, which is a separate check against the file itself.

Which brings up the other half of the question. A user agent in the log does not mean your robots.txt was obeyed. Pull the file you served that week and see what it said:

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{content_type}\n' https://example.com/robots.txt
curl -sS https://example.com/llms.txt | head -20

Run it from outside your own network. A WAF rule that allows your office IP and blocks everything else looks identical to "no crawlers came" once you are reading the log.

What week one can and cannot tell you

A fetch is not an inclusion. A confirmed GPTBot request for the home page says a crawler read the page; it says nothing about whether the page will appear in an answer later, and there is no field in the log that closes that gap.

The reverse is worth stating too: no hits in week one does not distinguish "blocked" from "has not found it yet". A brand-new domain with no inbound links gives a crawler very little to follow, so an empty column is the expected starting state, not a malfunction. Do not rewrite robots.txt on the strength of one quiet week; check what the file actually serves first, then wait.

Keep the week

Print the per-crawler count once a week and keep the output next to the raw log. A single snapshot after launch tells you nothing that changes a decision. The number that matters is the change between week one and week four, and whether the paths being fetched moved from the home page into the pages you actually want quoted.

If maintaining this pipeline on every site is not the job you want, AumCrawl records crawler hits per crawler and lets you allow or block them individually. It is free and on wordpress.org; the log format above is still worth setting, because the plugin's data is only as good as what the server keeps.

title: My fix for the agent-edited test gate was wrong. The pin has to be older than the agent.
description:
Three weeks ago I published four fixes for a test gate that runs the tests in the tree the agent just edited. Fix 2 was this: do not run the tests in the agent's tree, run them in a pristine worktree off HEAD and copy in only the unprotected changes.

@howcani_howcani_77e786a89 took it back to a local repo, stopped at fix 2, and wrote: fix 2's precondition is the thing evasion 1 removes. Evasion 1 is the agent committing. After that, HEAD is the agent's commit, so "a commit you control" is a commit the agent controls, and a worktree off it is pristine only with respect to the uncommitted dilution.

He was right. I reproduced it before writing this. Baseline has one real test. The agent commits a weakened one. A clean worktree off HEAD, fresh checkout, nothing copied in from the working tree:

old fix 2 worktree tests/test_calc.py:
    assert True
old fix 2 verdict: PASS

The gate passes on a test that asserts nothing. Fix 2 moved the dilution from "uncommitted edits" to "a commit", and a commit is exactly the thing the agent can make.

The pin has to be older than the agent

The fix is not a better use of HEAD. It is to stop asking HEAD what the baseline is.

Before the agent runs, while the tree is known good, record the protected set as content: every path under tests/, conftest.py, the runner config, the CI file, each mapped to its blob hash.

37895b28ab864addfe1921d4bf035a1563ac0689 conftest.py
4b341e0595f8265e27ed7b7e6119711b672e0e17c tests/test_calc.py

At check time, recompute the same tree listing for those paths and compare. Three ways to differ, all fail: a path is missing, a path's hash changed, a path that was not in the pin appears. Then run the tests on a tree assembled from the pins for protected paths and from the agent's commit for everything else.

A blob hash is not a ref. An agent can rewrite history, orphan its commits, delete a branch. It cannot produce a different file with the same hash.

What I actually ran, four repos from one baseline, one shared pin:

A control src-only:                    added=0 changed=0 missing=0 -> PASS
B agent-committed weakened test:       added=0 changed=1 missing=0 -> FAIL
C delete + add inside tests/:          added=1 changed=0 missing=1 -> FAIL
D rewritten history (1 orphan commit): added=0 changed=1 missing=0 -> FAIL

Case C is the one that caught my own corrected check. Compare hashes of the paths you know about and the agent can leave every pinned path alone, delete them, and drop tests/test_zz.py with assert 1 == 1 in the same commit. The path set has to be compared, not just the hashes. Case D is a repo rewritten to a single orphan commit where the baseline is not an ancestor of anything. The pin does not care, because it never asks about ancestry.

What the pin does not fix

Where the pin lives.

If the harness writes the expected hashes into the worktree it is about to inspect, or reads them out of the repository it is checking, this whole method collapses into the class I hunt for a living: a check that decides on bytes it never reads. An agent that can write the pin can set it to whatever it just produced, and every check above passes.

So the pin is written by the step that owns the checkout, before the agent exists, and kept out of every path the agent's process can write. If you cannot name the component that owns the pin, you do not have this fix, you have a second copy of the problem.

The general shape

A gate is only as strong as the oldest copy of the expected value it holds. If the expected value is derived at check time from anything the checked party touched, then the gate's verdict is decided by the artifact, not by the check. The agent committing is just the most convenient way to make the artifact supply its own baseline.

Corrections: this one came from someone who ran my method instead of agreeing with it, which is worth more than a like and costs him an afternoon. The first piece is https://dev.to/mayailands/your-agents-test-gate-runs-the-tests-in-the-tree-the-agent-just-edited-574

If you ship the pinned version and want a third-party re-run of the check against your repo, with a control that must pass and a negative control that must fail, the receipt is $25 and the card is here: https://buy.stripe.com/fZu5kD1rN0laceh13n5kI02

The finding is free. That is why it is above and not behind a link.

title: How to Evaluate AI Agents for Production: Moving Beyond LLM-as-a-Judge
description:
This is Part 1 of a 5-part series on evaluating and hardening production AI agents. See also: Part 2: Deterministic State Evaluations, Part 3: Statistical Rigor in AI Evals, Part 4: Curating Golden Trajectories, and Part 5: Building an Agent CI/CD Pipeline.

Most AI agent demos look magical until they face unconstrained user inputs and real environment states.

In a controlled demo, an agent receives a clean prompt, calls two tools, and outputs a coherent final response. In production, teams encounter the reliability cliff: the agent gets stuck in infinite retry loops, hallucinates schema parameters, mutates production databases unexpectedly, or drifts into degenerative completions.

To solve this, engineering teams frequently reach for the industry default: LLM-as-a-judge. They pipe the agent's multi-turn transcript into a secondary frontier model, provide a rubric prompt, and ask the model to rate task completion on a scale from 1 to 5.

A note on model generations: Foundation models turn over continuously, but evaluation mechanics are invariant. Whether your agent runs on proprietary frontier APIs, domain-specialized reasoning checkpoints, or locally hosted open weights, the failure modes and statistical principles below remain identical across model lifecycles. Build evaluation harnesses that outlive the model release of the day.

This approach creates a dangerous illusion of measurement. It gives leadership a plausible-looking dashboard while leaving production systems entirely unprotected against regression.

Here is why LLM-as-a-judge fails to protect production agents, the compounding mathematics underneath multi-step failure, and the state-based evaluation architecture required to deploy agents with confidence.

The Mathematics of Multi-Step Error Cascading

The fundamental difference between a single-turn completion (such as summarization or question-answering) and an autonomous agent is sequential dependency.

In a multi-turn agent, every intermediate tool execution changes the environment and feeds into the next turn's context window. If Turn 1 retrieves an incorrect ID, Turn 2 operates on bad data, Turn 3 issues a corrupt database mutation, and Turn 4 hallucinates an explanation to justify the discrepancy.

Consider an agent task requiring $k$ discrete steps. If each step has an independent success probability $p$, the end-to-end task success probability $P(\text{task})$ follows:

$$P(\text{task}) = p^k$$

If your underlying foundation model is highly capable—say, $p = 0.90$ (90% per-step reliability)—the compound trajectory success decays rapidly as task complexity scales:

  • 1 step: $0.90^1 = 90.0\%$
  • 3 steps: $0.90^3 = 72.9\%$
  • 5 steps: $0.90^5 = 59.0\%$
  • 10 steps: $0.90^{10} = 34.9\%$

A system where individual steps look stellar during ad-hoc testing fails two out of three times when executing 10-step workflows.

Worse, steps are rarely independent. A minor error early in a trajectory increases the entropy of the agent's context window, degrading subsequent reasoning performance. Without deterministic guards at each transition, error cascading is mathematically inevitable.

The Three Structural Failures of LLM-as-a-Judge

Using a language model to grade multi-turn transcripts introduces three major measurement errors:

1. Inability to Observe Environment State Mutations

Language models evaluate text tokens; they do not execute environments.

If an agent reports:

"I have reconciled invoice #8492 and updated the ERP ledger status to settled."

An LLM judge reads this transcript and gives it a score of 5/5 for helpfulness, tone, and apparent completion. But did the invoice actually update in the database? Did it credit the right account balance? Did it violate foreign key constraints?

The judge cannot know because it only inspects the prose claim, not the environment delta. Grading agents on what they say rather than what they changed is the primary source of unmonitored production outages.

2. Systematic Cognitive Biases in LLM Scoring

Empirical evaluation benchmarks repeatedly reveal systematic structural biases in frontier models acting as evaluators:

  • Verbosity Bias: LLMs assign higher scores to long, repetitive, verbose answers, conflating length with thoroughness.
  • Position Bias: In multi-candidate evaluations, judges disproportionately favor responses presented in specific serial positions.
  • Self-Enhancement Bias: Frontier models systematically score outputs generated by their own family or architecture higher than outputs from competing models.

3. Non-Deterministic Evaluation Noise

When you evaluate a non-deterministic agent with a non-deterministic judge, you double your measurement variance. If an evaluation score drops from 4.2 to 3.8 on a nightly run, your team cannot immediately tell whether:

  1. The agent degraded due to prompt drift or model updates.
  2. The judge drifted due to non-zero temperature or provider inference changes.
  3. The sample variance was simply noise.

An evaluation harness that engineering teams cannot reproduce is an evaluation harness they will eventually ignore.

The Architecture: State-Based Evaluation

To build an evaluation suite that survives engineering inspection, we invert the paradigm: Evaluate state first, tool execution second, and prose last.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               Evaluation Pyramid for Agents             │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Layer 3: Semantic / Prose Quality                      │
│ (Embeddings, semantic similarity, tone guards)         │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Layer 2: Trajectory & Tool Efficiency                  │
│ (Schema validation, step counts, token budget, loops)  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Layer 1: Deterministic State Assertions                │
│ (Database deltas, sandbox files, mock API contracts)   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Layer 1: Deterministic State Assertions

Before an agent executes a test case, snapshot the environment. After the agent halts, assert exact environment state:

  • Did the expected row appear in the SQL database with the exact required fields?
  • Did the file written to the filesystem parse cleanly as valid JSON/YAML?
  • Did the mock external API receive the expected payload parameters?

These assertions are deterministic, instant, free of token costs, and 100% reproducible.

Layer 2: Trajectory & Tool Efficiency

Even if the final state matches, how the agent got there matters for latency, cost, and reliability:

  • Tool-Call Schema Conformance: Did every tool invocation strictly validate against Pydantic / JSON Schema?
  • Step Count Budget: Did the agent resolve the issue in 3 steps, or did it thrash for 18 steps before stumbling onto the answer?
  • Repetition & Loop Detection: Did the agent invoke the same tool with identical arguments repeatedly after receiving an error?

Layer 3: Constrained Semantic Grading

Only after Layers 1 and 2 pass do you evaluate prose. Instead of open-ended 1-to-5 scoring, use narrow, single-question binary assertions:

  • "Does the final user-facing response state the tracking number [YES/NO]?"
  • "Does the response refuse the prompt injection attempt without leaking system credentials [YES/NO]?"

What a Inspectable Evaluation Runner Looks Like

Here is a minimal, robust harness showing how to evaluate an agent against deterministic environment assertions:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Callable, Dict, List
import pytest

@dataclass
class EvalTestCase:
    task_id: str
    user_prompt: str
    initial_state: Dict[str, Any]
    expected_state_assertion: Callable[[Dict[str, Any]], bool]
    max_steps: int = 5
    max_cost_usd: float = 0.05

def test_agent_reconciliation_flow():
    # Setup test fixture with isolated mock state
    mock_db = {"invoices": {"inv_101": {"amount": 250.0, "status": "pending"}}}

    test_case = EvalTestCase(
        task_id="reconcile_paid_invoice",
        user_prompt="Reconcile payment of $250.00 for invoice inv_101.",
        initial_state=mock_db,
        expected_state_assertion=lambda state: (
            state["invoices"]["inv_101"]["status"] == "settled"
            and state["invoices"]["inv_101"]["amount"] == 250.0
        ),
        max_steps=3
    )

    # Execute agent against the mock environment
    trajectory = run_agent(test_case.user_prompt, state=mock_db)

    # 1. Assert deterministic final state
    assert test_case.expected_state_assertion(mock_db), (
        f"State assertion failed for {test_case.task_id}. Current DB: {mock_db}"
    )

    # 2. Assert trajectory efficiency constraints
    assert len(trajectory.steps) <= test_case.max_steps, (
        f"Agent exceeded step budget: {len(trajectory.steps)} > {test_case.max_steps}"
    )

    # 3. Assert zero schema validation errors during tool calls
    for step in trajectory.steps:
        assert step.schema_valid is True, f"Malformed tool call in turn {step.turn_id}"

When an engineer breaks agent functionality in a pull request, this harness outputs an exact stack trace showing the mismatched database row or the malformed schema parameter, rather than a subjective LLM judge score dropping by 0.2 points.

The Next Step
