title: Capture and Resolve API Errors: Node.js Error Tracking for Pricing Rollouts
description:
Pricing rule rollouts should be observable as decisions, not just exceptions. Capture a stable request fingerprint, the rule version, flag state, tenant-safe cohort, and trace context at the API boundary; then connect that event to metrics and a replayable timeline. The deciding constraint in healthtech is incident reconstruction: an error report that says 500 is not enough to explain which price was calculated, under which rule, and why the request took that path.

TL;DR: Put structured error events at the boundary of the pricing operation, redact sensitive fields before export, and record the same bounded dimensions in metrics. Keep the event payload small. Keep the decision context durable. A useful record lets an engineer answer three questions without guessing: what failed, who was affected, and which rollout state produced it.

The before-and-after mental model

The weak model is a stack trace with a timestamp. It is quick to emit and hard to use. During an incident, someone has to join that trace to deployment logs, feature-flag audit records, request logs, and a database snapshot. Those sources rarely share the same identifier or clock precision.

The stronger model is a short chain:

request -> pricing decision -> error event -> metric -> trace timeline

The request carries a correlation identifier. The pricing decision records the rule revision and evaluated flag state. The error event records the failure class and a safe cohort key. The metric shows whether failures cluster by endpoint, rule revision, or cohort. The trace supplies timing across the API, flag evaluation, and pricing dependency.

Keep it boring.

That separation matters. OpenTelemetry describes metrics as a signal for measurements collected over time, which makes them useful for rates and distributions rather than for storing a full exception object. Keep high-cardinality context, such as an internal request identifier, in logs or traces. Use bounded dimensions in metrics.

For a healthtech pricing endpoint, the event might contain ruleRevision: "pricing-2026-04", flagState: "new-rule", and cohort: "pilot-a". It should not contain a patient name, diagnosis, full address, payment credential, or an unfiltered request body. The safe context is the context an on-call engineer needs to reconstruct the decision.

What should an API error event contain?

Start at the boundary. Error handling scattered across controllers produces inconsistent records: one path has a status code, another has a message, and a third serializes an entire exception. A single boundary handler can enforce the contract and apply redaction once.

type PricingContext = {
  ruleRevision: string;
  flagState: 'control' | 'new-rule';
  cohort: string;
};

type ErrorEvent = {
  eventName: 'pricing_api_error';
  requestId: string;
  route: string;
  method: string;
  status: number;
  errorType: string;
  retryable: boolean;
  pricing: PricingContext;
  traceId?: string;
};

function makePricingErrorEvent(
  error: unknown,
  request: { id: string; method: string; route: string; traceId?: string },
  pricing: PricingContext
): ErrorEvent {
  const knownError = error instanceof PricingDependencyError;

  return {
    eventName: 'pricing_api_error',
    requestId: request.id,
    route: request.route,
    method: request.method,
    status: knownError ? 503 : 500,
    errorType: knownError ? 'pricing_dependency_timeout' : 'unexpected_error',
    retryable: knownError,
    pricing,
    traceId: request.traceId
  };
}

class PricingDependencyError extends Error {}

The important part is the contract, not the class names. errorType is a bounded vocabulary. ruleRevision is deployable and searchable. flagState describes the evaluated state, not the flag's configured name alone. cohort is retained in the event because it can be necessary for reconstruction, but it should not automatically become a metric label.

Do not log the raw exception message by default. Messages often absorb upstream payloads. Classify known errors, attach a sanitized cause code, and keep the original exception available only in a controlled diagnostic path. A healthtech log pipeline should treat redaction as a data boundary, not a formatting preference.

How do you reconstruct a failed rollout?

Imagine the new rule is enabled for pilot-a. The API returns intermittent 500 responses for one pricing operation. The incident timeline should be readable without opening a patient record.

First, group errors by ruleRevision, flagState, errorType, and route. If failures appear only under pricing-2026-04, the flag state is a strong lead. It is not proof. A dependency timeout could affect both control and new-rule traffic, so compare both populations.

Next, follow one requestId through the trace and structured logs. Confirm that the request reached the intended rule evaluator, that the evaluator returned the recorded state, and that the pricing dependency saw the same trace. A mismatch means the telemetry contract is broken even if the endpoint response is correct.

Finally, compare the error event with the API response policy. A retryable dependency timeout should have a retryable classification and an appropriate response status. An invalid rule should fail closed according to the service's domain policy. The error event documents the decision path; it is not a second source of pricing truth. If the request says flagState: "new-rule" but the trace shows a control calculation, stop investigating the pricing formula first. The telemetry contract has already exposed a rollout problem, and the next check is the boundary where that context was copied or changed.

Dimension Question it answers
ruleRevision Did one rule revision introduce the pattern?
flagState Is the pattern limited to the rollout path?
errorType Is this validation, dependency, or unknown failure?
route Is one API operation affected?
requestId and traceId Can one failure be reconstructed end to end?

This is where before and after diverge. Before, the on-call engineer searches for a timestamp. After, the engineer tests a hypothesis. That difference reduces the chance of disabling a rollout that was only coincidentally near an unrelated dependency failure.

What will break this design in production?

The first trap is cardinality. A unique user, patient, invoice, or request identifier is valuable in an event and dangerous as a metric label. Metrics aggregate. Logs and traces provide lookup paths. Mixing those jobs creates noisy time series and a dashboard that cannot answer a simpler question.

The second trap is inconsistent flag capture. If the flag is evaluated in one module and errors are recorded in another, pass the evaluated context explicitly. Reading the flag again inside the error handler can produce a different answer after a configuration change. Record the value used by the pricing decision.

The third trap is retry duplication. A client or gateway can retry the same operation. Each attempt may be a real infrastructure event, but the business incident may be one failed operation. Include an attempt number or idempotency reference when the protocol provides one, and decide whether your alert counts attempts or operations.

The fourth trap is over-alerting on raw exception volume. Alert on a bounded signal that represents user impact: an elevated rate of 5xx responses, a sustained retryable dependency error rate, or a rollout cohort crossing a defined failure threshold. The exact threshold belongs to the service's traffic and risk profile; it should not be copied from a generic example.

I initially treated the stack trace as the center of error tracking. The correction was operational, not stylistic: incident reconstruction needs the decision inputs beside the failure classification. The stack trace became supporting evidence instead of the only clue.

Which trade-offs should the team choose?

A full trace on every successful pricing request may be unnecessary, while sampling every failed request can hide the context needed to understand a rare issue. Retain error events that pass the privacy filter, align trace sampling with error status when the tracing system supports it, and sample routine successes according to traffic needs. Document the policy so engineers know why a trace is absent.

There is also a tension between rich context and minimal data. Store a stable cohort key and rule revision, not a copied business object. Keep correlation IDs opaque. Apply retention by signal: high-volume metrics can outlive verbose events, while sensitive event payloads need a shorter and more deliberate retention period.

A small contract test catches regressions. Send one synthetic request through the control path and one through the new-rule path, force a known dependency error, and assert that the emitted event has the expected bounded fields and no prohibited body fields. Run it alongside the pricing service tests. Observability code is production behavior. It deserves a test.

The result is a rollout process with an evidence trail: flag evaluation, pricing revision, request correlation, classified failure, bounded metric, and trace timing. That trail supports a rollback decision without exposing clinical data or turning telemetry into a shadow database.

References

  • OpenTelemetry, “Metrics signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • OpenTelemetry, “Signals”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/
  • W3C, “Trace Context”: https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/
  • MDN Web Docs, “HTTP response status codes”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status
  • Node.js documentation, “Diagnostics Channel”: https://nodejs.org/api/diagnostics_channel.html

title: How to Handle Retries for Failed User Reminders Using Node.js Queue Workers
description:
Short answer: to handle retries for failed user reminders using Node.js, put each weekly learner digest on a queue, retry only transient failures with a finite policy, and send exhausted messages to a dead-letter queue. Make the worker idempotent because a standard queue can deliver the same reminder more than once.

For a one-person SaaS, the useful decision rule is narrow: choose the queue whose delivery boundary you can operate. I would evaluate Infrai when the service needs a plain HTTP handoff and does not need workflow joins or a long replay log. The queue can retry a delivery. The worker still owns the decision that prevents a duplicate email.

Which delivery boundary fits a weekly digest?

Option Where it is strong Boundary to accept Fit for this job
RabbitMQ Explicit acknowledgements, requeueing, and dead-letter exchanges Broker topology and lifecycle become your responsibility Teams that need detailed routing control
Amazon SQS Managed queues, visibility timeouts, and dead-letter queues AWS operations and queue semantics shape the design AWS-first products
BullMQ Delayed jobs and a Node.js-oriented worker API Redis becomes part of the reliability boundary Teams already running Redis
Infrai queues Queue operations through one REST surface, with no SDK to install It is not a workflow engine or a Kafka-style replay log Small services with an HTTP integration boundary

The recommendation is conditional. Try Infrai for the queue handoff when a small edtech service can call HTTPS, needs bounded retries for a weekly digest, and wants to outsource client-library maintenance. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That lowers the cost of checking a request contract from a Node worker or another language.

There is a second, different benefit for a one-person team. Infrai's verified breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, with one bill. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so I can inspect a capability before adding another integration. The same single key means the reminder worker does not need a new credential or a separate reconciliation task for every adjacent backend capability. It is an operational simplification, not proof that the queue is better than RabbitMQ or SQS.

Choose RabbitMQ when exchanges and routing rules are central. Choose SQS when managed AWS controls are the hard requirement. Choose BullMQ when Redis and its Node ecosystem are already in the stack. The right answer is the failure boundary you are willing to own.

How should I handle retries for failed user reminders using queues?

Start with a state transition. A weekly job creates one message per active customer. A worker consumes it and classifies the outcome:

  • A provider timeout, temporary network failure, or rate limit is retryable.
  • A malformed recipient or invalid payload is not retryable.
  • An exhausted retry goes to the dead-letter queue for review or manual intervention.

The retry count must be finite. Five attempts is a reasonable starting policy, but the product deadline matters more than the number. For example, if Monday's digest is still failing on Sunday night, another retry may compete with the next week's batch and confuse the learner. A digest that arrives after the next weekly issue may be worse than a controlled miss, so give messages an expiration window, record why an attempt stopped, and let support see the dead-letter entry. The failure policy is part of the customer promise, not just a queue setting.

The queue should enforce the delay. Do not keep a Node.js worker asleep while it waits. Infrai delayed messages are limited to 7 days, message bodies to 256 KB, and retention to 30 days. A standard queue is at-least-once, so requeueing is never a substitute for idempotency.

Here is the decision loop with the HTTP handoff included. It is runnable TypeScript and makes the delivery contract visible before you map retry and dead-letter to queue operations.

type Reminder = {
  id: string;
  customerId: string;
  recipient: string;
  attempt: number;
  expiresAt: number;
};

type Action = "ack" | "retry" | "dead-letter";

type DeliveryError = Error & { status?: number };

function classify(error: unknown, attempt: number): Action {
  if (attempt >= 5) return "dead-letter";

  const status = error instanceof Error
    ? (error as DeliveryError).status ?? 0
    : 0;

  if (status === 408 || status === 429 || status >= 500 || status === 0) {
    return "retry";
  }
  return "dead-letter";
}

function retryDelayMs(attempt: number): number {
  return Math.min(60_000, 1_000 * 2 ** Math.max(0, attempt - 1));
}

async function publishToInfrai(payload: unknown, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(`queue publish failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : Math.min(30_000, 1_000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }

  throw new Error("queue publish exhausted its retries");
}

async function processReminder(
  reminder: Reminder,
  sendOnce: (reminder: Reminder, idempotencyKey: string) => Promise<void>,
  record: (action: Action, reminder: Reminder, delayMs?: number) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<void> {
  if (Date.now() >= reminder.expiresAt) {
    await record("dead-letter", reminder);
    return;
  }

  try {
    await sendOnce(reminder, reminder.id);
    await record("ack", reminder);
  } catch (error) {
    const action = classify(error, reminder.attempt);
    await record(
      action,
      reminder,
      action === "retry" ? retryDelayMs(reminder.attempt) : undefined,
    );
  }
}

const reminder: Reminder = {
  id: "digest-2026-week-43-customer-17",
  customerId: "customer-17",
  recipient: "learner@example.edu",
  attempt: 1,
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 6 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1_000,
};

await publishToInfrai(reminder, reminder.id);

await processReminder(
  reminder,
  async (item, idempotencyKey) => {
    console.log("send once", { id: item.id, idempotencyKey });
  },
  async (action, item, delayMs) => {
    console.log({ action, id: item.id, delayMs });
  },
);

The same id must survive every retry. In the real sender, use it as the provider's idempotency key or check a durable delivery record before sending. A retry that creates a fresh identity is a duplicate-email generator.

That is the trade-off.

What makes a reminder retry safe?

There is an uncomfortable ordering choice. Mark the database row as sent before the provider call and a timeout can lose the reminder. Call the provider first and a lost response can produce a duplicate. Use the provider's idempotency feature when available; otherwise make the delivery record and the send boundary explicit in the design. The queue cannot solve that uncertainty for you.

Log the message ID, customer ID, attempt, action, error class, and next retry time. I would rather inspect five useful lifecycle records than one giant stack trace. The log should answer whether the fifth attempt failed or whether the same malformed message looped because every exception was treated as transient.

Do not let the worker implement its own unbounded retry loop. It should classify, acknowledge, requeue with a delay, or dead-letter. The queue owns redelivery timing. The worker owns idempotency. The dead-letter path owns human review.

When is a specialist better?

This design has clear limitations. The scheduling surface does not provide DAG or join primitives. It does not provide Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. Cron executions are capped at 900 seconds, so long work should be a cron trigger that enqueues a job and a worker that consumes it. Push targets must be publicly reachable over HTTPS, and a private endpoint will not receive them. There is no native debounce or throttle.

That is where the alternatives win. RabbitMQ is the better boundary when routing topology is a core feature. SQS is better when the team wants AWS-managed queue operations and its visibility-timeout model. BullMQ is better when Redis is already the shared operational dependency. A workflow product such as Temporal is the better choice when this digest is one step in a durable multi-stage process with joins. Those are real trade-offs, not footnotes: a specialist is the better choice when its native guarantee is the requirement.

For the smaller case, Infrai is worth trying: a weekly edtech digest, a Node.js worker, bounded retry rules, and a team that values an HTTP surface plus one credential across backend capabilities. The recommendation stops there. If the system needs long-lived workflow history, fan-out aggregation, or specialist broker routing, use the specialist.

If that boundary matches your system, start with the Node.js queue retry and dead-letter guide.

References

  • RabbitMQ dead letter exchanges
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • BullMQ retrying failing jobs
  • Temporal retry policies

title: MongoDB vs Postgres JSONB in 2026: Inserts, Lookups, Updates and Storage, Benchmarked
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Most "MongoDB vs Postgres JSONB" debates are fought with benchmarks from 2014 and opinions from Twitter. I run both in my day job and side projects, so I put the current versions, MongoDB 9.0.4 (released October 13, 2026) and PostgreSQL 18.6, on the same VM, loaded the same 200,000 order documents into each, and measured the things a real app does all day: inserts, lookups by an indexed field, containment filters, partial updates of nested fields, aggregations and disk usage.

The short version: neither one wins everywhere. Postgres answered B-tree indexed reads more than twice as fast through the Node.js drivers, but MongoDB loaded data almost 4x faster, updated nested fields about 50% faster and used 5.6x less disk. And one index choice that most JSONB tutorials recommend, a GIN index on the whole document, turned out to be the most expensive line in my Postgres schema.

TL;DR: MongoDB vs Postgres JSONB

If your app is relational with some flexible fields, keep it in Postgres and index the JSONB paths you query with B-tree expression indexes, not one big GIN index. If your data really is documents that get written and updated a lot, and disk or cache size matters, MongoDB did that work faster and far more compactly in my tests.

200,000 docs, 16 clients (median of 3) PostgreSQL 18.6 JSONB MongoDB 9.0.4
Bulk insert, 1,000 per batch 12,337 docs/s 46,448 docs/s
Single inserts 24,594 docs/s 18,506 docs/s
Point lookup by orderNo 44,701 ops/s (B-tree), 29,417 (GIN) 19,139 ops/s
Latest 10 orders of a customer 19,322 ops/s 8,855 ops/s
Containment filter, LIMIT 20 2,531 ops/s 4,605 ops/s
Count of 1,411 matching docs 2,094 ops/s 1,067 ops/s
Nested field update 16,786 ops/s 24,603 ops/s
Append to an array 16,542 ops/s 26,755 ops/s
Revenue by country (full scan) 182.8 ms 154.6 ms
Top 10 SKUs (unwind items) 161.3 ms 283.1 ms
Disk: data + indexes after load 308.4 MB 55.2 MB
Disk after 1.5 to 2.3 million updates 1,231.5 MB 138.8 MB

How I tested

Everything ran on one Linux VM: 8 vCPUs (Intel Xeon, KVM), 16 GB of RAM, Debian 13. The databases and the Node.js client shared the machine and talked over loopback TCP, so there's no network latency in these numbers. The VM is shared with other workloads, so I logged the load average and free memory with every result and re-ran everything after one early run stalled (more in the limitations).

  • PostgreSQL 18.6 (PGDG build) in its own cluster with shared_buffers = 512MB, max_wal_size = 4GB and otherwise default settings, including fsync = on and synchronous_commit = on.
  • MongoDB 9.0.4 Community, the official Debian 12 tarball, as a standalone server with --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 0.5 so both databases got the same 512 MB of cache. Everything else default: snappy compression, journaling on, default write concern.
  • Node.js 22.20.0 with pg 8.23.1 and mongodb 7.7.0, the latest npm releases on October 29, 2026.
  • Data: 200,000 generated e-commerce orders from a seeded random generator, the same documents for both databases. Each order has a customer, status, total, tags, a nested shipping object, 1 to 5 line items and an events array. That's about 770 bytes as JSON, 979 bytes per row as JSONB and 806 bytes as BSON.
  • Method: 16 concurrent clients (a 16-connection pool on both sides) in a closed loop for 10 seconds per test, 3 runs per test, and I report the median. Aggregations ran 5 times per run.

Every query I timed returned the same answer on both databases: for example, both found exactly 1,411 orders that are shipped, going to the UAE and tagged gift, and both aggregations returned identical totals.

The schema and the indexes

Postgres gets one jsonb column plus an identity key. To compare the two ways people index JSONB, I created both: a GIN index over the whole document and B-tree expression indexes on the fields the app looks up.

```sql title="postgres.sql"
CREATE TABLE orders (
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
doc jsonb NOT NULL
);
-- one index for any containment query (@>)
CREATE INDEX orders_gin ON orders USING gin (doc jsonb_path_ops);
-- B-tree expression indexes for the hot lookups
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX orders_orderno ON orders ((doc->>'orderNo'));
CREATE INDEX orders_customer ON orders
(((doc->>'customerId')::int), (doc->>'createdAt') DESC);






```js title="mongo-indexes.js"
db.orders.createIndex({ orderNo: 1 }, { unique: true });
db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 });
db.orders.createIndex({ status: 1, "shipping.country": 1 });
db.orders.createIndex({ tags: 1 });

Two things to know about the Postgres side. The query has to match the index: doc->>'orderNo' = $1 uses the B-tree, doc @> '{"orderNo": "..."}' uses the GIN index, and neither one can use the other's index. And JSONB has no date type, so createdAt is an ISO 8601 string. It sorts correctly as text, but in MongoDB it's a real Date.

Insert throughput

Inserts (median of 3) PostgreSQL 18.6 MongoDB 9.0.4
Bulk, 1,000 docs per call, all indexes 12,337 docs/s 46,448 docs/s
Bulk, without the GIN index 26,918 docs/s not applicable
Single inserts, 16 clients, defaults 24,594 docs/s (p50 0.485 ms) 18,506 docs/s (p50 0.571 ms)
Single inserts, synchronous_commit = off / { j: true } 31,459 docs/s 16,070 docs/s

For bulk loads MongoDB was 3.8x faster: 200,000 orders in 4.3 seconds against 16.2 seconds for Postgres with a multi-row INSERT ... SELECT unnest($1::jsonb[]). Half of the Postgres cost was the GIN index. Without it the same load ran at 26,918 docs/s, 2.2x faster.

Single inserts flipped the result. With 16 clients each inserting one document at a time, Postgres did 24,594 per second with every commit flushed to the WAL. Postgres groups concurrent commits into one flush, which is why durability cost it so little here. MongoDB's default write concern gave 18,506 inserts per second, and asking it to wait for the journal on every insert ({ j: true }) gave 16,070.

Point lookups: GIN vs B-tree expression index vs MongoDB index

Fetching one order by its unique orderNo is the most common query in most apps.

Lookup by orderNo (median of 3) 16 clients 1 client, p50 1 client, p99
Postgres, B-tree expression index (->>) 44,701 ops/s 0.057 ms 0.316 ms
Postgres, GIN jsonb_path_ops (@>) 29,417 ops/s 0.123 ms 0.506 ms
MongoDB, { orderNo: 1 } index 19,139 ops/s 0.076 ms 0.377 ms

The B-tree expression index was the fastest way to find one document in either database, and 52% faster than the GIN index on the same table. EXPLAIN shows why: the B-tree query is a plain index scan, while the GIN query is a bitmap index scan plus a bitmap heap scan with a recheck, and the planner guessed 20 matching rows for a unique value because it has no real statistics for containment. With GIN you also pay for an index that covers every key and value in the document.

MongoDB's own query planner used its fast EXPRESS_IXSCAN path, and with one client its p50 (0.076 ms) sat between the two Postgres indexes. With 16 clients it delivered less than half the throughput of the B-tree. I didn't profile the client side, but part of the gap is likely decoding: pg hands JSONB to V8's native JSON.parse, while the MongoDB driver decodes BSON in JavaScript.

Customer feed: the latest 10 orders

A compound index on customer and date, then ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10. Both databases read the index backwards from the newest entry and stopped after 10 rows.

Latest 10 orders for a random customer Ops/s p50 p99
Postgres, expression index on (customerId::int, createdAt DESC) 19,322 0.67 ms 2.40 ms
MongoDB, { customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 } 8,855 1.55 ms 4.50 ms

Postgres returned the 10 documents 2.2x faster. Same pattern as the point lookups: when the access path is a known B-tree, Postgres plus pg moved more rows per second.

Containment filters and counts

Now an ad-hoc filter: orders with a given status, shipping country and tag, such as shipped to the UAE with the gift tag. In Postgres that's one @> against the GIN index. In MongoDB it's a normal filter that used the { status, shipping.country } index and checked tags on the fetched documents.

SELECT doc FROM orders
WHERE doc @> '{"status": "shipped", "shipping": {"country": "AE"}, "tags": ["gift"]}'
LIMIT 20;

db.orders.find({ status: "shipped", "shipping.country": "AE", tags: "gift" }).limit(20);
Filter on 3 fields (4 rotating filters) Postgres GIN @> MongoDB
First 20 matches 2,531 ops/s (p50 5.76 ms) 4,605 ops/s (p50 2.86 ms)
Count all matches (1,411 for the UAE filter) 2,094 ops/s (p50 6.83 ms) 1,067 ops/s (p50 14.21 ms)

MongoDB was 1.8x faster at returning the first 20, because it can walk the compound index and stop as soon as it has 20 documents. Postgres builds a bitmap from the GIN index for all matches before it reads the first row, so LIMIT 20 saves less. For a full count Postgres was 2x faster: the GIN index matched all three conditions at once, while MongoDB had to fetch every shipped UAE order to check its tags. A tags field in MongoDB's compound index would change that, and so would a B-tree on the hot fields in Postgres. The point is that GIN gives you decent speed on any combination of fields without planning indexes, not the best speed on any one of them.

Partial nested updates

Updating one nested field is where the two storage engines differ the most. Here are three updates by orderNo: set shipping.status and updatedAt, push an event onto the events array, and increment a counter.

-- Postgres
UPDATE orders
SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{shipping,status}', to_jsonb($2::text))
WHERE doc->>'orderNo' = $1;

UPDATE orders
SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{events}',
  (doc->'events') || jsonb_build_array(jsonb_build_object('type', $2::text, 'at', now())))
WHERE doc->>'orderNo' = $1;

// MongoDB
db.orders.updateOne({ orderNo }, { $set: { "shipping.status": status, updatedAt: new Date() } });
db.orders.updateOne({ orderNo }, { $push: { events: { type: "note", at: new Date() } } });
db.orders.updateOne({ orderNo }, { $inc: { views: 1 } });
Updates by orderNo, 16 clients (median of 3) Postgres, all indexes Postgres, no GIN MongoDB
Set a nested field 16,786 ops/s 22,979 ops/s 24,603 ops/s
Append to an array 16,542 ops/s 22,154 ops/s 26,755 ops/s
Increment a counter 17,604 ops/s 23,298 ops/s 26,638 ops/s

MongoDB was about 50% faster than Postgres with the full set of indexes. jsonb_set reads like a partial update, but Postgres stores JSONB as one value, so every update writes a complete new copy of the row. Worse, it can't be a HOT (heap-only tuple) update once any index is built on an expression over doc, because Postgres only knows the indexed column changed. I checked this on a small table: 5,000 jsonb_set updates gave 0 HOT updates with a doc->>'orderNo' index and 2,215 without it. So every update also inserts new entries into every index, including the GIN index, which holds an entry for every value in the document. Dropping the GIN index made Postgres updates 32 to 37% faster and closed most of the gap.

Aggregations

Two reports over all 200,000 orders: revenue and order count per shipping country for shipped and delivered orders, and the 10 best-selling SKUs, which needs unwinding the items array.

SELECT doc->'shipping'->>'country' AS country, count(*) AS n,
       sum((doc->>'total')::numeric) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE doc->>'status' IN ('shipped', 'delivered')
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 3 DESC;

SELECT i->>'sku' AS sku, sum((i->>'qty')::int) AS qty
FROM orders, jsonb_array_elements(doc->'items') AS i
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC, 1 LIMIT 10;

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: { $in: ["shipped", "delivered"] } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$shipping.country", n: { $sum: 1 }, revenue: { $sum: "$total" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
]);
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $group: { _id: "$items.sku", qty: { $sum: "$items.qty" } } },
  { $sort: { qty: -1, _id: 1 } },
  { $limit: 10 },
]);
Full-collection aggregation (median of 3 x 5 runs) Postgres 18.6 MongoDB 9.0.4
Revenue by country (70% of orders match) 182.8 ms 154.6 ms
Top 10 SKUs (about 600,000 line items) 161.3 ms 283.1 ms

A split result. The grouped sum was close (MongoDB took 15% less time, which is inside the run-to-run noise for that Postgres query), and Postgres took 43% less time on the unwind. Postgres used parallel workers for these scans (2 per query by default) and still had to parse ->> paths and cast text to numeric for every row. EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed the revenue query sorting on disk with the default work_mem of 4 MB, which I left untuned. If reports like this matter, move the summed fields into real columns, or raise work_mem for the reporting role.

Storage size

After loading 200,000 orders PostgreSQL 18.6 MongoDB 9.0.4
Table / collection data 212.6 MB 45.6 MB (161.2 MB before compression)
Indexes 95.7 MB (GIN 71.9 MB) 9.7 MB
Total 308.4 MB 55.2 MB
Total without the GIN index 236.5 MB not applicable

MongoDB used 5.6x less disk. WiredTiger compresses collections with snappy and indexes with prefix compression by default, so 161 MB of BSON became 46 MB. Postgres only compresses a JSONB value when it's bigger than about 2 KB (the TOAST threshold), and these documents averaged 979 bytes, so none were compressed. The GIN index alone was larger than MongoDB's collection and all five of its indexes together.

Then I ran the update tests from the previous section and measured again. Those runs also grew the documents (new events, a views counter, an updatedAt field), so average document size went up by about a fifth in both databases.

After the update tests PostgreSQL, all indexes PostgreSQL, no GIN MongoDB
Updates applied 1,461,709 2,128,223 2,308,992
Total size 1,231.5 MB 627.0 MB 138.8 MB
Of which indexes 512.2 MB (GIN 466.0 MB) 50.6 MB 9.7 MB

Postgres grew 4x with autovacuum running at default settings, and the GIN index grew 6.5x to 466 MB even though no indexed value changed. MongoDB's indexes stayed the same size, because updating fields that aren't indexed doesn't touch its indexes. Its collection grew to 129.1 MB, of which 67.4 MB was free space WiredTiger will reuse. Postgres will reuse its dead space too after vacuum, but a heavily updated JSONB table with a whole-document GIN index needs much more disk and cache than the same data in MongoDB.

The same operations in Node.js

This is the module I used to check that each query does the same thing in both databases. A test inserted 3 orders, ran every function against both and asserted identical results. It passed.

```ts title="orders.mjs"
import pg from "pg";
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.PG_URL });
const mongo = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGO_URL);
const orders = mongo.db("shop").collection("orders");

// Insert
export const pgInsert = (doc) => pool.query("INSERT INTO orders (doc) VALUES ($1)", [doc]);
export const mgInsert = (doc) => orders.insertOne(doc);

// Point lookup: ->> matches the B-tree expression index; @> would go to GIN
export const pgByOrderNo = async (no) =>
(await pool.query("SELECT doc FROM orders WHERE doc->>'orderNo' = $1", [no])).rows[0]?.doc;
export const mgByOrderNo = (no) => orders.findOne({ orderNo: no });

// Customer feed: latest 10 orders
export const pgFeed = async (customerId) => (await pool.query(
SELECT doc FROM orders WHERE (doc->>'customerId')::int = $1
ORDER BY doc->>'createdAt' DESC LIMIT 10, [customerId])).rows.map((r) => r.doc);
export const mgFeed = (customerId) =>
orders.find({ customerId }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(10).toArray();

// Containment filter
export const pgFilter = async (status, country, tag) => (await pool.query(
"SELECT doc FROM orders WHERE doc @> $1::jsonb LIMIT 20",
[JSON.stringify({ status, shipping: { country }, tags: [tag] })])).rows.map((r) => r.doc);
export const mgFilter = (status, country, tag) =>
orders.find({ status, "shipping.country": country, tags: tag }).limit(20).toArray();

// Partial nested update
export const pgShip = (no, status) => pool.query(
UPDATE orders SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{shipping,status}', to_jsonb($2::text))
WHERE doc->>'orderNo' = $1, [no, status]);
export const mgShip = (no, status) =>
orders.updateOne({ orderNo: no }, { $set: { "shipping.status": status } });




Two driver details that cost me time. `pg` serializes a plain object to JSON for a `jsonb` parameter, but a JavaScript `Date` inside it becomes an ISO string, and it comes back as a string. And `pg` returns `numeric` and `count(*)` as strings (`"361.5"`, `"3"`), while MongoDB returns numbers, so convert before you compare or add.

## Which should you choose?

- **Your data is relational and some of it is flexible: Postgres JSONB.** Joins, foreign keys, transactions across tables and SQL reporting still matter more than raw document speed for most apps. Use B-tree expression indexes (or generated columns) for the paths you query often. They were the fastest lookups in this whole test.
- **Add a GIN index only when you need ad-hoc containment queries.** It made any combination of fields queryable, but it halved bulk insert speed, slowed updates by about a quarter and was the biggest object on disk, and it grew fastest under updates. If you only filter on a few known keys, index just those paths, for example a GIN index on `(doc->'tags')` queried with `doc->'tags' @> '["gift"]'`. It should cost far less, though I didn't measure that variant.
- **Your data is documents that get written and updated all day: MongoDB.** It loaded 3.8x faster, updated nested fields about 50% faster and stored the same orders in 18% of the space, which also means more of your working set fits in RAM.
- **Updates are frequent and documents are large: avoid whole-document rewrites in Postgres.** Put fast-changing fields like status, counters and timestamps in normal columns next to the JSONB, so updates can be HOT and don't rewrite every index.

If you're also deciding what else Postgres can absorb, I measured [Postgres full-text search against Elasticsearch and Meilisearch](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/postgres-full-text-search-vs-elasticsearch) and [Postgres job queues against BullMQ on Redis](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/postgres-job-queue-pg-boss-vs-bullmq). For primary keys on big tables, see [UUIDv7 in Postgres](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/uuidv7-postgres), and for the ORM layer, [Drizzle vs Prisma](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/drizzle-vs-prisma).

## Limitations of this benchmark

- One VM, a single node of each database, everything on loopback. No replica set, so MongoDB's write concern never waited for a second node, and Postgres had no replica either. Real networks add a round trip to every call.
- 200,000 documents of under 1 KB each, which fits in RAM. With a working set larger than memory, MongoDB's 5.6x smaller footprint would likely matter even more, but I didn't test that.
- The VM is shared with other workloads. My first full run stalled for about a minute while the VM was almost out of free memory, so I discarded it and re-ran everything. Then MongoDB crashed mid-run because a snapshot agent on the VM dropped a temporary file into its journal folder, so I restarted it with log file removal turned off (`log=(remove=false)`) and re-ran all MongoDB tests from scratch. Most tests stayed within 10% of their median across the 3 runs, but a few varied by up to 47% (one Postgres aggregation run, the GIN lookups and some update runs). That's why I report medians, and why I'd treat any gap under about 20% as noise.
- Node.js drivers on both sides, so client-side decoding (JSON vs BSON) is part of every read number.
- I didn't tune `work_mem`, autovacuum or fillfactor in Postgres, or anything in MongoDB beyond the cache size. I also didn't test transactions, sharding, schema validation or change streams.


---

*Originally published on [fabwaseem.com](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/mongodb-vs-postgres-jsonb).*

title: SQL Pattern Matching Without the Pain: LIKE, Wildcards, and the Gotchas Nobody Warns You About
description:
A practical guide to searching text in SQL using LIKE, wildcards, SUBSTRING and LOWER, with real examples and the mistakes that cost you hours.

Every app I've worked on eventually hits the same moment: someone types a few letters into a search box and expects the right row to show up.

Behind that tiny feature sits one of the oldest tools in SQL: pattern matching. It looks simple, but it has quirks that silently return wrong results, or make a fast query crawl.

In this post I'll walk through pattern matching using a small Employees table, then cover the gotchas I wish someone had told me earlier.

The setup 

CREATE TABLE Employees (
  EmpID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(50),
  Department VARCHAR(50),
  Email VARCHAR(50)
);

INSERT INTO Employees (EmpID, Name, Department, Email) VALUES
  (1, 'Alice Johnson', 'HR',      'alice.johnson@example.com'),
  (2, 'Bob Smith',     'IT',      'bob.smith@example.com'),
  (3, 'Charlie Brown', 'Finance', 'charlie.brown@example.com'),
  (4, 'Diana Prince',  'HR',      'diana.prince@example.com'),
  (5, 'Eve Adams',     'IT',      'eve.adams@example.org');

Five rows is enough. The goal is to understand the patterns, not to stress the database.

The two wildcards you need

LIKE understands exactly two special characters:

Wildcard Meaning
% any number of characters (including zero)
_ exactly one character

Everything else is matched literally. Once that clicks, most of the rest is just where you place them.

1. Starts with, ends with, contains

The position of % tells SQL what you mean.

-- Starts with 'A'
SELECT Name FROM Employees WHERE Name LIKE 'A%';
-- Alice Johnson

-- Ends with 'son'
SELECT Name FROM Employees WHERE Name LIKE '%son';
-- Alice Johnson

-- Contains 'IT'
SELECT Name, Department FROM Employees WHERE Department LIKE '%IT%';
-- Bob Smith (IT), Eve Adams (IT)

A quick way to remember it: the % goes on the side where you don't care what comes next. 'A%' means "I care about the start, anything can follow."

2. Filtering by domain

Pattern matching is great for light data cleaning, like finding emails from one domain:

SELECT Name, Email
FROM Employees
WHERE Email LIKE '%@example.com';

This returns Alice, Bob, Charlie and Diana. Eve is left out because her address ends in .org. Including the @ in the pattern matters. Without it, '%example.com' would also match something like bob@notexample.com.

3. "Second letter is v": two ways

This one is a nice puzzle because there are two valid solutions.

Using a function:

SELECT Name FROM Employees WHERE SUBSTRING(Name, 2, 1) = 'v';

Using the single-character wildcard:

SELECT Name FROM Employees WHERE Name LIKE '_v%';

Both return Eve Adams. Read the second one as: "one any character, then v, then anything."

I prefer the LIKE version. It's shorter, and it reads like the pattern it describes. SUBSTRING is better when you need to compare the extracted piece against something more complex.

4. Case-insensitive matching

Say you want everyone in HR, but your data might contain HR, hr or Hr:

SELECT Name, Department
FROM Employees
WHERE LOWER(Department) LIKE '%hr%';

Lowercasing the column and writing the pattern in lowercase makes the match independent of how the data was typed. You get Alice Johnson and Diana Prince.

The gotchas

Gotcha 1: LIKE isn't case-sensitive everywhere (or case-insensitive everywhere)

This is the biggest source of "works on my machine" bugs.

  • In PostgreSQL, LIKE is case-sensitive. It also has ILIKE for case-insensitive matching.
  • In MySQL and SQL Server, case sensitivity depends on the column's collation, and the common defaults are case-insensitive.
  • In SQLite, LIKE is case-insensitive for plain ASCII letters by default.

That affects the '%IT%' query above. On a case-insensitive setup, it would also match a department named Facilities, because "Facilities" contains "it". If exact case matters, don't rely on the default. Be explicit.

Gotcha 2: Searching for a literal % or _

What if you need to find a value like 50%_off? The wildcards get in your way. Use ESCAPE:

SELECT * FROM Promotions
WHERE Code LIKE '50\%\_off' ESCAPE '\';

The backslash tells SQL to treat the next character literally. Any time user input goes into a LIKE pattern, remember to escape these characters, or users can accidentally (or deliberately) match far more than they intended.

Gotcha 3: A leading % can make queries slow 

WHERE Name LIKE 'Ali%'   -- can use a normal index
WHERE Name LIKE '%ice'   -- usually cannot

With a pattern that starts with a fixed prefix, the database can jump into a regular index. With a leading wildcard, it generally has to scan every row. On five rows you'll never notice. On five million, you will.

If you need fast "contains" search on large tables, look at full-text search, or trigram indexes in PostgreSQL, instead of leaning on LIKE '%...%'.

Gotcha 4: NULL never matches 

SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Email LIKE '%@example.com';

A row where Email is NULL is not returned, and it won't be returned by NOT LIKE either. Comparisons with NULL evaluate to unknown, not true. If you need those rows, handle them with IS NULL or COALESCE.

Which tool should I use?

You want to... Reach for
Match a simple shape (starts, ends, contains) LIKE
Match by position _ or SUBSTRING
Ignore case reliably LOWER() / UPPER() (or ILIKE in PostgreSQL)
Match complex patterns Regex (REGEXP in MySQL, ~ in PostgreSQL)
Search large text quickly Full-text search

Wrapping up

Pattern matching is one of those topics that feels too basic to study, until a search feature returns the wrong rows in production. The core ideas are small:

  1. % means "anything", _ means "exactly one character".
  2. Where you place the wildcard defines the meaning.
  3. Case sensitivity depends on your database, so check it.
  4. Leading wildcards are fine for small data and costly for big data.

Try the queries above on your own data and break them on purpose. Adding a lowercase hr row or a NULL email will teach you more than reading about it.

If this helped, drop a comment with the weirdest LIKE bug you've run into. I'd love to hear it.

title: Building a Behavior-Based Email Welcome Flow Without Complex Automation
description:
Most welcome email systems follow a predictable pattern: subscribe, receive three generic emails, then join a newsletter.

I think we can build something more useful without introducing an expensive automation platform.

Consider an application with 400 newsletter subscribers. Some are beginners, while others already understand your product. Sending identical onboarding messages to both groups wastes an opportunity to personalize communication.

Here's how I would design a lightweight, event-driven welcome sequence with three branches, five possible emails, and a few simple tags.

1. Model Subscribers With Minimal State

I would start with three tags:

  • beginner
  • experienced
  • unengaged

Each subscriber also needs signup time, email preferences, and consent information.

const subscriber = {
  id: "user_123",
  email: "user@example.com",
  tags: [],
  subscribedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  consent: true,
  unsubscribed: false
};

For production, I would persist this information in a database rather than storing it in memory.

2. Email 1: Capture Intent Immediately

My first email delivers whatever someone requested during signup.

Below download link, I would include two options:

  • I'm just starting out.
  • I've been doing this a while.

Each link points to an authenticated preference endpoint.

For example:

GET /preferences?choice=beginner&token=...
GET /preferences?choice=experienced&token=...

One important detail: email security scanners sometimes follow links automatically.

I would therefore show a confirmation page before permanently updating preferences. Tokens must be signed, scoped, and expire after a reasonable period.

Actual preference changes should use a validated POST request.

3. Implement Three Branches

Once preference selection is confirmed, subscriber state determines upcoming emails.

function getWelcomeSchedule(segment) {
  const common = [
    { day: 0, template: "welcome" },
    { day: 8, template: "expectations" },
    { day: 12, template: "next-step" }
  ];

  const branches = {
    beginner: [
      { day: 2, template: "beginner-mistakes" },
      { day: 5, template: "beginner-checklist" }
    ],
    experienced: [
      { day: 2, template: "advanced-tactics" },
      { day: 5, template: "campaign-teardown" }
    ],
    unengaged: [
      { day: 3, template: "preference-reminder" },
      { day: 5, template: "general-example" }
    ]
  };

  return [...common, ...branches[segment]]
    .sort((a, b) => a.day - b.day);
}

This function returns five scheduled messages for any supported segment.

I would initially classify subscribers without a preference as unselected, using unengaged only after a defined inactivity period.

4. Schedule Emails Reliably

For a small application, a queue worker or scheduled job is sufficient.

Every scheduled message should have a unique key:

const jobKey =
  `${subscriber.id}:${templateId}`;

Before sending, I would check:

  1. Has this message already been sent?
  2. Is subscriber consent still valid?
  3. Has someone unsubscribed or reduced frequency?
  4. Has their preferred segment changed?

A database-backed uniqueness constraint and transactional job claiming can prevent duplicate sends across workers.

I would also suppress outdated branch messages whenever preferences change.

5. Measure Actual Engagement

Open tracking is increasingly unreliable because of privacy protections and automated activity.

I prefer measuring confirmed preference selections, meaningful clicks, replies, and unsubscribes.

Consider a hypothetical 400-subscriber cohort:

Segment Subscribers
Beginner 120
Experienced 80
No selection 200

Initial preference selection:

(120 + 80) / 400 * 100 = 50%

If another 20 subscribers choose a preference after receiving a reminder:

220 / 400 * 100 = 55%

That's a five-percentage-point increase in known preferences, not proof of improved revenue or retention.

For accurate reporting, I would exclude detected bot activity and track each cohort separately.

6. Avoid Overengineering

Small mailing lists rarely need complex customer-data infrastructure.

Before selecting an email service provider, I would evaluate automation support, API limits, webhook reliability, and pricing.

For additional platform context, Sprout24 maintains an independent email marketing software comparison directory.

I would also implement unsubscribe handling, bounce processing, retry limits, suppression lists, and relevant email authentication requirements before going live.

Final Thoughts

My preferred architecture is straightforward:

Signup → Welcome Email → Preference Selection → Branch Scheduling → Engagement Measurement

No complicated scoring engine is necessary.

I'd start with explicit user preferences, add behavior-based segmentation only when useful, and improve implementation using real subscriber feedback.

How would you handle preference changes while multiple email jobs are already queued?

Id be interested in comparing approaches using database jobs, queue workers, or serverless functions.

title: Automating tax calculation from Amazon VAT reports: a system design for VAT service providers
description:
For firms that provide cross-border VAT services, the most labor-intensive step usually isn't registration. It's calculating tax every filing period. Sellers send over their Amazon VAT Transactions Report, and accountants sort it in Excel by country, rate and deductible item, then copy the numbers into each country's return. With more countries and more sellers, both the error rate and the turnaround time go up.

We built an online platform for a cross-border tax compliance provider covering VAT registration and agent transfer, tax calculation, filing and payment, EPR and authorized representative services. This article covers only the tax calculation part: how the system turns an Amazon report into numbers ready to file. It should be useful for VAT service providers and tax agents who want to turn their service into a product.

The input: how the Amazon report is structured

The Amazon VAT Transactions Report has one row per transaction. Each row includes the transaction type, who collects the tax (Amazon or the seller), whether the buyer gave a valid VAT number, the ship-from and ship-to countries, the tax rate, gross and net amounts, currency and other fields.

Calculating tax comes down to deciding, for each row, "in which country, as what kind of supply and at what rate is this sale reported", then totaling by country and filing period.

Core design: classify first, then calculate

Instead of writing rules country by country, we first put every transaction into one of 7 sales categories. The classification combines three fields:

  • Tax collector: Amazon collects (as the deemed supplier) or the seller self-reports
  • Buyer VAT number: whether the buyer is a business with a valid VAT number
  • Ship-from / ship-to country: domestic sale, intra-EU cross-border sale or export outside the EU

Combined, these put each transaction into a category such as domestic sale, intra-EU distance sale, supply to a VAT-registered business, export or marketplace-collected. Each category has a fixed treatment: some are charged output tax at the local rate, some are reported at zero rate and listed separately, and for marketplace-collected sales the seller pays no further tax but still has to report them.

The benefit is that country differences collapse into one table of "how each country treats each category", instead of being scattered across hundreds of if-else branches. Adding a country means filling in that table.

The system has built-in cross-border rules for all 27 EU member states. Tax calculation is live for the UK and 8 EU countries: Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and Austria.

Input tax: C79, C88 and PVA

UK import VAT is the part most often missed, so the system handles three kinds of documents separately:

  • C79: the import VAT certificate issued by HMRC, which is the basis for reclaiming import VAT. The system collects C79 amounts per filing period and counts them as input tax
  • C88: the import declaration, used to reconcile import value and tax, and part of the supporting evidence
  • PVA (Postponed VAT Accounting): the seller pays no VAT at import and instead reports the same amount as both output and input tax on the return. The system puts PVA amounts in both boxes; the net effect is zero, but it must be reported

None of these are in the Amazon report, so sellers upload them separately. In the filing workspace they are separate items with reminders when something is missing.

The output: UK VAT Return boxes

The UK VAT Return has fixed boxes (Box 1 to Box 9) for output tax, EU acquisitions tax, input tax, net tax, total sales and purchases, and intra-EU supplies and acquisitions. Once transactions are sorted into the 7 categories and C79 / C88 / PVA are processed, every box can be derived directly, without an accountant reconciling spreadsheets by hand.

For the 8 EU countries, the system outputs totals that match the structure of each country's return.

Currencies and exchange rates

The currency of a transaction in the Amazon report isn't always the filing currency. The system fetches exchange rates daily and converts each transaction at the rate for its date. The rate source and conversion date are stored with each calculation so reviewers can trace them.

Workflow: tax calculation inside the filing workspace

Tax calculation isn't a standalone tool; it's one step in the filing workflow. The workspace moves through these states: awaiting report upload → awaiting tax confirmation → awaiting submission → being filed by the accounting firm → awaiting payment → filed.

  • Seller side: upload the Amazon report and deduction documents, see the calculated tax, confirm and submit
  • Operations side: review calculations and filings, manage payment proofs and receipts, with role permissions and audit logs

With tax calculation inside the workflow, sellers see "how much is due this period and why" instead of an Excel file they have to interpret themselves.

Engineering safeguards

Mistakes in tax data are expensive, so we put several safeguards in place:

  • 20 end-to-end automated tests covering the main calculation paths
  • A database schema comparison before each release so migrations don't drop fields
  • Calculation results keep the mapping from original rows to totals, so a reviewer can trace any total back to individual transactions

The platform went through 300+ iterations in about 4 months, with about 44 business pages, 77 API endpoints and 19 data models. The stack is React 19 + TypeScript + Koa + MySQL, with Alibaba Cloud for OCR and object storage.

Advice for VAT service providers

If you're thinking about turning manual tax calculation into a system, start here:

  1. Write your tax rules as a "category × country" table first. It takes no code, but it exposes the gray areas in your rules
  2. Model deduction documents separately from marketplace reports; they come from different sources on different cycles
  3. Make every result traceable to individual rows, so reviewers are willing to sign off
  4. Start with the UK and one or two EU countries, get the workflow running, then add countries

FXTech is an e-commerce technology agency and Shopify Partner based in Shenzhen, China. We build VAT compliance systems for VAT service providers, tax agents and cross-border e-commerce teams (we don't file taxes ourselves), and also build Shopify stores and headless DTC storefronts and optimize web performance. Case study: https://fxweb.dev/cases/#vat-compliance-saas . VAT solutions: https://fxweb.dev/vat/ .

title: Node.js Audio Transcriptions 503 — Portable Fallback Boundaries for Marketplace Moderation
description:
Short answer: treat 503 Service Unavailable and model available: false as two different facts, then make the fallback decision from a capability registry rather than from the HTTP status alone. In a marketplace moderation pipeline, the durable boundary is a provider-neutral transcription request and a stored result envelope; the provider adapter owns readiness checks, timeout policy, and translation of errors.

This is a boundary problem before it is a client-library problem.

That separation matters because an OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/transcriptions route can be reachable while the selected transcription model is not ready for that request. Retrying the same route blindly turns a temporary readiness signal into queue pressure. A fallback that changes providers without recording why also makes moderation audits difficult.

The decision rule I would put in the architecture record is narrow: retry a request only when the adapter can identify a transient condition and the operation is safe to repeat; use another provider only when its capability, region, audio constraints, and data policy have already been verified; otherwise keep the report pending for human review. No silent downgrade.

What does “model available: false” actually mean?

It is a readiness result, not a diagnosis of the whole service. The route may accept authentication and parse the multipart request while the model pool, deployment, or capacity allocation behind it cannot serve the requested operation. A 503 is likewise a service-availability response, not proof that the audio is malformed. RFC 9110 defines 503 as a temporary inability to handle the request and permits a Retry-After indication, but the client still has to decide whether repeating the operation is appropriate.

For moderation, I separate four states in storage: accepted, transcribing, waiting, and failed_permanently. waiting carries a reason such as provider_model_unavailable; it does not pretend that the transcript is empty. The distinction is operationally small and legally useful. An empty transcript can look like a user submitted no speech, while a waiting record says the system has not reached a conclusion.

The same request can fail at several boundaries:

Boundary Observable signal Correct interpretation Next action
Client validation 4xx before provider work File, auth, or request contract needs correction Do not retry unchanged
Route availability 503 or timeout before a result Provider may be temporarily unable to serve Apply bounded retry policy
Model readiness available: false, unavailable deployment, or capacity response This model cannot serve now Consult capability registry, then fallback or wait
Content result Successful response with low confidence or empty text A transcription exists but may need review Store provenance and use moderation policy

The table is deliberately boring. Boring boundaries survive incidents.

That is intentional.

How should a Node.js-compatible audio transcription client handle a 503 fallback?

The adapter should return a normalized outcome, not leak one provider's error vocabulary into the moderation service. The example below keeps the critical path explicit. It uses Python because the policy is easier to inspect as a small decision function; the same state transitions can sit behind a Node.js client.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

Outcome = Literal["transcript", "retry", "fallback", "wait", "reject"]

@dataclass
class Attempt:
    http_status: int | None
    model_available: bool | None
    retry_after_seconds: int | None
    request_replayable: bool
    audio_validated: bool

def decide(attempt: Attempt, attempts_used: int, fallback_ready: bool) -> Outcome:
    if not attempt.audio_validated:
        return "reject"
    if attempt.http_status == 200 and attempt.model_available is not False:
        return "transcript"
    if attempt.http_status == 503 and attempt.request_replayable and attempts_used < 2:
        return "retry"
    if attempt.model_available is False and fallback_ready:
        return "fallback"
    if attempt.http_status == 503 or attempt.model_available is False:
        return "wait"
    return "reject"

The limit of two attempts here is a policy example, not a universal number. It makes the boundary visible so it can be reviewed against queue depth, audio length, and the moderation service-level objective. A real worker should honor a valid Retry-After, add jitter, and cap total elapsed time. It should also persist an idempotency key or a stable report-attempt identifier before sending audio, because a timeout leaves the client uncertain about whether the provider completed the work.

There is a real trade-off here: a shorter deadline protects the queue but increases pending reviews, while a longer deadline improves completion probability but holds worker capacity behind one unavailable model. The right value depends on the moderation service-level objective and the cost of delaying a human decision; it is not a property of a compatibility route. Keep it explicit.

The long tail matters more than the happy path in this workflow. A report can arrive with an audio object that is valid, a provider route that is reachable, a readiness probe that passed 90 seconds ago, and a model that becomes unavailable while the worker is sending bytes. The worker therefore needs a durable transition for uncertainty, a retry budget tied to elapsed time rather than only attempt count, and a policy check before it sends the same object to a second destination. Those details are less attractive in a demo than a one-line fallback chain, but they are the difference between a recoverable delay and an untraceable moderation decision.

A Node.js implementation should use an AbortSignal for the request deadline, classify the response body without assuming every provider emits the same JSON fields, and record the adapter name separately from the model identifier. Do not turn an arbitrary fetch exception into a fallback. DNS failure, local cancellation, invalid credentials, and a provider-side 503 have different owners and different recovery paths.

Which fallback preserves provider portability?

Portability is not the ability to swap one URL for another. It is the ability to preserve the moderation contract while changing the speech engine. That contract should include the source object reference, content hash, language hint, duration if known, transcript text, segment timing when available, provider-neutral status, adapter identity, model identifier, attempt count, and timestamps. Provider-specific response fields can be retained as opaque metadata, but they should not be required to decide whether a report enters human review.

The capability registry needs more than a boolean. For each configured adapter, record whether transcription is enabled, accepted audio formats, maximum duration, supported languages, geographic or data-residency constraints, and current readiness with an expiry time. A stale true is not readiness; it is only the last observation. The registry should be advisory, with the live request remaining authoritative.

Option Portability boundary Failure surface Valid use case
Self-hosted Whisper-compatible worker Stable internal adapter and object-storage contract Capacity, model loading, accelerator scheduling Predictable traffic and controlled data handling
Amazon Transcribe adapter Normalized transcript envelope over a managed API Region, quotas, job lifecycle, and service availability Teams accepting asynchronous managed processing
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text adapter Same envelope, with provider-specific feature mapping Supported encoding, quotas, and feature differences Workloads already governed in that cloud
OpenAI audio transcription adapter Same envelope behind an isolated client Provider availability and request contract A separately approved external processing path

These are not interchangeable feature lists. Amazon Transcribe documents batch and streaming workflows; Google documents encoding and recognition configuration; OpenAI documents an audio transcription endpoint. The useful comparison is the boundary each adapter has to absorb, not which row appears most capable. A managed API can reduce local operations work while increasing dependence on its job model, region rules, and data-processing terms. A self-hosted worker can improve control while making capacity and model loading your responsibility.

The rejected option is a single global fallback chain embedded in the moderation handler: call provider A, then B, then C until any text comes back. It looks portable in a diagram and is dangerous in production. It can duplicate billable work, violate residency policy, reorder reports, and conceal a systematic language or audio-format gap. It is valid only for an explicitly non-authoritative enrichment path where duplicates are acceptable, policy permits every destination, and the result is labeled as enrichment rather than evidence.

The limitation is important: this adapter design does not make providers feature-equivalent. It is a poor fit when moderation depends on a provider-specific diarization, vocabulary, or streaming behavior that cannot be represented in the neutral envelope. In that case, keep the specialized path separate and document why portability is being traded away.

Portability has a boundary.

How do we test readiness without making it the product contract?

A readiness probe should be cheap, bounded, and separate from user audio. It can verify credentials, route reachability, a known-small fixture, and the adapter's ability to map a response into the normalized envelope. It cannot prove that a later report will have capacity, the same language coverage, or identical latency. I would expire the probe result quickly and treat a failed probe as a reason to stop sending new work, not as permission to erase queued work.

The test matrix should include a reachable route with model_available: false, a 503 with Retry-After, a timeout after the request was sent, malformed audio, a successful empty transcript, and a provider response that contains fields the adapter does not recognize. For each case, assert the stored state, retry count, audit event, and whether the fallback was allowed. Test the policy, not just the HTTP client.

Observability needs three correlated identifiers: the marketplace report ID, the transcription attempt ID, and the provider request ID when one exists. Metrics should distinguish waiting_provider, fallback_selected, permanent_rejection, and transcript_completed. Log hashes and metadata needed for correlation, not raw user audio or uncontrolled transcript content. A queue dashboard that reports only 503s cannot tell capacity trouble from invalid files; that is a poor dashboard and an even poorer incident signal.

My storage rule is strict: never overwrite the prior attempt when changing providers. Append an attempt record, link the resulting transcript to the successful attempt, and keep the policy decision that allowed the transition. This costs rows. It buys an explanation when a moderator asks why a report was delayed or why two engines produced different text.

The architecture decision

For marketplace moderation, choose an adapter layer with a provider-neutral result envelope, an expiring capability registry, bounded retries, and an explicit waiting state. Keep the audio object immutable and the attempt history append-only. A 503 may justify a short retry; model available: false should trigger a capability decision; neither should silently become a blank transcript.

That architecture leaves room for three provider adapters, a self-hosted worker, or a later engine change without moving provider assumptions into moderation policy. It also accepts an uncomfortable truth: sometimes the correct fallback is no transcription yet. Human review is a controlled state. Pretending otherwise creates a more expensive data-quality problem than the original outage.

References

  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • MDN, 503 Service Unavailable: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/503
  • OpenAI, Audio API reference: https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/audio
  • Amazon Transcribe Developer Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/what-is-transcribe.html
  • Google Cloud Speech-to-Text documentation: https://cloud.google.com/speech-to-text/docs

title: How we bundled Java 8 into a one-click Windows zip for our game
description:
Disclosure: I'm Snow, and I run SnowRSPS, a free custom 317 game server online since 2012.

Our game client is a Java 8 jar. For years the #1 support question was "it won't open." Players had no Java, the wrong Java, or a 32-bit PC. Here's what we shipped instead.

The layout 

SnowRSPS/
  Play SnowRSPS.bat   <- the only thing players click
  SnowRSPS.jar
  java64/             <- Java 8 runtime for 64-bit Windows 7/8/10/11
  java32/             <- Java 8 runtime for old 32-bit Windows
  README-EN.txt
  README-CN.txt

What the launcher does

  1. Picks the right runtime. It checks whether Windows is 64-bit and uses java64, otherwise java32. No system Java needed, no PATH changes.
  2. Survives odd folder names. Many of our players unzip to folders with spaces or Chinese characters, so every path is quoted and the script works from its own directory.
  3. Retries with less memory. If the JVM can't reserve the heap on a weak PC, it relaunches with a smaller -Xmx instead of failing silently.

Why a zip and not an exe

Unsigned .exe downloads get blocked more often by browsers. A zip with a .bat inside goes through more easily. Players still see Windows "protected your PC"; the README says: More info → Run anyway.

Build notes

  • Compile with compliance 1.8 so the bundled runtime can run it.
  • Eclipse → Export → Runnable JAR → "Package required libraries into generated JAR".
  • Ship two READMEs (English + Simplified Chinese). It cut down our support questions a lot.

Takeaways

Bundle the runtime, make the first click obvious, and add a fallback for weak machines.

If you want to see it in action: download the SnowRSPS client.

title: Why did my birthday move? A date-only bug across time zones
description:
Someone enters their birthday as 12 June. After travelling, they open the app and see 11 June.

They haven't changed it. One possible cause is that the app turned a calendar date into a moment in time, then displayed that moment in a different time zone.

Here's a small example of how that can happen, and what to test in an app that stores birthdays.

Watch the short video: Why did my birthday move?

From 12 June to 11 June

Suppose a birthday is 1994-06-12. An app saves it as midnight UTC:

1994-06-12T00:00:00Z

That timestamp identifies a moment. At that moment in Los Angeles, the local date and time are 11 June 1994, 17:00. If the app converts the timestamp to the device's time zone and takes the date, it will show 11 June.

The time-zone conversion is doing what it was asked to do. The problem is that a birthday was represented as a moment in the first place. Travelling doesn't change a correctly stored birthday.

Here's the conversion in Kotlin:

import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneId

val savedMoment = Instant.parse("1994-06-12T00:00:00Z")
val displayedDate = savedMoment
    .atZone(ZoneId.of("America/Los_Angeles"))
    .toLocalDate()

println(displayedDate) // 1994-06-11

The offset depends on the zone's rules for the date in question. Using a named zone such as America/Los_Angeles lets the time API apply those rules, including daylight saving time.

Keep a birthday as a date

For a birthday, the value we need is a year, month and day. In Java or Kotlin, LocalDate represents that without a time or time zone:

import java.time.LocalDate

val birthday = LocalDate.parse("1994-06-12")
val apiValue = birthday.toString() // "1994-06-12"
val loadedBirthday = LocalDate.parse(apiValue)

check(loadedBirthday == birthday)

The important part is what happens between those two operations. Agree on a date-only value in the API, for example:

{ "birthday": "1994-06-12" }

Then preserve it as a date through the server and database. For example, PostgreSQL's DATE type stores a calendar date without a time of day. On the way back, parse the value as a date and format it for the person's locale—without converting it through an instant.

On Android, java.time.LocalDate is available from API level 26. If you support older Android versions, check your project's Java API desugaring configuration and supported APIs.

Test the full round trip

A parsing test alone can't catch a conversion hidden in the API, database mapping or UI. Try a test that exercises the actual save and reload path:

  1. In UTC, enter and save 1994-06-12.
  2. Reload it and check that the API returns 1994-06-12 and the screen displays 12 June.
  3. Change the device or test environment to America/Los_Angeles, reload the same record and check both values again.
  4. Repeat with a zone east of UTC, such as Asia/Tokyo, and include dates near year boundaries and a leap day.

For an automated integration test, run the save and reload through your real serialization and persistence layers in each relevant test environment. Inspect what travels over the API as well as what appears on screen; a date-only string can still be converted incorrectly by a client.

Existing timestamp data needs care. Before migrating, establish what the stored timestamps meant and which time zone was used when the original dates were converted. A timestamp alone may not reliably reveal the intended birthday; don't apply a blanket conversion without checking the data and assumptions.

A birthday isn't the only date-only value: a due date or anniversary may be one too. Scheduled meetings and payment events, on the other hand, represent moments and need appropriate time-zone handling. Choose the representation based on what the value means.

References

  • Java LocalDate
  • Java Instant
  • PostgreSQL date and time types
  • Android Java API desugaring
