title: We kill -9 our database 21 times in 140 seconds, then read back every write. Here is what comes back
description:
A database earns trust by what it gives back after something goes wrong. So for Semurg we break a running node the ways real machines break, then read back every write the node acknowledged. These results are from the release published on 29 October 2026 (r11.138), on one bare-metal AMD EPYC server.

A killed process

32 writers kept writing while we killed the node with kill -9 21 times in 140 seconds, restarting it each time. Afterwards we read back all 32.2 million acknowledged writes, each at its newest acknowledged version. None was lost.

A full disk

We kept writing until the data volume filled. As it neared full, the node refused new writes by name (HTTP 507, "insufficient storage") and stayed healthy, and all 2,183,488 writes it had acknowledged read back. Then we grew the volume while the node kept running: writes were accepted again with no restart, and all 6,190,464 acknowledged writes read back.

A slow disk

We throttled the disk to 200 MB/s, then 40 MB/s, then 8 MB/s, under write load. The node got slower and never wrong: every acknowledged write read back at every level.

A frozen process

We paused the node 5 times for 15 seconds each under load, and all 15.2 million acknowledged writes read back. 80 client calls timed out during the pauses. None of those was an acknowledged write that went missing: a call that times out was never acknowledged, so the client sends it again, and every call sent again was stored.

A power cut

We replayed sudden power loss at the block device, on a datacenter drive with power-loss protection, 21 cuts in each of two data shapes. Everything acknowledged before the final seconds survived every cut, and nothing that read back was ever damaged. Writes acknowledged in the last seconds before a cut can be lost on ext4: at most 9.4 seconds in one shape and 4.7 seconds in the other, inside the 10-second bound we test against. Our goal there is zero, and we publish the number until we get there.

Why we test this way

The rule we hold ourselves to is simple: when the node cannot keep a write, it refuses that write at the moment you send it, by name, so nothing is accepted now and lost later. Every result above is on our durability page with the release it was measured on, and the tests run again on new releases.

What failure do you test your own database against before you trust it with data? A killed process, a full disk, a power cut, something nastier? I would like to hear what has bitten you.

Read more on our blog: https://one.semurg.io/blog/what-a-semurg-node-gives-back

This post was drafted with AI assistance and checked line by line against our published durability results.

title: The Happy Path Is Fully Tested; the Error Path Is Never Asserted
description:
Quick answer: A suite that covers every successful response but never asserts a failure gives you a false sense of safety: the happy path is the easy part, and the error path is where real systems break, retries, and surface data to users. Leaving 4xx and 5xx responses untested means a malformed error body, a missing field, or a wrong status code reaches production even though coverage reports look complete. Treat error responses as first-class behavior with explicit assertions, not as exceptions you hope never happen.

Coverage numbers hide this gap neatly. A test that calls the endpoint and asserts a 200 touches the success branch, and a tool reports the line as covered even though no test ever exercises the branch that returns a 422. Line coverage is not branch coverage. The failures that dominate incident reviews — a validation error with the wrong shape, an upstream timeout surfaced as a 500 with no detail, a rate-limit the client does not know how to handle — live in precisely those untested branches.

What "only happy path" looks like

The common pattern is a single test that sends valid input and asserts the success response. Invalid input, missing permissions, and upstream failures have no corresponding case. When the error-handling code later changes — or is generated by an agent that simplifies it — nothing fails.

// This is the only test. It proves success and nothing else. it("returns the order", async () => { const res = await getOrder("ord_123"); expect(res.status).toBe(200); expect(res.body.id).toBe("ord_123"); }); // None of these are asserted anywhere: // 404 when the order does not exist // 403 when the caller does not own it // 429 when rate limited // 502 when the upstream service is down

Assert the failure as behavior

Each error response is a contract: it has a status code, a documented body shape, and often headers the client acts on. Write a test per meaningful failure and pin those elements. For errors the handler triggers, send the input that causes it. For upstream failures, inject a stub that returns an error rather than relying on a real dependency.

These assertions do more than catch regressions; they document what a client should do when things fail. The retryable flag and the Retry-After header are the difference between a client that backs off and one that hammers a failing endpoint.

The error cases worth a test

Failure class What to assert Why it matters
Validation (400/422) Status and per-field error shape Clients render field-level messages
Not found (404) Problem details body Distinguish missing from forbidden
Permission (403) Status, no leaked resource data Authorization must not reveal data
Rate limit (429) Retry-After header Drives client backoff
Upstream error (502/504) Mapped status, retryable flag Avoid surfacing raw internals
Conflict (409) Current-state pointer Clients reconcile optimistic writes

Branch coverage and contract-driven checks

Configure coverage to report branch coverage and set a threshold so an untested error branch fails the build rather than quietly passing. Where responses are documented in OpenAPI, a contract test can verify each declared error status returns a body matching the schema, closing the gap even for cases you forget to hand-write. The spec lists every response the client must handle; generating tests from it means the documented failures cannot drift from the actual ones. This is especially valuable when an agent generates code, because the build enforces the error contract instead of trusting the model to remember it.

Frequently asked questions

My coverage is 90%. Aren't the error paths negligible?

Line coverage can be high while most error branches are never asserted, because a single success call may count the surrounding lines as covered. Check branch coverage and ask, for each declared error status, which test triggers it. The answer tells you more than the percentage.

Do I need a test for every single status code?

Cover every failure a client is expected to act on — validation, not-found, permission, rate-limit, and upstream mapping. Trivial duplicates can share a parameterized test, but each distinct behavior the client handles should have an assertion.

How do I test upstream failures without a flaky real dependency?

Inject a stub or mock at the boundary that returns the specific error, then assert how your handler maps it. Deterministic injected failures are faster and more reliable than waiting for a real service to time out.

What about error bodies that leak internal details?

Add an assertion that error responses do not include stack traces, internal hostnames, or query details. Testing the 500 path gives you a place to enforce that only safe, problem-shaped bodies reach clients.

This is part of the API Testing Guide — start there for a complete approach to tests that assert behavior rather than just green status codes.

title: An AI rewrite can be stale before you click Apply
description:
A document editor can show a perfectly reasonable AI suggestion that is already wrong to apply.

Imagine a paragraph in a shared creative brief:

The father leaves the room.

A writer asks an agent to rewrite it. While the suggestion is being prepared, a collaborator changes the brief:

The father stays and helps his daughter.

The agent returns a polished version of the first sentence. Someone clicks Apply. The problem is no longer the quality of the generated sentence. It is whether the proposal still refers to the document people are editing now.

A shared editing system can merge updates without understanding that a pending rewrite expresses an outdated decision. That requires a separate check in the proposal workflow.

Keep the proposal separate from the edit

The implementation examined here is in Breatic's public repository. Its document-edit tool returns a proposal card rather than immediately rewriting the shared document.

A proposal carries the target Space, a block ID, the block's original plain text, the proposed content, and its own proposal ID. Comments, rewrites and inserts use the same proposal shape, with different requirements for their targets.

The original text is important. An ID tells the application which block the model saw. It does not tell the application whether that block still says the same thing.

For a rewrite, the relevant check is conceptually this:

const block = findBlockById(currentDocument, proposal.blockId);

if (block === null) return { outcome: "blockGone" };
if (plainText(block) !== proposal.original) {
  return { outcome: "changed" };
}

This is an explanatory sketch, not a standalone API example. In the implementation, the check reads the editor's current ProseMirror document. It compares the block's plain text, not a full structural hash of every attribute and mark.

If the collaborator has rewritten the paragraph, the proposal is refused instead of silently replacing the new wording. The user can ask for another proposal against the current text.

A real example-project capture. The scene is illustrative; the rewrite has not been applied in this image.

Check again after asynchronous preparation

Putting the check in the click handler is not enough if the handler then awaits work.

The proposed Markdown has to become editor blocks. Preparing those blocks can also wait for media configuration. During that interval, another edit can arrive, the target can disappear, or the current editor can become read-only.

The landing function therefore checks the current state twice: before preparation and again after it finishes, immediately before the synchronous block write. A simplified outline is:

const initial = inspectCurrentState();
if (initial !== null) return initial;

const prepared = await prepareNewContent(proposal.body);

const ready = inspectCurrentState();
if (ready !== null) return ready;

writePreparedBlocks(prepared);

inspectCurrentState stands for more than the text comparison. It checks whether the request is still available, whether this proposal has already landed, the current write admission, whether the editor is editable, and the current target.

Notice what is absent from the second check: a target position saved before the await. The implementation looks up the block again by ID. A collaborator may have moved it, including into a table cell, without changing its words. The new content must be normalized for its current location.

Applying once needs a durable trace

A second click should not insert the same proposal again. A local applied = true flag does not explain what happened after a reload.

For inserted or rewritten content, the implementation derives root block IDs from the proposal ID and each output block's index. A later render can look for that trace in the shared document. Comments instead carry proposal metadata on their thread and must still have a range in the document to count as landed.

The trace describes the document's current state. If the write is undone and its output disappears, the proposal no longer counts as landed. If it is redone, the trace is there again.

The write is also bracketed as one undo step. Accepting a multi-block suggestion should not require a user to undo its fragments one by one, or undo text they typed just before accepting it.

Test the gap rather than the happy path

The useful regression case deliberately pauses asynchronous preparation. While it is paused, the test changes the target, removes it, or makes the editor read-only. It then releases preparation and checks the result.

The public test suite asserts that these cases return changed, blockGone, or readOnly, leave the current document intact, and do not add an undo item. Other cases move the target into or out of a table cell during preparation, and verify that output is normalized for the new location.

The tests also cover repeated application, undo and redo, and reading the resulting document through a second Yjs document. These are assertions present in the repository; this article does not report a new benchmark or a fresh run of the full suite.

What this check does not solve

The plain-text comparison is a deliberately narrow guard. It does not detect every formatting-only change or establish that the model's interpretation of the brief is correct. A final browser-side check is also not a distributed lock against every remote update that might arrive later.

Its job is more specific: refuse a proposal when the current local document no longer contains the text it was proposed against, and avoid using state captured before an asynchronous pause.

The practical place to review a collaborative AI editing feature is the moment between “the user accepted this suggestion” and “the shared document changed.” That interval has its own state, permissions and failure cases, even when the suggestion itself looks finished.

Implementation references

  • Proposal schema and original-text contract
  • Proposal generation without immediate document writes
  • Commit-time checks and undo boundary
  • Regression tests for changes during preparation

title: How to Learn SQL Joins (and Stop Mixing Up LEFT and INNER)
description:
For about two years I wrote SQL joins by trial and error. I'd type JOIN, run it, count the rows, feel uneasy, swap in LEFT JOIN, count again, and keep whichever number looked less wrong. It worked often enough that I never sat down and learned the thing properly.

Then a report I'd written quietly dropped every customer who hadn't placed an order. Nobody noticed for a month. That was the week I finally figured out joins, and the approach that stuck is pretty different from the Venn diagrams most tutorials open with.

Forget the Venn diagram for a minute

The circles are fine as a rough picture, but they hide the part that actually trips people up: joins don't combine sets of values, they match rows. One customer with three orders becomes three rows. A customer with zero orders becomes either zero rows or one row full of NULLs, depending on the join type.

So the question I ask now is always the same. For each row on the left, how many rows on the right match it, and what happens when the answer is zero?

That one question covers almost everything:

  • INNER JOIN keeps only rows with at least one match. Zero matches means the row disappears.
  • LEFT JOIN keeps every left row. Zero matches means you get one row with NULLs on the right side.
  • RIGHT JOIN is the same thing mirrored. I almost never use it; I flip the table order and write a LEFT JOIN so I'm always reading in one direction.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.
  • CROSS JOIN matches every row with every row, which is what you get by accident when you forget the join condition in old comma-style syntax.

Build two tiny tables and break them

Reading about joins taught me very little. Running them on data small enough to check by eye taught me a lot. Open SQLite, DuckDB, or the free DB Fiddle and make this:

CREATE TABLE customers (id INT, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT, customer_id INT, total INT);

INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Asha'), (2, 'Ben'), (3, 'Chen');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10, 1, 50), (11, 1, 20), (12, 2, 35), (13, 9, 99);

Asha has two orders, Ben has one, Chen has none, and order 13 points at a customer who doesn't exist. Before you run each query, write down how many rows you expect. Then run it.

SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;   -- 3 rows, no Chen

SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;    -- 4 rows, Chen with NULL

Guessing first is the important bit. When your guess is wrong, you've found the exact gap in your understanding, and that sticks far better than a correct answer you read off a page.

The two bugs worth memorizing

Most join bugs I've shipped or reviewed come down to two mistakes.

The first is filtering a LEFT JOIN in the WHERE clause:

SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total > 30;

That looks like "all customers, plus their orders over 30." It isn't. Chen's row has o.total = NULL, NULL > 30 isn't true, so Chen gets filtered out and you've rebuilt an inner join without meaning to. If you want to keep every customer, move the condition into the ON:

LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 30

The second is row multiplication. Join customers to orders, then join to a table of support tickets, and a customer with 3 orders and 4 tickets turns into 12 rows. Run SUM(o.total) over that and the number is quietly four times too big. The fix is usually to aggregate each side in a subquery or CTE first and join the summaries.

Turn every "wait, why?" into a flashcard

Here's the habit that made it stick for me. Any time a query surprised me, I wrote a card with the situation on the front and the reason on the back.

I LEFT JOINed and then filtered on the right table in WHERE. Why did rows vanish?
NULL fails the comparison, so unmatched rows are dropped. Put the filter in ON.

My SUM doubled after adding a second join. Why?
One-to-many on two sides multiplies rows. Aggregate before joining.

How do I find customers with no orders?
LEFT JOIN orders, then WHERE o.id IS NULL.

I review them on a growing schedule: the next day, a few days later, a week, two weeks. That's spaced repetition, and it's the reason I can still write an anti-join from memory instead of searching for it. If you're curious how the intervals get calculated, I wrote up how to implement spaced repetition (SM-2) in JavaScript.

Keep the cards about situations you'll actually hit at work. "What is a semi-join?" is trivia. "How do I check if a customer has any order without duplicating rows?" (answer: EXISTS) is something you'll need on a Tuesday.

Don't lose the good explanations

Plenty of what finally made joins click came from videos and blog posts, and I used to watch one, nod, and forget it by the weekend. That's part of why I built Recl. You share a video, reel, podcast or article to it from your phone or the Chrome extension, and it summarizes the key points, files it under a topic like "SQL", and brings it back on a spaced schedule so you see it again before it fades.

Read execution plans once you're comfortable

When the row counts make sense, run EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in Postgres) on a join and look at whether it picked a hash join, a nested loop, or a merge join. You don't need to tune anything yet. Seeing that the database is literally looping over rows and looking up matches makes the "how many matches per row" model feel real.

I still check row counts on every non-trivial query. The difference is that now I know what number to expect before I hit run, and that report from a few years ago would have been caught in about ten seconds.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves your videos, reels, podcasts and articles, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you remember what you learned.

title: The Save Button That Did Nothing
description:
Have you ever clicked Save on a long form and watched absolutely nothing happen?

No toast. No red text. No movement. Just a button that seems to be ignoring you.

That was our app. We build long forms: profile pages, multi-section settings, repeatable blocks like "contacts" or "addresses". Here's what kept happening:

  1. The user fills in the visible part of the form and clicks Save, which sits in a sticky header.
  2. Validation fails on a field far below the fold, or inside the third item of a repeatable list.
  3. Nothing visible happens. The user clicks Save again, then gives up or reports a bug.

The error was there all along, sitting politely at the bottom of the page where nobody could see it.

Server-side validation had the same problem. The form submits, the backend answers 400 with field errors, we map them into the form, and the screen still doesn't change.

We needed one consistent rule for every form: when validation fails, bring the first error into view.

What we were working with

  • React Hook Form (RHF) for form state, with Zod schemas through zodResolver.
  • MUI inputs, plus many composite controls: autocompletes, date pickers, chip selectors, custom list widgets.
  • React Router for navigation. Some forms are reused across tabs and routes.
  • A shared FormItem wrapper that renders the label, the control and the error message for every field.

"Doesn't RHF already do this?"

Sort of. RHF has shouldFocusError, and it's on by default. It focuses the first invalid field registered with a focusable ref.

It works well for plain inputs. But in our case:

  • Composite controls often don't expose a focusable ref, or they expose the wrong element.
  • Array-level errors (for example "add at least one contact") belong to no input, so there's nothing to focus.
  • Some fields are read-only displays of a value picked in a dialog. Focusing them is pointless.
  • Focus doesn't always scroll to a comfortable position. The field can land right under the sticky header.

So instead of chasing inputs, we decided to target the error message element.

The approach

Four small steps: mark, search, scroll, wait.

1. Mark: tag every error message with its field path

The shared FormItem already renders the error text. We add one attribute to it: the RHF field path.

{errorMessage && (
  <FormHelperText data-name={name}>
    {errorMessage}
  </FormHelperText>
)}

Why the error message and not the input?

  • It only exists when there's an error, so the selector never matches a valid field.
  • It works for any control type, including composites and custom widgets.
  • It works for errors with no input at all. A list-level error can render its own message with data-name="contacts".

Now every visible error has a predictable, framework-agnostic address in the DOM, like [data-name="contacts.2.email"].

2. Search: find the path of the first error

RHF errors mirror the shape of your form values:

// Plain field
{ title: { type: 'too_small', message: 'Required' } }

// Field array: sparse, only invalid items are present
{ contacts: [ , , { email: { message: 'Invalid email' } } ] }

// Array-level error
{ contacts: { type: 'too_small', message: 'Add a contact' } }

We need to turn each shape into a path that matches our data-name:

  • { title: {...} } → title
  • { contacts: [ , , { email: {...} } ] } → contacts.2.email
  • { contacts: { message: ... } } → contacts

The algorithm:

  1. Take the first key of the errors object. That's the first failing top-level field.
  2. Check whether its value has index keys ("0", "2", ...). If it does, it's a field array error.
  3. For a field array, take the first index present, then the first sub-field inside that item.
  4. Otherwise, use the top-level name as is.

How do you tell the two shapes apart? A plain FieldError has keys like type, message and ref. A field array error has "0", "2" and so on. One regex is enough:

const isIndex = (key: string) => /^\d+$/.test(key);

And "first index" really means the lowest one. JavaScript returns integer-like keys first, in ascending order, so Object.keys on a sparse error array always starts with the earliest invalid item.

3. Scroll: let the browser do it

Once we have a path, scrolling is a single DOM call:

document
  .querySelector(`[data-name="${path}"]`)
  ?.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'center' });

block: 'center' matters. With a sticky header, start often hides the field right under it. Centering keeps the label, the control and the message all visible. If you'd rather use start, set scroll-margin-top in CSS to the header's height.

Two extra details in the final version:

  • Focus, not just scroll. Seeing the field isn't enough for keyboard and screen-reader users. After scrolling, we focus the first focusable element inside the same FormItem.
  • Reduced motion. If the user has prefers-reduced-motion enabled, we jump instead of animating.

4. Wait: let the page settle first

Our layout scrolls the page container to the top on every route change. When a form is submitted and the app navigates or re-renders a route, both scrolls race and neither works.

The quick fix is a setTimeout with a guess, say one second. But is one second enough? On a fast laptop it's too long. On a slow phone it might be too short.

Instead of guessing, we wait for the error message to settle. On every animation frame, we check two things:

  1. Does the element exist yet?
  2. Is it in the same place as in the previous frame?

When both are true, nothing is moving anymore, and it's safe to scroll. Here's the core of it, simplified:

const check = () => {
  const element = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>(selector);
  const top = element?.getBoundingClientRect().top ?? null;

  if (element && top === lastTop) {
    callback(element);
    return;
  }

  lastTop = top;
  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(check);
};

This covers more than the route scroll. It also waits for content that renders late, like a list that loads its items or a section that expands with an animation. As a safety net, the loop stops after about a second (MAX_FRAMES) and scrolls to wherever the element is.

The helper returns a cancel function, and the hook returns it from the effect. A fast re-validation or an unmount never triggers a stale scroll. The effect also depends on location.pathname, so it runs again when the same form instance is shown on another route or tab.

A catch: isValid and server errors

A natural guard is to run the hook only when isValid is false. No errors, nothing to scroll to, right?

Not for server errors. setError doesn't touch isValid, because RHF derives it from schema validation only. When the client-side checks pass and the server returns a 400, isValid stays true, and a hook guarded by it would never scroll.

So the hook ignores isValid and reads the errors directly. If there's a path, it scrolls. submitCount is also in the dependencies, so submitting the same invalid form again scrolls again, even when the errors haven't changed.

Usage

Call the hook once per form:

const ProfileForm = () => {
  const form = useForm<ProfileFormValues>({
    resolver: zodResolver(profileSchema),
  });
  const { errors, submitCount } = form.formState;

  useScrollToFieldError({ errors, submitCount });

  return (
    <FormProvider {...form}>
      <FormItem name="title" label="Title">...</FormItem>
      <ContactsList name="contacts" />
    </FormProvider>
  );
};

Server errors work the same way. Map them into the form with setError, and the hook scrolls to the first one.

Trade-offs and limitations

  • "First" means first key, not first on screen. Top-level key order follows the order errors were added. That usually matches field order, but it isn't guaranteed. For a stricter version, collect all matching elements and pick the one with the smallest getBoundingClientRect().top.
  • One level of nesting. contacts.2.email works. sections.1.items.3.name doesn't. A recursive walk fixes that if you need it.
  • "Settled" is a heuristic. "Didn't move since the last frame" is a good signal, but it isn't an explicit "layout is ready" event. If your app has one, use it. MAX_FRAMES caps the wait either way.
  • Convention-based. It only works if every error message renders data-name. Putting that in one shared FormItem made it easy to enforce.

Conclusion

A small amount of code removed a whole class of "the Save button does nothing" reports. The ideas carry over to any form library:

  • Address errors, not inputs. Tag the error message with the field path. It exists only when needed and works for every kind of control.
  • Derive the path from the error tree. An "index keys" check tells plain fields from field arrays.
  • Let the browser scroll. scrollIntoView({ block: 'center' }) handles sticky headers well. Then move focus for accessibility.
  • Don't guess delays. Wait until the element stops moving, cancel on cleanup, and re-run on route change and re-submit.

Full code

waitForSettledElement.ts 

// Safety net if the layout never settles: ~1s at 60fps.
const MAX_FRAMES = 60;

// Calls `callback` once the element exists and hasn't moved
// since the previous frame. Returns a cancel function.
export function waitForSettledElement(
  selector: string,
  callback: (element: HTMLElement) => void,
) {
  let frameId = 0;
  let frames = 0;
  let lastTop: number | null = null;

  const check = () => {
    const element = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>(selector);
    const top = element?.getBoundingClientRect().top ?? null;
    frames += 1;

    if (element && (top === lastTop || frames >= MAX_FRAMES)) {
      callback(element);
      return;
    }

    if (frames < MAX_FRAMES) {
      lastTop = top;
      frameId = requestAnimationFrame(check);
    }
  };

  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(check);

  return () => cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);
}

scrollToFieldError.ts 

import { waitForSettledElement } from './waitForSettledElement';

const FOCUSABLE = [
  'input:not([disabled])',
  'textarea:not([disabled])',
  'select:not([disabled])',
  'button:not([disabled])',
  '[tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])',
].join(', ');

function prefersReducedMotion() {
  return window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')
    .matches;
}

function reveal(message: HTMLElement) {
  message.scrollIntoView({
    behavior: prefersReducedMotion() ? 'auto' : 'smooth',
    block: 'center',
  });

  // Keyboard and screen-reader users need focus, not just scroll.
  message
    .closest('[data-form-item]')
    ?.querySelector<HTMLElement>(FOCUSABLE)
    ?.focus({ preventScroll: true });
}

// Returns a cancel function.
export function scrollToFieldError(path: string) {
  const selector = `[data-name="${CSS.escape(path)}"]`;

  return waitForSettledElement(selector, reveal);
}

getFirstErrorPath.ts 

import { type FieldErrors } from 'react-hook-form';

type ErrorNode = Record<string, unknown> | undefined;

const isIndex = (key: string) => /^\d+$/.test(key);

function hasIndexKeys(node: ErrorNode) {
  return node !== undefined && Object.keys(node).some(isIndex);
}

function getArrayFieldPath(name: string, node: ErrorNode) {
  // Integer-like keys come first, in ascending order.
  const index = Object.keys(node ?? {}).find(isIndex);
  if (index === undefined) {
    return '';
  }

  const item = node?.[index] as ErrorNode;
  const [subField] = Object.keys(item ?? {});

  return subField ? `${name}.${index}.${subField}` : '';
}

export function getFirstErrorPath(errors: FieldErrors) {
  const [name] = Object.keys(errors);
  if (!name) {
    return '';
  }

  const node = errors[name] as ErrorNode;

  return hasIndexKeys(node)
    ? getArrayFieldPath(name, node)
    : name;
}

useScrollToFieldError.ts 

import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { type FieldErrors, type FieldValues } from 'react-hook-form';
import { useLocation } from 'react-router';

import { getFirstErrorPath } from './getFirstErrorPath';
import { scrollToFieldError } from './scrollToFieldError';

type Config<T extends FieldValues> = Readonly<{
  errors: FieldErrors<T>;
  submitCount: number;
}>;

export const useScrollToFieldError = <T extends FieldValues>({
  errors,
  submitCount,
}: Config<T>) => {
  const { pathname } = useLocation();

  useEffect(() => {
    // Don't check isValid: setError() doesn't change it,
    // so server errors would be skipped.
    const path = getFirstErrorPath(errors);
    if (!path) {
      return;
    }

    return scrollToFieldError(path);
  }, [errors, submitCount, pathname]);
};

FormItem.tsx (simplified) 

import { type FC, type PropsWithChildren } from 'react';
import {
  FormControl,
  FormHelperText,
  FormLabel,
} from '@mui/material';
import { useFormState } from 'react-hook-form';
import { get } from 'lodash';

type Props = PropsWithChildren<Readonly<{
  name: string;
  label: string;
}>>;

export const FormItem: FC<Props> = ({ name, label, children }) => {
  const { errors } = useFormState({ name });
  const errorMessage = get(errors, name)?.message as
    | string
    | undefined;

  return (
    <FormControl
      data-form-item
      error={Boolean(errorMessage)}
      fullWidth
    >
      <FormLabel>{label}</FormLabel>
      {children}
      {errorMessage && (
        <FormHelperText data-name={name}>
          {errorMessage}
        </FormHelperText>
      )}
    </FormControl>
  );
};

Field array example 

import { useFieldArray, useFormContext } from 'react-hook-form';
import { FormHelperText, TextField } from '@mui/material';

type Props = Readonly<{ name: 'contacts' }>;

export const ContactsList = ({ name }: Props) => {
  const { control, register, formState } =
    useFormContext<ProfileFormValues>();
  const { fields } = useFieldArray({ control, name });

  const listError =
    formState.errors.contacts?.message ??
    formState.errors.contacts?.root?.message;

  return (
    <>
      {listError && (
        <FormHelperText error data-name={name}>
          {listError}
        </FormHelperText>
      )}

      {fields.map((field, index) => (
        <FormItem
          key={field.id}
          name={`${name}.${index}.email`}
          label="Email"
        >
          <TextField {...register(`${name}.${index}.email`)} />
        </FormItem>
      ))}
    </>
  );
};

Schema used in the examples 

import { z } from 'zod';

const contactSchema = z.object({
  email: z.email('Invalid email'),
});

export const profileSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(1, 'Required'),
  contacts: z.array(contactSchema).min(1, 'Add a contact'),
});

export type ProfileFormValues = z.infer<typeof profileSchema>;

title: Building an AI Video App on Cloudflare Workers with TanStack Start
description:
I run a small AI video web app: users upload a character photo and a short motion clip, and a hosted video model renders the character performing those moves. The whole thing (UI, API, auth, payments, storage and the job pipeline) runs as one Cloudflare Worker. No servers, no containers, no separate queue service.

This post walks through the architecture and the handful of problems that turned out to be interesting. If you're considering Workers for anything that handles large files or long-running third-party jobs, most of this transfers.

The stack

  • TanStack Start + React 19 for SSR and file-based routing, built with Vite and the Cloudflare Vite plugin
  • A single Worker entry (src/server.ts) that hands requests to TanStack Start's handler
  • D1 (SQLite) through Drizzle ORM for users, credits and jobs
  • R2 for uploads and finished videos
  • KV as a cache
  • Workers AI for a vision-model safety check on uploaded photos
  • Better Auth for email/password and Google sign-in
  • Cloudflare Email for transactional mail, behind a small provider interface
  • GitHub Actions deploying with wrangler deploy on every push to main, plus per-PR preview URLs

TanStack Start's server functions (createServerFn with a Zod validator and middleware chain) replace a separate API layer. The client calls them like ordinary async functions, and they run inside the same Worker with direct access to the bindings.

Problem 1: large uploads without blowing up memory

Motion clips can be tens of megabytes. Buffering that in a Worker is a bad idea. Instead, the upload route takes the raw file as the request body and streams it straight into R2:

// simplified
const key = `uploads/${userId}/${crypto.randomUUID()}.mp4`;
await env.BUCKET.put(key, request.body, {
  httpMetadata: { contentType: request.headers.get('content-type') ?? '' },
});
return Response.json({ key });

The client then passes that key to the "start job" server function. Uploads are deleted as soon as a job has used them, and an R2 lifecycle rule removes anything older than a day as a safety net. That keeps storage costs flat and means user-provided material doesn't sit around.

Problem 2: pricing a video by length without downloading it

Pricing is per second of motion video, so the server needs the clip's duration before charging. Reading the entire file just to get one number defeats the point of streaming.

MP4 and MOV files store their duration in the mvhd box inside moov. So the server uses R2 range reads to walk the top-level box headers (8â€“16 bytes each), skips over mdat without reading it, fetches only the moov box, and parses timescale and duration from mvhd. Typically that's a few kilobytes read instead of the whole file. When the job is submitted, the video body goes to the model provider as a stream, again never held whole in memory.

Problem 3: jobs that outlive the request

Video rendering takes a few minutes, far longer than a request should stay open. Queues or Durable Objects would work, but a simpler pattern is enough:

  1. Start: one request validates input, runs the photo check, charges credits, submits to the provider and writes a row to an effect_job table with the provider's request ID.
  2. Advance on poll: the client polls a status server function. Each poll asks the provider for status and moves the job forward. When it's done, the result is copied into R2 under the user's files. When it fails, the credits are refunded.
  3. Notify: on completion, an email goes to the user ("your video is ready") so they can close the tab.

Because the status call is idempotent (it only moves a job forward from its stored state), duplicate polls from multiple tabs are harmless.

Problem 4: refunds that happen minutes later

The codebase has a withCredits helper that charges, runs a callback and refunds if the callback throws. That's perfect for synchronous AI calls but useless here: the job can fail five minutes after the request that charged for it has finished.

The fix was to store the spend on the job row. When a poll discovers a failure, it refunds exactly what that job cost and marks the row as refunded, so the refund can't happen twice. Treat the job row as the source of truth for money, not the call stack.

Problem 5: safety checks before charging

Every photo passes through a Workers AI vision model via the AI binding before any credits move. It flags sexual content and recognizable public figures (both always refused) and applies extra rules for photos that appear to include minors. If the check itself errors, the photo is refused rather than let through. Running it first means users are never charged for a request that would be rejected anyway.

Problem 6: private files, shareable thumbnails

Finished videos are private. They're served from a route that checks the owner's session. But generating a first-frame poster image uses Cloudflare Media Transformations, which needs to fetch the video by URL. The answer was short-lived signed links: the video route accepts either the owner's session or a valid signature, and the poster pipeline uses the latter, then stores the WebP through the Images binding.

Local development against remote resources

One opinionated choice: local dev and end-to-end tests connect to the remote D1, R2 and KV ("remote": true on each binding in wrangler.jsonc) rather than local emulators. That removes a whole class of "works locally" bugs around SQLite versions and R2 behaviour, at the cost of needing a dev database. For a solo project that trade has been worth it.

Would I do it again?

Yes. The single-Worker model keeps operations close to zero: one deploy, one log stream, costs that scale with usage, and no idle servers. Its constraints (no Node-only APIs, careful memory use, request time limits) pushed the design toward streaming and stateless polling, which ended up simpler than a queue-based design.

If you want to see the result, the app is live at MotionControlAI. It's an independent project, not affiliated with Kling AI or Kuaishou, even though it runs their motion control models. There's a plain-English guide to how Kling Motion Control works if you're curious about the model side.

title: When Strict Mode reruns Effects: inspect subscription setup and cleanup
description:
When Strict Mode logs an Effect setup twice, check whether cleanup ran between the setups and how many subscriptions remain. Reducing the setup count to one does not establish that cleanup works.

A small subscription was compared in React 19.3.0 development and production builds. Initial behavior also differed between wrapping the root in Strict Mode and wrapping only part of the tree.

Count registration and removal without external communication

The test subscription target is a Set. Setup registers a handler, and a local button invokes all registered handlers. There are no network connections or notification services.

function Subscription({ room, cleanup }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const handler = () => trace.events.push(`message:${room}`);
    trace.active.add(handler);
    trace.events.push(`setup:${room}`);
    if (cleanup) {
      return () => {
        trace.active.delete(handler);
        trace.events.push(`cleanup:${room}`);
      };
    }
  }, [room, cleanup]);
  return <output id="room">{room}</output>;
}

trace.active contains registered handlers, and trace.events records their order. The normal version uses cleanup: true; the deliberately incomplete comparison uses false. The room can change from A to B, and the root is unmounted at the end.

Separate bundles were built with development and production values for process.env.NODE_ENV. In the root-wide condition, <StrictMode> wraps the element rendered by createRoot. In the partial condition, it wraps only Subscription beneath a parent outside Strict Mode.

Placement changed initial setup and cleanup

Build and placement Initial setups Initial cleanups Handlers remaining after initial processing
Development, root Strict Mode, with cleanup 2 1 1
Development, no Strict Mode, with cleanup 1 0 1
Development, child-only Strict Mode, with cleanup 1 0 1
Production, root Strict Mode, with cleanup 1 0 1
Development, root Strict Mode, without cleanup 2 0 2

The normal development root logged setup:A → cleanup:A → setup:A during initial processing. It removed the earlier subscription before setting it up again.

The official Strict Mode documentation distinguishes the extra development setup/cleanup cycle from the condition where initial Effects are not rerun because Strict Mode does not wrap the root. Check where Strict Mode is placed before interpreting repeated Effect logs.

The table counts Effect work. It does not establish component-function invocation counts or DOM painting counts.

Omitting cleanup accumulated handlers

Pressing the local notification button once after initial setup logged one message:A with cleanup and 2 without it. The next step changed the room to B.

Development root condition After initial registration After changing room After unmount
With cleanup 1 1 0
Without cleanup 2 3 3

The normal version logged cleanup:A → setup:B on the room change and cleanup:B on unmount. Without cleanup, the A handlers remained while a B handler was added. They stayed in the Set after unmount too.

The comparison shows what remains when the implementation omits its removal step. Each case discards its Set; the incomplete version was not integrated into an application.

Check the matching teardown before limiting calls

For this example, the fix is to remove the same handler that setup registered. A room change removes the old room's subscription before registering the new one. The useEffect reference describes cleanup with previous values followed by setup with the new values when dependencies change.

This experiment does not apply the extra-execution scenario to API writes, payments, or email delivery. Its scope is a subscription with matching registration and removal. If real logs differ, investigate actual unmounts and remounts or development-tool updates as well as Strict Mode placement.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152 and no React Compiler. The fixture code and results for the 5 conditions include room changes and unmounts as well as initial processing.

title: SQL: WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT — Why Your Query May Return the Wrong Employees
description:
A SQL query can run successfully and still return the wrong result.

Imagine your manager asks you to find the three highest-paid employees in the IT department.

You write a query, execute it, and get three rows. Everything looks fine.

But are those really the three highest-paid employees?

Let's use a simple example to understand where things can go wrong.

Sample Data

Consider the following "employees" table:

CREATE TABLE employees (
emp_id INT,
name VARCHAR(30),
dept VARCHAR(30),
salary INT
);

emp_id| name| dept| salary
101| Amit| IT| 60000
102| Neha| HR| 75000
103| Rahul| IT| 85000
104| Priya| IT| 50000
105| Kiran| IT| 90000
106| Sneha| Finance| 95000
107| Raj| IT| NULL
108| Meera| IT| 70000

Our requirement:

Find the three highest-paid employees from the IT department. Employees with missing salaries should be excluded.

  1. Using LIMIT Without ORDER BY

Let's start with a query that looks reasonable:

SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
LIMIT 3;

This query returns three employees from the IT department.

But there is a problem.

We haven't told SQL how to sort the employees.

The database is free to return qualifying rows in an order that does not represent salary ranking.

So, getting three employees does not mean getting the three highest-paid employees.

  1. Adding ORDER BY

Let's improve the query:

SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 3;

Now the records are sorted by salary, from highest to lowest.

However, there is one more detail worth understanding.

What happens when an employee's salary is NULL?

The position of NULL values in sorting depends on the database.

For example, MySQL and SQL Server generally place NULL values last with descending order, while PostgreSQL and Oracle generally place them first.

This means the result may differ between databases.

  1. The Correct Query

If the requirement says employees with NULL salaries must be excluded, don't depend on the database's default sorting behaviour.

Add an explicit condition:

SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
AND salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 3;

Expected Output

emp_id| name| salary
105| Kiran| 90000
103| Rahul| 85000
108| Meera| 70000

Now we get exactly what the manager asked for.

Here's what SQL does:

  1. "WHERE" filters employees belonging to the IT department.
  2. "salary IS NOT NULL" removes employees without a salary.
  3. "ORDER BY salary DESC" sorts employees from highest to lowest salary.
  4. "LIMIT 3" returns only the first three records.

Remember These Three Clauses

Clause| Purpose
WHERE| Filters records
ORDER BY| Sorts records
LIMIT| Restricts the number of returned rows

A small mistake in any of these clauses can change the result of a business report.

One more thing: "LIMIT" is supported by MySQL and PostgreSQL. Oracle and SQL Server use different row-limiting syntax.

Try This Yourself

What would happen if we removed this condition?

AND salary IS NOT NULL

Would the query return the same three employees in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server?

Think about how each database handles NULL values when sorting in descending order.

Share your answer in the comments.

Learn More

For more practical examples, SQL interview questions, and explanations of filtering and sorting, visit:

"Restricting and Sorting Data in SQL — Sankalan Data Tech" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/restricting-sorting-data-sql-faq.html)

SQL #SQLTutorial #SQLInterview #Database

title: Why Empathy is a Mobile Developer's Greatest Tool
description:
Why Empathy is a Mobile Developer's Greatest Tool

As engineers, it is incredibly easy to get caught up in the technical details. We obsess over milliseconds of render time, the elegance of our state management, and achieving a 100% crash-free rate.

But sometimes, in our pursuit of technical perfection, we lose sight of the most important element: The User.

Designing for the Real World

A perfectly optimized app is useless if it frustrates the person using it. Empathy in mobile development means stepping out of the IDE and into the user's shoes.

Consider these scenarios:

  • The One-Handed User: Is your core navigation reachable with a thumb while holding a coffee?
  • The Low-Connectivity User: Does your app gracefully handle a sudden drop to 3G, or does it show an infinite loading spinner?
  • The Anxious User: When a payment fails, do you show an obscure HTTP 500\ error, or a calm, actionable message?

Bridging the Gap

Great engineers don't just write code; they solve human problems. By collaborating closely with UX designers and actively listening to user feedback, we can build products that aren't just fast, but feel genuinely delightful to use.

Next time you build a feature, ask yourself: How will this make the user feel? That simple shift in perspective is what separates good apps from unforgettable ones.

Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy said on the company's third quarter earnings call that AWS can become a $1 trillion annual revenue business in the next five to ten years. The comment came with numbers attached. AWS segment sales grew 39 percent year over year to $46.0 billion, which Amazon described as the fastest growth in nearly five years and the sixth straight quarter of acceleration. That leaves AWS at a $184 billion annualized revenue run rate. Jassy framed the current moment as the early stage of an inflection driven by enterprise demand for AI capacity.

The ambition is paired with spending. Amazon continues to expect 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and Jassy told analysts the company expects to spend meaningfully more in 2027, with what he called a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns. Cash capex was $75.9 billion in the third quarter alone. He forecast that AWS revenue growth stays north of 40 percent in both 2027 and 2028. Supporting figures from the call include a $578 billion backlog growing at triple digit rates year over year, an AI accelerator installed about every 14 seconds, and AWS operating income of $17.8 billion at a 38.7 percent operating margin. AI revenue inside AWS is growing at triple digit rates year over year, and inference already accounts for well over half of AWS AI revenue.

Investors focused on the cash burn. Amazon shares fell about 6 percent in extended trading after the report. Quarterly revenue of $201.9 billion came in slightly below analyst expectations, as did earnings per share of $1.89, and free cash flow was an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months as equipment purchases rose. For context, Microsoft earlier in the week lowered its own 2026 capex outlook to $170 billion while Alphabet held its guidance, and Amazon's full year 2025 capital spending was roughly $128 billion. Amazon also guided fourth quarter revenue to a range of $240 billion to $247 billion, whose midpoint came in below analyst expectations, and operating income to $28.5 billion through $33.5 billion. Jassy opened by noting that there has never been a business with a trillion dollars of annual revenue and that Amazon may have two of them in the next five to ten years, naming AWS and the retail business.

IMPACT: AWS is now sized like a national cloud utility, so its capital plan has become a direct read on how fast AI infrastructure demand is expected to grow through 2028.
