title: Build, Test, Optimize: Exploring Amazon Connect Customer Agentic CX Designer (ACXD)
description:
Customer experience automation is evolving beyond traditional chatbots and rigid decision trees. Modern systems need to understand customer intent, retrieve information, interact with business applications, execute multi-step workflows, and know when to involve a human.

AWS is bringing these capabilities together with Amazon Connect Customer Agentic CX Designer (ACXD) — a visual, no-code environment for building, testing, and optimizing agentic customer experiences.

What makes ACXD interesting is its combination of two approaches:

  • Deterministic workflows: For predictable business rules, validations, routing, and controlled outcomes.
  • Agentic AI: For understanding natural language, reasoning through customer requests, retrieving knowledge, and coordinating multi-step interactions.

Let's explore how it works and how developers can think about building a practical customer experience with it.

1. What Is Amazon Connect Customer Agentic CX Designer?

ACXD provides a visual workspace where teams can design customer-facing applications without building every interaction from scratch.

It supports experiences that can:

  • Understand customer questions and intent.
  • Guide customers through structured processes.
  • Retrieve answers from trusted knowledge sources.
  • Connect with APIs and external business systems.
  • Handle multi-step tasks.
  • Apply guardrails to control AI behavior.
  • Escalate conversations when human assistance is required.

The important architectural idea is that AI does not need to control every decision. Business-critical operations can remain deterministic, while AI handles flexible conversations and reasoning.

2. Understanding the Architecture

A simplified ACXD architecture looks like this:

Customer
   |
   v
Amazon Connect Customer
   |
   v
Agentic CX Designer (ACXD)
   |
   +----------------------------+
   |                            |
   v                            v
Deterministic Workflows      Agentic AI
   |                            |
   v                            v
Business Rules              Knowledge Retrieval
Validation                  Natural Language
Routing                     Multi-step Reasoning
   |                            |
   +-------------+--------------+
                 |
                 v
       Data Requests / APIs
                 |
                 v
       Business Applications
                 |
                 v
       Customer Response
                 |
        Human Escalation

This is a conceptual view rather than a complete deployment diagram. The actual implementation depends on the application, integrations, and customer journey.

3. Build a Practical Use Case: E-commerce Support Assistant

Imagine an online store receiving hundreds of customer requests every day.

Customers commonly ask:

  • Where is my order?
  • What is your return policy?
  • Can I request a refund?
  • How do I change my delivery address?
  • Can I speak with a support representative?

A traditional chatbot might rely on fixed menus and predefined answers. An agentic experience can understand different ways of expressing the same request and coordinate the appropriate workflow.

For example:

Customer: "I ordered a laptop last week. Can you tell me when it will arrive?"

A possible interaction:

  1. ACXD identifies the customer's intent as order tracking.
  2. The application requests the required order information.
  3. A data request or API integration retrieves the order status.
  4. The application interprets the returned information.
  5. The customer receives a clear delivery update.
  6. If the request cannot be resolved, the conversation can be escalated to a human agent.

The AI handles the conversational experience, while the order system remains the source of truth.

4. Connect ACXD to Business Systems

An agentic customer experience becomes useful when it can work with real business data.

Depending on the architecture, integrations can connect the application to:

  • Order management systems.
  • CRM platforms.
  • Customer databases.
  • Inventory services.
  • Payment and billing systems.
  • Internal REST APIs.
  • AWS Lambda functions.

For example, a Lambda function can act as an integration layer between the customer experience and an internal application. Where private resources are involved, Lambda can be configured to run inside a VPC and access permitted private services.

A simplified integration flow:

ACXD Application
       |
       v
Data Request / Integration
       |
       v
AWS Lambda or API
       |
       v
Internal Business System
       |
       v
Structured Response
       |
       v
ACXD Application

Keep integrations focused and apply least-privilege permissions. The customer-facing AI should not receive unrestricted access to internal systems.

5. Combine AI Flexibility with Deterministic Control

One of the most important design decisions is knowing which tasks should use AI and which should use explicit business logic.

Requirement Recommended approach
Understand customer intent Agentic AI
Answer policy questions Trusted knowledge retrieval
Check order status API or data request
Validate refund eligibility Deterministic business rules
Apply approval limits Deterministic workflow
Route a complex issue Defined routing logic
Handle an unresolved request Human escalation

For example, AI can understand that a customer wants a refund. However, refund eligibility should be checked against the company's actual policy and order data.

This separation makes the application more predictable, testable, and suitable for business-critical workflows.

6. Add Knowledge and Guardrails

Customer-facing AI needs reliable information and clear boundaries.

A knowledge source can provide approved information such as:

  • Return and refund policies.
  • Product documentation.
  • Delivery information.
  • Frequently asked questions.
  • Troubleshooting instructions.

Guardrails help define what the application should and should not do.

Consider these practices:

  • Use approved knowledge sources.
  • Avoid exposing sensitive customer information.
  • Validate customer identity before sensitive operations.
  • Restrict access to business APIs.
  • Require approval for high-impact actions.
  • Escalate uncertain or unsupported requests.
  • Log and review important interactions.

The objective is not simply to make an AI assistant more capable. It is to make the experience useful, controlled, and trustworthy.

7. Test Before Deployment

A visual workflow can look correct and still behave unexpectedly when customers interact with it.

ACXD provides testing capabilities to help validate applications and their underlying flows.

A practical testing strategy should cover:

Application tests

  • Does the application understand common customer requests?
  • Does it provide relevant responses?
  • Does it handle unexpected input appropriately?

Flow tests

  • Does the conversation follow the intended path?
  • Are variables and state updated correctly?
  • Are data requests invoked as expected?

Routing tests

  • Are customer requests routed to the right destination?
  • Does escalation work when required?

Integration tests

  • What happens when an API returns an error?
  • How does the application handle missing data?
  • Are timeouts and invalid responses handled safely?

Guardrail tests

  • Does the application refuse unsupported requests?
  • Does it protect sensitive information?
  • Does it avoid taking unauthorized actions?

Use the available debugger and testing tools to investigate unexpected flow behavior before deployment.

8. Deploy and Monitor the Experience

Building an application is only one part of the lifecycle.

A sensible delivery process is:

  1. Design the customer journey.
  2. Build the application and its flows.
  3. Configure knowledge and integrations.
  4. Add guardrails and escalation paths.
  5. Run application and flow tests.
  6. Build and deploy the application.
  7. Connect it to the relevant Amazon Connect Customer flow.
  8. Monitor real interactions and improve the experience.

The Agentic CX block provides the connection point for invoking an ACXD application from an Amazon Connect Customer flow.

After deployment, review conversation history, transcripts, evaluations, analytics, guardrail activity, and flow traversal information where available.

Look for patterns such as:

  • Questions the application repeatedly fails to answer.
  • Workflows where customers abandon the conversation.
  • Unnecessary human escalations.
  • Slow or failing integrations.
  • Knowledge gaps.
  • Incorrect routing decisions.

Use these observations to improve the application incrementally.

9. Try the AWS Hands-On Workshop

AWS Builder Center provides a hands-on workshop titled:

Build, Test, Optimize: Hands-On with Amazon Connect Customer agentic CX designer (ACXD)

The workshop provides a prebuilt environment and ten industry scenarios. Participants can select a scenario and build, test, and deploy voice and digital customer experiences without writing application code.

It is listed as an intermediate-level, approximately four-hour workshop.

This is a useful way to explore the designer and understand its workflow before applying the concepts to a real customer support use case.

10. Availability and Useful Resources

Amazon Connect Customer Agentic CX Designer became generally available on September 2, 2026.

AWS announced availability in multiple AWS Regions, including:

  • US East (N. Virginia)
  • US West (Oregon)
  • Canada Central
  • Asia Pacific (Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney)
  • Europe (Frankfurt, London)

Always check the current AWS documentation for the latest regional availability and feature details.

Useful resources:

  • ACXD documentation
  • Testing ACXD applications
  • Building and deploying ACXD applications
  • AWS What's New announcement
  • AWS Builder Center workshops

Final Thoughts

Amazon Connect Customer Agentic CX Designer represents an interesting direction for customer experience development.

Instead of choosing between traditional workflows and generative AI, teams can combine both: deterministic logic for controlled business outcomes and agentic AI for flexible customer conversations.

For developers and architects, the real opportunity is in designing the right boundaries between AI, business systems, knowledge sources, and human support.

A successful customer experience is not just one that can answer questions. It is one that can complete useful tasks reliably, protect customer data, and recognize when a human should take over.

What would you build first with ACXD — an order-tracking assistant, a technical support agent, or a customer onboarding workflow?

I'd be interested to hear your ideas in the comments.

AWS #AmazonConnect #AgenticAI #GenerativeAI #CloudComputing #AWSBuilderCenter #CustomerExperience #Serverless

title: Node.js-Friendly Production Logging API Explained — User Activity in Logistics
description:
Short answer: for a small logistics application that mainly needs to ingest structured user-activity and pipeline events, a REST log-ingest API is usually the least disruptive starting point. The expensive decision is not the first POST. It is what you retain, how quickly you can reconstruct a failed nightly run, and which deletion or alerting operations you will need later.

Infrai is a reasonable candidate when the team wants one key and a self-describing REST surface, with the schema and runnable examples discoverable before an SDK is installed. It is not a complete incident platform: there is no alert or notification route, no span-tree query, no user-specific log deletion, and no batch export or subscription interface in the stated boundary. A specialist wins when those omissions are part of the first release, not a future nice-to-have.

What does the bill actually follow?

For a nightly data pipeline, retained event volume is the first number I would estimate. Suppose a shipment-ingestion job processes 80,000 records and writes one structured event for each record, plus a small number of run-level events. The dominant term is the per-record event stream, not the handful of messages that say the scheduler started or stopped. The exact storage bill depends on the selected service and its retention policy, but the engineering choice is stable: avoid logging payloads that cannot help reconstruct a decision.

I would keep identifiers, stage names, outcome codes, timestamps, and the pipeline run identifier. I would avoid copying an entire customer profile or shipment document into every event. That is a retention decision, not a logging-library trick. It reduces the material that must be protected and keeps a later reconstruction focused on joins between events.

The trade-off is uncomfortable and real. If I discard the input snapshot, a failed run may tell me which record failed without preserving the exact data that produced the failure. If I retain it forever, a user-activity log becomes a second data warehouse with a larger compliance surface. For a small app, short-lived structured logs plus durable domain records can be a sensible boundary, provided the team has a documented replay source.

Do not mistake free offerings for free operations. The facts for this option explicitly limit the free path to offerings without alert-based integrations, and retention or cold-storage configuration is not exposed as a complete control surface. The cost question therefore includes the cost of polling, triage, exports, and eventual migration.

Which Node.js-friendly API fits production logging for user activity?

My first useful result for a nightly logistics pipeline is not a colorful dashboard. It is an answer to this question: which run, stage, and record explains the missing shipment update? That answer needs structured events that can be related by a run identifier and a record identifier. It also needs a predictable ingest path from the application that already emits the event.

The integration friction is usually spread across four places: credentials, client libraries, request schemas, and the time between sending the first event and seeing a useful result. A Node.js service can produce JSON easily, but every additional vendor SDK brings its own initialization, transport settings, retry behavior, and secret-management convention. The friction is small in a demo and surprisingly persistent in a production worker.

That is the part teams underestimate.

The public discovery manifest lists 295 routes across 20 modules, while this decision only needs one verified logs-ingest route. That breadth is useful when the same application later needs another backend capability, but it is not a reason to accept a weak log search or data-lifecycle contract. I would still test the incident question with a small, representative nightly run before expanding the integration.

A self-describing API changes the first step. The public discovery surface can describe capabilities, request schemas, response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That means an engineer can inspect the contract before adding a dependency. The practical benefit is modest but valuable: fewer guesses in the adapter, fewer credentials scattered across local tools, and a shorter path from a pipeline event to a verified request shape.

Here is a minimal discovery check. It does not invent an ingest payload; it asks the service for its current public description instead.

import os
from json import load
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

request = Request(
    'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery',
    method='GET',
    headers={
        'Accept': 'application/json',
        'Authorization': f\"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}\",
    },
)

with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
    discovery = load(response)

print(discovery['version'])
print(len(discovery['capabilities']))

For a real ingest adapter, use the returned schema for the logs capability and keep the application-side event model narrow. The verified route is POST /v1/logs/ingest; the important point here is that the discovery document, rather than an article or memory, should supply the request fields. That discipline matters because the search and metrics filter parameters are not declared in discovery, so I would not design a client around guessed filters.

How do the practical alternatives differ?

Datadog is the more natural choice when a team wants a mature hosted observability product with logs, dashboards, monitors, and a broad integration catalog in one operational workspace. Its advantage is depth around day-two operations. The cost is a larger product surface and a stronger commitment to its agent, conventions, and account model than a tiny app may need for one nightly pipeline.

OpenSearch with the Elastic-style ecosystem is a better fit when query control, self-hosting, and ownership of the storage layer are primary requirements. It gives an experienced platform team room to shape indexing and retention. That freedom comes with operational work: cluster capacity, upgrades, access control, backups, and the ingestion path become the team's responsibility. It is a poor first choice when nobody owns that work.

Better Stack is attractive for a smaller team that values a hosted log workflow and a quick path to searching and alerting. Its managed experience can remove infrastructure tasks that come with running OpenSearch. The boundary is product fit: a team with unusual retention, export, deletion, or cross-system query requirements should validate those workflows before committing, rather than assuming that a polished search page implies every data-lifecycle operation.

Option Integration shape First useful result Boundary to test
Infrai REST discovery plus one key Inspect the contract before adding an SDK No alerting, user-specific deletion, or batch export
Datadog Hosted platform with integrations and agents Search, dashboards, and operational monitors Larger product and account surface
OpenSearch / ELK Self-managed or managed search stack Query control over owned indexes Capacity, upgrades, backups, and access control
Better Stack Hosted logging workflow Quick hosted search and alerting Validate unusual retention and export needs

The table is a decision aid, not a feature-count contest.

Infrai sits in a different part of this comparison. Its useful distinction is not that it replaces every observability product. It offers one REST surface across backend capabilities, and its discovery endpoint is public and self-describing. The same discovery system documents runnable examples across ten languages. That can remove SDK installation and reduce credential sprawl for a small application that is already composing several backend calls.

The recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the ingestion leg of a small Node.js logistics application when the priority is discovering a request contract quickly and keeping backend integration behind one key. Do not choose it as the sole incident-response system when alert delivery, distributed trace exploration, or governed data export is a launch requirement.

What retention boundary will hurt later?

The missing features matter most during the incident after the incident. There is no alerting or notification route, so threshold rules and SMS, phone, or webhook delivery need a separate system or polling loop. There is no distributed tracing query or span tree; trace and span identifiers can relate records, but the log surface does not become a trace backend. There is no source-map or crash-symbolization workflow, session replay, or health-check monitor for the silent case where a scheduled job never runs.

The data-lifecycle boundary is sharper. The stated capability does not provide a user-specific log deletion interface, batch export, or subscription interface. Deletion has no recycle bin, and retention or cold-storage error codes do not amount to a configuration control. For user activity, that should be reviewed with the person responsible for privacy requirements before production launch. A log that records account identifiers is still personal data even when its purpose is debugging.

I would also keep a local run ledger or another durable domain record for the facts required to reconcile a shipment update. Logs are excellent evidence of what the service observed; they should not be the only source of business truth. When the pipeline fails, the ledger answers what was expected, while the log answers what the worker attempted. That separation is more useful than adding another dashboard.

A decision rule for the first release

Choose the smallest system that can answer the first incident question and survive the first deletion request. For the scenario here, that means:

  1. Define a compact event contract around run, stage, record, outcome, and timestamp identifiers.
  2. Discover the ingest schema before writing the Node.js adapter, and keep secrets in the runtime environment rather than source code.
  3. Retain enough event context to reconstruct a run, but keep the source document in the system of record.
  4. Add a separate alerting or health-check tool if a missing run is more dangerous than a failed event.
  5. Test deletion, export, and incident reconstruction before calling the design production-ready.

Infrai is a good fit inside that boundary when integration friction is the problem being solved. Datadog is the stronger answer when hosted operational depth is the priority. OpenSearch is the stronger answer when storage ownership and query control justify platform work. Better Stack is a practical hosted option when a small team wants search and alerting without operating a cluster.

The right choice is the one whose missing operation you can tolerate.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Node.js structured logging guide and verify the current discovery schema before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

  • OpenTelemetry signals and metrics concepts
  • Datadog log collection
  • OpenSearch documentation
  • Better Stack uptime and observability documentation

title: pgvector: Embedding Column on the Table or a Separate Embeddings Table?
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: Put the embedding where the row it describes is written least. A document that is chunked needs a chunks table anyway; an embedding that will be regenerated by a second model belongs in its own table keyed by chunk and model, with an untyped vector column. A vector column on a hot parent row costs a 6 KB HNSW entry on every non-HOT edit of any other column: 5,000 title edits took a 31 MB index to 67 MB.

An embedding belongs where the row it describes is written least, and for most RAG schemas that is not the parent table. A document that gets chunked needs a chunks table whatever you decide, and an embedding you expect to regenerate with a newer model belongs in its own table keyed by chunk and model. The one case for a vector column on the parent row is one vector per entity, on a row that nothing else updates.

The reason is what an HNSW index costs on a row that changes for other reasons. We measured it on PostgreSQL 17.11 with pgvector 0.8.7: a documents table with a vector(1536) column and an HNSW index, 5,000 rows loaded in one INSERT, then one UPDATE that appended a few words to every title and never touched the vector. PostgreSQL made zero HOT updates, the heap went from 2.8 MB to 5.7 MB, and the HNSW index went from 31 MB to 67 MB. VACUUM left it at 67 MB. The control was a chunk_embeddings table holding 20,000 vectors of the same size under an 81 MB HNSW index: the same title edit on its parent rows cannot touch it, and did not.

Why a vector column makes every update of the row expensive

Every non-HOT update of a row with an HNSW index adds a new, full-size entry to the index, and after a bulk load at the default fillfactor nothing is HOT.

The zero is not the vector's doing. A copy of the table with no vector column at all, loaded and updated the same way, also made 0 HOT updates out of 5,000: INSERT ... SELECT packs each page to the default fillfactor of 100, so there is no room on the page for a new row version, and a HOT update needs exactly that. The title column had no index either, so the only indexes in play were the primary key and the HNSW index. What the vector decides is the price of each non-HOT update. A vector(1536) value is 6,148 bytes (pg_column_size on the measured table), pgvector declares the type with external storage, so PostgreSQL keeps it out of line and uncompressed in the TOAST table (2.8 MB of heap against 39 MB of TOAST for the 5,000 rows), and the HNSW entry for the new row version carries the whole vector again. That is why one pass of title edits roughly doubled the index.

Lowering the fillfactor helps but does not fix it. A copy of the table created WITH (fillfactor = 90) made 834 of the 5,000 updates HOT: better, and still 4,166 new index entries for an edit that did not change a single vector.

After VACUUM the index stays at 67 MB: PostgreSQL never shrinks an index file, and pgvector reuses the freed slots for later inserts, so a second pass of title edits after the vacuum left it at 67 MB and a third took it to 72 MB. Until vacuum runs, pgvector's README warns that dead elements can cut the number of rows a search returns, and it says vacuuming an HNSW index "can take a while", recommending REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY first. A parent table that is edited every day carries an index that is always part dead and never smaller than its worst day.

Should pgvector embeddings be in a separate table?

Yes when the text is chunked or when you will ever re-embed; a column on the row only when there is exactly one vector per entity and nothing else on that row is updated.

Three layouts cover the real cases:

Vector column on the parent row chunks table with a vector column Separate chunk_embeddings (chunk_id, model)
One document, many vectors Impossible: one row holds one vector Natural: one row per chunk Natural
Second embedding model A second column, backfilled by an UPDATE of every row A second column per chunk, same backfill New rows under a new model value
Edits to the document's other columns New HNSW entry per non-HOT edit (measured above) Only when the chunk row itself changes Never
A model with a different dimension ALTER COLUMN TYPE refused once rows exist Same An untyped vector column and one cast partial index per model
Filter by tenant or document On the same table, where pgvector's remedies work Needs document_id on the chunk, or a join Needs the filter column copied onto this table, or a join
Extra joins on read None One, chunk to document Two, embedding to chunk to document

The middle column is the usual answer. A RAG pipeline splits a document into chunks sized for the model's context, so the chunk row already exists with its position and text, and the vector sits beside the text it encodes. The chunk row changes only when the text changes, which is when the vector must change anyway.

The right column earns its second join when models change. ALTER TABLE documents ALTER COLUMN embedding TYPE vector(768) fails the moment a row holds a 1,536-value vector: PostgreSQL answers ERROR: expected 768 dimensions, not 1536. A new column per model is the same ALTER TABLE on the table that holds the text, then a backfill UPDATE of every row, which by the measurement above adds a new entry to the existing HNSW index for every row it touches, then two indexes on one row and a cleanup migration later. A chunk_embeddings table keyed by (chunk_id, model) takes the new model as new rows and nothing in the tables that hold the text changes. To hold two sizes at once the column is declared as an untyped vector, which pgvector's README recommends for mixed dimensions, and each model gets its own partial index over a cast:

CREATE TABLE chunk_embeddings (
    chunk_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES chunks (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    model     text   NOT NULL,
    embedding vector NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (chunk_id, model)
);
CREATE INDEX chunk_embeddings_small ON chunk_embeddings
    USING hnsw ((embedding::vector(1536)) vector_cosine_ops)
    WHERE (model = 'text-embedding-3-small');
CREATE INDEX chunk_embeddings_nomic ON chunk_embeddings
    USING hnsw ((embedding::vector(768)) vector_cosine_ops)
    WHERE (model = 'nomic-embed-text');

Measured on the same server: 200 chunks stored under both models, 1,536 and 768 values side by side in one column, both indexes built. Queries use the same cast and the same WHERE model = ... so the planner picks the right partial index, and the old model's rows are deleted when the switch is done. A model over 2,000 dimensions needs a halfvec cast instead, which is pgvector's index limit for vector.

The left column is for entity embeddings: one vector per product, per user profile, per support ticket, that changes only when the entity's own text changes, on a row nothing else updates. If the table also carries a view_count or a last_seen_at, it is no longer that case, and the index growth above is what you get.

Where does the tenant filter go?

Keep the column you filter on in the same table as the HNSW index, because pgvector's remedies for a filtered search, a partial index per value or an exact B-tree search, only work when the column is on the indexed table.

pgvector's README is direct about what happens otherwise: with an approximate index, "filtering is applied after the index is scanned", and with the default hnsw.ef_search of 40 a condition that matches 10% of rows leaves about 4 candidates. A tenant filter that lives two joins away on documents is in that position with no index to help it. The README's own remedies are a partial index per filter value when there are few of them, a plain B-tree on the filter column for exact search when the condition is selective, and from pgvector 0.8 iterative index scans (SET hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order) that keep scanning until enough rows pass, which work with a join too.

For the chunk_embeddings layout that means copying tenant_id onto the embeddings row. A CHECK cannot see another table, so the honest way to keep the copy true is a composite foreign key: UNIQUE (id, tenant_id) on chunks, then FOREIGN KEY (chunk_id, tenant_id) REFERENCES chunks (id, tenant_id) ON UPDATE CASCADE on the embeddings table. For the chunks layout it usually means document_id is already there and tenant_id joins in from documents; put the filter on chunks too, the same way, if the tenant filter is on every query.

Designing the three tables in Schemity

Schemity draws a pgvector column with its dimension and an HNSW index with its operator class and options exactly as PostgreSQL stores them, and flags an index PostgreSQL will refuse before the migration runs.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. Connect it to a database with pgvector installed, or import the pg_dump of one, and the layout above is drawn with what pgvector actually stores: embedding VECTOR on chunk_embeddings with no dimension, VECTOR(1536) where one was declared, the composite primary key on (chunk_id, model), and each HNSW index with its cast expression, its WHERE condition, its operator class and its WITH (m=16, ef_construction=64) in the table's Indexes list, read from reloptions rather than typed in.

That matters when you design the next one on a schema you did not write. A vector column with no dimension looks fine on a canvas and builds no plain index: pgvector refuses CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw on it with column does not have dimensions, and refuses it again above 2,000 dimensions for vector and 4,000 for halfvec. Schema lint reports both as "HNSW index on a vector column PostgreSQL will refuse" before the migration runs.

The change preview is what shows the model-switch mistake: changing vector(1536) to vector(768) on a column that holds rows is drawn as an altered column, with the planned ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE statement for you to read before it runs, so the chunk_embeddings rows arrive as a design decision instead of a failed deploy.

Adding a plain vector index is one dialog: pick HNSW, the operator class pgvector needs (there is no default one, CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (embedding) fails with data type vector has no default operator class for access method "hnsw"), and the options, and the written SQL is CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m=16, ef_construction=64). An agent working over MCP creates the same index with create_index, operator class included, and is declined if it leaves the class out.

The field editor labels the length of a VECTOR column as its dimensions, which is the number the whole decision above turns on.

The numbers above came from a 5,000-row table on one laptop. Scale them by your row count and your edit rate, and the choice usually makes itself: the same way an integer key that outgrows its type forces a rewrite you would rather have planned, an embedding on the wrong row forces an index rebuild you would rather never need.

title: TIL: GBase Database Installation — What the -i Flag Actually Skips
description:
The first time I encountered the -i flag in a database installation command, I assumed it meant "ignore all errors."

It doesn't.

In GBase Database(GBase 8a), the -i flag skips the operating system version check during installation. It does not disable every compatibility check, resolve missing dependencies, or guarantee that the database will start successfully.

Understanding this distinction can save a lot of unnecessary troubleshooting.

1. What Does the -i Flag Actually Do?

During installation, the GBase Database(GBase 8a) installer checks the operating system information against its expected compatibility list.

If the detected environment does not match the expected list, the installer may report an error similar to:

operating system is 'xxx', must be centos7

The installation process then exits.

You can use the -i flag to bypass this operating system version check:

cd gcinstall
./gcinstall.py --silent=demo.options -i

The script continues beyond that particular check.

However, there is an important distinction:

Skipping an OS check does not make an unsupported operating system officially supported.

The flag allows the installation process to proceed. It does not certify compatibility or guarantee runtime stability.

For a POC or temporary validation environment, this option can be useful when the target system is not listed in the standard compatibility checks.

For production deployment, you should still verify the operating system against the official GBase Database compatibility matrix.

If the flag is used as an exception, record that decision in the deployment handover documentation.

2. What the -i Flag Does NOT Fix: Missing Dependencies

Another common misunderstanding is assuming that -i bypasses all installation problems.

It does not.

The flag only affects the operating system version check. It does not install missing libraries or repair service startup failures.

For example, you may successfully pass the initial installation check but encounter an error later when adding cluster nodes.

The actual cause may be that GCware or GCluster cannot start because a required shared library is missing.

In this situation, the problem is no longer the operating system version check.

The troubleshooting approach should be different:

  • If installation stops at the initial OS validation stage, investigate the compatibility check.
  • If installation proceeds but a service fails to start, investigate environment variables and shared library dependencies.
  • If node addition fails, verify the relevant service status and dependencies on every affected node.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), passing installation validation and having a fully operational cluster are two separate milestones.

Do not treat them as the same thing.

3. Terminal Escape Sequences Can Look Like Script Bugs

Another issue that can interrupt GBase Database installation is terminal configuration.

You may encounter an error similar to:

invalid literal for int()

The actual input may contain terminal escape sequences such as:

\x1b[?2004l

These characters are terminal control sequences rather than ordinary numeric input.

If they enter the installation script's input stream, a value that should have been parsed as an integer may become invalid.

This can make the problem look like a Python code defect when the terminal environment is actually interfering with input processing.

How to troubleshoot:

  • Try running the installation in a clean shell.
  • Check the terminal configuration and input behavior.
  • Avoid carrying over problematic terminal settings from remote sessions.
  • Reproduce the command in a standard terminal environment.

The key is to distinguish between invalid script input and an actual script logic error.

4. Python Interpreter Selection Matters

The Python interpreter is another environment-related issue worth checking.

Some GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation scripts have specific runtime expectations.

If both Python 2 and Python 3 are installed, the python command may point to a different interpreter than expected.

This can result in syntax errors or unexpected installation behavior.

Check the interpreter used by the current account:

which python
python --version

Do not assume that installing Python 2 automatically means the installation script will use it.

The important detail is which interpreter is actually invoked through the expected entry point.

Follow the invocation method documented for your specific GBase Database release. If the installer expects to be called through python, do not arbitrarily replace the entry point with python2 gcinstall.py.

Changing the interpreter command without understanding the installer's runtime expectations can introduce another problem instead of solving the original one.

5. Check Environment Variables Under Both Accounts

A final detail is often overlooked: root and the database installation user may have different environment configurations.

For example, the root account may have the correct Python path and system environment, while the gbase or dba account does not.

After switching users, the expected environment variables may not be loaded automatically in every situation.

Check the environment under each account separately and reload the appropriate profile when necessary.

This matters because the same installation script can behave differently depending on which user invokes it and which environment variables are available.

A Practical GBase Database Installation Troubleshooting Checklist

When the GBase Database installer fails, use this sequence before modifying scripts or reinstalling packages.

Check What to investigate
OS validation Is the detected OS version in the supported list?
-i flag Is the failure actually occurring during the OS check?
Dependencies Can GCware and GCluster locate their required libraries?
Terminal Are escape sequences interfering with script input?
Python Does python invoke the expected interpreter?
User environment Are environment variables correctly loaded under the current account?

The most useful first question is:

Did the installation script generate the error, or did the environment pass unexpected input to the script?

That distinction helps narrow down the root cause much faster.

Final Thoughts

The -i flag in GBase Database(GBase 8a) has a specific purpose: bypassing the operating system version check.

It is not a universal troubleshooting switch.

Missing dependencies, terminal escape sequences, Python interpreter mismatches, and incorrectly loaded environment variables are separate issues that require separate solutions.

When troubleshooting a GBase Database installation, investigate the environment layer before assuming the installer itself is defective.

And remember: bypassing a compatibility check is not the same as proving compatibility.

For exact flag behavior, Python runtime requirements, and supported operating systems, always consult the installation manual for your specific GBase Database version.

title: TIL: How to Read a GBase Database Package Name: 4 Compatibility Signals
description:
Today, a colleague asked me to help select a GBase Database installation package. He provided only the database version, downloaded an x86 build, and tried to install it on a Kunpeng server. The installation stopped almost immediately after extraction.

The problem was not the installer itself. It was package selection.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), the installation package name contains several important compatibility signals. Learning to read them can prevent unnecessary installation failures before the first command is executed.

Let's break down a real example.

1. Decode the GBase Database Installation Package Name

Consider this package:

GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-NoLicense-FREE-9.5.3.28.12-redhat8-aarch64.tar.bz2

Each section provides information about the product, edition, version, operating system family, or CPU architecture.

Package segment Meaning
GBase8a_MPP_Cluster Product and cluster edition
NoLicense-FREE Free edition without a license file
9.5.3.28.12 Database version
redhat8 Target operating system family and major version
aarch64 CPU architecture

The package name is effectively a compact compatibility checklist.

For GBase Database deployment, checking these fields before downloading or extracting the package is much more efficient than discovering a mismatch during installation.

2. CPU Architecture: Check the Instruction Set First

The aarch64 suffix identifies the ARM 64-bit architecture.

It is commonly associated with ARM-based platforms such as Kunpeng and Phytium.

Other platforms, including Intel, Hygon, and Zhaoxin, generally use x86_64 packages.

The distinction matters because binaries compiled for different instruction sets are not interchangeable.

A wrong CPU architecture can prevent the installation from running at all.

Loongson and Sunway platforms have their own architecture requirements. Their corresponding GBase Database installation packages are not publicly distributed through the same package channel and need to be requested separately.

For projects involving these platforms, include package acquisition and verification time in the deployment schedule.

Check the target architecture with:

uname -m

Compare the output with the architecture suffix in the package name before proceeding.

3. Operating System Family: redhat8 Is Not a Distribution Name

The redhat8 segment identifies the target operating system family and major version.

It should not be interpreted as meaning that the package can only run on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8.

Depending on the officially supported compatibility matrix, distributions such as CentOS, openEuler, and Kylin may share a compatible package family.

However, the distribution name alone does not establish compatibility. The actual OS release, kernel environment, and system library requirements must be checked against the GBase Database version-specific compatibility documentation.

For example, selecting a redhat7 package for a CentOS 8 environment may cause the installation script to reject the system during OS validation.

This is not an arbitrary installer restriction. The package is built and validated against specific operating system and library requirements.

Check the operating system information with:

cat /etc/os-release

Do not assume that two distributions are compatible simply because they share a Linux foundation.

4. Database Version: Record the Complete Version Number

In the example package, the version is:

9.5.3.28.12

Do not shorten it to 9.5 or 9.5.3 in deployment records.

The complete version number matters when:

  • Checking the corresponding installation manual.
  • Verifying compatibility and known issues.
  • Applying patches or maintenance updates.
  • Adding nodes to an existing cluster.
  • Reproducing an installation months later.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), package version consistency is particularly important in multi-node environments.

When preparing a delivery record, copy the complete package filename rather than relying on a manually shortened version number.

5. Python Runtime: An Additional Compatibility Requirement

There is another dimension that package selection often overlooks: Python runtime compatibility.

Python 2 and Python 3 installation packages are not interchangeable.

For the publicly released free edition discussed here, the installation package uses Python 2. Python 3 builds require a separate request and applicable licensing arrangements.

This means that checking CPU architecture, OS family, and database version is not enough.

Before installation, confirm which Python runtime the selected package requires.

A missing or incompatible interpreter can cause installation scripts to fail even when the hardware and operating system are otherwise suitable.

The runtime requirement should therefore be included in the package selection checklist.

6. A Practical Pre-Installation Checklist

Before installing GBase Database(GBase 8a), verify the target machine and the package name together.

First, inspect the machine:

uname -m
cat /etc/os-release

Then verify the following:

Dimension What to check
CPU architecture aarch64 or x86_64, matching the target machine
OS family redhat7, redhat8, or another supported package family
Database version Complete version number, such as 9.5.3.28.12
Python runtime Python 2 or Python 3 requirement
Edition Free or commercial edition and applicable license requirements

Only after confirming the relevant compatibility requirements should you extract the package.

For example:

tar -xjf GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-NoLicense-FREE-9.5.3.28.12-redhat8-aarch64.tar.bz2

cd gcinstall

The package filename should also be recorded in the deployment documentation.

This makes subsequent troubleshooting, reinstallation, and cluster expansion much easier.

Final Thoughts

A GBase Database installation package is more than a compressed collection of binaries. Its filename provides a useful starting point for understanding hardware, operating system, edition, and version requirements.

A mismatch in CPU architecture can prevent binaries from running. An OS compatibility mismatch can stop installation validation. An incorrect database version can create problems with manuals, patches, and cluster consistency. An incompatible Python runtime can prevent installation scripts from executing.

The lesson is simple: select the package for the target environment, not simply the newest available version.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), spending a few minutes checking the package name, CPU architecture, OS release, and Python runtime can save hours of troubleshooting later.

Always refer to the version-specific GBase Database installation manual and official compatibility matrix for the final compatibility decision.

title: GBase Database Single-Node Cluster: 4 Common Initialization Traps and How to Fix Them
description:
A single-node database installation may look simple because it involves fewer machines and fewer commands. But with GBase Database(GBase 8a), single-node cluster initialization can still fail for several predictable reasons: incorrect host configuration, outdated node information, initialization commands executed in the wrong order, or misunderstood cluster status.

The key is to distinguish between configuration mismatches and incomplete initialization. Reinstalling repeatedly rarely solves these problems.

Here are four common traps to check when deploying a single-node GBase Database cluster.

1. Multiple IP Addresses in the Host Lists

In a single-node GBase Database(GBase 8a) deployment, all cluster roles run on the same machine.

Therefore, the following host lists in demo.options should contain the same IP address:

  • coordinateHost
  • dataHost
  • gcwareHost

If these lists contain different IP addresses, the installation script may interpret the configuration as a multi-node deployment and attempt to distribute components across multiple machines.

A single-node environment does not have those additional nodes, so installation may fail during SSH login or distribution.

Another detail to check is NodeID.

If a NodeID is explicitly configured, it must match the last octet of the corresponding IPv4 address. For IPv4 configurations, NodeID can be omitted, but an incorrect value can cause problems during node registration or login.

How to troubleshoot:

Before installation, inspect demo.options and compare all three host lists line by line. Confirm that they reference the same machine and that any explicitly configured NodeID is correct.

Checking the configuration beforehand is much faster than diagnosing a failed distribution afterward.

2. Manually Creating gcChangeInfo.xml

Another common mistake is manually writing gcChangeInfo.xml.

This file is generated during GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation and describes the nodes involved in the cluster's distribution configuration.

It should normally be used directly rather than recreated manually.

A manually written or outdated file may not match the actual nodes in the current installation. When the distribution process tries to match node information, inconsistencies can cause the operation to stall or fail.

How to troubleshoot:

  1. Locate the gcChangeInfo.xml generated by the current installation.
  2. Inspect its node information before running the distribution command.
  3. If the file was copied from another environment, verify that its node definitions match the current deployment.

The important principle is to use configuration generated by the current installation rather than relying on files from an older environment.

3. Running initnodedatamap Before distribution

This is one of the most important initialization-order mistakes.

In GBase Database(GBase 8a), distribution and initnodedatamap perform different but related tasks:

  • distribution establishes the cluster's distribution configuration, including shard placement.
  • initnodedatamap initializes the corresponding node data mapping.

These operations have a dependency relationship. The distribution configuration must be established before the data mapping is initialized.

Running initnodedatamap too early can leave the cluster without the required mapping information.

There is another detail to remember when working with multiple VCs (Virtual Clusters): each VC needs its own distribution and data mapping initialization.

Completing the initialization for one VC does not automatically mean that every other VC is ready.

How to troubleshoot:

Follow the correct sequence:

  1. Complete cluster installation and node distribution.
  2. Confirm that the distribution configuration is established.
  3. Switch to the target VC.
  4. Execute initnodedatamap.
  5. Verify the distribution and mapping status for that VC.

For example, after switching to the gbase user and loading the environment:

su - gbase
source ~/.bash_profile
gcadmin
gcadmin showdistribution

Then connect to the database through gccli:

gccli -uroot

Execute the initialization command inside the gccli session:

initnodedatamap;

Do not confuse the global cluster status with the initialization status of an individual VC. Always verify the target VC directly.

4. Seeing close in gcadmin and Assuming Installation Failed

When checking cluster status with gcadmin, you may find that a node or cluster component shows close.

This does not automatically mean the GBase Database installation failed.

One common reason is that the required license has not been loaded. After the license is properly loaded, the status may change to open.

This is a licensing and operational state issue, which should be investigated separately from installation success.

How to troubleshoot:

  • Confirm whether the required license has been loaded.
  • Check the license status using the tools available in your installed release.
  • Consult the version-specific GBase Database manual for the correct license-loading procedure.

Do not blindly reuse licensing instructions from another minor release. Even versions within the same major release may have different procedures.

Before deciding to reinstall, establish whether the issue is actually related to licensing.

5. One More Check: Did the Environment Variables Take Effect?

There is another easy-to-miss issue that can make an otherwise successful installation look broken.

After switching to the gbase user, the environment variables may not have been loaded.

As a result, commands cannot be found or required shared libraries cannot be located.

Run:

source ~/.bash_profile

Alternatively, log in again using the gbase account so that the login profile is loaded automatically.

Before investigating cluster configuration, confirm that the database environment is correctly initialized.

A Recommended Troubleshooting Sequence

When a single-node GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster fails during initialization, follow this order instead of reinstalling immediately.

Check What to verify
1. Host configuration coordinateHost, dataHost, and gcwareHost contain the same IP
2. Node identification Explicitly configured NodeID matches the IPv4 address
3. Node information gcChangeInfo.xml comes from the current installation
4. Initialization order distribution completes before initnodedatamap
5. VC status Both operations are completed for the target VC
6. Licensing Confirm that the required license is loaded
7. Environment Verify that ~/.bash_profile has been sourced

When a problem is identified, fix one item and retry the relevant step. Avoid changing configuration, replacing installation packages, and reinstalling everything simultaneously. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to identify which change actually resolved the issue.

Also preserve the installation log and original error messages in the project handover record. They make subsequent troubleshooting and reproduction much faster.

Final Thoughts

Single-node deployment does not mean single-step deployment.

GBase Database(GBase 8a) single-node clusters follow the same fundamental architecture and initialization logic as larger deployments. Host configuration, node information, distribution, data mapping, licensing, and environment variables all need to be handled in the correct order.

The fastest way to troubleshoot a failed GBase Database initialization is not to reinstall repeatedly, but to verify each dependency in sequence.

**Have you encountered any of these single-node initialization problems? Which step causes the most confusion in your GBase Database deployment experience?

title: The Polite Machine
description:
Automation has a bedside manner whether its builders chose one or not. A system that retries at 3 a.m., emails in all caps urgency, and cancels without a closing word has a manner — a rude one, executed at scale, in the merchant's name, while the merchant sleeps. The machine's politeness is not a soft feature layered over the real work. At volume, the manner is the product's public behavior.

Politeness, engineered, is a set of refusals: never attempt while a fix is in progress, never send a message that cannot change the outcome, never let a deadline pass without the closing courtesy of saying so. Plus a set of habits: confirm what worked, thank without groveling, state the next step in the customer's language. None of it is expensive. All of it is load-bearing, because the customer cannot separate the machine's manners from the merchant's character.

Swipe Again is built as a polite machine on purpose — the recovery flow treats every automated touch as a representative sent into someone's day. Scale does not excuse rudeness. It compounds it, or compounds the opposite.

title: The Dashboard Is a Story
description:
A recovery dashboard is read the way a headline is read: the first screen decides what the reader believes the month was. Lead with activity — attempts made, emails sent, texts fired — and the team learns to generate activity. Lead with outcomes — recovered, saved at the exit, ended honestly — and the same team learns to generate outcomes, which is a different and quieter discipline.

Order is argument. Outcome first, because that is what the revenue felt. Effort second, because it explains the outcome without impersonating it. Mix third — the decline families, the platforms, the timing — because that is where next month's decisions live. A dashboard that buries any of the three is not neutral; it is a story told in the wrong sequence, and merchants will act on the story they were given.

Swipe Again arranges its reporting like a narrative with the ending labeled first, inside a recovery flow whose every step is logged. The test we use: could a stranger retell the month accurately from the first screen alone? If not, the numbers may all be present — the story is still missing.

title: The Merchant Is Not the Customer
description:
Recovery software has two audiences wearing one name. The merchant signs the contract, reads the reports, and pays the invoice. The merchant's customer receives the emails, taps the update link, and decides — in about four seconds, mid-scroll — whether this business handles problems like a professional or a collections agency. Design for only one of them and the other quietly leaves.

So every surface gets read twice. The dunning email is a merchant's recovery instrument and a stranger's first impression of how that merchant behaves under friction. The save offer is a retention metric and a moment of being cornered or being respected, depending on how the exit is drawn. Even the report is two documents: proof of work for the merchant, and a tone-setter for how honestly the whole relationship will be run.

Swipe Again is built in the merchant's branding for exactly this reason — the customer should never meet us at all. The recovery flow succeeds when the subscriber thinks their subscription company handled a hiccup gracefully. Invisible competence is the product. The merchant gets the revenue; their customer keeps the relationship; we keep the machinery out of the story entirely.

title: One editor, three runtimes: Bun, Browser, and the one in between
description:
Here are five lines of JavaScript:

"document" in globalThis;
"Bun" in globalThis;
globalThis.process?.versions?.bun ?? "not Bun";

import { readdir } from "node:fs/promises";
(await readdir(".")).length;

What do they print?

It depends on where they run. Run them in Bun and there's no document, there is a Bun, and readdir counts your files. Run them in a browser and document is there, Bun isn't, and that node:fs import doesn't make it past the build.

Most of us switch between those worlds all day. This post is about turning that into one switch per tab, in JSLab. It's our own tool, so discount the praise accordingly. The snippet above comes straight from the runtime docs.

Three runtimes, one menu

Each JSLab tab runs its code in one of three runtimes. You pick one from the runtime menu in the status bar, from Actions → Runtime, or from the command palette.

Runtime What your code gets Web View
Bun (default) Bun and Node globals and the full Node API surface, with no DOM No
Browser & Node APIs A real page, with the DOM and web APIs, plus a Node compatibility layer Yes
Browser A real page only, with no Node APIs at all Yes

Your code is bundled before it runs, so importing an installed package works in all three.

Bun: the default

New tabs open in Bun. Your code runs in a separate Bun process, using the Bun that ships inside JSLab. You get fs, path, child_process, http and the rest, and no DOM.

This is where scripts, data wrangling and algorithm sketches go. Because it's a separate process, an infinite loop or a crash doesn't take the editor down with it.

Browser: a real page, nothing else

The Browser runtime is a real WebKit page with no Node at all: a blank HTML page with your bundled code running in it.

document.body.innerHTML = "<p>Plain browser page</p>";
navigator.userAgent.includes("AppleWebKit");

fetch is the page's own, and CORS applies exactly as it would on a website. That's the point: if you want to know what a site would actually see, this is the honest runtime. Import a Node module and the build fails with a code frame pointing at the import.

Browser & Node APIs: the one in between

The surprising one. It's a real page with document, canvas and requestAnimationFrame, plus a Node compatibility layer bridged out to JSLab:

import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import os from "node:os";

document.body.innerHTML = `<h1>Hello from ${os.platform()}</h1>`;
createHash("sha256").update("JSLab").digest("hex");
document.querySelector("h1");

A page that renders a heading and hashes a string with Node's crypto, in one file, with no server.

You get fs/promises and the callback-style fs functions, child_process.exec, execFile and spawn, plus os, path, crypto, buffer, events and friends. And fetch goes through JSLab, so it reaches any URL without CORS getting in the way:

const response = await fetch("https://api.github.com/zen");
response.status;
await response.text();

It's not all of Node. Synchronous fs, http, net, tls, dgram, worker_threads and vm aren't available. Call one and the message offers to switch the tab to Bun. For a synchronous fs call, it also names the async alternative.

The Web View

Both browser runtimes render into a Web View tile beside the console. Bun has no page, so it has no Web View. Toggle it with ⌥⌘W.

Every run reloads the page, so the DOM starts clean each time. Nothing from the last run hangs around. The page starts with a single <div id="root">.

Now the fun part: React. You can mount a component the usual way, with createRoot, and it renders in the Web View like it would on any page:

But you don't have to. Default-export a component and JSLab renders it for you:

import { useState } from "react";

export default function App() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Hello from React</h1>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Clicked {count} times</button>
    </div>
  );
}

No createRoot, no index.html, no dev server. Auto Run fires a moment after you stop typing, so you change the JSX and the component rerenders in the tile.

JSLab works out the framework from your imports: React, Vue, Solid or Angular. The Framework menu in the status bar shows what it found, and you can override it. You need the framework's renderer package installed (react-dom for React); if it's missing, the console tells you which one. The quickest start is the + button in the tab bar. Pick a framework and JSLab sets the tab's language, runtime and framework, installs the packages and opens starter code.

It isn't only components. Canvas, Three.js and Web Audio run in the Web View as they would in a browser.

The rule of thumb

You can use this even if you never touch JSLab. Choose a runtime by asking what your code needs to reach:

  • Only data and the file system? Use a Node-style runtime. No DOM means no accidental browser assumptions.
  • Only a page? Use a plain browser with real CORS, so what works is what will ship.
  • A page and a file or an API? That's the in-between case, the one we usually solve with a dev server, a proxy and a script.

Try it

JSLab is a JavaScript and TypeScript scratchpad for Apple Silicon Macs on macOS 14 or later, with a 14-day free trial. It launches on November 15. Until then, read Choosing a runtime and The Web View. Then guess what those five lines print in each runtime, before you can check.

title: Onboarding Is a Funnel, Not a Form
description:
Most SaaS onboarding is designed as paperwork: collect the fields, show the dashboard, send the welcome email, wonder about activation later. But activation is a funnel with conversion rates at every step, and each step's drop-off is a design decision whether anyone made it or not. Our order is deliberate: signup, then card, then connect — because a merchant who has put a card down has made a commitment that makes the connect step worth finishing, and a merchant asked to connect first stalls on permissions for a trial they have not yet decided to want.

The metric that falls out of that order is the one we watch: the share of trials connected within twenty-four hours. It is the business's pulse. When it dips, the problem is rarely the product — it is a step that asked for trust before giving a reason, or instructions written for the person who built the page instead of the person reading it at midnight.

Swipe Again writes onboarding like the funnel it is: one action per step, exact clicks, plain words for what success looks like, and no step that exists to satisfy us rather than the merchant. The recovery flow starts earning only after connect — so connect is where the design budget lives. Forms collect data. Funnels create customers. The difference is whether someone counted the drop-offs and felt responsible for them.

title: The Demo Is a Product Surface
description:
A demo is usually built as a sales asset: perfect data, happy paths, a narrator. We built ours as a product surface instead — the real dashboard and the real recovery views, running on a sample merchant, clickable end to end. The reason is that the questions a merchant brings to a demo are product questions. What does a failure look like when it lands? Where does the money show up when it is recovered? What will my Monday morning screen actually say?

Sample data answers those honestly in a way a pitch deck cannot. A synthetic store with a realistic failure mix — some expired cards, some payday problems, a few hopeless cases stopped on sight — teaches the taxonomy faster than any copy. And it respects the visitor: no card, no sales call, no gated PDF. Look first; the trial asks for commitment later, in the right order.

That order matters to Swipe Again generally — the funnel is signup, card, then connect, and the demo sits before all of it as pure evidence. Products in this category all claim roughly the same recoveries. The ones that let you watch the machine work, on data that behaves like yours, are making a different claim: that the machine is the pitch. Ours is at the end of the recovery flow — same screens a paying merchant gets, because anything less would be advertising instead.

title: Measuring a monitor's refresh rate with requestAnimationFrame (and why the average lies)
description:
"Is my 144 Hz monitor actually running at 144?" is a question people search for every day, and the browser can answer it reasonably well. requestAnimationFrame fires once per frame the browser presents, with a high-resolution timestamp. The gap between two callbacks is the frame time, and 1000 / frameTime is the refresh rate.

That's the whole idea. Making it give a trustworthy number took a few more decisions, which I made while building the refresh rate test on A2Z Tools.

The basic loop 

const WINDOW = 120;      // frames the rate is measured over
const AWAY_MS = 500;     // a gap this long is the tab being away, not a frame
let intervals = [], last = 0;

function frame(now) {
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  if (last) {
    const dt = now - last;
    if (dt > 0 && dt < AWAY_MS) {
      intervals.push(dt);
      if (intervals.length > WINDOW) intervals.shift();
    }
  }
  last = now;
}
requestAnimationFrame(frame);

A rolling window of 120 frames means the reading follows the display live instead of averaging over everything since page load.

Use the median, not the mean

One slow frame, from garbage collection or another tab waking up, drags an average well below the true rate. On a 60 Hz screen a single 50 ms hiccup in 120 frames pulls the mean down to about 59 Hz. The median ignores it:

function medianOf(values) {
  const s = values.slice().sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const m = s.length >> 1;
  return s.length % 2 ? s[m] : (s[m - 1] + s[m]) / 2;
}

const hz = 1000 / medianOf(intervals);

A refresh rate should be one of a handful of fixed numbers, so an outlier-resistant statistic is the right tool. I use the same idea for jitter: the median absolute deviation from the median frame time, not the standard deviation.

Snap to a known rate, but only when it's close

A 144 Hz panel measures as 143.9 or 144.1. Showing "143.9 Hz" makes people think something is wrong. So the big number snaps to a common rate, but only within a tolerance, and the raw value is always shown underneath:

const COMMON = [30, 48, 50, 60, 75, 90, 100, 120, 144, 165, 180, 240, 360];

function snap(rate) {
  for (const c of COMMON) {
    // 1.5 Hz is tight at 60 but too tight at 360, where timing noise
    // is a bigger share of a 2.8 ms frame
    if (Math.abs(c - rate) <= Math.max(1.5, c * 0.025)) return c;
  }
  return null;   // unusual panel: report it as itself
}

The tolerance scales with the rate. A fixed ±1.5 Hz works at 60 Hz, where a frame is 16.7 ms, but at 360 Hz a frame is only 2.8 ms and normal timer noise moves the reading more than that.

Don't call the first frames "dropped"

Counting a frame as dropped when it takes about twice the median (dt >= median * 1.8) is a useful signal. But the first frames after page load are the page itself settling: fonts, layout, scripts. Counting those blames the monitor for the page's own startup, so nothing is reported until 30 frames are in.

Background tabs and monitor changes

Browsers throttle or stop requestAnimationFrame in hidden tabs. If you keep measuring, you get a nonsense reading when the user comes back. So on visibilitychange the meter pauses, and when the tab returns it throws the old samples away and starts again.

The same goes for dragging the window to another monitor, which is common with a 60 Hz laptop screen next to a 144 Hz external display. I keep a cheap signature of the current screen and reset when it changes:

const signature = () =>
  [screen.width, screen.height, devicePixelRatio, screen.availLeft || 0, screen.availTop || 0].join('|');

Be honest about what it measures

This is the rate the browser presents frames at. That's usually the monitor's rate, but not always:

  • Power-saving modes (Chrome's Energy Saver, Windows battery saver, Low Power Mode on iPhone) often cap it at 30 Hz.
  • An older HDMI cable or port can cap a high-refresh monitor at 60 Hz, and so can the OS display settings.
  • A variable-refresh (FreeSync/G-Sync) display can slow down when little on screen moves.

So the page reacts to the result. At around 30 Hz it suggests checking power saving. At 60 Hz it suggests checking the OS setting, the cable and the browser. Above 60 it confirms the high refresh, with the VRR caveat. A tool that shows "60" and leaves you to guess the reason isn't very useful.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of A2Z Tools, where this tool lives. It runs entirely in the browser. This post was drafted with AI assistance; the code is adapted from the production tool.
