title: The Connect Page Is the Revenue Page
description:
Every SaaS product has a page where the money actually changes hands, and it is rarely the pricing page. For a recovery tool, it is the connect page — the moment a merchant who has signed up, started a trial, and handed over a card decides whether to grant access to the platform where their revenue lives. Everything before that moment is intention. Everything after it is product. The connect page is the hinge.

So it gets the discipline other pages beg for: instructions in simple words, the exact clicks in order, one action per step, and a plain statement of what success looks like when it works. No jargon about scopes or tokens where a merchant can see it. No optional detours. A merchant who stalls here does not stall because the product failed — they stall because the page asked them to be a developer for ninety seconds.

Swipe Again treats connect as the revenue page it is: card first, then connect, with the share of trials connected within twenty-four hours watched as the business's vital sign. Stripe connects fastest — an approval in Stripe's own window, no keys to paste — and we say so, because the honest ranking helps merchants start where success is quickest. The recovery flow cannot recover anything for a merchant who never connects. The least glamorous page in the product is the one the whole business flows through, and it is written like it.

title: Node.js Text Classification: Implementing Structured Output with a GPT API
description:
Node.js Text Classification: Implementing Structured Output with a GPT API

TL;DR: For a Node.js implementation of text classification using a GPT API, the important design choice is not which text model sounds best. It is whether the classifier returns a contract that the review queue can validate, retry, and safely apply twice. Put the model behind a narrow adapter, require a small structured result, reject malformed output, and make the write path idempotent.

A report classifier should be treated like an unreliable dependency in a production queue. The useful result is a label, a confidence value with a defined meaning, and enough trace context to explain why a human reviewer received the item. Everything else is optional prose.

Retries are part of the design.

Make the write conditional.

How should Node.js implement text classification using a GPT API?

Start with the workflow, not the prompt. A media report might arrive with a report ID, the reported text, a policy category, and a review priority. The classifier should return a bounded object such as category, priority, needs_human_review, and reason_code. The consumer must know what each field means before a model is called. The same boundary applies when implementing the client in Node.js: the JavaScript adapter can call the GPT API, but the queue worker should own validation and state transitions.

A free-form answer is hard to operate. It can contain a plausible label with a misspelled key, a confidence score on an unknown scale, or an explanation that quietly changes the decision. A schema makes those failures visible at the boundary. It also gives the team a place to decide what happens when the model cannot classify the report: route it to human review, rather than inventing a fifth state in application code.

The word “confidence” deserves care. Unless the serving system defines and calibrates it, treat that number as a signal for triage, not as a probability that the label is correct. The decision rule belongs to the service owner.

I first thought the prompt was the main implementation detail. The queue contract turned out to matter more: a beautifully worded answer still needs a valid category before it can create review work.

The incident lesson: duplicate delivery is a classification problem too

I approach this path with the same concern I bring to cron and queue workers: a retry is normal, and a duplicate delivery is not an exceptional event. Suppose a worker classifies report rpt_157, times out while acknowledging the queue message, and receives the same message again. If classification and the state transition are coupled to an unguarded insert, the second attempt can create two review tasks. The label may be right and the system can still be wrong.

The invariant is simple: the report ID is the idempotency key for the business decision. Store the decision with a uniqueness constraint, or use a conditional update that only advances the report from its expected prior state. Record the model request separately from the applied decision if audit detail matters. Do not use a generated request ID as the only deduplication key; retries generate new requests.

Here is the preventative shape in Go. A Node.js service can use the same interface boundary with a typed function and a schema validator. The classifier is an interface, so tests can return malformed data, a transient error, or a valid decision without contacting a provider. The repository owns the conditional write. That ownership matters during the awkward interval after a model response has been received but before the queue acknowledgement is durable: a worker crash can replay the message, and only the business-key check can distinguish a new decision from a repeated application.

type ModerationReport struct {
    ID   string
    Text string
}

type Decision struct {
    Category         string `json:"category"`
    Priority         string `json:"priority"`
    NeedsHumanReview bool   `json:"needs_human_review"`
    ReasonCode       string `json:"reason_code"`
}

type Classifier interface {
    Classify(context.Context, ModerationReport) (Decision, error)
}

type DecisionStore interface {
    ApplyOnce(context.Context, string, Decision) (bool, error)
}

func Process(ctx context.Context, c Classifier, s DecisionStore, r ModerationReport) error {
    d, err := c.Classify(ctx, r)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := validate(d); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = s.ApplyOnce(ctx, r.ID, d)
    return err
}

ApplyOnce should report whether it applied a new decision or found an existing one. The worker usually does not need to call the model again merely because the queue redelivered the message. If the first attempt failed before a durable decision, a retry remains useful. That distinction is the point of keeping the idempotency check at the business boundary.

The trade-off is deliberate: validation and replay code add maintenance, but accepting arbitrary prose moves that cost into every downstream consumer. This pattern is a poor fit for one-off exploration where outputs are disposable; it is a better fit for moderation records that can trigger human work.

This advice does not apply unchanged to exploratory labeling, where every run is intentionally a new experiment. Use a run ID there, keep outputs immutable, and compare runs explicitly. Production review state has a different contract.

How should the model boundary be tested?

The prompt is one input to a larger protocol. Test the protocol with fixtures that represent the failures operators actually see: an unknown category, missing keys, extra prose around JSON, an empty report, a request timeout, and a valid response delivered twice. The expected result is not always “retry.” A schema violation can be a quarantine or human-review event; a transport timeout can be retried with a bounded policy.

Keep a small golden set of reports that has been reviewed by humans. It should contain ambiguous language and examples near category boundaries, not just easy cases. Measure disagreements by category and inspect the false positives that create review load. A single aggregate accuracy number hides the operational cost of sending too many benign reports to an urgent queue.

Use two separate budgets: a request deadline and a retry budget. A deadline prevents one stuck call from holding a worker forever. A retry budget prevents a bad dependency or malformed contract from multiplying queue pressure. Backoff should include jitter, and permanent validation failures should stop retrying until a person or a controlled replay fixes the input.

Where do observability and deployment fit?

Log a correlation ID, report ID, classifier version, schema version, latency, outcome class, and retry count. Do not put the complete report text or sensitive user content in ordinary logs by default. A reviewer needs to find the decision; an operator does not need a second copy of the report in every log line.

Dashboards should separate transport errors, schema failures, rejected inputs, human-review fallbacks, and successful applications. Alert on queue age and fallback rate, not just HTTP error rate. A service can return successful requests while the classification contract is drifting and the review queue is filling with manual work.

Roll out changes as data migrations, even when no database table changes. Version the output schema, preserve the old parser during a transition, and replay a fixed evaluation set before changing the application rule. If the category vocabulary changes, migrate stored decisions deliberately; do not let a prompt edit silently reinterpret historical moderation records.

Choosing an implementation without choosing a vendor

The decision criteria are concrete. Prefer an integration that can enforce structured output or make validation practical, expose bounded request controls, and return enough request metadata for tracing. A hosted API, a self-hosted model, and a library wrapper each move different responsibilities between your team and the serving layer. The wrapper may shorten initial code while leaving versioning, retries, and schema enforcement to your service. A direct client may expose more control while requiring more adapter code. A self-hosted path can change deployment and capacity work without removing the need for idempotent writes.

For a Node.js team, using a familiar SDK can reduce adapter code, while a direct HTTP client can make request and retry behavior easier to audit. Neither choice supplies the business idempotency rule for you.

The reference integration documentation for a popular chat abstraction is useful for understanding how a wrapper presents model calls, but it is not a substitute for your production contract. Keep the adapter narrow enough that changing the serving path does not change the queue semantics.

For this media workflow, I would accept a slightly slower path that produces a validated, auditable decision over a faster path that emits attractive prose. Human review is the fallback. The system should make that fallback explicit.

Sources

  • https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/chat/openai/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9333

title: What building wedding invitation websites taught us about the phones guests really use
description:
At Invifest we make invitations and guest management for weddings and every big moment. Each family gets its own invitation website: every function with its date, time, venue and map pin, dress codes, the family's own song, and an RSVP for each function. The link goes out on WhatsApp.

That last part changes everything about how we build. The person opening the link is rarely the couple. It is a grandmother on a four year old Android phone, inside WhatsApp's in-app browser, with battery saver on. Here is what that guest taught us.

1. With every animation switched off, the page must still be whole

Reduce Motion on iPhone, Low Power Mode and Android battery savers stop CSS animations dead. If a block only reaches opacity: 1 through a keyframe, it stays invisible forever for that guest. The same settings make scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' }) do nothing at all.

Our rule now:

  • The resting state is visible. Animation is decoration on top, never the thing that reveals content.
  • Every reveal driven by an IntersectionObserver gets a timeout fallback that shows the block anyway.
  • Every automatic scroll has an instant fallback.

And we test it instead of guessing:

await page.emulateMediaFeatures([
  { name: 'prefers-reduced-motion', value: 'reduce' },
]);

2. 100vh is the wrong height on an iPhone

On iOS Safari, 100vh is the height with the toolbar hidden. A "full screen" cover built on it hides its bottom edge, often the button that matters, behind the toolbar. We write every screen-tall block as 100vh first and 100svh right after it (older browsers keep the first), use dvh for fixed overlays, and pad every fixed bottom bar with env(safe-area-inset-bottom) in pages that use viewport-fit=cover. A small lint in our build fails any screen-tall 100vh that has no svh beside it.

3. The WhatsApp preview is the real front door

Most guests decide whether to open the invite from the preview card in the chat. So every invite has its own og:image, title and description, made for that family. When the picture changes we give the file a new name (-v2), because WhatsApp and the CDN both keep the old one for days.

A related trap: never request a new file's URL while the deploy that adds it is still running. A single-page app answers every unknown path with its HTML shell and a 200, and the CDN will happily keep that HTML under your image's name for a week. We check the content type and size of a new asset, not just the status code.

4. One app, many invitations

Every invitation used to be its own small app. Now each one is a folder of words (a short YAML card) plus the family's own files, and one React app builds all of them. Artwork that more than one invitation uses lives once in a shared library and a card points to it, so a fix in one place reaches every invite. A family's own photos and song never leave their folder.

5. A guest should see only their functions

An Indian wedding can have eight functions over three days, and not every guest is invited to all of them. Instead of one invite for everyone, each side or group gets its own link with only its functions, and the RSVP is per function, so the family knows the headcount for the Haldi and the Sangeet separately. We wrote more about this in inviting guests to selected functions.

6. Elders do not install apps or log in

No app, no login, no "open in browser" step. The invite opens straight from the chat, the map pin opens the phone's own maps app, and the text is large enough to read without glasses. Our notes on digital invitations for elderly guests go deeper.

7. Changes should be as easy as saying them

Families ask for changes the way they talk: "make the Sangeet start at 7" or "add Nani's name here". So each family gets a review link where they tap the spot on the invite and simply say what they want. We read it as a list of changes tied to exact places on the page.

If you are building anything that elders open from WhatsApp, these rules carry over. And if you are planning an Indian wedding, here is how an invitation website comes together.

Written by the team at Invifest, India.

title: How to Detect Circular Dependencies in Java, TypeScript, Python and Go
description:
A circular dependency is rarely written on purpose. It shows up one reasonable import at a time — a service that needs a helper, a helper that needs a constant from the service — until three classes can no longer be changed without the other two. This guide covers how to find them in Java, TypeScript, Python and Go, how to break them, and how to stop new ones in code review.

Why they matter

  • Changes ripple. Every class in the cycle can be affected by a change to any other.
  • Testing gets heavy. To test one piece you have to construct the whole cycle.
  • Runtime bugs. In Node.js a circular require or import can hand you a module that hasn't finished initialising, so a value is undefined at load time. Spring Boot has refused circular bean references by default since 2.6.
  • Splitting becomes impossible. A cycle can't be extracted into separate services or packages without breaking it first.

Java

ArchUnit lets you write the rule as a unit test, failing the build when packages form a cycle:

slices().matching("com.myapp.(*)..")
    .should().beFreeOfCycles()
    .check(importedClasses);

In Spring, a startup failure about circular references between beans is the framework telling you the same thing at runtime. Resist re-enabling spring.main.allow-circular-references; fix the cycle.

TypeScript and JavaScript

madge builds the import graph and lists cycles; eslint-plugin-import catches them while you edit:

npx madge --circular --extensions ts src/

// .eslintrc
"rules": { "import/no-cycle": "error" }

Python

Pylint reports import cycles as cyclic-import (R0401), and pydeps can draw the module graph with the cycles highlighted:

pylint --disable=all --enable=cyclic-import mypackage
pydeps mypackage --show-cycles

Moving an import inside a function makes the error go away but keeps the cycle; treat it as a temporary patch.

Go

The compiler does the package-level work for you: an import cycle between packages is a build error. Cycles between types inside one package are still allowed, and a large package can hide a tangle of structs that all depend on each other.

How to break a cycle

  1. Invert one dependency. Have A depend on an interface it owns, and let B implement it.
  2. Extract the shared part. If both sides use the same types or helpers, move them into a third module both depend on.
  3. Use an event instead of a call. When B only needs to know that something happened in A, A can publish an event rather than calling B.
  4. Merge them. If two classes can't work without each other, they may really be one.

Stop new cycles in pull requests

Language tools check one language and usually one level — packages or files. Archynt builds a class-level graph for Java, TypeScript, Python and Go and finds every cycle in it. On a pull request it analyses both the base and the head commit and reports only what the PR changed: a new cycle of four or more classes fails the check, a smaller one warns. The same analysis flags god classes, single points of failure and dead-code candidates.

For public repositories it's a free GitHub Action — no account and no token shared:

name: Archynt architecture scan
on: pull_request

jobs:
  archynt-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - uses: archynt/pr-check-action@v1
        with:
          language: java # java | go | node | python

Private repositories use PR checks through the GitHub App, and the class diagram shows where each cycle sits in the codebase.

FAQ

What is a circular dependency?
Two or more modules or classes that depend on each other, directly (A uses B and B uses A) or through a chain (A → B → C → A). None of them can be understood, tested or changed in isolation.

Why are circular dependencies bad?
They couple pieces that should be independent: a change in one ripples through the whole cycle, tests need the entire cycle wired up, and in some runtimes they cause real bugs, such as half-initialised modules in Node.js or bean creation failures in Spring.

Does Go allow circular imports?
No. The Go compiler rejects import cycles between packages with an "import cycle not allowed" error. Types inside the same package can still depend on each other in a cycle.

How do I fix a circular dependency?
Usually by inverting one dependency through an interface, extracting the shared part into a module both can depend on, or replacing a direct call with an event. Merging the two pieces is the right answer when they were never really separate.

Originally published on archynt.com.

title: I wrote MobX from scratch in 150 lines. Here's every bug I hit
description:
I'm preparing for senior React Native interviews, and one kind of task keeps showing up: "write your own state manager". Redux is the usual target. I picked MobX instead, because I've used it for years and realized I couldn't explain what happens between store.count++ and the re-render.

The finished version is about 150 lines: observable, autorun, computed, action, and a React hook. Getting there took a lot more than 150 lines of wrong code. This post goes through the bugs in the order I made them. Every output below comes from running the code.

The core: track on read, trigger on write

MobX doesn't ask you to declare dependencies. A reaction runs once, MobX watches which fields it reads, and from then on it reruns only when one of those fields changes.

You need two pieces for that. A global variable that says which reaction is running right now, and a Proxy that records reads and announces writes:

type Reaction = (() => void) & { deps: Set<Set<Reaction>> }

let currentReaction: Reaction | null = null

export const observable = <T extends object>(object: T): T => {
  const reactionsByKey = new Map<string | symbol, Set<Reaction>>()

  const track = (key: string | symbol) => {
    if (!currentReaction) return
    let reactions = reactionsByKey.get(key)
    if (!reactions) {
      reactions = new Set()
      reactionsByKey.set(key, reactions)
    }
    reactions.add(currentReaction)
    currentReaction.deps.add(reactions)
  }

  const trigger = (key: string | symbol) => {
    const reactions = reactionsByKey.get(key)
    if (!reactions) return
    [...reactions].forEach((reaction) => reaction())
  }

  return new Proxy(object, {
    get(obj, key, receiver) {
      track(key)
      return Reflect.get(obj, key, receiver)
    },
    set(obj, key, value, receiver) {
      if (Object.is(Reflect.get(obj, key, receiver), value)) return true
      const result = Reflect.set(obj, key, value, receiver)
      if (result) trigger(key)
      return result
    },
  })
}

Every key has a Set of reactions that read it. autorun puts itself into currentReaction, calls your function, and every get along the way adds it to the right Sets.

A few Proxy details matter here. The set trap has to return true, because a falsy result throws a TypeError in strict mode. Reflect.set already returns a boolean, so passing it through is enough. Object.is skips writes that don't change anything, and unlike === it treats NaN as equal to NaN, so writing NaN over NaN doesn't wake anyone up. The receiver argument decides what this is inside getters and setters on the object. It confused me enough that it gets its own post.

Almost every line above was a bug fix at some point.

Bug 1: a reaction that listens to fields it stopped reading

My first autorun just set currentReaction, called the function and cleared it. Dependencies only ever got added. Here's what that does to a conditional read:

const s = observable({ show: true, name: 'Bogdan' })

autorun(() => console.log('render:', s.show ? s.name : 'hidden'))

s.show = false
s.name = 'Ivan'

render: Bogdan
render: hidden
render: hidden

After show became false, the function no longer read name. It still reran when name changed, because it was still sitting in the Set for name from the first run. In a React app this is a component that re-renders because of data it doesn't display.

Dependencies have to be rebuilt on every run. Before calling the function, remove the reaction from every Set it's in, and let the run add it back where it still belongs. That's why each reaction keeps deps, a Set of the Sets that contain it. Without the link back, there's no way to find those Sets:

const cleanup = () => {
  reaction.deps.forEach((set) => set.delete(reaction))
  reaction.deps.clear()
}

With cleanup the same code prints two lines.

Bug 2: the Set that never ends

Cleanup fixed bug 1 and broke something else. My trigger iterated the Set directly:

reactions.forEach((reaction) => reaction())

const s = observable({ count: 0 })
autorun(() => console.log('count:', s.count))
s.count = 1

count: 0
count: 1
count: 1
count: 1
count: 1
...

It never stopped. I had a guard that threw after a few runs, otherwise the tab would just hang.

Set.prototype.forEach visits entries that are added while it's iterating. If you delete an entry and add it back, it goes to the end of the Set and gets visited again. That's exactly what a reaction does: cleanup deletes it from the Set for count, then the function reads count and track adds it back. forEach sees a "new" entry and calls it, and the same thing happens again.

You can see it without any reactivity:

const set = new Set(['x'])
let visits = 0
set.forEach((v) => {
  if (++visits > 3) return
  set.delete(v)
  set.add(v)
})
visits // 4

The fix is to iterate over a copy, [...reactions]. Vue 3 copied the Set in triggerEffects in the same way, until 3.5 replaced Sets with linked lists. I hit this bug a second time later, when I wrote batching.

Bug 3: a nested autorun steals tracking from its parent

If an autorun creates another autorun, the inner one overwrites currentReaction. When it finishes and resets it to null, the outer one keeps running with no reaction to attach reads to:

const s = observable({ a: 1, c: 1 })

autorun(() => {
  autorun(() => console.log('inner a:', s.a))
  console.log('outer c:', s.c)
})

s.c = 2

Nothing happens on s.c = 2. The outer reaction read c while currentReaction was null, so it never subscribed.

The fix is a stack, but you don't need an array for it. Each run remembers the previous reaction and puts it back at the end, in finally so that an exception in the function doesn't leave the wrong reaction behind:

const previousReaction = currentReaction
try {
  currentReaction = reaction
  cleanup()
  fn()
} finally {
  currentReaction = previousReaction
}

After this change, s.c = 2 prints outer c: 2.

Bug 4: dispose that didn't dispose

autorun returns a function that stops it. It needs two things: cleanup() to remove the reaction from all Sets, and an isDisposed flag. The flag covers the case where trigger already copied the Set and the reaction is in that copy when it gets disposed. Without the flag, it would run one more time after you stopped it.

Later I moved the shared code into a helper and passed the flag as an argument:

const makeReaction = (isDisposed: boolean, fn: () => void) => {
  const reaction = () => {
    if (isDisposed) return
    // ...
  }
}

export const autorun = (fn: () => void) => {
  let isDisposed = false
  const reaction = makeReaction(isDisposed, fn)
  // ...
  return () => { isDisposed = true }
}

A boolean is passed by value. isDisposed = true in dispose changes the variable in autorun, and the helper still has its own false. The check has to read the variable through a closure, either by keeping it in the scope where the reaction is created or by passing a getter.

Hooking it up to React

The first hook was useState plus useEffect: run an autorun in an effect and push the selected value into state. Two things went wrong.

I wrote setState(value). When the selected value is a function, React calls it as an updater instead of storing it. The safe form is setState(() => value).

The selector you pass changes on every render, because it's usually an inline arrow. The autorun is created once, so it would keep calling the selector from the first render. The latest selector goes into a ref, updated in useLayoutEffect, and the autorun reads selector.current.

The second version uses useSyncExternalStore, which React 18 added for exactly this, and which avoids tearing in concurrent rendering:

export const useObserver = <T,>(fn: () => T) => {
  const selector = useRef(fn)

  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    selector.current = fn
  }, [fn])

  const subscribe = useCallback(
    (onStoreChange: () => void) =>
      autorun(() => {
        selector.current()
        onStoreChange()
      }),
    []
  )

  return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, fn)
}

subscribe has to be stable. If it's a new function on each render, React unsubscribes and subscribes again every time. The autorun calls selector.current() only to subscribe to whatever it reads, and onStoreChange tells React to call getSnapshot again.

There's a known trap I left unsolved. If the selector returns a new object or array, for example store.items.filter(...), getSnapshot returns a new reference on every call. React warns that the result of getSnapshot should be cached and then re-renders in a loop. A real implementation memoizes the snapshot.

computed: a cache that knows when it's stale

computed is a derived value that is lazy and cached:

const total = computed(() => cart.price * cart.qty)

total.get() // computes
total.get() // returns the cached value
cart.qty = 3 // marks it stale, doesn't recompute
total.get() // recomputes

It should recompute only when a field it actually read has changed. Its function also has to be pure. It can only depend on observable fields. If it reads a plain variable or Date.now(), nothing will ever tell it the value changed.

Bug 5: isDirty started as false

My first get() was if (isDirty) { value = fn(); isDirty = false } with isDirty initialized to false. The first call returned undefined, and nothing ever set the flag to true. That one's easy to find.

Bug 6: subscribing the function that computes

Then I needed something to set isDirty = true when a dependency changed. I reused the autorun machinery: a reaction that runs fn with tracking, and get() calls it when the value is stale.

The problem is which function ends up in the Sets. During tracking, currentReaction was the evaluator itself. So when cart.qty changed, trigger called the evaluator directly, bypassing get() and its isDirty check:

const total = computed(() => cart.price * cart.qty)
total.get()  // 200, evaluator calls: 1
cart.qty = 3 // evaluator calls: 2
total.get()  // 200

The value was recomputed eagerly when nobody asked for it. The result was thrown away, because trigger ignores return values. isDirty stayed false, so get() kept returning 200 from then on.

A computed needs two separate things. One is what trigger calls, and for a computed that function only marks it stale:

const markDirty = () => { isDirty = true }

The other is the tracked run of fn that happens inside get(), with markDirty as the current reaction. That way the fields subscribe markDirty, and fn runs only when someone reads the value.

Bug 7: two functions called fn

At this point autorun and computed had the same block: save the previous reaction, set the current one, clean up, run, restore in finally. I moved it into a shared createReaction:

const createReaction = (fn: () => void) => {
  const reaction = Object.assign(() => fn(), { deps: new Set() })
  const cleanup = () => { /* ... */ }
  const run = () => {
    const previousReaction = currentReaction
    try {
      currentReaction = reaction
      cleanup()
      return fn()
    } finally {
      currentReaction = previousReaction
    }
  }
  return { reaction, cleanup, run }
}

Inside createReaction, fn is the reaction callback: markDirty for a computed, and for an autorun a callback that calls run(). The user's function lives in a different scope with the same name. So the computed's run() executed markDirty and returned undefined, and the autorun did callback → run → callback → run until Maximum call stack size exceeded.

The function to run has to come in as an argument:

const run = <T,>(work: () => T): T => {
  const previousReaction = currentReaction
  try {
    currentReaction = reaction
    cleanup()
    return work()
  } finally {
    currentReaction = previousReaction
  }
}

The computed calls run(fn) with its formula, the autorun calls run(fn) with its body, and the parameter of createReaction gets a name that can't be confused with either, like onTrigger.

The autorun's callback calls run, which only exists after createReaction returns. This works:

const callback = () => {
  if (isDisposed) return
  run(fn)
}
const { reaction, cleanup, run } = createReaction(callback)
reaction()

A closure captures the variable, not its value. callback is created before run exists, but it isn't called until reaction() on the last line, and by then run is initialized. Calling callback() before the destructuring would throw "Cannot access 'run' before initialization".

action: five ways batching broke

Every write triggers reactions right away, so two writes run an autorun twice, and the first run sees a half-updated state:

autorun(() => console.log(cart.price, cart.qty))
cart.price = 200 // 200 2
cart.qty = 5     // 200 5

action should collect the writes and run each affected reaction once at the end. Values are still written immediately, so reading cart.price inside the action returns the new value. Only reactions wait.

Bug 8: a queue of Sets

My first version put the Set of reactions for each changed key into a queue. price and qty have separate Sets, and the same autorun is in both:

autorun: 100 2
autorun: 200 5
autorun: 200 5

The queue has to hold reactions. A Set<Reaction> deduplicates them on its own.

Bug 9: the queue was never cleared

The next action ran every reaction from the previous one again. clear() after the flush.

Bug 10: a nested action ended the batch early 

action(() => {
  action(() => { s.a = 2 })
  s.b = 2
})

The inner action set isBatching = false when it finished, so s.b = 2 ran reactions immediately. Each action has to remember the previous state of the flag, restore it, and flush only if it was the outermost one. MobX uses a counter, globalState.inBatch, and runs reactions when it drops back to zero. A saved boolean does the same job.

Bug 11: computed went stale inside an action 

const total = computed(() => s.price * s.qty)
total.get()

action(() => {
  s.qty = 3
  console.log(total.get())
})

total inside action: 200
total after action: 300

I had put the batching check into trigger: during an action, queue every reaction instead of calling it. That included markDirty. The computed didn't learn it was stale until the action ended, so get() inside the action returned the old value.

A computed doesn't need batching at all. Marking it stale is cheap and the recompute is lazy anyway. The question is where the decision belongs. You can teach trigger the difference between kinds of reactions, but then the Reaction type needs a flag. I moved the check into the autorun's callback instead, and trigger went back to calling everything:

const callback = () => {
  if (isDisposed) return
  if (isBatching) {
    batchingDelayedReactions.add(reaction)
    return
  }
  run(fn)
}

MobX is built the same way. When a value changes, it calls onBecomeStale_ on every observer. A computed reacts by propagating "maybe changed" to its own observers. A reaction calls schedule_(), which pushes it onto globalState.pendingReactions, and the list runs when the batch ends.

Bug 12: flushing while still batching

With the check inside the reaction, the next run of my tests printed nothing after the action. The flush loop called each queued reaction while isBatching was still true, and each one put itself back into the queue and returned. The flag has to be reset before the flush.

Bug 13: an exception left the flag on

If the function passed to action threw, the code after it never ran, isBatching stayed true, and from then on every write in the app was queued and never flushed. Restoring the flag and flushing go into finally. The flush runs over a copy of the queue, for the same reason as bug 2.

The final version:

let isBatching = false
const batchingDelayedReactions = new Set<Reaction>()

export const action = (fn: () => void) => {
  const previousBatching = isBatching
  isBatching = true

  try {
    fn()
  } finally {
    isBatching = previousBatching
    if (!previousBatching) {
      const reactions = [...batchingDelayedReactions]
      batchingDelayedReactions.clear()
      reactions.forEach((reaction) => reaction())
    }
  }
}

My tests cover four cases: two actions in a row, a nested action, a computed read inside an action, and an exception followed by a plain write. All four pass now. Before this version, each of them failed in a different way.

What's still missing

One gap is visible right away:

const total = computed(() => cart.price * cart.qty)
autorun(() => console.log('total:', total.get()))
cart.qty = 3

This prints total: 200 once, and nothing after qty changes. Inside get() the current reaction is markDirty, so the autorun never subscribes to price or qty, and the computed has no observers of its own. To fix it, a computed has to act as an observable: track whoever calls get(), and notify them when it becomes stale.

Even with that fixed, MobX does a lot more. Its graph avoids glitches: when two computeds depend on the same field and an autorun reads both, the autorun runs once and never sees one updated and one stale. A computed with no observers stops listening to its own dependencies. There are observable Map and Set, async actions with flow, comparers, onBecomeObserved hooks, trace and spy. That's why the production build of MobX 7.1.3 is around 14.7 KB gzipped, against my 150 lines.

What I got out of it is that I now know where all of that comes from. In an interview, "MobX tracks reads through Proxy" is the short answer. The cleanup, the copy before iterating, the restore in finally, and the batching check in the reaction are what the follow-up questions are about.

New posts go to my Telegram channel first: t.me/umaniuk_dev

Questions, or a senior mobile role you think I'd fit? Message me on Telegram: @umaniukbogdan

title: crustc ports rustc to C and builds it with GCC
description:
The crustc repository is C code that you compile with GCC and GNU make into a working Rust compiler. Point make at a matching LLVM build and the binary it produces reports rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c712ea946 2026-06-16), then goes on to build core, alloc and std. The author built it on ARM64 Linux with GCC 13.3.0 and the LLD 18.1.3 linker. An unoptimized build takes about 78 seconds of wall time (937 seconds of user time with make -j20). It still needs LLVM at runtime, because rustc uses LLVM, so the repo asks you to supply libLLVM.so.22.1-rust-1.98.0-nightly from the matching nightly toolchain rather than shipping a binary.

That is rustc itself, translated to C and built by a C compiler. The repo is a demo for cilly, the author's Rust-to-C toolchain and, by their count, the 14th attempt at the problem over three years (rustc_codegen_clr was an earlier public one). cilly is a Rust library that generates C plus a rustc backend plugin. Instead of handing MIR to LLVM for machine code, it emits C and passes that to whatever C compiler you nominate for the target. Compiling rustc with itself through that path is the flashiest thing to show, so that is what the repo does.

The useful engineering is that cilly does not assume a fixed C dialect. It emits "witness" programs and compiles them to learn what the target compiler and platform actually support: a file containing _Thread_local int KEYWORD_TLS_SUPPORTED; only compiles if the compiler has _Thread_local, so that tells cilly whether it can use the keyword. It queries type layouts, sizes, alignments, character encoding (ASCII) and integer representation (two's complement), with fallbacks where it can. The author aims to assume nothing outside ANSI C, works around newer-standard hazards like strict aliasing, and documents the few unavoidable assumptions ((void*)(uintptr_t)(ptr) round-trips, CHAR_BIT == 8) with runtime asserts where possible. The cost is that output is target-specific. C generated for Arm64 will not run on riscv32; you regenerate per target.

cilly can also talk to a C compiler over TCP, with UART floated as a possibility. You run rustc on an ordinary Linux box and let cilly drive a small C server on the target, which covers platforms that have no C cross-compiler at all. The author used this to build small Rust programs for x86 Plan 9 VMs from an Arm64 Linux host; the binary printed Hello, world! and carried a rust_begin_unwind symbol. cilly can embed markers in its object files, cache its IR, and emit a directory of makefiles, so the end product is a tree you build with a C compiler and make.

Compiling Rust through C does not undo Rust's safety guarantees. The borrow checker and type system run in rustc's frontend, which cilly does not touch; crustc is rustc, so those checks still happen before any C is emitted. The change is in the codegen trust base: you are now relying on cilly's translation and a C compiler to be correct, on top of the documented assumptions above. The author is candid that the demo is rough. They are chasing optimization-related bugs and recommend building without optimizations, both because enabling them "may break stuff" and because they choke on larger Rust files. Generated code is mostly ABI-compatible with normal rustc output, with a known exception on Arm64, where rustc picks an sret convention that C cannot express for small structs under 16 bytes.

The target user is anyone who maintains Rust that people keep asking to run on old or obscure hardware, the recurring "Rust doesn't support Plan 9" objection whenever a project moves off C. The stated goal is targets that have a C compiler but no LLVM or GCC Rust backend. It is not there yet. The author says cilly is not ready for public consumption and that real use waits on the full toolchain. crustc is the evidence it works: a Rust compiler that builds from C with stock GCC and make, self-hosting included.

title: Low-Latency LLM Chat Streaming — First-Token Tradeoffs for Healthtech Catalog Enrichment
description:
A catalog chatbot should optimize for the first useful token, but the platform decision should optimize for the next provider migration. For the stated comparison, GPT-4o-mini is the leading interactive choice at roughly 200 ms time to first token, with streaming enabled; Claude Haiku is a credible alternative at roughly 300 ms when its speed-and-quality balance fits the evaluation better. Put either behind an adapter, count the prompt before dispatch, and keep the chat event format independent of the provider.

Short answer: use a small streaming model for the user-facing turn, make prompt length visible, and treat provider portability as an operational contract. The answer changes if the SLO is about completed answers, tool calls, or clinical review instead of perceived responsiveness.

The incident lesson is a boundary, not a model ranking

The bounded production scenario is a product-catalog enrichment chat: a merchandiser pastes a supplier description such as "sterile polymer tubing, 3/8 in, non-DEHP", and the assistant proposes normalized attributes for search and review. A slow blank screen makes the workflow feel broken even when the final answer is accurate, so the first SLO should cover streaming TTFT, followed by completion latency and an explicit human-review path for uncertain fields.

The decision is not a permanent ranking. It is a boundary choice. A smaller model generally streams faster, but prompt size, network distance, and output length still affect the result. Measure TTFT with the same region and prompt shape before changing the model, then keep a fallback whose output can be rendered by the same chat UI.

The invariant is simple: the UI may depend on a stream, but the rest of the system must depend on an adapter. If a provider changes its request format, the catalog workflow should not.

Measure the seam.

How should an LLM streaming chat handle low latency?

The comparison needs a clear boundary. GPT-4o-mini is the leading choice for this narrow goal: the supplied comparison puts it near 200 ms TTFT and identifies it as the fastest streaming option for chat interfaces. Claude Haiku is around 300 ms TTFT, a reasonable trade when speed and answer quality need a different balance. Cohere Rerank is useful for ordering retrieved catalog candidates, but it is not a replacement for a conversational generation model; putting it in the same latency race would be a category error.

Option What it contributes here Boundary to keep visible
GPT-4o-mini Fastest stated streaming path, about 200 ms TTFT Validate extraction quality on the catalog vocabulary
Claude Haiku About 300 ms TTFT with a speed-and-quality balance A slower first token may be acceptable under a quality-first SLO
Cohere Rerank Candidate ordering after retrieval Reranking does not generate the chat response

The practical choice is therefore not “which vendor wins forever?” It is “which adapter meets the interactive SLO while preserving an exit path?” A provider-neutral service can run GPT-4o-mini today, expose the same internal event stream for Haiku tomorrow, and use reranking only where retrieval needs it. That is portability with a testable interface, not a claim that all models are interchangeable.

What does the preventative path look like in Go?

The request below uses the OpenAI-compatible chat surface, sends an explicit method, streams the response, and honors Retry-After on rate limits. The model and base URL are supplied through environment variables so the adapter can switch models or providers without changing the request path. The credential is also read from the environment.

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type chatEvent struct {
    Choices []struct {
        Delta struct {
            Content string `json:"content"`
        } `json:"delta"`
    } `json:"choices"`
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    model := os.Getenv("MODEL_ID")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if key == "" || model == "" || baseURL == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_BASE_URL, and MODEL_ID are required")
    }

    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "model":  model,
        "stream": true,
        "messages": []map[string]string{{
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Normalize attributes from: sterile polymer tubing, 3/8 in, non-DEHP",
        }},
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    resp, err := request(context.Background(), key, baseURL, body)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    scanner := bufio.NewScanner(resp.Body)
    for scanner.Scan() {
        line := scanner.Text()
        if !strings.HasPrefix(line, "data: ") || line == "data: [DONE]" {
            continue
        }
        var event chatEvent
        if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(strings.TrimPrefix(line, "data: ")), &event); err != nil {
            continue
        }
        if len(event.Choices) > 0 {
            fmt.Print(event.Choices[0].Delta.Content)
        }
    }
    if err := scanner.Err(); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

func request(ctx context.Context, key, baseURL string, body []byte) (*http.Response, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/")+"/chat/completions", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            responseBody, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(responseBody)))
        }
        return resp, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

This example is intentionally small. A production adapter should finish consuming the stream, associate each emitted event with an internal request record, and record TTFT separately from total completion time. The token-count capability can check prompt length before inference; trimming duplicated supplier text is often a better latency intervention than chasing a different model. That check is especially useful when descriptions contain repeated regulatory or packaging text.

The retry loop is appropriate for the read-like inference request shown here because it does not create a catalog record. If a surrounding workflow writes enrichment results, give that write a client-supplied idempotency key and make the consumer tolerate duplicate delivery; a 24-hour default deduplication window is useful only when the key is stable. I don't treat a chat stream as a substitute for those storage semantics.

Is one backend surface worth the coupling?

For this workflow, the one-key REST shape is a real portability advantage. A service that can send HTTP can call it, so a Go adapter does not acquire an SDK version as a second dependency. The discovery surface is public and self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples across 10 languages; that helps a platform team replace a provider without rewriting every application. The second advantage is operational breadth: 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one key, so catalog inference and adjacent backend capabilities do not require a new credential for every integration. That reduces the specific friction of rotating secrets, teaching each service a different request convention, and reconciling separate bills. Infrai is a reasonable fit when that unified REST boundary and single credential matter more than choosing specialized services independently.

The alternative stack is concrete: OpenAI for inference, Sentry for error capture, and Datadog for metrics and logs means three legitimate products, three credential sets, and glue code for request correlation, retry semantics, dashboards, and retention. A team may prefer those specialized controls. The combined surface has a cost that should be said plainly: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Portability improves only if the adapter and data export story are tested before an incident.

There are hard boundaries here. Audio transcription is present in the catalog but currently unavailable, voice sessions are pending and limited to the western region, there is no dedicated moderation endpoint, and image upscale is limited to Lanczos. That limitation makes the combined surface a poor fit if the project is primarily voice or audio transcription; use a specialized provider there. For text moderation, the stated fallback is a chat model with json_schema; for this catalog assistant, human review remains the right boundary for consequential normalization.

The decision rule

Choose GPT-4o-mini when the user is waiting for the first token and the roughly 200 ms TTFT target is the dominant SLO. Choose Claude Haiku when its roughly 300 ms first-token profile is acceptable and the speed-quality balance better matches evaluation results. Add Cohere Rerank for retrieval ordering, not generation. Keep all three behind an adapter, count prompts before dispatch, and make telemetry part of the same request path.

That is the useful outcome of the comparison: faster streaming improves the chat experience, but a provider boundary protects the catalog workflow from becoming a model-specific product. The first token gets attention; the evidence trail keeps the decision reversible.

Sources

  • OpenAI, Chat Completions API: https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat
  • Anthropic, Claude models overview: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models
  • Cohere, Rerank overview: https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank-overview
  • OpenTelemetry, HTTP semantic conventions: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/http/

title: Why Flat-Text PDF Parsing Breaks RAG (And How Spatial 2D Grounding Fixes It)
description:
When building Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, the standard ingestion step usually looks like this:

  1. Read a PDF file.
  2. Dump all text content into a single flat string.
  3. Split the string into 500-token chunks with some overlap.
  4. Generate vector embeddings and store them in a vector database.

While this works for simple blog posts or single-column articles, it breaks down completely when applied to production documents like financial reports, scientific papers, and legal contracts.

The Three Hidden Failures of Flat-Text Ingestion

1. Table Flattening

PDF files do not store tables as HTML table elements or markdown grids. They store independent text strings positioned at absolute coordinates, combined with vector stroke lines.

When a standard parser strips away positioning, rows and columns collapse into a single stream. A table comparing quarterly revenues across three divisions becomes a scrambled sequence of numbers. By the time your chunk reaches an LLM, the relational context is destroyed.

2. Multi-Column Reading Order

Dense academic papers and annual reports frequently use two-column or three-column layouts. A naive parser reads across horizontal bands, interweaving sentences from the left column with sentences from the right column. The resulting embeddings represent garbled nonsense.

3. The Lack of Visual Provenance

When an LLM produces a critical answer, such as an interest rate or an EBITDA figure, users need to verify it. If your RAG system only stores raw text chunks, the best you can show the user is a quoted string. You cannot point to the exact page, line, or table cell where the
fact originated.

The Current Trade-off: Fast and Blind vs. Accurate and Slow

Right now, developers face two extremes:

• Legacy C-based Parsers (PyMuPDF, Poppler, PDFium): Extremely fast, but originally designed for rendering pixels onto desktop screens rather than feeding structured spatial trees into AI pipelines. They also introduce heavy C/C++ compilation toolchains, breaking in
lightweight container environments.
• Vision-Language Models and OCR (Marker, Docling, Nougat): These rasterize pages into images and run deep learning models to predict layout. While accurate, they require GPUs, cost significant compute per page, and introduce seconds of latency per document.

The Alternative: Spatial RAG with Native 2D Grounding

The coordinate geometry needed to reconstruct document structure already exists inside the PDF content streams, you do not need a GPU to rediscover it.

This is why I built RasgaPDF (https://github.com/MartinsMessias/rasgapdf): a lightweight, pure Rust PDF engine built specifically for Spatial RAG.

Instead of outputting an unstructured string, the engine reconstructs the document as a spatial 2D hierarchy with exact coordinates:

{
  "page_number": 1,
  "width": 612.0,
  "height": 792.0,
  "rotation": 0,
  "text_blocks": [
    {
      "bbox": { "x0": 60.0, "y0": 70.6, "x1": 384.6, "y1": 82.7 },
      "lines": [
        {
          "bbox": { "x0": 60.0, "y0": 70.6, "x1": 384.6, "y1": 82.7 },
          "text": "Revenue increased by 14% year-over-year..."
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "tables": [
    {
      "bbox": { "x0": 60.0, "y0": 121.0, "x1": 540.0, "y1": 245.0 },
      "markdown": "| Metric | 2025 | 2026 |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n..."
    }
  ]
}

Visual Citation in User Interfaces

Because every chunk retained its physical bounding box ([x0, y0, x1, y1]), your frontend can render the original PDF page and draw an exact translucent highlight over the source passage. The user gets instant, trustworthy verification without hunting through a 50-page
document.

Pure Rust: Zero C/C++ Toolchains

By implementing the ISO 32000-1 specification natively in safe Rust:

• cargo build and pip install work without MSBuild or C compiler installations.
• Memory safety is enforced at compile time.
• A dense 12-page academic paper parses in approximately 15 ms on a single CPU core.

Native Integration with LangChain and LlamaIndex

You do not need to write custom spatial wrappers. RasgaPDF integrates directly into standard AI orchestrators:

    from rasgapdf import RasgaPDFLoader

    # Load with physical 2D metadata preserved in every Document chunk
    loader = RasgaPDFLoader("financial_report.pdf", mode="elements")
    docs = loader.load()

    first_chunk = docs[0]
    print(first_chunk.page_content)
    print(first_chunk.metadata["bbox"])
   # {'x0': 60.0, 'y0': 70.6, 'x1': 384.6, 'y1': 82.7}

Conclusion

If your RAG system is hallucinating data or failing on complex documents, the problem is often not your embedding model or prompt, it is flat-text ingestion destroying spatial context before the model ever sees it.

Preserving 2D physical coordinates gives you reliable tables, accurate reading order, and verifiable visual citations at native speed.

• GitHub: https://github.com/MartinsMessias/rasgapdf
• Interactive Playground: https://martinsmessias.github.io/rasgapdf/

How are you currently handling table extraction and citation verification in your RAG pipelines? Let us discuss in the comments below.

title: Why In-Context Translation Beats Traditional JSON Localization: Trying Tolgee
description:
Managing internationalization (i18n) with raw JSON files is tedious and error-prone. Here is how Tolgee's in-context translation streamlines developer localization.

Internationalization (i18n) is one of those features every engineering team knows they need, but almost everyone dreads setting up.

The traditional localization workflow usually looks like this:

Developers define translation keys in nested JSON files (en.json, es.json, de.json).

Every UI copy update requires a pull request and git merge conflict resolutions.

Non-technical translators have no visual context for where strings actually live on the screen, leading to awkward truncation and broken layouts.

I recently tested Tolgee
—an open-source localization platform built specifically to bridge this gap. Here is what makes its developer experience standout.

The Killer Feature: In-Context Translation

What separates Tolgee from traditional Translation Management Systems (TMS) is in-context editing.

When running your app in development or staging with the Tolgee SDK:

You simply hold Alt (or Option on Mac) and hover over any text on your screen.

Tolgee highlights the text with a subtle bounding box.

Click on it, and a clean translation modal pops up right inside your app.

text
[ Your Live Web App Screen ]
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Welcome to Open Payments │
│ [ Alt + Click ] │
│ │ │
│ ▼ │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ Tolgee In-Context Editor │ │
│ │ Key: landing.hero.welcome_title │ │
│ │ Translation: Bienvenido a Pagos... │ │
│ │ [ Save & Sync ] │ │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Translators and product managers can adjust wording directly in the live UI, see exactly how long the text looks in the layout, and save the change straight to the cloud or self-hosted backend. Zero developer intervention needed.

Clean Integration with Modern Frameworks

Tolgee provides native SDKs for React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, and vanilla JS. In Next.js (App Router), wrapping your layout takes less than 5 minutes:

tsx
import { TolgeeProvider } from "@tolgee/react";
export default function RootLayout({ children, locale }) {
return (
apiUrl={process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_TOLGEE_API_URL}
apiKey={process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_TOLGEE_API_KEY}
staticData={/* pre-baked locale files for production */}
>
{children}

);
}

In production, you don't even have to query Tolgee's API dynamically if you don't want to—their CLI can export static snapshot files into your build pipeline so production builds remain ultra-fast and static.

Key Benefits for Engineering Teams

No More Git Merge Conflicts in .json Files: Translations live in Tolgee and are fetched or pulled during build, keeping pull requests focused purely on code logic.

Context-Rich Screenshots: When translators edit strings via in-context translation, Tolgee automatically captures a screenshot of the surrounding DOM elements so reviewers understand the exact visual context.

Open-Source & Self-Hostable: If your company has strict compliance requirements and can't use external SaaS clouds, Tolgee is 100% open-source under Apache 2.0 and can be deployed with Docker in one command.

Final Verdict

If your team is still emailing spreadsheets or copy-pasting translation strings into giant JSON dictionaries, switching to in-context translation is a night-and-day upgrade.

Check out their open-source repository at github.com/tolgee/tolgee-platform
.

How does your team handle localization in production? Let me know in the comments! 🌍
