title: Seven small scripts I no longer write
description:
Every project I have worked on that used a Redis-style store ended up with a folder of tiny Lua scripts. They were never complicated. Read a number, compare it with something, write one or two keys, return. But each of them had to be loaded, called by its SHA, kept in step with the application code, and explained to the next person who opened the folder.

When I started Ruvio I went through that folder and asked a plain question for each script: is this a command that nobody has written yet? Surprisingly often the answer was yes. This post is the list of the ones that made it into the server, with the exact replies you get back. Everything below was run against the 0.4.0 release.

1. Move money only if there is enough

The classic one. Take 30 credits from a wallet and put them in escrow, but only if the wallet holds at least 30. Nobody should ever see the money in both places, or in neither.

SET {user:42}:wallet 50
TRANSFER {user:42}:wallet {user:42}:escrow 30
# 1) 20  -> wallet after
# 2) 30  -> escrow after
TRANSFER {user:42}:wallet {user:42}:escrow 30
# (nil)  -> only 20 left, nothing changed

Both balances change in one WAL record, so a crash cannot leave you with only half of the move on disk.

Keep both keys in one slot

TRANSFER works on two keys of the same slot. The {user:42} hash tag in the key names is what puts them there, in a single server as well as in a cluster.

When the balances are fields of one hash, HTRANSFER account:7 available held 30 MAX 1000 does the same between two fields and also refuses if the destination would pass the cap.

2. Sell the last ticket once

DECRBY happily goes below zero, so the usual fix is a script that reads the stock first. TAKE subtracts only when the key holds enough:

SET stock:ticket-42 500
TAKE stock:ticket-42 2
# 498   -> took 2, 498 left
TAKE stock:ticket-42 1000
# (nil) -> not enough, the key is unchanged

The mirror image is a counter with a ceiling, for seats in a room or members in a team:

INCRBY seats:room-9 1 MAX 120
# 57    -> joined
# (nil) -> room is full, nothing was written

3. A daily counter that cleans up after itself

This one is so small it hurts. You want a per-day counter that disappears tomorrow. With plain INCR you need a second EXPIRE call, and if you only want to set the deadline when the key is created, you are back to a script or a MULTI block.

INCR hits:user-7:2026-10-29 EX 86400
# 1     -> first hit, the day's deadline is set
# 2, 3… -> later hits leave the deadline alone

EX and PX on INCR and INCRBY only apply when the call creates the counter. Later calls do not push the deadline forward.

4. Keep the newest value, whatever order writers arrive in

Event consumers that run in parallel love to write an older watermark after a newer one. IFGT and IFLT on SET compare against the stored integer and only write when the new number wins:

SET watermark:orders 1700000200 IFGT
# OK    -> written
SET watermark:orders 1700000100 IFGT
# (nil) -> stored number is greater, nothing written
SET price:best 499 IFLT PX 3600000
# OK    -> new lowest price, expires in an hour

Integers only

A stored value that is not a number is an error and stays as it was. I prefer that to a silent string comparison.

5. A rate limit in one round trip

Fixed window, sliding window and token bucket are all LIMIT. The reply is the allowance that is left, and a refused call is not counted:

LIMIT api:key-7 3 60000
# 2
# 1
# 0
# (nil) -> window is full, this call was not counted
LIMIT api:key-7:burst 10 1000 TOKENS COST 2 WITHRETRY
# 1) 8  -> 8 tokens left
# 2) 0  -> no need to wait

WITHRETRY puts the wait in the reply, so the number for a Retry-After header comes from the server rather than from a guess in the client.

6. Pop the jobs that are due

A sorted set with the run time as the score is the simplest scheduler there is. The awkward part was always "give me what is due and remove it" without two workers picking the same job.

ZADD {jobs}:due 100 job:9 200 job:10 300 job:11
ZPOPBYSCORE {jobs}:due 150 COUNT 10
# job:9 -> due and removed in the same call
ZMOVEDUE {jobs}:due {jobs}:ready 250 COUNT 100
# 1     -> job:10 moved to the tail of the list {jobs}:ready

ZMOVEDUE hands due members to a list queue in one recorded step, up to 10,000 per call. Both keys must share a slot; without the {jobs} tag the server answers CROSSSLOT, as it should. There is a whole post on delayed jobs if you want the stream version too.

7. Save only if nobody else saved first

Two people open the same profile, both press save. With SETV every write returns a version and a write that names an old version is refused:

SETV profile:ada "v1"
# 1
SETV profile:ada "v2" 1
# 2
SETV profile:ada "v3" 1
# ERR version mismatch

No WATCH, no retry loop around MULTI.

What I did not turn into commands

Not every script deserves to become a command. Anything with real business rules, several branches and a dozen keys is still better as code in your application, or as a script if you really need it next to the data. Ruvio runs Lua for exactly that. The commands above made the cut because they are small, they come up in almost every codebase, and they share three properties:

  • All or nothing. Either the whole thing happens or nothing is written, not to the key and not to the log.
  • One record. A refused call leaves no trace, and an accepted one is a single WAL record that replicas apply the same way.
  • A typed method. Each one is a method in all six clients, so there is no script text to send and no reply to parse by hand.

There is also a speed side. Every one of these is measured against the script it replaces on the benchmarks page, together with the memory each key takes. I will let the table speak there rather than paste numbers here.

All six first-party clients have a typed method for each command, so in C# the first example is await db.TransferAsync(...) and not a string you send and parse. The original post has tabs under each example with the same steps in all six languages.

I used Claude to help edit this post; the commands and outputs were run by me against the 0.4.0 release.

Originally published on ruviodb.com. Ruvio is open source: github.com/salihcantekin/ruvio.

description:
BioSmart es una plataforma inteligente para agricultura urbana, trazabilidad de donaciones y e-commerce ecológico. No es un proyecto de clase — está desplegado y funcionando.

👉 Demo en vivo 👉 Código fuente

La arquitectura
┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐
│ React 18 │────▶│ Express.js │────▶│ Neon DB │

│ AI (Go 1.26) │
│ pgx/v5 │
└──────────────┘
🧠 GopherMind AI: el motor en Go
Esta es la parte que más me enorgullece. Construí un pipeline cognitivo de 15 fases en Go puro:

Sanitización CUSUM — detección de cambios en las series temporales de sensores
Filtro Hampel — eliminación de outliers sin perder señal real
Predicción multi-motor — múltiples modelos generan predicciones independientes
Fusión Bayesiana — combina las predicciones con pesos probabilísticos
Detección de drift Page-Hinkley — identifica cuando el modelo se desactualiza
Calibración de confianza — cada insight tiene un score de fiabilidad
¿Por qué Go y no Python?
Goroutines + Channels: análisis simultáneo de múltiples racks hidropónicos sin bloquear
Zero-Copy: el pipeline procesa datos sin copias innecesarias en memoria
Compilado: latencia mínima en las respuestas de la API de IA
HMAC-SHA256: cada insight lleva firma de integridad para auditoría IEEE
// Ejemplo simplificado del pipeline
func (gm *GopherMind) Analyze(rack RackData) Insight {
sanitized := gm.cusumSanitize(rack.Readings)
filtered := gm.hampelFilter(sanitized)
preds := gm.multiPredict(filtered) // goroutines
fused := gm.bayesianFuse(preds)
drift := gm.pageHinkley(fused)
insight := gm.calibrate(fused, drift)
insight.Signature = gm.hmacSign(insight)
return insight
}
🌍 Globo 3D con Three.js
La landing tiene un globo terráqueo interactivo que visualiza las donaciones globales en tiempo real. Implementé una transición fluida de vista 3D (Three.js) a vista 2D satelital (Leaflet.js) según el nivel de zoom.

🛒 Marketplace multivendedor
Google OAuth 2.0 con Passport.js
RBAC (control de acceso por roles): Usuario, Vendedor, Admin
Cloudinary para imágenes optimizadas
Catálogo público responsivo con cálculo en tiempo real
📊 Dashboard IoT
Paneles interactivos con datos meteorológicos, sincronización virtual de sensores Arduino y control simulado de granjas hidropónicas urbanas.

Stack completo
Capa Tecnologías
Frontend React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Recharts, Three.js, Leaflet.js
Backend Express.js, Node.js, Drizzle ORM, Passport.js, JWT, bcryptjs
IA Go 1.26, pgx/v5, HMAC-SHA256
DB Neon DB (PostgreSQL Serverless)
Storage Cloudinary
Deploy Vercel
Lo que aprendí
Go para IA no es loco — si tu pipeline es determinístico y necesitas concurrencia real, Go aplasta a Python en rendimiento
Three.js + Leaflet.js se pueden combinar con transiciones fluidas si manejas bien los estados de cámara
Drizzle ORM con TypeScript es brutal para esquemas complejos — typesafe de verdad

title: A Java IDE in Your Browser, With Your Files in Your Browser
description:
If you're used to opening a page and immediately changing an app, installing a Java development environment is a substantial detour. I want your first encounter with Codename One to be the app running.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Our new browser IDE is a highly experimental, very early preview. Open it, press Run and start changing the Java. It has a project tree, multiple files and an application preview. Think of the Playground growing into a proper IDE workspace.

I'm calling it Not a Cloud IDE because the editing, compilation for preview and application execution happen in your browser. Your project files stay in that browser's storage. The ordinary build server enters the workflow when you request a cloud build.

Start with an app on the screen

The first visit opens a GettingStarted project. Press Run in the top toolbar. The editor compiles Java and shows the application beside its source. This screenshot shows that starter running in the public preview:

You can start with a small edit. Inside the starter's runApp() method, this replaces its initial screen with a counter:

Form hi = new Form("First app", BoxLayout.y());
Label count = new Label("Trips: 0");
Button add = new Button("Add a trip");
int[] trips = {0};
add.addActionListener(event -> count.setText("Trips: " + (++trips[0])));
hi.addAll(count, add);
hi.show();

The starter already imports the UI and layout classes. Run it, click the button and change the label. The point of this first exercise is to shorten the distance between an idea and a visible result.

Compiler errors appear against the source. Completion, hover information and source navigation help you explore the API. They don't amount to a full Java language server or IntelliJ's refactoring model, and I don't want to present them that way.

What runs where

The site delivers the editor and toolchain. Dependencies may need downloading too. That doesn't make the editing session a remote machine: there is no server-side workspace running your development loop.

A cloud build is an explicit handoff of build inputs to the existing Codename One service. It is separate from local preview and doesn't back up your editable workspace. Opening the IDE also doesn't make the whole workflow available offline.

Browser storage is local storage

The toolbar says Saved only in this browser · No cloud backup. Take that literally. Signing in on a second computer or switching browser profiles won't bring your project along.

Use Download ZIP to keep a backup and take the project to your desktop. Clearing the site's browser data or using private browsing can erase your local work. The export gives you a project you can continue building with the usual Maven or Gradle tools.

This is also why I like the approach for getting started. You can try the framework in a page, then keep the code when you're ready to set up a local environment.

Where the experiment ends today

This will not replace IntelliJ. We can't reproduce the full Java ecosystem, every desktop tool and every build plugin inside JavaScript. Browser preview supports a defined subset of dependency and build behavior; projects outside that subset need a local build.

Backend projects can be created, edited and exported, but there is no backend runtime in the browser. Full stack preview currently runs the client only. Don't expect Wayline's backend to start inside the editor tab.

The IDE exposes settings, GUI Builder and cloud-build actions, but this is early software. A successful browser preview is also not proof that every device API will behave identically on a phone. Check your real targets as the project grows.

Make the first experiment small

Last week's Playground compiler showed real Java compilation in a page. The IDE gives that loop a workspace you can grow beyond one snippet.

Try the counter, change its layout and download the project. That is the experience I want to make ordinary: a person curious about Java can see their own change running before spending the afternoon configuring tools.

This closes our weekly release series. Between a full-stack ride-hailing application and a browser workspace, we're working on both ends of the same problem: getting you to the part of an application that is yours.

Discussion

What is the first small app you would try if opening a page were all the setup it needed?

title: Sunsetting Rune, and why I'm writing in WordCraft now
description:
Earlier this month I started building Rune, a word processor for Linux and Omarchy with AI built right into the writing surface. Today I’m archiving it, and I’d like to tell you why.

Why I built Rune

Word processors on Linux felt like a choice between heavyweight ports and plain text editors pretending to be word processors. And every one of them treated AI as a sidebar plugin. I wanted the opposite: a fast, native app where the model is part of the page, where you can ask it to fix a paragraph and the fix lands right in your document as one undo step.

Rune got further than I expected. It went from an idea to version 0.8.7 in about two weeks, with packages for Arch, Debian and Fedora, an AppImage for most other distros, headers and footers, tables, and sign-in for ChatGPT and OpenRouter.

What I learned

Quite a lot, honestly. Rune started on LibreOfficeKit and ended up as a single Qt process that reads and writes ODF itself, because the first design had a performance ceiling I couldn’t get past. Along the way I learned to test real files instead of trusting documentation. That habit caught a bug in Qt’s own ODF writer, where a table right after a list silently disappeared when LibreOffice opened the file. By the end, Rune was checked by 504 automated tests. I’ll carry that way of working into everything I build next.

Then I found WordCraft

Recently I came across WordCraft, a fast, open-source word processor written in Rust by the ArtCraft team. I tried it, and it’s really good.

It does what Rune set out to do, and more. It has a ribbon and styles, works with .docx natively along with .odt, Markdown and more, exports PDF, and has track changes and comments, offline spelling and grammar, footnotes, a table of contents, and citations in APA, MLA, Chicago and IEEE. It runs on Linux as a Flatpak, plus macOS, Windows, FreeBSD and the web.

The part that really got me is how it treats AI. Its commands are available through a command-line tool, a JSON control channel and an MCP server, so AI assistants can work inside your documents. That’s the idea I was chasing with Rune, done in a more open way: you bring whichever assistant you like.

It’s still in development, but it’s already well past where Rune is.

Why archive instead of compete

I could keep going. But I’m one person, word processors are a lot of work to maintain, and the world doesn’t need two small open-source editors chasing the same idea when one of them is already further along. I’d rather spend my time on things only Nine Point Labs can build, and send you to the better tool.

So Rune is archived. The code stays up under the MIT license, along with the existing releases, if you’d like to learn from it or fork it. The README now points to WordCraft.

Give WordCraft a try

If you write on Linux, or anywhere really, please give WordCraft a try. The source is on GitHub if you’d like to dig in or help out.

Thank you to everyone who tried Rune or sent a kind word about it. It meant a lot.

Originally published on The Word from Nine Point Labs.

title: Rustidian: Obsidian but fast, a native Rust Markdown notebook
description:
Obsidian took 3.77 s to show a note in a paired startup test. Rustidian took 0.61 s.

I built Rustidian because Obsidian was slow to start for me, even after I tried to optimize it. Speed and efficiency are its operating principle: a native Markdown notebook in Rust, with no Electron and no account. It opens your ordinary Markdown folders as they are.

What you get today

  • Wiki links, backlinks, tags, aliases, properties and bookmarks
  • A graph of your notes
  • Tables, callouts, images, syntax highlighting and Mermaid diagrams
  • Live editing, source and reading modes
  • Linux: a .deb package or a portable archive

Coming next

  • LaTeX math that renders as you type
  • An Agent tab that runs Claude Code, Codex or Elpis in a terminal beside your notes, inside your vault folder

Try it

Install it from the README in one command, open a copy of your vault, and see how fast a note can open.

If speed matters to you, star it on GitHub: it helps other people find it. Contributors are welcome.

👉 https://github.com/MasihMoafi/rustidian
